Department DEPARTMENT OF MEDICINE AND AGING SCIENCES Website https://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-studio/scienze-infermieristiche-ed-ostetriche-area-sanitaria  Admission Requirements Required Knowledge for Admission Admission requires possession of a university degree or diploma enabling registration as a Nurse, Pediatric Nurse, Midwife, or equivalent qualification.
Admission to the Master's Degree Program is quota-based under Law 264/1999 and includes an admission exam consisting of a multiple-choice test.
Curricular Requirements For professionals holding a degree in class SNT/1 or L-SNT1, no academic debts are required.
Candidates holding the enabling qualification obtained through University Diplomas may also apply if they have completed at least 20 ECTS in SSD MED/45 for Nurses and MED/47 for Midwives, and 50 ECTS in internship activities.
For candidates holding the Professional Nurse, Childcare Supervisor, and Midwife Diploma obtained under the previous non-university curriculum and recognized as equivalent qualification, admission requirements and academic debts will be specified in the Study Program Didactic Regulations.
Personal Preparation Verification The suitability of personal preparation will be assessed using methods specified in the Study Program Didactic Regulations.
Enrollment is not permitted for first-cycle graduates with academic debts, whether regarding curricular requirements or personal preparation suitability.

SECTION: Admission Requirements
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/614

Admission Requirements To be admitted to the Study Program, the student must hold a three-year Bachelor's degree in Nursing/Midwifery or a University Diploma enabling practice in the professions of Nurse/Midwife, Pediatric Nurse, or another equivalent qualification, enabling the practice of the profession of Nurse/Midwife as required by current regulations, or another foreign degree deemed suitable.
Admission to the program is nationally regulated under Law 264/1999, with the number of places set annually by a decree of the Ministry of Education, University and Research.
Admission to the Study Program occurs through a competitive examination, the date and mode of which are determined annually by the Ministry of Education, University and Research and published in a specific call issued by the University (www.unich.it).
Selection is carried out through evaluation of academic qualifications and a multiple-choice quiz focusing on:
- theory/practice relevant to healthcare professions included in the Master's Degree class in Nursing and Midwifery;
- general culture and logical reasoning; regulation of the practice of healthcare professions included in the Master's Degree class in Nursing and Midwifery and health legislation;
- scientific-mathematical culture, statistics, computer science, and English;
- humanities and social sciences culture.
For professionals holding a degree in the SNT/1 or L-SNT1 class, no academic deficiencies are required. Candidates holding the enabling qualification obtained through University Diplomas may also apply if they have completed at least 20 CFU in the SSD MED/45 for Nurses and MED/47 for Midwives, and 50 CFU in internship activities.
For candidates holding a Professional Nurse, Childcare Supervisor and Midwife Diploma obtained under the previous non-university system and recognized as equivalent, the admission requirements and academic deficiencies will be specified in the Study Program's Didactic Regulations.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
Master's graduates, at the end of the training path, are able to:
• conduct interpersonal conversations with users and operators, exercising adequate listening skills, adapting them to the context, the nature of the problems addressed and the objectives to be achieved;
• present their thoughts in written and oral form, in a reasoned manner and with language appropriate for different interlocutors and contexts;
• conduct negotiations with effective communication, methodological rigor and convincing arguments;
• lead work groups and meetings exercising appropriate leadership;
• interact appropriately with other professionals in the planning and implementation of multiprofessional interventions;
• manage and resolve conflicts;
• manage educational relationships directed at the assisted population, staff and students at various levels;
• manage educational relationships directed at the assisted population, staff and students at various levels;
• reprocess the principles and techniques of the helping relationship at a more advanced level to be able to provide colleagues with consultation for complex relational situations;
• act as a mentor to train and develop competencies in aspiring leaders in clinical and organizational settings;
• adopt supportive managerial styles to support colleagues in conducting projects, teaching and supervision, negotiation, conflict resolution and counseling.
The development of written and oral communication skills, also in English, will be carried out through laboratory activities, discussion of case studies and exemplary relational situations in subgroups, and presentations in plenary sessions. Internship with supervised experiences by expert tutors in various contexts with debriefing sessions to reflect and reprocess relational experiences with users and the team in simple and complex healthcare settings.
The verification of these skills occurs in the form of seminars at the end of a professional internship period during which Master's graduates must prepare a written dissertation, subsequently presented orally.

URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/614

Judgment Autonomy (making judgments)
Master's degree graduates, upon completion of the training path, are able to:
• develop complex analyses and formulate autonomous reflections and evaluations of a scientific, legal, ethical and deontological nature, through multidisciplinary discussion, to support decisions necessary for addressing complex problems in the management of care, organizational, training and research processes related to the exercise of nursing and midwifery functions;
• anticipate and evaluate the effects resulting from their decisions and activities, assuming the consequent social responsibility;
• integrate high ethical standards and values into daily work activities and projects.
The teaching tools aimed at achieving the following skills include the dissertation of student-compiled works containing the phases of constructing an intervention project in the care setting, demonstrating the ability to analyze, manage and interpret data with judgment autonomy by using existing literature material and producing original and innovative data in a multidisciplinary and multidimensional perspective (also in preparation for the final exam).

Orientation in entry The orientation in entry is coordinated by the Department of Medicine and Aging's Orientation Delegate. The delegate collaborates with the Course of Study's orientation contact. Orientation activities, given the nature of the Course, are carried out exclusively at the facility or during events organized by the University or the School of Medicine and Health Sciences.
The Teaching Director provides detailed information about the study course and student services through the student listening service and is the main point of reference for students. Organizes an orientation meeting for new students coinciding with the start date of first-year lectures. The Course of Study has a designated Teaching Director.
The Disability and Specific Learning Disorders (DSA) Service, activated in accordance with Law 17/99 and Law 170/2010, under the Coordination of Equality Policies and Disability led by the Rector's Delegate for Disabilities, is addressed to students with disabilities and DSA, promoting, implementing, and managing services to ensure access and integration in all aspects of university life from the welcome phase, through ongoing support, to exit support.
For more information:
https://orientamento.unich.it/servizi-gli-studenti/disabilita-e-dsa Orientation and ongoing tutoring The ongoing orientation is primarily expressed through the ongoing tutoring activity, carried out by tutors and teachers of the Course of Study, typically during office hours, and aimed at assisting students in resolving their issues.
Additionally, designated reference teachers are available for students to request personalized tutoring services and agree on the corresponding implementation methods. The list of available tutors is regularly updated on the Course of Study's internet page.
Throughout the academic year, thematic meetings on managing and organizing the study path and study methods are proposed.

- guidance for preparing curriculum vitae,
- verification of employability profile,
- facilitation for recent graduates

For this reason, the Course does not have mandatory partnerships with external facilities suitable for employment placement but refers to University facilities when necessary.

SECTION: Student Opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/614

Student Opinions From the results of student opinions for the academic year 2022/2023, it emerges that the Study Program has an average rating of 3.64 out of 4, a score slightly higher than the previous academic year (3.62).
The results show that, as last year, all courses received a score above 3. It is noted that for several courses (25 out of 31), the score is above 3.5, with 7 courses scoring above 3.8.
Additionally, student interest in the topics of various courses has slightly increased, with a score of 3.66 (previous year 3.63), and overall the Study Program has seen an improvement in scores for questions related to teaching methods and course organization, lecture schedules, and presentation of exam topics, highlighting a good organization of the Study Program's teaching.
No courses have reported critical situations.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [M645] NURSING AND MIDWIFERY SCIENCES
TYPE: MASTER'S DEGREE
CURRICULUM: GRADUATE OPINIONS
SECTION: GRADUATE OPINIONS
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/614

Graduate Opinions The available data, collected on the Alma Laurea website and referring to 20 interviewed graduates out of 25 in the calendar year 2022, show that 95% attended more than 75% of the required courses.
The study load related to the courses required by the Degree Course was judged in 2022 to be appropriate to the course duration by 80% of the respondents.
Regarding the evaluations expressed on the organizational aspects of the exams in our Course (exam sessions, information, reservations), 60% of the 2022 respondents always feel satisfied (previous year 53%).
The relationship with professors is judged overall satisfactory by 90% of respondents.
68.8% of our graduates in 2022 graduated on time (previous year 57.9%). In 2022, twenty-five (25) students obtained the degree in Nursing and Midwifery Sciences at our University.
More than 50% of graduates reside outside the region, confirming the high attractiveness of the Master's Degree Course.
The high school diploma represents the most common pre-university education among graduates (76%).
70.0% of graduates were working students during their studies. 60% of respondents would enroll again in the same Master's Degree Course.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Master's graduates must have demonstrated the ability to apply knowledge and understanding. At the end of the training path, they are able to:
• analyze relevant policies to provide healthcare, understand and use laws and regulations to ensure patient care quality,
evaluate socioeconomic and healthcare policy trends and issues at local, state, and international levels; make high-quality, cost-effective decisions in the use of resources for care and training;
• analyze major ethical issues and how these can influence care,
ethically evaluate decision-making from both personal and organizational perspectives and understand how these two dimensions can create conflicts of interest;
• take responsibility for the quality of their professional practice;
• appropriately use nursing and midwifery theories and those from related fields to provide effective and innovative leadership and/or training;
• create person-centered clinical and educational environments respecting cultural diversity and different relational and learning styles;
• act as a professional role model providing guidance to students, colleagues, and users;
• apply leadership and management theories to develop collaborative alliances between different healthcare professions in their work context;
• apply leadership and management theories to develop collaborative alliances between different healthcare professions in their work context;
• develop evidence-based practice using research to introduce changes and improve practice.
The knowledge and understanding mentioned above will be acquired through attending lectures, exercises, seminars, cognitive mapping; discussion of cases in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions, guided and independent personal study.
The verification of learning outcomes is primarily conducted through oral and/or written exams, in-course or final, staged case studies, project work, and reports.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
Master's graduates, at the end of the training path, are able to:
• evaluate their performance based on professional practice standards and organizational criteria, continuously identifying their educational needs in relation to the nature and complexity of problems to address and the strategic and operational approaches to manage, in order to implement their professional improvement plan;
• independently adopt effective strategies to continue learning throughout their professional life, both formally and informally, through further training paths;
• use complete information systems, software, and databases to collect, organize, and catalog information; identify a problem, conduct a literature review on the topic, critically analyze the problem and current knowledge, develop a strategy to apply research in practice, and facilitate the dissemination of research results.
Learning skills are acquired through the overall study process, particularly through individual study, preparation of individual projects, and activities carried out in preparation for the thesis.
Verification of these skills occurs within specific laboratories through the assessment of the ability to query databases, access international bibliographies on topics proposed within the teaching, and illustrate aspects of novelty introduced by scientific research; identify which issues in different areas of competence pose further questions for research development and in which directions.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Master's graduates must have demonstrated knowledge and understanding.
Knowledge and skills:
• reinforcing content, theoretical, interpretive, operational, and research models specific to nursing and midwifery sciences acquired in the first cycle;
• to understand the work processes of healthcare organizations, personnel management strategies, and professional accreditation and evaluation systems in order to promote the integration of nursing and midwifery teams with other professionals for achieving safe, effective, efficient, relevant, culturally sensitive, appropriately documented, and competent service delivery;
• to create a professional environment that promotes excellence in nursing and midwifery practice, fosters effective communication, promotes decision-making, responsibility, and autonomy of professionals;
Expected learning outcomes, expressed through the European descriptors of the degree title (DM 16/03/2007, art. 3, comma 7)
(Quadro A4.b.1 SUA)
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding):
• to create an effective learning environment both formally and in laboratories and clinical contexts;
implement various teaching strategies based on educational theories and evidence-based practices;
• to develop competency profiles, formulate learning objectives, select appropriate learning activities, design basic curricula, and implement them based on educational principles and theories, revising curricula based on current societal and healthcare trends.
Understanding:
• of complex phenomena and problems in healthcare, of interest to nursing and midwifery professions, placing them within the broader demographic-epidemiological, socio-cultural, and political-institutional context;
• of nursing and midwifery care, organizational, and educational processes connected to population health problems, functioning of healthcare and social systems, and specific professionalization pathways;
• of the historical-philosophical evolution of respective disciplinary fields in order to analyze them critically.
The knowledge and understanding mentioned above will be acquired through attending lectures, exercises, seminars, guided and independent personal study.
The verification of learning outcomes is primarily conducted through oral and/or written exams, preparation of papers, and project work.

- Maurizio Rivera Di Renzo, Course instructor (Coordinator)
- Paola Borrelli, Course Chair (Member)
- Marta Di Nicola, Course instructor (Member);
- Carlo Della Pelle, Course instructor (Member).
Tasks: The Course Quality Assurance Coordinator is responsible for: - coordinating GAQ activities; - maintaining direct relationships with the University Quality Office, the Evaluation Unit, and the Joint Faculty-Student Committee; - periodically updating the Course Chair on the progress of Course quality assurance; Members of the GAQ are responsible for: - supervising the implementation of quality assurance within the Course; - monitoring indicators for continuous process control and improvement; - promoting a quality culture within the Course; - planning and controlling the efficiency of contextual services; The GAQ also conducts monitoring and self-evaluation of the training path to identify strengths and weaknesses to be reported within the Course. These activities are aimed at designing corrective and preventive actions for identified issues and implementing improvement plans to be proposed to the Chair and the Course Council.
Work Planning and Implementation Deadlines The Review Group has decided to meet during the Didactic Area Council meetings, and at least every three months.
At these meetings, the Group will examine emerging issues and problems, propose suggestions to the Council, and systematically collect relevant data. The Group is responsible for drafting the Annual Review Report according to deadlines set by the University and the MIUR.
Brief Description of Affiliated and Integrative Activities Students will be provided with basic epidemiology knowledge for analyzing and understanding population health issues. The course also aims to train professionals capable of planning, managing, and evaluating care services with a focus on quality improvement.
Students will also receive basic knowledge to undertake research activities in various fields of medicine.
Course Description Brief Master's graduates in Nursing and Midwifery Sciences, in accordance with Article 6, paragraph 3 of Legislative Decree 30 December 1992, No. 502 and subsequent amendments, and in accordance with Law 10 August 2000, No. 251, Article 1, paragraph 1, possess advanced cultural and professional training to intervene with high competence in care, management, training, and research processes relevant to the professional figure and capable of responding to both priority population health issues and quality service-related issues.
Upon completion of the two-year theoretical-practical specialist training path, leading to 120 CFU, Master's graduates develop an integrated approach to organizational and management problems of healthcare professions, characterized by mastery of healthcare management techniques and procedures and methodological knowledge in scientific research.
Admission to the Course is nationally quota-based, with the requirement of a three-year Bachelor's degree in Nursing/Midwifery or a University Diploma enabling the practice of Nursing/Midwifery, Pediatric Nursing, or another equivalent qualification, enabling the practice of Nursing/Midwifery as required by current regulations, or another foreign degree deemed suitable.
External Effectiveness Alma Laurea analysis with data updated to April 2023 indicates that, at the employment level, 100% of graduates are employed three years after graduation.
Three years after graduation, Chieti graduates report a job satisfaction level of 7.6 (on a scale of 10), equal to the average of the degree class across all universities.
Three years after graduation, 53.8% of graduates report using their acquired skills to a high degree (national average 46.3%).

Course Description:
Year 1: Aimed at providing conceptual and methodological models of the four competency areas of the Master's graduate:
a) Management Area - principles and methods of healthcare economics and planning, in-depth administrative and labor law.
b) Quality Area - healthcare planning and accreditation, methodologies for managing clinical-organizational risks, regulations protecting workers.
c) Research Area - medical and social statistics methods, critical literature analysis, research methodology, and evidence-based healthcare practice.
d) Disciplinary Area - theories and philosophy of Nursing and Midwifery Sciences and applications to care and midwifery processes.
An internship activity is planned, related to the specific scientific-disciplinary sector of the class, aimed at producing a scientific research paper on a topic chosen by the student, submitted for approval by the instructor, to improve a relevant professional problem.
Year 2: Aimed at applying and contextualizing the theoretical models and methodologies learned in the four competency areas of the Master's graduate, with specific reference to future work contexts:
a) Management Area - in-depth strategies for directing and managing professional and healthcare services based on efficiency and effectiveness criteria, human resource management, design of organizational integration tools, and quality performance evaluation.
b) Research Area - analysis of organizational, pedagogical, and clinical-professional research studies, design and implementation of studies in nursing and midwifery, and training in deducing implications for practice.
c) Training Area - in-depth design and management of basic and advanced training systems specific to nursing and midwifery professions, and continuing education activities. Theoretical models of social psychology, group psychology, and adult learning theories.
d) Disciplinary Area - in-depth relevant care and midwifery processes to design innovative models with strong impact on care quality for users.
An internship or internship activity is planned, related to the specific scientific-disciplinary sector of the class, aimed at producing a scientific research paper on a topic chosen by the student, submitted for approval by the instructor, to improve a relevant professional problem. Internships are carried out in accredited services chosen by the student (Nursing and Midwifery Directorates, Training Services, Research Centers, Quality Offices, Organizational Consulting Companies in Healthcare).
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Practical Training Agreements No internships/practical training are currently planned at entities and companies.

Considering the educational objectives of the Course and the expanding professional opportunities in management, research, and teaching, it is deemed useful to sensitize Healthcare Agencies and Universities to build an interdisciplinary network to intensify dialogue and promote specific skills in respective sectors, offering further opportunities to Master's graduates.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data In the academic year 2022/2023, 54 students were enrolled, as specified in the Ministerial Decree. The majority of students (25/54) come from other Italian regions, demonstrating the Course's attractiveness.
Currently, a total of 103 students are enrolled in the Master's Degree in Nursing and Midwifery Sciences, of which 86 are in progress.
In the calendar year 2022, 33 students obtained the degree, including 10 with a grade of 110/110 with honors, 3 with a grade of 110/110, and 10 in the 105-110/110 range.
Final Exam Characteristics To be admitted to the Master's final exam, the student must have passed all course exams and received a positive evaluation on internship learning outcomes.
The final exam consists of a discussion of a Research Thesis focusing on the deepening of managerial, training, professional, and applied research themes.
Final Exam Procedure To be admitted to the Final Exam, the student must have regularly attended didactic activities, passed all course exams, and received a positive evaluation on internship learning outcomes as per the current Study Plan.
The Final Exam consists of the preparation and discussion of a Research Thesis with originality as per paragraph 5 of Article 11 of DM 270/2004, focusing on the deepening of managerial, training, professional, and applied research themes within their professional field.
The Thesis is prepared and elaborated under the guidance of a Supervisor (Course instructor) selected by the graduate from the figures specified in the Course Didactic Regulations. The possibility of co-supervisors (internal or external to the Course) is provided.
On the day of the Final Exam, the graduate presents and discusses their work within a maximum of fifteen minutes, under the guidance of the Supervisor and with the aid of selected and meaningful slides, before a Committee of Faculty members consisting of at least seven and no more than eleven members. The Examination Committee is usually composed of Supervisors and other faculty members and may be chaired by the Course Coordinator. On the day of the Thesis discussion, the Committee will provide a comprehensive evaluation in hundredths, with possible honors, considering the entire study path of the candidate. The score attributed to the graduate's work derives from the sum of the base score (obtained from the weighted average of course exams in hundredths), the score attributed to the Thesis, and the score attributed to the entire study path. Specifically, the evaluation of the Thesis and the study path contribute to a score from 0 to 8 points as follows:
- quality of the dissertation from 0 to 3 points;
- content and methodology used from 0 to 5 points.
The Committee may, with unanimous opinion, award:
- an additional point to candidates who participated in internationalization paths or to those graduating on time;
- honors to candidates who achieve a final score greater than 110 with a study path characterized by one or more honors.
The possibility for the student to prepare the work in English is provided.

Program, Texts, and Objectives Rationale for the establishment of the interclass course The interclass course LM 5 (Archival Science and Library Science) - LM 84 (Historical Sciences) Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times is born from the consolidated experience of the link between the two fields: indeed, the archival and library science field is based on SSD M-STO/08, namely Archival Science and Library Science, which is a historical sector. Conversely, there is no serious historical research that does not rely on a careful knowledge of primary and secondary sources. Therefore, when designing the course, it naturally arose to develop it in two tracks that will be in constant and close dialogue, mutually feeding each other on a methodological plane and on an application plane of the most recent research acquisitions, particularly regarding the use of digital resources for both organization and cataloging tools as well as for research tools. In this way, students and teachers of the course will be able to mutually exchange knowledge and skills in a fruitful and enriching manner.

Communication Skills
Graduates must be able to clearly and unambiguously communicate the results of their studies and the underlying knowledge, both to specialist and non-specialist audiences. Communication skills are also linked to mastery of written and spoken use of at least one European Union foreign language, including disciplinary terminology.
The development of communication skills is supported by laboratory activities and is fostered through the presentation and evaluation of written and oral student work. Communication skills will also be continuously assessed at various levels of learning evaluation.
Expected learning outcomes in terms of communication skills may be evaluated through traditional assessment methods (oral and/or written exams).

SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5118

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgements)
Graduates, based on the research and analysis methods learned in their study path, will be able to receive, interpret and manage complex cultural data within broad reference frameworks, with their own mature critical spirit, attentive to scientific, social and ethical implications.
To foster the achievement of autonomy of judgment, interdisciplinary connections between teaching activities are provided through the organization of seminars and conferences on common topics. Additionally, some teaching activities conducted in seminar form involve assigning in-depth topics for students to report on during lessons.
Autonomy of judgment will be verified at different levels of learning assessment tests.
The acquisition of increasing autonomy of judgment will be periodically assessed during written and/or oral examinations, where students can demonstrate having personally assimilated and critically understood the examination content; furthermore, through discussions between teachers, students and representatives of professional realities.

International Mobility Unit Students will be encouraged to engage in international mobility, with orientation and support activities for studying abroad, primarily through opportunities arising from specific agreements established with foreign universities for the Course of Study in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times, as well as the University's Lifelong Learning Programme Erasmus. International mobility orientation will be carried out in collaboration with the Coordinator for the LLP/Erasmus Programme and the Coordinator for International Relations of the Department of Letters, Arts and Social Sciences.
In line with the University's strategic guidelines, the Department of Letters, Arts and Social Sciences and the Department of Languages, Literatures and Modern Cultures have already implemented initiatives to promote the internationalization of teaching and research by increasing the number of research collaboration agreements and cooperation with international partners for the mobility of teachers and students, and international conventions. Data being processed for this year show signs of recovery after the difficulties caused by the Covid-19 pandemic. For example, taking another Course of Study from DiLASS, the LM 14 in Modern Philology, the iC10 indicator showed an increase in ECTS credits earned abroad by LM14 students in 2021 (5.7 in 2021 compared to 3.7 in 2020), and it is expected that the Course of Study in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times will contribute to fostering international exchanges through agreements and collaborations with foreign universities offering study programs with similar training paths. Partnership agreements are currently being studied with Enssib (École Nationale Supérieure des Sciences de l'information et des Bibliothèques) in Lyon, the national reference body in France for training librarians and information specialists; with Babeș-Bolyai University in Cluj-Napoca, Romania, for historical aspects; and with the University of Nantes and the University of Utrecht for aspects more related to medieval studies. Thanks to specifically formulated agreements, it will be possible to provide students of the Course of Study in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times with an expedited pathway to complete part of their studies abroad at one of the partner universities.

Career Guidance The CdS will establish a Steering Committee to ensure an active, effective, and continuous relationship with organizations representing the world of work and professions, continuing the activities already carried out through internships and internships: archives, libraries, institutes and research centers, publishing houses and multimedia production companies, cultural associations are the main interlocutors in this regard. The Steering Committee will consist of, in addition to CdS representatives, representatives of the relevant social partners, particularly entities and institutions related to the training profiles provided by the CdS, both in the private sector and public-ministerial sector.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
At the end of the program, the student:
is able to apply heuristic and hermeneutic techniques, conceptual tools, and the most up-to-date methodological approaches, as well as the specific terminologies of the various disciplines involved, to independently propose critical interpretations of historical events and the original reconstruction of some of their significant aspects;
possesses the ability to apply knowledge through skills acquired in the fields of document, manuscript, and printed book disciplines, to the management and valorization of archival and library heritage, in the field of source research, analysis, and study of historical sources, according to different historiographical traditions and research methodologies, proposing original interpretative lines;
is able to transmit such knowledge for educational purposes both in study contexts and other settings, both in person and through telecommunications tools related to knowledge dissemination. They will also have acquired some skills and competencies related to the English language, common to all training areas, the educational offer, and teaching methodology.
is able to expand, diversify, and deepen their historical and archival knowledge gained during previous studies, thanks to direct contact with sources and documents and the use of a laboratory-based teaching approach, supported by the necessary digital skills for research contexts, in the fields of digitization, database creation, archival science and library science, and the use of information technology in areas such as Public History and Digital History.
The high interdisciplinarity will guarantee a variety of approaches and topics covered in the courses and laboratories. This approach contributes to making the CdS effective in training the various professional profiles it encompasses and allows the acquisition of specific competencies and the achievement of specific educational objectives, useful for applying the theoretical knowledge acquired.

From an organizational perspective, lectures and remote classes will be complemented by classes in archives and libraries, as well as laboratories where innovative teaching methods can be tested in small groups. This aims to promote the active role of students in the learning process from a socio-constructivist perspective, where the teacher acts as a mediator capable of stimulating students to express themselves and collaborate, together contributing to the construction of knowledge (role-playing, Problem-Based Learning, etc.).

These competencies form the basis of the following professional activities to be carried out in public, private, and accredited private structures, within editorial offices and archives, libraries, and museums. Additionally, solid knowledge in the field of digital humanities allows for continuous updating in research fields in both public and private sectors, as well as in educational and training contexts.

The teaching tools used to achieve the above objectives include both frontal lectures and interactive and laboratory activities. Assessment methods include oral or written exams.

Ability to Learn (learning skills)
Graduates must have developed learning abilities enabling mostly independent study or, at least, a high level of responsibility. Tutoring activities support students toward full autonomy in research. The achievement of expected results will be verified during the process through laboratories, internships, stages, and reports on specific topics.

Learning abilities will be periodically evaluated within individual courses using traditional assessment methods (oral interviews, exercises, written tests), as well as within various laboratory and internship activities.

Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
At the end of the study program, the master's graduate acquires advanced theoretical and methodological knowledge, as well as interdisciplinary and specific knowledge related to historical research, source identification, historiographical trends, and research topics. They know and recognize concepts of periodization and those of continuity, change, and rupture in the formation of chronologies. They identify and interpret interdisciplinary research methods, placing history in relation to other disciplines, not only humanistic. They know heuristic, editing, and source analysis techniques and are able to use bibliographic and archival research tools. They can compare different types of documents. They can navigate various chronological spans, topics, research areas, and different theories for managing archives, libraries, conservation institutions, and research bodies related to their field.

These knowledge bases underpin the professional activities detailed in section A4.a to be carried out in public, private, and accredited private structures, within editorial offices and archives, libraries, and museums. Additionally, solid knowledge in the field of digital humanities allows for continuous updating in research fields in both public and private sectors, as well as in educational and training contexts.

These knowledge bases are acquired through frontal lectures, seminar activities, laboratories, and internships. Assessment methods refer to oral and written exams during examination sessions and a final thesis exam.

Brief Description of Related and Complementary Activities The Master's Degree in Archival Science and Library Science (LM-5) and in Historical Sciences (LM-84) requires the acquisition of a total of 12 CFU in related activities between the first and second year.

What primarily characterizes the proposal of the "Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times" study course, as already highlighted in section A.4.a, is its nature as an interdisciplinary course (between LM 5 and LM 84) and the delivery method that includes innovative teaching forms. This second aspect is not only reflected in remote delivery but also in in-person lectures held in places dedicated to the conservation and valorization of documents and library materials, as well as other forms of "source" useful for historical research.

Therefore, related activities aim to highlight and emphasize the specific objectives of the Course through in-depth and expanded educational offerings for both Archival Science and Library Science (LM 5) and Historical Sciences (LM 84), fostering knowledge and understanding of phenomena related to written culture in their various manifestations, from antiquity to the contemporary world, broadening the range of methodological proposals while keeping in mind the need to acquire theoretical and practical competencies related to the use of different textual types. On one hand, the goal is to propose courses that open broader horizons, crossing disciplines in dialogue with history and prioritizing other types of sources beyond written ones; on the other hand, opportunities for reflection on the deep philological attention necessary for a correct contextualization and precise analysis of any source, starting from, as is obvious in a historical context, all forms and manifestations of writing, from wall graffiti to writing on papyrus, parchment, paper, in documentary or library contexts. Through related activities, an opportunity for in-depth learning related to subjects useful for completing and enriching the personal background of graduates is offered.

Brief Course Description The Master's Degree in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times is one of the master's courses comprising the educational offer of the DiLASS, Department of Letters, Arts, and Social Sciences, affiliated with the School of Humanistic Studies of the 'G. D'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara. It is a two-year interdisciplinary course structured into "Archival Science and Library Science" (LM-5) and "Historical Sciences" (LM-84), responding to the need to provide graduates with a specific cultural and professional training that enables them to:
● understand the orientations and languages of historiography and the most recent methods of investigation, characteristic of historical sciences, with an interdisciplinary approach;
● understand the languages of historical communication, both in the form of specialized research and in the form of historical culture dissemination in new application contexts, taking into account the latest technologies and new media;
● manage library and documentary heritage on any support, analog and digital, based on current legal regulations and using updated theoretical and practical tools for the protection, valorization, and promotion of archives and libraries;
● carry out study, research, training, and educational activities on archival and library heritage through services designed to facilitate independent resource retrieval by users for their individual research.

To acquire these competencies, the Master's Degree in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times will offer: I) a common training for all students on themes related to the scientific fields characterizing the course, namely those related to historical studies and those concerning the production, conservation, valorization, and use of written and audiovisual heritage; II) studies related to digital humanities, archival and library regulations, and the study of ancient books (particularly for the LM 5 path), as well as opportunities for in-depth learning related to a correct philological and hermeneutic approach to sources, especially for the LM 84 track; III) specific training aimed at directing students toward professionalization in four educational areas: 1) professional area; 2) cultural management area for public, private, and accredited private sectors; 3) research area; 4) teaching and training area. These specific educational areas will provide master's graduates with competencies in sectors particularly sought after by the labor market and at the forefront of innovative technologies for critical analysis, research, and understanding of a diverse range of sources and historical and archival research methodologies, applicable to teaching, managerial, or research activities.

Professional Profile and Employment Prospects The proposed study paths aim to refine the preparation acquired during the three-year degree, contributing to forming qualified students who can further pursue studies to work in secondary school and university teaching; engage in research and the protection and valorization of archival and library heritage, thanks to the acquisition of specialized historical, critical, and operational skills. The professional opportunities offered by the two paths into which the Master's Degree in Historical Sciences and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times is structured are connected to the ability to organize and classify complex historical, archival, and library problems coherently, designing and communicating appropriate solutions within the relevant fields. Graduates may therefore assume responsible roles:
● in activities related to cultural services and initiatives sectors;
● in specific institutions such as archives, libraries, museums, cultural centers, and foundations with cultural purposes;
● in study and research centers, public and private;
● in governmental and local institutions within cultural services sectors, and in the recovery and valorization of activities, traditions, and local identities with an economic and cultural promotion perspective;
● in publishing, particularly in the dissemination of historical information and culture, with special attention to new forms of historical communication connected to Information and Communication Technologies (Digital and Public History).

Master's graduates in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times find placement in research and in public and private institutions, both Italian and foreign, such as archives, libraries, and museums, as well as in entities with responsibilities in the cultural services sector, such as journalism, specialized and digital publishing. They may also continue their studies to become secondary and university teachers.

The possession of a Master's Degree in Archival Science and Library Science (LM-5) is a legally and contractually required qualification for public competition for the professional profile of Area III, Archivist and Librarian Officer, within the roles of the Ministry of Culture.

The Master's Degree in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times, like any Master's Degree, will be recognized throughout Europe based on the 2005/36/EC Directive of the European Parliament and Council of September 7, 2005, concerning the recognition of professional qualifications, currently subject to a recognition procedure. Master's graduates will therefore be able to access roles reserved for those holding a Master's Degree in other parts of Europe.

Specific Educational Objectives of the Course and Description of the Study Path Master's graduates in Historical Studies and Written Heritage from Antiquity to Contemporary Times, after a training path focused on the study of documents, manuscripts, books, and digital supports, and on tools, methods, historiographical traditions, and specialized research approaches for various historical periods, will be able to:
1. Acquire, evaluate, and ensure the preservation of current, deposit, or historically significant archives, guaranteeing their accessibility and public use, also through microfilm, digital supports, or other means;
2. Conduct analyses and research aimed at editing archival sources, even in a digital environment;
3. Catalog, classify, and index public and private library collections with particular attention to preservation, accessibility, and public use;
4. Valorize documentary and library material, both ancient and modern, manuscript and printed, through promotion activities, exhibitions, events, and promoting specific services for users;
5. Conduct research, describe, and interpret past events and documents using historical sources of various types;
6. Master the methodologies of historical sciences, primarily through knowledge of the research techniques required for the retrieval, analysis, and critical use of sources;
7. Analyze past phenomena through specific knowledge of human cultures and civilizations, as well as theories and methodologies of social and economic sciences;
8. Recognize the key aspects of a historical period in its various dimensions, based on a general knowledge of world history from its origins to the present and a critical elaboration of the most current themes, such as new "global" history and gender issues;
9. Build an autonomous research capacity;
10. Use the main information technology tools;
11. Communicate results in written and oral form, at least in a foreign language commonly used in disciplinary scientific communication;
12. Promote the knowledge of history through dissemination activities, exhibitions, events, and the design of multimedia content;
13. Plan and coordinate public and private cultural management activities;
14. Plan and coordinate teaching, training, and research activities.

DESCRIPTION OF THE STUDY PATH The path through which the specific educational objectives of the CdS are achieved is organized according to the following chronological sequence:
1. In the first year, disciplines will cover the following areas: archival science, bibliography and library science, with particular attention to digital information management, codicology, and paleography. Students must also acquire advanced knowledge and skills in Greek, Roman, and medieval history. Foreign language skills are also acquired during the first year.
2. In the second year, training activities focus on providing adequate preparation in the field of digital humanities applications, as well as administrative law sources in the archival and library context.
Also in the second year, tools are provided for acquiring knowledge and skills in modern and contemporary history, with particular attention to the Balkan and Adriatic regions of Europe, as well as the history of the Italian Republic, Islamic countries, and the economy. Additionally, activities providing transversal knowledge and skills, ranging from classical and Christian medieval archaeology to anthropology and geography, are concentrated. Furthermore, linguistic, literary, and philological disciplines are significant.

Practical-laboratory and internship activities are distributed between the first and second years.
These activities can be carried out based on student interest at:
- Public or private libraries with particular attention to cataloging and preservation methods for ancient texts.
- Museum structures.
- State and/or private archives.
- Archaeological sites.
- Sites of particular historical-artistic interest.

MOTIVATIONS FOR DELIVERING TEACHING IN MIXED MODE AS PER D.M. 289/2021
The decision to deliver the course in mixed mode (type b) stems from the significant presence of non-practical-laboratory training activities, which can be effectively delivered remotely. Specifically, the affected activities fall primarily within the historical field, which can be effectively delivered without the need for physical presence in the classroom.

Remote delivery will affect training activities within the following scientific disciplines, not exceeding 27% of the total for non-practical-laboratory activities, which will always be delivered in person:
- L-ANT/02 Greek History
- L-ANT/03 Roman History
- M-STO/01 Medieval History
- M-STO/02 Modern History
- M-STO/03 Eastern European History
- M/STO/04 Contemporary History.

Consultation with Representative Organizations of Production of Goods and Services, Professions (Course Establishment)
The first formalization of the establishment process for the new interdisciplinary LM 5 (Archival Science and Library Science) and LM 84 (Historical Sciences) CdS occurred during a meeting held on March 28, 2023, convened by the Coordinator of Relations with Conventional Structures of DiLASS, in agreement with the presidents of the CdS in Letters and Master's in Philology, and attended by the DiLASS Placement Delegate. Public and private, national, and local entities participated, including the Director of the Abruzzo and Molise Archival and Bibliographic Superintendency, Directors of State Archives of Chieti and L'Aquila, the National Tostiano Institute, the Marrucino Theater, the Atri Cathedral Archive, faculty, and students of the University.

This was followed by further steps and moments of discussion, partially documented in two detailed reports by the Abruzzo and Molise Archival and Bibliographic Superintendency, which show that current national regulations foresee a strong demand for archivists and librarians. At the same time, new perspectives requiring in-depth expertise and knowledge of methods and themes of historiography, beyond the teaching field, have been highlighted. These touch on the dimensions of public historical communication and its use within the framework of new media and new professions connected to it, such as the design of history-based multimedia content: diverse, broad, and varied is the audience looking for professionals in documents, books, and history.

Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam consists of preparing and discussing a research-based thesis, developed by the student under the guidance of a supervising faculty member affiliated with a scientific-disciplinary sector in which the student has passed at least one exam.

The thesis supervisor must be a faculty member active in the scientific-disciplinary sector of the discipline in which the student is graduating.

Procedure for Conducting the Final Exam From the thesis and its discussion, also prompted by the supervisor and all members of the graduation committee, the progress made by the graduate in their training path and the general and specialized qualification of their preparation may emerge.

After the presentation of the supervisor and co-supervisor, the candidate presents their work, possibly using multimedia tools, and engages in discussion with the committee, justifying the choices made during their research.

The candidate can thus demonstrate the variety of topics, methodological and historiographical issues, sources, and investigation tools applied in their original research within one of the disciplinary areas provided by the study path. In particular, they can demonstrate the ability to use, with appropriate methodologies and knowledge of the most important and updated research trends in their field of investigation, a wide range of historical sources (archival, documentary, library, literary, etc.) and the most suitable and effective investigation techniques and tools in their areas of interest.

The weight of the final exam corresponds to 9 CFU.

The final exam is evaluated by a committee appointed by the Department Director, who also sets the schedule. The judging committee consists of a minimum of seven faculty members, including the Chair. The majority of committee members must be tenure-track professors from the University. The Chair of the Committee is, among the members, the first-category professor with the greatest seniority or, in the absence thereof, the associate professor with the greatest seniority. The Chair must ensure full regularity in the conduct of the exam and adherence of the final evaluations to the general criteria established by the bodies responsible for the course.

The committee awards up to a maximum of 6 points for the final exam, with reference criteria including synthesis ability, scientific accuracy, argument coherence, and expressive clarity demonstrated by the candidate in the written thesis and oral presentation. Students who have completed a study experience within the ERASMUS program and international conventions (OVERSEAS) are awarded an additional 1 point. The judging committee expresses the overall grade in hundredths, considering the curriculum and the final exam, and unanimously may award the highest grade with honors. The minimum passing grade for the exam is 66 out of 100.

Admission Methods ART. 4 REQUIRED KNOWLEDGE FOR ACCESS AND ADMISSION METHODS
4.1 Required knowledge for access a. To enroll in the Master's Study Program, one must hold a Degree under the Old System, a Degree, or a three-year university diploma, or another foreign academic qualification recognized as suitable.
b. Additionally, to be admitted to the Study Program, students must, in accordance with DM 270/04, art. 6, paragraphs 1 and 2, possess knowledge of the fundamental elements of pedagogical knowledge and its connections with the knowledge of other humanities and social sciences.
c. The criteria and methods for evaluating the required knowledge for admission to the Master's program are specified in this Didactic Regulation and regulated as follows.
4.2 Admission methods
4.2 a. Those who hold a Degree in Pedagogy or Educational Sciences (pre-509/99); a three-year Degree belonging to Degree Class Cl-18 (ex DM 509/99) or L-19 (ex DM 270/2004) or equivalent may enroll in the Master's Degree Program in Pedagogical Sciences (LM-85).
Provided they meet the above requirements, candidates may be admitted to the Master's Degree Program in Pedagogical Sciences (LM-85) if they achieved a degree grade of at least 85/110 in the academic qualification that grants access to the program.
4.2 b. Those holding academic qualifications different from those listed above may also enroll in the Master's Degree Program in Pedagogical Sciences LM 85, provided they have earned a minimum of 30 CFU in the pedagogical-psychological-sociological-philosophical field, according to the following distribution:
a. 18 CFU in pedagogical SSDs (M-PED)
b. 6 CFU in psychological SSDs (M-PSI) or philosophical SSDs (M-FIL);
c. 6 CFU in sociological SSDs (from SPS 07 to SPS 12 inclusive).
Provided they meet the above requirements, candidates may be admitted to the Master's Degree Program in Pedagogical Sciences (LM-85) if they achieved a degree grade of at least 85/110 in the academic qualification that grants access to the program.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills (communication skills)
All teaching activities, even through the possibility of experimenting with models and techniques aimed at improving the quality and effectiveness of one's communication, generally aim to enhance communication skills.
Graduates will particularly acquire the ability to:
improve their relational skills;
identify communication techniques acting in texts and authors related to the educational research field;
critically evaluate the quality and effectiveness of different expository choices;
develop observation and listening skills towards others;
optimize the effectiveness of their own communication;
understand different communication modalities in interpersonal relationships;
manage, through communication, potential critical situations in their professional context.
They will also acquire functional and interpersonal communication skills aimed at team building and team leadership.
Finally, the course aims to develop students' communication skills through the targeted use of various communication tools currently available, by educating in the choice of strategies and channels most suitable and functional to the content to be transmitted.
Expected learning outcomes in terms of communication skills will be periodically verified through traditional assessment methods and through comparisons with different professional realities.

The President has committed to studying with the University office the possibility of a double degree agreement with foreign partner universities.
The Erasmus Department Delegate has been replaced and is now Prof. STEFANIA ACHELLA. In March 2021, a specific seminar was held with Erasmus contacts, Dr. Conte from the University International Office, and Erasmus students or those who had experienced this. The very effective online seminar on Teams.
Workplace support Graduates of the Course benefit from the Curricula services, a search engine implemented by the University for the performance of labor market operator functions, following accreditation granted by the Ministry of Labor, which authorized its registration in the Informatic Register of Intermediary Agencies from January 2, 2012.
This new task stems from the desire to complete the support path for graduates entering the labor market, already initiated in 2004 through the activation of the University Program Start, and subsequently the Ministry Program FIxO, a centralized Placement Service aimed at providing services to graduates during the delicate transition from study to work.
All students of the Course complete professional internships at occupational settings and are constantly supported by a database providing access to some contractual and labor market regulation information sheets.
Additional operational tools are provided to deepen one's competence in terms of self-promotion aimed at employment, also through online checks on the acquired training.
Workplace orientation activities aim to provide graduates with knowledge elements facilitating interaction with the world of work and can be carried out through various means, such as Internships, Traineeships, and Project Work. To this end, a strong collaboration with the world of work is activated, which in most cases demonstrates sensitivity and interest in the projects presented by universities.
The common goal becomes facilitating students' entry into the world of work and contributing, through the dissemination of knowledge and skills, to the socio-economic growth of the territory.
The Course has also benefited from the opportunities offered by the University of Chieti-Pescara 'G. d'Annunzio', as promoter and coordinator of the InnovAction project, presented within the LLP - Leonardo da Vinci program (People in the Labour Market) and approved by the European Union through the Italian National Agency for Leonardo (ISFOL), which provides scholarships for transnational internships lasting 24 weeks in European Union countries.
Finally, it is necessary to emphasize that the training path is structured to access the new competition classes and qualifications A18 (formerly 36/A) and A19 (formerly 37/A).

Student Opinions Data for the first semester of the 2023-2024 academic year (starting March 2024) for courses held in the first semester confirm the course's appreciation in line with the average.

ACADEMIC YEAR 2021 2022
Regarding the Pedagogical Sciences degree course for the 2021-2022 academic year, 308 questionnaires were processed from student opinion surveys. All 15 teaching activities were surveyed, and the average score for the Pedagogical Sciences degree course based on student surveys is favorable, with an average of 3.46. Regarding overall satisfaction, Pedagogical Sciences students express an appreciation of 3.30%, slightly below the social area average of 3.33% and slightly below the university average of 3.31%.

Regarding logistical and organizational aspects, the Pedagogical Sciences degree course scores 3.51, compared to the social area average of 3.52 and the university average of 3.47.

Regarding teaching effectiveness, the Pedagogical Sciences degree course achieves a student score of 3.56, higher than both the social area average of 3.52 and the university average of 3.49. Detailed responses to different questions are provided, covering various aspects. Notably, students highly appreciate the interest teachers generate during lessons and their availability, scoring 3.66, which is higher than the social area average of 3.62 and the university average of 3.59. Similarly, teachers' clarity in exposition receives a score of 3.52, compared to the social area average of 3.48 and the university average of 3.46. Teachers also stimulate interest in the discipline, achieving a score of 3.51 for the entire degree course, compared to 3.45 for the social area and 3.42 for the university.

Regarding exam modalities, clarity is at social area levels, with the Pedagogical Sciences course scoring 3.59 compared to the social area average of 3.59 and the university average of 3.55, remaining fully in line with the average. Slightly higher appreciation is observed for Pedagogical Sciences regarding the coherence of teaching in relation to what is reported on the course website. The alignment of teaching with previously declared content on the website is recognized with a score of 3.58 for Pedagogical Sciences, compared to 3.55 for the social area and 3.50 for the university.

Regarding teaching materials and their adequacy, or the study load required, it is at the university level, though slightly less proportional than the social area (3.30 vs. 3.27 for Pedagogical Sciences), but overall positive results are confirmed for both the interest in teaching and the preliminary knowledge students possess to understand exam topics, fully in line with the university.

ACADEMIC YEAR 2020/21
Specifically regarding the B6 student opinion survey, the Pedagogical Sciences degree course receives a score of 3.46, a highly favorable score exceeding last year's averages. The analytical summary of evaluations shows students particularly appreciate teachers' availability to clarify topics and the coherence of teaching with what is declared on the website. Regarding the CUN areas present in the degree course, the score is good and exceeds three points in all areas. Scientific disciplinary sectors all significantly exceed three points, and individual courses also show good performance, as in the previous year. Data is somewhat underestimated by non-attending students. Student responses confirm the trend of previous years of substantial student satisfaction, with the entire degree course scoring nearly 3.5.

The general evaluation synthesis shows attending students positively evaluate the study course, assigning a score of 3.43. 90% of degree course students declare themselves fairly and fully satisfied. Scores are respectively 33% for 'more yes than no' and over 56% for 'decidedly yes'. Greater dissatisfaction is found among non-attending students, although over 70% of non-attenders declare themselves generally satisfied. 40% respond with 'more yes than no' and 31% with 'decidedly yes'. This does not diminish the need for the degree course to improve its performance regarding impact on non-attending students. These students number 245, unable to attend due to work reasons; very few, 5 units, state that attendance is not useful for exam preparation.

Regarding courses, attending students show widespread satisfaction with the training offer and teachers, with scores well above 3. Slightly lower scores are observed for courses among non-attending students.

ACADEMIC YEAR 2019-2020 - Situation Analysis
The evaluation system allows all students to express specific and detailed evaluations of individual courses, structures, and all aspects of university life through an anonymous and automated procedure. Student opinions and evaluations are promptly processed by the NdV and forwarded to the Course Director, relevant teachers, and structures, with potential issues discussed by academic bodies to identify possible solutions.

BEFORE ANALYZING THE DATA, IN PERSONAL JUDGMENT, IT IS OBSERVED THAT STUDENT VALUES AND EVALUATIONS EXPRESSED IN THIS CONTEXT ARE NOT CONFORMING TO THE PARTICULAR SITUATION IN WHICH TEACHING, DUE TO THE CORONAVIRUS PANDEMIC, WAS DELIVERED.

FOR EXAMPLE, THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN ATTENDING AND NON-ATTENDING STUDENTS IS ENTIRELY INCOHERENT WITH THE SITUATION THAT AROSE IN THE SECOND SEMESTER, SINCE CLASSES COULD BE RECORDED AND MADE AVAILABLE TO THOSE WHO MISSED THE LIVE SESSION.

THEREFORE, THE QUESTIONNAIRE, NOT APPROPRIATELY MODIFIED (WHICH COULD HAVE BEEN DONE BY UTILIZING SPECIFIC PROFESSIONAL EXPERTISE AVAILABLE AT THE UNIVERSITY), HAS ITS VALIDITY COMPROMISED BY AN INADEQUATE FORMULATION FOR THE NEW SITUATION. Additionally, no question was asked about the technical IT service.

Regarding the 2019-2020 academic year, data confirms widespread student satisfaction. Our students express decisive satisfaction with the degree course, responding 'Decidedly yes' for 53.9% (Table 3). This exceeds the social area average ('Decidedly yes' 49.2%) and the university average ('Decidedly yes' 47.1%). Responses with 'more yes than no' account for 36.9%.

The main reason for not attending classes (Table 4) is work-related causes, almost 70%, nearly double the social area and university totals.

Regarding teacher opinions, in our degree course, only 60% of courses were rated low, though still well above the university average. Teachers are mostly satisfied (46% 'Decidedly yes' and 30% 'more yes than no'), though at a lower level than the social area average (54% 'Decidedly yes' and 34% 'more yes than no') and the university average (55% 'Decidedly yes' and 34% 'more yes than no').

Strengths and Weaknesses.
Strengths include: constant attention to balancing teaching loads across both semesters and accommodating requests from previous academic year surveys for more exam sessions.
The didactic regulation continues to be revised annually, updating it for clearer specialization of the Master's degree, as planned, including scientific and professional development seminars. In-course orientation has proven highly effective, positively impacting the entire course management, particularly through constant attention to student requests and problem resolution, including administrative issues.

EXAMINING THE QUESTIONNAIRE RESULTS FOR THE 2019-2020 ACADEMIC YEAR, the overall positive evaluation of courses and teachers by students is confirmed, with scores above 3 (3.42). Student surveys confirmed the validity of the current course structure regarding teaching load, topics covered, organization, adherence to lecture schedules, and teacher and tutor availability.

On May 15, 2020, the CDS Council for PEDAGOGICAL SCIENCES LM 85 discussed data from the Student, Graduates, and Teachers Opinion Survey on the university website (https://www.unich.it/sites/default/files/report_opinioni_studenti_2020.pdf; https://www.unich.it/sites/default/files/rilevazione_opinione_laureandi_aa_2018-2019.pdf; https://www.unich.it/sites/default/files/rilevazione_opinione_docenti_aa_2018-2019_f.pdf). It emerged that the course received satisfaction from students, graduates, and teachers; participation in the survey should be encouraged, and the President recommends all to complete the questionnaires.

The opinion survey confirmed the persistence of long-standing logistical issues, such as insufficient classrooms and equipment.

Regarding the complete opinion survey for the 2019-2020 academic year:
ATTENDING STUDENTS, THE MAJORITY (221), BELIEVE THEIR BASIC PREPARATION IS ADEQUATE AND THAT THE COURSE'S TEACHING LOAD SHOULD NOT BE INCREASED. STUDENTS ARE GENERALLY SATISFIED WITH THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN DISCIPLINES. THE MAJORITY ARE ALSO SATISFIED WITH THE QUALITY OF TEACHING MATERIAL. HOWEVER, THEY REQUEST GREATER TIMELINESS IN PROVIDING ADDITIONAL SUPPORT MATERIAL.

STUDENTS ARE GENERALLY SATISFIED WITH THE DAILY AND TIMETABLE SCHEDULING OF CLASSES. REGARDING INTERMEDIATE EXAM PROOFS, ABOUT HALF OF STUDENTS REQUEST THEM, WHILE THE OTHER HALF IS AGAINST.

A SIGNIFICANT NUMBER OF STUDENTS REQUEST SUPPORT ACTIVITIES SUCH AS SEMINARS AND EXERCISES, WHICH THE TEACHING STAFF, DUE TO STRUCTURAL REASONS (SPACE AVAILABILITY) AND/OR TEACHING LOAD, CANNOT FULLY PROVIDE.

BASED ON THE DATA, SUPPORT ACTIVITIES WOULD BENEFIT NON-ATTENDING STUDENTS, ESPECIALLY IN COURSES WHERE FUNDAMENTAL KNOWLEDGE IS LACKING. ADDITIONALLY, THE PANDEMIC-IMPOSED CLOSURE PROBABLY CAUSED DISCOMFORT FOR STUDENTS, PARTICULARLY NON-ATTENDERS.

Graduate Opinions Academic Year 2021-2022
Data on graduates in Pedagogical Sciences for the year 2022. Regarding satisfaction with the completed degree course, there were 52 graduates and 40 interviewed. Of these, over 75% of the students attended more than half of the required courses, compared to almost 70% of those enrolled at the university. This low attendance rate among Pedagogical Sciences students compared to other courses at the university can be explained by the fact that the Pedagogical Sciences degree attracts many people who are already working and employed.
16% attended between half and three-quarters of the courses;
a small 10% attended between a quarter and half of the courses;
a small 20% attended less than a quarter of the courses.
Regarding the study load of the courses, most of the interviewed students consider the study load appropriate, and this figure is slightly higher than the university average;
furthermore, according to a small 40% of the interviewed students, the study load is appropriate for the duration of the degree course. Therefore, the study load of the Pedagogical Sciences degree is widely supported by almost all graduates who have already completed their studies.
Regarding exam organization, exam sessions, schedules, and information, a little over one-third of graduates consider it satisfactory: 35% compared to 40% at the university; most graduates, 58%, believe that more than half of the exams are well-organized, compared to 45% university-wide.
Regarding relationships with professors, just under one-third of graduates declare themselves highly satisfied, just under half are predominantly satisfied, while approximately 15% are highly dissatisfied.
Overall, 35% of graduates are satisfied with the degree course, compared to 45% of graduates at the university.
About half, 48%, are fairly satisfied, compared to 45% of graduates at the university, while 12% are dissatisfied.
When asked if they would enroll in university again, over 60% of graduates would re-enroll, and almost 70% would enroll in the same degree course or another course at the university, thus remaining loyal to the university. A 10% would enroll at another university and in another degree course.
Regarding employment status, the following were interviewed in 2022:
- Graduates from 2021 (one year after obtaining the degree)
- Graduates from 2019 (three years after obtaining the degree)
- Graduates from 2017 (five years after obtaining the degree).
One year after graduation, 14 were interviewed, with an average age of 29 years, all women, with an average grade of 107.6. Over one-third participated in or are engaged in post-graduation training. 64.3% are employed. Most, 55%, work in intellectual, scientific professions requiring high specialization; 44% are employed on an open-ended contract, 22% on a fixed-term contract; 33% have other contractual forms; 11% work in Smart Working; 44% work part-time, with an average of 24 weekly working hours. 44% work in the public sector, 22% in the private sector, and one-third in the non-profit sector. Most work in services. Additionally, they predominantly work in the South, over three-quarters, and in the Northeast, 22%.
Regarding the use of skills acquired through the degree, over half, 55%, consider them highly utilized; 44% consider them utilized to a lesser extent, compared to the professional training acquired at university, which is considered very appropriate by 77%. Conversely, 22% of respondents consider the professional training acquired at university to be poorly appropriate. Obviously, the high correlation rate between degree title and profession is due to legal requirements for teaching; only 11% perform work not requiring a degree; however, the degree is considered necessary even if not required, and useful for 44% of people. Regarding the effectiveness of the degree, satisfaction with current work. Two-thirds express that the degree is very effective in performing the job and finding satisfaction with the current work, which is considered fairly effective. 33% are satisfied with the work performed on a scale from one to ten, with a collective score of 8.2 points.
Regarding student career monitoring for the academic year 22-23 in the Pedagogical Sciences degree course: at the first year, 13 students have earned at least 12 CFU; 11 students have between 18 and 30 CFU, and four students have between 45 and 60 CFU for the second year. We have four students with up to 36 CFU and 26 students with between 36 and 60 CFU; 12 students have between 90 and 120 CFU. Regarding the second year off-track, we have six students. There are also those who have earned up to 36 CFU, 19 students from 36 to 60 CFU, and 21 students from 90 to 120 CFU.
Enrolled students for the 22-23 academic year: 29 first-year students and 89 second-year students, for a total of 118 enrolled students, of which 47 are off-track.
Regarding enrolled students for the academic year 22-23. The Pedagogical Sciences degree course has 43 enrolled students. Total enrolled: 118, of which 71 are on-track and 47 off-track.
Regarding geographical origin of enrolled students for the academic year 2022/2023, Pedagogical Sciences shows 5 people from the same municipality, 9 enrolled from another municipality in the province, 5 from other municipalities in the region, and 24 from other regions.
