Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and service production, professions (Establishment of the course)
On May 8, 2018, the Department Council of the Department of Legal and Social Sciences established an investigative commission composed of the Director, Prof. Fornari, and Prof. Guarriello, Gambini, and Civitarese to elaborate a proposal for a Master's Degree Course in the Legal Sciences degree class, as per DM 77/2018, as the natural continuation and completion of the Bachelor's Degree Course in Legal Services for Business (L-14).
The commission met on multiple occasions to discuss the cultural profile and architecture of the CdS, and carried out one-to-one meetings and interviews with representatives of national and international organizations of the business world and professions. Among these: National Confindustria and the European Confederation Business Europe, sectoral business associations and national trade unions (metal-mechanical, food, construction, chemical-energy), Chamber of Commerce, National Confartigianato, National Order of Customs Brokers, National Register of Industrial Property Consultants, National Association Federtrasporti, National Order of Labor Consultants, AIGE-European Association of Business Lawyers, some Human Resources and Industrial Relations departments of transnational companies or groups, the International Arbitration Chamber, some Legal Departments of large companies or Law Firms specialized in International Trade Law.
Continuous dialogue with stakeholders, supported by sector studies and documents on employment trends at national and international level (see CdS design document), contributed to building the CdS project as much as possible in line with the training needs present in the local and national labor market, focusing on the qualifying training objectives in relation to the expected professional outcomes, centered on the figure of the legal expert in internationalization and innovation of business, capable of supporting from within or as an external consultant strategies of internationalization and organizational innovation processes.
The consulted organizations positively welcomed the novelty represented by the Master's degree class SC-GIUR for the training of the figure of a business legal expert or general counsel, professions not regulated that today concern only graduates of the single-cycle Master's Degree in Jurisprudence (L-MG/01), the Master's Degree in Administrative and Legal Sciences of Public and Private Organizations (L-M 63), and European Studies (L-M 90), usually after completing a second-level Master. The opportunity offered by the new degree class to accelerate the training of such a figure for direct insertion into the labor market was strongly emphasized and accompanied by the proposal to establish the achievement of the LM SC-GIUR as a prerequisite for entry to specific professional registers requiring qualified legal competencies accompanied by economic-business competencies.
On October 18, 2018, a consultation table was convened with social partners (see attached minutes) where a detailed proposal for a Master's Degree Course was presented. The numerous stakeholders present expressed strong appreciation for the initiative, fully responsive to the needs present in the regional productive fabric and more broadly in Central-South Italy, where there is an objective shortage of professional figures expert in legal issues related to business internationalization and technological innovation (privacy, patents, intellectual property protection, etc.). Some indications and suggestions were positively accepted: the non-alternativity of the courses in International Taxation and Customs Merchandising, both necessary for the training of an international business legal expert; the progressive introduction of courses taught in English to acquire full mastery of the international specialist jargon in view of the full internationalization of the Study Course; the availability to host students in internships also at foreign sites and to carry out company tutor functions for specialized thesis; the interest in holding professionalizing seminars, testimonials, and company visits and drafting conventions for professional internships.
Some participants in the consultation expressed interest in participating in the Steering Committee of the new Master's degree class, which was subsequently established on December 13, 2018 (attached minutes), composed of 4 teachers of the CdS (Prof. Guarriello, Gambini, Civitarese, and Puoti) and 4 representatives of organizations of interest for the CdS LM: Chieti-Pescara Confindustria, the Regional Abruzzo Director responsible for territorial cohesion and europrojecting, the President of the local Order of Labor Consultants, a representative of an international professional studio. These are stakeholders interested in the cultural and professional profiles of the CdS graduates, who offer their collaboration through professionalizing initiatives for students (internships, traineeships, laboratories) and, through the Steering Committee, will carry out periodic monitoring of the CdS representing the actual needs of the labor market, the correspondence of the knowledge, skills, and competencies of the training path, evaluating the potential for development and the need for periodic updating of the CdS training profiles and proposing modifications/improvements.
The in-person consultation was supplemented by interviews with stakeholders who could not be present at the above meeting (see attached letter and responses from managers of national and international companies, international law firms, AIGI-National Association of Business Lawyers, AGICONSUL-National Association of Legal Consultants, experts, Regional Abruzzo offices, MISE Trademarks and Patents Office, ICE, etc.) who responded expressing appreciation for the initiative and making additional proposals, some of which were positively accepted, including: strengthening the area related to innovation issues (the course in Innovation Economics and Networks SECS-P/06 was introduced) and integrating communication strategy profiles into the course (the course in Social Innovation and Communication SPS-09 was introduced).
On October 25, 2018, the Department Council unanimously approved the Master's Degree Course.
Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and service production, professions (Subsequent consultations)
On February 28, 2024, the CdS Council modified the composition of the Steering Committee by including new stakeholder representatives: in particular, the composition was expanded to include representatives of public administrations, companies, and consulting firms, and professional orders interested in the training of the Giurinn Master's graduate.
The new Steering Committee, convened on April 4, 2024, discussed with the academic component of the CdS, discussing the strengths of the study plan and its correspondence with the training needs required by the labor market and professions, showing great interest in the proposed training offer, considered of very high level. Particular attention was paid to the new international path built with the University of Rouen, for the potential enrichment of knowledge and skills provided to our students who will spend a semester of study abroad, as well as to incoming students from the University of Rouen, to whom the course intends to offer a qualifying training experience both theoretically and practically, through cycles of professionalizing seminars and laboratories carried out in collaboration with stakeholders.
It was also discussed to activate a more intense participation of interested parties in the training of individual students through forms of company/professional tutoring to be activated already in the first year of the Master's course, through presentation meetings with students and matching with respective sponsors based on self-candidacy, project evaluation, forms of involvement in laboratory activities.
The Steering Committee also discussed how to promote the Study Course through their networks and sponsorship forms.
Entry, progression, and exit data The CdS enrolled 18 students in 2022, adding to those of the previous academic year, giving a total of 44 students enrolled in the Master's degree, of whom 35 in course, 9 out of course, and 34 regular. It is therefore noted a decrease in new enrollments (from 20 last year). Students are predominantly from the L-14 Bachelor's degree, while the origin from other degree classes is marginal (one student from Sociology and Criminology, one from Management Sciences, one from Economics and Commerce). This is a circumstance largely anticipated and noted also in Almalaurea data, which underlies the very establishment of the new degree course, aimed at guaranteeing the continuation of studies for L-14 Bachelor's graduates, who until now did not have their own Master's degree class and who mostly continued their studies at Jurisprudence courses or other Master's courses. Some students enrolled in the CdS are already engaged in work activities, justifying a certain slowdown in the study path: of the total 20 students in the 2021 cohort, 3 explicitly withdrew from studies. Of the 44 enrolled students, 35 are in course and 9 out of course: for these, a careful verification will be carried out to determine whether they are students close to graduation or if the delay is more consistent and relates to the failure to take curricular exams. The CdS Council will discuss this and adopt measures to facilitate in-course orientation and to facilitate the completion of missing exams, as was done last year. In 2021, the average number of exams passed per student was 4.85 with acquisition of 45.7 CFU; while in 2022 the average number of exams passed per student increased to 6, with 59.3 CFU acquired, showing an excellent improvement. One first-year student, having completed the first-year exams in the July session, requested and obtained the abbreviation of the CdS.
Regarding the number of students enrolled in the CdS, which remains abnormally low, to strengthen entrance orientation and organize a social campaign to increase the number of new enrollments from outside the region, the CdS has already carried out initiatives before summer to make known the characteristics and job opportunities offered by the new Master's degree course in order to increase the source of new students. It has also decided to remodulate the entry requirements to facilitate the enrollment of students from other degree classes.
Characteristics of the final exam The final exam, consisting of the preparation of a paper on a topic agreed with the supervisor, who oversees the research work providing indications and suggestions and verifies its completeness and formal correctness, aims to verify the final achievement of expected learning outcomes (acquired knowledge, competencies: analytical, linguistic, transversal, relational, technological, communicative).
It can take the form of a written dissertation, also in a foreign language, aimed at presenting the research topic through chapters and paragraphs, accompanied by notes and an adequate bibliographic apparatus.
It can be the subject of the final exam the design activity, carried out under the supervision of a teacher and/or a company tutor, aimed at participating in competitive national or international calls for companies and organizations, through the complete preparation of a project idea, suitable partnership networks, also international, and a financial plan.
It can be the subject of the final exam the preparation of a study report, monitoring, or feasibility analysis regarding a complex reality, through the collection and interpretation of data, their systematic organization, detection of criticalities, and proposal of corrective solutions.
In each type, the final exam must demonstrate full acquisition of the knowledge necessary for the conscious use of the tools and techniques learned.
Mode of conducting the final exam The paper constituting the final exam, which the CdS attributes great importance to as a completion of the training path, quantified in 16 CFU, must be of adequate consistency for the topic treated and the specific characteristics of the chosen type.
It is presented and discussed before a graduation committee convened by the School's Academic Secretariat and composed of at least 7 teachers, presided over by the CdS President or the most senior professor, in which for each candidate the supervisor and co-supervisor are indicated.
The graduation committee may be optionally integrated for each candidate by the company tutor who followed the application research activity during the curricular internship or traineeship in company/entity, who will express their evaluation of the activity carried out and the results achieved by the candidate.
If the final exam concerns a study and research activity or internship carried out partially abroad, the supervisor also presents the evaluation of the foreign professor or company tutor who followed the research path of the graduate.
The supervisor introduces the candidate's work, inviting them to present the key contents before the graduation committee. At the end of the presentation, the co-supervisor discusses with the candidate the results achieved, the methodology used, the knowledge contribution, and the practical applications of the investigated topic.
The committee expresses an evaluation by assigning a merit score between 1 and 6 points in relation to the mastery of the topics covered, the correctness of the methodological approach followed, the degree of analytical depth of the issues, the richness and variety of sources consulted, the language property, and the originality of the results achieved. The paper can be written and presented in a foreign language.
An overall judgment is also formulated by the committee based on the candidate's academic career through the assignment of an additional score that cannot exceed 4 points for in-course candidates and 2 points for out-of-course candidates.
In assigning this score, the committee will give strong consideration to Erasmus experience or the international path followed, particularly for students who have spent at least six months abroad and obtained a minimum of fifteen CFU (thirty CFU for the double degree), as well as company experience that has stimulated the development of an applied research project.
The award of honors is conferred unanimously, on proposal of the graduation committee President, for works particularly meritorious in terms of the candidate's personal effort and the innovativeness/relevance of the results achieved.
For anything not expressly provided, the CdS conforms to the SEAGS School's Regulations on Final Exam Procedures (Attachment)
Summary of the technical report of the evaluation nucleus - SUA Sheet The design of the CdS, although carried out with tight timelines, is adequate and convincing. The cultural and professional profiles of the figure the CdS intends to form are clearly defined. Direct consultation with stakeholders is adequate at the local level, although not entirely at the national level. The cultural and professional profiles, functions, and competencies are consistent with learning outcomes and training activity objectives. Entry requirements and methods for verifying courses are adequately defined. The monitoring of the CdS is consistent with the University's AQ system.

Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission Access to the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences at the University of Chieti-Pescara requires both specific curricular requirements and adequate personal preparation.
1. Curricular requirements.
The following subjects may apply for admission to the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences at the University of Chieti-Pescara.
1.1 Those who hold a Degree in Philosophy class L-5 (ex DM 270/04), a Degree in Philosophy class 29 (ex DM 509/99) or a four-year Degree in Philosophy 'old system' obtained at any Italian university.
1.2 Those who hold one or more degrees, specialist degrees or master's degrees ex DM 509/99 or ex DM 270/04 and have acquired a minimum number of CFU in CUN areas 10 and 11. The determination of the SSDs of these areas and the minimum number of CFU for each area or group of SSDs is delegated to the didactic regulations of the study course.
1.3 Those who hold one or more degrees of the old system or degrees obtained abroad and have, in substance, acquired the same requirements as in point 2.
Verification of curricular requirements will be carried out by a commission established by the Course Council of the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences.
2. Personal preparation.
Subject to meeting the curricular requirements above, the following subjects may be admitted to the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences at the University of Chieti-Pescara.
2.1 Those who have obtained a grade of 90 or higher in the fields of philosophy, literature, psychology, sociology or history in their degree, specialist degree, master's degree or 'old system' degree. In the case of degrees obtained abroad, verification of a degree grade equivalent to the current definition will be carried out by a commission established by the Course Council of the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences.
2.2 Those who, in the absence of the above requirement, have been positively evaluated by a specific commission established by the Course Council of the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences. This commission will assess the applicants' knowledge and skills in the disciplinary fields defined by SSD M-FIL. The methods, timing and number of assessments will be determined by the commission.

Admission Requirements Admission to the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences at the Chieti-Pescara University is regulated as specified below.
1.
All individuals who hold a Degree in Philosophy class L-5 (ex DM 270/04), a Degree in Philosophy class 29 (ex DM 509/99), or a four-year Degree in Philosophy 'old system' obtained at any Italian university may directly enroll in the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences at the Chieti-Pescara University without further formalities.
2.
Additionally, all individuals who do not hold the qualifications specified in the previous point may enroll in the aforementioned Master's Degree if they possess one or more degrees, specialist degrees, or Master's degrees ex DM 509/99 or ex DM 270/04, and meet the following two requirements.
1°) Have acquired at least 60 CFU in one or more of the following SSD, or SSD defined as equivalent by law: all those whose name begins with the codes M-FIL, M-GGR, M-PED, M-PSI, M-STO, L-ANT, L-ART, L-FIL-LET, L-LIN, as well as M-DEA/01, IUS/19, IUS/20, L-OR/17, L-OR/20, SPS/01, SPS/02, SPS/08.
2°) Of the aforementioned 60 CFU, have acquired at least 30 CFU, obtained by passing at least four exams, in the following SSD, or SSD defined as equivalent by law: all those whose name begins with the code M-FIL, as well as IUS/20, L-OR/17, M-STO/05, SPS/01, SPS/02.
Verification of the possession of these requirements will be carried out by the Council of the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences, or by a committee appointed by such body, or, in urgent situations, by the Head of the Study Program.
3.
Additionally, all individuals who do not hold the qualifications specified in the previous points may enroll in the aforementioned Master's Degree if they possess one or more degrees of the old system or degrees obtained abroad, and meet, in substance, the same requirements as in point 2.
Verification of the possession of these requirements will be carried out by the Council of the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences, or by a committee appointed by such body, or, in urgent situations, by the Head of the Study Program, who will examine the candidate's academic record and determine the equivalences between semester or annual courses of the old system or foreign courses and courses structured in CFU.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The educational path aims to enhance in students the communication skills necessary to clearly and rigorously present their knowledge to both specialist and non-specialist audiences. To this end, the Study Course intends to provide theoretical tools and methodologies enabling students to understand the specific characteristics of the audience for philosophical communication, identifying and implementing expository strategies aligned with the theoretical objectives pursued and the identified interlocutors.
Specifically, the Study Course promotes knowledge of philosophical communication strategies to develop in students the following abilities.
- Correctly identify the different communication techniques operating in philosophical texts.
- Identify the relationship between expository strategies and the historical context in which authors and texts are situated.
- Decipher with insight the conceptual architecture underlying individual texts, recognizing in different authors the connection that variously intertwines philosophical reflection and expository choices.
- Evaluate with discernment the quality and effectiveness of different expository choices.
- Identify rhetorical strategies functional to different contexts and use them autonomously with perspicacity and critical acumen.
At the same time, the Study Course introduces students to the knowledge and practice of the multiple communication tools currently available, habituating them to present acquired knowledge in forms most suitable for the chosen communication media and directing them toward two goals.
- Create a solid and organic structure, well articulated in its different parts and marked by a coherent sequence of steps, within which to present their knowledge and research results, both orally and in writing.
- Correctly use different expressive structures, varying and adapting them according to the requirements of the different communication media adopted.
These objectives can be achieved through three types of activities.
- Activities in each course guiding students to present theoretical knowledge acquired during lectures in written and oral reports, applying them to topics and objects chosen in agreement with the instructor, with the specific intent, as mentioned, of fostering in students a full capacity to express their knowledge coherently.
- Activities of reading and commenting on texts in the original language, allowing students to grasp the constant features of philosophical communication across different languages and expressive forms.
- Activities, also interdisciplinary, of studying and using different communication techniques, with the aim of developing the ability to autonomously use different languages in various communication contexts.
To verify the competencies acquired by students in various disciplinary fields, each course or laboratory must identify, according to the specificity of each discipline, in-course assessments, written or oral exams, or final exercises.

SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgments)
Graduates of the Program will be able to identify, select, and use appropriate methodologies functionally to solve problems within their disciplinary area and to conduct autonomous research activities on topics related to their field of competence and understanding. Such research may involve both the critical analysis of texts with subsequent deepening of the historical and cultural context in which they are situated, as well as research on diverse issues related to different fields (such as, for example, the philosophy of science, logic, ethics, aesthetics, the universe of religions, environmental issues). Specifically, the Master's program aims to provide tools that enable philosophical research to interact with other disciplines, thus operating effectively in other areas, such as economics and business communication.
Specifically, graduates will acquire the following abilities.
- Ability to use bibliographic research tools judiciously, both to deepen their disciplinary field and to connect distinct fields and disciplines.
- Ability to critically evaluate acquired data to draw methodologically correct conclusions.
- Ability to critically interpret acquired knowledge to define, structure, and fully conduct autonomous research on authors, texts, and issues related to their field of competence.
- Ability to adapt their knowledge functionally to the needs of public discussion.
These objectives will be achieved primarily through teaching activities provided by various disciplines, which will guide students to effectively use the methodologies discussed and analyzed during lectures, identifying, applying, and developing coherent strategies appropriate to the conceptual-historical-philosophical, logical, theoretical, and ethical framework within which they propose to operate. The results achieved may also be confirmed through training experiences provided by the Program's regulations, such as internships and traineeships, allowing students to apply theoretical knowledge in practice.
To verify the competencies acquired by students in various disciplinary areas, each course or laboratory must identify, according to the specificity of each discipline, in-course assessments, written or oral exams, or final exercises. The ultimate verification of these competencies is constituted by the final exam and the preparation of a Master's thesis, during which each student - under the guidance of a faculty member - will have the opportunity to use methodologies connected to a specific area of philosophical research to explore authors, texts, and problems of the philosophical tradition. This will be done by constructing a reasoned, updated, and judicious bibliography on the subject of competence; using within an autonomous and rigorous reflection process the conceptual strategies identified both in the author addressed and in the critical literature used; critically and carefully evaluating the collected data to draw correct conclusions; and using the acquired theoretical knowledge in ways functional to public discussion.
To promote a fruitful interaction of philosophical competencies with other cultural and professional fields, such as the business field, students may also prepare their Master's thesis by utilizing appropriate training internships at partner companies.

STUDENT OPINIONS The overall evaluation of the Study Course by attending students for the 2023-24 academic year, according to currently available data, reports favorable results for the teaching staff, achieving an average score of 3.58/4. Based on these average evaluations, the different courses within the CUN area are equivalent in the obtained evaluation, as are the different courses according to the SSD. According to student opinion, the study course succeeds in meeting the expectations of enrolled students, surpassing the university average and also the humanities area average, achieving a score of 3.53. Students also express satisfaction with the logistical-organizational aspects, positioning the Master's program in Philosophical Sciences with a score of 3.59, higher than the university average and that of other humanities master's programs. The result achieved by teaching effectiveness is also very important, surpassing the university average and the average of other master's programs once again, with a score of 3.66. For this last academic year, it is not possible to go into detail, but if we take the results from last year, we see that the majority of students believe that the courses presuppose the appropriate level of basic knowledge - Additionally, the majority of students also consider it appropriate to keep the teaching load unchanged. Regarding the possibility of introducing or improving synergy with other courses, the majority of students believe it is not significant. Even non-attending students provide a good overall evaluation of the Study Course (3.38/4), improving on the previous year's data. This score is also reflected in the distribution by CUN areas and SSD. It is interesting to note that more than half of the students declare not attending due to work reasons, approximately 20% due to overlap with other courses (which are not part of LM78), and others for unspecified additional reasons. Of the non-attending students, only a very few request the activation of evening courses; the same percentage suggests reducing the overall teaching load and introducing intermediate exams. It should be added that at the meeting of the Parity Committee of Teachers-Students of the Department, held on March 14, 2023, whose minutes were sent to the Coordinator, no major issues were reported, but suggestions from student representatives that the Coordinator transmitted to his colleagues. In any case, it will be the Coordinator's responsibility to bring the results of the student opinion survey to the attention of the Council at the next meeting. No institutional procedures have been activated for the management of complaints and dissatisfaction, this because thanks to the not excessive number of students and the excellent representation work carried out by the delegated students as well as the student tutors, there has always been direct management by the Coordinator. Additionally, it is recalled that the Department, as regulated by the University, has the position of Student Guarantor.

Opinions of Graduates According to the opinions of graduates, the study load of the course's teachings is appropriate for the duration (57.1% definitely yes, 28.6% more yes than no), with a result 10 points better than the university D'Annunzio's average. The organization of exams appears to need improvement, as for some it is always satisfactory (24.6%) while for other graduates it is satisfactory for only half of the exams (57.1%). A commendable result is achieved by the course in the evaluation of graduates regarding their relationship with professors; students declare themselves definitely satisfied for 42.9% and more yes than no for 28.6%. The majority of graduates are also overall satisfied with the degree course, although here the average of 42.9% is slightly lower than the university's average. Decisively positive results are obtained in the evaluation of computer workstations, equipment for other teaching activities, and library services. An important result concerns the demand for potential re-enrollment at D'Annunzio University: for 85.7% of respondents, the choice would again fall on the Philosophical Sciences course, with a score exceeding the university's by more than 10 points.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The knowledge and skills acquired in the Study Course will enable those who obtain, at the University of Chieti-Pescara, the Master's degree in Philosophical Sciences to independently navigate the critical debate regarding the different areas of historical-philosophical inquiry, conduct research on topics related to various philosophical disciplines, and apply the tools of philosophical research to the questions and challenges posed by scientific research and interpersonal relationships, even at the corporate level. Graduates, after completing the training path, will be able to express their historical-critical, theoretical, and moral competencies in original forms to identify, understand, and solve problems related to areas such as scientific and educational research, corporate communication, ethical, legal, and environmental issues, and propose, on topics related to their disciplinary field, personal, competent, and methodologically grounded solutions. To verify the abilities acquired by students to understand and apply the knowledge offered in various disciplinary areas, each course or laboratory will identify, according to the specificity of each discipline, in-course assessments, written or oral exams, or final exercises. The training path concludes with a final thesis defense.

Learning Skills (learning skills)
The Study Course refines the abilities of sustained attention and application through activities that enhance critical sensitivity and acumen necessary for deepening knowledge and developing it in new disciplinary areas. This objective will be pursued both through seminar and assisted study hours provided within each discipline, and through training activities such as internships and traineeships. To verify the competencies acquired by students in various disciplinary areas, each course or laboratory must identify, according to the specificity of each discipline, in-course assessments, written or oral exams. The achievement of this objective will be fully expressed in the final evaluation related to each discipline, which concludes and defines the systematic interactions between teachers and students activated during lectures.

Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Upon obtaining the degree conferred by the Study Course, the student will possess an analytical understanding of the development of philosophical thought and its speculative components from antiquity to the contemporary world, and a secure competence in the methodologies and issues related to historiography, logic, theoretical philosophy, and moral philosophy. Specifically, thanks to the training activities provided in the Study Course, students will first refine their knowledge of philosophical thought from antiquity to the contemporary world and develop specialized competencies and theoretical tools to independently navigate the critical debate regarding the different areas of historical-philosophical inquiry; secondly, they will acquire advanced competencies in the methods and issues related to theoretical philosophy and moral philosophy to confidently navigate current debates and apply, in an interdisciplinary perspective, the tools of philosophical research to central issues of scientific research and interpersonal relationships. To verify the knowledge and abilities acquired by students in various disciplinary areas, each course or laboratory will identify, according to the specificity of each discipline, in-course assessments, written or oral exams, or final exercises. The training path concludes with a final thesis defense.

Brief Course Description The Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences at the University of Chieti-Pescara develops along four interconnected educational directions. First, it provides theoretical and methodological tools to understand different eras, contexts, and thematic areas of philosophical traditions developed over nearly three thousand years of human history, from ancient Greek-Archaic times to the present. To this end, students are offered a wide range of historical-philosophical courses dedicated to presenting and examining all periods of the history of philosophy: antiquity, Middle Ages, Renaissance, first and second modernity, contemporary era. Second, the Study Course aims to refine the ability to critically identify original research lines, develop them rigorously, and communicate them competently. To this end, students will acquire specific knowledge in the fields of theoretical philosophy, practical philosophy—moral and political—and philosophy of science. Equipped with these tools, they will be able to navigate current debates and independently conduct their research. In particular, they will be able to integrate philosophical inquiry tools with central issues of scientific research, ethics, and economics, and law. Third, the Study Course, together with a solid curriculum in a first-level degree course, enables students oriented toward secondary school teaching to acquire the knowledge and requirements necessary to enter the training or competitive pathways for access to this professional field. It also provides preparation and qualifications for entry into competitive procedures for higher education training courses aimed at scientific research. Finally, but not least in importance, the Study Course is designed to train professional figures capable of operating in political and economic sectors requiring the cross-disciplinary competencies peculiar to philosophical training: for example, the field of corporate management and human resources, communication and creative design, or the promotion of rights, the promotion and evaluation of biomedical and scientific research, and cultural mediation between disciplines, worldviews, lifestyles, and societies.

External Effectiveness The most recent data provided by AlmaLaurea, updated as of April 2023, despite the small number of respondents, highlight the following regarding the employment rate. We can see that one year after obtaining the degree, the employment rate of our graduates is higher than that of our university (71.4%), remaining equal at five years after graduation but appearing lower than the university's average. The time taken to enter the labor market, measured in months from the start of the job search to securing the first position, is significantly shorter compared to the university average. However, a reassuring data point shows that our graduates use their degree-acquired competencies to a high extent in their work: while only 20% report using their competencies in the first year, this percentage reaches 80% at five years. The average monthly net salary is nearly identical between the course and the university, but graduates' satisfaction with their work is higher than the university average in both the first year and at five years after graduation. These results will be discussed in detail at the next Course Council meeting.

Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description Within the disciplinary framework defined by the Master's Degree class LM-78 (Philosophical Sciences), the Master's Degree in Philosophical Sciences at the University of Chieti-Pescara sets three specific educational objectives. 1) To ensure a highly specialized preparation in historical-philosophical and philosophical-theoretical terms. 2) To offer students the opportunity to acquire the competencies required by current regulations to participate in selection procedures for secondary school teaching staff in the areas of teaching classes currently designated as A-18 'Philosophy and Human Sciences' and A-19 'Philosophy and History', as per DPR 19/2016. 3) To offer students the opportunity to acquire competencies necessary for productive insertion into a variety of corporate contexts. The training paths leading to these three objectives are not separable and do not result in distinct curricula. Rather, they are conceived as defined but interconnected and interdisciplinary pathways, within which students are given the freedom and responsibility to define some details of their training. In this context, the Course is structured to provide students with the theoretical and methodological tools necessary to independently and competently navigate different eras of the philosophical tradition and its various thematic areas. To this end, the educational offer allows the development of high-level critical competencies indispensable for both in-depth exploration of philosophical texts from a historical perspective and for adequately highlighting their complex conceptual architecture and theoretical and axiological implications. It also aims to strengthen students' ability to use acquired competencies to understand and evaluate, with autonomy and maturity of judgment, the various issues related to different areas of philosophical knowledge and those where philosophical research tools can be profitably applied, such as scientific, economic, juridico-political, ethical, and religious fields. The historical-critical analysis of philosophical texts is also aimed at acquiring linguistic and conceptual tools to organize research results scientifically and in personal and original forms, both in oral and written expression. The training path is completed by two sets of courses. On one hand, those aimed at conferring adequate linguistic competencies, enabling students to master the philosophical lexicon in various thematic areas and different expressive registers and genres, as well as to communicate acquired knowledge in Italian and at least one other European Union language. On the other hand, courses necessary to understand the fundamental elements of the economic world and various corporate realities, especially in the field of human resources. This design translates into a training path consisting of a single curriculum but with a versatile profile. It is designed to ensure, first, a highly specialized preparation in historical-philosophical and philosophical-theoretical terms. Nevertheless, it also offers the necessary scientific-disciplinary competencies for students who plan to work in secondary school teaching in classes A-18 'Philosophy and Human Sciences' and A-19 'Philosophy and History', following the completion of the required qualification and competitive pathways. Finally, the Study Course enables students to acquire competencies necessary for effective insertion into a variety of corporate contexts. This does not involve strictly technical knowledge but preparation for culturally oriented roles, such as human resource management, problem solving, marketing and communication, and the role of connecting different competencies present within a single company or different companies.

Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Traineeship Agreements The current Course Regulations do not provide for curricular internships classified as independent training activities. In previous years, some internship agreements with entities and companies were activated. It is emphasized, however, that entities and/or companies that previously hosted graduates of the Course have renewed their availability. After a long pause due primarily to regulations and practices strongly penalizing non-qualifying internships, fruitful attempts have been made to activate agreements with local companies for specific training in human resource management. The pandemic emergency period has not favored the signing of new internship agreements. The Course Council must address this opportunity for planning in the coming years, considering what has been done, what is underway, and what still needs to be done to open our Course to the interaction requests from territorial subjects.

Note: The Study Course does not have a Steering Committee. Experience shows that in-depth, timely, and interactive consultations with various stakeholders at national and local levels allow both optimal and constructive emergence of societal expectations regarding graduates of this Course and, equally importantly, active involvement of the stakeholders themselves in a dynamic and virtuous process of defining and clarifying both the intentions and their social and economic role and the resources on which to rely for detailing and achieving those intentions. The 'place' where reflection, deepening, and provision of elements regarding the employment potential of graduates (to be understood as the contribution of graduates to the overall economic-cultural improvement of their conditions and society) occur is the Quality Assurance Group of the Course, which interacts with stakeholders on one hand and with the Course Council on the other, in a unified perspective of defining the educational offer and building fruitful interaction between civil society in general, stakeholders in particular, Course Council, and graduates.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data The number of enrolled students in the Course has increased from 19 to 21. These data should be considered within a context of constant democratic decline affecting Abruzzo for several years, as almost all enrolled students come from this region. Most enrolled students hold a degree in Philosophy; however, graduates in Education Sciences, Political Sciences, and Sociology are also noted. The presence of students over 25 years of age is noted, indicating interest in the philosophical field among mature individuals, possibly for a second degree. The majority of enrolled students complete the required exams within the regular two-year period, with excellent results. In particular, no course failures are reported in the first year, while some are reported in the second. Withdrawals are extremely rare. The total study duration exceeds two years, likely due to students' ability to access qualification courses to acquire the credits necessary for the teaching training path. Final grade statistics confirm the high level of enrolled students. At the end of the three-year presidency, it is necessary to communicate to the Council members the enrollment and registration trends recorded during this period to monitor and plan changes for potential improvement of the educational offer.

Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam must be the result of a methodologically precise and correct research, with some original contribution. It will consist of the elaboration and discussion of a thesis on topics strictly related to philosophy, or on issues involving a broad philosophical reflection on ethical and socio-political questions emerging at various levels in the current cultural universe. To be admitted to the final exam, students must demonstrate advanced knowledge, in written and oral form, of at least one European Union language other than Italian, with reference to disciplinary lexicons. To promote, in line with the specific educational objectives outlined above, the interaction between philosophical research tools and the multifaceted corporate world, the final exam may optionally be conducted based on a training internship at partner companies.

Conduct of the Final Exam Nature of the final exam.
The final exam consists of the following acts:
- Student presentation of a written document, called 'thesis', on a specific topic related to one of the courses in their study plan and developed under the supervision of a teacher, called 'supervisor', in collaboration with a second expert in the field, called 'co-supervisor';
- 'Approval' of the thesis by the supervisor and co-supervisor;
- 'Graduation session', i.e., discussion and approval of the thesis before a dedicated committee, called 'graduation committee';
- Evaluation by the committee of the student's entire study path, the thesis, and its discussion.
Guidelines and notes regarding the thesis's editorial characteristics are available in the 'Teaching' section of the Department of Philosophical, Pedagogical, and Economic-Quantitative Sciences website.

Thesis Topic and Language.
- The student may write the thesis only in a discipline whose course (called 'affiliated course') has been or was taught within the Course. Additionally, the student must have passed the exam related to that discipline or been exempted from it.
- The thesis must normally be written in Italian, the language in which the thesis discussion before the graduation committee will be conducted, except as provided by Article 35, Paragraph 4 of the University's Academic Regulations, which states: "The final thesis and the respective written work and thesis may be conducted in a foreign language, upon favorable and motivated opinion of the Course Council, ensuring the possibility of effective evaluation due to sufficient expertise within the teaching body. In any case, the written work and thesis in a foreign language must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian."
Student Responsibilities.
Submit via email to the Supervisor and Co-Supervisor the Thesis Assignment Request Form (available in the Student Secretariat's Forms section). The form must include the signature of the student and the Supervisor/Co-Supervisor and be retained until the degree is obtained.
UPLOAD TO ESSE3 (Restricted Area – Conferment of Degree Section):
✓ Final Degree Conferment Form (available in the Student Secretariat's Forms section);
✓ Receipt of completing the AlmaLaurea questionnaire;
✓ Final thesis in .pdf format (it is strongly recommended to upload as soon as possible to allow the Supervisor/Co-Supervisor timely approval, necessary for admission to the final exam – no modifications can be made to the thesis after the deadline).
- The Student Secretariat may require the student to submit additional documentation or complete further administrative procedures necessary for the final exam. The student must be aware of the Student Secretariat's regulations and their schedule and comply with them.

Designation and Responsibilities of Supervisor and Co-Supervisor.
- Only a teacher with a formal relationship with the University of Chieti-Pescara 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' and who has taught or previously taught the course in question may serve as supervisor.
- The co-supervisor may be a teacher with a formal relationship with the University of Chieti-Pescara 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' or an external expert; if an external expert serves as co-supervisor, the Course Council must have previously verified the expert's scientific and/or professional qualifications related to the thesis presented by the student.
- The supervisor is responsible for guiding the student in preparing the thesis to achieve the specific educational objectives of the Course, through the acquisition of knowledge, the ability to apply it, independent judgment, communication skills, and learning abilities as described in the Course description.
- Approval of the thesis by the supervisor and co-supervisor is manifested through approval on ESSE3 of the PDF file uploaded by the student.

Designation and Responsibilities of Graduation Committee.
- The appointment and composition of the graduation committee are governed by Article 37, Paragraphs 1-4 of the University's Academic Regulations, which states: "1. Graduation committees for final exams, master's degrees, and specialization diplomas are appointed by the Head of the Competent Department or, after consulting the Departments, by the Director of the relevant School, if established, who also sets the work schedule. It is possible to operate simultaneously with multiple committees. 2. Graduation committees consist of at least five and no more than seven members for bachelor's and specialization diplomas; at least seven and no more than eleven members for master's degrees, including the Chair. 3. The majority of committee members must be tenure-track professors of the University. 4. The Chair of the Committee is, among the members, the full professor with the greatest seniority or, in the absence, the associate professor with the greatest seniority, unless otherwise determined by the Academic Regulations of the Competent Structures. The Chair must ensure the full regularity of the exam and the adherence of final evaluations to the general criteria established by the bodies responsible for the Course."
- Per Article 35, Paragraph 5, Letter d, of the University's Academic Regulations, it is specified that, subject to the provisions of Article 37, Paragraph 3, any individual whose scientific qualifications regarding the thesis topics to be discussed in a given session have been verified by the Course Council may serve as a committee member.
- The graduation committee evaluates the student's entire study path, the presented thesis, and its discussion; at the end of the evaluation, it issues either a failure or a pass, expressed as a final degree grade. In case of passing, the committee proclaims the student a doctor in the degree class they are enrolled in and declares the final degree grade.

Determination of Final Degree Grade.
- The final degree grade ranges from 66 to 110 and is composed of the sum, up to a maximum of 110 points, of the weighted average of the grades of passed exams, expressed in hundredths, and the thesis grade.
- The weighted average of the grades of passed exams, expressed in hundredths, is obtained by expressing in hundredths the weighted average of the grades of passed exams, expressed in thirtieths. Grades of simple pass or exam completion do not contribute to the weighted average. Grades for exams taken outside the plan do not contribute. All grades (expressed in thirtieths) of passed exams included in the study plan contribute to the weighted average, including those acquired in autonomously chosen activities (called 'TAF D'), with the following two clarifications: a grade of '30 and lode' contributes with a value of 30.10; grades associated with excess CFU from autonomously chosen activities exceeding the plan's CFU requirement do not contribute to the weighted average.
- Following the thesis discussion, if the graduation committee deems the final exam passed, it assigns a thesis grade ranging from 0 to 6 points. This score is assigned considering the quality and scope of the thesis and the student's proficiency in presenting the topics clearly and eruditely.
- If the sum of the weighted average expressed in hundredths and the thesis grade exceeds 110, the graduation committee may award the 'lode'. The 'lode' is awarded as an expression of the significance of the results achieved by the student in the thesis work. The award of the 'lode' must be proposed by the supervisor, approved by the co-supervisor, and unanimously agreed upon by the thesis committee.

Conduct of the Final Exam.
The modalities of conducting the final exam are governed by Article 35, Paragraphs 9 and 11, of the University's Academic Regulations, which states: "9. The student may withdraw from the exam until the moment the President of the Committee dismisses them to proceed with the grade decision, which occurs without the student's presence or that of outsiders. 11. The conduct of graduation, master's, specialization, and doctoral exams is public, and the act of announcing the final result is public."

Final Exam Schedule.
The definition of the final exam schedule is governed by Article 36 of the University's Academic Regulations, which states: "1. The final exam schedule for obtaining a degree and a master's degree is set annually by the prevailing Department or School, if established, and must include at least four sessions distributed across three terms: from May to July; from October to December; from February to April. 2. Final exams for each academic year must be conducted by April 30 of the following academic year; students enrolled in the previous academic year may take them without re-enrollment."

Reference Clause.
For matters not expressly regulated above, refer to the University's Academic Regulations and applicable laws.

Admission Procedures Access to the Master's Degree course in Sciences and Technologies of Geology of the Earth and Planets (LM-74) is open.
Adequate preparation:
Individual preparation verification is conducted through an interview aimed at assessing general preparation in scientific, technological fields, and knowledge of the English language. Various pathways allow for a wide variety of admission types and offer various disciplines the opportunity to access specific areas of Earth and Planets Sciences. Educational pathways are structured to enable students from different three-year courses to culturally and methodologically integrate into the topics of the Study Course. English language assessment may be replaced by presenting a certificate of knowledge at B2 level (QCER).
Curricular requirements:
Access to the Master's Degree in Sciences and Technologies of Geology of the Earth and Planets (Class LM-74) is possible with a Degree in Class of Geological Sciences L-34 or Class of Sciences and Technologies for Environment and Nature L-32.
For all those holding Degrees in other technical-scientific Classes, the following curricular requirements are required:
at least 6 CFU (university credits) in total in mathematical and computer disciplines (SSD - scientific-disciplinary sectors - MAT/xx, without constraints on individual SSD and/or INF/01);
at least 6 CFU in chemical disciplines (SSD CHIM/xx, without constraints on individual SSD);
at least 50 CFU in SSD GEO/xx and/or ICAR/xx and/or FIS/xx and/or BIO/xx and/or AGR/xx.
If the curriculum is deemed satisfactory, the Course Council will approve admission to the Master's Degree Course by issuing the required approval. Otherwise, student preparation verification occurs through an interview that may lead to the issuance of approval for admission, with the proposal of a personal study plan, in agreement with the Regulations even with derogation from what is specified in this Regulation.

Program, texts and objectives Note regarding selected sectors and credits for characteristic activities The Master's Degree course in Sciences and Technologies of Geology of the Earth and Planets expands the educational aspects and knowledge that can be acquired in specific and modern fields such as the study of planets, fossil and renewable resources, the application of quantitative methods to solve environmental problems, and seismotectonics. This implies the activation of various curricula requiring a wide range of disciplines.
Naturally, this necessitates an expansion of the regulatory intervals. In particular, the two areas 'Geological Paleontology' and 'Geomorphological and Applied Geological' require substantial intervals. Indeed, Applied Geology and Geomorphology support teaching paths encompassing applied geological aspects related to environmental management and risk mitigation. While sedimentology and structural geology are relevant to teaching paths concerning the structure and evolution of the Earth, including planets, and the crust structure and risks associated with seismicity.
Naturally, the course must also provide a foundation of knowledge that allows for the cross-use of teachings.
In this way, the graduate will be able to address, in the workplace, not only specific topics but also more diversified responsibilities without diminishing traditional aspects such as applied geology, mineral-petrology, and geomorphology. Characteristic activities therefore involve a broad spectrum of knowledge that also increases students' exposure to innovation.
To enable this expansion of knowledge and to cover these cutting-edge scientific and technical aspects, it was necessary to widen the credit intervals in various areas, which will however be assigned in the planned teaching of each individual curriculum in line with the specific objectives reported in the A4.a framework.
Note regarding credits for other activities The 'student's choice' CFU interval has been expanded, raising the maximum value to 18 to allow acquisition of CFU in SSD necessary for access to FIT paths Communication skills (communication skills)
Students must be able to communicate their scientific activities, ideas, results, and methods used to obtain them clearly and unambiguously.
The scientific method must be well reflected in their presentations through a logical, concise, and rigorous manner of presenting results.
Students must use technical-scientific language properties, know how to define data and result quality, and clarify which data are original and which are from the literature. Additionally, they must be able to manage previous information and clarify its use. Probably this action is one of the most difficult, but it must permeate the entire CdS with lessons that should always be carefully prepared and well structured.
Students are exposed to a series of Seminars given by nationally and internationally renowned scientists. Moreover, many examples include oral presentations with PowerPoint.
A guide for students on scientific presentations is currently being prepared.
Regarding written communication, annually some seminars are organized on how to write scientific papers and proposals.
The assessment of communication skills will occur through the evaluation of clarity of exposition and language properties during:
- oral exams, written and practical tests;
- presentations of specific topics in posters or essays, also through computer tools, during and at the end of training activities;
- presentation of the thesis work in the final exam of the course, which will allow evaluation of the style of the work and the graduate's ability to synthesize.

Autonomy of judgment (making judgments)
Graduates must be able to assess the quality of work performed by themselves and others, and be able to understand innovations and whether these are truly the result of technological developments rather than being influenced by secondary or marketing purposes. They must be able to determine if the results of work produced by themselves or others are valid and sustainable. These abilities will be developed through external and individual activities involving field studies, laboratory work, and computer environments, thereby requiring active participation from the student and recognition of how well they apply their theoretical knowledge. This can be further deepened through optional internships with the professional world, research, and industry. The most important verification of possessing these abilities is the master's thesis, which must be developed autonomously by the student using conceptual and practical tools representing the state of the art in research, with a thorough and comprehensive elaboration.
More interactive exams, both written and oral, can significantly contribute to evaluating autonomy of judgment, especially if during the course there are field or laboratory discussions that become an integral part of the assessment. Additionally, at least one written essay on scientific topics, both specialized and general, must be prepared per academic year according to the procedures specified in the academic regulations.

In order to promote and publicize the activities and contents of the Master's Degree LM/74 at the UdA, a series of informative events will be organized across the Abruzzo region, aimed at communicating the relevance of the geology degree course for preparing young people from Abruzzo and neighboring regions to face natural and anthropogenic disasters.
The action will be carried out in a coordinated and agreed manner between regional and provincial civil protection with particular attention to provincial capitals and will be implemented through a series of meetings with the population, also during other public events, to emphasize the importance of the geologist's role and their multiple applications in modern society.
The aim is to increase awareness of the need to train a new generation of geologists capable of collaborating and communicating their knowledge more immediately to bodies and institutions related to the protection of health and the environment, as well as to mitigate specific risks such as earthquakes, landslides, floods, and acute or chronic emergencies related to pollution.

Brief course description The Master's Degree Course in Sciences and Technologies of Geology of the Earth and Planets guides students towards comprehensive and advanced training in the field of Geosciences. The didactic methodological approach is multi-disciplinary and multi-scale, theoretical and practical, aimed at understanding and describing quantitatively past phenomena related to the lithosphere-atmosphere ecosystem, for the management and control of corresponding current territorial and environmental processes. The Course simultaneously offers a traditional and naturalist methodological approach and an innovative, digital, and technological quantitative approach. All curricula are organized into frontal lessons and laboratories and include professional internships.

The Master's degree program is divided into three interconnected curricula, which are:
Applied Environmental Geology, Georesources and Environmental Sustainability, Structural Geology and Geophysics for Seismic and Volcanic Risk.

The curriculum in "Applied Environmental Geology" has a strong applied identity, with emphasis on environmental problems that society is facing. It provides methodological, technical, and scientific skills for:
- Multidisciplinary site analysis and high-professional geotopic mapping, carried out with new technologies; numerical modeling applied to the environment
- Study and management of exogenous phenomena (floods, landslides), anthropogenic (pollution), and climatic (extreme weather events).
- Geological characterization and modeling of the subsurface for the realization of large works and infrastructure (bridges, tunnels, railway tracks, etc.), for the search for natural resources (water, renewable resources), for environmental sustainability and geomorphological susceptibility.

The characteristic study subjects are those of the Applied Geology (Geo/05) and Geomorphology (Geo/04) groups.

The curriculum in "Georesources and Environmental Sustainability" has a strong component dedicated to the sustainability of anthropic and natural systems. It provides methodological, technical, and scientific skills for:
- Study of reservoirs for the production and storage of fluids (gas, CO2, geothermal); study of fossil and renewable energies (geothermal, hydrogen) aimed at managing the energy transition and the sustainable use of environmental resources
- Mineral-petrographic and geochemical characterization of environmental resources for their sustainable recovery and use; petrographic and geomechanical analysis of rocks for the use of geomaterials in the industrial field, conservation, and valorization of architectural and historical-cultural heritage
- Fighting climate change, waste, and recycling

The curriculum in "Structural Geology and Geophysics for Seismic and Volcanic Risk" has a dual identity, theoretical and applied, dedicated to understanding complex endogenous phenomena (earthquakes and volcanoes) of the past and present and the tectonic and geodynamic context that determines and controls them, aimed at developing strategies for reducing and mitigating territorial risks at a global level.
It provides methodological, scientific, and technical skills, both fundamental and cutting-edge, enabling new strategies for controlling and managing territory and also highlighting the managerial role of the geologist. In particular, it trains in:
- Geological survey, morphotectonic and structural analysis for digital geotopic mapping and three-dimensional modeling; reconstruction of regional and local, superficial and deep deformation models, also aimed at identifying and defining energy sources (e.g., deep geothermal);
- Seismology and seismic and geophysical analysis for seismotectonic analysis and seismic hazard; volcanology and volcanotectonics, geological and geophysical investigations for local seismic hazard (microzonation), as well as archaeoseismology;
- Analysis of data and metadata and technical-scientific activities for managing seismic and volcanic emergencies.

All curricula provide the foundational training for a wide range of professional activities for geologists and geophysicists, including Professional Geologist (for geological characterization of territory for water resource exploration, study of landslides, floods, and extreme weather events, site remediation, support for design and construction of small and large works, seismic microzonation, etc.), Geologist in Public Bodies (ISPRA, National Geological Service and Regional Geological Service, National and Regional Environmental Protection Agencies, Local Authorities), in Companies and Service Companies; Researcher in Universities and National and International Research Centers.

Workplace Guidance The workplace guidance is carried out in collaboration with the University Placement Office, which promotes a series of activities aimed at facilitating the integration of graduates into the job market. The CdS works closely with the Placement Office, and the forms of collaboration are established on an ongoing basis.
Some meetings with stakeholders and interested companies are organized. The success of these meetings is difficult to assess, however, Alma Laurea data provide a generally positive picture of the employment rate of Master's graduates.
This year, a series of meetings between students and the job market will be formalized through seminars, poster presentations, and direct contacts. These meetings will serve to expose students to the job market while allowing the job market to become familiar with our teaching and students.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Master's graduates will have:
- improved their general knowledge of Geological Sciences, supplemented by a comprehensive understanding of at least one technical-scientific field of Earth Sciences;
- analytical and synthesis skills;
- ability to address geological issues and proceed with their analysis and solution;
- understanding of interactions within the geosphere and terrestrial/planetary processes applicable to various fields of geosciences such as earthquakes, environment, materials, planetary exploration, and our planet;
- ability to design, plan, and implement a strategy to solve problems in Earth Sciences;
- ability to conduct research activities.
The Master's Degree is strongly based on practical activities closely linked to the progression of frontal lectures. Applied Petrography Laboratories, GIS and Remote Sensing Laboratories, seismic profile processing, and planetary data analysis are the main indoor activities that will enable students to acquire operational skills for the job market. These are complemented by significant fieldwork activities both in Italy and abroad. This interaction between theoretical lectures and indoor and outdoor practical activities allows students to gain a broad spectrum of multidisciplinary experiences.
To the entire teaching activity within the courses, an internship may be added, which can be carried out in professional offices, industry, or research centers. Finally, the Master's Thesis, which is necessarily experimental, allows students to apply the knowledge and work methodology acquired throughout the training path in areas of greater interest.
Assessment Tools The verification of knowledge and understanding abilities will take place through oral exams, essays, individual or team work, quizzes, and written and oral exams during and at the end of the training activities. The structure of the assessment develops throughout the Master's program, interacting continuously with students through both formal and informal activities, with a continuous 'dialogue' between teachers and students. This structure cannot be separated from common teaching activities and a high teacher/student ratio.
Organizational Structure and Responsibilities at University Level The University organization is based on the figure of the Magnificent Rector, who manages, guides, and proposes all academic activities. He is assisted by the Academic Senate and the Board of Directors. The resolutions of these bodies directly influence the activities of the CdS, which are however monitored by the University Quality Assurance Office (PQA). The PQA maintains close contact with both the Department Parity Commission and the specific CdS. The PQA acts as a liaison between the CdS and the Rector and Academic Senate, reporting directly to these bodies. The Evaluation Unit is an independent body with which the PQA interacts and transmits its resolutions to the various CdS.

The decision-making process of the Study Course develops annually, starting in spring and ending in late winter of the following year, as follows:
The Advisory Committee, upon the Study Course President's indication, with an online procedure starting in March and April, elaborates its comments and provides opinions in the form of questionnaire responses or documents.
The Study Course Parity Committee elaborates its report based on stakeholders' opinions if available. The Committee identifies critical issues and situations requiring intervention, and also analyzes the Study Course as a whole.
The Review Committee analyzes the Parity Committee's report and prepares a final document on the Study Course's status, providing a specific proposal for solutions to critical issues or borderline situations.
The Study Course President, together with the Council, acquires the documents of the three Committees, analyzes them, and proposes a plan to mitigate critical issues, improve teaching standards, and carry out necessary operations for active support from University structures to improve quality.

Description link: Activities for orientation Link inserted: https://orientamento.unich.it Ability to apply knowledge and understanding
The ability to apply knowledge will be provided to the student through extensive practical activities carried out mainly in the field. The Study Course has developed a strong program of field activities, considering that a geologist must primarily apply their knowledge in the field. A series of excursions and field trips will provide students with the means to apply their theoretical knowledge in practice. Particular attention is paid to interdisciplinary problems requiring additional effort to simultaneously apply the necessary knowledge for problem-solving.

This more informal assessment will be taken into consideration for the final grade. Both field notebooks and laboratory notes will be considered.

- quickly integrate into work environments, easily adapting to new scenarios and complex situations;
- continue educational activities, also for professional updating, either independently or through further courses (PhD, Masters, etc.), in relation to their career ambitions and professional goals.
