Specific educational objectives of the course and description of the study path The Master's Degree in Geosciences and Geological Technologies of the Earth and Planets is composed of a complex set of objectives that include skills in a wide range of fields and disciplines. The primary objective is to train a geologist capable of intervening in various aspects of geoscience related to territory and environment, while also being aware of the scientific aspects related to environmental changes. However, our graduate must be able to face the labor market in all professional fields.

The Master's Degree provides students with competencies regarding the general aspects of the genesis of energy and mineral raw materials, with particular attention to current ecological and environmental sustainability issues. It also includes a comparison between the various aspects of fossil and renewable energy systems. In this context, an important educational objective is to provide specialized knowledge for managing the energy transition through the study of geology and the subsequent analysis of factors controlling the development of fossil energy sources, with particular reference to low-impact sources (natural gas) for their role in the near future, traditional renewable sources (e.g., geothermal), decarbonization (CO2 storage), and the identification and exploitation of hydrogen sources. Through the application of main analysis techniques and systems, the course aims to provide knowledge for identifying, exploiting, and managing such georesources within an environmental sustainability context. Additionally, it provides competencies for identifying, analyzing, and utilizing geo-materials within an environmentally compatible context.

Another important objective is the ability to acquire methodological and technical skills for analyzing geomorphological processes and geo-environmental dynamics, as well as mastering the scientific method of investigation and the techniques for processing and analyzing experimental data, and the ability to transfer geomorphological knowledge results to interdisciplinary and international work contexts. This knowledge is based on understanding the physical landscape's physiography to analyze hazards related to different agents and morphogenetic processes, and the ability to identify areas susceptible to destructive phenomena and modifications. This will achieve the objective of providing skills and knowledge for proper territorial planning and designing interventions aimed at preventing, correcting, and mitigating environmental disasters at various scales, including those induced by human activity. Naturally, an objective related to identifying and mitigating natural disasters cannot be separated from the analysis of earthquakes and seismicity.

A final objective concerns creating knowledge to understand the variability of large-scale geological systems and their evolution. This objective is developed through the study of planetary systems and provides the ability to analyze, through understanding different planetary systems and their evolution, the reasons for the formation of a wide geological variability.

The study path unfolds through several educational fields and sectors, such as structural geology, applied geology, sedimentology, and planetary geology. These topics are naturally accompanied by other components, such as petrography, which provide completeness in preparation and objectives.

The course may be structured into curricula that will include common courses on the knowledge of geomorphological environments and sedimentary and tectonic processes of the Earth and/or Planets. The curricula will then differ through courses in various disciplinary fields. One will focus on environmental-geological aspects and geomorphological knowledge, used to develop skills for intervention on natural hazard analysis and related risks. Another will deepen aspects related to fossil and renewable resources and their impact on global changes. A further educational profile may be that of earthquake geology, seismicity, and seismic risk. A specific profile may develop knowledge in planetary geology.

Lectures represent the core of teaching, but the course will also include a strong commitment to practical activities both in the field and in the laboratory, with the possibility of participating in internships primarily in industrial settings. Curricula may be offered in a mixed mode with two semesters in person and two in a telematic mode, up to a maximum of two-thirds of the courses delivered in telematic mode for the planetary geology curriculum.

Opinions of organizations and companies with internship/curricular or extracurricular internship agreements The Master's Degree in Geosciences and Geological Technologies requires a mandatory internship of 150 hours (6 CFU) for a period of approximately 3/6 months.

The internship activity can be carried out either in the internal laboratories of the d'Annunzio University (internal internship, under the guidance of a university professor) or outside the University (under the guidance of a company tutor) or alternatively, it can be carried out abroad in the form of Erasmus+ Traineeship.

Overall, the experience of tutors with interns is evaluated very positively, although interest in potential further collaborations with the intern is not significant.

Regarding the evaluation of interns, it is necessary to note that many internships are internal, and therefore not always comparable to evaluations by company tutors. In general, evaluations are good regarding both pre-existing and acquired competencies.

In any case, the Course of Study can commit to promoting more internships at external structures that bring students closer to the labor market or even research beyond regional borders.

Consultation with representative organizations at national and international levels for goods and services production, and professions (Course establishment)

The Course of Study bases its consultations with stakeholders on two recently established committees.

The first is the National Interest Committee, composed of the National College of Presidents of Geology and Geophysics Courses of Study at the Universities of Padua, Bologna, Turin, Ferrara, and Bari, and representatives of ISPRA - Rome, Pro.Civ.Naz. Catania, ANISN - Aosta, Liri Basin Authority, ConScienze Perugia, ENI Milan, INOGS - Trieste, AssoMineraria Rome, Natural Sciences Museum Florence, ConScienze, ENEA Rome, Professional PA, Tuscany Region - Florence, CNG Salerno, CNR-IRPI Perugia, INGV - Rome.

Additionally, on June 16, 2016, the Course of Study Council decided to establish the Local Advisory Committee, composed of the President of the Abruzzo Geologists' Order and a representative of: Abruzzo Archaeological Superintendency, National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology, National Association of Natural Sciences Teachers, Energy Policy Service, Air Quality and SINA, Abruzzo Region, Thales Alenia Space, Laboratory of Geology University of Lyon 1.

The Course of Study's decision-making process develops annually, starting in spring and ending in late winter of the following year, as follows:

The Advisory Committee, through a telework procedure starting in March and April, elaborates its comments and provides opinions in the form of responses to questionnaires or documents.

The Parity Committee of the Course of Study elaborates its report based on stakeholders' opinions.

The Review Committee analyzes the Parity Committee's report and prepares the final document on the Course of Study's status, providing a specific analysis of criticalities.

The Course of Study President, together with the Council, acquires the documents from the three Committees, analyzes them, and proposes a plan to mitigate criticalities, improve teaching standards, and carry out necessary operations to actively support the University's quality structures.

From the consultations conducted, the Local Advisory Committee's opinion on teaching in general was highly positive, noting good quality in both basic and applied teaching structures. Additionally, it identified some criticalities to be addressed in the ongoing activities of the two advisory committees, particularly regarding skills to be strengthened.

On September 29, 2016, the National Interest Committee was consulted for a specific opinion on changing the course name from Master's Degree in Geosciences and Geological Technologies to Master's Degree in Geosciences and Geological Technologies of the Earth and Planets.

The Local Committee gave a favorable opinion, reaffirming the uniqueness of d'Annunzio at the national and European level and highlighting the strong investment made by the Course of Study on this topic. The judgment given on the course name change, which can be summarized by Dr. Galadini (INGV-Rome), member of the Course of Study's Advisory Committee: "The success of universities is also linked to diversification, the ability to provide products that students (and more generally stakeholders) cannot find elsewhere. Clarifying a diversification from a simple title is therefore important. If this is added to the growing attention to planetary characteristics, with various perspectives in a not-immediate future, then the positive judgment on the choice is reinforced."

At this occasion, broader course topics regarding student entry into the labor market and the presence of certain themes within the course were also discussed.

A series of meetings and assemblies with students were organized prior to institutional consultations. From these meetings, it was understood that students consider it a priority for the Course to develop immediately from the first year into Curricula, and that such curricula allow the Master's Thesis to be completed within the fourth semester. It is also emphasized that it is necessary to diversify the educational profiles by expanding from Planetary Sciences and mineral-petrographic fields to include earthquake geology. Additionally, there is a request to strengthen internship activities.

The Local Interest Committee was consulted, and various comments and suggestions were presented. Generally, satisfaction was expressed for the inclusion of courses in English and for the development of topics such as Planetary Sciences, Seismotectonics, and Mineral-Petrographic. It is hoped that the professional geologist's preparation will be enhanced by particular attention to design skills. It is also suggested that in Seismotectonics, a course on Quaternary Geology be included. These and minor suggestions have been largely accepted.

The Parity Committee has resumed some of the criticalities highlighted by the Interest Committee.

Entry, progression, and exit data The students enrolled in the 2022-2023 academic year number 10, showing a significant decrease compared to previous academic years (29 in 2021-2022, 23 in 2020-2021, and 26 in 2019-2020), partly due to the activation of a new Master's Degree in Planetary Geosciences in the same LM-74 class, which has effectively absorbed the similar educational path previously present in this Master's Degree.

Approximately 94% of enrolled students are aged between 21 and 28 years, while the remaining approximately 6% are over 28 years old.

Regularly enrolled students account for about two-thirds of total enrolled students, with no dropouts between the first and second year.

In terms of CFU, less than 45% of students acquire at least 40 CFU; students who acquire the required CFU (60 CFU) after the first year average ≤60%.

Most students (>60-70%) graduate within one year beyond the course duration.

Characteristics of the final exam The final exam for the Master's Degree in Geosciences and Geological Technologies of the Earth and Planets consists of a thesis conducted under the guidance of a Supervisor, presented by the student before the Degree Committee. The thesis must be of an experimental nature; it must be original and presented in the form of a written report. Final evaluation criteria and the assignment of the graduation score consider the student's academic record during the Master's Degree, the quality of the final exam, and any other relevant elements.

Final exam procedure The final exam is held in public before a committee composed of at least seven professors from the Course of Study, specifically appointed by the Department of Engineering and Geology Director.

During the thesis defense, the student has 15 minutes to present their work, followed by approximately 5 minutes for questions from the committee.

The Master's Thesis must represent the complete development process of a scientific or technological research, from the idea's conception to the final report. The thesis must contain the scientific rationale and analysis of the idea's originality. The report must be clear and distinguish between data presentation, interpretation, and discussion. The thesis must be comprehensive and allow for a complete evaluation by the Committee.

The final exam is assessed on three elements:
a. The written thesis report
b. The oral presentation of the thesis
c. The discussion

During the thesis defense, the student will be evaluated on the following aspects:
1. Consistency between thesis objectives and achieved results.
2. Clarity in presenting objectives and methodology, synthesis ability, and technical language proficiency.
3. Ability to illustrate the originality of the work compared to the current state of the art.
4. Critical analysis skills for results (and comparison with the current state of the art).
5. Ability to argue in direct confrontation (questions posed).

The final grade is expressed based on the weighted average of exam scores in 110ths. The thesis grade is expressed as a value from 0 to 10 and is added to the average. The honor is proposed by one of the committee members and must be unanimously accepted.

The Faculty has adequately equipped, appropriate, and effective spaces. Department DEPARTMENT OF MEDICAL, ORAL AND BIOTECHNOLOGICAL SCIENCES Website https://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-studio/scienze-e-tecniche-delle-attivita-motorie-preventive-e-adattate-area-scientifica Teaching Method Conventional Admission Requirements Check Yes Course Teachers View list Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission To access the Master's Degree in Sciences and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Physical Activities, it is required to hold a three-year University Degree or a University Diploma of three-year duration, or another foreign degree recognized as suitable (as provided by Article 6, paragraph 2, of Ministerial Decree 22 October 2004, No. 270).
Students holding a three-year Degree in Sports Sciences (class L-22, pursuant to DM 270/04; or class 33, pursuant to DM 509/99) or a four-year Degree in Sports Sciences may enroll in the Master's Degree in Sciences and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Physical Activities, with full recognition of the 180 CFU.
For students holding a Degree not belonging to class L-22 or L-33 (Sports Sciences) or a Master's Degree or a University Diploma, or another foreign degree recognized as suitable pursuant to current regulations, the competent academic body will conduct a specific assessment of the previous academic record and personal preparation.
The methods for assessing the student's personal preparation are defined by the course's academic regulations.
Admission Methods For direct admission to the Master's Degree in Sciences and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Physical Activities, it is necessary to have obtained the three-year Degree with a grade of 95/110 or higher.
For those who have obtained the three-year Degree with a grade below 95/110, enrollment will be subject to passing a qualifying test, to be taken at the beginning of the Academic Year, typically in October, consisting of multiple-choice questions related to Anatomy, Biochemistry, Physiology, Biology, and Physical Activity in different age groups.
The Master's Degree in Sciences and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Physical Activities does not have a limited enrollment quota.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate in Sciences and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Physical Activity must be able to:
- clearly and correctly explain to collaborators at various levels the different protocols of adapted physical and sports activity, both already consolidated and personally modified or designed, for optimal application;
- use appropriate technical terms in interaction with other professional figures, for the implementation of a project and a training path;
- differentiate and adapt teaching communication according to age and different physical needs.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [LM67] SCIENCES AND TECHNIQUES OF PREVENTIVE AND ADAPTED MOTOR ACTIVITIES
TYPE: Master's Degree
CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/545

Judgment Autonomy
The Graduate in Sciences and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Motor Activities must be able to autonomously judge:
- the psychophysical needs of individual subjects related to age, gender, specific health conditions, and socio-cultural context;
- the potential physical, psychological, and social benefits resulting from the continuous practice of an adequate adapted motor or sports activity;
- the physical, psychological, and social risks that subjects may face when engaging in unadapted motor and sports activities;
- the necessary health interventions and collaboration with other professional figures to better adapt motor and sports activities to individual subjects;
- the conditions for the onset of acute events, with evaluation of vital parameters and preparation of first aid techniques.
This autonomy will enable the Master's Graduate to interact as an equal with other professionals in the socio-health field, in order to integrate motor activity programs with preventive and therapeutic programs derived from other fields and competencies.

Ass. training periods The Internships, which represent the only mandatory attendance activity of the entire educational path, consist of practical training periods to be carried out at structures, internal or external to the University, or at institutions or public or private bodies (Hosting Entities), identified by the Master's Degree Course and contracted with the University, through the School of Medicine and Health Sciences to which the Master's Degree Course belongs.
For each academic year, the Course Council annually plans the available Internships for students. For each activity, a Training and Orientation Project is prepared, containing the objectives and methods of the Internship, indicating its duration and the presence times of the Intern at the Hosting Entities. The training and orientation activity is followed and verified by an Academic Tutor, appointed by the Course Council, and by a Corporate Tutor indicated by the Hosting Entity. For each activity, attendance of at least 75% of the hours specified in the Training Project is required, and the attribution of the corresponding CFU is conditional upon a final positive evaluation, expressed through a suitability assessment by the Tutors.
The choice of locations and Internship activities is primarily aimed at offering students experiences that may prove useful for their training and therefore for introduction to the world of work.
As of April 30, 2024, the number of first and second-year students who have completed their Training Internship is 197.
Monitoring is carried out through a form that the student is required to complete and return to the Academic Secretariat to formalize the acquisition of CFU related to the completed Internship.
The monitoring of External Internship activities is conducted through the administration of a questionnaire to both students and Tutors of the contracted structures.

However, the Master's Degree Course has actively engaged, at both local and national levels, in identifying a professional field for S.T.A.M.P.A. graduates.
In this regard, a working group is active at the Abruzzo Region (Prot. 0044859/18) aimed at promoting, through the recruitment of structures where S.T.A.M.P.A. and Sports and Physical Activities Sciences graduates operate, preventive and adapted physical activity as a primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention tool.
This initiative led to the promulgation of Regional Decree 700/18, which approves the creation of 'Safe Gyms' and 'Health Gyms' where S.T.A.M.P.A. graduates must necessarily operate. The importance of this initiative became evident after the publication of Legislative Decree No. 36 of February 28, 2021, which specified the role of graduates in motor sciences, creating the professional figure of the preventive and adapted physical activity kinesiologist.
Subsequently, with Decree 659/19, the Abruzzo Region decided to entrust the professional training and updating of graduates in 'Motor Sciences' (L22) and Master's graduates in 'Preventive and Adapted Physical Activity' (LM67) to the University of G. D'Annunzio of Chieti-Pescara UNICH and the University of L'Aquila UNIVAQ, to provide qualified professionals who will operate in the aforementioned 'Health Gyms' and 'Safe Gyms', and to approve the convention scheme between the Abruzzo Region Department of Health, the University of G. D'Annunzio of Chieti-Pescara and the University of L'Aquila, concerning the operational and economic commitments to enable inter-institutional collaboration for the purpose of professional training and updating of graduates in 'Motor Sciences' and Master's graduates in 'Preventive and Adapted Physical Activity', to provide highly qualified personnel operating in structurally and professionally adequate gyms named 'Health Gyms' and 'Safe Gyms', appropriately recognized and certified, dedicated respectively to primary prevention and treatment of the most common non-communicable chronic diseases sensitive to physical exercise. Access calls for the training courses are being prepared.
The Master's Degree Course is preparing a system for monitoring and evaluating the effectiveness of the career guidance actions implemented in recent years, specifically those related to the 'SAFE GYMS' Project.

Graduate Opinions GRAPHICS INSERTED IN THE ATTACHED PDF According to the ALMALAUREA database, in the calendar year 2022, 99 students obtained their Master's Degree, of which 92 were interviewed. The examined group totals 87.
The average grade was in line with the previous year's results and not dissimilar from the national average. From the cited data, it also emerges that a good percentage of graduates obtained their degree on time.
The percentage of attending graduates is as follows:
- attended more than 75% of courses regularly: 59.3% (58.7% nationally): compared to the previous year, there has been a decline both locally and nationally;
- attended between 50% and 75% of courses regularly: 25.9% (22.1% nationally): compared to the previous year, there has been an increase both locally and nationally.
It can be deduced that well over 80% of graduates attended more than 50% of the courses. This figure is slightly higher than that observed at other universities.
Regarding the teaching load, approximately 90% of interviewed graduates consider it adequate: this figure is in line with the average for all universities.
With regard to satisfaction regarding the course organization, 90% of graduates declare overall satisfaction, and this figure is nearly in line with the total class average across all universities. Similarly excellent is the relationship with professors, with a satisfaction rate of 95%, which is in line with the national average.
The percentage of graduates who attended more than 50% of the scheduled courses has increased: this rise could also be attributed to the online availability of teaching materials provided by professors and the resumption of in-person teaching activities.
The overall satisfactory judgment is confirmed by the fact that 84% of graduates would enroll in the same course at our university again, while only 7.4% would choose a different one. Encouraging is the increasing number of those who would choose the same Master's program and university again.
Slightly above the average of all universities is the satisfaction rating for exam organization in our course (over 90%).
The evaluation of the facilities available to the Bachelor's program, which, although needing improvement, still ensure good delivery of frontal teaching, can be considered satisfactory; indeed, the satisfaction level of classrooms is slightly above the national average.
The evaluation of laboratory equipment is good and similar to the national average: likely, the creation of three new laboratories dedicated to 'Motor Sciences' between 2019 and 2020 has contributed to improving the satisfaction of recent graduates compared to previous years.
The evaluation of computer equipment has improved, with 69% of graduates expressing satisfaction; this can also be attributed to the course's off-campus location, which prevents students from accessing all services available on campus.
The data regarding graduate opinions will be discussed in the upcoming meetings of the Bachelor's Council (September 2023).

Brief Course Description CHARACTERISTICS AND OBJECTIVES
The Master's Degree Course in Science and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Motor Activities (S.T.A.M.P.A.), lasting two years, offers advanced preparation in the field of preventive and adapted motor activities for various conditions of motor ability decline and disability.
The Course, which continues the training path started with the three-year degree in Science of Motor Activities and Sports, developing theories, methodologies, and operational content primarily related to biomedical sciences and motor education sciences, ensures our Master's graduates the capabilities expected of graduates of the class, who, with broad decision-making powers and autonomy, must be able to use advanced cultural, methodological, and technical-practical tools, necessary for:
- design and implement motor activity programs aimed at achieving, recovering, and maintaining the best psychophysical well-being conditions for subjects in various age groups and physical conditions, with attention to gender specifics;
- organize and plan specific activities and lifestyles useful for disease prevention and quality of life improvement through physical exercise;
- prevent postural defects and recover the motor system post-rehabilitation, aimed at maintaining physical efficiency;
- program, coordinate, and evaluate adapted motor activities for people with disabilities or individuals in clinically controlled and stabilized health conditions.
These competencies will be achieved through the study of motor and sports disciplines, biomedical, psychopedagogical, and sociological disciplines. The contributions of these disciplines provide the student with a structured cultural framework that allows interpreting, with a multidisciplinary approach, both the motor and health conditions of subjects and the context in which the intervention must be placed.
Complementing traditional teaching, the course includes 300 hours of training internship at external organizations and structures connected to the University, where competencies are consolidated through direct professional experience.
WORKING AREAS With the acquisition of competencies, graduates will be able to obtain a professional qualification aimed at designing, conducting, and managing motor activities aimed at achieving and maintaining optimal physical efficiency and well-being; motor activities focused on general and specific prevention and overcoming pathologies related to sedentary lifestyles and incorrect habits within initiatives promoted by public bodies or private structures; motor activities for the elderly at public bodies and private structures; adapted educational, recreational, and sports motor activities for disabled individuals at institutions and specialized bodies, including those operating within the private social sector.
The course provides the possibility of access to advanced training for secondary school teachers.
FROM THE THREE-YEAR TO THE MASTER'S DEGREE For direct admission to the course, it is necessary to have obtained the three-year degree with a grade of at least 95/110. For those who have obtained the three-year degree with a grade below 95/110, enrollment will be subject to passing a qualifying test consisting of multiple-choice questions on Anatomy, Biochemistry, Physiology, Biology, and Motor Activities in different age groups, which is normally held at the beginning of the academic year.
External Effectiveness The Bachelor's Course, within its competence, strives to increasingly facilitate contact between graduates and the job market by implementing all necessary and useful strategies. Some of the most important initiatives are described in the following section (C3). Given the absence of a specific professional register, the Master's Degree Course has worked to establish a working table whose consultations are conducted at the institutional level with local ASLs, the Abruzzo Region, Sports Federations, and CONI. Other initiatives have been undertaken with Sports Associations, School Institutes, and rehabilitation-contracted structures to enhance the professional prospects of graduates and, where possible, offer a wider range of internship activities for students.
With regard to employment, the percentage values demonstrate how good training is fundamental in professional and work matters:
- 75% of graduates are employed five years after graduation; the data is lower than the national average (83.9%).
Regarding employability, it should be noted that the time to enter the job market is approximately 4.4 months from the start of the search to finding the first job compared to the national average of 5.3 months.
Five years after graduation, 66.7% of graduates who found employment after obtaining their degree state they use the skills acquired during the specialized training path to a high degree (a figure lower than the national average of 73.1%).
The average salary of working graduates is €1,309; this figure is improving compared to the previous five-year survey (€1,216) and higher than the national average (€1,266).
The data will be presented and discussed during the September 2023 Master's Course Council meeting; at the same time, corrective measures to be implemented where necessary will be presented.
Specific Course Objectives and Description of the Training Path The Master's Degree Course in Science and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Motor Activities continues the training path of the three-year degree in Science of Motor Activities and Sports, developing theories, methodologies, and operational content primarily related to biomedical sciences and motor education sciences.
The training path aims to acquire in-depth knowledge and competencies in motor fields for prevention in healthy subjects, post-rehabilitation re-education, and functional maintenance or recovery in subjects with both acute and chronic conditions.
The Course also aims to teach graduates the main risk factors for subjects with various conditions, both acute and chronic, in different age groups, and the effects that drugs, most commonly used in frequent therapies, can have on physical exercise.
The acquired competencies will allow graduates to work in an integrated and coordinated manner in a team of health and well-being professionals, where motor activities are of fundamental importance in promoting health and primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention of major socially relevant pathologies.
Finally, the Course aims to provide graduates with specific skills for achieving the best psychophysical efficiency in subjects with congenital or acquired psychomotor disabilities, adapting motor activities to the specific needs of subjects, both in the developmental and adolescent and adult age.
For this purpose, the Course must provide advanced knowledge in movement biomechanics, functional evaluation of physical exercise, and psychopedagogical foundations, necessary for programming individual and group activities of an educational, recreational, and sports nature, to be carried out in free time and socio-cultural animation, which are also fundamental for implementing different training paths applicable within primary and secondary schools.
Opinions of Organizations and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements (Curricular or Extra-curricular) The offer of curricular internships, carried out both at external structures/organizations and at the CLM's own structures, is annually evaluated and adjusted thanks to a control tool developed by the Master's Course: an online questionnaire on internship activities and validity based on evaluation forms.
This tool constitutes a form of continuous consultation to collect information regarding the cultural and professional level of interns, as well as observations and requests for new and/or different competencies deemed of interest.
Through the questionnaire tool, students can evaluate the hosting structures, and simultaneously, these structures can evaluate the students as a whole.
The data collected through the questionnaire administration will be evaluated in the September 2023 Master's Course Council meeting, as the documentation return was recently completed; at that time, any necessary corrective measures will also be presented.
Both internship activities and meetings represent a form of continuous monitoring that allows the Master's Course to obtain significant information to effectively guide the training curricula.
Students' evaluations of internships have a direct impact, meaning that in recent academic years, internship sites with poor evaluations were not confirmed for the following year.
Additionally, any student complaints are collected directly by the Bachelor's Course Secretariat, particularly by administrative staff dedicated explicitly to student relations.
Based on the opinions collected through the online questionnaire, starting a few years ago, the Master's Course has decided to significantly implement 'in-house' internship activities, and in particular, to leave only internships at secondary education schools as external activities for the first year of the course.
This organization has had positive effects on the students' curricular training.
This, although requiring a significant economic effort, was decided in accordance with student opinions, who requested to concentrate internships in closer locations, with an obvious time saving, and also to have the opportunity to interact with highly specialized professionals.
The Master's Degree Course also participates, for several years now, in the working table established by the Abruzzo Region (protocol no. 00444859/18) for promoting physical exercise as a form of primary and secondary prevention.
This working table led to the Regional Resolution for the establishment of Safe Gyms and Health Gyms; these gyms, registered in the regional registry, have as an indispensable requirement, among others, the presence of a three-year graduate or a STAMPA graduate, and will be the only ones to which S.S.N. doctors and Sports Medicine doctors will refer their patients for primary or secondary/tertiary preventive activities based on physical exercise.
There is still an ongoing convention with AUSL Chieti-Lanciano-Vasto for the creation of a multidisciplinary outpatient clinic focused on promoting an adapted motor activity program dedicated to women with breast cancer; the convention has also enabled the creation of a specific internship for STAMPA students.
The collaboration between CONI and the Master's Course remains active and fruitful, allowing the realization of highly applied internship activities and the organization of thematic meetings, aimed at teachers, instructors, and students, on various aspects characterizing the world of both sports and adapted motor activities.
The comparison with the school world is possible thanks to specific agreements with Abruzzo Region Secondary Education Institutes, where internships are activated that allow students to participate in decisions regarding the organization and programming of school activities.
The previously described activity, and in particular that related to the Abruzzo Region's working table, has allowed contact with representatives of the Region itself, representatives of the three-year and Master's Courses related to Motor Sciences at the Universities of Chieti-Pescara and L'Aquila, delegates of Abruzzo ASLs, representatives of Sports Doctors and General Medicine Doctors, and representatives of Professional Associations that include the largest number of three-year and Master's graduates; this opportunity allows creating a Steering Committee that, including the mentioned figures, together with representatives of the School Offices, CONI, and the Regional Sports School, can support the Master's Course in best directing the preparation of future students.
Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Levels - of Goods and Services Production, Professions (Course Establishment)
The acquired competencies will allow graduates to work in an integrated and coordinated manner in a team of health and well-being professionals, within which motor activities are of fundamental importance in promoting health and primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention of major socially relevant pathologies.
The graduate in Science and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Motor Activities can work in public and private structures for the elderly or disabled, associations, to design and implement post-rehabilitation, re-educative, and recreational motor and sports programs, adapted and personalized to different age, ability, and the presence of stabilized chronic pathologies.

In detail:
- thanks also to Prof. Claudio Robazza, member of the internal PQ and Director of the Regional Sports School, the comparison with CONI has strengthened over time and has been concretized in the joint organization of applied internships, highly professionalizing seminar activities within curricular courses, and roundtables open to teachers, instructors, and students;
- the comparison with the school world and motor education has been maintained through both the internship activities organized at schools and through the 'School in Motion' project, aimed at primary school first and second grade students (approximately 23,000 children/year) focused on promoting correct lifestyles. This project, active from 2015 to 2020, included, among other things, the intervention of three-year graduates in primary school classes, the possibility for students of the Study Course to carry out internship activities in schools, and finally the collaboration of the Study Course for research on the school population and the study of work protocols. This project allowed verifying the technical, scientific, and operational qualities of young graduates enrolled in the activities. The judgment of School Directors and Reference Teachers, recorded during specifically organized meetings and also through the administration of a questionnaire, highlighted strong appreciation of the Study Course graduates by teachers, who also emphasized the need to consolidate the presence of specialist educators in motor sciences within primary schools;
- the regional projects 'Health Gyms' and 'Safe Gyms' (https://www.dmsi.unich.it/il-progetto-regionale-palestre-della-salute-e-palestre-sicure), implemented since 2020, represent the outcome of a long period of comparison and reflection, starting in 2018, between the Presidencies of CdS UdA and the University of L'Aquila, the Abruzzo Region Health Office, category representatives (Italian Committee of Motor Sciences), General Medicine Doctors, and Regional Sports Doctors, on the role and competencies that three-year and Master's graduates in motor sciences must have for the prevention and management of exercise-sensitive pathologies (obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, colon and breast cancer, Alzheimer's disease, etc.). It is believed that these projects, together with 'School in Motion', may impact the employment profile of graduates in the near future, and therefore the comparison with these institutions has been (and is) deeply useful for guiding the Study Course's educational choices;
- simultaneously, the Study Course has continued to monitor the demand for competencies in the job market and the professions sector (amateur sports associations, private entities, gyms, etc.) through a stakeholder survey. This is a monitoring system based on evaluation forms completed by hosting entities and conventioned subjects for student internship activities. This tool constitutes a form of 'continuous consultation' to collect information regarding the cultural and professional level of interns, as well as observations and requests for new and/or different competencies deemed of interest. The questionnaire is administered to all structures hosting CL-STAMPA students for curricular internships.
The offered training would be especially suitable for the requests of sectors dedicated to well-being, health, and leisure, while greater efforts should be dedicated to training operators in the sports sector. Strong appreciation of the Study Course students by primary school teachers, while secondary school teachers and a.s.d. operators have highlighted the need for a greater practical-application component in student preparation.

Final Exam Characteristics The final exam consists of an original written and discussed thesis, predominantly experimental, on a topic relevant to the specific and qualifying training objectives of the Study Course, agreed upon with a professor of the Course itself.
Final Exam Execution Method The Master's Degree in Science and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Motor Activities is obtained following a positive outcome of a final exam for the acquisition of 6 CFU, through which the student accumulates the 120 CFU required by the study plan.
The final exam consists of a public discussion, in front of a specific Commission composed of at least 7 and no more than 11 professors, of an original compilative or experimental thesis, prepared by the student under the supervision of a professor of the Master's Course, called the Supervisor, and any external co-supervisors. The Commission, predominantly composed of Supervisors, is appointed by the School of Medicine and Health Sciences upon proposal from the Master's Course President.
To be admitted to take the final exam, the student must:
- have passed all exams related to the courses specified in the study plan;
- have obtained the qualification in internship activities;
- have fulfilled the administrative obligations specified by the Student Secretariat.
The final exam, which constitutes an important individual training opportunity to complete one's path, aims to engage the student in a process of formalization, planning, and development.
The thesis content must be related to the themes related to the Master's Course's training objectives.
The evaluation of the final exam will be based on the following criteria:
- level of depth of the work done and state of the art;
- critical engagement;
- cultural maturity and ability to personally elaborate the graduate;
- accuracy of execution.
The graduation grade is expressed in hundredths with possible honors, whose attribution, in case of a grade of at least 110/110, is at the discretion of the examination committee and is decided without the adoption of specific automatic calculation mechanisms.
The minimum score for obtaining the degree is 66/110.
The graduation grade is determined by:
- the weighted average of the grades obtained in the curricular exams, expressed in hundredths;
- the honors obtained in the profit exams (0.1 point per honor);
- the time of completing studies within the legal duration of the Master's Course (2 points for those who graduate on time in the summer and autumn sessions; 1 point for those who graduate on time in the extraordinary session);
- the student's participation in recognized international exchange projects (2 points);
- the points assigned by the commission to the final exam (maximum 6 points for compilative theses and maximum 9 points for experimental theses).
Three graduation sessions are provided (summer, autumn, and extraordinary).
The topics covered in the theses are numerous and related to the training path. For example, some of the topics covered are:
- evaluation of coordination abilities in subjects in developmental age;
- chinesiological treatment in elderly subjects;
- study of the psycho-motor effects of swimming training in adolescent age;
- evaluation of the effectiveness of physical exercise in subjects with Type II diabetes;
- design of pathways for social inclusion and psychophysical well-being of individuals with intellectual disability;
- realization of strategies to promote motor activity and physical exercise in schools.
Technical Report Summary of the Evaluation Committee The course covers a scientifically and professionally relevant area and is consistently positioned at optimal levels in relation to its class, enrolled students, and graduates. The Faculty has adequately equipped, suitable, and effective spaces. The Faculty can currently count on a minimal specific teaching staff. The proposed organization, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's training offer.

ADMISSION TO THE MASTER'S DEGREE COURSE IN FOOD SCIENCE AND HEALTH IS CONDITIONED ON AN ASSESSMENT OF THE STUDENT'S INITIAL PREPARATION, WHICH WILL OCCUR AFTER VERIFYING THE POSSESSION OF THE REQUIRED ACADEMIC QUALIFICATIONS.
ADEQUATE PREPARATION WILL BE ASSESSED IN DISCIPLINES COVERED BY THE FOLLOWING SSD CODES: BIO/13, CHIM/03, BIO/10, BIO/09, BIO/19, BIO/14, MED/42, MED/49.
THE PERSONAL PREPARATION ASSESSMENT WILL BE CONSIDERED FULFILLED IF THE GRADUATION GRADE IS EQUAL TO OR HIGHER THAN 95 OUT OF 110.
CANDIDATES POSSESSING ONE OF THE FOLLOWING QUALIFICATIONS MAY BE ADMITTED:
- DEGREE IN DIETETICS (CLASS SNT/3 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR CLASS L/SNT3 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- DEGREE IN BIOMEDICAL LABORATORY TECHNIQUES (CLASS SNT/3 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR CLASS L/SNT3 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- DEGREE IN FOOD AND AGRICULTURAL SCIENCES (CLASS 20 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR L-26 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- DEGREE IN BIOTECHNOLOGY (CLASS 1 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR L-2 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- DEGREE IN BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES (CLASS 12 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR L-13 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- MASTER'S DEGREES IN BIOLOGY (CLASS 6/S UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR CLASS LM-6 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- MASTER'S DEGREES IN BIOTECHNOLOGY (CLASSES 7/S, 8/S, 9/S UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR CLASSES LM-7, LM-8, LM-9 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- MASTER'S DEGREES IN PHARMACY AND INDUSTRIAL PHARMACY (CLASS 14/S UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR CLASS LM-13 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- MASTER'S DEGREE IN FOOD SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (CLASS 78/S UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR LM-70 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
- MASTER'S DEGREE IN AGRICULTURAL SCIENCES AND TECHNOLOGY (CLASS 77/S UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 509/1999 OR LM-69 UNDER MINISTERIAL DECREE 270/2004)
ENROLLMENT FOR STUDENTS COMING FROM BACHELOR'S DEGREE PROGRAMS (OR EQUIVALENT FOREIGN QUALIFICATIONS) DIFFERENT FROM THOSE LISTED WILL BE SUBJECT TO THE POSSESSION OF AT LEAST 60 CFU:
- 20 CFU AMONG: FIS/07, SECS-S/01, SECS-S/02; CHIM/01, CHIM/03, CHIM/06; AGR/13; INF/01, CHIM/09, CHIM/10, AGR/15
- 30 CFU AMONG: BIO/09, BIO/13, BIO/10, BIO/14, BIO/16, BIO/19
- 10 CFU AMONG: MED/42, MED/49, IUS/01, MED/44, MED/07
THE MINIMUM REQUIRED KNOWLEDGE IN THE VARIOUS DISCIPLINES, AS WELL AS THE DETAILED MODALITIES OF THE ASSESSMENT, WILL BE DETAILED IN THE COURSE'S DIDACTIC REGULATIONS UNDER 'CULTURAL REQUIREMENTS FOR ADMISSION' AND PUBLISHED IN THE STUDY PLAN.
THE NUMBER OF STUDENTS ADMITTED TO THE MASTER'S DEGREE COURSE IN FOOD SCIENCE AND HEALTH IS PROGRAMMED BASED ON THE AVAILABILITY OF TEACHING STAFF, TEACHING FACILITIES (CLASSROOMS, LABORATORIES) FOR CONDUCTING PRACTICAL ACTIVITIES, AND ESPECIALLY THE AVAILABILITY OF INTERNSHIP POSITIONS (MANDATORY), IN LINE WITH EUROPEAN UNION RECOMMENDATIONS, APPLYING THE PARAMETERS AND GUIDELINES SET BY THE UNIVERSITY AND THE COORDINATING BODIES.

Admission Procedures For enrollment in the Master's Degree in Sciences of Nutrition and Health, regarding curricular requirements, graduates from classes of degree other than those indicated in the required knowledge for access must have acquired at least 60 CFU in basic and/or characterizing training activities, distributed as follows:
- minimum 20 CFU in total of: FIS/07, SECS-S/01, SECS-S/02; CHIM/01, CHIM/03, CHIM/06; AGR/13; INF/01;
- minimum 30 CFU in total of BIO/09, BIO/13, BIO/10, BIO/14, BIO/16, BIO/19;
- minimum 10 CFU in total of MED/42, MED/49; IUS/01
If the applicant does not possess the required curricular requirements, they cannot finalize enrollment in the course until they have acquired them through passing specific exams.
The admission of such students will be subject not only to the acquisition of the specified CFU but also to the evaluation of their previous university path (e.g., relevant and compatible degrees for research and technical roles in Biological Sciences - (2.6.2.2.1) and biologists and similar professions - (2.3.1.1.1)).
In accordance with Article 6, paragraph 2 of DM 270/2004, the verification of the applicant's adequate preparation, which must be carried out after confirming the possession of curricular requirements, is conducted by a dedicated Commission appointed by the Course Council through an interview. The applicant's personal preparation is considered proven for graduates who obtained a degree grade above 95/110. If candidates exceed the maximum limit set for the class (65 students), a selection will be carried out through a test. In case of equal scores, priority will be given to the younger candidate by age.
Upon positive verification results, the applicant may finalize enrollment in the Master's Degree within the deadlines specified in the University Study Plan.

Program, texts and objectives The reasons for using sectors already included in the decree for the class The need to consider aspects related to health requires prioritizing, among the characterizing biomedical disciplines, the sector BIO/12 - Clinical Biochemistry and Clinical Molecular Biology, especially to ensure the acquisition of skills applicable in the job market. This strategy immediately results in including the sector BIO/10 among the related activities, with in-depth study of the part specific to food biochemistry, in harmony with other disciplines consistent with food characterization.
Regarding the SSD AGR/15, it is present both among the characterizing training activities and among the related training activities. This choice follows the need to provide specific content, as requested in consultations with social partners, such as: the influence of technologies, techniques and processing systems on food composition modification, with enrichment of potentially toxic substances and reduction of high-quality components (antioxidants, vitamins, aromas).
The motivation for including the sector BIO/14 among the related activities is linked to the need to include the course in Food Toxicology.

Communication Skills (communication skills)
Master's degree graduates in Science of Nutrition and Health must demonstrate the ability to communicate clearly, using appropriate language and terminology, as well as synthesis, information, knowledge, and solutions to various issues related to nutrition and health.
Master's degree graduates must be able to communicate in writing and orally, and through innovative computer solutions, with interlocutors of different knowledge and cultural levels, and in highly diversified contexts.
Communication skills must be particularly effective in highlighting the strengths of the topics and the ability to interact, both in technical-scientific environments and in mass contexts.
Acquisition of these skills will be achieved through specific opportunities:
- Frontal lectures, seminars, and ad hoc presentations, group work;
- Specific initiatives: surveys, demographic and anamnestic data collection techniques, physical activity diaries, collection and processing of questionnaires
- Use of computer tools (teleconferences, chat, virtual classroom).
Monitoring of Communication Skills will be conducted through the evaluation of paper and computer-based materials from individual and group work, and especially through the defense of the thesis.

Judgment Autonomy (making judgments)
Master's degree holders must demonstrate having developed judgment autonomy capable of ensuring, both in the collection and interpretation of literature and/or specific analysis data, and in the management of concrete issues in professional activity, rational solutions, also in terms of strategic planning and coherent resolution aligned with the training path undertaken, theoretical and practical.
The acquisition of judgment autonomy will also be guaranteed through internship periods, with activities and attendance at facilities in specific public and private contexts, requiring personal abilities alongside consolidated teaching knowledge.
Judgment autonomy, primarily monitored through the final exam, must also enable the resolution of non-standardized issues.

Incoming Orientation:
Students will have access to various welcome points represented by the 'Help Stations' located within the Chieti Campus, dedicated to providing information about the University and the territory to facilitate student access, offering support and assistance in finding services to address the variability of their needs. Services include bike sharing (free rental service) and medical assistance (support for medical and dental emergencies). Next to the Help Stations, there are information points provided by the University for the presentation of the Study Programs of the School of Medicine and Health Sciences, offering promotional materials for the Study Programs, organizing presentation meetings, and assisting interested students.

Regarding the specific activities offered by the Study Program, incoming orientation will be guaranteed by a pool of tutor professors who will organize specific meetings with students aimed at presenting the educational objectives, professional profile, and employment and professional opportunities for graduates, as well as enrollment options for working students or those living away from the campus (part-time enrollment).

Regarding the availability of effective tools for self-assessment of recommended entry knowledge, self-assessment tests will be provided, preparatory for any preparatory courses organized by the School in the macro-areas characterizing the Study Program.

In-course Orientation: The in-course orientation will include the role of 'Teaching Assistant', covered by teaching staff, aimed at complementing standard activities with additional exercises, student office hours, dissemination of teaching materials, etc., in relation to the courses offered by the program.

The enhancement of the service will be directed by any identified criticalities, which will be detected through the use of quality assurance tools provided by the Quality Office, such as indicators related to the monitoring of student careers, or reports from Parity Committees.

Students will also be encouraged to participate in international mobility, with orientation and support activities for studying abroad, primarily through opportunities provided by the Lifelong Learning Programme Erasmus. International mobility orientation will be carried out in collaboration with the LLP/Erasmus Program Coordinator and the Departmental Coordinator for International Relations of the Department of Innovative Technologies in Medicine and Dentistry.

Outgoing Orientation:
Outgoing orientation will be based on active involvement of the territory, already demonstrated through extensive consultation with companies from relevant sectors (agri-food, pharmaceutical, collective catering) and public institutions, which have guaranteed internship and employment opportunities. This interest will be formalized through appropriate agreements following the formal accreditation of the Study Program.

Students may also benefit from the University's Placement Service, accredited as a job agency by the Abruzzo Region, through the University's Post-Graduation Orientation Program S.T.A.R.T. (Internships, Traineeships, Advanced Training, Research, Territory and Placement), managed through the online platform JOB.

Career Guidance Given that the University Job Placement office carries out activities to facilitate entry into the workforce through multiple services and initiatives, and detailed information on the office's planned activities is available at the URL: https://orientamento.unich.it,
the Course has joined the 'Master's Degree Course Project' promoted by the Rector and Professor Davide Quaglione, committing to building a mechanism for companies (or more generally entities whose activities align with the relevant professional outcomes) to take on students starting from the 2024/2025 academic year. This aims to improve graduate employability.
Therefore, the Course will operate according to these steps:
1) Identify a portfolio of companies/external entities to contact and verify their availability to participate in the project;
2) With them, identify the activities to include in the 'student guidance' process during the internship, such as mentoring, coaching, curricular internships, support in thesis writing, and potentially the goal of employment at the end;
3) Identify the most available and motivated students for the specific path and build a ranking with the company in case of multiple applications, to minimize the risk of companies dealing with insufficiently motivated students;
4) Identify monitoring and control mechanisms for the guidance process to respond promptly in case of emerging issues.
The Course participated in the Presentation Day of the I Career Day of the University of Chieti-Pescara G. d'Annunzio on May 29, 2024, in collaboration with the MAW - awesome people, great results employment agency.
The event provided further details on how to be more attractive to Generation Z through innovative solutions, sharing Gen Z workforce data, discovering how to engage young talents, and informing about various participation modalities: Career Game, Workshop, Stand Uni-Park, and more.
The Course promoted the University's Career Service & Placement Sector initiative, in collaboration with Fastenal, regarding the Mock interviews - Simulated Interviews in English event to familiarize students with interview types, from traditional to unexpected ones, aiming to exercise and prepare students' mindset for any job interview scenario.

http://zeus.unich.it/teledidattica/#insegnamenti Student opinions In light of the new methods for administering questionnaires regarding student opinions on attended teaching activities, it is recorded that the number of collected forms for evaluation is congruent and significant. This allows us to consider the expressed judgments increasingly truthful. In particular, the number of evaluated courses has reached almost total coverage, thus fully describing the situation of the Study Program.
564 questionnaires were processed, from which the level of 21 training activities is derived: 47.62% at level A (n=10) and 52.38% at level B (n=11). None at level C or D. The evaluated courses have increased by 44% compared to the previous cohort; in particular, level B courses have decreased from 56% previously.
The average evaluation of the 13 Study Programs in the scientific area is 3.37, while that of the 21 training activities of the Nutrition and Health Master's Degree Program is 3.48, significantly higher. Aggregated data for the scientific area, composed of 14 active courses, report an evaluation based on 15,047 processed questionnaires with 304 out of 378 training activities (80.42% coverage) and an average of 3.43.
For SAS, 448 questionnaires were processed, with 22 out of 26 training activities (84.62% coverage) and an average of 3.52.
The average of questions D0, D1, and D3 (overall satisfaction macro-indicator) for SAS is 3.41, higher than the scientific area's 3.32 and the University's 3.35.
For logistical-organizational aspects (D9, D13, D14, and D16), SAS reports 3.56, higher than the scientific area and University averages, both at 3.48.
With an average of 3.57, the teaching effectiveness macro-indicator (D20, D121, and D22) also exceeds the scientific area's 3.47 and the University's 3.48.
The number of valid forms has fluctuated with an upward trend from A.A. 2019-2020 (10 forms) to A.A. 2020-2021 (25 forms) to A.A. 2021-2022 (20 forms).
The average score of the Study Program has decreased from 3.23 in A.A. 2019-2020 to 3.21 in A.A. 2020-2021 and 3.19 in A.A. 2021-2022. This trend contrasts with the upward trend of the scientific area's scores (3.04, 3.12, and 3.12 for the three academic years) and the University's average scores, which also increased (3.11, 3.23, and 3.23 for the three academic years).
It should be noted that the very low score for question D7 (what is your judgment on the classrooms where lessons and exercises are held?) of 2.90 in A.A. 2019-2020 has increased over time to 3.10 in A.A. 2021-2022. The very low score of 2.58 for information technology equipment remains.
Very few forms were collected for teacher opinion surveys (n=4), so the Study Program's score of 3.90 is not convincing.
Non-attending students gave an overall average score of 3.41.
The main reasons for not attending Master's courses in the scientific area, also for this program, are primarily two: work and 'other unspecified reasons'. Among suggestions, requests are made to reduce the overall teaching load by eliminating repeated topics across multiple courses, thus improving coordination between courses and providing teaching materials in advance.
The main reasons for not attending Master's courses in the scientific area, also for this program, remain similar to the previous cohort: primarily work and 'other unspecified reasons'. Among suggestions, requests are made to reduce the overall teaching load by eliminating repeated topics across multiple courses, thus improving coordination between courses and providing teaching materials in advance.

Graduate Opinions The compilation of Form B7 (Graduates' Opinions and Satisfaction with the Completed Course of Study) of the SUA CdS 2023 was carried out following the recommendations of the University Quality Assurance Body (PQA) and based on the updated statistical data file provided by PQA and the U-Gov Didattica e Ricerca Information Systems Sector.
Form B7 – Graduate Opinions The most recent Almalaurea survey 2023, updated data as of April 2023, on the profile of SAS graduates from G. d'Annunzio University in 2022, for which 42 out of 44 graduates were interviewed, has highlighted the results to be analyzed below.
42 graduates completed the questionnaire, of whom 25% were male and 75% female, with a completion rate of 95.5%.
The average age at graduation is 27.9, of which 22.7% are under 23 years old, 43.2% are between 25-26 years old, and 34.1% are 27 years or older.
The data on origin indicate that 25% come from the same province as the university location, 45.5% from other provinces in the Abruzzo region, and 29.5% from other regions. None from abroad. Notably, 61.9% travel less than an hour to reach the university for more than 50% of the study period.
19% of graduates have at least one parent with a degree (11.9% both parents and 7.1% only one), while 81% have parents without degrees.
Social class distribution is between 20-30% across high class (26.2%), middle white-collar (21.4%), middle autonomous (21.4%), and working class (31%).
The access diploma is 77.3% high school, predominantly scientific high school (45.5%) and classical (22.7%). Meanwhile, 9.1% come from technical institutes and 13.6% from professional institutes. The average diploma grade is 82.7 out of 100.
100% of graduates completed their previous degree. Graduates come from 25% the same university, 38.9% from other central universities, and 36.1% from southern/island universities. The average grade of the bachelor's degree was 105 out of 110.
The choice of the master's course was primarily (40.5%) driven by both cultural and professional factors.
56.8% enroll regularly or with a one-year delay, while 43.2% enroll with two or more years of delay.
The average exam score is 28.4, and the average graduation grade is 109.4.
70.5% graduate one year late, 22.7% two years, and 6.8% three years, which is the maximum number of years late. Thus, the average master's duration is 2.5 years, and the average graduation delay is 0.5 years.
Although attendance is not mandatory, 69% regularly attend more than 75% of courses. Only 16.7% received scholarships. Compared to other scientific degrees, 69.0% of respondents regularly attend more than 75% of courses, compared to 64.4% at the university. 95.2% completed curricular or recognized work internships, of which 54.8% outside the university.
The time spent on the thesis is 5.4 months.
61.9% of graduates have work experience, of which 19.2% is related to their studies.
21.4% and 52.4% are definitely and mostly satisfied with the degree course, close to national university averages. 42.9% and 42.9% are satisfied with the relationship with professors, a higher value than the national average of 30%. 54.8% and 33.3% are definitely and mostly satisfied with the relationship with students.
85.7% use classrooms they consider always or almost adequate for 27.8% and often adequate for 50%, in line with university values.
Only 28.6% use computer workstations, while 54.8% do not use them despite their availability. 50% consider them adequately numbered, compared to 71% of national universities.
Only 38.1% used the library service, compared to 50.2% of national universities.
71.4% used teaching facilities such as laboratories for practical activities, of which 60% often adequate and 20% always adequate. Averages exceed those of national universities.
Only 38.1% used dedicated study spaces, and 57.1% did not use them despite their availability.
Regarding post-graduation study orientation services, only 52.4% used them, with 18-27% considering them adequate, insufficient, or definitely inadequate. 52.4% participated in career orientation training, with 18.2-36.4% considering it satisfactory, insufficient, or not satisfactory.
57.1% used job search support, with 16-33% considering it satisfactory, insufficient, or not satisfactory.
59.5% used the job placement office, with 20-28% considering it satisfactory, insufficient, or not satisfactory.
35% and 40% are satisfied with student secretariats.
The exam organization service is always satisfactory for 31%, satisfactory for more than half of exams for 57.1%, and for less than half for 11.9%.
The study load is definitely adequate for the course duration for 50%, mostly yes for 31%, mostly no for 16.7%, and definitely no for 2.4%.
66.7% would re-enroll in the same course, compared to 69% of national universities, and 23.8% would choose another university, compared to 19.7% of national universities.
Language skills are predominantly English with 31% and 23.8% at least B2 written and spoken. 2.4% speak Spanish, with no other languages reported.
88.1% have at least basic knowledge of navigating the internet, 66.7% of word processors, 61.9% of spreadsheets, 81% of presentations, and 76.2% of operating systems.
61.9% intend to continue studies with a master's (40.5%), while 38.1% do not intend to continue.
Regarding aspects considered relevant in job search, 81% consider acquiring skills decisive, 76.2% career opportunities, 69% earning potential and job security, 69% alignment with studies, and 61.9% social utility of work. 76.2% mention economic independence, and 71.4% the opportunity to use acquired skills.
Graduates are available to work in the public sector for 59.5% and in the private sector for 61.9%. 71.4% full-time, 59.5% part-time, and 61.9% with smart-working.
81% prefer to work in their province of residence, 76.2% in the province and region of studies, 38.1% in northern Italy, 59.5% in central Italy, and 33.3% in southern Italy. 28.6% in Europe and 23.8% in non-European countries. 40% are available for work trips with relocation, and 31% without relocation. 23.8% for limited trips, and only 2.4% for no trips.
The employment rate after one year is 52.9%, compared to 67.9% of national universities. Data for 3 and 5 years are not available. The time to enter the labor market from the start of the search to finding a job is not yet available.
