- Abruzzo Psychologists' Order, whose representativeness is considered national: the meeting held on October 31, 2017 (see attached minutes), with the President and a councilor of the Abruzzo Psychologists' Order, aimed to present the current structure of the Master's degree and reflect on the employment opportunities for psychologists;

- Psychological Director, Internship Tutor, Head of the Clinical Psychology Service of the Mental Health Department, ASL of Pescara: the meeting held on October 26, 2017, focused on discussing the skills to be acquired in clinical psychology and the professional opportunities for clinical psychologists in Territorial and Hospital Psychology.

From the direct consultations, indications emerged regarding the importance for the reference professional figure of the following skills: project design, coordination, and implementation of scientific research; ability to evaluate the outcomes of psychosocial interventions from an evidence-based perspective; ability to manage complex and multiproblematic clinical situations from a transversal case management perspective; ability to provide support to individuals and families and analyze and improve relational and communication aspects between users and socio-health operators; clarity on the definition of roles of clinical psychologist and psychotherapist; knowledge of professional ethics and the code of ethics.

On September 4, 2019, the Advisory Committee of the Master's Degree in Clinical and Health Psychology met at the premises of the Department of Psychological, Health, and Territorial Sciences (see attached minutes). Present were: Course Director and AQ Group Coordinator, representatives of: Alumni UdA, Territorial Area Foro-Alento, Francavilla al Mare (CH), Focolare Maria Regina Association onlus, Scerne di Pineto (TE), CSM Nord ASL Pescara, DSM ASL Lanciano-Vasto-Chieti, Abruzzo Psychologists' Order. The following points emerged from the meeting:

- Importance of framing the psychologist profession in the health sector and sensitizing political and institutional worlds to favor further occupational spaces for psychologists, particularly in health and hospital settings;

- Need for a seminar discussion between the Abruzzo Psychologists' Order, the Medical Association, and the Regional Health Department;

- Need to develop further contexts where psychologists can be integrated.

It was decided to schedule meetings with the Advisory Committee and other interested parties biennially, aimed at analyzing the consistency between course content and the dynamics of training demand, examining subsequent ex-post results.

It was decided that the systematicity of the survey would be biennial due to the recognition and stability of the clinical psychologist professional figure in various institutional and health contexts (Ministry of Health, SSN, etc.).

On January 5, 2021, a questionnaire was sent to all members of the Advisory Committee to evaluate training needs and professional opportunities, also in relation to Bill n. 2751 on the qualifying degree, which would entail significant regulatory changes to LM-51. The questionnaire (see attached) was prepared by the Course Director and the AQ group.

From the analysis of the questionnaires, it emerges that most representatives of professional organizations have had experience with graduates of the degree course who completed at least six months of internship at their locations. The operators' evaluation was satisfactory in all cases, considering that the degree course provides adequate training to meet professional needs. Essential basic skills that graduates should possess were indicated: theoretical and operational knowledge of research methods, diagnostic abilities, and management of interviews and the ability to work in networks, ability to design interventions for different population groups. Operators consider that graduates of the degree course have important strengths, consisting in a good level of in-depth theoretical knowledge of basic psychology, motivation for knowledge in the context of personal growth and psychological assistance to others, representing in some cases an added value to the patient care process. Three social cooperatives present in the Advisory Committee also declared to have hired psychologists from the degree course with permanent contracts in the last five years.

Critical issues were also identified. Practical skills in familiarity with diagnostic tools, operational management of different phases of the interview and setting, and formulation of diagnosis were found to be deficient. From this perspective, it is evident that the main deficiency in university preparation for the clinical psychologist professional figure is the lack of clinical experience, a problem that immediately affects the most important gap in university training for clinical psychology, namely the absence of outpatient clinical settings. This structural deficit is common to all Italian universities regarding clinical psychology training, including our degree course.

For the degree course programming, further significant elements emerged regarding the use of online teaching (DAD) for clinical psychology training, the qualifying degree, and the need to promote greater dialogue with public institutions for adequate programming of the relationship between demand and supply of psychologists in the market.

The Course Director and the AQ Group Coordinator participated in 2022 in a series of meetings organized at the national level (within the Assembly of the College of Professors and Researchers in Clinical Psychology of Italian universities, at the Congress and Assembly of the Italian Psychological Association), aimed at designing the reorganization of the LM-51 regulations in accordance with Law n. 163/2021, concerning provisions on university qualifications, which modifies the modalities through which it will be possible to obtain professional qualification for the psychologist profession in the future. The documents and guidelines produced by the Academic Psychology Consultation (CPA), the Italian Psychological Association (AIP), and the National Order of Psychologists (CNOP) were also examined.

On November 14, 2022, the Advisory Committee of the Master's Degree in Clinical and Health Psychology met. The members were informed of the letter and spirit of the June 2022 Interministerial Decrees, which impose a profound transformation of the regulations of the LM-51 degree courses as qualifying degrees starting from the 2023/2024 academic year. The philosophy behind the reorganization of the degree course and its teaching regulations was explained: redistribution of CFU over two years, attention to professionalizing content of teaching courses, organization of part of the Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) within the degree course and part of it at external contracted structures, organization of teaching silence periods to allow students to attend external internships. The Director of the Center for Studies of the Focolare Maria Regina Association onlus of Scerne di Pineto (TE) highlighted the positive and critical aspects of the experience of our degree course's interns at the Scerne di Pineto structure. Regarding the new qualifying degree, she emphasized the need for a selection of students requesting internships at their structure due to the specific nature of interventions, hoping that students are adequately informed and prepared for the type of work required. She also expressed concerns that the reduction of didactic CFU might lower the quality of theoretical preparation of students, which has so far been optimal. She hopes that teaching courses will be particularly attentive to practical preparation for the psychologist profession, an aspect structurally deficient in university psychology degree courses due to the lack of structures allowing clinical practice.

The representative for the Social Cooperative Orizzonte of Pescara, a psychologist, agreed with the analysis of her colleague and shared both the experience and concerns regarding future preparation of interns. In particular, she emphasized the lack of maturity expressed by students in requesting internships, as each structure has its own specificities. A passive attitude of simply requesting the structure's frequency is not motivating, as she believes that only a proactive and somewhat creative attitude can allow students to fully value the educational experience of the internship, which can be a source of growth for both the student and the structure, especially if, as in her case, it is a social cooperative whose specific activity involves proposing innovative socio-health projects. Not surprisingly, many of our degree course interns in the past have had the opportunity to continue their experience at her cooperative through employment contracts after obtaining professional qualification. From this perspective, she expresses great concern that an excessive number of interns might undermine the optimal tutor-student ratio and thus the real motivation for training among future interns.

The delegate for the Parity Commission for Internships University-Order of Psychologists of the Abruzzo Region expressed doubts about another aspect of the future external internship. The time required for internalization and metabolism of professional training is necessarily long, and the future organization of the TPV, as expressed in the Interministerial Decrees, consisting of a reduction of internship hours and the abolition of continuous semesters, might undermine the essential time for proper professional work training.

The delegate of the Abruzzo Psychologists' Order emphasized the importance of giving adequate space in teaching courses to the Psychologists' Code of Ethics, as it is an obligatory reference point for professional action and therefore for the professionalization of future psychologists.

On February 10, 2023, a joint meeting was held with the Directors of the Master's Degree in Psychology and the Three-Year Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of the University d'Annunzio with the President of the Abruzzo Psychologists' Order for the organization of the TPV in coordinated manner, both in view of the admission procedures for the 2023/2024 academic year and for the coordination of the internal TPV. The meeting took place within the activities of Consultation with Representative Organizations, as the inclusion of the TPV in the educational activities required for the qualifying degree necessitates constant coordination with the professional order. During the meeting, both the Order President and the Course Directors expressed their respective motivations in outlining criticalities and possibilities for organizing the TPV. After thorough discussion, criteria for a common procedural line were established with the full agreement of the Psychologists' Order.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data
According to data provided by the University Quality Office, in the 2022/23 academic year, the number of students enrolled in the Clinical and Health Psychology degree course is 212. Regarding the geographical origin of students, the majority of new students (80.19%) come from other regions.

Regarding the type of diploma obtained, 41.51% come from high schools, 31.60% from magistral institutes, 14.62% from technical institutes, 4.72% from professional institutes, and the remaining (7.55%) from other types of schools. The percentages regarding the graduation exam score of new students are as follows: 62.56% obtained a score up to 80, 33.65% a score between 80 and 99, 2.84% a score of 100, and 0.95% a score of 100 with honors.

In the cohort enrolled in the 2021/22 academic year, the percentage of CFU acquired in the first year compared to the required CFU is 74.7%, with an average of 6.93 exams passed per student. When moving to the second year of enrollment, only 3.7% of students made an explicit withdrawal.

Regarding the duration of the study course, the percentage of graduates in 2022 is 68.51%. 24.31% obtained the degree one year late, and the remaining (7.18%) two or more years beyond the course duration. An improvement action implemented by the degree course to reduce the number of students outside the course timeline and that has already led to a desired decrease compared to the previous academic year involves adding extraordinary exam and graduation sessions.

Characteristics of the Final Exam
Students are admitted to the final exam discussion who obtain a suitability judgment of the Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) and pass the Practical Evaluation Test (PPV) that precedes the thesis discussion, as provided by the new regulations of DM n. 654/2022 regarding professional qualification for psychologists.

The final exam consists of the preparation of an original work by the student under the supervision of a supervisor and a co-supervisor. The work consists of a written document related to a topic connected to clinical and well-being psychology and related disciplines, which must be clearly defined and argued rigorously and originally, with empirical, bibliographic, or logical-theoretical contributions. The final exam thus represents a learning experience on a specific topic where the student searches for information, formulates hypotheses, and argues and supports their conclusions. Through the final exam, it will be possible to evaluate the achievement of expected results in terms of knowledge, application skills, communication skills, independent judgment, and autonomous learning ability. The course regulations establish the modalities for taking the exam and determining the final score.

Final Exam Procedure
The final exam consists of the preparation of an original work by the student under the supervision of a supervisor and evaluated by a co-supervisor.

Students are admitted to the final exam discussion who obtain a suitability judgment of the Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) and pass the Practical Evaluation Test (PPV) that precedes the thesis discussion.

The graduation exam will, as legally required, be public and conducted according to a predetermined program, with each candidate having an average exam duration of 15 minutes, divided into a first part for the thesis presentation and a second part for discussion. Candidates are encouraged to use audiovisual aids for presentations.

The Commission, whose composition is established by the University's teaching regulations, evaluates each candidate considering the overall academic performance, thesis content, and final exam execution; the evaluation is expressed in hundredths.

The score assigned to the thesis and its presentation ranges from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 6 points, according to the following scale:

- 0-1: sufficient

- 2-3: fair

- 4-5: good

- 6: excellent

The Commission may exceptionally award an additional point to the maximum 6 points if: a) the student has a starting grade of 103; b) the thesis and presentation are particularly appreciated and brilliant; c) the supervisor assumes responsibility for attesting to the quality of the student's preparatory work; d) the Commission unanimously agrees on awarding the additional point.

The criteria for evaluating the score to be assigned to the thesis include:

1. Ordered and coherent organization of topics treated in the work;

2. Mastery of specialized language and discipline-specific terminology;

3. Originality of the thesis topic;

4. Level of in-depth treatment of the topic;

5. Accuracy of bibliographic research;

6. Relevance assigned to the most recent literature on the thesis topic;

7. Completeness of the treatment of the thesis topic;

8. Expressive and presentation skills of the work.

The exam is considered passed with a minimum score of 66/110. If the maximum score (110/110) is achieved, the Commission may award the honor on unanimous decision.

Summary of the Technical Report of the Evaluation Committee
The resources made available to the degree course are appropriate, effective, and fully commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. More critical is the situation in terms of university teaching staff if all the proposed regulations are activated. The course covers the class of psychological sciences in the University's educational offer, positioning itself at optimal levels (in reference to the class) in terms of enrollments and registrations. The proposed regulation, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the University's goals of rationalization and qualification of its educational offer.

Admission Requirements Required Knowledge for Access Admission to the course requires holding a Bachelor's degree or equivalent title (Italian or foreign) that documents a study curriculum consisting of at least 90 CFU within the psychological scientific-disciplinary sectors (M/PSI). These CFUs must be distributed as follows: a) a minimum of 18 CFUs in total across sectors M-PSI/01, 02, 03; b) a minimum of 6 CFUs in SSD M-PSI/04; c) a minimum of 12 CFUs in total across SSDs M-PSI/05, 06; a minimum of 12 CFUs in total across SSDs M-PSI/07, 08. Additional admission requirements include (a) knowledge of English at a minimum B1 level, certified by passing a university-level English language exam or an external language certification; (b) completion of 10 CFUs of Practical-Evaluative Internship certified by the Bachelor's degree curriculum. In the absence of the application of Law 163/2021 and subsequent adjustments, those who have obtained a Bachelor's degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques (L-24) under the previous curriculum and have not completed the 10 CFUs corresponding to professional training activities may request recognition of activities carried out and certified during the Bachelor's program (DM n. 654/2022, art. 6, para. a and b), as well as request enrollment with reservation and acquire the 10 CFUs, in addition to the 120, during the Master's program (DM n. 654/2022, art. 7). The adequacy of personal preparation is verified through the weighted average of grades obtained in the Bachelor's degree profit exams related to the above-mentioned SSD M-PSI, useful for compiling a merit ranking.

Admission Procedures The Master's Degree Course in Psychology is subject to locally regulated quota-based admission governed by an annual call. The total number of available places is 120, consisting of 114 places for Italian, EU, and non-EU citizens residing in Italy (Article 26 of Law No. 189 of July 30, 2002), 3 places reserved for non-EU citizens residing abroad, and 3 places reserved for students of the Marco Polo Program from China.
To successfully complete the Course of Study (CdS), students must have knowledge of psychophysiological processes underlying behavior and a solid foundation in core psychology areas, such as general psychology, social and work psychology, and developmental psychology. Additionally, knowledge of statistical and psychometric methods as well as familiarity with computer procedures for data processing is required.
Admission to the CdS is regulated annually by a specific admission call.
Eligible applicants are students holding a Bachelor's Degree or an equivalent qualification obtained in Italy or abroad, provided they comply with current ministerial regulations. Specifically, the following are admitted to selection: a) graduates in Class L-24, under Decree 270/2004, and graduates in Class L-34, under Decree 509/1999, who meet the above-mentioned curricular requirements. Admission for foreign students is also subject to proof of Italian language proficiency, verified through an assessment interview. In all cases, compliance with the aforementioned requirements will be evaluated by a committee established by the Course Council.
Admission to the CdS is granted, in order of merit ranking and until available places are exhausted, to candidates who have achieved a weighted average of 23/30 or higher.
If the number of eligible candidates is fewer than the available places, candidates ranked below the admission threshold will undergo an interview to assess their knowledge in the disciplinary areas of the Course of Study and the chosen curriculum, for the purpose of determining eligibility. The interview will explore knowledge of fundamental theories, specific constructs, and the most commonly used methods of analysis, diagnosis, and research.

Communication Skills
Students are required to demonstrate the ability to clearly and appropriately present knowledge and ideas developed through critical reflection on the covered topics, using discipline-specific terminology. They must also demonstrate the ability to consider others' perspectives to promote and support constructive discussions with diverse interlocutors. These skills will be particularly developed and assessed during practical exercises and presentations of reports on topics covered during the didactic and experiential activities.

Autonomy of Judgment
Students are required to demonstrate the ability to: a) independently formulate critical judgments in reading and interpreting the reference scientific literature; b) formulate well-founded evaluations of the phenomena under investigation based on observational and instrumental data, while considering the principles of professional ethics; c) evaluate research/intervention proposals and projects, taking into account situational factors that apply in the contexts where they are implemented. These skills will be particularly developed and assessed during active discussions, throughout the teaching process, practical exercises/laboratory activities, and the entire preparation process for the thesis. The experience of the Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) will further contribute to the development of autonomy of judgment, with the dual added value that 1) the circumstances in which it will be required will have practical and situational relevance, and 2) the maturation of decision-making ability will be subject to monitoring and evaluation for the successful completion of the TPV.

Orientation in Entry The Study Course actively participates, in collaboration with the Delegates for Orientation of the Department and the School of Medicine and Health Sciences, in the initiatives of the University Orientation Service, such as Open Days and the Student Fair - Campus Ud'A Orienta - aimed at high school students. The Committee organizes annually two orientation meetings in spring - aimed at students of the three-year Study Course in Psychological Sciences and Techniques of the Department of Psychological, Health and Territory Sciences of the Chieti University (Open Day). The purpose of the meetings is to promote knowledge of the Study Course, fostering the development of university and career planning. During these meetings, Study Course professors present the distinctive aspects and objectives of the course, the study plan, the curricular internship, the possibility of studying abroad, and career prospects. Representatives of the academic secretariat and students are also present, illustrating the services. Additionally, as part of permanent orientation, the Committee offers a desk service managed by senior students with teaching tutoring grants, responding to questions raised by students (tutoringpsicologia@unich.it).
The Study Course publishes an online Study Guide at the beginning of each academic year, illustrating the study plan, course programs, professor office hours and contact details (email and phone), and all useful information for the self-orientation process for new students and enrolled students (both attending and non-attending), as well as for external interested parties. For orientation in entry for students with disabilities, the Study Course relies on the initiatives of the University's Study Rights, Tutoring and Disability Office. The Office has established a Disability and DSA CON_TE_STO Service, which provides services and initiatives to promote conscious and active participation in university life for students with disabilities (and/or disabilities), DSA or BES and with specific temporary needs. The Department (DNISC) relies on a delegated professor for disability, Professor Brunetti, with whom the Study Course coordinates to enhance and improve initiatives. Orienting and in-course tutoring The orienting and in-course tutoring activities are promoted by the Course Orientation Committee and delivered through differentiated methods:

All students are then regularly invited to participate in numerous scientific events (seminars, conferences) organized by the Course faculty.
To enhance in-course tutoring activities, the Course has equipped itself with a computer laboratory (shared with the CCdSS of DILASS), where support activities for bibliographic research and thesis writing can be organized.

Assigned Training Periods The training offer of the previous non-licensing framework provides a curricular alternating study-work experience (Stage) lasting 100 hours (4 CFU) to be completed in at least 1 month in external structures contracted with the School of Medicine and Health Sciences. The contracted structures are entities operating mainly in the territory: a) social enterprises (third sector organizations such as non-profits, associations, committees, foundations, consortia, social cooperatives, etc.) registered with the respective regional registers; b) public bodies (ASL, Hospitals, Prisons, etc.); c) private companies contracted with public bodies; d) private companies with a study-work alternation project consistent with the training objectives of the Stage.
The Stage activity continues to be implemented and supported by the CdS, through: a) an internal tutoring service that continuously monitors students' experiences by interviewing them at the end of the Stage period and analyzing evaluation forms on the quality and effectiveness of the experience and the relationship with the structures; b) a monitoring activity of the structures to interface with the responsible persons for proposing improvements to the offer; c) the activation of new agreements, subject to the evaluation of the requirements possessed by the structures requesting them.
The CdS also provides an online service for searching sites where information on the offer and access modalities is collected. The Didactic Office supports students in the activation procedures.
The periodic verification of the operational status of the contracted structures for Stage confirms the operation of 70 structures (33 in Abruzzo and 37 in other central-south regions) (see PDF).
To monitor the effectiveness of the training experience, the intern must complete an evaluation form of the structure and the overall Stage experience. The structure's tutor is also required to provide an evaluation of the intern at the end of the Stage. Both evaluations are essential for certifying the 4 CFU acquired through the Stage activity. The summary table of the last three years is available in the attachment.
Analysis of the evaluation forms shows high satisfaction regarding all reported items, such as the welcome received, the quality of tutoring and activities offered, and the perceived usefulness of the experience for training purposes. The evaluations of the last two years, on a scale ranging from 1 (poor) to 4 (excellent), are generally very high (above 3.50), indicating that the experience is formative both for understanding the characteristics of a work environment and for professional orientation. In confirmation of this positive assessment, numerous students continue to engage with the structures known through Stage via volunteering activities.
Starting from the 2023-24 academic year, with the implementation of the new licensing framework, 20 CFU of curricular evaluative practical internship (TPV) have been included in the Training Offer (OF), which can be acquired through one of the following methods:
a) up to 6 CFU with internal TPV within the Course of Study (in accordance with the specific Didactic Regulations) and at least 14 CFU at qualified external structures contracted with the University;
b) 20 CFU entirely acquired at qualified external entities contracted with the University.
The CdS has appointed a TPV Coordinator, Prof. Rosalia Di Matteo, member of the University-Order of Psychologists of the Abruzzo Region Parity Commission for Internships (CPT), and a TPV Commission consisting of the same Coordinator, the Chair of the CdS, Prof. Giorgia Committeri, and one member for each curriculum to better manage the organization of external TPV: Prof. Francesca Romana Alparone for the Social, Work, and Organizational Psychology curriculum, Prof. Marcella Brunetti for the Cognitive Neuroscience curriculum, and Dr. Giulio D'Urso for the Developmental Psychology curriculum.
The Didactic Office supports students in the procedures for activating new agreements with external entities. The outcome is subject to the evaluation of the requirements possessed by the structures requesting them by the Didactic Office and the assessment of the training project by the CPT.
Regarding TPV conducted internally at the university, in the 2023-24 academic year, the Training Offer includes (up to a maximum of 6 CFU, in blocks of 2 CFU) activities in the form of:
- Supervised Practical Experiences (EPS): 1 CFU modules for deepening specific aspects of the profession or the use of professional tools. These modules are activated annually as part of the Course of Study's training offer and can be completed in the first or second year;
- Supervised Laboratory Activities (ALS): practical activities supervised within a Course of Study laboratory for a number of CFU to be agreed upon with the laboratory's responsible instructor. These activities are permanent and can be completed in the first or second year.
It is possible to complete internal TPV in a mixed format (EPS + ALS) provided the total CFU always equals a multiple of 2. All activities are mandatory, and are carried out by both regular faculty and highly qualified external professionals (see link).

International Mobility Section The Course ensures students' overseas training through agreements with foreign universities, managed by a dedicated Commission composed of the Department Delegate for Neurosciences, Imaging and Clinical Sciences, Professor Giorgia Committeri, the Course Delegate Professor Sergio Di Sano, and Dr. Ilaria Giovannelli, in collaboration with the University's Internationalization and Erasmus Office.
Since the 2018-19 academic year, the Course has consistently increased the number of contracted European and extra-European locations where students can carry out study and/or research periods, including thesis preparation. Currently, the number of such locations has risen to 38.
All mobilities are offered through competitions advertised via the University website, the Course website, and the Course's social media pages. During the publication of the calls, the Course organizes meetings to present the mobility calls to students; during these meetings, students who have already completed their stay provide testimonials, raise awareness, and encourage their peers to undertake the overseas experience.
The Course ensures support for those intending to complete a training period abroad through constant coordination with central offices, which provide administrative support and mentoring by former Erasmus students, and through the Erasmus Commission, which accompanies, monitors, and supports the experience, also through online meetings. Additionally, the Course financially supports international mobility for students, allocating an additional sum in the form of expense reimbursement based on the annual availability of teaching funds.
Thanks to this effort, student mobility within standard Erasmus programs (Study and Traineeship) has significantly increased, reaching an average of 10 per year (2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24). For the 2024-25 academic year, 15 scholarships were awarded, indicating a growing trend.
Beyond standard Erasmus programs (Study and Traineeship), since 2022 the Course has been actively organizing additional internationalization opportunities in the form of Blended Intensive Programmes (BIP), which include an online component and an in-person component in collaboration with at least two foreign universities, and Short International Mobility (MIB) lasting one or two weeks.
In September and October 2022, the Course organized the first University-wide Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) with ISPA in Lisbon and the University of Latvia, involving 5 students from the Course (selected via a specific call) and 15 students from foreign universities.
In the 2023-24 academic year, 8 students participated in a BIP organized in Riga by colleagues from the University of Latvia together with the University of Tallinn (Estonia) and Mykolas Romeris University (Lithuania). The Course also organized a new BIP in collaboration with the University of Stockholm and the University of Granada, scheduled between late April (online component) and early June (in-person component), involving 3 selected Course students alongside doctoral students.
Additionally, six different Short International Mobility (MIB) programs were organized, allowing students to attend one week of intensive courses on specific topics. The first took place in Riga in November 2023 and the second in Crete in February 2024, with participation from 4 Course students. The remaining will take place between May and July 2024 in Lublin, Rouen, Riga, and Lisbon. For these, 38 applications were submitted for 25 available places, some of which are also open to students from other psychology courses and doctoral candidates.
The meeting to present the Erasmus Study 2023-24 call was held online on 16 February 2023 via a dedicated Teams channel, while the meeting to present the Erasmus Traineeship 2023-24 call was held online on 26 April 2023. For the presentation of the Erasmus Study 2024-25 call and opportunities for short mobility (BIP and MIB), the Course organized an in-person meeting on 12 March 2024, attended by numerous students from both the first and second year of the course (approximately 90). On 29 April 2024, an online meeting was held with Erasmus Study scholarship winners to support them in preparing their Learning Agreement.
Information on calls and the BIP and MIB programs organized is visible at the link below.

Student opinions The evaluation of the quality and effectiveness of the educational process includes, among the most important actions, the analysis and reflection on the perceived satisfaction of *students* during their study path. For this purpose, the evaluation questionnaire elaborated by the University Quality Assurance (PQA) is used, with particular attention to the following questions: interest in the topics covered (D0), adequacy of prior knowledge (D1), adequacy of study load to the credits assigned to the course of interest (D3), adequacy of teaching materials (D9), coherence of the teaching delivered (D13), respect for the schedule of teaching activities (D14), mode of conducting exams (D16), satisfaction with teachers (D20), clarity of exposition (D21), and availability to provide clarifications (D22).
The survey was made public by the PQA through a comprehensive report on student opinions for the academic year 2021-22, available on the website;
The opinion of *students* was analyzed and discussed by the CCdS at the meeting of July 13, 2023.
Contextual data show that, compared to the triennium examined, in 2021/22 the number of correctly completed questionnaires by students increased compared to the previous biennium: 1,029 forms completed against 975 in 2020-21 and 1,004 in 2019-20, with a coverage of 90.91% of courses (40/44 courses), significantly improved compared to the previous two years (79% in 2020-21; 82.5% in 2019-20) and higher than the area average (87.39%) and the University average (87.39%).
The average evaluation of teaching activity remains stable at 3.50/4.00 (3.45 in 2020-21) and constant within the Level A threshold (from 3.5 to 4 inclusive), in line with the reference area (3.46%) and University (3.43%) scores.
60% of courses fall within Level A, with a slight improvement compared to the previous academic year. Only one course falls within Level C (2.33%), none within Level D.
Scores assigned to questions in the macro-indicators also remain constant over the triennium.
Breaking it down:
- Overall satisfaction appears good, at 3.31/4.00; students find the course topics interesting, but evaluate slightly more negatively the adequacy of preliminary knowledge to tackle the programs and the study load of exams. Scores for these indicators remain within Level B. Specific scores are reported below.
o D0 Are the topics of the course interesting? 3.47
o D1 Were the preliminary knowledge sufficient for understanding the topics in the exam program? 3.31
o D3 Is the required study load proportional to the credits assigned? 3.25
- Teaching effectiveness is evaluated very positively (3.59), and all indicator scores fall within Level A.
o D20 Does the teacher stimulate interest in the subject? 3.52
o D21 Does the teacher explain topics appropriately considering the complexity of the subject? 3.56
o D22 Is the teacher available to provide clarifications during lessons and/or office hours? 3.69
- Logistical-organizational aspects are also considered very satisfactory (3.59), as all indicators fall within Level A.
o D9 Is the teaching material adequate for studying the subject? 3.45
o D13 Was the teaching delivered consistently with what was declared on the course website? 3.57
o D14 Are the schedules for lectures, exercises, and other teaching activities respected? 3.64
o D16 Were the exam modalities clearly defined? 3.53
All macro-indicators align with University and area averages and are slightly higher.
The update of data for the academic year 2022-23 confirms, to date, the positive evaluations collected in 2022. Overall satisfaction rises to 3.41, exceeding University and area averages, while macro-indicator values remain constant.
The 2022 CPDS had highlighted areas for improvement in satisfaction regarding the didactic experience, particularly concerning the completeness of information on programs and exam modalities, the organization of the teaching calendar, and the timing of publishing the thesis session calendar, confirming also the noted dissatisfaction regarding the lack of study rooms, different from the library, where group work related to teaching programs could be carried out. Regarding this, the CCdS has no capacity for action.
Overall data confirm that actions taken to maintain the strengths of the CCdS and address criticalities are yielding positive results. The CCdS educational activity is perceived as more than satisfactory, with no significant critical situations or new issues compared to the past. The CCdS has nonetheless prepared measures to: a) increase participation of students and teachers in the opinion survey, for example by scheduling reminder emails starting from the last third of the teaching cycle; b) improve coordination of teaching programs within the disciplinary areas constituting the curricula and implement greater control over syllabus content; c) improve the distribution of teaching schedules in the academic calendar, avoiding overly tight daily schedules and overlaps between the schedules of TAF B, C, and D courses of the same year.
It is noted that the CCdS has an internal system for managing complaints and suggestions, but continues to support and encourage the role of student representation in collegiate bodies and the value of open dialogue between teachers and students.
Students can further refer to the centralized University-level complaint management system, https//www.unich.it/parla-con-noi, also promoted on the CCdS website.
