Graduate Opinions GRADUATE OPINIONS The analysis of data provided by the AlmaLaurea survey (updated report 2023) on the perceived effectiveness of the training process by graduates shows that the Course of Study has maintained, in recent cohorts, the excellent results that have always characterized it, considering that in 2022 graduates completed all or part of their teaching activities through distance learning (DAD) and experienced the restrictive phases of the pandemic infection.

Almost 100% of graduates (89/90) correctly responded to the survey in the academic year 2022. Attendance was more than satisfactory: 68.5% attended more than 75% of the courses in the study plan, 23.5% attended between 50% and 75% of the courses, and only 5.6% attended between 25% and 50%.

Regarding the regularity of the training path, 61% graduated on time, while 18% graduated with less than one year of delay (delay index=0.8).

Graduates' satisfaction with the completed study path is very high (54% are very satisfied and 43% satisfied), stable over the three years (2020 96%; 2019 96%) and higher than the national class average and the university average.

Almost all graduates expressed a very high level of satisfaction for all aspects concerning the teaching experience, exceeding the national class and university averages, and 79% would enroll in the same course again.

Specifically, all graduates feel satisfied with the relationship with teachers (98.4%, of which 49.4% very satisfied, 49.4% satisfied); 94.4% considered the study load adequate (56.2% very adequate, 38.2% adequate); satisfaction with exam organization (appeals, schedules, information, reservations) was also good, with 47.2% finding it always or almost always satisfactory and 38.3% satisfactory for more than half of the exams.

Improvements are also noted in evaluations of teaching facilities: 34.6% (25% in 2021) rated classrooms always or almost always adequate, 48.1% (36.4% in 2021) often adequate, and only 16% rarely or never adequate (28% in 2021); 34.5% (21% in 2021) rated equipment for other teaching activities (laboratories for practical activities) always or almost always adequate, 45.5% (49% in 2021) often adequate, and only 18% rarely or never adequate.

The improvement continues in evaluations of computer workstations: 79% (68% in 2021) rated them sufficient in number and often adequate; the percentage of users increased (61.8% against 29% in 2021), approaching the national average (65.9%) and slightly exceeding the university average (58.1%), indicating that the enhancement of workstations (implemented through a 2019 agreement with DILASS for shared use of an IT classroom with 23 workstations) has achieved the desired outcome. It seems confirmed that the negative percentages of previous years were linked to the institution and maintenance of distance learning due to the pandemic emergency.

For the same reason, there is an improvement in the use (70.8% against 59% in 2021) and evaluation of library services, with 39.7% (37% in 2020) rating them very positive and 55.6% (51% in 2021) rating them fairly positive.

A high percentage of graduates used post-graduation orientation services (86.5%), but evaluations indicate partial dissatisfaction with support services for job search (64% dissatisfied) and job placement in general (48% dissatisfied); evaluations for orientation services for post-graduation study improved slightly, with half of users declaring themselves very or quite satisfied. The Course of Study orientation committee strengthened work-oriented initiatives in 2022-23 with numerous testimonials, seminars, and meetings with doctoral program coordinators, masters, professionals, and graduates already placed in the sectors of interest for the three Course of Study curricula. It is hoped that this effort will improve evaluations. The curricular internship service has also increased agreements with public and private entities to offer more direct contact opportunities with the world of work.

Overall, the data highlight the perception of a more than good quality of the teaching offer, from the perspective of courses, teaching staff, and facilities. However, concern is expressed for future years since the implementation of the qualifying degree, if not adequately supported by the university, could return negative values for evaluations on classrooms and equipment for laboratories/practical exercises and Practical Evaluation Internship, and negatively reflect on overall satisfaction with the teaching path. This concern has been jointly expressed by the Course of Study departments on multiple occasions and formal settings (Course Council, Department Council, School of Medicine and Health Sciences Board) and through a joint letter to the Rector and DG.

Applying knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
A Psychology graduate is required to have the ability to use acquired knowledge in practical activities and concrete situations; to frame empirical data in appropriate theoretical models; to evaluate psychological phenomena based on solid knowledge. Graduates must demonstrate the ability to interpret data, design research, or collaborate in its design in an original way, to set up and conduct psychological interventions in specific contexts. This ability will be: 1. encouraged through practical exercises and/or laboratory activities closely linked to theoretical lessons and aimed at acquiring and managing tools for analysis, intervention, and evaluation; 2. promoted and consolidated through the Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) experience, carried out in qualified public or private healthcare structures accredited and contracted with the National Health Service (SSN) (see D.I. 654/2022) and university-contracted, aimed at building a situated learning path for procedural and relational skills foundational to the profession, and experimenting with them in operational contexts; 3. evaluated through passing exams, practical tests/reports on exercise topics and in-depth readings, as well as through laboratory activities and the TPV practical evaluation.

Learning skills (learning skills)
An advanced ability to reflect on study topics and integrate new information based on an original and autonomous elaborative process is required. The graduate in this course must therefore qualify for their ability to 'learn how to learn', in order to design the development of their own training in relation to specific goals. This ability will be developed and verified mainly during the presentation of projects and analysis of literature during thesis preparation.

Knowledge and understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The Psychology graduate, at the end of the training path, knows, understands, and appropriately uses the basic concepts, scientific language, methodology, and application tools of the psychological discipline, specifically tailored to the disciplinary areas reflected in the curricula constituting the Course of Study: - knows and understands the main explanatory theories in cognitive psychology, neuropsychology, neuroscience, developmental psychology, social psychology, group and community psychology, work and organizational psychology, along with the most relevant contributions of related disciplines in philosophical, anthropological, sociological, pedagogical, methodological, economic, and biomedical fields; - knows and understands the main evaluation methods in cognitive psychology, neuropsychology, neuroscience, developmental psychology, group and community psychology, work and organizational psychology; - knows and understands the main research methods and data analysis methods of cognitive psychology, neuropsychology, cognitive neuroscience, developmental psychology, social psychology, group and community psychology, work and organizational psychology. These knowledge and understanding abilities are acquired through frontal lessons, seminars, group discussions, exercises, and individual study using updated texts on recent theoretical and methodological directions of the disciplines, as well as international scientific articles, which provide updates to knowledge and improve understanding, illustrating recent research results and future perspectives. They will be verified through oral and/or written passing exams related to individual teaching subjects.

Organization and responsibility of AQ at Course of Study level The Course of Study carries out AQ activities through the following bodies, whose composition, competencies, and responsibilities are described below. Names are listed in the Referents and Structures section.

1) Course of Study Chair Responsibility: coordinates the Course of Study AQ system and oversees compliance with obligations set by regulations, with the collaboration of the Parity Commission (CPSD) and the Course of Study AQ and Review Group (GAQ/R), in line with university central bodies' AQ guidelines. The Chair annually compiles the SUA Course of Study in collaboration with GAQ/R, the Orientation and Erasmus commissions, and the Internship and Placement coordinators; annually monitors the preparation and/or update of teaching syllabi, with the help of the Course of Study Teaching Commission; is responsible, in collaboration with GAQ/R, for commenting on the indicators of the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA); is responsible and guides the annual and cyclical review of the Course of Study (RRC).

2) Parity Commission Composition: one representative of the Course of Study teaching body; one representative of the Course of Study students.

Responsibility: monitors the teaching offer and quality of teaching activities, services provided to students, and the sustainability of the Course of Study from the perspective of teaching facilities, study, and in-depth learning.

3) Quality Assurance/Review Group (GAQ/R)
Composition: five reference teachers of the Course, the Department's ReAQ-Didattica, one representative of technical-administrative staff, one representative of the students in office.

Responsibility: organizes and implements the Course of Study self-assessment system and suggests improvement initiatives for quality assurance. Reads critical indicators for annual monitoring (SMA) and collaborates in commenting; drafts the cyclical review report (RRC), analyzing the process (document analysis, including CCdS minutes, data reports, and single commissions' reports from the last three years) through which the Course of Study achieved current results, highlighting criticalities, strengths, and improvement opportunities, and proposing corresponding objectives, indicators, and target values. The GAQ/R organizes meetings with stakeholders and supports the Course of Study Chair in all AQ system activities, including SUA-CdS preparation.

4) Course of Study Council Composition: teachers responsible for courses and student representatives enrolled in the Course, elected according to the General University Regulation.

Responsibility: annually deliberates on the content of SUA and the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA); periodically (at least every 5 years) deliberates on the content of the cyclical review report (RRC); collaborates in the smooth running of the Course of Study AQ; ensures the functioning of the Course of Study in all aspects.

The Course of Study also benefits from the support of ReAQD, as the coordination figure between PQA and the Department.

Planning of work and implementation deadlines The Course of Study, to improve its performance and ensure smooth operation of quality assurance activities, has defined and planned the following management organization:

- The Course of Study Council meets monthly to examine, discuss, and deliberate on all necessary measures for the smooth functioning of the course.
The Course of Study Council during the year, following the established timeline, approves the comments on the Course of Study indicators (SMA – Annual Monitoring Sheet prepared by GAQ/Review and Course of Study Chair by December 15); analyzes any suggestions from consultations with organizations representing goods and service production and professions (within the deadlines for modifying the teaching offer or curriculum); analyzes, within the time for inclusion in SUA-CdS (September 30), student opinions, CPDS report (January/February), GAQ/Review observations, preordering, based on the review report, any improvement actions and possible curriculum modifications; approves, by the end of May, the teaching regulations and inclusion of relevant parts in the Study Manifesto; approves the planning of the teaching offer to be delivered (with corresponding teaching coverage) for the following academic years to be submitted to academic bodies for approval; evaluates, by July 31, the GAQ/Review report on the second semester's performance, examines and aligns individual course programs, checks the correctness and inclusion of syllabi (by June 30/September 30).

- The GAQ/Review, with the collaboration of the Department's Teaching AQ Responsible, during the year analyzes Course of Study indicators for the preparation of the Annual Monitoring Sheet; monitors the first semester teaching performance, analyzing student (and graduate) opinions; proposes a possible redefinition of specific Course of Study objectives and training path, considering possible outcomes of consultations with organizations representing goods and service production and professions; updates SUA-CdS within the deadlines indicated in the 'Guidelines for SUA Compilation'; monitors the second semester teaching performance by June 30; examines the adequacy and update of study programs by the end of July.

The Course of Study also ensures the appropriate relationship between delivered teaching and research conducted in the disciplinary areas of the Course of Study curricula; promotes, in the spirit of continuous improvement, a constant update of programs for different courses and accurate monitoring of laboratory and internship training activities. The responsible parties for this process are the Course of Study Teaching Commission and the syllabi and e-learning activity coordinators.

In the 2023-24 academic year, the Course of Study also joined an initiative promoted by the Department's Teaching AQ Responsible, who organized a seminar cycle on innovative teaching for the entire teaching body.

Annual Review The Course of Study, through the GAQ/Review Group, conducts a self-assessment process aimed at detecting the suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of its training activities, and thus implementing appropriate correction and improvement initiatives, whose effects will be evaluated in the next Review.

The Review was structured over two different cycles:

1. Compilation of the Annual Monitoring Sheet, for evaluating the results of correction and improvement interventions based on quantitative indicators provided by ANVUR, carried out by GAQ/Department AQ Responsible in dedicated meetings by December 15; Course of Study Coordinator prepares a critical synthetic comment by December 31, 2019;
2. Preparation of a Triennial Cyclical Review Report of the Course of Study training project, by GAQ and Review Group, analyzing the process through which the Course of Study implemented its training project, the strengths contributing substantially to achieving educational goals, the quality of services offered to students, the adequacy of the overall course organization (infrastructure, human and technological resources), the permanence of the validity of training goals, and the appropriateness of initiatives for connecting with the world of goods and service production, and professions.

The 2015-2018 Cyclical Review Report was prepared by the Review Commission by October 31, 2018, and submitted for approval to the competent bodies. The RRC and Course of Study AQ evaluation suggested substantial modifications to the Course of Study curriculum, with a redefinition of the overall training project, its educational goals, and the teaching offer plan. The new curriculum came into effect in the 2019-20 academic year.

An update of the 2018 RRC was necessary due to the ANVUR visit for the Course of Study accreditation, which took place on December 2-6, 2020.

In connection with the implementation of Law Decree 163/2021 on qualifying degrees, which imposed a change in the teaching curriculum, a new RRC was completed in January 2023.

Course of Study Design The Master's Degree Course in Psychology has undergone substantial modifications to the curriculum (2018-19; 2023-24) following a process of reflection on the internal coherence of the training project and its response to the cultural and scientific progress psychology has undergone since the course's establishment, as well as to the evolution of the profession and current job placement opportunities for graduates, also considering the territorial scope.

A new modification became necessary in the 2023-24 academic year for the inclusion of 20 CFU of Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) in the training path, in application of Law Decree 163/2021, which made the Master's Degree in Psychology qualifying.

The GAQ/Review Group conducted a thorough document analysis of the Course of Study's performance over the last three years, considering SUA-CdS, CPDS reports, SMA sheets, ANVUR indicator comments, student opinions (provided by the University PQA and emerging from direct consultations), graduate employment opinions (provided by AlmaLaurea), and consultation outcomes with social partners.

Following this analysis, the Course of Study training project was positively evaluated and still responsive to the set goals, so no changes were made to the definition of curricular learning areas (see Attachment) and the professional profiles of graduates, which remain responsive to current labor market dynamics and the latest developments in its requirements regarding the professional expenditure of the Psychology degree.

Brief Description of Affine and Integrative Activities In accordance with Ministerial guidelines, the Course of Study offers 12 CFU per curriculum dedicated to affine and integrative activities (TAF C) within the disciplinary areas of human and social sciences and biomedical sciences. The wide choice of courses allows students to personalize their professional profile following their individual interests and directives.

In particular, among humanities courses, those in philosophical and anthropological fields contribute to grounding knowledge of the main psychological theories on mind functioning, emotions, language, basic cognitive processes, and collective behavior organization, which find their historical roots in these disciplines. They also allow for deeper exploration and explanation of moral competence exhibited by humans, foundational to many socially relevant behaviors and general social functioning, as well as the social construction of concepts of normality and deviance and the complex interplay between social phenomena and collective representations.

Economic courses complete the basic theoretical training, enabling understanding of the connection and increasing contamination between economic rationality theory and psychology of reasoning and economic decision-making, as well as the role of intuition and emotional and affective components in decisions.

Sociological courses, on the other hand, contribute to achieving application-oriented goals, aimed at understanding the position occupied, function performed, and purpose served by law in society and how this influences and is influenced by the world of work. These courses also provide methodologies for organizing and planning services and skills for business development and improving entrepreneurial opportunities.

Biomedical area courses contribute to understanding human behavior from a bio-genetic and evolutionary perspective and refine clinical-diagnostic competencies in cases of mental and cognitive disorders due to altered psychological functioning in adults and children, or following brain injuries.

The offer is completed by a 4 CFU English language course aimed at equipping students with disciplinary vocabulary and dialogue, reading, and writing skills for overseas training experiences; as well as enabling them to independently consult international scientific literature, necessary for deepening study topics, also in preparation for the thesis, and for continuous updating once entering the world of work and profession.

Brief Course Description The Master's Degree Course in Psychology aims to train graduates with advanced cognitive, methodological, and operational tools in the macro-areas of cognitive and neuropsychology, developmental psychology, social psychology, work, and organizations. It is structured into three curricula named 'Cognitive Neuroscience', 'Developmental Psychology', and 'Social Psychology, Work, and Organizations', which share a strong theoretical foundation based on knowledge of classic psychology authors and theories, aligned with recent approaches, and a view of psychological functioning and human behavior as complex, systemic, dynamic, and multidimensional phenomena. The training path integrates theoretical knowledge with applied methodologies and practical tools for psychological and psychometric investigation, computer procedures for research data analysis, and the design and evaluation of specialized interventions directed at individuals, groups, communities, work contexts, and organizations. These skills are developed through teaching activities using active and interactive methodologies, including frontal lessons, seminars, laboratories, and guided practical experiences aimed at learning operational tools and preparing for the Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) experience.

English language competencies (B2 level) are also enhanced.

The training path is completed with courses in biomedical and humanistic areas, specific to the reference curriculum content, aimed at promoting students' knowledge in areas related to psychological training and allowing personalization of training goals.

Professional training for psychological intervention in the above-described curricular areas is carried out through a 20 CFU curricular internship, performed in external contracted structures for at least 14 CFU, under the supervision of an internal tutor at the structure, in accordance with the provisions of Law 163/2021 on qualifying degrees.

External Effectiveness Information on the employment prospects of the Master's Degree in Psychology primarily comes from the AlmaLaurea survey. However, it is important to refer to the programmatic document disseminated by CNOP for the 2020-24 national counseling, which highlights the critical relationship between the number of psychologists relative to the national population (one psychologist per 535 inhabitants), placing Italy at the global peak and essentially defining the difficulty for psychologists to quickly and effectively enter the workforce. Additionally, the document notes that, despite a good growth in the profession's market share over the last twenty years (+10% average annual), the average annual income is distributed very unevenly between older and younger professionals, with peaks of 19,000 Euros in the 60-65 age group and less than 6,000 in the under-30 group, placing it among the lowest for average income at one and five years (average 1,331.00 Euros/month).

Data from the 2022 survey show that only 29.5% of 61 surveyed graduates (61/79) found employment one year after graduation, compared to 53% of the national class. 22% work in the public sector, 66% in the private sector, and 11% in the non-profit sector; these data are fairly aligned with the national average, except for the non-profit sector where employment percentage doubled (20.3%). 33% have a fixed-term contract and the same percentage a training contract, 6% benefit from a scholarship or research grant. The average monthly salary is 965 Euros. These data are aligned with national averages. Only 33.3% perform work requiring a degree by law, but overall, a high percentage of employed individuals use their degree-acquired skills to a significant extent. 72% consider the professional training received very effective for their work, compared to 49% nationally; 7.3% are satisfied with their work (scale 1-10), in line with class values.

Even three years after graduation, the employment rate (63.8%) remains lower than the national class average (78.6%); employed individuals took an average of one year to find their first job, in line with the national average, during which they likely completed the professional internship. Monthly average net salary increases slightly to 1,136 Euros, still in line with the national average. 50% of employed individuals use their degree-acquired skills to a significant extent, and 7.8% (scale 1-10) are satisfied with their work.

The employment rate increases satisfactorily at five years after graduation (72%), but maintains the gap with the national average (84%). Employed individuals took about seven months to find their first job, in line with the national average. Monthly average net salary increases slightly (1,270 Euros) and remains slightly lower than the national average (1,387). Significantly higher, compared to the national average, is the percentage of employed individuals (73%) who perform work using their degree-acquired skills to a significant extent; the satisfaction level for their work (7.4% on scale 1-10) remains consistently high, again in line with the national average.

These data will be discussed in the first useful Course of Study Council.

In conclusion, the data offer a fairly positive picture; the first job for Psychology graduates is typically found in less than one year, fairly aligned with the national average, with a similarly high percentage (above 50-60%) of employed individuals using their degree-acquired skills to a significant extent at three and five years. The employment rate increases over time since graduation but remains consistently lower than the national average for Master's graduates in general. Regarding this, the latest AlmaLaurea report highlights that territorial differences remain significant, both in terms of residence and geographical distribution of study. Those residing in the North have a higher probability of being employed compared to those residing in the South; similarly, for geographical distribution of study, Psychology graduates from the North have a higher probability of finding employment compared to those who studied in the South.

The Course of Study is very active regarding exit orientation and placement events and initiatives (see Table B5) and maintains regular relationships with professionals in the sectors of interest for the curricula, facilitating contact between students and the local labor market.

Reasons for Establishing Multiple Courses in the Class The project to establish two Master's Degree courses, named Psychology and Clinical and Health Psychology, responds to the intent of offering two specific training and professionalizing paths: the first directed towards understanding psychological processes—cognitive, emotional, and social—that characterize mental functioning both individually and in groups, and the second more typically directed towards intervention in situations of psychological discomfort and suffering. Therefore, due to their different purpose, the two courses refer to rather different theoretical and methodological premises, more formative and general in the first case and more applied and experiential in the second. While the first course deepens the understanding of mechanisms guiding human behavior and its development, both typical and atypical, the second deepens the techniques and models of intervention used in the various and diverse areas of clinical psychology. It is believed, in accordance with DM 270, that offering two independent courses better responds to the specialist nature of the Master's Degree and better reflects the trend of psychology training at the national level. It is also believed that this offer allows for the formation of different professional profiles, facilitating easier entry into the labor market and providing more targeted preparatory training for the third level of education, consisting of specialized schools, master's degrees, and doctoral courses.

Finally, it is emphasized that the proposal for two differentiated and autonomous Master's paths meets the indications and guidelines present in the Europsy model, regarding suggestions for the second phase of training (equivalent to the Master's Degree) concerning student preparation for independent professional practice as a psychologist.

In the Europsy model, the professional areas of education, work, and organizations, and neuroscience, whether directed towards psychological practice or experimental research, are clearly distinct from the professional area of clinical and health psychology; therefore, the Europsy model suggests that the knowledge and specialized skills to be acquired, as well as internship activities and basic research skills, come from specific training curricula, respectively represented by the two different Master's Degree courses proposed.

Specific Training Objectives of the Course and Description of the Training Path The Master's Degree Course in Psychology provides advanced preparation for the psychological profession in various areas where it can be applied, such as cognitive psychology and psychobiology, developmental and educational psychology, social psychology, work, and organizations, with particular attention to training in the field of cognitive neuroscience and its applications in cognitive and emotional rehabilitation for adults and children and research in all the above-described areas. The specific objective is to train a psychology professional with solid theoretical foundations, capable of applying the methodology and tools of psychological and psychometric investigation, computer procedures for research data analysis; also capable of designing, implementing, and evaluating interventions directed at individuals, groups, communities, work contexts, and organizations, even in difficult and conflict situations, in full autonomy and in a collaborative manner, while being aware of the ethical aspects and issues related to professional activity. The training plan must also take into account the clinical dimension, both for the nosological framing of psychopathology in adults and in developmental age, and for the foundations of diagnosis and treatment.

The graduate also acquires advanced knowledge, in written and oral form, of at least one European Union language (English language) in addition to Italian, with reference to disciplinary lexicons, which they will have the opportunity to practice and refine, if necessary, in international mobility experiences (for study and traineeship) at sites with which an agreement has been established.

Specific training objectives are achieved through three differentiated curricula at the level of content of frontal teaching and practical/laboratory activities, traceable to different learning macro-areas. The curricula share characteristic activities aimed at maintaining a unified training perspective, with a core oriented towards a solid understanding of cognitive and neuropsychological processes underlying individual functioning, also in an evolutionary perspective, and towards a deep understanding of collective social functioning, community, and organizational, as well as the methodology for designing and intervening in these areas. Ample space is given to methodological aspects, psychological investigation tools, psychometric techniques, and data analysis. Students will have ample opportunity to personalize their curriculum by inserting optional affine disciplines consistent with their training-professional project and choosing characteristic disciplines to strengthen their preparation in a specific area of psychological activity.

Professional training objectives, necessary for obtaining the qualification for the profession, are achieved through practical training activities (20 CFU of TPV, DL 163/2021) contextualized and supervised, involving direct observation and execution of activities aimed at situated learning and development of procedural and relational skills fundamental to the profession. These activities include the application of tools and protocols for prevention, diagnosis, qualification/rehabilitation, and support in psychological contexts, directed at individuals across the lifespan, groups, communities, and social and work organizations. They also include the application of research protocols in the fields of neuroscience, neuropsychology, developmental and educational psychology, social psychology, and work psychology.

- Training objectives in the cognitive neuroscience area. Specific training objectives in this area consist of providing knowledge and skills in cognitive neuroscience, with specific reference to understanding typical and atypical cognitive functioning throughout the lifespan, and enhancing basic and higher cognitive functions and their recovery in case of dysfunction. These competencies are acquired through characteristic courses dedicated to deepening the main cognitive and affective processes—and their neural correlates—also in an evolutionary perspective, the methods and techniques used to study them, neuropsychological and mental disorders, and the methods for their evaluation and rehabilitation. The training path is further realized through knowledge and understanding of social and community phenomena useful for professional practice. Affine and integrative courses offer a range of choices between bio-genetic, neurophysiological-psychiatric, philosophical, and economic fields, allowing flexibility for the individual training project. The graduate expert in this area will be able to operate independently and interact with other professionals involved in caring for individuals, providing the contribution of psychological specificity to case reading and analysis, as well as to the appropriate use of investigation and intervention tools regarding behavioral and (neuro)cognitive-affective functioning.

- Training objectives in the development-education area. Specific training objectives in this area consist of providing knowledge and skills regarding psychological abilities and their functioning during the period from birth to school age, adolescence. Viewing human development as a multidimensional and dynamic phenomenon, specific objectives are achieved through characteristic courses on cognitive, communicative-linguistic, affective, social, and emotional development, studied in typical and at-risk conditions. These objectives are completed with advanced knowledge of the neural specialization and integration process in building the first development and knowledge and understanding of adaptation processes in school and psycho-social contexts. Competencies are also acquired on methodological tools for observing and evaluating abilities in the above-described areas. Biomedical area affine courses complete the knowledge of atypicalities in developmental age, regarding neurodevelopmental disorders and dysfunctional growth forms; a wide choice of courses in humanistic fields—philosophical, anthropological, pedagogical, sociological, economic—also allows for personalization of the training project. The graduate expert in this area will be able to operate independently and in collaboration with other figures in services offering consultation, planning, evaluation, and intervention on psychological issues in developmental age.

- Training objectives in the social-work-organizations area. Specific training objectives in this area consist of providing specialized knowledge of cognitive, affective, and behavioral aspects involved in interaction processes and intra-group and inter-group dynamics at various levels of social life, along with skills on methodological and technical tools necessary to enhance the capabilities and potential of individuals and groups in social, work, and organizational contexts, considering these as multidimensional and dynamic realities. The training path is structured in the characteristic disciplinary areas of social psychology, work and organizational psychology, cognitive psychology, and neuroscience, aiming to provide the theoretical and methodological tools necessary to analyze, interpret, and evaluate social behavior as the result of interaction between intraindividual cognitive and affective processes (attitudes, perception, language and communication, attributions, emotions) and contextual and situational variables, from the micro level (characteristics and dynamics of small groups-team) to the macro level of complex social and organizational systems. The training project is further directed towards knowledge and understanding of collective phenomena and the generative capacity of participatory processes, also aimed at shared decision-making. Competencies are also acquired for using appropriate tools for analysis, evaluation, and intervention in social, work, and organizational contexts. Affine and integrative training activities offer a range of choices among General Sociology, Business Economics and Management, Moral Philosophy, Genetics, ensuring flexible training for individualized project design. The graduate expert in this area will be able to carry out, in full professional autonomy and in collaboration with other figures, actions aimed at developing human potential and individual and collective empowerment; managing change and innovation in social, institutional, educational, and productive contexts; and evaluating and recovering psychological and psychosocial discomfort connected to aspects of community and work life.

Opinions of Entities and Companies with Stage/Internship Agreements Currently, 68 agreements are active for curricular internships (stages) with private entities, non-profits, and companies (30 in Abruzzo and 35 in other central-south regions).

Contracted structures host Course of Study students for a study-work alternation experience (Stage) lasting 100 hours (4 CFU) to be completed in no less than one month. These are entities operating mainly on the territory: a) social enterprises (third-sector enterprises such as non-profits, associations, committees, foundations, consortia, social cooperatives, etc.) registered with respective regional registers; b) public entities (ASL, Hospitals, Prisons, etc.); c) private companies contracted with public entities; d) private companies with a study-work alternation project consistent with the Stage's training objectives.

To monitor the effectiveness of the trainees' training, tutors complete a performance evaluation sheet for the trainees. A positive evaluation is an essential requirement for verbalizing the 4 CFU acquired through the Stage activity.

From the analysis of evaluation sheets, high satisfaction emerges regarding all reported items, such as the level of involvement in activities, the quality of the relationship with operators and service users. Evaluations from the last three years, on a scale from 1 (poor) to 4 (excellent), are generally very high (above 3.70) with a positive trend over the three years, indicating excellent appreciation.

The Stage is a regular agenda item for every Course of Study Council, and the progress of agreements and outcomes is continuously monitored.

Consultation with Organizations Representing Goods and Service Production, Professions (Course Establishment)
The Course of Study has established a permanent consultation table with representatives of the professional order, third-sector organizations, USL services in Pescara, Lanciano-Vasto, and Chieti, local productive companies, and national research institutions.

Consultations were conducted in dedicated meetings and through questionnaires, involving a total of 37 stakeholders distributed between private and third-sector representatives (17), hospital departments, research and training in neuropsychology, rehabilitation, neurosurgery, and psychiatry (11), hospital departments in obstetrics, neonatology, and neuropsychiatry, schools, and educational institutions (9).

The teaching offer was overall evaluated as valid and responsive to the needs of the present realities. Additionally, points for reflection and suggestions for improvement emerged, such as increasing the hours dedicated to practical exercises/laboratories, to be carried out outside the university and in collaboration with organizations representing production, services, research, and profession; 2) inclusion of at least one course of SSD-M-PSI/08 in the teaching offer. Proposals were presented and discussed with the Course of Study Council at the April 19, 2021 meeting.

The approval of the law decree on qualifying degrees (ex DL n.163/2021) enabled the implementation of all the above suggestions, with a partial modification of the teaching curriculum. A Practical Evaluation Internship (20 CFU) was thus introduced to be carried out predominantly (min. 14 CFU) in qualified external contracted structures, and a course in clinical psychology area was added to all curricula's teaching offer as an affine activity (TAF C). These modifications were agreed with the regional professional order, with whom two meetings were held (November 9 and December 14, 2022), and discussed at the table on February 6, 2023. Important suggestions were collected to improve the effectiveness of the training path for student placement in contracted structures. Participants particularly recommended strengthening the participation of qualified experts and professionals for the practical part of teaching courses (Guided Practical Experiences) and for the Practical Evaluation Internship quota provided by the Degree Course.

Consultation with Organizations Representing Goods and Service Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
Due to the curricular structure of the Course of Study, the consultation table with social partners and stakeholders gathers representatives of diversified working realities, in line with the profiles and professional outcomes of each curriculum.

Consultations began in 2014-15 and continued with sufficient regularity, involving new interlocutors over time based on changes to the training project, as detailed in previous SUA-CdS.

The method used for the consultation process achieved its purpose, obtaining useful information to direct training activities towards the interests of the labor market, while simultaneously creating interest in the professional profiles of the Course of Study graduates.

The first consultations led to modifications of the teaching offer plan (OF) with the introduction of a 4 CFU curricular internship (TAF F), the inclusion of a characteristic course (TAF B), already present in the curriculum of the Psychology of Groups, Communities, and Organizations, named 'Community Psychology and Social-Psychological Project Design' (SSD M-PSI/05), also in the study plans of the other two curricula with an associated practical application activity (EPG2 and EPG3) linked to this course (TAF F) and tailored to each curriculum's profile. Additionally, seminar activities led by representatives of the business world and third-sector associations were introduced during lessons to best combine theoretical knowledge with professional practice. It was also agreed that the strong potential of the Psychology of Groups, Communities, and Organizations curriculum in training and promoting a professional profile of interest to productive companies would be strengthened by focusing more on the area of work and organizational psychology with SSD M-PSI/06 courses.

The inclusion (2018) in the table of the responsible for the Cognitive Rehabilitation Service at the San Valentino Hospital (Prof. Stefano Sensi) and the Neurosurgery Operative Unit (UOC) at the Pescara Hospital (Prof. Annunziato Mangiola) facilitated the inclusion of a course dedicated to neuropsychological evaluation in the teaching offer. Consultation with the UOC Neurosurgery responsible also led to an expansion of the sites for curricular internship, with the addition, among contracted sites, of the Neurology Clinic at the Chieti PO (Responsible Prof. Marco Onofrj) and the Mental Health Department of the Lanciano-Vasto-Chieti USL (Responsible Prof. Massimo Di Giannantonio).

The consultation process described above and the preparation of the Cyclical Review Report stimulated a careful and in-depth reflection on the current relevance and validity of the Course of Study training project, leading to a proposal for curriculum modification, which redesigned the cultural and professional profile of Psychology graduates, with greater adherence to the characteristics and requirements of the labor market, also at the territorial level.

The new curriculum came into effect in the 2019-20 academic year, and a new consultation plan was scheduled for February 2020, but the unexpected health emergency due to the COVID-19 pandemic imposed a suspension of consultations. These resumed in September 2020 with an online questionnaire data collection, involving 37 stakeholders distributed between private and third-sector representatives (17), hospital departments, research and training in neuropsychology, rehabilitation, neurosurgery, and psychiatry (11), hospital departments in obstetrics, neonatology, and neuropsychiatry, schools, and educational institutions (9). The survey concerned: a) the correspondence between the professional profiles identified for the Course of Study and the expectations of the labor market; b) the coherence between the teaching activities framework, expected learning outcomes, and the professional profiles identified by the Course of Study; c) the actual interest of the labor sectors towards the professional profiles for which the training is directed. The survey results highlighted strengths and criticalities discussed in a remote meeting on November 23, 2021, attended by 15 stakeholders and GAQ Course of Study members. At this meeting, some points for reflection and suggestions for improving the OF emerged. In particular, the redefinition of some courses, the introduction of a clinical psychology course (SSD M-PSI/08) in all curricula's teaching offer as an affine activity (TAF C), and increasing, in each characteristic course, the hours dedicated to practical exercises/laboratories, to be carried out outside the university and in collaboration with organizations representing production, services, research, and profession. Proposals were presented and discussed with the Course of Study Council at the April 14, 2021 meeting.

The approval of the law decree on qualifying degrees (D.L. n. 163/2021) enabled the implementation of all the above suggestions, with a new partial modification of the teaching curriculum. A Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) (20 CFU) was thus introduced to be carried out predominantly (min. 14 CFU) in qualified external contracted structures, and a course of SSD M-PSI/08 (Clinical Psychology) was added to all curricula's teaching offer as an affine activity (TAF C). These modifications were agreed with the regional professional order, with whom two meetings were held (November 9 and December 14, 2022), and discussed at the table in two sessions on February 6 and 13, 2023, attended by a total of 20 representatives of productive companies, employment agencies, hospital services, IRRCS, research and training institutions. Important suggestions were collected to improve the effectiveness of the training path for student placement in contracted structures for the internship. Participants particularly recommended strengthening the participation of qualified experts and professionals for the practical part of teaching courses (Guided Practical Experiences) and for the TPV quota provided by the Degree Course (≤ 6 CFU).

Following these suggestions, starting from the 2023-24 academic year, internal TPV activities with mandatory attendance have been introduced in the OF, carried out by both structural teachers and highly qualified external professionals. They are delivered in the form of (1) Supervised Practical Experiences (EPS), i.e., 1 CFU modules for in-depth study of specific professional aspects or the use of professional tools; and (2) Supervised Laboratory Activities (ALS), i.e., practical supervised activities to be carried out within the Degree Course's Laboratory for a number of CFU to be agreed with the laboratory's responsible teacher.

The Course of Study has planned for autumn 2024, at the end of the first year of the new qualifying degree and thus the first activation of EPS and ALS, a new consultation with social partners and stakeholders aimed at presenting the numerous internal TPV activities in the OF and their progress; at the same time, the Course of Study intends to present the new regulation for external TPV, which will be activated in the 2024-25 academic year and carried out in the second semester of the second year. This consultation will provide important feedback on the quality of promoted actions and the organization and implementation of both internal and external TPV. Additionally, it will allow for the potential inclusion of new EPS in the OF to be approved in subsequent months.

The consultation will take place in two meetings, one for stakeholders of the "Cognitive Neuroscience" and "Developmental Psychology" curricula and one for stakeholders of the "Social Psychology, Work, and Organizations" curriculum, which differ substantially from others as they mainly involve companies and third-sector entities.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data The number of students enrolled in the Course of Study in the 2022-23 academic year amounts to 80 units out of a total of 292 enrolled, of which 194 in course, 89 out of course, and 192 regular. More than 50% of new students come from a region different from the university location, and almost all have obtained a high school diploma. The enrollment trend is declining compared to the previous academic year (112 units), and this data might indicate that graduates have postponed enrollment in the Master's Degree for one year to enroll in the new qualifying Course of Study effective in 2023-24. Regarding the 2021-22 cohort, students took an average of 6 exams in 2021 and acquired 69% of the total CFU; students from 2022 took an average of 3 exams and acquired 36% of the total CFU. These data might reflect a generalized difficulty, widespread across the university, linked to pandemic fatigue that has particularly affected younger population groups, significantly increasing psychological distress. This could be compounded by difficulty adapting socially and to the university environment.

24% of the 2020-21 cohort continued in the same course for the second year; of these, 48.78% acquired more than 40 CFU in the first year of the course; 12% acquired less than 20 CFU, and 6.5% was inactive with 0 CFU; 57.72% passed exams with an average grade between 28 and 30, while 26.8% with an average grade between 24 and 27.

In the calendar year 2022, 90 students graduated, of whom 64% on time, with a delay index of 0.21 (AlmaLaurea data), stable compared to the previous year; the percentage of those graduating with two years of delay remains stable at 10%. To improve the regularity of the study path, the Course of Study has implemented a monitoring of enrolled students' careers since the 2018-19 academic year, within the framework of ongoing orientation, identifying students with significant delays in passing exams early and offering them necessary support to remain in course (see Table B5 "Ongoing Orientation"). However, the number of students who have undergone re-orientation and support meetings in the last two years has been low, preventing the service from functioning well.

The good academic performance of students is reflected in the average graduation grade (AlmaLaurea 2022 data), which is 109.6 with an average exam grade of 28.

These data will be discussed in the first useful Course of Study Council.

Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam for the Master's Degree in Psychology – class LM-51 – qualifies for the exercise of the psychologist profession (pursuant to Articles 1 and 3 of Law n. 163/2021) and includes the completion of a practical evaluation of professional skills acquired through the internship within the course of study, following the acquisition of the relevant qualification.

The final exam further consists of the presentation and discussion of the thesis, elaborated originally by the student under the guidance of a teacher teaching the subject of the thesis and acting as supervisor.

The thesis is the concluding product of the Master's Degree career, implying the acquisition and mastery of the skills necessary for conducting independent research and in-depth work in the psychological field. These skills concern: - the reasoned choice of a relevant topic in psychological research and theory; - critical understanding of specific literature, particularly the theoretical and methodological issues characterizing the chosen topic; - the realization of empirical work through scientific investigation methodologies; - autonomous use of tools for data collection and subsequent statistical analysis; - logical and linguistic competence necessary for the oral and written presentation of the work done.

The thesis is then submitted to the evaluation of another teacher expert in the subject, acting as co-supervisor.

Final Exam Procedure The qualifying practical evaluation (PPV) for the exercise of the psychologist profession is unique and conducted orally. It focuses on the activities carried out during the Practical Evaluation Internship (TPV) and the links between theories/models and professional practices, as well as aspects of legislation and professional ethics. Successfully passing the PPV is a requirement for admission to the final degree exam.

The final exam consists of the presentation and discussion of the thesis, elaborated originally by the student under the guidance of a teacher teaching the subject of the thesis and acting as supervisor. The thesis is then submitted to the evaluation of another teacher expert in the subject, acting as co-supervisor. The final exam is conducted, by legal obligation, in public form; each candidate has approximately 10 minutes for the oral presentation of the thesis work, with the possible use of audiovisual means, and 5 minutes for discussion, during which they respond to questions from the co-supervisor and the committee. The thesis can also be written in English, with prior authorization from the Course of Study Council, and must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian.

The Degree Committee assigns the graduation grade to the candidate considering the overall progression of their career, the thesis content, and the quality of the presentation.

The starting score is the weighted average of the grades obtained in passing exams, converted to a hundredth [(average exams × 11) ÷ 3], rounded to the nearest integer (n ≤ 0.5 for rounding down, n > 0.5 for rounding up).

The Degree Committee can assign up to 6 points for the final exam, considering the following indicators:
a) Originality and relevance of the contribution within the reference disciplinary field;
b) Overall quality of the work (accuracy, methodology, bibliography);
c) Quality and clarity of the written work (structure, composition, language property);
d) Quality and clarity of the presentation (exposition, language property, relevance);
e) Mastery of the problem as emerges from the presentation and discussion;
f) Completeness of the treatment as emerges from the presentation and discussion.

Each indicator is evaluated by the Degree Committee based on the following criteria:
- Sufficient if necessary and sufficient elements are present: 1 pt
- Fair if identifiable interesting elements are present: 2 pt
- Good if identifiable appreciable elements are present: 3 pt
- Distinct if identifiable meritorious elements are present: 4 pt
- Excellent if identifiable relevant elements are present: 5 pt
- Outstanding if identifiable notable elements are present: 6 pt

Candidates with a starting score of at least 103 points may receive an additional 2 points (maximum) for academic merit for the following reasons:
- Thesis discussion within the legal duration of the course: 1 pt
- Participation in international mobility programs (training activities for at least 12 CFU or internship of at least 2 months within Erasmus Study, Erasmus Traineeship, Overseas programs, or study/research activities documented at foreign institutions for the purpose of writing the Master's Thesis): 1 pt

The total score thus determined expresses the joint judgment of the Degree Committee.

The graduation grade (starting score + committee score) is expressed in hundredths, and the exam is considered passed with a minimum grade of 66/110.

Honors (Lode) may be awarded, with the unanimous opinion of the Committee, upon request (motivated and argued in detail) by the supervisor and supported by the co-supervisor, to candidates who achieve a score of at least 110/110. Even with equal or higher scores, honors are awarded only in cases of high scientific and/or methodological quality of the work recognized unanimously by the Committee.

STUDY PLANS INFORMATION General information regarding the current academic year Duration 2 years Regulation 2017 Status Open Credits 120 CFU Language Italian Type Master's Degree Course Regulation Reform 270/04 Degree Class LM-87 - Class of Master's Degrees in Social Services and Social Policies Interuniversity Course No Open Access Location CHIETI (Sustainable User Capacity: 59) Department DEPARTMENT OF BUSINESS ECONOMICS Website https://www.dea.unich.it/

Admission Requirements Required Knowledge for Access In reference to the curricular requirements, all holders of a three-year degree in Social Services (L-39), or another degree obtained abroad, recognized as suitable, are admitted to enrollment in the master's degree program in Policies and Management for Welfare (LM-87).

Additionally, candidates holding any three-year degree or foreign equivalent degree, who possess a total of 30 CFU in one or more of the following scientific-disciplinary sectors (SSD): SPS/07, SPS/08, SPS/09, SECS-P/07, SECS-S/01, SECS-S/05, SECS-S/06, M-PSI/04, M-PSI/05, M-PSI/06, M-PED/01, M-DEA/01, IUS/09, IUS/17, IUS/10, SPS/02, SPS/03, SPS/04, SPS/06, SECS-P/02, SECS-P/10, with a minimum of one third of CFU in sociological sectors as professionalizing for the type of studies, and the remaining CFU in other sectors, may enroll in the Master's Degree Program in Policies and Management for Welfare (LM-87).

In reference to the assessment of the candidate's personal preparation, admission to the study program in Policies and Management for Welfare (LM-87) is subject to evaluation through an interview by a Commission appointed by the Course Council.

If the Commission deems the graduate's knowledge and skills sufficient, it issues a suitability judgment allowing enrollment.

Candidates who have achieved a grade of at least 80/110 are exempt from the interview to ensure the possession of the required qualifications and preparation. This minimum threshold is set at 80/110.

If the candidate's curricular level and knowledge, while deemed suitable by the Commission, are still considered to require further deepening, the Commission may allow enrollment by directing the candidate to a personalized path for the acquisition of additional knowledge and skills deemed necessary for successful enrollment in the Master's Degree Program, through the deepening of subjects indicated by the Commission, with appropriate assessments.

For all matters not covered in this article, refer to the current regulations and the University Teaching Regulations.

Admission Methods In reference to the curricular requirements, all holders of a three-year degree in Social Services (Italian or foreign, regardless of denomination or recognized equivalent by the Course Council), are admitted to enrollment in the master's degree program in Policies and Management for Welfare (LM-87).

Additionally, candidates holding any three-year degree or equivalent Italian or foreign degree, who possess a total of 30 CFU in one or more of the following scientific-disciplinary sectors (SSD): SPS/07, SPS/08, SPS/09, SECS-P/07, SECS-S/01, SECS-S/05, SECS-S/06, M-PSI/04, M-PSI/05, M-PSI/06, M-PED/01, M-DEA/01, IUS/09, IUS/17, IUS/10, SPS/02, SPS/03, SPS/04, SPS/06, SECS-P/02, SECS-P/10, with a minimum of one third of CFU in sociological sectors as professionalizing for the type of studies, and the remaining CFU in other sectors, may enroll in the Master's Degree Program in Policies and Management for Welfare (LM-87).

In reference to the assessment of the candidate's personal preparation, admission to the study program in Policies and Management for Welfare (LM-87) is subject to evaluation through an interview by a Commission appointed by the Department Council.

If the Commission deems the graduate's knowledge and skills sufficient, it issues a suitability judgment allowing enrollment.

Candidates who have achieved a grade of at least 80/110 are exempt from the interview to ensure the possession of the required qualifications and preparation. This minimum threshold is set at 80/110.

If the candidate's curricular level and knowledge, while deemed suitable by the Commission, are still considered to require further deepening, the Commission may allow enrollment by directing the candidate to a personalized path for the acquisition of additional knowledge and skills deemed necessary for successful enrollment in the Master's Degree Program, through the deepening of subjects indicated by the Commission, with appropriate assessments.

Program, texts and objectives Note regarding the selected sectors and credits for characterizing activities The scope of the characterizing field "Psychopedagogical, anthropological and philosophical disciplines" is determined by the logic of strengthening courses that have a functional vocation for managing socio-cultural complexity and diversity in welfare systems.
Communication skills
The graduate possesses the following skills:
- Management and control of the internal and external communication area, understood as a set of areas for the production, circulation and consumption of information products, whose central function is that of service;
- Competent communication regarding the performance of the profession (projects, research reports, documents);
- Competent communication in the use of information technologies Communication skills will be acquired through theoretical courses in sociology, pedagogy, psychology, and professional methodology, as well as through an internship.
The verification of communication skills acquisition occurs through the evaluation of the student's comprehension, exposition and argumentation abilities within the training activities, internship and final exam, as well as through the evaluation of the reports and written documents prepared by the student within the individual activities that require them.

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgements)
The graduate must possess solid theoretical knowledge and develop skills and abilities useful for managing complexity and formulating judgments with full autonomy, even based on limited or incomplete information, while fully respecting the protocols of research and social action.
The autonomy of judgment is monitored through:
- assessment methods, oral and/or written, planned during and at the end of the courses;
- assessment methods for professionalizing experiences through the organization of seminars and workshops using innovative teaching methodologies and other high-level training activities;
- verification of internship activities through the presentation and discussion of a report by the students;
- verification of the final exam through the discussion of a compilation and/or experimental work.

Training Periods Administrative Contact: Cinzia Colangelo (ufficio.tirociniclass@unich.it)
The Course of Study provides for the completion of curricular internships for 10 CFU in the field of social service and assistance professions. These activities represent the completion of the theoretical and practical training provided by the study path through direct contact with occupational realities where students will exercise their profession. For the internship, the Course of Study has specific conventions with public or private entities operating in the social intervention, socio-assistive, and socio-health areas. The entities and organizations where students carry out their internships are mainly those with a socio-health vocation, socio-assistive welfare, local welfare, and, more generally, those operating in the welfare area.
The Course of Study assists students in carrying out internships through a dedicated service that handles the signing of new conventions and collects and analyzes the evaluation forms completed by the tutor to assess the effectiveness of the internship.
Assistance for carrying out internships includes:
1) Reception in Front Office and Back Office with the parties interested in the internship activity;
2) Promotion of new conventions;
3) Support and maintenance of relationships with the conventioned structures;
4) Collection and management of forms and documentation related to the activation of the internship;
5) Coordination with the external supervisor of the hosting entity/organization;
6) Assistance/accompaniment to the intern for the elaboration of the internship training project by the responsible Academic Tutor.
All Academic Teachers of the Course Council are academic tutors for the various internships. All information and necessary documentation to activate and manage the internship are provided through a dedicated section on the Course website, which also lists the conventioned entities:
https://pmw.unich.it/pagina-enti-convenzionati-e-modulistica-attivazione-nuove-convenzioni-1058
The Course of Study has over 300 active conventions with various local entities, national associations, cooperatives, including the following: ASL 1 of Avezzano-Sulmona-L'Aquila, ASL 2 of Lanciano-Chieti, the Municipality of Chieti, the Prefecture of Chieti, ANFFAS, the Municipality of Pescara, the Province of Pescara, the Union of Municipalities of Vomano, the Basilicata Region, various juvenile prisons, ASL of Benevento, and numerous Italian municipalities.
Between January and December 2023, 48 students started their internship, none abroad.

Student Opinions Compared to 2020/21, the satisfaction index shows a mean of 3.62. It remains at very good levels and in line with the previous year (3.55). Specifically, the percentage of courses with an average rating of 3.5 or higher (Band A) has slightly decreased from 89% to 75%.
The following specific evaluations are highlighted:
- level of interest in course topics: 3.59;
- study load required for individual courses proportional to assigned credits: 3.55;
- adequacy of teaching materials for studying the subject: 3.61;
- consistency between taught courses and those declared on the CdS website: 3.64;
- adherence to class schedules by instructors: 3.66;
- clarity in defining exam modalities: 3.64;
- instructor's ability to stimulate and motivate students toward the discipline: 3.65;
- instructor's ability to present topics appropriately according to subject complexity: 3.48;
- instructor's availability during lessons and office hours to clarify topics covered: 3.66.
Although slightly lower than 2020/21, these evaluations do not indicate issues, remaining within the upper range of the University's Band A ratings.
The CdS has activated the Teaching Commission, aimed at analyzing the alignment of various Syllabi with the training objectives specified in the Dublin Descriptors, as well as the consistency between the information on the CdS website regarding courses and the Syllabi. The evaluations expressed by students confirm the effectiveness of this synergy. Beyond the Teaching Commission, student opinions are presented and discussed within the Department's AQ Group, the Course Council, to identify appropriate corrective actions and reorganize the academic calendar. The 2021/22 opinions were discussed in the Course Council meetings of September 11, 2023.
This comparison is also conducted by considering the observations from the CPDS, which reports to the Department on student observations, as well as the presence of student representatives in Councils and the AQ Group. The observations are nearly minimal and concern some difficulties encountered by individual students in completing internships.
The CdS, to manage emerging issues, through the Course Director accepts student complaints via the following communication channels: francesco.ferzetti@unich.it and didattica.dea@unich.it.
