Graduate Opinions The data regarding graduate opinions were extracted from Almalaurea (updated as of April 2023) and integrated with University statistics. The Almalaurea survey covers 92% of total graduates in the calendar year 2022, amounting to 38.
Regarding study duration, 65.6% of respondents, compared to 69.4% in 2021, graduated on time, while 18.8%, compared to 22.6% in 2021, obtained their degree one year after the planned course duration. This data shows a slight decline in the regularity of the academic path.
83% of respondents (89% in 2021; 89% University average) considered the teaching load generally appropriate for the study duration, while the percentage of graduates overall satisfied with the relationship with professors decreased to 88.6% (95.4% in 2021; 92.3% University average).
Adequate and above University average appreciation was noted for classrooms, laboratories, and computer equipment, respectively at 89.3% (80% University average), 86.7% (72.5% University average), and 61.5% (53% University average).
The proportion of graduates overall satisfied with exam organization increased from 82.8% in 2021 to 85.7% (86% University average). In summary, the percentage of graduates who are definitely or more satisfied with the course of study rose to 83% (90% University average) from 81.2% in 2021. Indeed, 71.4%, compared to 68.8% in 2021, would enroll again in the same course at the University (73.7% University average). The increase in these data positively rewards the course of study.
The data related to previous analyses were discussed in the course of study on September 13, 2022; the data from the latest analyses are discussed in the course of study on September 11, 2023.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The planned training path enables the Master's graduate to acquire the following knowledge, skills, and abilities:
- Define, coordinate, and lead programs and projects in the field of social services and high-level socio-health integration;
- Plan, organize, and manage actions, projects, and interventions in the field of social policies and services from a managerial perspective;
- Direct services managing complex interventions in the social field;
- Design and conduct analyses and research on the territory, also in sociological contexts, with knowledge of methods and techniques of social research and social services;
- Conduct qualitative and quantitative evaluations of interventions, services, and social policies;
- Apply knowledge and techniques related to quality assessment systems for services.
- Design governance, accountability, organizational, and communication systems in social enterprises and other civil society organizations;
- Design governance, accountability, organizational, and social communication systems in the areas of reference of public administrations;
Didactic tools aimed at achieving the ability to apply knowledge include, besides the set of teaching activities (frontal lessons, self-learning, etc.), practical internship activities. Other fundamental tools are represented by the use of computer tools, consultation and/or processing of databases, bibliographic research, text research, and thesis preparation for the final exam.
Verification methods for learning outcomes consist of:
- Oral and/or written exams, scheduled during and/or at the end of courses;
- Internship activities through presentation and discussion of periodic reports (direct and indirect internship) by students;
- Final exam through discussion of a written report.

Learning Skills (learning skills)
During the training path, the graduate develops learning and self-learning abilities through processing information acquired via activation of interpretive schemes, connected to previous knowledge and experiences, leading to modification of their own schemes, reasoning in a pluriparadigmatic way, formulating hypotheses and anticipations, with the ability to construct an adequate mental representation for problem solving in front of a problem.
The graduate also develops learning and self-learning abilities, particularly reflecting on these, through the ability to interact and share meaning construction processes, developing metacognitive abilities.
The graduate is accompanied in learning conceived as an active and personal declination of knowledge.

Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Graduates will achieve:
- Advanced knowledge of sociology, social research methodology, and social services;
- Advanced knowledge in economic-legal, mathematical-computer, psycho-pedagogical, anthropological, and historical disciplines;
- Knowledge of the socio-economic context of reference with application of sociological quantitative and qualitative analysis models;
- Advanced knowledge for designing interventions and services in the social field within a broad framework of integration between policies;
- High ability to forecast, read, and analyze social phenomena;
Verification of learning outcomes occurs through:
- Verification methods, oral and/or written, scheduled during and at the end of courses;
- Professionalizing experiences with seminars and laboratories using innovative teaching methodologies and other high-level training activities;
- Verification of internship activities through presentation and discussion of a report by students;
- Verification of the final exam through discussion of a compilative and/or experimental report.

Organizational Structure and Responsibilities at University Level The Quality Assurance Office plays a central role in promoting the culture of Quality and Quality Assurance (QA), ensuring compliance with the Quality Assurance Requirements set forth in Annex C of Ministerial Decree 30 January 2013, n. 47.
For the QA of study courses, in particular, it organizes and verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-CdS of each study course at the University; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for teaching activities in accordance with planned and declared procedures; regulates and verifies periodic course review activities; evaluates the effectiveness of improvement interventions and their actual consequences; ensures correct information flow to and from the Evaluation Unit and the Parity Committees of teachers and students.
For the QA of departmental research, in particular, it verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-RD of each Department; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for research activities in accordance with planned and declared procedures; ensures correct information flow to and from the Evaluation Unit.
The Quality Assurance Office is composed of the Rector's delegate for 'Quality', a full-time professor of the first rank who has opted for full-time work, responsible for overseeing the Office's activities, along with three professors of the first rank belonging to the following ERC (European Research Council) fields: Physical Sciences & Engineering; Social Sciences & Humanities; Life Sciences.

Organization and Responsibilities for QA at Course Level Course Coordinator for ReAQD: Prof. Daniela Di Berardino The Department of Business Economics has established within itself a system of bodies and committees involved in the Quality Assurance process for study courses and in managing the primary processes of the courses affiliated with the Department.
This system is structured into bodies with specific competencies and responsibilities for QA, being involved in monitoring the primary processes connected to teaching. These bodies are listed below:

Course Coordinator: Prof. FRANCESCO FERZETTI
Responsibility: Coordinates the QA system of the course and oversees compliance with obligations set forth by regulations, with the collaboration of the Quality Assurance Committee/Group, the Parity Committee of Teachers and Students (CPDS), in accordance with the guidelines of the University's central bodies on QA and the directions of ANVUR. The Coordinator, with the collaboration of the QA Group, leads the cyclical and annual review of the course, drafting the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA) and the Cyclical Review Report (RRC), and proceeds with the insertion of the SUA-CdS, with the collaboration of the QA Group. According to annual deadlines, it handles teaching coverage and redefines the training path and objectives, based on periodic consultations with social partners. Finally, it promotes a quality-oriented culture within the Course Council.

Quality Assurance Committee/Group and Review Group
Composition: Course Coordinator, AQ Coordinator at the Department of Business Economics (Prof. Daniela Di Berardino), Department professors (Prof. Maria Teresa Giusti and Prof. Stefano Camillo Pasotti), a student representative, a technical-administrative staff representative (Cinzia Colangelo).
Responsibility: The QA and Review Group oversees the quality management policy of the course; specifically, the coordinator manages all quality activities and the specific committees established within the Department for monitoring the primary processes of the course. The coordinator also maintains direct relationships with the PQA and the Parity Committee of Teachers and Students. The Course Coordinator is constantly updated on the activities of the Department committees. The QA Group as a whole oversees compliance with the quality policy, regulations, and rules, in line with PQA guidelines and ANVUR directions, proceeding with periodic monitoring of indicators, analysis of criticalities, evaluation of possible improvement actions, convening active Department committees for information on requirements from AVA 3. The QA Group collaborates in drafting the SUA-CdS, SMA, and RRC.

Parity Committee of Teachers and Students
Composition: Committee Coordinator and course professor (Prof. Antonio D'Andreamatteo), a course professor, and a student representative.
Responsibility: The committee monitors the training offer, teaching quality, and contextual services provided to students by professors and structures, with particular emphasis on criticalities, which are periodically communicated to the Course Coordinator, the Course Council, and the Department's Teaching AQ Coordinator.

Course Council
Composition: Professors responsible for courses and student representatives enrolled in the course, elected according to the procedures set forth in the University's General Regulations.
Responsibility: The Council deliberates on the content of the SUA, the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA), and evaluates and deliberates on the related improvement proposals identified by the Course Coordinator and the QA Committee; periodically, it deliberates on the content of the Cyclical Review Report (RRC); collaborates in implementing the quality improvement policies of the course.

The quality policy in the course is also exercised through decentralized activities within the committees activated in the Department as follows:
- Teaching Committee: Members are professors responsible for scientific areas represented in the training path; it harmonizes teaching programs and evaluates the quality of the training offer, as well as verifies the completeness of syllabi inserted by professors;
- Orientation Committee (divided into entry, mid-course, exit, and placement): Evaluates student opinions on tutoring initiatives, monitors careers, welcomes and guides new students, monitors the effectiveness of curricular internships and placement, plans and evaluates the effectiveness of support services for entering the workforce;
- International Relations Committee: Coordinates services for student mobility, provides support and orientation for Erasmus students;
- Relations with Territory Committee, Steering Committee, and Course Coordinator: Monitors employment effectiveness, consults social partners, redefines training offer, activates agreements;
- Communication Committee: Coordinates contextual services supporting students, updates information documentation on the course (student guide, course functioning, e-learning platform, social networks, department website), manages relations with media;
- Credit Recognition Committee: Verifies access and admission requirements to the course. The Academic Secretariat and the Department Internship Office also collaborate in acquiring information.

Work Planning and Implementation Deadlines for Initiatives The QA Committee meets periodically, according to the schedule summarized in the attached model, to carry out the following activities:
- Within the appropriate timeframes for entering information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), SMA (October-December), and RRC (at least 3 months before internal deadlines), proceed with hearing the specific Department Committees regarding the implementation of QA within the course;
- Within the appropriate timeframes for entering information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), SMA (October-December), and RRC (at least 3 months before internal deadlines), proceed with analyzing and evaluating interventions aimed at continuous improvement of the course in various organizational aspects, monitoring teaching indicators, with particular reference to student, graduate, and candidate opinions, contextual services, external effectiveness of the study course, Erasmus path, effectiveness of curricular internships, and results of actions taken.
The reference indicators are drawn from the Department Strategic Plan (% students out of course contacted; % recovered out of course, enrolled, internationalization), from internal surveys by the Internship Office and the Orientation Committee (student opinions; opinions of organizations and companies; career monitoring, quality forum results), and from analyses provided by the University's Applied and Teaching Department (enrolments, career monitoring, student opinions, employment).

- Within the appropriate timeframes for entering information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), collegial meetings for final discussion of frameworks and drafting the SUA;
- Between February and May, coordinate with the Course Coordinator to redefine specific training objectives of the course, based on consultations with social partners, for defining the requirements necessary for teaching coverage and programming the training offer. Based on indications from the Evaluation Unit and the Teaching Delegate, the Department AQ Coordinator will liaise with the Course Coordinator before approving the training offer to allow timely verification regarding the sustainability of the course and the consistency of training objectives with the planned offer, also verifying the effectiveness of elective courses in the course, with biennial checks;
- By the annual deadline set by the PQA (October-December), at least two meetings for analyzing SMA indicators and evaluating causes and improvement proposals;
- Periodically, verify the correctness and proper insertion of syllabi, in concert with the Teaching Committee;
- Periodically, through the Coordinator of the QA/Review Group and the Course Coordinator, promote a quality culture within the course, both within Councils and through periodic communications to Department committees, as well as participating in training events related to the requirements for course quality.

Improvement initiatives emerging from periodic meetings are periodically highlighted in the Course Council to plan improvement actions, as evidenced by the minutes of the Course Council meetings.

Brief Course Description The Course of Study in Policies and Management for Welfare is aimed at training specialist social assistants, achieved through the structuring and offering of a theoretical and practical training path capable of integrating sociological, economic, legal, and pedagogical profiles.
This path also benefits from an additional strengthening of its training potential through knowledge and skills acquired within curricular internships and activities useful for entering the workforce. Therefore, the training path is appropriately oriented towards acquiring high-level abilities for analyzing and interpreting social phenomena relevant to welfare, for the planning, design, organization, managerial management, and evaluation of social and socio-health services, within the context of interventions, services, and social policies.

External Effectiveness The data provided by Alma Laurea for 2022 on the employment rate of graduates (updated as of April 2023) one year after obtaining the degree describes a generally stable situation compared to the previous year for the 45 respondents, amounting to 68.2% of graduates (66), with a slight decrease in employed individuals only in the first year after graduation.
Indeed, 60% of respondents report working one year after graduation; 80% report working three years after graduation; 91.7% report working five years after graduation. All percentages are higher than the University average. The data indicates an excellent increase at three years after graduation with an increased employment opportunity at five years after graduation.
Graduates who report using acquired competencies at a high level in their work are 48.1% one year after obtaining the degree; 50% at three years; and 72.7% at five years (57.1% total University class average at five years).
The average monthly salary one year after graduation is, on average, €1,076 for both women and men; at five years after graduation, it is on average €1,301.
On a scale from 1 to 10, job satisfaction at five years after graduation is 8.2 (8.0 at University); 7.8 one year and 7.4 two years after graduation.
100% of respondents, in work started before graduation, noted an improvement in professional skills.
25.9% of respondents have an indefinite-term contract, while the majority of employed individuals (55.6%) have a fixed-term contract; 7.4% have a training contract; 3.7% are self-employed; 3.7% continue in the research sector with a scholarship or research grant.
One year after the degree, the majority of respondents (40.7%) work in the private sector, the same percentage (40.7%) works in the non-profit sector, while 18.5% works in the public sector.
The considered indicators, examined as a whole, confirm the good ability of the Master's Course in Policies and Management for Welfare to form skills useful for entering the workforce, in line with the course's professionalizing vocation. Furthermore, the data confirms the course's attractive capabilities and its effectiveness compared to national data and the University average.
Data for the year 2021 was discussed in the Course of Study on September 13, 2022. For 2022 data, the reference minutes are from the Course of Study on September 11, 2023.

Specific Training Objectives and Description of the Training Path Graduates of the Master's Degree Course in 'Policies and Management for Welfare' must:
1. Acquire advanced knowledge in the fields of sociological, economic, legal, mathematical-statistical, and computer disciplines for decision-making and pedagogical purposes.
2. Possess advanced knowledge of models, methods, and techniques for evaluation in social sciences.
3. Possess advanced methodological knowledge of applied management for local welfare systems.
4. Possess a high ability to analyze and interpret social phenomena through a multidisciplinary approach to the disciplines provided.
5. Possess advanced knowledge of methods for designing, defining, and conducting social analyses and investigations on people, organizations, companies, and territories.
6. Possess advanced knowledge of the fields of knowledge and intervention of the social assistant.
7. Possess knowledge of social reporting.
8. Possess methodological knowledge and advanced skills related to scenario analysis, governance, planning, programming, management, and control of organizations and companies operating in welfare systems (Public Administrations, private companies operating in service sectors, civil society organizations).
9. Be able to use at least one European Union language, in addition to their own, with particular regard to terminology specific to the social field.
Depending on the number of students enrolled in the course and emerging professional needs, differentiated study paths may open.
In addition to theoretical lessons, exercises, and training internships at public bodies, private for-profit companies, and civil society organizations, further knowledge useful for entering the workforce is provided.
The two-year Master's study path is structured following a training path that initially focuses on sociological and social service disciplines, identified in the study of research methods, planning, programming, and evaluation for social management and planning. Subsequently, the path proposes psycho-pedagogical, anthropological, socio-historical, philosophical, and ethical-deontological disciplines, legal and political-managerial disciplines, and internship activities. Language knowledge completes the path.

Opinions of Organizations and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements The Course of Study provides curricular training internships for which students have an initial contact with services and bodies where their professional work will be carried out. Internships are conducted at public and private bodies operating in welfare systems; specifically in the area of social intervention, socio-assistential, and socio-health sectors. Local Authorities, ASLs, territorial health services, and Third Sector organizations are involved in the training internship. The Course of Study has over ninety active agreements with public and social private organizations for conducting internships.
Internship activities are designed to place students in contact with the fields and sectors connected to the profession of the Specialist Social Assistant. The bodies most interested in which students have carried out internships are those with a social, socio-health, and socio-assistential vocation.
The internship experience is evaluated through a personal sheet completed for each student at the end of training. The sheet allows for recording student opinions, as well as opinions and judgments of the internal tutor at the host body. Completion of the sheet precedes access to the internship exam by the competent evaluation committee of the Course of Study.
Number of internship students: 47. Analysis of data collected via each student's personal sheet highlights very positive evaluations. Values related to the intern's motivation for carrying out the internship exceed 90%. Positive judgments expressed regarding basic competencies possessed by students exceed 90%, as do those for transversal competencies and expectations regarding the internship activity. Indicators show similar trends regarding personal commitment, integration into the work environment, relational skills demonstrated by the student, involvement in the host body's activities, and autonomy.
Students have shown excellent relationships with the host body and the objectives set by the training project have been successfully achieved. The data examined is confirmed also regarding the host body's judgment of the internship activity, considered very useful by 77.4% of bodies and useful for the remaining 22.6%. Values are confirmed in the overall evaluation of the internship experience: rated very satisfactory in 91% of cases and satisfactory in 9%. Judgments expressed by tutors on individual students followed are very positive in all cases. Therefore, no criticalities are reported in internship activities.
Data for 2022 is discussed in the Course of Study on September 11, 2023.

- Prof. Franco Blezza (Chairperson of the Master's Degree Course in Policies and Management for Welfare LM-87);
- Prof. Vincenzo Corsi, Gabriele Di Francesco, Maria Teresa Giusti, Stefano Pasotti, Francesco Ferzetti;
- Vice-chairperson of the Regional Order of Social Assistants; Treasurer of the Order of Social Assistants; Secretary of SUNAS (National Union of Social Assistants); Social Assistant of the Chieti Municipality; a representative of the profession in the field of Social Assistants; a freelance Social Assistant; student representatives in the Governance Bodies of the Course and members of the 'Parity Committee'.
During the meeting, in a calm and extremely collaborative atmosphere, various topics related to the characteristics of work and necessary competencies of the Specialist Social Assistant and the parallel training path were examined.
The Course Coordinator noted that it is increasingly difficult to find suitable and available sites for internships due to the strong contraction of employment opportunities in recent years. It is also emphasized that in Public and Private Bodies, the top functions of Specialist Social Assistants are often covered by other professionals not adequately prepared for the profession. Specialist Social Assistants should instead have a more appropriate weight.
This leads to the shared necessity, by participants at the table, of indirect internships, which can partially address students' training needs. Participants also expressed appreciation for the activated and functioning indirect internship courses at the study course. The table expressed the hope that such types of internships be intensified for better preparation.
Regarding training issues, the inclusion of new disciplinary fields, among related and integrative disciplines, is positively evaluated for the possibility of filling potential gaps and thus equipping students with appropriate tools for undertaking the tasks proper to the profession.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data
ENTRY Based on data acquired by the University Quality Office as of August 28, 2023, in the Statistics section, students entering in 2022/23 amount to 64 enrollments, a figure substantially in line with the previous academic year (66).
Total enrolled in the Course of Study are 179, of which 69% are on track, a figure perfectly in line with the previous period.
Geographical origin confirms a decent attractiveness of the Course of Study, which enrolls students also from outside the region, amounting to 36% of enrollments, exactly in line with last year.
A large part of the 2022/23 enrollments have obtained a Master's degree or similar (42%), followed by high school graduates (25%), technical and professional institutes (23%), with the remainder from other forms of education. The clear preference for the Course of Study by students from humanistic fields is confirmed, which constitutes the primary target of the Course of Study.
Integrating data with SICAS surveys, it emerges that there are 2 entries, that the 2022/23 enrollments are predominantly women (93%) and belong to the target age group for Master's courses, i.e., 20-24 (52%). 81% have obtained a degree at the same University (85% last year), with a strong incidence of graduates from the L-39 Course in Social Services (63.4%) and L-40 Sociology (17.6%), while the percentage of graduates from other Italian Universities rises to 19%, compared to 15% in the 2021/22 academic year. These data highlight that the Course of Study, on one hand, represents a natural continuation of the three-year path and, on the other, shows an increase in the Course of Study's attractiveness to graduates from outside the University. 27% of enrollments have obtained a three-year degree with a grade of 110 or higher, between 106-109, and a grade equal to or below 100. This reveals the good profile of students entering and denotes, in systemic terms, an increase in knowledge and skills of students in the overall study path, considering that Master's students belong for 61% to high school graduates who obtained a grade below 80 at graduation.

PATH The path data refers to the 2021/22 cohort and is acquired from statistics provided by the PQA, updated as of June 2023, and integrated with the Sicas system for the same cohort.
The renewal rate for the second year slightly decreases from 91% to 85%. Indeed, 4 explicit withdrawals and 6 non-renewals are reported, with no outgoing transfers or passages.
Data provided by the University confirms a situation of regularity and continuity in career progression, improving compared to the 2020 cohort. Among those continuing to the second year, 39% have earned more than 40 CFU, compared to 29% of the previous cohort. However, the percentage of inactive students increases to 21%, compared to 16% of the previous cohort, and the percentage of those not earning any CFU in the first year rises from 3.6% to 10%. Overall, however, students of the 2021 cohort earned 56% of the required CFU, a value increasing compared to the previous cohort. This data is partial as it does not account for autumn and extraordinary sessions in progress. It is observed that the average number of exams taken increases from 5 to 6, with an average grade of 28. These data highlight an improvement in career regularity and the quality of the learning path.

EXIT Data on graduates for the calendar year 2022 shows 38 graduates, of which 63% graduated on time, a figure significantly improved compared to 48.5% in 2021. Half of the graduates obtained a grade of 110 or higher, 16% obtained a grade between 105-110, and the rest a grade below 105.
Past data were discussed in the Course of Study on September 13, 2022, while current data are discussed in the Course of Study on September 11, 2023.

Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam requires the presentation and discussion of a written thesis of at least 200,000 characters, also in digital format, elaborated personally by the student under the guidance of a supervisor. It will broadly address policies and management for welfare analyzed in their theoretical, methodological, and technical-applicative dimensions.

Method of Conducting the Final Exam The degree is awarded upon passing a final exam, which is assigned 18 CFU.
The Master's final exam requires the presentation and discussion of a written thesis of at least 200,000 characters, also in digital format, elaborated personally by the student under the guidance of a supervisor. The final exam and the corresponding thesis may be conducted in a foreign language upon favorable and motivated approval by the Course Council, ensuring the possibility of effective evaluation due to sufficient competencies within the teaching body. In any case, a thesis written in a foreign language must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian.
In particular, the work may consist of a broad critical review of the literature or field research of a project or analytical type, in one of the disciplines present in the path followed and characteristic of the chosen study direction. Consistency around the topic that gives the title to the thesis, an organic and logical articulation of the subject, and a sufficiently broad and related bibliography to what is presented in the text are required.
The graduation exam is public and takes place according to a predetermined program, with each candidate having an average exam duration not exceeding twenty minutes, with a portion dedicated to presentation and a portion to discussion.
For the evaluation of the final exam, the student's academic record is taken into account, using the average as a base to which additional points may be added, up to a maximum of 7 points. The variation from minimum to maximum score will also consider qualitative variables, which will be evaluated case by case by the Committee.
Candidates are evaluated with a grade expressed in hundredths, taking into account also the overall career progression of the student, with possible unanimous mention of honors; the minimum score for passing the final exam is 66/110.
Committees for evaluating Master's final exams are appointed by the Department Director. The judging committees are composed of at least seven and no more than eleven members, including the Chairperson.

Summary of the Technical Report of the Evaluation Unit The Evaluation Unit expresses a favorable opinion regarding the technical feasibility of the proposed modification, discussed and approved in consultation with representative organizations at the local level of production, services, and professions.

Admission Requirements The Master's Degree Course, Master's Degree, in Planetary Sciences is open to candidates who meet the admission requirements. In particular, candidates who have obtained an Italian Laurea (Bachelor Degree equivalent) in the class of Geological Sciences L-34 or in the class of Sciences and Technologies for Environment and Nature L-32 can access the Master's Degree Course, Master's Degree. For candidates holding a degree in other technical-scientific classes, specific curricular requirements are required: at least 6 ECTS in total in mathematical and computer science disciplines (SSD - scientific disciplinary sectors - MAT/xx, without constraints on individual SSD and/or INF/01); at least 6 ECTS in chemical disciplines (SSD CHIM/xx, without constraints on individual SSD); at least 12 ECTS in SSD GEO/xx; at least 50 ECTS in SSD GEO/xx and/or ICAR/xx and/or ING/xx and/or FIS/xx and/or BIO/xx and/or AGR/xx and/or ING-IND/xx.
For foreigners and Italian citizens with foreign degrees, admission is subject to the possession of qualifications equivalent to Italian ones in the Earth Sciences class. If, on the other hand, the candidate possesses another degree in scientific and technological subjects, it is necessary to have followed courses for at least 60 hours in mathematics and computer science, at least 60 hours in chemistry, and at least 500 hours in geological, engineering, physical, biological, and agronomic subjects. An interview, also online, may be required in case there is a need for clarification on the qualifications presented.
In addition, a good knowledge of the English language is required, which can be attested by a B2 level certification for non-native English speakers or, in the absence of certification, by means of an interview, also online. Knowledge of the Italian language is not required since the course is entirely taught in English.
Starting from the academic year 2023/2024, Master's Degree, Master's Degree, in Planetary Sciences will include the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degree, which will issue a joint degree from the Universities d'Annunzio (Italy), Nantes (France), and Coimbra (Portugal). For Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degree candidates only, access to the Master's Degree Course in Planetary Sciences is limited to the number of scholarships available under the program. The selection of candidates will be based on their qualifications and an interview conducted by a joint commission of the three universities.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
IN ITALIAN
For planetary science to have an impact, good communication is essential. Students will be taught the ability to communicate effectively and discuss research topics, methods, and results intelligently and persuasively. The communication skillset will be developed through the development of the following elements:
• Ability to communicate and discuss research topics, methods and results, in English;
• Ability to present results in a graphic format: the student must be able to produce drawings, images and other graphic tools with a high scientific content and image rendering. The graphic structure must clearly identify the scientific concept or data set to be highlighted. It must also be differentiated for the communication system used such as publications, PowerPoints, posters;
• Data processing, analysis, and presentation: data processing, analysis and their representation are a key element for scientific communication. How to process data and how to make it accessible to colleagues and the public is of primary importance. Understanding whether a table, a graph or a written report is more effective can make research more understandable and accessible to the science community and the public. The student will learn to be autonomous in these choices;
• Ability to work in groups: group work is now an essential element, and the student must be able to work together with his colleagues demonstrating that in the future, in his field of work, he will be able to work effectively in groups, sharing responsibilities and behaving in a serious and concrete way to achieve the common goal.

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
IN ITALIAN:
Since this course is inherently interdisciplinary both in its focus and teaching method, it is crucial that students learn to properly distinguish the geological, geophysical, physical, and mineralogical processes that guide the origin and evolution of the Solar System. Students will acquire the ability to judge, integrate, and interpret information from multiple sources in a coherent manner using the scientific method. The scientific method teaches students to make logical inferences about natural phenomena and iteratively test these inferences against data obtained from observations, experiments, fieldwork, and modelling. Students will learn to gather and interpret data from multiple sources, integrating and critiquing evidence so that they can properly interpret the data. Students must also be open to updating and even changing interpretations based on new observations and/or tests using new experiments or modelling. The skillsets thus acquired will be assessed through exercises and oral and written exams.

Ability to apply knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
IN ITALIANO:
Adopting a multi-disciplinary approach, the program of this master's degree combines classroom lectures, laboratory work, fieldwork, remote sensing and in-situ probe data processing and analyses, and modeling techniques to enable students to acquire the necessary skills to obtain a robust and practical knowledge of geological, geophysical, mineralogical, and physical processes on Earth and other planetary bodies. Students will learn fieldwork both for studying terrestrial processes and for studying processes analogous to planetary processes. Additionally, students will learn to competently use software and digital tools to access, process data, and perform analyses and modeling. Further laboratory experiences can complement observational and theoretical results and data. Verification of this activity will be carried out through practical exercises and testing. Some of these tests will be performed in the field.
IN ENGLISH:
Adopting a multi-disciplinary approach, this master's program combines classroom lectures, laboratory work, fieldwork, remote sensing and in-situ probe data processing and analyses, and modeling techniques to enable students to acquire the necessary skills to obtain a robust and practical knowledge of the geological, geophysical, mineralogical, and physical processes on Earth and other planetary bodies. Students will learn how to do terrestrial and terrestrial analogue fieldwork. In addition, students will learn to competently use software and digital tools to access/process data and perform analyses and modeling. Further laboratory experiences can complement observational and theoretical results and data. The verification of this activities will be performed by practical exercises and testing. Some of these tests will be performed in the field.
Learning skills
IN ITALIANO:
Additionally, to provide students with a robust background in planetary sciences, the master's program aims to turn students into lifelong learners. This program will impart learning skills to students that will provide them with a high level of analytical proficiencies, enabling them to conduct research which will add to the larger body of scientific knowledge. Scientific knowledge is accumulative based on prior research and achievements, so students will learn through coursework how to obtain a broad background of topics under study, for example by engaging in bibliographic research to better understand and define research objectives and interpret outcomes. Students will also learn to consult and master the use of numerous scientific databases housing digital data from terrestrial investigations and planetary space missions. In addition to coursework and fieldtrips, students will have the opportunity to extend their learning opportunities by attending extra-curricular seminars and courses as well as annual summer schools.
IN ENGLISH:
In addition, to providing students with a robust background in planetary sciences, the master's program aims to turn students into lifelong learners. This program will impart learning skills to students that will provide them with a high level of analytical proficiencies, enabling them to conduct research which will add to the larger body of scientific knowledge. Scientific knowledge is accumulative based on prior research and achievements so students will learn through coursework how to obtain a broad background of topics under study for example by engaging bibliographic research to better understand and define research objectives and interpret outcomes. Students will also learn to consult and master the use of numerous scientific databases housing digital data from terrestrial investigations and planetary space missions. In addition to coursework and fieldtrips, students will have the opportunity to extend their learning opportunities by attending extra-curricular seminars and courses as well as annual summer schools.
University communications to CUN As anticipated in the previous academic year, a new organizational change is being presented to restore the "interuniversity" characteristic of the Master's Degree course.
Previously, due to the pandemic, the mandatory mobility between the three universities was abandoned. Currently, the limiting factors for international exchanges have diminished, and it seems stability has been achieved to resume the initial project as previously accredited.
Therefore, the international and interuniversity course is being restored, based on mandatory mobility and aimed at issuing a joint degree by the three Universities.
The Master's Degree course, as proposed, is supported by an EMJMD program.
We emphasize that in the previous organizational change, we clearly stated "our absolute intention to restore the course as originally designed, once pandemic conditions permitted."
It follows that this latest request is an announced and due act. The consortium agreement will be available in its updated version based on the timing and procedures of the three Universities forming the consortium.
Knowledge and understanding
IN ITALIANO:
The student will gain a robust understanding of the geological, geophysical, mineralogical, and physical processes of the planets, including Earth, moons, and other bodies of the Solar System. Learning will be conducted via lectures, exercises, laboratories, and field activities. Learning will be facilitated by data analyses, modeling, fieldwork, and experimental work as well as access to remote sensing ground observations and space mission data. Students will learn to use software and digital tools to access and process remote sensing and in-situ robotic probe data and to process and analyze such data. Students will have the opportunity to gain real-world skills by participating in internships and working with teaching staff and their research. The knowledge obtained in the coursework will enable the student to define, plan, and develop scientific operations for research and analyses. Students will learn to effectively communicate scientific and technical results. The tools used, both conceptual and technical, for terrestrial and extra-terrestrial bodies will be basically the same, but their field of application will be different both in the type of data and in the observational methods. Students' knowledge will be verified through proficiency tests, such as practical, oral and/or written tests, cartographic products, and written reports.
IN ENGLISH:
The student will gain robust understanding of the geological, geophysical, mineralogical, and physical processes of the planets, including the Earth, moons, and other bodies of the Solar Systems. Learning will be conducted via lectures, exercises, laboratories, and field activities. Learning will be facilitated by data analyses, modelling, fieldwork, and experimental work as well as access to remote sensing ground observation and space mission data. Students will learn to use software and digital tools to access and process remote sensing and in- situ robotic probe data and to learn to process and analyse such data. Students will have the opportunity to get real- world skills by participating in internships and working with teaching staff and their research. The knowledge obtained in the coursework will enable the student to define, plan and develop scientific operations for research and analyses. Students will learn to effectively communicate scientific and technical results. The tools used, both conceptual and technical, for terrestrial and extra-terrestrial bodies will be basically the same, but their field of application will be different both in the type of data and in the observational methods. Students' knowledge will be verified through proficiency tests, such as practical, oral and/or written tests, cartographic products, and written reports.
Organizational structure and responsibilities at university level The organizational system of the University is based on the figure of the Rector, who is responsible for managing, guiding, and proposing all academic activities. The Rector is assisted by the Academic Senate and the Board of Directors. Decisions made by these bodies directly influence the activities of the Study Courses, which are monitored by the University Quality Assurance Office (PQA). The PQA maintains close contact with both the Departmental Joint Committee and the individual Study Courses. The PQA acts as a mediator between the Study Courses and the Rector and the Academic Senate, directly communicating with these bodies. The Evaluation Committee is an independent body with which the PQA collaborates and to which it transmits decisions to the various Study Courses.
Organization and responsibilities of quality assurance at Study Course level Quality Assurance (QA) will be implemented through a mixed model, based on the Quality Assurance/Evaluation Committee of the Consortium, which will report to the control system of the individual Universities. These, in turn, will proceed with evaluation within their competence.
Regarding the d'Annunzio University, the QA structure is based on the Joint Committee, which monitors the educational offer and the quality of teaching and student services provided by the faculty and structures.
Additionally, there is the Steering Committee, which provides opinions and comments on the relationship between the Study Course and the professional world, monitors key activities for student educational development, and provides suggestions to the Study Course. The Steering Committee meets as needed, also remotely, upon the convocation of the Study Course Chair. The Study Course Chair may also contact members of the Local Steering Committee and Student Representatives, and may involve other representatives of interest groups if necessary. On special occasions, they may also organize assemblies with the student body to discuss key elements of the Study Course.
The decision-making process of the Study Course develops annually, starting in spring and ending in late winter of the following year. The Steering Committee, upon the indication of the Study Course Chair, elaborates its comments and provides opinions in the form of responses to questionnaires or documents, through a remote procedure beginning in March and April. The Joint Committee of the Study Course also elaborates its report based on stakeholder opinions, if available, identifying critical issues and situations requiring intervention, as well as analyzing the Study Course as a whole.
The Review Committee analyzes the Joint Committee's report and elaborates a final document on the status of the Study Course, providing a specific proposal for solutions to critical issues. The Study Course Chair, together with the Council, acquires the documents from the three Committees, analyzes them, and proposes a plan to mitigate critical issues, improve teaching standards, and carry out necessary operations for effective support of the University structures in quality improvement.
The result of this procedure is transmitted to the Quality Assurance/Evaluation Committee of the consortium structure coordinating the Study Course. This committee adopts the results, incorporating them into the final report.

Work planning and implementation deadlines During the period May-June, a consultation with the Steering Committee is carried out through the presentation of a questionnaire and data processing, in collaboration with the results of the National Interest Committee.
In July, a meeting is held between the Study Course Chair, the Joint Committee, and the Quality Assurance Group to identify and standardize procedures and documentation processing.
In September, the Study Course Chair presents a report to the Council to describe the current state of Quality Assurance procedures and preliminarily identify intervention lines.
During October and November, the Joint Committee carries out its work.
In December, the Quality Assurance Group carries out its work, presents and approves the document by the Study Course Council, and subsequently transmits it to the relevant consortium bodies.
Annual review The annual review will be carried out by the Quality Assurance Group, which will also base its work on the report of the consortium structure.

Brief course description IN ENGLISH The Master's Degree in Planetary Sciences aims to train experts in the field of planetary sciences, in order to prepare them for careers in universities, research centers, and industry. Graduates of the program will acquire in-depth knowledge in planetary sciences and solar system exploration. This degree course is aimed at geologists, physicists, naturalists, and engineers, provided they hold a Laurea Triennale degree or equivalent.
The course offers a blended learning approach, with the first and third semesters being offered in both in-person and distance learning formats, and the second semester being entirely in-person. The fourth semester will be dedicated entirely to an internship and the development of the Master's thesis. All course exams and thesis discussions are held in person.
In the first year, in the first semester, students will take the following courses: Planetary Geophysical Exploration (6 ECTS), Planetary Astrophysics (6 ECTS), Solar System Exploration (6 ECTS), Extreme Geological Events on Earth and Planetary Bodies (6 ECTS), and Introduction to Astrobiology (6 ECTS). In the second semester of the first year, students will take courses in Planetary Geology (6 ECTS), Planetary Analogues Field Work (6 ECTS), Planetary Mapping and Data Analysis (6 ECTS), Planetary Materials (6 ECTS), and Comparative Sedimentology (6 ECTS).
In the second year, in the first semester, students will take courses in Remote Sensing for Space Exploration (6 ECTS) and Earth Observation Analysis (6 ECTS), Global Changes (optional) (6 ECTS), Astrobiology (optional) (6 ECTS), and Planetary Interiors (6 ECTS). In the second semester, students will carry out an internship (6 ECTS) and work on their Master's thesis (30 ECTS).
For the Joint Degree (EMJMD), students will follow the courses according to the agreement established in the consortium agreement between Nantes Université, Universidade de Coimbra, and Università G. d'Annunzio.
All courses are taught in English.
IN ITALIANO La Laurea Magistrale in Planetary Sciences è finalizzata alla formazione di esperti nel campo delle scienze planetarie, al fine di prepararli per carriere in università, centri di ricerca e industrie. I laureati del programma acquisiranno conoscenze approfondite in scienze planetarie e nell'esplorazione del Sistema Solare. Questo corso di laurea è rivolto a Geologi, Fisici, Naturalisti e Ingegneri, purché siano in possesso di un titolo di Laurea Triennale o titolo di studio equivalente.
Il Corso offre una didattica mista in presenza e a distanza, con il primo e il terzo semestre a scelta dello studente e il secondo semestre in presenza. Il quarto semestre sarà interamente dedicato a un tirocinio e all'elaborazione della Tesi di Laurea Magistrale. Gli esami dei corsi e la discussione della tesi di laurea sono in presenza.
Nel primo anno, primo semestre gli studenti seguiranno i seguenti corsi: Planetary geophysical exploration (6 ECTS), Planetary astrophysics (6 ECTS), Solar System exploration (6 ECTS), Extreme geological events on Earth and planetary bodies (6 ECTS) e Introduction to Astrobiology (6 ECTS). Nel secondo semestre del primo anno, gli studenti seguiranno i corsi: Planetary geology (6 ECTS), Planetary analogues field work (6 ECTS), Planetary mapping and data analysis (6 ECTS), Planetary materials (6 ECTS) e Comparative sedimentology (6 ECTS).
Nel secondo anno, primo semestre, gli studenti seguiranno i corsi: Remote sensing (6 ECTS), Earth observation analysis (6 ECTS), Global changes (optional) (6 ECTS), Astrobiology (optional) (6 ECTS) e Planetary Interiors (6 ECTS). Nel secondo semestre, gli studenti svolgeranno un tirocinio (6 ECTS) e lavoreranno alla Tesi di Laurea Magistrale (30 ECTS).

Reasons for establishing multiple courses in the class The Master's Degree 'International Master in Planetary Geosciences' belongs to the class of Master's Degrees LM-74. Indeed, the Department of Engineering and Geology already has an active teaching program in the LM-74 class. Unfortunately, the fact that the International Study Course is organizationally impossible to integrate with the existing Curriculum makes it necessary to create another, different Study Course. The choice of the LM-74 class is necessary because planetary sciences are firmly linked to geological sciences. In fact, the same methods used for studying planets are used for studying Earth. Indeed, there has been an evolution in the approach to studying planets, which until the first half of the last century was almost exclusively the domain of astrophysics/astronomy. Now, with planetary missions, both orbital and in-situ, the analysis tools are predominantly geological, making Earth Sciences apply the same type of observation and analysis of processes (which are similar) to planets and minor bodies in the Solar System. Not surprisingly, there are numerous departments worldwide named Earth and Planetary Sciences, and especially in the United States, there are numerous Study Courses in Earth and Planetary Sciences.
Therefore, the establishment of a Study Course in LM-74 parallel to the existing one is proposed. The teaching staff respects the legal relationships.
Solar System exploration is now fully underway with three main objectives: i) human exploration of Mars and the Moon, with the latter involved in the establishment of a permanently inhabited base; ii) exploration of the outer Solar System using satellites; iii) robotic exploration of rocky and icy planets in the Solar System. This scientific and technological effort must be accompanied by the European educational system. Currently, there are few examples in Europe of integrated Study Courses that provide substantial preparation in this field. An exception is the Planetary Sciences path of the Master's Degree in Geological and Planetary Sciences offered by d'Annunzio University.
The proposed Master's Degree will provide scientifically qualified personnel for participation in and organization of planetary space missions. There is a clear need to produce geoscientists capable of participating in these activities, entering the job market with their employment in national and European Space Agencies, in research for data analysis, planetary mission planning, scientific instrumentation construction, etc. These activities can also be developed in the aerospace industry, which consists of multinational companies, Astrium, Thales Alenia Space, Airbus, but also smaller realities up to micro-enterprises.
Specific educational objectives of the course and description of the educational path IN ITALIANO:
The educational objective of the Master in Planetary Sciences is to provide students with the knowledge and skills necessary to become experts in the analysis and interpretation of planetary mission data, organization of space missions, definition of scientific objectives for the exploration of the Solar System, and definition of requirements and development of scientific instrumentation and experiments. The interdisciplinary nature of the Master of Planetary Sciences program focuses on the geological, geophysical, mineralogical, and physical processes of planets, including Earth, natural satellites, and other bodies such as meteorites, asteroids, and dwarf planets in the Solar System.
Understanding the formation of the Solar System and its evolution and the processes that produced and continue to affect Earth, other planets, and associated planetary systems has both observational, including experimental, and theoretical aspects. One of the educational objectives of this master's degree is to provide an in-depth preparation in how to analyze, interpret, and produce observational planetary science. Observational planetary science includes remote sensing data, including data from terrestrial ground observations and space missions, as well as terrestrial fieldwork for both Earth-specific processes and terrestrial analogues to planetary processes. Courses include field geological surveying so students can learn about both terrestrial processes and processes analogous to planetary processes. In addition, experimental coursework allows the study of terrestrial/planetary processes, the results of which can provide information both on the observables expected from space missions and theoretical work. Theoretical planetary science uses modeling to study and investigate various terrestrial and planetary phenomena while using observational and experimental data as inputs into modeling. Coursework includes training on how to process data, analyze it, and model it to study and investigate various terrestrial and planetary phenomena.
The educational program is designed to have a group of courses dedicated to providing students with a strong foundation in planetary sciences, while a second group of courses will provide more advanced topics in planetary sciences. This master's program has an interdisciplinary teaching staff with diverse backgrounds in geology, geophysics, mineralogy, and astrophysics as well as direct participation in terrestrial analogue fieldwork projects and current and upcoming space missions in the Solar System. Students will benefit by gaining experience in Earth and planetary science projects and space missions. In addition, the program provides students with the opportunity to do internships and independent research. Students will also learn methods to effectively communicate scientific results to the scientific community and the professional world. The knowledge and experience gained during the course will allow the graduate in Planetary Sciences to have the knowledge and skillset to pursue a career path in academia, research institutes, national and international space agencies, and industry for both Earth and extra-terrestrial bodies.

3. Proposal for activation of new Study Courses
- The International Master's Degree 'International Master in Planetary Geosciences' is the result of a collaboration between three European Universities: Université de Nantes (France), Università d'Annunzio (Italy), and Universidade de Coimbra (Portugal). Each of the three Universities will deliver one semester of courses. The first semester will be held at the University of Coimbra, the second at d'Annunzio, and the third at Nantes; the fourth semester will be dedicated to internships and the thesis. The course will be taught in English and will issue a joint degree. The Master's Degree 'International Master in Planetary Geosciences' belongs to the class of Master's Degrees LM-74. Indeed, the Department of Engineering and Geology already has a Master's Degree course in the LM-74 class. Unfortunately, the fact that the Study Course is organizationally impossible to integrate with the existing Curricula makes it necessary to create another, different Study Course.
The choice of the LM-74 class is necessary because planetary sciences are firmly linked to geological sciences. In fact, departments studying planets are also linked to the study of Earth. Indeed, there are departments worldwide named Earth and Planetary Sciences, and especially in the United States, there are numerous Study Courses in Earth and Planetary Sciences. Therefore, the establishment of a new Study Course in LM-74 parallel to the existing one is proposed. The teaching staff respects, from the first year of delivery, the legal requirements for the entire duration of the Master's Degree course as per DM 6/2019 (Annex A, Table K), including 2 teachers per Partner University and 3 teachers from UdA. Solar System exploration is now fully underway with three main objectives:
- i) human exploration of Mars and the Moon, with the latter involved in the establishment of a permanently inhabited base;
- ii) exploration of the outer Solar System using satellites;
- iii) robotic exploration of rocky and icy planets in the Solar System. This scientific and technological effort must be accompanied by the European educational system.
Currently, there are few examples in Europe of integrated Master's Degree courses that provide substantial preparation in this field. An exception is the Planetary Sciences path of the Master's Degree in Geological and Planetary Sciences offered by d'Annunzio University.
In this scenario, the proposed Master's Degree will provide scientifically qualified personnel for participation in and organization of planetary space missions. There is a clear need to produce geoscientists capable of participating in these activities, entering the job market with their employment in national and European Space Agencies, in research for data analysis, planetary mission planning, scientific instrumentation construction, etc. These activities can also be developed in the aerospace industry, which consists of multinational companies such as Astrium, Thales Alenia Space, Airbus, but also smaller realities up to micro-enterprises.
This Master's Degree is aimed at graduates in Geology, Natural Sciences, Engineers, and Physicists. Admission requirements, in addition to holding a degree equivalent to a three-year degree, also require knowledge of English at a level above B2 (CEFR).
Admission will be evaluated and decided by an Admission Team composed of a Chair and a representative from each of the three involved Universities.
The knowledge acquired will be broad and will be provided by three of the most important sites in Europe in the field of planetary science and exploration. Coimbra will provide a foundation in astrophysics and planetary sciences in general. d'Annunzio will provide a solid theoretical and practical preparation on planetary geology. Nantes will provide in-depth insights into the different applied fields of planetary geology.
There are 18 students per academic year, all beneficiaries of a Scholarship available through the European Erasmus Mundus program, to which the consortium of the three Universities will submit the funding project.
The fourth semester will be dedicated to the completion of the thesis work, which can be carried out at the three sites of the Master's Degree or at other sites if accepted by the Faculty of the Master's Degree.
The Master's Degree at the three sites represents a continuity with the three-year undergraduate courses and the doctoral courses present in the three Universities, which also concern Solar System exploration.

LM-74 INTERNATIONAL MASTER IN PLANETARY GEOSCIENCES (CHIETI)
Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and services production, professions (Course establishment)
IN ITALIANO:
The Master's Degree in Planetary Sciences was established to train experts in the field of planetary sciences in response to the growing interest in this sector both within industries and in research centers and universities. This degree provides high-level skills for those who wish to pursue a career in industries, space agencies, research institutions, and universities dealing with planetary sciences and the exploration of the Solar System. In the academic year 2022/2023, the international Master in Planetary Geosciences was activated. The International Master's Degree in Planetary Geosciences is part of the GeoPlanet consortium. This consortium organizes a series of activities, including the Strategic Partnership GeoPlaNet. The GeoPlaNet consortium, coordinated by the University of Nantes, includes about twenty partners: European Space Agency, Jet Propulsion Laboratory (NASA/Caltech), University of New Mexico, University of Washington, Centro de Astrobiologia (Madrid), Observatoire Royal de Belgique, Open University (UK), IRSPS/Univ. d'Annunzio, University of Padua, University of Bern, Charles University (Czech Republic), University of Coimbra, University of Porto, Institute of Earth Sciences of Academica Sinica (Taiwan), Conservatoire National (Brazil), DLR (German Space Agency), Earth Science Institute (Japan), University of Atacama, Agricultural University of Athens. The consultation with the active stakeholder committee in 2022/2023 provided an extremely positive opinion on the activation of the Master's Degree, recognizing the strong interest in the course both nationally and internationally.
The demand for a more comprehensive education in the field of planetary sciences, not limited only to the field of geosciences, led to the need to rename the Planetary Geosciences course to Planetary Sciences from the academic year 2023/2024. This change represents a response to the growing needs of the national and international job market and research institutions that require highly qualified personnel in the field of planetary sciences. Following the restructuring of the Planetary Sciences course, the stakeholder group was updated to be in line with the new needs of the course. Among the members of the stakeholder group we find leading figures in the field of planetary sciences, from space agencies and space industries: Dr Rosaly Lopes (NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, USA), Prof. Luciano Iess (University La Sapienza, Italy), Prof. Pascal Allemand (University of Lyon, France), Dr Christina Plainaki (Italian Space Agency, Italy), Dr Fabrizio Capaccioni (Institute of Astrophysics and Space Planetology, INAF, Italy), Dr Daniel Mege (Space Research Centre Polish Academy of Sciences, Poland), Dr Armando Tempesta (Thales Alenia Space Italy). The first stakeholder group consultation is scheduled for February 24, 2023. The stakeholder group will be consulted periodically at least once a year to ensure the highest quality of education offered.

Characteristics of the final exam IN ITALIANO:
The final exam consists of a written dissertation on an original research topic. The topic must concern a subject of broad scientific or technological interest. The dissertation must demonstrate that the student has mastered the knowledge of the course of study, and that they are able to use the acquired knowledge and skills to provide new insight into a technical-scientific subject in an in-depth and autonomous way. The dissertation must be defended in front of a commission composed of members who can be both internal and external.
IN ENGLISH:
The final exam consists of a written dissertation on an original research topic. The topic must concern a subject of broad scientific or technological interest. The dissertation must demonstrate that the student has mastered the knowledge of the course of study, and that they are able to use the acquired knowledge and skills to provide new insight into a technical-scientific subject in an in-depth and autonomous way. The dissertation must be defended in front of a commission composed of members who can be both internal and external to the program.
Method of conducting the final exam IN ENGLISH The final exam consists of a public presentation of the thesis in front of a committee composed of at least seven teachers from the Degree Course, appointed by the Director of the Department of Engineering and Geology. During the presentation, the student has 30 minutes to present their work and another 15 minutes to answer questions from the committee.
The Master's Thesis should represent the complete development process of a scientific or technological research project, from the idea phase to the final draft. The thesis should include a scientific rationale and an analysis of the originality of the idea. Additionally, the thesis should be clear and distinguish between the presentation of data, their interpretation, and the discussion of the same. Finally, the thesis should be comprehensive and allow for a complete evaluation by the committee.
The evaluation of the student is based on three elements: the written work of the thesis, the oral presentation of the thesis, and the discussion. During the defense of the thesis, the student is judged on the coherence between the objectives of the thesis and the results achieved, the clarity of the presentation, the ability to illustrate the originality of the work, the ability to critically analyze the results, and the ability to argue in direct comparison.
For Italian degree, the final grade is expressed based on the weighted average of exam grades on a scale of 110. The grade for the thesis is expressed on a scale of 0 to 10 and is added to the average. A distinction can be proposed by one of the members of the committee and must be unanimously accepted.
The thesis must be written in English, but upon request of the student and with the approval of the Board of Studies, it can be written in another language of the European Union.
The dates of the Master's Degree sessions and the deadlines are available on the Final Exam page of the Master's Degree Course.
For EMJMD, the final grade will follow the consortium agreement between Nantes Universitè, Universidade de Coimbra, Università G. d'Annunzio.
IN ITALIANO La prova finale consiste in una presentazione pubblica della tesi davanti ad una commissione composta da almeno sette docenti del Corso di Laurea, nominati dal Direttore del Dipartimento di Ingegneria e Geologia. Durante la presentazione, lo studente ha 30 minuti di tempo per esporre il proprio elaborato e altri 15 minuti per rispondere alle domande della commissione.
La Tesi di Laurea magistrale deve rappresentare il percorso completo di sviluppo di una ricerca scientifica o tecnologica, dalla fase di elaborazione dell'idea alla stesura dell'elaborato finale. La tesi deve contenere un razionale scientifico e un'analisi dell'originalità dell'idea. Inoltre, l'elaborato deve essere chiaro e distinguere tra l'esposizione dei dati, la loro interpretazione e la discussione degli stessi. Infine, la tesi deve essere esaustiva e consentire una valutazione completa da parte della Commissione.
La valutazione dello studente si basa su tre elementi: l'elaborato scritto della tesi, l'esposizione orale della tesi e la discussione. Durante la difesa della tesi, lo studente viene giudicato sulla coerenza tra gli obiettivi della tesi e i risultati raggiunti, la chiarezza espositiva, la capacità di illustrare l'originalità del lavoro, la capacità di analisi critica dei risultati e la capacità di argomentare in un confronto diretto.
Per il tiolo di studio Italiano, il voto finale viene espresso sulla base della media ponderata dei voti degli esami in 110 decimi. Il voto per la tesi è espresso in un valore da 0 a 10 e si somma alla media. La lode viene proposta da uno dei membri della commissione e deve essere accettata all'unanimità.
La tesi deve essere scritta in lingua inglese, ma su richiesta dello studente e con l'approvazione del Consiglio di Corso di Studi, può essere scritta in un'altra lingua dell'Unione Europea.
Le date delle sedute di Laurea Magistrale e lo scadenzario sono disponibili sulla pagina Prova finale del Corso di Laurea Magistrale.
Per il titolo di studio congiunto (EMJMD), il voto finale sarà espresso in accordo a quanto stabilito nel consortium agreement tra Nantes Universitè, Universidade de Coimbra, Università G. d'Annunzio.
Summary of the technical report of the evaluation committee - SUA Sheet The activation of the Master's Degree, consistently with the strategic planning of the University for the period 2019-2023, contributes to opening the educational offer to the international context. The design was carried out following an in-depth analysis of professional profiles and the possible career prospects for graduates, and following consultation with social partners, which proved sufficiently representative at territorial, national, and international levels.
The functions and competencies are described with sufficient precision and are consistent with the professional profiles. For the disciplinary competencies of the members of the Evaluation Committee, the path appears sufficiently consistent with the formed professional profiles. Improvements are needed in the verification methods for personal preparation for admission to the Master's Degree.
The structural resources and teaching staff appear generally adequate.
The monitoring of the Study Course is consistent with the University's Quality Assurance system.

Department DEPARTMENT OF INNOVATIVE TECHNOLOGIES IN MEDICINE & DENTISTRY Website https://www.dtimo@unich.it  Admission Requirements Required Knowledge for Admission Candidates who hold a five-year Upper Secondary School Diploma may be admitted to the Master's Degree Course in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis (CLMOPD). Admission to the course occurs following the successful completion of a test established by specific ministerial decrees indicating the procedures and content of the admission tests for university courses with national programmed access.
The didactic organization of CLMOPD requires that students admitted to the first year possess adequate knowledge of the Italian language (for candidates competing for places reserved for citizens of countries not belonging to the European Union) and adequate initial preparation achieved through previous studies.
In this context, all students who have passed the admission exam for the M.Sc., but answered correctly to less than half of the maximum score for individual topics in Physics, Chemistry, Biology, will be admitted with a compulsory educational requirement for one or more of the relevant disciplines, which they must address by October 31 of the following calendar year. Failure to comply will be governed by the provisions of the University's Didactic Regulations.
To enable students to acquire CFU related to additional compulsory educational requirements, the Course Council may establish preparatory didactic activities to be carried out during the first year of the course and which must be attended compulsorily by students in debt.
The assessment of results achieved in preparatory didactic activities will occur within the evaluation of the corresponding courses. Students who fail to address the compulsory educational requirement will not be allowed to take the second-year profit exams, effectively establishing a pre-requisite.

Admission Procedures To be admitted to the Master's Degree in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis, one must hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent. An adequate initial preparation is also required, in accordance with current national regulations for access to courses with a numbered quota.

1. Admission to the Master's Degree in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis occurs following the successful completion of a specific entrance examination based on ministerial decrees regarding the procedures and content of entrance examinations for university courses with national numbered quotas.
2. The number of admissions to the first year is defined in accordance with Article 3, paragraph 2 of Law No. 254 of September 2, 1999, considering resources in terms of teaching staff, laboratory technicians, tutors, instructors, classrooms, pre-clinical teaching laboratories, and necessary equipment to achieve professional training objectives.
3. Students admitted to the first year must possess adequate initial preparation acquired through previous studies.
In light of the above, all students who have passed the entrance examination for the Master's Degree, answering correctly to less than half of the maximum score for individual topics in Physics and Mathematics, Chemistry, Biology, will be admitted with a compulsory educational obligation for one or more of the mentioned disciplines, which must be remedied by October 31 of the following calendar year. Failure to comply will be regulated in accordance with the University's Academic Regulations. To enable students to acquire CFU related to Compulsory Educational Obligations, the Course Council may establish preparatory teaching activities to be carried out during the first year of the course, which students in debt must attend compulsorily.
The verification of results achieved in preparatory teaching activities will occur within the evaluation of the corresponding courses. Students who fail to remedy the compulsory educational obligation in one or more of the mentioned subjects will not be allowed to take the second-year profit examinations, effectively establishing a prerequisite.
4. The enrollment and registration deadlines are specified in the Study Plan.
For the academic year 2023/2024, the Course Council approved a number of places equal to 46, distributed as follows:
- n. 40 places reserved for EU students, as well as non-EU students residing in Italy, in accordance with Article 26 of Law No. 189 of July 30, 2002;
- n. 6 places reserved for non-EU students residing abroad, in accordance with Article 46 of DPR No. 394 of August 31, 1999;
