Training Periods Association Students in our program carry out most of their professional training periods within the relevant Department. Indeed, the Department of Innovative Technologies in Medicine and Dentistry provides equipment that positions 'd'Annunzio University' at the forefront of the national landscape, having on-site equipment, instrumentation, and facilities more than adequate to optimally complete the 90 CFU of professional training required by their educational path.
In fact, the equipment of the DiTmo Department, where the program is based, includes the following:
- 36 state-of-the-art dental units;
- 1 manikin room with 50 workstations total, equipped with dental arches and latex gums for practical exercises in periodontics, prosthetics, dental materials, and laboratory prosthetic technologies;
- 1 microscope room with 25 workstations for anatomy and histology exercises;
- 1 Anatomage anatomical room. The table is interactive, already used by the most important Medical Schools worldwide, and allows a level of exploration and learning beyond what any cadaver could offer, thus enabling first and second-year students to gain a deeper understanding of General Anatomy and Anatomy of the stomatognathic apparatus;
- 1 computer room with 40 workstations;
-
Students have the opportunity to work, as first operators under the guidance of a tutor (usually the instructor, a specialist, or a volunteer doctor), on patients who visit the Dental Clinic for conservative, endodontic, prosthetic, orthodontic, periodontal, implantological, etc. procedures (approximately 5,000 per year) and are often invited to participate free of charge in the specialization and/or update courses organized periodically by the Department.
Non-professional training periods are carried out at the clinical departments of the S.S. Annunziata Hospital and at the Biomedical Sciences Museum in Chieti. Biological science training periods are conducted in the laboratories of the Departments.

Career Guidance The degree program promotes the employability of its graduates through the provision of 3 specialization schools, specifically in Oral Surgery, Orthodontics, and Pediatric Dentistry, as well as the organization of annual Master's programs and Advanced Training and Update Courses by the Department of Innovative Technologies in Medicine and Dentistry, which hosts the degree program in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis.
- Level II Master in Sports Dentistry;
- Level II Master in Management of the Head-Neck District Function, in relation to neuro-muscular balance in pediatric, adult, and sports patients;
- Level II Master in Prosthetics and Implantology: Aesthetic-Functional Analog and Functional Rehabilitation;
- Level II Master in Conscious Sedation and Emergency Management in Dentistry;
- Level II Master in Clinical Periodontics and Periodontal Surgery;
- Level I Master in Dental Hygiene and Non-Surgical Periodontal Therapy;
- Update Course in Zygomatic and Pterygoid Implants.
The theoretical sessions of the aforementioned courses consist of lectures delivered by highly qualified speakers, who remain available for in-depth discussion with participants. The clinical sessions include live procedures on patients, accompanied by case preparation, treatment planning, and discussion of the performed interventions. The practical sessions involve exercises in diagnostic and therapeutic techniques on manikins, animal tissues, and patients.
Recently, the CLOPD Council confirmed the composition of the Steering Committee, aimed at organizing specific meetings with the world of work. In line with the C.U.N. document 'Guide to Writing Academic Regulations' and for the purpose of implementing Ministerial Decree 270/04 and subsequent decrees, it has become necessary to establish continuous contact with the world of work, both to communicate the objectives of the proposed educational offer and to foster active collaboration in identifying the knowledge, skills, and professional competencies to be achieved through bachelor's and master's degree courses, so that they can be effectively applied in the workplace. The 'G. d'Annunzio' University of Chieti Pescara has established a Placement Office to guide its graduates into the world of work. Each Department has appointed its own delegate. Other initiatives The Advisory Committee intends to extend its initiatives beyond national borders, considering that, compared to the past, there is greater difficulty in the insertion of our graduates into the job market, especially in medium-short terms.
In particular, it aims to establish frequent contacts with international public and private operators in other countries where, in recent years, there have been shortages of specific healthcare operators in the dental sector.
It is worth noting that unilateral contacts with English operators have, in recent years, enabled us to secure employment contracts in public hospital structures in the United Kingdom for our graduates who have a good command of English. The Committee's intention is certainly to intensify contacts with these operators and also with the relevant UK public authorities to establish a convention with British hospital facilities, aimed at training professionals capable of meeting the supply needs of dentists in Anglo-Saxon countries.
Furthermore, to make student support in the job market more effective, the course of study, in consultation with the Department of Innovative Technologies in Medicine and Dentistry, to which it is attached, and subject to available financial resources, increased in 2021 the number of research doctorates, post-doctoral positions, scholarships, and research grants offered to graduates in Dentistry and Prosthetics.
We do not know if, following the UK's Brexit and especially due to bureaucratic difficulties created by the pandemic, it will be possible to continue placing our graduates within the UK healthcare system, as the UK's exit from the European Union could create issues regarding foreign workers' ability to find employment opportunities as was the case in the past.
Another initiative repeated in 2021: Professor T. Zulli, within the English language course, continued to hold seminars for the in-depth study of scientific English and terminology related to Anglo-Saxon healthcare organization, not only for first and second-year students but for all students in the course of study.

Student opinions The opinions to be inserted are derived from the pre-exam questionnaire to which students are subjected before taking their assessment exams and are updated as of 31.08.2023.
The questionnaires processed for the study program in Dentistry totalled 2176 and involved 106 training activities out of 107, covering 99.07% of the courses offered by the study program.
The questionnaire presented a series of questions of the following type:
- Do you find the topics of this course interesting?
- Is the study load required for this course proportional to the credits assigned?
- Is the available teaching material adequate for studying the subject?
- Are the schedules for lectures, exercises, and other teaching activities respected?
- Are the examination methods clearly defined?
- Does the professor stimulate interest in the subject?
- Does the professor present the topics appropriately according to the complexity of the subject?
- Is the professor available during lectures and/or office hours to clarify the topics covered?
and other questions regarding the detailed programs and exam dates.
To the above questions, students, considering a scale from 1 to 4, expressed a rating ranging from a minimum of 3,36 to a maximum of 3,50, achieving an average of 3,45.
For a clearer and more comprehensive overview of the scores given by our students, the following comparative summary table based on macro-indicators may be very useful:
- Overall satisfaction of the Dentistry study program: 3,45 (compared to 3.33 for the health area and 3,35 university-wide);
- Logistical and organizational aspects: 3,51 for Dentistry (3,45 for the health area and 3,48 university-wide);
- Teaching effectiveness: 3,53 for Dentistry (3,43 for the health area and 3,47 university-wide).
No critical issues were found, i.e., modules that did not reach at least 2,5 in the average score.
In conclusion, the average score obtained by our study program was 3,45. Considering that the evaluation scale ranges from 1 to 4, we can consider ourselves satisfied with the quality of the courses and the level of satisfaction achieved among students in the Dentistry study program.

Applying Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis must have acquired knowledge of the foundations for qualitative and quantitative understanding of biological, physiological, and pathological phenomena for maintaining oral health and dental therapies, including practical training within professional disciplines.
In particular, the professional internship must enable the student to acquire specific competencies in restorative dentistry, endodontics, periodontology, prosthesis, orthodontics, and gnathology, oral surgery, special oral and maxillofacial pathology, pediatric dentistry, clinical oral and maxillofacial medicine, clinical prerequisites, preventive and community dentistry, dental hygiene, dental anthropology, dental materials, laboratory prosthesis technologies, industrial bioengineering, clinical pathology, anesthesiology and emergency treatment, otorhinolaryngology, neurology, through clinical activities performed on patients in accordance with the Ministry's Teaching Ordinance.
To achieve the educational objectives, graduates must acquire physiological and pathological knowledge of general medicine and perform clinical activities throughout the study program, carried out with technical-professional autonomy as a primary operator under the guidance of dentists from university or contracted facilities, in line with the specific requirements of the TPV.

Learning Skills
The Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis must have developed learning skills necessary to pursue further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis must acquire a solid foundation in basic disciplines, medical disciplines relevant to dentistry, and dental disciplines, and must be able to critically evaluate issues related to the pathological state of the stomatognathic apparatus within a unified vision that considers the general health status of the individual patient.

MODE OF ACQUISITION AND VERIFICATION: Learning occurs through frontal lectures, laboratories, and clinical exercises, and is assessed through written and/or oral exams, clinical exercises, project evaluations, and practical activity assessments. Verification and assessment of acquired knowledge and competencies are conducted through methods independently determined by professors via comprehensive or ongoing assessments. Through the professional competencies acquired via the internship within the study program, particularly the TPV, the Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis must reach the level of practical knowledge required for professional licensure.

Organization and Responsibility of AQ at Course Level The AQ Group has scheduled bi-monthly meetings throughout 2023 to monitor the following aspects related to teaching delivery:
- Verification of frontal lectures and practical exercises, correspondence between assigned CFU and actual delivery, based on detailed programs reflecting the educational path for acquiring knowledge and competencies as specified in the Teaching Regulation;
- Verification of professional internships at clinical departments for small student groups, ensuring each student is assigned patients with diverse pathologies to intervene as a primary operator under tutor supervision;
- Monitoring activities to systematically implement ongoing assessments for gradual learning verification, and to activate targeted supplementary lessons for addressing learning deficits identified by students;
- Ensuring all teaching activities (lectures and internships) are conducted either in the morning (08:30–14:00) or afternoon (14:30–19:00) to allow students to dedicate part of their day to continuous self-directed or assisted study in designated university campus spaces, avoiding unnecessary time loss.

The responsible for the Department of Innovative Technologies in Medicine and Dentistry for Quality Assurance in teaching and research, to which the program is attached, is Professor Gabriella Mincione.

AQ Group members participated in processes related to SUA-CdS, SMA, and Cycle Review elaborations.

Program of Work and Implementation Deadlines The Council of the Course of Study schedules work on a quarterly basis, based on resolutions concerning faculty, student procedures, and other aspects related to the management and coordination of teaching activities.

Specifically, during the academic year 2023/2024, the following Council sessions were held to address and define the mentioned topics:
- Session of October 19, 2023;

The minutes of the aforementioned Council meetings, duly approved and submitted to Higher Academic Bodies for ratification of resolutions, are deposited and available for consultation at the Presidency Offices of the C.d.S. in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis and at the Presidency of the School of Medicine and Health Sciences.

Brief Description of Affine and Integrative Activities Affine and integrative activities aim to provide additional knowledge and competencies within the field of dental sciences. A primary educational objective of the C.d.S. in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis is to train professionals capable of operating in any dental environment with diverse patient types.

Affine and integrative activities within dental and maxillofacial disciplines contribute to achieving this objective by providing knowledge and competencies to evaluate, through diagnostic phases, oral cavity pathologies and appropriate therapies to restore correct masticatory and periodontal function of the entire stomatognathic apparatus.

Affine and integrative activities also aim to provide additional knowledge that complements basic and characteristic disciplines, particularly regarding oral cavity pathologies. These courses contribute to the multidisciplinary training of dental professionals and aim to equip them with essential competencies to promote an appropriate approach to problematic patients, thereby optimizing their performance and expected outcomes.

Therefore, some affine and integrative activities included in the study plan of the C.d.S. in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis are particularly effective in providing theoretical-practical knowledge regarding teaching and educational technologies in the broader context of distance learning.

Briefly, the S.S.D. (Scientific Disciplinary Areas) where these affine and integrative activities are conducted, as specified in our study plan, are:
- BIO/17: HISTOLOGY;
- MED/03: MEDICAL GENETICS;
- MED/04: GENERAL PATHOLOGY;
- MED/30: VISUAL APPARATUS DISEASES;
- MED/46: LABORATORY MEDICINE TECHNIQUES

Brief Course Description The Master's Degree Course in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis, class LM-46, was activated in the academic year 2009-2010 by the Faculty of Medicine and Surgery Council in accordance with the Ministerial Decrees of March 16, 2007, which redefined the classes of degree courses and master's degree courses in line with the D.M. n. 270 of October 22, 2004, respecting the freedom of teaching, as well as the rights and duties of professors and students. The relevant Teaching Regulation, which governs the study program and specifies its organizational aspects, was reformulated for the 2017/18 cohort by the Course Council in its meeting of July 20, 2016, and approved by the Department of Medical, Oral, and Biotechnological Sciences and the School of Medicine and Health Sciences to align with the University's Teaching Regulation issued under D.R. N. 863 of December 16, 2013. The study program has a six-year duration, requires the acquisition of 360 CFU, and is based on the following types of training activities: basic, characteristic, affine or integrative, student choice, and final exam. The general framework of training activities is reported in the table attached to the Teaching Regulation (specified in another sheet), identifying the number and type of scientific-disciplinary areas and the CFU assigned. The academic year is organized around annual courses starting in the first week of October and ending no later than May of the following year. Educational objectives are achieved through courses identified and approved by the Course Council before the start of each academic year's lectures. For further information about the C.d.S., refer to the School of Medicine and Health Sciences portal, www.med.unich.it, link Dentistry.

External Effectiveness The Interuniversity Consortium ALMALAUREA continuously monitors the employment status of Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis graduates at our University: the selected group covers the calendar year 2022 and includes 58 graduates. 55 graduates completed the questionnaire, representing a 94.8% completion rate; of these, 60% were male and 40% female, with an average age of 27.4 years at graduation.

In the selected group, 38.2% of the 2022 graduates had prior university experiences, of which 7.3% had obtained a degree in previous careers and 30.9% had not completed their studies and enrolled in the C.d.S. in Dentistry. The average graduation grade was 104.1, and the average study duration was 6.5 years, with 59% graduating on time and 97% regularly attending more than 75% of the required courses.

18.2% utilized scholarships; 20% completed study periods abroad or within the Erasmus program or other EU initiatives, with 100% of exams taken abroad validated in the C.d.S. study plan.

The average time spent preparing the thesis was 12 months.

Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description The objective of the Master's Degree in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis is to train a professional capable of practicing dentistry. The general objectives and structure of the teaching ordinance described below refer to the contents of the new Ministerial Decree on New Degree Classes – Regulation for Master's Degree Courses, which defines Master's Degree Courses in compliance with European Union directives, the University's Teaching Regulation, LEGGE 8 November 2021, n. 163, and the Interministerial Decree n. 653 of 5-7 2022. The teaching ordinance requires the acquisition of 360 CFU over 6 years. The distribution of the 360 CFU is determined in accordance with the conditions specified in the decree's attachments, which establish the CFU to be assigned to disciplinary areas including essential training activities for dental training.

For the university credit (CFU), equivalent to 25 hours of student effort, and the ratio of CFU to hours of frontal lectures/exercises/laboratory and CFU to hours of professional internship, refer to the University's Guidelines and the course's Teaching Regulation. The remaining CFU quota is available for the student's independent or assisted self-study.

Pursuant to Interministerial Decree n. 653 of 5-7 2022 and LEGGE 8 November 2021, at least 30 CFU will be acquired through a practical-evaluative internship, i.e., a professional training path aimed at acquiring specific competencies and diagnostic and clinical-therapeutic skills in the prevention, diagnosis, and therapy of oral and maxillofacial diseases, related to disciplines such as oral surgery, restorative dentistry, endodontics, implantology, oral pathology and medicine, pediatric dentistry, special dentistry, orthognathodontics, periodontology, and prosthesis.

The holders of professional courses are responsible for the related internship. The physiological and clinical knowledge of general medicine and oral-maxillofacial disciplines acquired through the training activities included in the teaching plan and clinical practical activities determine and define the professional profile of the dentist operating in European Union countries.

Upon completion of six years, the Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis must have acquired the knowledge, technical skills, and practical preparation to enter the dental profession in both private and public settings. The graduate must be able to perform activities related to the prevention, diagnosis, and therapy of dental, oral, jaw, temporomandibular joint, and related tissue diseases, as well as dental rehabilitation, prescribing all necessary medications and devices for professional practice. The graduate must possess a level of professional, cultural, decisional, and operational autonomy enabling continuous updating, having followed a training path characterized by an holistic approach to oral health issues of healthy or ill individuals, also in relation to their physical and social environment.

In general, the first two years focus on basic training activities to familiarize students with the structure and functions of the human body, including courses addressing the doctor-patient relationship and the principles underlying scientific methodology. Students also acquire information-technology skills to receive technological innovations in various branches of dentistry.

The subsequent three years involve the study of medical, surgical, and specialist disciplines with particular reference to clinical issues related to oral and maxillofacial pathologies. These training activities occur concurrently with the study of dental disciplines and the professional clinical internship.

The sixth year focuses on acquiring specific competencies and diagnostic and clinical-therapeutic skills, particularly through clinical and practical-evaluative internship (TPV). TPV CFU can only be acquired through activities performed as a primary operator under direct supervision of a professor-tutor at university or National Health Service facilities following a convention. Pursuant to Article 2, paragraph 9 of DM n. 653 of 5-7 2022, TPV credits are acquired in the sixth year of study, with a maximum of 30% of the total credits possibly acquired in the fifth year.

Consultation with National and International Organizations Representing Goods and Services Production and Professions (Course Establishment)
The general objectives and structure of the study plan refer to the contents of the new Ministerial Decree. The Master's graduate in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis must acquire a solid foundation in medical disciplines relevant to dentistry and dental disciplines. The course specifically provides the competencies necessary to practice the full range of general dentistry, identifying treatment priorities; learning the fundamentals of human pathology by integrating physiological and pathological study with clinical methodology and diagnostic procedures; controlling cross-infection to prevent physical, chemical, and microbiological contamination in professional practice; analyzing scientific literature and applying research results to therapy reliably; developing an interdisciplinary clinical case approach; educating patients in appropriate and effective oral hygiene techniques; correctly interpreting legislation concerning dentistry practice in the European Union; organizing and guiding the dental team using the full range of available auxiliary personnel; deepening knowledge regarding the development of a multicultural society. Graduates have employment opportunities in the field of independent dental practice and in managerial roles at levels I and II within the National Health System or in private clinics contracted with it.

Final Exam Characteristics Pursuant to Articles 1 and 3 of Law 8 November 2021, n. 163, the final exam for the single-cycle Master's Degree in Dentistry and Dental Prosthesis - class LM-46, which qualifies for the dental profession. For this purpose, the final exam includes the performance of a Practical-Evaluative Test (PPV) of professional competencies acquired through a Practical-Evaluative Internship (TPV) within the study program, aimed at verifying the candidate's practical preparation level for professional licensure, preceding the final exam.

The PPV is organized through the student's discussion of three multidisciplinary clinical cases treated as a primary operator during the TPV, involving multidisciplinary treatment plans covering most disciplines of the TPV.

The PPV judging committee has a balanced composition between university professors and members designated by the National Dental Board Commission. Additionally, a member registered with the Dental Board is invited to participate in the graduation session. To pass the PPV, students receive a qualification, after which they proceed to the thesis defense.

The final exam, accessible after acquiring at least 350 credits and granting an additional 10 CFU, consists of presenting and discussing a thesis developed by the student under the guidance of a supervisor.

The Master's degree grade (ranging from a minimum of 66 to a maximum of 110, with possible honors) is assigned by a designated committee in a public session, taking into account the student's entire study path. The organization of the final exam, composition of the committee, and evaluation criteria are defined by the Master's Degree Course's Teaching Regulation.

Conduct of the Final Exam The C.d.S. sets three dates within the summer, autumn, and extraordinary sessions each academic year. The final exam session involves the candidate presenting an original thesis under the guidance of a supervisor or co-supervisors. The presentation, which may be in English, has no time constraints and may include slides, photos, panoramas, videos, especially in the presence of clinical cases or research conducted on archived clinical records from the Department of Innovative Technologies in Medicine and Dentistry.

The committee, consisting of a minimum of seven to a maximum of eleven members, may ask questions and request clarifications regarding specific topics in the thesis after the candidate's presentation. After the presentation, candidates are asked to leave the hall while committee members assign each candidate a score from 0 to a maximum of 7. Each professor considers the following elements in assigning the score:
- Thesis presentation by the candidate;
- Clarity of images projected via PowerPoint;
- Quality of answers to committee questions.

The average of the scores assigned by committee members contributes to determining the final degree grade. Candidates are then invited to return for the proclamation by the committee chair.

Students have 10 CFU dedicated to thesis preparation at university or basic facilities. This activity, called 'Thesis Internship,' must be performed outside official teaching hours, not overlapping with student-choice activities (ADE), and must be requested from the supervisor at least six months before the graduation date, with the thesis submitted to the General Student Office. For the Master's degree, a thesis must be presented, developed by the student under the guidance of a supervisor and possibly co-supervisors. The thesis may also be written in a foreign language previously agreed upon. Students intending to complete the Thesis Internship in a specific discipline must submit a formal request to the thesis supervisor, including their curriculum (list of exams passed and grades, list of optional activities attended, laboratory or clinic internships, or any other training activities). The supervisor, upon verifying available slots, accepts the request and may assign a tutor to monitor and certify the student's activities.

The final degree grade, expressed in hundredths, is determined by the following parameters:
a) The average of grades obtained in curricular exams, expressed in hundredths;
b) Points assigned by the Graduation Committee during the thesis discussion, obtained from the average of individual scores assigned by committee members, up to a maximum of 7 points;
c) Points for each honor received in profit exams (0.1 point per honor);
d) Years of study (1 point for graduates on time).

Honors may be awarded with a unanimous committee decision to candidates achieving a final score of 111 or higher.

Admission Procedures The Master's Degree in Medicine and Surgery is a nationally regulated access course. Admission requirements are governed by national laws and ministerial regulations.
Admission procedures and content are established annually through ministerial decrees, which also specify deadlines, requirements, and registration procedures for the admission test.
The Admission Notice, published annually on the University website (www.unich.it), indicates the deadlines and procedures for registering for the test at the chosen location.
Specifically for the 2024-25 academic year, the Ministerial Decree MUR n.472 was published on 23/02/2024, establishing access procedures for the upcoming student cohort.
To be admitted to the Master's Degree in Medicine and Surgery, candidates must hold a Secondary School Diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent.
Enrollment in the course is conditional upon passing an Admission Test administered twice in person at university locations on 28 May 2024 and 30 July 2024. The first test, scheduled during the school year, may also be taken by candidates enrolled in their final year of secondary school. Candidates may participate in both tests and choose the higher score for inclusion in the ranking. The test will be identical for all students and consist of 60 multiple-choice questions covering reading skills, acquired knowledge, logical reasoning and problem-solving, biology, chemistry, physics, and mathematics.
The number of admitted students for the first year of the CLMMC is nationally regulated (closed quota) annually based on national medical workforce needs and the local training capacity of each Medicine and Surgery course.
Enrollment is granted to students ranked within the predetermined number of admitted students.
After enrollment, as required by Article 6 of DM 270/2004, specified in the Medicine and Surgery Course Regulations and detailed in SUA Sheet A3a - Required Knowledge for Access, each student's need for Additional Educational Requirements (OFA) is assessed based on admission test scores in Biology, Chemistry, and Physics.
To this end, the Course Council has established a threshold score below which enrolled students are assigned Additional Educational Requirements (OFA) to be fulfilled in the first year of the course. The percentage of correct answers in the admission test related to Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics questions is evaluated to assign OFA in the most deficient area(s).
The Additional Educational Requirement (OFA) to be fulfilled will be communicated to the student, who must attend recovery activities to address the identified educational gaps. OFA will be considered fulfilled upon passing the relevant course examinations in the disciplines covered by the OFA.

Communication skills
Graduates must be able to communicate clearly and unambiguously their conclusions, knowledge, and underlying rationale to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, as well as to their patients in the manner required by the circumstances.
Therefore, they must be able to:
1) Listen attentively to extract and synthesize relevant information on all issues, understanding their content.
2) Apply communication skills to facilitate understanding with patients and their relatives, enabling them to share decisions as equal partners.
3) Communicate effectively with colleagues, the Faculty, the community, other sectors, and the media.
4) Interact with other healthcare professionals involved in patient care through efficient teamwork.
5) Demonstrate basic teaching abilities and appropriate attitudes when instructing others.
6) Demonstrate good sensitivity towards cultural and personal factors that enhance interactions with patients and the community.
7) Communicate effectively both orally and in writing.
8) Create and maintain good medical documentation.
9) Summarize and present appropriate information to meet audience needs, and discuss achievable and acceptable action plans that represent priorities for the individual and the community.

Making Judgements
Graduates must have the ability to integrate knowledge and manage complexity, as well as formulate judgments based on limited or incomplete information, including reflection on the social and ethical responsibilities related to the application of their knowledge and judgments.
Making Judgements is progressively acquired and verified throughout the course in examination assessments (oral, written, and practical exams) conducted during the training path.
Therefore, in various contexts, they must be able to:
Critical Thinking and Scientific Research:
1) Demonstrate in professional activities a critical approach, constructive skepticism, and a creative attitude oriented towards research.
2) Consider the importance and limitations of scientific thinking based on information obtained from diverse sources to establish the cause, treatment, and prevention of diseases.
3) Formulate personal judgments to solve analytical and complex problems ('problem solving') and independently seek scientific information without waiting for it to be provided.
4) Identify, formulate, and solve patient problems using the foundations of scientific thinking and research based on information obtained and correlated from various sources.
5) Be aware of the role that complexity, uncertainty, and probability play in decisions made during medical practice.
6) Formulate hypotheses, collect, and critically evaluate data to solve problems.
Professional Values, Skills, Behavior, and Ethics:
1) Identify the essential elements of the medical profession, including moral and ethical principles and legal responsibilities underlying the profession.
2) Respect professional values including excellence, altruism, responsibility, compassion, empathy, reliability, honesty, integrity, and commitment to following scientific methods.
3) Be aware that every physician has the obligation to promote, protect, and improve these elements for the benefit of patients, the profession, and society.
4) Recognize that good medical practice depends closely on interaction and good relationships between physician, patient, and family, safeguarding well-being, cultural diversity, and patient autonomy.
5) Demonstrate the ability to correctly apply principles of moral reasoning and make appropriate decisions regarding possible conflicts in ethical, legal, and professional values, including those that may arise from economic distress, commercialization of healthcare, and new scientific discoveries.
6) Respond personally to the need for continuous professional improvement with awareness of one's own limitations, including those of medical knowledge.
7) Respect colleagues and other health professionals, demonstrating the ability to establish collaborative relationships with them.
8) Fulfill the moral obligation to provide medical care in the terminal phases of life, including symptom and pain palliative therapies.
9) Implement ethical and deontological principles in handling patient data, avoiding plagiarism, maintaining confidentiality, and respecting intellectual property.
10) Effectively plan and efficiently manage one's time and activities to address conditions of uncertainty and exercise the ability to adapt to changes.
11) Exercise personal responsibility in caring for individual patients.

Orientation and ongoing tutoring The orientation and ongoing tutoring activities are organized and regulated by the Course Council, in accordance with the University and Master's Degree Course Teaching Regulations.
In particular, the Master's Degree Course in Medicine and Surgery provides distinct tutoring roles:
a) the TEACHER-TUTOR role, to which a small number of Students are assigned for the execution of supplementary tutorial teaching activities and/or support planned based on students' needs or requests to a Coordinator/teacher of a Course Unit or to the Course Chair.
This tutorial activity constitutes a genuine teaching task. Each Teacher-Tutor must coordinate their functions with the teaching activities of the courses sharing the same educational objectives and may also be involved in preparing materials for tutorial teaching. All teachers of the Course, upon specific request, carry out tutorial activities, also in small groups, and are required to be available to perform Tutor duties.
Clinical Tutors are also included in this category, represented by doctors with university, hospital, and General Medicine roles operating in the hospital facilities and territory of the Chieti-Lanciano-Vasto and Pescara ASLs. Selected by the coordinators of professional training internships in various disciplines, they play a fundamental role in the clinical training of students during curricular professional training internships and practical assessment internships (TPVES). In the context of TPVES, the tutor:student ratio is typically 1:1 to maximize learning.
b) STUDENT-TUTORS. Annually, calls for assignments are published to incentivize didactic-integrative, preparatory, recovery activities, and tutoring for deserving students regularly enrolled in the IV, V, and VI years of the Master's Degree Course in Medicine and Surgery and for Medical Research Doctorate Courses.
Winning students of the Master's Degree Course and 'senior' students of the Course who receive tutoring assignments are engaged in activities aimed at guiding and assisting students throughout their academic journey, managing a listening and information point called MED-POINT, and drafting and updating a 'Student-to-Student' Guide to the Medicine and Surgery Course, published on the Course website, while collaborating with teachers in conducting practical exercises and pre-clinical internships.
Typically, Student-Tutors are also involved by teachers in didactic-integrative recovery and support activities for students who have requested academic support or who, based on career monitoring, are experiencing specific difficulties with certain courses.
Methodological tutoring interventions have also been carried out for students facing difficulties in study methodology, promoting the formation of study groups for individual exam preparation.
The 2022 and 2023 calls provided assignments for 150 hours for an extremely limited number of Course students (respectively 3 and 4 students), who were mainly employed for orientation activities upon entry and as digital tutors.
Students can find all information on orientation and ongoing tutoring activities by accessing the Course website in the 'Orientation and Tutoring' folder, which lists the request procedures and the lists of available teaching and clinical Tutors. Evaluation forms for Tutors are also available in anonymous form. Students are requested to complete the Tutor evaluation questionnaire available on the Course website, expressing an opinion on tutoring activities (Tutors and facilities visited) and their effectiveness, with the possibility to add comments. It is also specified that this completion is voluntary, anonymous, but important for evaluating different activities/structures and for guiding and optimizing future choices. Collected questionnaires are discussed by the CTP and results reported to the Course Council.
c) Additionally, for information on administrative procedures, to receive assistance and information on the educational offer or IT service support (exam booking and ADE, frequency verification, booking of professional training internships), or to request personalized assistance for personal academic issues, the Course has made available for many years a 'SUPPORT FOR TEACHING OF THE MEDICINE AND SURGERY MASTER'S DEGREE COURSE' desk at the Course Chair (Monday to Friday, 10:00-18:00) and a dedicated email (supporto.didatticamedicina@unich.it) capable of interfacing directly and in real time with the Course Chair, Student Secretariat, and all relevant offices.
d) Furthermore, CONTEXT SERVICES for G. d'Annunzio University students, launched in 2013, are active and include:
1) The Psychological Listening and Orientation Counseling Service (SAPCO) for students experiencing psychological issues affecting study capacity and performance. The service provides individual psychological counseling paths.
2) The Specific Learning Disorders (SDSA) service offers students with DSA individualized consultations by specialized operators, aimed at facilitating student integration and improving quality of life.
3) The Student Disability Orientation and Welcome Service (SOASD) is for students with disabilities, as well as their families, and provides essential support by activating necessary support interventions (physical accompaniment/study support/welcome and orientation upon entry/ongoing orientation/exit orientation) to guarantee the right to education.

Assistance for Training Periods For the completion of training periods in external structures to the University, normally a convention or agreement is activated, upon proposal by a faculty member of the Degree Course, between the School/University and the external public or private Italian or foreign structure (other University, Research Center, Entities, hospital structures, health facilities) that will host the student, in order to ensure adequate academic and scientific support from the hosting structure and the necessary insurance coverage.
The completion of internships and traineeships in external structures, in Italy or abroad, may be aimed at carrying out activities to acquire specific skills, approved by the Degree Course, or to the realization/integration/completion of the Thesis, upon approval by the Supervisor and the Degree Course.
Students wishing to carry out an internship/traineeship in an external structure (national or international) with which no convention is currently in place are directed by the Degree Course Presidency to a Tutor faculty member of the relevant scientific area, who proceeds to identify and contact the University/Research Entity deemed suitable to establish a convention or agreement.
Alternatively, students may choose on their own initiative an external university and organize an overseas study period independently (Free Movers/Visiting Students).
Free Movers students may obtain an additional score on their Degree grade for periods exceeding one month by submitting appropriate certification from the host University/Structure.
On return to the university, students are asked to complete the evaluation questionnaire available on the Degree Course website, expressing an opinion on the structures visited. It is also specified that this completion, necessarily non-anonymous, is optional but important for evaluating different sites and guiding the choices of other students.

Career support The University's Career Guidance, Tutoring and Placement Office offers, among other services, a Placement desk providing various career orientation tools, such as:
- information on labor regulations and contracts,
- guidance for preparing curriculum vitae;
- verification of employability profile;
- facilitation for recent graduates;

Additionally, the Office publishes a START bulletin board with offers from public and private entities/companies providing internship, traineeship, apprenticeship, and training/research opportunities (START program) for students and graduates. Information is also provided regarding VAT registration and setting up start-up businesses.
Information can be obtained at the following address: https://placement.unich.it Regarding employment opportunities for graduates in Medicine and Surgery, it is necessary to note that obtaining the degree is part of a complex training path that, until the 2019-20 academic year, required passing a State Exam for Professional Qualification after the degree. This State Exam has now been integrated into the degree program starting March 2020, so the Medicine degree qualifies for the profession of Medical Doctor. The natural path for a Medicine and Surgery graduate, after obtaining the degree, involves enrolling in a Specialization School at universities, following successful completion of an admission exam, or in a training course for General Medical Practitioner qualification offered by local health authorities. After completing the specialization or General Medicine training, the specialist doctor can be employed by public or private hospitals, or practice independently. Medicine and Surgery graduates may also be employed in research institutions, both public and private, pharmaceutical companies, and national or international health organizations.
In this context, consultations with representatives of Medical Councils, General Medicine associations, and local private healthcare providers are particularly informative regarding employment opportunities for graduates in local or national settings across various specializations or in General Medicine.
Career Integration Pathways and study paths linked to High-Level Apprenticeship do not apply to the Medicine and Surgery Degree Course.

Other initiatives The Course of Study has progressively activated and/or implemented a series of initiatives aimed at enhancing students' vocational potential (e.g., through the Excellence Pathway), and providing knowledge on emerging or socially relevant themes (e.g., major emergencies from natural disasters (earthquakes/floods/snow), disaster medicine, nuclear-biological-chemical-radiological risk, or violence and abuse against minors and newborns) via Elective Teaching Activities (ADE).

The level of interest generated by different initiatives is also indirectly measured by the number of students enrolling in each activity. Therefore, proposals that do not reach an adequate number of enrollments are not repeated the following year.

The Course of Study has also joined national initiatives proposed by the Permanent Conference of Presidents of Master's Degree Courses in Medicine and Surgery, such as the Progress Test, Training Test, and recently the TECO-M test, to monitor students' progressively acquired transversal and disciplinary knowledge.

EXCELLENCE PATHWAY An Excellence Pathway (EP) was established starting from the 2013-14 academic year, reserved for second-year students of the Master's Degree Course in Medicine and Surgery who are deserving and interested in conducting in-depth and research activities.

The Excellence Pathway represents an additional and integrative training path consisting of interdisciplinary seminar-type teaching activities and laboratory and/or clinical internships aimed at motivating and enhancing the talent of the most deserving students.

The Excellence Pathway is an important tool to allow students to approach and integrate into activities related to clinical and/or laboratory research, facilitating a more conscious choice of future prospects.

The Excellence Pathway, lasting three years and structured into different Curricula, is accessible annually to a limited number of students who have completed all first-year exams with an average grade of at least 27/30 by the extraordinary session of the enrollment/registration year, as defined by the Excellence Pathway Regulations of the Master's Degree Course in Medicine and Surgery, Article 12 of the University Teaching Regulations, and the Course of Study Teaching Regulations.

Students who complete the EP while maintaining the above requirements throughout the three years will be awarded a study prize equivalent to the tuition fees and university contributions paid for enrollment in the final year of the course, and a score within the framework of the graduation incentives.

The activation of the EP for 6 students in the 2013-14 academic year was renewed for 8 students in 2014-15, 10 students in 2015-16, 12 students in 2016-17, 11 students in 2017-18, 10 students in 2018-19 with an offer of 11 training curricula, and for 10 students in 2019-20 with an offer of 10 different translational curricula, for 12 students in 2020-21 with an offer of 10 different curricula, for 10 students in 2021-22 with an offer of 8 different curricula, and for 10 students in 2022-23.

The call for the 2023-24 academic year, approved by the Department Council (DMSI) on the recommendation of the Course of Study in March, is currently being published and will be open to 9 students.

This initiative generates significant interest among students, evidenced by the large number of applications submitted annually by deserving students interested in this training initiative. To date, only 3 out of the 89 students admitted to the Excellence Pathway have been unable to complete it.

INTEGRATED TEACHING ACTIVITIES BY EXPERTS ON SOCIAL IMPACT Numerous integrated teaching activities planned for the 2023-24 academic year focus on medically and socially relevant topics not immediately covered by the integrated course programs, thus providing useful enrichment for Medicine and Surgery students. Examples include: Child abuse and maltreatment; Risk Management tools; Ethics of communication between patient and doctor; Medical-legal assessment of victims of maltreatment, sexual violence, domestic violence, stalking: role of ASL; Gender medicine; Certifications and prescriptions in General Practice; Hospice and palliative care; Clinical use of blood and blood components (ADE conducted in collaboration with the Italian Red Cross) and many others.

INTEGRATED TEACHING ACTIVITIES BY THE COMMISSION ON MAJOR RISKS AND MAJOR EMERGENCIES OF MILITARY HEALTH The Course of Study has promoted a convention with the A.N.S.M.I. Military Health Interforces Association to conduct Elective Teaching Activities (ADE) on aspects related to major emergencies from natural disasters (earthquakes/floods/snow), rescue operations, hostile environments, disaster medicine, and nuclear-biological-chemical-radiological (NBCR) risk.

Activities have been conducted annually since the 2015-16 academic year (3 ADE activities), in 2016-17 (5 ADE activities), and in 2017-18 and 2018-19 (5 ADE activities).

In the 2019-20 and 2020-21 academic years, the number of ADE activities was reduced (3 ADE activities conducted online) due to the health emergency that directly involved the Commission members.

The ADE on Major Emergencies has been scheduled again for the 2023-24 academic year.

Teaching activities have been conducted, also using operational area videos, by medical officers directly involved in various major emergency operations from the Emergency and Rescue Units of the Carabinieri, Army, Air Force, Navy, and Police.

INTEGRATED TEACHING ACTIVITIES BY UNICEF In the 2018-19 academic year, Elective Teaching Activities (ADE) were activated for Medicine and Surgery students as a pilot project in Italy in collaboration with the Chieti UNICEF Committee, conducted by doctors and psychologists to provide fifth and sixth-year students with tools to identify all forms of violence and abuse against minors and newborns.

ADE activities were regularly conducted in the 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, and 2022-23 academic years, though during the COVID-19 emergency they were conducted online.

In the 2023-24 academic year, these ADE activities have been restored in person.

PROGRESS TEST/TRAINING TEST/TECO-M Annually, the Medicine and Surgery Course of Study has participated for over ten years in the national Progress Test (PT) promoted by the Permanent Conference of Presidents of Master's Degree Courses in Medicine and Surgery.

The Progress Test has served as a useful national tool to evaluate students' preparation in Medicine and Surgery Courses across different locations, thus representing an indirect tool to assess the quality of Italian Medicine and Surgery Courses.

In the 2017-18 academic year, 1,021 students from the second to sixth year voluntarily took the PT, and in 2018-19, 1,036 students did so, representing participation rates between 83% and 92% of enrolled students per year. Individual student results are published exclusively on their personal web page, allowing them to verify if their knowledge progresses proportionally to their academic year, thus serving as a self-assessment tool.

Aggregated results by cohort/year and by area (Basic Sciences and Clinical Sciences) and/or discipline are presented and discussed annually at the Course of Study Council to evaluate potential knowledge gaps regarding specific questions. It thus serves as a useful tool to assess the average preparation level of each student cohort.

In particular, the 2018-19 PT served as a true 'dress rehearsal', a 'Training Test', in preparation for the new written exam, with closed-question bank, of the state examination for medical and surgical licensure as per DM.58/2018.

In the 2019-20 academic year, the Training Test, scheduled for April, was suspended due to the COVID-19 emergency. Additionally, the elimination of the written state examination for licensure has limited its preparatory and training value, though it continues to serve as a useful tool to assess the average preparation level of students comparatively across different locations.

In this context, the Permanent Conference of Presidents of Master's Degree Courses in Medicine and Surgery, in collaboration with ANVUR, proposed conducting a test called TECO-M in the 2020-21 academic year to assess students' transversal and disciplinary competencies. The TECO-M test, conducted in April, was administered remotely in a pilot phase only to third and sixth-year students who voluntarily participated.

Information regarding all initiatives proposed by the Course of Study is available at the Course of Study's web address.

Student Opinions The Student Opinions survey has been in effect for the Master's Degree Program in Medicine and Surgery for over ten years, following the recommendation of the University's Evaluation Unit (NdV) and therefore the University's Quality Assurance Unit (PQA), using a common online questionnaire for all University degree courses, prepared according to AVA guidelines, which students access via personal password to express, in complete anonymity, their evaluation of attended courses by answering the proposed questions, as well as providing comments and/or personal suggestions in the notes. Students can choose to express their evaluation either during the lecture semester, at the time of exam registration, or to express no evaluation. Following the recommendation of the PQA and the Chair of the Course (CdS), teachers encourage the completion of the questionnaire during the lecture semesters, emphasizing the importance of their evaluations and comments for individual teachers/courses, as well as to report specific teaching and/or organizational issues of the Course. The PQA proceeds to a detailed analysis of the annually collected data, making available by the end of July the analytical evaluations to the individual teachers responsible for the various teaching modules and to the Course Directors. Annual data is published annually in aggregated form on the University's PQA website (see the 2023 Student Opinion Report attached). Course Directors have access to both the students' evaluations of individual teaching modules and the aggregated results. The effectiveness of this system largely depends on the active collaboration of students, which has been very high for first-year students but has gradually decreased in subsequent years, as evidenced by the number of evaluations for first-year courses compared to those for final-year courses. Annually, the results of the 'Student Opinions' surveys are presented and discussed in the Course Council meetings. Analyzing individual questionnaire responses has allowed the identification of some critical issues, leading to the planning of appropriate actions, often through tutoring interventions by teachers or student-tutors, but also, based on student proposals, implementing targeted actions to improve the organization/delivery of teaching activities, particularly for courses with critical evaluations. The effort of the Course, individual teachers, and student representatives in encouraging students to complete the questionnaire, emphasizing its importance and role, has resulted in a significant number of evaluations (valid questionnaires) that have progressively increased from 5,292 evaluations in the academic year 2013-14 to 26,263 evaluations in the academic year 2022-23. Simultaneously, the number of courses evaluated (considering a minimum of 6 evaluations per course) has progressively increased from 61% of courses offered in 2013-14 to 99.02% in 2022-23. It is important to note that the SARS-COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent activation of distance learning affected student participation in extracurricular academic activities, thus reducing the number of evaluations collected during the academic years 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22. Overall, the average scores assigned to the Course by students in the evaluation questionnaire have shown a progressive increase: from an average score of 3.15 (out of a maximum of 4.0) in 2015-16 to 3.26 in 2019-20, 3.32 in 2020-21, and 3.35 in 2021-22. For the academic year 2022-23, the average score, calculated based on partial data provided by the PQA as of July 31, 2023, is 3.32. This score (as reported in the attached PDF) essentially reflects a decreased overall satisfaction (questions D0, D1, D3: average score of 3.26 in 2022-23 compared to 3.29 in 2021-22) and a decreased evaluation of teaching effectiveness (questions D20, D21, D22: average score of 3.35 in 2022-23 compared to 3.40 in 2021-22), while the evaluation of logistical and organizational aspects remains relatively stable (questions D9, D13, D14, D16: average score of 3.35 in 2022-23 compared to 3.36 in 2021-22). Analyzing the detailed responses reveals, in the partial data for 2022-23, slightly lower scores compared to the previous biennium for the interest in topics covered in the course (question D0); the study load/CFU ratio (question D3); and the ability of teachers to stimulate interest and provide clarifications during lectures and/or office hours (questions D20 and D22). The progressive increase in the average score naturally reflects the percentages of courses with scores categorized into four levels: Level A: scores from 3.5 to 4.0; Level B: scores from 3.0 to 3.5; Level C: scores from 2.5 to 3.0; Level D: scores from 1.0 to 2.5. In the triennium 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22, the number of courses with Level A evaluation increased from 4 (1.99%), 3 (1.51%) to 22 (10.84%), while the partial data for 2022-23 indicates 16 (7.88%). Conversely, although no course falls under Level D, courses with Level C, albeit sporadically, were 1 in 2020-21 and 2 in 2021-22 and 2022-23 (see the attached Student Opinion PDF). To further value student opinions and encourage self-assessment, results are presented and discussed in Course Council meetings as well as in smaller meetings with teachers to address specific issues/requests. In Course Council meetings, results are presented both in aggregated form and comparatively with other courses at the University, with each module and each academic year analyzed individually. To encourage student and teacher participation, an annual 'Top Ten' ranking is presented, including the names of teachers and their respective teaching modules that received the highest scores. The Student Opinion results are attached to the Course Council minutes and made available on the Course website. It should be noted that students can freely present issues to the academic office, either directly or through their representatives, and that the University has activated a Customer Satisfaction procedure accessible online at https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi, where students can report specific issues. The summary documents related to the 'Student Opinion Survey' 2021 and 2022, made available by the PQA and containing the final data for the academic years 2019-20 and 2020-21-22, were presented and discussed in the Course Council meetings on September 13, 2021, September 14, 2022, and September 2023, during which preliminary results for the 2022-23 academic year evaluations collected as of July 31, 2023, were also presented. Regarding Student Opinions on CLINICAL INTERNSHIPS, the current online survey allows evaluation of clinical internships included in Integrated Courses as a whole, without providing insights into student opinions on individual clinical tutors assigned during the internship. Since it is important to understand the detailed evaluation of individual tutors to better select clinical tutors, in addition to the continuous monitoring of student judgments on clinical internships as direct feedback and through their representatives, the Course has prepared an evaluation form to be distributed along with the student's Practical Evaluation Booklet for the State Exam (TPVES) starting in October. The Course has also initiated the collection of Student Opinions on ELECTIVE TEACHING ACTIVITIES (ADE) on a sampled basis, to better guide the ADE offering, which is remodeled annually. The satisfaction index, verified also by the number of students choosing different ADE offerings, provides an indirect satisfaction index and determines the renewal of the offered activities in the following academic year or their elimination. The block of in-person teaching activities starting in March 2020, at the beginning of the second semester, and the subsequent resumption in mixed mode for the academic year 2020-21 due to the current health emergency caused by COVID-19 has significantly interfered, in some cases blocked, the monitoring activities related to Clinical Internship and Elective Teaching Activity opinions. Therefore, the low number of collected forms in the academic years 2020-21 and 2021-22 does not allow for a reliable assessment.

STUDENT OPINIONS DISTANCE LEARNING Starting from the academic year 2020-21, our University has accepted the request of the Didactic Commission of CRUI by including in the student opinions questionnaire 12 questions related to the EVALUATION of DISTANCE TEACHING (DAD).
The data provided by PQA's 2022 Report and regarding the valid questionnaires collected in the academic year 2020-21 for the courses of the Study Program show that: 26% of the courses were delivered in person or in blended mode (in person and simultaneously online), while 34% of faculty delivered lessons online.
Considering the University's decisions for the academic year 2020-21 regarding teaching, which allowed all students to freely choose the attendance mode for lessons, students declared they chose to attend exclusively (69%) or predominantly (12%) lessons in distance mode, residing in 67% of cases in another city or country and only in 33% in the same city where the course is held. Distance mode did not interfere with communications with faculty, which occurred through various modes: in person, during lessons, via email or phone, and through in-person or distance appointments.
The majority of students reported having access to a PC (71%), smartphone (16%), or tablet (12%) for personal use (82%), but connectivity issues were reported, interfering with 14% of students' satisfactory access to teaching.
Overall, 87% of students reported overall satisfaction with the distance and blended teaching methods adopted for the academic year 2020-21.
OPINIONS OF GRADUATES PQA made available the first Report in 2019 regarding the opinions of graduates in Medicine and Surgery who submitted a graduation application in the academic year 2017-18, for a total of 280 responses; in the 2020 Report, regarding graduates who submitted a graduation application in the academic year 2018-19, responses were 158; in the 2021 Report for the academic year 2019-20, responses were 229; in the 2022 Report, regarding graduates of the academic year 2020-21, responses were 179; and in the 2023 Report regarding graduates of the academic year 2021-22, responses were 169.
In the academic year 2018-19, the average score of 3.23 attributed to the Study Program in Medicine and Surgery was higher than in previous years, in line with the average scores attributed to Health Area Study Programs and slightly above the University average (3.16).
In the academic years 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22, a clear decrease in the average scores attributed to the Study Program was recorded, respectively 3.09, 3.06, and 3.05. This decrease, recorded in the academic year 2019-20 also in the average scores of Health Area Study Programs (3.14) and the University, can be explained by the difficulties caused by the suspension of all in-person activities in the second semester of the academic year 2019-20, which necessarily initially suspended all activities in the academic year 2019-20 and then significantly limited the number of students admitted to clinical departments and university laboratories in the academic years 2020-21 and 2021-22, making it difficult to prepare experimental graduation theses and carry out qualifying clinical internships. It is worth noting the entry into force of DM 58/2018, which establishes the qualifying degree for the Medicine and Surgery Study Program, anticipated compared to national programming to respond to the increased demand from all healthcare structures for qualified doctors to be immediately employed in the national healthcare service.
The analysis of scores related to individual questions provided useful elements to highlight and address the most perceived issues by graduates, as well as to highlight the strengths of the Study Program. Scores between 3 and 2.5 indicate a criticality, while scores between 1 and 2.5 are considered indicators of serious criticality.
For the Medicine and Surgery Study Program, no scores indicating serious criticality were recorded. However, questions with scores between 2.5 and 3 were discussed in the meetings of the Council on September 25, 2019, September 30, 2020, September 13, 2021, and September 14, 2022, with corrective actions planned.
In particular, for the academic years 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22, the critical issues relate to questions: D9: judgment on teaching equipment (laboratories), also reflected in scores attributed to the University; D11: adequacy of study load relative to course duration; D12: evaluation of support provided by the university for internship or training activities.
Graduates of the academic years 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22 assigned a slightly lower score than previous years to question D3: "Overall organization (schedule, exams) of courses provided during the reference period" and a score below 3.00 and below the University average to question D9: "Judgment on equipment for other teaching activities (laboratories, practical experiences) during the reference period," highlighting the organizational difficulties that Health Area Study Programs had to face during the pandemic, particularly for practical activities. Indeed, these questions show criticality specifically in Health Area Degree Courses.
On the other hand, many strengths of the Medicine and Surgery Study Program were highlighted by scores above the University average, for example in the academic year 2019-20: D5: Secretariat Service (3.03 compared to 2.93); D7: Classrooms; D8: Computer equipment; D10: Library services.
All graduates highly evaluate the overseas experience (average evaluation of 3.87 in the academic year 2021-22) and also positively evaluate the support provided by our University, assigning an overall score of 3.23.
The satisfaction level (D16) appears slightly increased among graduates of the academic year 2018-19, who report overall satisfaction in 90% of cases, and 70% would enroll again in the same course at this University, compared to 18% who would enroll again in the same degree course but at another University and 9% who would change both the degree course and the University.
Also in the academic year 2019-20, the satisfaction level remains high (85% report overall satisfaction, and 57% would enroll again in the same course at this University, 36% would change University). Overall, the satisfaction level expressed in the academic years 2017-18/2019-20 is substantially stable, obtaining scores of 3.08, 3.16, and 3.13 respectively, while it appears decreased in the academic years 2020-21 and 2021-22, with scores of 3.01 and 3.00. This decrease, discussed in the Study Program Council, reflects, at least in part, the difficulties and limitations necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly for the conduct of qualifying internships, which required a very tight scheduling, and restrictions on guest access to Graduation Sessions to maintain the required numbers and distancing.
STUDENT CRITICITIES AND PROBLEMS Any criticalities or problems are reported directly by the concerned student or communicated through Student Representatives and addressed directly to the Study Program Director or by Tutor faculty, who work to identify the most appropriate solutions while operating with impartiality and independence of judgment.
Also, the Study Program Council, parallel to the Academic Senate's decision of September 17, 2019, which accepted the request of Student Representatives in the S.A., pending operational guidelines from central bodies, approved the President's proposal to establish one or more Student Guarantors for the Study Program. Moreover, students can freely report criticalities to the Study Program's Academic Secretariat or use the University's Customer Satisfaction procedure, expressing specific criticalities directly to the online service accessed by connecting to the website https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi. The results of Student Opinions and Graduates' Opinions are made available on the Study Program's website.
