Graduate Opinions The data made available on the Alma Laurea website and related to interviewed graduates show a constant progressive increase in graduates of the CdL who report having attended more than 75% of the required courses (with percentages of 77.7% of graduates in the calendar year 2019, 84.3% in 2020, 89.4% in 2021, and 88.4% in 2022), always significantly higher than graduates of the same class (percentages of 66.7% in 2019, 71.3% in 2020, 72.3% in 2021, and 70.7% in 2022).
The progressive improvement in attendance percentages seems to indicate the success of strategies (such as expanding study areas, opening the new Medical-Scientific Library, campus spaces available until 8 PM, and some classrooms and libraries open until 10 PM) implemented by the Degree Course and the University, which has allowed optimizing course attendance while also providing dedicated spaces and time for personal study and the performance of professional activities.
Additionally, the 2020-21 academic year was particularly challenging due to the pandemic, but the CdL adopted measures to ensure educational continuity, including the use of online platforms and the scheduling of recovery sessions.
The Master's Degree in Medicine and Surgery is required for access to Medical Specialization Schools. Graduates in Medicine and Surgery will find employment opportunities in various clinical, health, and biomedical professional roles both nationally and internationally.
The introduction of the national ranking and subsequent roll-downs have resulted, starting from the 2013-14 academic year, in enrollment periods not always compatible with the attendance requirement, with mid-year enrollments and the consequent difficulty for these students to acquire the necessary attendance to take the first-year profit exams, even though the CdL organized attendance recovery courses at the end of the first semester and during the second semester, which allowed almost all new enrollments to recover.
Additionally, the numerous appeals accepted by the TAR have allowed enrollment above the quota or with reservation for a significant number of students (notably the 2014-15 cohort, which included 320 students against a potential capacity of 222 students, and which in the 2019-20 academic year, now in the sixth year of study, still consists of 285 students), creating organizational issues regarding teaching facilities (classrooms and laboratories), which are now affecting the professional practical training for the state exam (TPVES) (in teaching laboratories and clinical departments), causing discomfort for students and increasing the teaching and organizational load for faculty, who have had to re-modulate/reprogram and, in some cases, repeat teaching activities, in order not to penalize students' careers, allowing the recovery of lost teaching activities.
In the 2018-19 to 2022-23 cohorts, the majority of students come from Abruzzo (with percentages of 45.0%, 44.7%, 53.9%, 45.4%, and 49.76%, respectively), with significant numbers also coming from the Adriatic regions, primarily Apulia, Marche, and Molise. Smaller percentages come from Veneto, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna, Sicily, Campania, Umbria, Tuscany, Piedmont, Basilicata, Calabria, Lazio, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, and Trentino-Alto Adige, as well as non-EU students primarily from Israel.
The prevalence of female students in the 2018-19 to 2022-23 cohorts is 65.4% (compared to 65.9%, 58.2%, and 58.4% in the previous triennium), while the percentage of students aged 17-19 has decreased significantly (42.7% in 2018-19, 39.3% in 2019-20, 44.9% in 2020-21, 50% in 2021-22, and 42.6% in 2022-23), indicating increasing difficulties in accessing Medicine.
The progressive increase in the age of enrollment can be attributed to the limited access to the course due to the quota system, representing an increase in students who, while waiting to pass the entrance exam, enroll in other university studies, often requesting the recognition of prior studies upon enrollment in the Medicine and Surgery CdL.
The most frequent secondary school of origin for the 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, and 2022-23 cohorts is the Scientific High School (63.3%, 66.6%, 63.7%, and 61.6%, respectively), followed by the Classical High School (22.9%, 15.8%, 19.7%, and 22.2%, respectively), with minimal percentages from other secondary school types.
The distribution of high school graduation scores in the 2018-19 to 2022-23 cohorts shows a progressive increase in the percentage of students who achieved a score of 100/100 or 100 with honors, rising from 33.6% in the 2018-19 cohort to 40.9% in the 2022-23 cohort.
The first-year curriculum monitoring for the 2021-22 cohort indicates that students, on average, earned 52.44 CFU (out of 60), consistent with the previous two cohorts (52.76 CFU in 2019-20 and 53.66 CFU in 2020-21), with an average grade of 25.60 out of 30 (compared to 26.77 in 2019-20 and 27.26 in 2020-21), and an average of 5.18 exams taken, compared to 5.27 and 5.23 exams per student in the previous cohorts.
The average CFU earned and exams taken across all cohorts (from 2009-10 to 2021-22) remain within a range of 48.09 to 54.97 CFU, representing 80.15% to 91.61% of the required 60 CFU for the first year, with an average of 4.66 to 5.29 exams.
The detailed analysis of CFU earned by the 2021-22 cohort shows that 83.03% of students earned more than 40 CFU (compared to 86.7% in 2019-20 and 86.24% in 2020-21), indicating a progressive increase in the number of students who earn at least two-thirds of the required CFU in the first year.
Conversely, the percentage of students earning between 21 and 40 CFU has decreased (10.10%, 10.58%, and 8.04% over the triennium).
Regarding exam grades, only 33.04% of the 2021-22 cohort achieved grades between 28 and 30/30 (compared to 55.32% and 62.43% in the previous two cohorts), while the percentage of students with grades between 24-27 increased (56.25% compared to 38.83% and 32.28%), and the percentage of students with grades between 18-23/30 remained relatively stable (4.79% in 2019-20, 3.17% in 2020-21, and 4.46% in 2021-22).
Analysis of exam results by session for each cohort does not reveal specific difficulties in passing any particular exam.
The partial monitoring of the 2022-23 cohort, excluding data from the autumn 2023 and extraordinary 2024 sessions, shows a good performance, with students having taken an average of 4.1 exams and earned 41.82 CFU (71.68% of the required CFU) by September 8, 2023, with an average grade of 25.94.
Overall, student performance has improved in terms of both CFU acquisition and grades in the last three academic years compared to previous cohorts.
The percentage of students progressing to the second year of the course for the latest cohorts is 96.81% for the 2019-20 cohort (86.7% with more than 40 CFU), 98.41% for the 2020-21 cohort (86.24% with more than 40 CFU), and 91.96% for the 2021-22 cohort.
A significant issue is the variability in enrollment timing due to ranking roll-downs, which extend throughout the academic year, interfering with attendance requirements for the first year (e.g., enrollments for the 2021-22 cohort until July 2022 and for the 2022-23 cohort as late as September 2023), particularly affecting second-semester attendance for some students, even though recovery courses were provided.
For the 2016-17 cohort (the last completed), the progression of CFU earned was as follows:
- First year: 175 out of 182 students (96.15%) earned CFU (range 1-60), with 157 students (86.26%) earning 41-60 CFU and 18 students (9.89%) earning 1-40 CFU.
- Second year: 92.6% (163/176) of students earned 61-120 CFU (compared to 84.8% and 87.79% in the previous completed cohorts).
- Third year: 83.81% (145/173) earned 121-180 CFU (compared to 73.3% and 77.71% in previous cohorts).
- Fourth year: 80.8% (139/172) earned 181-240 CFU (compared to 70.2% and 74.39%).
- Fifth year: 69.76% (120/172) earned 241-300 CFU (compared to 58.5% and 63.19%).
- Sixth year: 61.98% (106/171) earned 301-360 CFU (compared to 55.9% and 57.14%).
The progressive improvement in student career data is confirmed by the percentage of graduates in the 2016-17 cohort (the last completed), which stands at 58.47% (100/171), higher than previous cohorts (49.2%, 45.04%, 48.2%, and 47.82% from 2012-13 to 2015-16).
The Course in Figures: Overall data on the student population of the CdL
Analysis of all students enrolled in any curriculum of the Medicine and Surgery CdL shows that the ratio of students currently enrolled (1,300) to the total enrolled (1,799) remains relatively stable in the 2022-23 academic year (72.26% compared to 72.16%, 71.97%, 71.64%, 71.37%, and 72.52% over the previous five years).
In the 2019-20 academic year, the 250 total graduates earned their degree as follows: 43.2% on time (including 7.20% early graduates), 23.20% one year late, and 33.60% two or more years late.
In the 2020-21 academic year, the 188 total graduates earned their degree as follows: 38.3% on time (including 4.79% early graduates), 25% one year late, and 36.7% two or more years late.
In the 2021-22 academic year, the 208 total graduates earned their degree as follows: 45.2% on time (including 1.92% early graduates), 19.71% one year late, and 35.10% two or more years late, consistent with the previous biennium.
Overall, in the calendar year 2022, 62.96% of students (119/189) graduated on time or one year late, compared to 65.23% (152/233) in the calendar year 2021.
In the 2021-22 academic year, the percentage of students who achieved a grade of 110/110 or 110/110 with honors (55.77%) was in line with the 2020-21 academic year (55.31%), but lower than previous years (62.9% and 60.4% in 2018-19 and 2019-20), reflecting the pandemic's impact on student careers.
The analytical and statistical data on student careers, useful for monitoring the results of teaching activities, were prepared by the PQA and made available through the S.I.Ca.S. (Student Career Indicators System) and M.E.P. (Coortes Profit Exam Monitoring) systems on the PQA website.
The annual data on student enrollment and progression, provided by the PQA, were presented and discussed in the Degree Course Councils on September 13, 2021, September 14, 2022, and will be presented in the September 2023 Council, where student and graduate opinions for the 2022 calendar year will also be discussed.
Characteristics of the Final Exam
The Degree Exam, or Final Exam, involves the discussion of a dissertation (Thesis) on a topic previously agreed upon with a Supervisor. The thesis must be written originally by the student under the guidance of the Supervisor; a Co-Supervisor may also be appointed. The roles of Supervisor and Co-Supervisor are determined by the Degree Course Council and listed in the Degree Course Regulations (http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/medicina-e-chirurgia).
The thesis can be written in Italian or English.
Students have 18 CFU dedicated to thesis preparation.
To be eligible for the Degree Exam, students must have completed all courses, passed the related exams, and earned 360 CFU (including at least 60 in professional training activities) over six years. Students must also submit a request to the Student Secretariat following the annual procedures published on the Degree Course website (http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/medicina-e-chirurgia).
Additional information is published on the website http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/medicina-e-chirurgia.
The Degree Grade is determined by the average of grades from curricular exams, the evaluation assigned by the Committee during the thesis discussion, and any additional evaluations, following the procedures outlined in the Degree Course Regulations (http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/medicina-e-chirurgia).
The Degree Grade is expressed out of 110.
Final Exam Procedure
Decree Law March 17, 2020, No. 18, Article 102, states that the completion of the Master's Degree in Medicine and Surgery (Class LM-41) qualifies for the medical profession, provided the successful completion of practical training (TPVES) as specified in DM No. 58/2018.
The Final Exam consists of presenting and discussing a written dissertation (Thesis) developed originally by the student under the guidance of a Supervisor, before a Degree Committee composed of 7-11 faculty members, as required by current regulations.
In the Final Exam Committee for the Abilitant Master's Degree in Medicine and Surgery, a representative of the relevant Professional Order must participate (MUR Note No. 9758 of April 14, 2020), verifying the proper conduct of the final exam for subsequent registration on the Professional Register. The candidate accesses the exam after completing a study path that includes a positive evaluation of the TPVES as per DM No. 58/2018.
The thesis can be written in Italian or English. A Co-Supervisor may be appointed.
To be eligible for the Final Exam, students must:
1. Complete all courses in the Study Plan and pass the related exams;
2. Earn a total of 360 CFU over six years;
3. Receive a positive evaluation for the TPVES as per DM No. 58/2018;
4. Submit the required documentation to the Student Secretariat by the deadlines specified annually on the Degree Course website (http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/medicina-e-chirurgia), including:
   a) The online downloadable Thesis Title Request form, indicating the chosen topic and signed by the Supervisor;
   b) The Graduation Request within the session deadlines.
The Degree Exam is typically held during the following periods:
- First session (SUMMER): July-September
- Second session (AUTUMN): November-January
- Third session (EXTRAORDINARY): March-April
For cohorts enrolled starting from the 2009-10 academic year (LM-41 curriculum), the Degree Grade is determined by the following parameters:
A) BASE SCORE: Calculated as the arithmetic mean of 36 grades (as per DM March 16, 2007), expressed out of 110, including 35 grades from mandatory curricular courses and the final grade for elective activities (ADE), calculated based on the average of all ADE activities taken and passed.
B) THESIS EVALUATION: A maximum score of 7 points derived from the average of scores assigned by each committee member based on:
   1) Scientific quality and originality of the thesis;
   2) Quality of presentation and mastery of the topic;
   3) Critical abilities, biological and clinical knowledge, and skills demonstrated during the discussion.
C) BONUS POINTS: Up to a maximum of 7 points, awarded for:
   1) Study duration;
   2) Number of honors achieved;
   3) Documented training activities, including participation in international exchange programs or study stays (abroad or in Italy), or other activities demonstrating special commitment to training, as per the Degree Course Regulations (http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/medicina-e-chirurgia) and approved by the Degree Course Council.
The TOTAL GRADE, calculated by summing A + B + C, is rounded to the nearest whole number after the final sum.
The HONORS (Lode) can only be awarded with a unanimous committee decision to candidates who achieve a final score of 113/110 or higher.
The ACADEMIC MENTION, in addition to the Honors, can only be awarded with a unanimous committee decision to candidates who graduate on time with a base score of at least 108/110 and have completed a particularly significant scientific thesis.
Additional information or announcements regarding the Final Exam are published on the Degree Course website.

Admission Procedures Students wishing to enroll in the LM in Languages, Literatures and Modern Cultures must submit an application for pre-assessment of eligibility requirements via the University's dedicated platform (operational guidelines are included in the Study Plan published annually at the beginning of August).
The LM in Languages, Literatures and Modern Cultures is open to graduates from classes L-11 and L-12 (ex-DM 270), classes 3 and 11 (ex-DM 509), four-year degrees in Foreign Languages and Literatures (Modern), and students holding degrees obtained at foreign universities, provided their academic record demonstrates a structured three-year study of the two languages to be continued in the Master's program.
It is recalled that, pursuant to DM 270/2004, current access requirements for the A-24 Foreign Languages and Cultures teaching category in secondary education institutions require 36 CFU in language and 24 in literature. Students intending to pursue teaching, if they do not possess these credits, may acquire them through appropriate selection of elective courses and/or off-plan courses during the study plan compilation.
Additionally, graduates from other classes (new system ex-DM 270, previous system ex-DM 509, old four-year degrees, and foreign universities) who have acquired at least 26 CFU in the first language and 26 in the second language; at least 6 CFU in scientific-disciplinary sectors L-LIN/01 or L-LIN/02, or in the philology of one of the two study languages; at least 6 CFU in one of the scientific-disciplinary sectors M-STO/02, M-STO/04, L-ART/06, M-GGR/02 or similar; and at least 6 CFU in one of the sectors L-FIL/LET are admitted.
Candidates lacking these requirements may acquire the missing CFU by enrolling in single courses at the D'Annunzio University or other legally recognized universities and passing the relevant exams before submitting the pre-assessment application.
Foreign students without an Italian degree must provide certification or demonstrate, through a specific test, possession of Italian language skills at B2 level.
For degrees obtained abroad, students must submit, in addition to the degree equivalence declaration, the study plan with course syllabi, translated and legalized.
In all cases, the Council reserves the right to assess the relevance of acquired competencies for each individual application.

URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/12

Communication Skills (communication skills)
Graduates of the Master's degree program must be able to argue and communicate clearly and effectively, also in the foreign languages studied, ideas, problems and solutions, both to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
In particular, they must demonstrate:
- Ability to communicate, orally and in writing, based on critical-literary texts, information, ideas, problems and difficulties to specialist and non-specialist interlocutors.
- Ability to translate and conduct critical analysis of literary texts (from and into the languages studied).
- Ability to communicate orally and in writing in their own language and in the languages studied within professional activities and relationships.
- Ability to interact with others and lead collaborative activities.
- Ability to process and present experimental data using multimedia systems.
The acquisition of these skills will be assessed, in addition to the usual forms of verification at the end of each disciplinary course, through learning level assessments to which students will be subjected upon enrollment in the Master's program, at the end of the first academic year, and before the final thesis defense.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [LM37] MODERN LANGUAGES, LITERATURES AND CULTURES
TYPE: Master's Degree
SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/12

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
Graduates of the Master's degree course must demonstrate having developed autonomous judgment capabilities and the ability to manage complex issues based on limited information, as well as the capacity to expand the acquired judgment autonomy in relation to socio-cultural and ethical-scientific implications connected to their field of reference.
In particular, they must demonstrate:
- Ability to select, analyze and interpret highly specialized texts and to translate literary text types from and into the languages studied.
- Ability to analytically identify problems and formulate appropriate solutions.
- Ability to locate and evaluate data and information sources concerning cultural materials (literary, aesthetic and historical in nature).
- Ability to address diverse themes within work contexts consistent with the course's specificities.
The acquisition of these skills will be assessed, in addition to standard verification methods at the end of each disciplinary course, through learning level assessments to which students will be subjected upon enrollment in the Master's degree course, at the end of the first academic year, and before the final thesis defense.

Training Periods STAGES AND INTERNSHIPS A stage or internship refers to a period of training and work orientation at a partner organization or company affiliated with the Department of Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures. The duration of a stage is calculated based on the CFU to be acquired as specified in the student's curriculum: 1 CFU corresponds to 25 working hours. A stage may serve as a basis for the final thesis, which must be previously agreed upon with the supervisor of the final project. The administration and coordination of external stages and internships are entrusted to the Teaching Tutor and Member of the Department's Orientation Committee, Dr. Lorena Savini.
Requests for participation in internships must be submitted at any time of the year to the Teaching Tutor, Dr. Lorena Savini (email: tutorato.lingue@unich.it) for the preparation of the training project.
The number of CFU associated with the "AAF stages and internships" entry in the study plan from the academic year 2023-2024 is organized as follows: 4 CFU Internship at partner organizations, 2 CFU participation in professional development seminars OR 6 CFU Internship at partner organizations.
LM37 Internships: 18+15
Method of acquiring CFU:
Stages can only be completed starting from the third year of a three-year degree program and from the second year of a master's degree program. CFU acquired through stages cannot be supplemented by other qualifications held by the student (other courses, language certifications, ECDL, professional development seminars). At the end of the stage, the student must submit: the signed attendance sheet completed by the company tutor, accompanied by their stage report and a report written and signed by the company tutor, and a copy of the authorized and registered training project. All documentation must be provided in original. CFU will be automatically added to the student's record only after approval by the Course Council.

International Mobility Office In addition to lectures and opportunities for direct contact with foreign students within the Department, students are offered numerous possibilities for study stays at foreign universities within the Erasmus program.
Students can go to a foreign university for a period ranging from four to nine months to carry out study activities equivalent to those conducted at their home university, such as attending courses, taking exams as planned in the Learning Agreement, and preparing their thesis.
International mobility for students is guaranteed through various Erasmus agreements and International Conventions with different countries.
The Department of Languages, Literatures and Modern Cultures currently has numerous bilateral Erasmus agreements with various foreign universities and some international conventions.
Conventions:
University of Vlora Lazarevic Albania Polotsk State University, Novopolotsk Belarus Universidade Presbiteriana Mackenzie, Brazil De Abreu Brazil The Universidade Federal de Goiás, Brazil De Abreu Brazil Universidad Estado Amazonas UEA De Abreu Brazil University of Macau De Abreu China Universidad de La Habana Solinas Cuba Universitè Bordeaux Montaigne D'Angelo France Masarikova Univerzita, Brno D'Angelo Czech Republic Institute for Literature and Arts, Belgrade Lazarevic Serbia Universidad Politecnica de Madrid D'Angelo Spain University of Neuchatel Del Gatto Switzerland University of Tunis El Manar, Tunisia Perolino Tunisia Ivan Franko University of Lviv, Ukraine Lazarevic Ukraine Bishop Grosseteste University, UK Costantini UK Salem State University, USA Costantini USA Nazareth College, NY Ettorre USA Students can spend between three to twelve months in Erasmus at a foreign university for study, thesis preparation, or internship, which will subsequently be recognized by their home university upon completion of the Learning Agreement (minimum 12 curricular CFU). Students can also go on Erasmus for thesis preparation, earning up to 15 CFU. Students may also participate in Erasmus traineeships during their studies or immediately after obtaining their degree.

Additional initiatives The Study Course provides a series of professionalizing Seminars. These consist of frontal activity hours with an expert speaker addressing one or more specific topics to complement the content offered by the curricular teaching.
The quantity and quality of seminar proposals are evaluated and approved by the Course Council.
Attendance is open to students of all years. Attendance will be recorded by signing at the end of each lesson.
For this item in the study plan, no more than 2 CFU can be acquired through participation in conferences, where "conference" does not refer to a seminar or professionalizing module, but to one or more study days on literary or cultural topics, different from the orientation towards the world of work.
Professionalizing seminars can be attended from the first year of the course, and the CFU acquired each time, if insufficient to cover the number required by the student's curriculum, may be supplemented by other titles held by the student (other courses, language certifications, ECDL).
Students may request CFU recognition for this item after enrolling in the second year of the Master's Degree, by submitting a request to the Department Student Office.
The CFU will be automatically inserted into the student's academic record and DO NOT need to be recorded in the transcript.
Along with orientation initiatives at entry and during the course, the initiatives mentioned above have contributed to an increase in enrollments for the 2020-2021 academic year (204 students compared to 194 in the 2019-2020 academic year). [source: PQA Monitoring 2020]
In addition to professionalizing seminars, teachers from the four Study Courses based in the Department of Languages offer a series of cultural initiatives and seminars/conferences/scientific conferences, to which students can participate to enrich their training and deepen their skills (see link).

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Master's graduates of the Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures Program acquire the critical and philological skills necessary for advanced linguistic and literary text analysis. The theoretical-methodological skills possessed by graduates of this Master's program enable them to engage in specialized teaching in linguistic, literary, and translation fields, as well as collaborate in publishing and international cultural cooperation.
Graduates will benefit from a rich educational offering organized into lectures, exercises, computer laboratory activities, and seminar activities applicable to specific areas of competence and aimed at developing a work and research methodology.
The high specialization and excellent project management and relational skills developed during the training process enable graduates to apply their knowledge in various national and international work contexts: managing linguistic expert roles in international cultural cooperation institutions and Italian institutions abroad (Embassies, Consulates, Cultural Institutes); operating as intercultural experts for diplomatic and administrative institutions in minority language and immigration/emigration areas in Italy and abroad; performing significant roles in public and private entities, publishing industries, and cultural and heritage institutions such as state archives, libraries, superintendencies, scientific editorial offices, etc.; exercising high-responsibility roles in intercultural and interlinguistic communication within artistic, journalistic, and multimedia fields; pursuing literary and technical-specialized translation expertise in the cultural and publishing industry; and continuing studies by accessing research doctorate courses in linguistic, philological-literary, and historical-cultural fields.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
Master's degree graduates must demonstrate adequate learning abilities and methodologies to independently develop further study and expand their knowledge.
In particular, they must demonstrate:
- Full development of the four linguistic skills and achievement of translation competence in languages A and B for highly specialized texts within the course's reference field.
- Full competence in the reference framework of selected foreign languages and literatures.
- Ability to present study outcomes orally and in writing, following methodologies and utilizing information technology tools.
The acquisition of these skills will be assessed not only through standard verification methods at the end of each course but also through learning level assessments to which students will be subjected upon enrollment in the Master's program, at the end of the first academic year, and before the final thesis defense.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Master's graduates in Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures possess in-depth linguistic and literary knowledge of at least two foreign languages, in addition to Italian. The acquisition of linguistic and philological-literary competencies provides graduates with the necessary tools for a critical and methodological approach across various disciplines. This mature theoretical and practical training offers versatile application of skills in multiple cultural, artistic, historical, and aesthetic contexts. However, graduates will develop competencies in cultural communication and literary and philological domains. This interdisciplinary training also enables graduates to master specific methodological tools for sociological and critical-philological analysis of literary texts in international cultural contexts.

The vast majority of teachers teaching in the Program belong to the Department of Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures, which hosts the study course.
The Study Course benefits from the collaboration of the teaching staff (administrative personnel: Ettore Nicolucci, Paolo Veggetti) and the teaching tutor, Dr. Lorena Savini.

Planning of Work and Implementation Deadlines To ensure effective management aimed at improving alignment with objectives over time, the Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures Study Course has defined a general planning of main activities based on internal needs and deadlines set by regulations. This includes periodic meetings of the Parity Commission, Quality Assurance Commission, and Program Council. In particular, the Parity Commission and Quality Assurance Commission meet before the deadlines set by regulations and present their reports to management bodies before the deadlines. Additionally, the Program Quality Manager coordinates with the Department's teaching staff to monitor the smooth operation of Program activities, ensuring work is conducted as planned.
The planning, annual or multi-year depending on the subject, follows this scheme:
1. Annually, the Program reviews or revises the educational objectives, proposing updates in time for inclusion in the SUA-CdS (March-April).
2. Similarly, the Program reassesses the validity of the educational path annually, within the time needed for inclusion of any updates in the SUA-CdS (January-February).
3. The Program proposes to the Department Council the teaching coverage for the following year, indicating any shortages or issues in the delivery of standard teaching (January-February).
4. Analysis of data from student, graduate, and alumni opinion surveys is conducted during the summer (July-September).
5. The survey on training demand, through meetings with social partners, institutions, and companies involved in producing goods and services, occurs at least twice a year (February-March and September-October).
6. Periodic evaluation of the Program's activities in various areas: infrastructure (classrooms and laboratories) and their improvement, student opinions on teaching activities, analysis of knowledge and skill outcomes, occurs before each Program Council meeting, during meetings with other Program Chairs of the Department of Modern Languages, and during Quality Assurance meetings held at least quarterly.
7. Annual evaluation of the results of correction and improvement interventions occurs between November and December.
8. Redefinition of educational objectives (in relation to social partner consultations) is typically every three years, and always in time for inclusion in the SUA-CdS.
Since autumn 2021, a process to improve the educational offer has been initiated by the Chair, taking advantage of the possibility offered by DM 133 of February 2, 2021, to add new TAF C entries without proceeding with a full curriculum reform. The improvements introduced include:
A. Reversal of TAF C for Year I (M-STO/02 L-ART/06) with TAF C for Year II (L-LIN/02).
Motivation: Courses in the L-LIN/02 sector are highly characteristic of Class LM37, which also prepares for teaching and research. It is therefore considered that such competencies should be acquired at the beginning of the Master's program to lay solid foundations for students' professional use of foreign languages in their reference fields.
B. Addition to Year II TAF C, as an alternative to M-STO/02 (Modern History course) and L-ART/06 (History and Critique of Cinema course), of the sectors: M-GGR/02 (with the course Tourism Geography) and L-FIL-LET/14 (with the course Literature Theory).
Motivation for adding M-GGR/02: This scientific sector is extremely useful for completing students' transversal knowledge, preparing them to work not only in teaching and research but also in cultural promotion and tourism.
Motivation for adding L-FIL-LET/14: This scientific sector is extremely useful for completing students' transversal knowledge, especially to develop critical reading and analysis skills of literary texts, which are fundamental educational goals of the Program.
For the 2023-2024 cohort, in line with initiatives promoted in the University's three-year programming plan, the CFU for "Training and Orientation Internships" were increased from 4 to 6, and the final thesis from 18 to 16.
For the 2024-25 cohort: To make the Program's educational offer more functional to its professional goals, in line with suggestions from stakeholders, the following changes are implemented:
A. Renaming of language courses to 'Language and Translation' for both academic years.
B. Expansion of the Educational Linguistics course (TAF C; 6 CFU) to TAF D (9 CFU) to allow students to take both Educational Linguistics and Italian L2 Teaching courses.
C. Addition of Italian Linguistics (L-FIL-LET/12) to Year II TAF C to enable students to acquire CFU necessary for teaching.
D. The final thesis is reduced to 14 CFU (within the range set by the curriculum) to establish a 2 CFU writing workshop (in addition to Courses, Internships, and Training). There is a strong need to improve students' writing quality and knowledge of textual types, as required by educational goals.
Summary of Affine and Integrative Activities Within the definition of the Program's curriculum, 'Affine and Integrative' activities (TAF C) aim to integrate the core course plan (TAF B), making the overall educational framework fully functional and relevant to the Class's educational paths.
Students, based on their educational interests, can choose from a range of disciplines in linguistic, language teaching, literary-critical, historical, geographical, and broader cultural fields.
Historical and geographical knowledge, as well as knowledge related to audiovisual-multimedia fields, allow students to contextualize philological-literary knowledge within diachronic, diatopic, and diamesic perspectives.
Linguistic and language teaching knowledge enable students to deepen their metalinguistic skills, fundamental for the professions of translator and educator/instructor, which are two of the preferred career paths for Program graduates.
The deepening of literature theory provides a solid foundation for working with literary texts professionally (as translator, critic, teacher, or communicator) and relates knowledge of literatures in the studied languages.
Brief Course Description Qualifying educational objectives of the Master's Degree course are:
- Achieve advanced knowledge of the history of literature and culture of European and American civilizations in their various expressions.
- Achieve high competence in at least two of the European and American languages and civilizations, along with theoretical tools for their comparison.
- Acquire theoretical and practical tools for linguistic and literary analysis, translation, and teaching of literatures and languages.
- Be able to use main information technology and multimedia tools in specific areas of competence.
- Possess written and oral mastery of at least two European Union languages, in addition to Italian.
Expected Learning Outcomes To obtain the degree, students must demonstrate consolidated and expanded linguistic-cultural competencies and the ability to understand issues and epistemological horizons typical of a Master's level. They must also demonstrate in-depth knowledge of the most up-to-date bibliographic tools, awareness of recent research developments in their field, and the ability to elaborate and apply original ideas.
In particular, they must demonstrate:
a) In-depth knowledge of European and American cultures in literary, philological, artistic, and anthropological aspects.
b) Acquisition of competencies necessary to apply literary and linguistic analysis from an intercultural perspective, including literary translation, as well as acquisition of techniques related to linguistic and literary teaching.
c) In-depth knowledge of the relevant literatures in the curricular languages.
d) Good knowledge of information technology and multimedia systems and related instrumental management skills.
The acquisition of these skills will be assessed, in addition to standard verification methods at the end of each course, through learning level assessments to which students will be subjected upon enrollment in the Master's program, at the end of the first academic year, and before the final thesis defense.

Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements The Program has conducted a survey of opinions from entities and companies that have signed internship/training agreements (curricular or extracurricular). It is noted that entities and/or companies that previously hosted students and graduates of the Program have renewed their availability and expressed highly positive evaluations of the students' commitment in their activities.
Additionally, in the first semester of academic year 18-19, a questionnaire was sent to stakeholders. Questions related to:
1. Partners' expectations regarding skills and competencies beyond linguistic ones of interns;
2. Organization of internships by the departmental structure;
3. Positive and negative aspects of the experience;
4. Utility of the internship for the hosting structure.
Almost all responses were received, allowing for analysis of the results. It is clear that stakeholders prioritize competencies such as 'teamwork' or 'commitment' alongside linguistic knowledge of our students. They find the organization of internship activities very functional and believe the internship experience improves operational activities in the hosting sectors.
The pandemic prevented this activity during academic year 2019-20.
For academic year 2020-2021, the consultation was conducted on March 29, 2021.
Generally, entities and companies appreciate the linguistic preparation of students; additionally, the Caritas representative highlights their good preparation in language teaching.
They also noted aspects to enhance or improve, possibly through specific seminars, including:
- Practical skills in using programs such as PowerPoint and Excel; Cristina Ceccherelli suggests including tasks requiring PowerPoint creation in assessments to help students learn to use it as needed;
- Skills in using translation technology tools (CAT-tools);
- Development of relational skills (practical use of language, understanding/explaining concepts in language; interacting with clients, writing correct emails, letters, quotes, etc.);
- Development of sector-specific skills (drafting quotes, estimating delivery times, calculating words, characters, translation service prices);
- Greater depth in economic-legal competencies;
- More targeted training for sectors present in the territory.
Regarding the most useful languages, entities and companies confirm the utility of widely used languages: English and Spanish, followed by German, French, Russian, and then 'exotic' languages; they suggest favoring the choice of a well-known, widely used language (English, Spanish, French, German) and a less known one for a more original market qualification. Fabrizio de Lellis (Caritas) notes the absence of courses in Indic, Urdu, and Farsi languages in Programs, which are highly requested for migrant integration, and the near absence of foreign students pursuing a language degree in Italy, who would be ideal for employment in social and school integration sectors.
2021-2022 Academic Year
For 2021-2022, social partners were consulted on May 17, 2022, in a joint meeting with Programs L11, L12, LM38.
In the context of enhancing the educational offer of the four Programs, the key points emerging from the discussion, which received broad consensus, are:
- Stakeholders' appreciation for this annual working table and active involvement in aligning university paths with labor market needs;
- Need to complement linguistic competence with sector-specific knowledge (economic, legal, tourism techniques, company functioning, travel agency operations, etc.);
- Opportunity to enhance techniques for using foreign languages in professional contexts: from customer psychology to public communication techniques;
- Need to enhance practical aspects and spontaneous use of foreign languages at all levels;
- Need to enhance information technology skills (Excel, PowerPoint, cloud usage, etc.) and, especially post-pandemic, digital skills (company websites, digital teaching modules) and specialized communication via social networks;
- Request to establish a more immediate and continuous connection between the Department and the labor market through a dedicated space on the new website for job/internship proposals from companies; some stakeholders (Spazio Matta) suggest organizing open days for students to experience such work firsthand;
- Request to involve students representing the Programs in such discussions.
Francesco di Tommaso and Alessandro Fontana suggest developing more targeted professional seminars aligned with the needs expressed and offer their expertise (legal and technical translation first, tourism sector second).
Maria Donata Cerere emphasizes that cross-cutting competencies cannot be acquired through simple seminars and suggests including specialized disciplines (or even curricula) in the educational offer: economics, information technology, etc. Her intervention provides an opportunity for Maria Chiara Ferro and Marco Trotta to clarify that the freedom to intervene on the educational offer is always constrained by ministerial regulations; therefore, multiple needs must be balanced.
Vincenzo Longo and Sebastian Valentini offer the perspective of language teachers. Praising the numerous internships in schools already offered by the four Programs to students as an excellent opportunity to determine if they are suited for teaching, they note a certain theoretical knowledge gap in students' preparation from a language teaching perspective, suggesting the implementation of practical modules to develop problem-solving and digitalization of teaching materials.
Gregorio Palama, active in IT communities, emphasizes the importance of linguistic and cultural competencies in his field, where people with diverse backgrounds interact and communicate.

Characteristics of the Final Thesis Students are admitted to the final thesis after acquiring all credits set by the curriculum and demonstrating at least C1 level CEFR proficiency in the study language. This proficiency is verified during the second-year language exam, whose content is structured to achieve C1-level linguistic skills.
The final thesis consists of a text of at least 120 pages (2,000 characters each, including spaces), addressing a topic consistent with the Program's educational objectives, characterized by:
- Development of the topic in light of the most recent acquisitions in the field,
- Integration of the chosen topic into interdisciplinary contexts,
- The treatment must contain elements of critical originality.
The topic must be agreed upon with a Program teacher and supported by a second teacher from the LM37 Program or the Department.
The examination committee for awarding the degree is appointed by the Department Director and consists of at least seven members, official professors of the Department. The Chair of the Committee is held by the Program Council Chair or a first-tier professor appointed by the Director.
Final Thesis Examination Procedure The examination committees for final thesis evaluations are appointed by the Department Director, who also sets the work schedule. Composed mostly of professors from the University, committees consist of at least seven members, including the Chair and Supervisor. The Chair must ensure the full regularity of the examination and adherence of final evaluations to criteria established by the Program's governing bodies.
In assigning scores, the committee starts from the weighted average of grades obtained by the student in course exams. To this weighted average, a score for the thesis evaluation (between 0 and 5) is added, considering the thesis scope, writing precision and analysis, and argumentative and/or translation effectiveness.
Additionally, the following bonus points are awarded:
1 point for students not out of course at the time of graduation;
1 point for students who participated in international mobility;
1 point for students who passed at least three exams with a grade of 30 with honors.
The final thesis consists of a text of at least 120 pages (2,000 characters each, including spaces), addressing a topic consistent with the Program's educational objectives, characterized by:
- Development of the topic in light of the most recent acquisitions in the field,
- Integration of the chosen topic into interdisciplinary contexts,
- The treatment must contain elements of critical originality.
Thesis topic examples: 'Goldoni's Mémoires: Literary and Linguistic Aspects', 'The Don Giovanni Myth in European Novels', 'Dualism in English Literature', 'The Reader's Role According to Textual Pragmatics Theories'.
The Program Council, in agreement with the Supervisor, reserves the right to assess the eligibility of a final thesis written in a language other than Italian, provided it is accompanied by an adequate Italian summary.
Summary of the Technical Report by the Evaluation Unit The Program covers a central area in the humanities, scientifically and professionally relevant, consistently positioned at optimal levels in terms of enrollments and students relative to its class. The Department has adequate, suitable, and effective facilities, and following an advanced restructuring program of the Pescara Campus, new teaching and scientific spaces will be acquired in the short term, fully aligned with the new programming and its implementation prospects. The Department can rely on a specific teaching staff for basic and characteristic disciplines, widely adequate to the new programming and its implementation prospects. The proposed curriculum, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the University's goals of rationalizing and qualifying its educational offer.

Department DEPARTMENT OF MODERN LANGUAGES, LITERATURES AND CULTURES Website https://www.lingue.unich.it/didattica  Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission All students holding a first-level degree (Bachelor's degree in 'Foreign Languages and Literatures' (L-11) and Bachelor's degree in 'Linguistic Mediation and Intercultural Communication' (L-12)) are admitted to the course.
Admission procedures ADMISSION and verification of required knowledge for access:
The LM38 course in Foreign Languages for Business and International Cooperation admits graduates from classes L-11 and L-12 (ex-DM 270), classes 3 and 11 (ex-DM 509), four-year degrees in Foreign Languages and Literatures (modern), and students holding degrees obtained at foreign universities, provided their academic record demonstrates structured study over a three-year period in two of the languages offered in the Master's program (having acquired a minimum of 26 CFU for each language). In any case, the council reserves the right to assess the relevance of acquired competencies for each specific request.
Additionally admitted are graduates from other classes (new organization ex-DM 270, previous organization ex-DM 509, old four-year degrees, and foreign universities), who have acquired at least 26 CFU in the first language sector, 26 CFU in the second language sector, among the following offered in the study program:
L-LIN/04 LANGUAGE AND TRANSLATION - FRENCH L-LIN/07 LANGUAGE AND TRANSLATION - SPANISH L-LIN/12 LANGUAGE AND TRANSLATION - ENGLISH L-LIN/14 LANGUAGE AND TRANSLATION - GERMAN L-LIN/21 SLAVIC STUDIES L-OR/12 LANGUAGE AND LITERATURE - ARABIC L-OR/21 LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES OF CHINA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA At least 6 CFU in scientific-disciplinary sectors L-LIN/01 and similar;
At least 6 CFU in scientific-disciplinary sectors M-STO/02 or M-GGR/01 and similar;
At least 12 CFU for each literature related to the two chosen languages;
At least 6 CFU in INF/01 and similar sectors.
Candidates not meeting these requirements may acquire missing CFU by enrolling in single courses at the 'd'Annunzio' University or other legally recognized universities and passing the relevant exams before submitting a request for re-evaluation.
International students without an Italian degree must provide certified proof or demonstrate through a specific test that they possess Italian language skills at B2 level.
For degrees obtained abroad, students must submit, in addition to the equivalence declaration, the study plan with course syllabi, translated and legalized.
The Course Council reserves the right to verify each case individually.

Program, texts and objectives Note regarding the selected sectors and credits for characterizing activities Notes regarding characterizing activities It is proposed to include the discipline "Didactics of Italian as a Second Language" (SSD: L-LIN/02) in category B as a characterizing activity, since the LM38 study class is recognized among the Master's Degree classes for the purpose of the competition for the teaching qualification class A 023 - Didactics of Italian as a Second Language. Students enrolled in the LM38 Study Program have repeatedly expressed, individually, in groups or through student representatives, the need to include the L-LIN/02 SSD subject in the LM38 Study Plan, as they have long been forced to take it as an off-plan exam. It is also recalled that currently, not only for the aforementioned teaching qualification class but also for teaching foreign languages, students must have earned 12 CFU in the L-LIN/02 disciplinary sector during their study path. For these reasons, many Italian universities include in the Master's Degree Program LM 38 subjects from the aforementioned disciplinary sector.
Note regarding credits for other activities Notes regarding other activities In line with initiatives promoted in the University's three-year Programming Plan, the CFU for "Training and Orientation Internships" are increased from 4 to 6 to align with the objectives of the aforementioned plan, linked to indicator B-1 (proportion of enrolled students: 6 CFU acquired for curricular external internships at the University in the reference calendar year). This modification aims to make the LM38 Study Program's educational offer more functional to its professional goals, in line with recommendations from stakeholders.
Thus, the number of CFU for the Final Exam becomes 16 CFU (previously 18 CFU).
The RaD (Rapporto di Attività Didattica) regarding "Other Activities" is therefore modified to minimum 29 - maximum 35 CFU to provide corresponding flexibility within the CFU range for this area: specifically, intervention is made on "Training and Orientation Internships": minimum 6 - maximum 8 CFU, and on "Final Exam": minimum 14 - maximum 18 CFU.
Communication skills (communication skills)
Graduates of the Master's Degree program must be able to argue and communicate clearly and effectively, also in the foreign languages studied, ideas, problems and solutions, both to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
In particular, they must demonstrate:
- Ability to communicate, orally and in writing based on targeted text types, information, ideas, problems and difficulties to specialist and non-specialist interlocutors.
- Ability to translate and critically analyze specialist texts (from Italian to Languages A and B, and from Languages A and B to Italian).
- Ability to communicate, in written and oral form, in their own language and in Languages A and B within professional activities and relationships (commercial transaction).
- Ability to interact with others and lead collaborative activities.
- Ability to process and present experimental data using multimedia systems.

SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/13

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
Graduates of the master's degree course must demonstrate that they have developed autonomous judgment capacities and are able to manage complex issues even based on limited information, and are able to expand the autonomy of judgment achieved to the socio-cultural and ethical-scientific implications connected with their reference field.
In particular they must demonstrate:
- Ability to collect and interpret highly specialized texts and to translate textual types (language and translation of languages A and B).
- Ability to formulate analytical problems, ideas and autonomous solutions.
- Ability to express judgments that include reflection on important social, scientific and ethical issues.
- Ability to address diverse work areas and themes; ability to retrieve and evaluate information sources, data, linguistic-cultural literature, historical and geographical.

A valuable initiative promoted by the LM38 CdS and the Head of the Pescara Campus Library, Dr. Benedetta Maino, consisted of organizing two orientation days to present and promote all services and electronic resources offered by the Pescara Campus Library. These meetings, held by Dr. Loriana Tazzi on May 9 and June 4, 2019, primarily for graduating students, focused on bibliographic research assistance, catalog consultation (OPAC; SBN; MAI AZALAI, etc.), access to specialized databases (MLA; JSTOR; PROJECT MUSE; TORBOSA, etc.), and the use of Google Scholar, Google Books, Open Access. Given the great utility of the initiative, it was decided to repeat it periodically.
Support services for students, graduates, and students with disabilities: In 2020, Prof. Beatrice Fedi was appointed as the Department's disability coordinator. In this role, with the support of the Teaching Manager, Fedi carries out reception and ongoing teaching management, particularly regarding examination modalities (timing, equivalent forms of assessment, etc.) and the organization of internships at external entities and organizations (preparing the entity for student reception, programming essential supports to ensure autonomy during the internship activity, etc.).

Training periods Courses, internships and traineeships are provided by the Regulations in the second year of the Study Course. Therefore, a support service is available for students of the course in preparation for their external training period. The service is provided by the teaching tutor, Dr. Lorena Savini. The duration of an internship is calculated based on the CFU to be acquired as specified in the student's study plan. These CFU are automatically inserted into the student's academic record.
At the link: https://www.lingue.unich.it/node/6861 information on internship offerings and access procedures can be found. Students may also identify companies or other organizations of their knowledge or interest willing to host them, following the signing of a convention with the Department or the Study Course. The activities of trainees and the satisfaction of organizations and companies where they operate are monitored through questionnaires and periodic meetings. Generally, internship results are positive from both companies and organizations, as well as from students.
An additional internship opportunity is offered through the Erasmus+ traineeship program. The possibility to take courses, internships and traineeships allows students to gain contact with the working world, with very positive results. Undertaking activities at public and/or private organizations may also, optionally, serve as the topic for the final thesis.
Finally, for students with disabilities, the Teaching Tutor is responsible for organizing internships at external organizations (preparing the organization for student reception, planning essential support to ensure independence during the internship or traineeship activity, etc.).

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [LM38] FOREIGN LANGUAGES FOR BUSINESS AND INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
TYPE: Master's Degree
SECTION: Student opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/13

Student opinions Student evaluations are conducted through an online questionnaire, where students can anonymously express their satisfaction index regarding the organization of the study course, didactic activities, and infrastructure. Each individual teacher has access to the evaluation results concerning their own courses, and the Course Director can view the overall judgments of the Course. Student opinions are periodically discussed within the Course Council, the Parity Committee, Department Councils, and contribute to improving the organization and quality of the delivered teaching. The LM38 Course has also taken note of observations and improvement proposals from teachers and students through discussion in collegiate bodies and quality assurance bodies, as well as in other meetings organized by the Presidency (such as President-student representatives meetings), where it is possible to receive any complaints from the student body and develop resolution strategies.
The latest available evaluations (from 1 to 4), provided by the University Quality Assurance Unit (reference year 21-22), once again show a good state of the LM38 Course's educational process. A total of 1,043 questionnaires were processed, as reported by the PQA, involving 32 out of 47 teaching activities, representing a coverage rate of 68.9%. The overall Course average is 3.52, slightly higher than the Humanities Area average (10 active Courses) of 3.51. Compared to previous years, the figure shows a steady increase and is undoubtedly encouraging for a definitive recovery, especially after the difficult years of the pandemic. Regarding the overall student satisfaction, the consolidated reference figure aligns with the University average (3.31) and is roughly in line with the Humanities Area average (3.36). The score for logistical-organizational aspects—3.60—exceeded both the University's furthest score (3.47) and the Humanities Area's closest score (3.55). The didactic effectiveness score was also highly positive at 3.62 compared to the University (3.49) and Humanities Area (3.59). It is interesting to note that student comments on teachers' availability to clarify content during lessons and office hours were fully satisfactory: LM38 3.72; University 3.59; Humanities Area 3.68. Similarly high—3.57 compared to University (3.42) and Humanities Area (3.52)—was student satisfaction with the stimuli and motivation teachers provide during lessons, where topics are presented appropriately to the complexity of the subjects: 3.57 (University 3.46 and Humanities Area 3.56). Students also appreciated the consistency between the actual delivery of courses and what was declared in the teacher's Syllabus: Course 3.66; University 3.50; Humanities Area 3.60.
Students who responded to the questions also found the topics presented by their teachers interesting at a score of 3.45, slightly higher than the University (3.43) but relatively lower than the Humanities Area (3.50). They also considered the study load required by the course to be proportionate to the assigned credits at 3.31 (University 3.29; Humanities Area 3.35) and the teaching material adequate for studying the subject at 3.50 (University 3.39; Humanities Area 3.48).
However, a critical point concerns students' preliminary knowledge at the start of courses. In several cases, this knowledge was barely sufficient for understanding exam program topics. Attention should therefore be focused more carefully on this aspect to implement targeted improvement measures.
Finally, among the suggestions provided, students consider it appropriate to maintain the current teaching load and do not view positively the possibility of introducing potential synergies with other courses. They also request additional teaching materials (photocopies, handouts, slides, etc.).
For the 2020-21 academic year, teaching was unfortunately affected by the resurgence of the pandemic.
In 2020-21, the overall average score for the LM38 Course evaluation was 3.40, a slight increase from 3.39 in 2019-20, but still slightly below the general 2018-19 figure (3.42), after several years of steady growth starting from 3.27% in 2015-16, 3.38% in 2016-17, and 3.40 in 2017-18. As can be seen, the 2020-21 figure is identical (slightly rising) to that of 2017-18, despite the multiple serious organizational and management difficulties related to the outbreak and spread of the Covid-19 pandemic (distance or blended learning).
Regarding student evaluations in 2020-21, it is also interesting to note that the vast majority of students considered themselves substantially satisfied with the educational offer within the Course: regarding the quality of courses and their syllabi, the interest in topics presented and stimuli from teachers, clarity of exposition during lessons, teachers' availability for further clarification and repetition of scientific content, appropriateness of teaching load relative to CFU, consistency with what was declared on the Course website, respect for lesson schedules, and overall approval of examination methods. 51.10% of student opinions, regarding the aspects mentioned above, were decidedly positive; 40.36% responded more yes than no; 6.41% more no than yes; 2.13% decidedly no.
However, there remains work to be done to improve the methods, forms, and content of teaching delivered in the LM38 Course, hoping to exit the health emergency as soon as possible, which has hindered educational programs and annual academic activities.
For example, in 2020-21, the figure for teachers' didactic availability towards students, both during lessons and office hours, was confirmed and slightly increased compared to the previous academic year: 3.66% against 3.64% in 2019-20. On the other hand, the parameter regarding students' preliminary knowledge needs improvement: in 2020-21, the figure was 3.03%. This value is slightly improved compared to 2018-19 and 2019-20 (3.09% and 3.11%, respectively). Critical issues continue to relate to factors such as student numbers, contractual courses, and limited classroom capacity at the Pescara Campus (Viale Pindaro). These are indeed problems that diminished during the pandemic, but on which the LM38 Course, like other Courses in the Department of Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures, has limited influence.

# Comprehensive Analysis of the "Lingue Straniere per l'Impresa e la Cooperazione Internazionale" Master's Program

## Program Overview
The "Lingue Straniere per l'Impresa e la Cooperazione Internazionale" (Foreign Languages for Business and International Cooperation) is a Master's program (LM38) offered by the University of Chieti-Pescara (Università degli Studi "G. d'Annunzio") through the Department of Modern Languages, Literatures, and Cultures. This program is unique in the Abruzzo region and has consistently maintained strong enrollment and graduation rates.

## Student Enrollment and Graduation Data

### Recent Enrollment Trends (2020-2023)
- **2020-2021**: 162 new enrollments (370 total students)
- **2021-2022**: 122 new enrollments (336 total students)
- **2022-2023**: 126 new enrollments (320 total students)

The program has shown resilience after pandemic-related challenges, with a slight recovery in enrollment numbers. The program has a strong regional appeal, with students coming from across Italy (particularly from Southern Italy) and a small number from abroad.

### Graduation Performance
- **2022**: 110 graduates (1 with 110 and lode, 7 with 110, 35 with 105-110, 30 with 105)
- **2021**: 107 graduates (1 with 110 and lode, 63 in course, 26 one year beyond course, 17 two years beyond course)
- **2020**: 96 graduates (38 with 105, 27 with 105-110, 24 with 110 and lode, 7 with 110)

The program consistently produces high-quality graduates with strong academic performance, particularly in the 105-110 range.

## Curriculum Development Based on Stakeholder Feedback

The program has undergone significant curriculum revisions based on regular consultations with stakeholders (businesses, organizations, schools, etc.):

### Key Revisions (2017-2023)
1. **Increased language course hours**:
   - First year: 8 to 10 CFU
   - Second year: 6 to 9 CFU

2. **Added specialized courses**:
   - "Informatica per le discipline umanistiche" (Computer Science for Humanities) instead of basic computer skills
   - Courses in economics and law (with choice between economic and legal tracks)
   - Added courses in Geography, Arabic Literature, Modern History, and Film Theory

3. **Enhanced practical skills**:
   - Focus on digital tools (Excel, PowerPoint, cloud usage)
   - Added courses on international marketing
   - Emphasis on translation skills (particularly legal translation)

## Stakeholder Consultations

The program has held numerous consultations with stakeholders since 2016, with the most recent in March 2024. Key themes from these consultations include:

1. **Digital skills**: Strong demand for improved Excel, PowerPoint, cloud usage, and digital communication skills
2. **International focus**: Need for knowledge of EU funding opportunities and international marketing
3. **Translation skills**: Demand for specialized translation abilities, particularly legal translation
4. **Regional connections**: Emphasis on strengthening ties with the Adriatic region (Eastern Europe/Balkans)

The program has responded by:
- Creating specialized courses in digital tools for humanities
- Adding courses on international marketing
- Developing stronger connections with Adriatic region organizations
- Organizing professional seminars focused on industry needs

## Final Thesis Requirements

The final thesis requires:
- Minimum 120 pages (each page at least 2000 characters)
- Can be written in a foreign language (with Italian summary)
- Must be on a topic related to program disciplines
- Must be supervised by a faculty member
- 16 CFU credit value

The evaluation considers:
- Quality of written work
- Language skills (must have at least C1 level in both languages)
- Overall academic performance

## Program Strengths

1. **Unique regional position**: The only program of its kind in Abruzzo
2. **Strong stakeholder connections**: Regular consultations with businesses and organizations
3. **Curriculum relevance**: Continuous updates based on industry needs
4. **High graduate quality**: Consistently high academic performance
5. **International focus**: Strong emphasis on international cooperation and business

## Challenges and Future Directions

1. **Digital skills development**: Need to further strengthen students' digital competencies
2. **International internships**: Addressing student resistance to remote internships
3. **Adriatic connections**: Strengthening ties with Eastern European/Balkan regions
4. **Post-pandemic recovery**: Continuing to rebuild connections with stakeholders after pandemic disruptions

The program has demonstrated a strong commitment to adapting to industry needs while maintaining academic rigor, making it a valuable educational option for students seeking careers in international business, translation, and cross-cultural communication.

Admission procedures The verification of personal preparation is mandatory in all cases and can only be accessed by students possessing the required curricular qualifications; in particular, the possession of curricular requirements cannot be considered as fulfillment of the personal preparation verification.
Admission occurs through the evaluation of the student's previous academic record and possible interview. The adequacy of the individual student's personal preparation is assessed according to the procedures specified in the Study Course Teaching Regulations. Any additional curricular requirements in terms of CFU must be acquired before the personal preparation verification.
If the essential requirements are not met, admission cannot proceed.
In addition to the essential curricular requirements, an adequate level of personal preparation is required for access to the Study Course.
Graduates of the Bachelor's degree in class L-23 and graduates of the Bachelor's degree in class L-7 are considered to possess the admission requirements and may proceed directly to enrollment.
For graduates from other classes, the assessment of personal preparation will be conducted by assigning points to the following elements:
- Results achieved in the educational path up to a maximum of 20 points as follows: 1 point for each passed exam with a score of 28/30 or higher, up to a maximum of 5 points; (P - 80)/2 points for a graduation grade of P/110 with P > 80 (0 points if P does not exceed 80).
- Congruence of the candidate's educational path with the training objectives of the Study Course up to a maximum of 60 points as follows: 1 point for each CFU in the sectors ICAR/01, ICAR/02, ICAR/06, ICAR/07, ICAR/08, ICAR/09, ICAR/10, ICAR/11, ICAR/12, ICAR/13, ICAR/14, ICAR/17, ICAR/18, ICAR/19, ICAR/20, ICAR/21, ICAR/22, GEO/05, GEO/09, ING-IND/10, ING-IND/11, ING-IND/22, ING-IND/31, up to a maximum of 60 points.
Candidates who, based on these criteria, achieve a score equal to or higher than 50 points are considered to possess an adequate level of preparation and may proceed directly to enrollment.
Regarding English language proficiency at least B2 level (according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages), this may be documented by a certificate issued by an accredited certification body or verified through an interview during the student's academic record evaluation procedures.

CURRICULUM: Program, texts and objectives
SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/664

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The ability to communicate objectives and implementation methods for interventions, even complex ones, necessary in the design and construction site phases, to interact with local realities and competent bodies in defining the optimal solution, is essential for the effective integration of master's degree graduates into the professional world. It is therefore important for the master's graduate to possess appropriate communication tools and to have verified mastery through targeted simulations. The master's degree course will therefore provide all the tools to consolidate and further develop students' communication skills, both written and oral, and communication through graphical representation, as well as through the use of computer and telecommunication tools. These objectives will be pursued through frontal lessons and exercises, and primarily by requiring students, in various courses, seminars, and the final thesis, to present both oral and written and/or computerized versions of their work, particularly the fundamental design documents for the construction site.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [801M] CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING
TYPE: Master's Degree
SECTION: Critical Judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/664

Critical Judgment (making judgements)
The master's graduate must possess, at the end of the study course, their personal critical judgment regarding the decisions to be made in the context of governing the operations of transformation and management of the built environment. He will therefore be able to assume autonomous decision-making responsibilities and actively participate in the decision-making process in even multidisciplinary contexts. Advanced critical reasoning skills will be developed through progressive involvement in research activities, through the analysis and interpretation of experimental data, theoretical results, and models. To promote the formation and growth of critical judgment, and to stimulate the capacity for individual critical analysis, the master's degree course will provide both technical-scientific tools and socio-cultural references in both theoretical and application-design courses, as well as in the cultural initiatives that will be activated. The development of critical judgment will also be encouraged through contribution to both practical and research projects, in which the student will be stimulated to develop their critical spirit and make decisions, both individually and in work groups.

Assigned training periods The internship activity is aimed at enabling students to acquire professional practice experiences, administrative procedures, site management, etc. The internship period takes place at public or private structures previously contracted with the Department where the Construction Engineering Study Course is based.
Before the start of the internship activity, the 'Training Project' must be defined, to be agreed upon with the academic tutor and countersigned by the tutor from the public/private structure.
At the end of the internship period, the student must prepare a 'Summary Report' of the experience, which must be signed by the student and countersigned by the academic tutor and the tutor from the public/private structure before being submitted to the Course Committee.
The Course Committee, through the coordination of the Committee for Guidance and Coordination with the Territory (CIRT), establishes various agreements with private firms, companies, and/or public bodies to activate the training internships required by the academic curriculum.
The CIRT has been tasked with creating a database of companies available for internships.
A list of companies and firms with which agreements for internships already exist is currently being published on the new version of the website in the dedicated page: https://idclm24.unich.it/pagina-modalit-1545, where, for greater clarity, the procedures already described in the academic regulations and mentioned above will also be published.
The list of agreements concluded in the last three years is attached in PDF.
To ensure an adequate quality standard, questionnaires (attached in PDF) have been prepared to be administered to both students and host entities. See the CIRT meeting minutes of November 28, 2023, for further details. The results of the administered questionnaires will be processed and analyzed during the next academic year.
The INGEO Department has numerous collaboration agreements with foreign universities and research laboratories where Erasmus Traineeship experiences can be carried out.

International Mobility Section At the Department of Engineering and Geology, numerous collaboration agreements with various foreign universities are in place; these collaborations promote and support student mobility for internship and training periods abroad, which students are directed towards.
All agreements, falling under the new program called Erasmus+, have multi-year validity.
As reported in the 2023 LM24 RRC, particularly in point D.CDS.2.4 Internationalization of Teaching, the CdS benefits from the strategy to enhance internationalization carried out by the INGEO Commission for Internationalization, coordinated by Prof. Pagliaroli from 2021 and then by Prof. Sara Amoroso from 2023.
Within this strategy, Erasmus agreements with other foreign campuses have been revised and expanded; a bonus has been introduced in the graduation score for students who have earned CFU abroad; a semesterly Erasmus questionnaire has been implemented and regularly administered to identify factors hindering students' overseas experiences; annual awareness seminars have been organized by students who have already completed Erasmus experiences; an economic contribution from the INGEO Department has been introduced to increase overseas stay scholarships; a preliminary correspondence table between LM24 Course of Study exams and those of the consortium foreign campuses has been prepared to facilitate student choices and recognition upon return.
The work of the INGEO Commission is carried out at the CdS level by the Erasmus Working Group, appointed by the CdS on 15.12.2023, composed of Prof. Amoroso, INGEO Delegate for Internationalization and Erasmus Delegate for Engineering courses, Prof. Masciotta, Erasmus Representative for L23-LM24 Courses of Study, and a student representative for both the L23 and LM24 Courses of Study.
To promote student participation in overseas training activities, the correspondence tables between courses offered within the CdS and those available at various Erasmus campuses with active exchange agreements are particularly important.
The availability of such correspondence tables facilitates both the organization of overseas activities by students and the approval of Erasmus study plans by the CdS Council.
The results of this activity, subject to continuous revision to account for changes in course offerings, are available on the web page https://idclm24.unich.it/pagina-studiare-allestero-1781, where a guide for completing the learning agreement is also available for students of the CdS.
The page also contains an updated list of selectable overseas destinations.
