Student opinions STUDENT OPINIONS FROM ATTENDING STUDENTS The study program takes student opinions into account through discussion moments of the results of opinion surveys conducted within the study program. These results are also thoroughly discussed in the Joint Teaching and Student Committee (CPDS), contributing together with possible corrective actions for emerging issues to the annual CPDS report, which is transmitted and presented also at the study program council meeting.
Analysis of the temporal trend of overall ratings shows a rising trend from 2016-17 to 2022-23 with a value of 3.56 in the latest survey. Examining the macro-indicators (overall satisfaction, logical-organizational aspects, teaching effectiveness) for 2022-23 shows satisfactory results as scores are significantly higher than the average of the scientific area and university. Examination of individual indicators also does not reveal criticalities, with ratings well above the average of the scientific area and university.
It is worth noting the maintenance of the study program's strengths with higher scores in the following areas: students' interest in the courses offered (demonstrating a well-calibrated teaching offer that also meets market expectations), respect for schedules and availability of teachers (demonstrating teachers' appropriate attention to students).
Regarding the evaluation of individual teaching activities, there are no particular criticalities: no courses received an average score below 3 from students. Lower ratings primarily refer to the high study load not proportional to credits according to students (indicator D3). Teaching effectiveness is high for all courses.

Graduate Opinions GRADUATE AND GRADUATING STUDENT OPINIONS The sample surveyed by Almalaurea (graduates from the calendar year 2022), consisting of 18 respondents out of 30 graduates (60%), can be considered sufficiently representative.
The comparison with other universities shows that approximately half of the respondents (49% between 'definitely yes' and 'more yes than no' compared to 71% national) considered the study load appropriate for the duration of the course.
The organization of exams in terms of exam sessions, schedules, information, etc., is considered always satisfactory by 27.8% of respondents and by more than half of the exams for 50%.
Also excellent are the percentages of respondents who reported being satisfied with their relationships with faculty: a decidedly positive judgment for 33.3% and positive for 61.1%, compared to national data of 23.5% and 65.4% respectively.
All respondents are satisfied with the degree course (100% compared to 92% of the national data).
However, the judgment on classrooms is slightly lower, with a positive rating of 56% compared to a national data of 77%.
The data for those who would enroll again in the same course is positive at 61.1%, although lower than the national data (73.4%).
The employment rate one year after graduation is slightly lower than the national data (83% compared to 89%), while it is higher at five years (96% compared to 93% national).
The opinion of graduating students 21-22 shows scores almost always lower than those of the university. The main issues concern: adequacy of classrooms, computer equipment, laboratories, support for internship activities. These are issues already partially highlighted by students during CPDS meetings.
DISCUSSIONS OF THE RESULTS OF GRADUATING STUDENT OPINIONS AT THE COUNCIL The results of the opinions of graduates and graduating students above were presented and discussed in detail at the CdS Council meeting on 17.11.2023, alongside those of students and faculty. See the minutes at the link:
https://idclm24.unich.it/pagina-verbali-1749
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding will be referred to situations characterized by significant complexity, set within broad contexts, also interdisciplinary. Graduates will therefore be able to integrate acquired knowledge and independently conduct analysis, design, and management activities for even complex constructions. These objectives will be pursued through the teaching courses of the areas 'Architectural and Urban', 'Structural and Risk', 'Energy and Sustainability'; these will be delivered using both theoretical and design approaches, and will be accompanied by practical-experimental activities, also through the interdisciplinary approach between the areas characterizing the degree course, strengthened by specific integrated courses, in which to concretely simulate the acquisition of the acquired knowledge. The verification of achieving the ability to apply knowledge and understanding will primarily occur through the execution of projects and during the preparation of the thesis. Considering that the training of the master's engineer is oriented towards achieving a multidisciplinary attitude to connect topics and competencies even strongly differentiated from each other, all training activities present in the teaching regulations contribute almost equally to achieving and verifying the abilities to apply knowledge and understanding. The multidisciplinarity of the Construction Engineering course will find strong expression also through the 'Built Cultural Heritage' area, where an holistic approach is fundamental for the correct management of the design and management process.
Learning Skills
The master's degree course will provide students, beyond specific knowledge, a methodological approach to study that will enable future professionals to independently initiate a process of 'continuous learning'. The objective of the study course is therefore the provision of a work method, in addition to specific knowledge. This objective will be pursued through the alternation of traditional training moments (frontal lessons) with other moments more dedicated to the development of self-organization, critical synthesis, and personal research skills (exercises, laboratories, thesis).
Knowledge and Understanding
The master's graduate must achieve, through the courses of the 'Architectural and Urban' area, knowledge and understanding of the typical themes of Building Systems Engineering directed at the built environment, both historical, contemporary, and to be designed, in their individuality and integration. They must be able to interpret, through the courses of the 'Structural and Risk' and 'Energy and Sustainability' areas, regulatory requirements and territorial, building, structural, and plant project elaborations. They must acquire, through the courses of the 'Structural and Risk' and 'Energy and Sustainability' areas, mastery in managing the building process and its technical, constructional, and economic aspects. They must develop, through the courses of the 'Built Cultural Heritage' area, design skills, in structural, plant, and management fields, necessary for a historical built heritage to be addressed with specific methods and tools that respect and preserve its characteristics. The privileged tools for developing such knowledge are: frontal lessons, active participation in exercises, individual or group project work, and guided personal study. The verification of knowledge acquisition primarily occurs through oral and/or written exam tests.

Brief Course Description The master's degree in Construction Engineering is a course with open access. However, it requires a preliminary assessment of entry curricular requirements.
The master's degree in Construction Engineering is aimed at training graduates who can govern and direct the design, realization, maintenance, and decommissioning of the built environment; a sector that expresses consistent and continuous demand, especially in the context of necessary rehabilitation of existing built heritage and the realization of new high-innovation buildings, generally guaranteeing significant responsibility and satisfaction.
The training path includes three distinct curricula that address major themes discussed both by the international community in the 2030 Agenda, Renovation Wave, NextGeneration EU, and Paris Agreement for 2050, and by the national community through PNRR guidelines and incentives for building heritage rehabilitation.
The first curriculum, starting from the observation that we live in fragile territories from multiple perspectives, focuses on risk themes of different nature and how design must evolve to mitigate them.
The second curriculum, starting from the recognition of ongoing climate change and high exploitation of our planet's resources, focuses on energy impacts of the built environment sector and sustainability in designing new structures and rehabilitating existing ones.
The third curriculum, entirely delivered in English, focuses on the rehabilitation of built cultural heritage, starting from the recognition that Italy hosts a fundamental part of the world's cultural heritage, and that design in this area requires a different approach and way of thinking about engineering design, fostering strong interdisciplinarity.
Theoretical activities are always accompanied, according to the specificity of each course, by practical, laboratory, and design exercises to develop transversal application skills of acquired knowledge.
The study course requires the completion of a training internship to be carried out at companies, public or private bodies, professional orders, or internal technical structures within the University.
The teaching offer defines a designer figure who, due to their technical-scientific training, is eligible for registration in the Senior Engineers' Professional Register, Civil Environmental Section.
External Effectiveness ANALYSIS OF ALMALAUREA DATA The surveys conducted in 2022 on graduates one year after graduation involved a sample of 46 graduates, of whom 30 responded to the questionnaire: the collected data therefore represents a relatively representative reference of 65%. The gender ratio of the surveyed sample corresponds to 72% men and 28% women. The average age at graduation is 28.5 years with an average course duration of 3.6 years. The percentage of master's graduates who participated in post-graduation training courses is 33%.
The employment rate of the surveyed group is 83%; of these, 28% continued working in the same job started before graduation, 16% continued with a different job than before graduation, and 56% started working only after graduation. 84% perform intellectual, scientific, and highly specialized professional activities.
8% of graduates found work in the public sector and 92% in the private sector (68% in industry and 32% in services).
71% of graduates who continued their previous job noted an improvement in their work due to the degree.
80% of graduates consider the degree very effective in their work.

Specific Course Objectives and Training Path Description The master's degree course aims to train a figure capable of adhering to and responding to the transformations of the operator's role in the building system, at a professional level, characterizing our time. While the architect traditionally controls the design segment but not the overall construction process, and the civil engineer often adopts a highly specialized role that risks not adequately influencing decision-making levels, the master's graduate in Construction Engineering will have training focused on controlling the entire construction process, both before (programming, economic and productive cycle control) and after (realization, management, maintenance). The new figure is that of a director of the transformation activities of the built environment, considered as an integrated system, able to collaborate with other sector operators without the fragmentation and disconnection that currently characterize their relationships. In other words, the master's graduate in this class will be a designer responsible for various phases of the programming, construction, transformation, management, and maintenance of the built environment.
Consequently, the study path is structured to form a master's graduate who must deeply understand theoretical-scientific aspects, technical tools, and operational methods related to the construction system, and be able to use such knowledge to identify, formulate, and solve complex problems or those requiring an interdisciplinary approach. They will therefore be able to know and integrate different architectural, technological, structural, plant, energy, and economic aspects in the various phases of the construction lifecycle, from ideation, to site, to commissioning, to operation.
In summary, it is the training of a versatile professional who can competently integrate different technical and regulatory knowledge and work with high responsibility in construction sites, even complex ones, in free professions, public and private bodies, in the various phases of the built environment lifecycle, from programming to management.
The master's degree in Construction Engineering, as stated, aims to complete the preparation of the first-level graduate by providing the skills necessary for entering the labor market and profession, as well as the tools required for further specialization in specific or scientifically advanced fields, and for continuing studies at higher education levels such as Master's and PhD.
The training path is structured into multiple curricula, delivered in Italian or English, involving the following learning areas:
ARCHITECTURAL AND URBAN AREA: It provides the skills necessary to elaborate and articulate a project at different scales of the built environment, from building to urban scale: it provides the skills necessary for developing and understanding the project in its functional, technological, and planning aspects.
STRUCTURAL AND RISK AREA: It aims to provide skills for evaluating and quantifying the risk associated with building works to develop and control the structural design of a work even in the most complex situations, where seismic, geological, and hydraulic calculations come into play. The themes of Risk and Structures are in a field of strong expansion and particular attention both in Abruzzo and throughout the national territory, where the Engineer must be able to evaluate and quantify the level of risk present both at urban and building scale to design safely, whether for existing structures undergoing rehabilitation or new constructions. This area, among other things, aims to train a figure capable of designing seismic retrofitting and improvement interventions for existing structures or designing new constructions with the seismic reliability required by current regulations. Particular attention is devoted to training professionals capable of evaluating and preventing risk in its multiple forms, referring to the different material types typical of the Italian territory (reinforced concrete, steel, masonry) and different structural types (buildings, infrastructure, bridges).
ENERGY AND SUSTAINABILITY AREA: It is aimed at providing the knowledge necessary to consider energy issues present in the design of building works, both at the building scale and at the urban context scale. The international historical context sees sustainability as a fundamental element for future generations and identifies energy as one of the pillars of the 2030 Agenda globally. The awareness that the building sector is one of the main contributors to energy demand and consumption at national and European levels highlights the need to train an Engineer capable of designing while considering both seismic aspects of the territory, i.e., structural design knowledge, but also energy saving and environmental sustainability, through a multidisciplinary approach that sees holistic design as the key to global optimization of the building system. Energy aspects are now increasingly valued and binding in the design of new buildings and the conversion of existing ones; energy-saving technologies in these areas are highly evolved, and the Engineer must be continuously updated to comply with regulatory requirements. Environmental sustainability of buildings is another theme covered by this area, both in terms of Architectural and Urban Design and innovative and bio-compatible construction materials. The theme also encompasses the achievement of management requirements for constructions and fire safety management.
BUILT CULTURAL HERITAGE AREA: This area focuses on training Engineers who possess technical and humanistic knowledge to intervene on historically and artistically significant constructions. Alongside historical insights into existing constructions, the theme deals with the study of materials and the historical development of construction techniques of cultural heritage. The themes addressed are linked to the awareness that monumental works and existing artistic and cultural heritage require highly specific design interventions to ensure their consolidation and preservation without altering their character and value, or in full respect of their identity. The theme of preservation, maintenance, and promotion of historically and artistically significant monuments will be addressed and deepened through a multidisciplinary approach starting from historical and restoration knowledge, passing through geotechnical, structural, and energy aspects, to reach managerial and informational knowledge necessary for their use in line with technological evolution.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements The course requires an obligatory training internship to be carried out during the study period with hosting entities that have established conventions with the CdS. The internship regulations also allow individual students to propose a hosting entity with which the CdS will establish an appropriate convention after verifying the minimum required criteria.
The CdS, through the coordination of the Committee for Orientation and Territorial Coordination (CIRT), prepares several conventions with private firms, companies, and/or public bodies to activate the training internships required by the teaching regulations.
The CIRT has been tasked with creating a database of companies available for internships.
An updated list of companies with existing conventions for internships is being published on the new version of the website in the dedicated page:
https://idclm24.unich.it/pagina-modalit-1545 where, for greater clarity, the modalities for activating and conducting curricular internships will also be published, as described in the teaching regulations.
The list of conventions established for internships in the last three years is provided in the attached PDF.
To ensure an adequate quality standard, at the end of the internship, electronic questionnaires are distributed on a platform to both students and hosting entities to evaluate the effectiveness of the internship and any improvement actions to be taken.

Summary of the Regional Coordination Committee's Opinion The Committee, having examined the proposal for the establishment of the aforementioned educational initiative and considering that the master's degree aims to train professionals capable of implementing various phases of the programming, management, maintenance, and rehabilitation of the building process, unanimously approves the establishment of the Master's Degree in Construction Engineering (LM-24).
Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Level - of Goods and Service Production, Professions (Course Establishment)
Representative organizations were consulted at the time of establishing the master's degree in Building Systems Engineering, formulated in accordance with the regulations set forth by DM 270/04, and expressed a favorable opinion on the realization of a teaching project oriented towards training construction professionals capable of entering the labor market broadly and responding adequately to the demand for both new constructions and management of existing structures according to emerging trends even at the European level.
In particular, the consultation led to identifying the graduate in the class as a versatile specialist who can work with high responsibility in construction sites, even complex ones, in free professions, public and private bodies, in the various phases of the building production cycle and the lifecycle of the built environment, from design to maintenance.
Over time, these objectives have been verified in practice, and it was agreed to make some path improvements to give the course a more distinctive identity through a reorganization of the teaching regulations and a more explicit and immediately understandable name.
In its new formulation, the course in 'Construction Engineering' provides a curriculum structure that, on one hand, allows students to choose the study direction that best aligns with their cultural aspirations and career ambitions, and on the other hand, addresses the main themes that will characterize the building and civil construction world in the coming years.
The specific themes of the new teaching offer were illustrated during two meetings held in December 2019.
At the first meeting held in Pescara on December 12, 2019, the following were invited:
- Engineering and Architecture Professional Orders of the provinces of Chieti and Pescara
- Geometers' Colleges of Chieti and Pescara
- Mayors of the municipalities of Chieti and Pescara
- Presidents of the provinces of Chieti and Pescara
- Abruzzo Region
- Confindustria Chieti Pescara
- ANCE
- Officials of the Regional Civil Engineering Service
Representatives of the Engineering and Architecture Professional Orders of Pescara and Chieti attended, and for Confindustria, a representative of Walter Tosto Spa participated.
The expansion of the teaching offer was favorably received by the social partners present at the meetings.
In particular, the theme of Risk and Structures was appreciated not only for the broad educational offer on structured courses but also for the attention to existing constructions and hydrogeological risk, for which good professional opportunities are expected. The theme of Sustainability and Energy was appreciated for the attention to energy sustainability at the building and urban scale, combined with structural skills, necessary in a fragile territory. The theme of Engineering and Management of Built Heritage was appreciated for the multidisciplinary approach proposed to preserve and conserve historical architectural constructions, albeit primarily focused on structural, energy, and management aspects.
At the second meeting held in Pescara on December 16, 2019, all students enrolled in the Bachelor's (L23) and Master's (LM24) courses in Construction Engineering were invited. To encourage student participation, teachers who would have taught the courses coinciding with the meeting also attended.
The specific themes were all positively received by students, who proposed deepening some topics within the planned courses.
Regarding the Topography and GIS Courses (ICAR/06), the possibility of deepening drone-based surveying with practical activities was requested.
Regarding the training internships provided in the new teaching offer, it was clarified that conventions would be established with the entities where the internship periods can be carried out to ensure adequate training requirements for interns. This will also favor the opening and possible positive outcomes from and towards the business world. To this end, the positive dialogue that took place in the first meeting with the Engineering and Architecture Professional Orders of the provinces of Chieti and Pescara was highlighted.
Regarding the Sustainability and Energy theme, it was observed that themes related to electrical systems and energy recovery in buildings, for example through mini-wind and mini-hydro, should be included in the programs to be carried out in individual courses.
For courses related to BIM skills, it is suggested to explore in the future the possibility of accrediting students who take such exams for BIM use at the Professional Orders, in light of recent sector regulatory innovations.
Finally, students suggest associating training activities with visits to external realities that allow increasing the synergies of engineers in training with future professional activities.
The students' observations will contribute to defining the content of the courses, and the feasibility of the requests will be verified.
At the end, among the present students, approximately 45% declared interest in the Risk and Structures theme, 50% in the Sustainability and Energy theme, and 5% in the Engineering and Management of Built Heritage theme, while recognizing the importance of offering all disciplines in English for the latter.
It is planned to make consultations systematic and periodic, involving all interested representatives both to have external monitoring and to remain aligned with the evolution of the labor market.
Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Level - of Goods and Service Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
Based on the meetings held during the initial accreditation phase and the elements emerging over the years, the following institutions have been identified as stakeholders for the Construction Engineering LM24 course: Confindustria (Chieti-Pescara), ANCE (Chieti and Pescara), Ente Scuola Edile (Chieti and Pescara), Engineering and Architecture Professional Orders (Chieti and Pescara), Geometers' Colleges (Chieti and Pescara), Province of Pescara, and schools in the provinces of Chieti, Pescara, and L'Aquila (classical and scientific high schools, geometry institutes).
Until 2019, meetings with these organizations were held at a temporal frequency dictated by the need to modify the training path; this allowed the study path to be adjusted to meet the changing needs of the labor market. The non-optimal response in participation from stakeholders, as per the attached minutes, and the need to implement a quality model in managing relations with external subjects led, in the second half of 2019, to the establishment of a Committee for Orientation, which, involving both CdS faculty and responsible stakeholders, aims to make the occasions for discussion more regular and better receive the indications emerging from them.
At the same time, extended meetings with CdS students were held to highlight and address any criticalities or anomalies detected by them; the meetings held so far have seen a large and active participation: 17/11/2015 (approximately 40 students present, L23 + LM24), 08/03/2016 (approximately 150 students present, L23 + LM24), 16 December 2019 (approximately 80 students present, L23 + LM24).
From the meetings held in 2019 with the Committee for Orientation and students, the reform of the LM24 master's path with the introduction of the two curricula in 'Risk and Structures' and 'Sustainability and Energy' was developed, operational from the 2020/21 cohort.
At the Course of Study Council meeting on March 27, 2020 (point 4), it was decided to expand the Committee for Orientation by establishing a Work Group composed of the following subjects: Chairs of L23 and LM24 Courses, Prof. Vincenzo Sepe, Prof. Guido Camata, Prof. Giuseppe Brando, Prof. Gianmichele Panarelli, Student Representatives L23 and LM24, Presidents of Provincial Engineering and Architecture Professional Orders Councils, the President or delegate of Confindustria for the provinces of Chieti and Pescara, and the President of ANCE for the provinces of Chieti and Pescara. The Work Group activities focus, besides periodic meetings with stakeholders, on managing and continuously revising the hosting entities for curricular internships.
At the Committee for Orientation meeting on October 26, 2021, it assumed the current name of "Committee for Orientation and Territorial Coordination" (CIRT).
On July 20, 2022, an assembly was held, in mixed presence-online format, to illustrate the reasons for the training project to the main stakeholders, namely the master's students in Construction Engineering LM23. After a first illustration of the practical implications and potential outcomes of the current degree path, an unanimous positive judgment and a shared strategic vision of the project were recorded. The assembly was followed by an online questionnaire, which expanded the participant base and fully confirmed the previously expressed judgments.
On October 21, 2022, a meeting was held with the Engineering Professional Orders of the Chieti and Pescara territories, where the University "G. d'Annunzio" is located; the Engineering Professional Order of the Calabria Region; the certification company ABIcert; the company Archliving of Ferrara; the company Energylab3 of Pescara; ANCE Marche; the Department of Infrastructure and Transport of the Abruzzo Region. The subjects involved were chosen by involving a national-scale geographical area and intercepting a variety of public and private subjects adequately representative of the future work environments of Construction Engineering graduates. The stakeholders involved expressed an extremely positive judgment on the proposed teaching offer, identifying the necessary interdisciplinarity that is currently decisive for success in the labor market.
The CIRT was reconvened on November 28, 2023, with the presence of the INGEO Director, the new L23 (Prof. De Bellis) and LM24 (Prof. Pagliaroli) Chairs, internal CIRT members (Coordinator Prof. Brando). Among the stakeholders, the Presidents of the Engineering Professional Orders of Pescara and Reggio Calabria, and the company Energylab3 of Pescara attended. In the meeting, stakeholders were updated on the interdepartmental degree project in Civil Engineering and Building Systems, discussed the possibility of involving professional categories for choosing topics for thesis work by proposing to establish a Commission at the Pescara Order. Finally, the opportunity to re-submit the request to hold state exams at the Pescara and Chieti sites was discussed, discussing the reasons that previously led to the rejection of the request.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data The number of enrollments for 2021/22 (22) is decreasing compared to the 20/21 data, which recorded a value of 41 units. Data on enrollments for the academic years 2022-23 and 2023-24 indicate a number of enrollments almost identical to 21-22: overall, the number of enrolled students was 23 and 24 units, respectively.
Based on the analysis of disaggregated data, available for 22-23 on the S.I.Ca.S platform (Student Career Indicators System),
the vast majority of the student body consists of graduates in class L23 from the same university continuing their studies with the master's in class LM24. The CdS's target audience remains stable in embracing a geographical area extending from Abruzzo (largely dominated) to Molise and Puglia.
The male/female ratio of enrolled students is approximately 2.
Regarding student careers, there is a paritarian relationship between regular and off-course students. Dropouts are a negligible percentage. The average time to obtain the degree has increased in recent years from 2.7 years (average value of 2016-2020) to 3.8 years of 2020-2022.
The English-language curriculum 'Engineering Management of Cultural Heritage' reported zero enrollments for the 2023-24 academic year. The analysis of criticalities related to this path led to identifying the following aspects to address: adequate visibility on the Universitaly portal, effective promotion of the curriculum, financial coverage for foreign external faculty, late opening of pre-enrollment procedures on Universitaly and at UdA with consequent impacts on visa timelines for non-EU students.
DISCUSSIONS OF ENTRY, PATH, AND EXIT DATA AT THE COURSE OF STUDY COUNCIL The results of entry, in-progress, and exit data of the CdS are normally analyzed every year in the CdS in November/December to have a clear and comprehensive view after the closure of regular enrollments, scheduled for the beginning of November. The last discussion took place at the council meeting on 17.11.2023, together with the analysis of student career data.
IMPROVEMENT ACTIONS The increase in the percentage of graduates in progress compared to the geographical area and national data was adequately addressed in the 2023 RRC with the identification of improvement actions (see comment on indicator IC02, https://pqa.unich.it/sites/st16/files/allegatiparagrafo/08-01-2024/lm-24_ingegneria_delle_costruzioni.pdf).
In the last two years, the activity of the Social Work Group has been strengthened to improve the knowledge of the CdS in the target areas. The interdepartmental path with Civil Engineering LM23 has been renewed to increase the attractiveness of the study course. The orientation activities have been renewed (see section B5 of the SUA Orientation in Entry, where projects and schools involved in 2023-24 are described in detail).
The teaching offer of the third English-language curriculum, by increasing the internationalization of the CdS, should attract foreign enrollments. Regarding this last point, the creation of a technical committee with the INGEO Director, chairs of English-language courses in INGEO (including LM24), INGEO Internationalization Representative, and University Administrative and Governance Bodies has allowed the analysis of criticalities encountered by foreign students in enrollment (meeting of 16.01.2024) and the forced closure of the 23-24 delivery. The initiatives identified have enabled the opening of pre-enrollment procedures at the end of March 2024, making it more concrete to have enrollments in 23-24. This initiative is accompanied by the promotion of the path on departmental and Engineering social media, at University events (International Student Fair - Tirana 15-16 March 2024), and through the restructuring of the LM24 website.
Final Exam Characteristics The final exam consists of the development of a project or theoretical-experimental thesis on topics related to the master's degree courses, to be developed under the supervision of a faculty member. The final exam will be conducted through the execution of projects and during the preparation of the thesis.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding will be referred to situations characterized by significant complexity, set within broad contexts, also interdisciplinary. Graduates will therefore be able to integrate acquired knowledge and independently conduct analysis, design, and management activities for even complex constructions. These objectives will be pursued through the teaching courses of the areas 'Architectural and Urban', 'Structural and Risk', 'Energy and Sustainability'; these will be delivered using both theoretical and design approaches, and will be accompanied by practical-experimental activities, also through the interdisciplinary approach between the areas characterizing the degree course, strengthened by specific integrated courses, in which to concretely simulate the acquisition of the acquired knowledge. The verification of achieving the ability to apply knowledge and understanding will primarily occur through the execution of projects and during the preparation of the thesis. Considering that the training of the master's engineer is oriented towards achieving a multidisciplinary attitude to connect topics and competencies even strongly differentiated from each other, all training activities present in the teaching regulations contribute almost equally to achieving and verifying the abilities to apply knowledge and understanding. The multidisciplinarity of the Construction Engineering course will find strong expression also through the 'Built Cultural Heritage' area, where an holistic approach is fundamental for the correct management of the design and management process.
Learning Skills
The master's degree course will provide students, beyond specific knowledge, a methodological approach to study that will enable future professionals to independently initiate a process of 'continuous learning'. The objective of the study course is therefore the provision of a work method, in addition to specific knowledge. This objective will be pursued through the alternation of traditional training moments (frontal lessons) with other moments more dedicated to the development of self-organization, critical synthesis, and personal research skills (exercises, laboratories, thesis).
Knowledge and Understanding
The master's graduate must achieve, through the courses of the 'Architectural and Urban' area, knowledge and understanding of the typical themes of Building Systems Engineering directed at the built environment, both historical, contemporary, and to be designed, in their individuality and integration. They must be able to interpret, through the courses of the 'Structural and Risk' and 'Energy and Sustainability' areas, regulatory requirements and territorial, building, structural, and plant project elaborations. They must acquire, through the courses of the 'Structural and Risk' and 'Energy and Sustainability' areas, mastery in managing the building process and its technical, constructional, and economic aspects. They must develop, through the courses of the 'Built Cultural Heritage' area, design skills, in structural, plant, and management fields, necessary for a historical built heritage to be addressed with specific methods and tools that respect and preserve its characteristics. The privileged tools for developing such knowledge are: frontal lessons, active participation in exercises, individual or group project work, and guided personal study. The verification of knowledge acquisition primarily occurs through oral and/or written exam tests.

Admission Procedures Admission is permitted for students who have obtained a three-year degree belonging to classes L-8 and L-9, in accordance with D.M. 270/04. Degrees of different classes will be evaluated by the Didactic Commission of the Study Program on a case-by-case basis. The adequacy of the student's preparation (Article 6, paragraph 2 of D.M. 270/04) will be verified through a written entrance test, which may be administered remotely, aimed at verifying the student's competencies in the fundamental areas of Biomedical Engineering (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology). The test will include a sufficient number of multiple-choice questions for each of the mentioned fundamental areas, with the entire test duration not exceeding two hours, and will be conducted at least one month before the start of lectures. The test evaluation, expressed in thirtieths, will be communicated to students within two weeks from the actual test date. For students with a minimum grade of 70/110 in the three-year degrees of classes L-8 or L-9, this verification is considered satisfied and does not need to be carried out. The ability to correctly use the English language, in written and oral form (at least at level B2), will be verified based on the previous academic record or certifications or certificates, or through specific tests held before enrollment, which may take place concurrently with the entrance test, or through a specific oral test if the student meets the curricular requirements (coming from classes L-8 or L-9) and the minimum degree grade (70/110) as stated above.

Communication Skills (communication skills)
The Master's graduate in Biomedical Engineering, given the inherently interdisciplinary nature of the Course, is constantly in contact with people with diverse expertise, often different from their own. They are therefore required to express themselves to colleagues with lexically correct and appropriate language for the various specialized contexts in which they operate, in order to be understood without ambiguity or hesitation.
Such communications must be effective both orally and in writing, both during public presentations (for example, to an audience of colleagues) and during informal conversations (for example, during a work meeting).
The communication skills necessary to achieve these capabilities, both in written and oral form, are developed during the institutional teachings and verified during examinations.
The acquisition of communication skills is also verified through the evaluation of the ability to present scientific reports and through discussion with a peer audience. In particular, the production of original works in the form of presentations or posters on issues of interest to the teachings will be encouraged, in order to train participants in public communication.
The student's ability to work individually or in a group will also be evaluated through the drafting of reports to complete partial examination tests or to accompany the laboratory sections of the teachings.

SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/2105

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
The master's degree in Biomedical Engineering provides highly interdisciplinary cultural preparation, enabling graduates to address complex biological/medical issues by considering various aspects of phenomena and multiple possibilities for data acquisition/processing/experimental-scientific-technological actions. The biomedical engineer is therefore able to independently evaluate the most suitable strategies and technologies for solving specific problems, while being aware of the costs inherent in various alternatives and the associated timeframes. They will thus be able to consciously acquire, process, evaluate, and propose complex information to their superiors (if applicable) or develop it independently (if applicable).
The acquisition of judgment autonomy is assessed during learning evaluations, prioritizing the student's ability to address practical problems and apply problem-solving models learned in lectures to new cases or those not treated in a standard manner.

Graduate Opinions Since the course started this year, there are no graduates yet.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The master's graduate, depending on the specific educational path chosen, will be able to apply their knowledge and understanding, adapting them to the different curricula. For the curriculum focused on biomaterials and biomechanics, master's graduates will acquire the ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to analyze the characteristics of existing materials and use them to design and manufacture devices (typically a prosthesis), to design and develop drug delivery systems, to model the functioning of artificial organs, or to design new materials when opportunities/necessities arise. For the curriculum focused on telemedicine and advanced prosthetics (sensorized and automated), master's graduates will be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to manage a healthcare database and connect it with reference healthcare facilities, making health data available as needed, to manage medical telepresence systems for diagnostic or surgical purposes, and to design and develop advanced prosthetic systems (sensorized and automated). For the curriculum focused on medical robotics and human-machine interfaces, master's graduates will be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to collect and interpret neuroscience data, to design and personally oversee the manufacturing of medical robotics equipment, and to design and develop human-machine interface systems.
The achievement of these learning objectives will be attained through i) critical reflection on the individual study proposed by the course, appropriately stimulated and verified by instructors, ii) study of practical cases during various taught modules, iii) extensive participation in the proposed teaching laboratories (which will be mandatory).
The verification of the ability to apply knowledge and understanding will be conducted through the aforementioned global exams and/or intermediate verification tests, carried out through oral and/or written and/or practical methods, depending on the module considered.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
The master's graduate in Biomedical Engineering, due to the multidisciplinary nature of the course, has the ability both to advance in studies with a high degree of autonomy and to independently deepen specific topics not covered in the courses, for example by consulting sector journals, databases, etc.
Practical exercises and tests provided for a variety of modules will complement the student's theoretical knowledge and concept learning with practical aspects.
The acquisition of learning skills is verified throughout the course, during exams, and culminates with the internship period and thesis work.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The master's graduate in Biomedical Engineering possesses in-depth knowledge in the classical disciplines of industrial and information engineering (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, thermodynamics, thermal transport properties, development of predictive/descriptive theoretical models, basic computer science), as well as in the application disciplines specific to the course curricula (biomechanics, biomaterials, telemedicine, telediagnostics, tele-surgery, image analysis, neuroscience, medical robotics). This highly interdisciplinary range of modules (mathematics, computer science, materials science, medicine, biology) enables students to develop cross-context understanding abilities.
As a result of this educational approach, students acquire the ability to understand and solve complex, interdisciplinary problems, using both known and innovative strategies.
These knowledge and understanding abilities are achieved both through participation in lectures, exercises, laboratories, seminars, and/or internships, and through individual study hours as specified in the activated training activities.
Learning verification prioritizes intermediate checks, where the module is segmented into smaller, more easily assimilated parts (so-called 'intermediate tests'), with verification conducted during the teaching period to allow students to complete verifications within the course's scheduled timeline. Traditional verification methods are also implemented in parallel, understood as verifications covering the entire module content (referred to here as 'global exam tests'), conducted during the examination sessions designated by the University. Both intermediate tests and global exam tests are conducted orally, in writing, or through practical exercises, depending on the module considered.
Organization and Responsibility of Quality Assurance at the Course Level Quality Assurance within the course is managed through the Quality Assurance Group, composed of the Course Director and one of the reference faculty members.
The Quality Assurance Group will closely collaborate with the University Quality Assurance Office.
A dedicated email box will also be activated for students to submit observations and complaints, managed by the INGEO Teaching Office at reclami@LM21.unich.it. Any other documents deemed useful to justify the activation of the Course of Study Reference Faculty Curricula Brief Description of Related and Complementary Activities The course includes a common related activity across different curricula, namely the study of Micro- and Nanofluidics, essential for understanding and developing hydraulic circuits used in prosthetic/robotic systems and correctly modeling the shapes and composition of biomaterials for implants.
Additional elective related and complementary activities are also provided for each curriculum, as follows:
- Elements of biomechanics and modeling of natural and artificial organs, to provide students with an understanding of the mechanical behavior of biological systems;
- Elements of biomaterials for specific applications in prosthetics, artificial organs, and dentistry, with reference also to nanostructured materials;
- Elements of cloud systems, neural networks, Internet of Things, and cybersecurity, to provide skills related to telemedicine and information security;
- Elements of omics sciences, to provide the necessary skills to understand and develop emerging fields such as proteomics, genetic engineering, and molecular pathology;
- Elements of tele-surgery and telediagnostics, for skills related to telemedicine and medical robotics;
- Elements of neuroscience, related to developing skills in artificial intelligence, telemedicine, and medical robotics;
- Elements of prosthetics in hard tissues and orthopedics, to provide skills related to the design of general bone prosthetic systems;
- Elements of translational medicine, to provide skills in surface sterilization, surface-organism interactions, and general medicine;
- Elements of pharmacology, for skills related to drug delivery systems and generally to pharmacological treatments related to prosthetic implants;
- Elements of histology, to provide skills in prosthetics and interactions between biomaterials and body tissues.
Brief Course Description Biomedical Engineering is a highly interdisciplinary field that uses engineering methods and technologies to describe, understand, and solve medical-biological problems. Biomedical Engineers are therefore able to i) design and develop new materials and methodologies for disease diagnosis and treatment, ii) design, develop, and maintain simple and complex devices used in biomedical contexts, iii) understand, rationalize, and design the organizational structures (human, computer, logistical, and resource-related) connected to healthcare organizations, aiming to reduce associated costs and maximize benefits for users of these organizations, iv) define methods, processes, and standards related to the use and safety of technologies applied to health.
To acquire these competencies, the Master's program in Biomedical Engineering will offer:
- Common training for all students in topics related to the characteristic scientific-disciplinary sectors (SSD) (ING-IND/34 and ING-INF/06), such as Biomaterials Science, Biomechanics, Computer Science, Biophysics, Electronics, Prosthetics, Biorobotics, and related medical disciplines such as Histology, Anatomy, Physiology, and Dentistry.
- Specific training, divided into separate curricula characterized by homogeneous disciplines, all linked to biomedical thematic areas, namely Materials and Technologies for Biomedicine, Telemedicine, Virtual Hospital, and Rehabilitation Technologies, and Advanced Medical Robotics and Human-Machine Interfaces. This specific training will provide students with competencies in the following high-growth, high-value sectors: Tissue Engineering Systems and Processes, Biomedical Instrumentation, Imaging Techniques, Telemedicine, Information Systems for Healthcare Database Management, Biorobotic and Prosthetic Systems, Neuroscience. All thematic areas included in the outlined curricula are consistent with the characteristic SSDs and/or specific SSDs related to training needs.
The main employment opportunities are in the biomedical sector, both in research and technological application; a significant portion of graduates will be absorbed by sectors related to hospital services and elderly care, which represent a substantial fraction of productive companies in the Abruzzo region. Regarding contract types, master's graduates in Biomedical Engineering can find employment both in the private sector (pharmaceutical companies, Medical Device manufacturers, healthcare and rehabilitation services, companies developing and maintaining digital medical and dental systems, both on-site and via telemedicine, companies designing and developing biomaterials) and in the public sector (hospitals, care facilities, institutions related to the biomedical world such as the National Health Institute, Italian Pharmaceutical Association, university sector, and public research bodies). Master's graduates in Biomedical Engineering can also engage in all aspects of independent practice (designer, manufacturer of custom medical devices, technical arbitrator, expert witness, court expert, etc.), as well as participate in public body competitions such as ASL, National Health Institute, etc.
Specific Course Learning Objectives and Educational Path Description The Master's graduate in Biomedical Engineering (IB) is a professional with broad, multidisciplinary, and integrated knowledge, capable of successfully entering the workforce and high-technology professions in the medical-biological field, specifically in the dental and biomaterials sectors, Virtual Hospital (telemedicine) and advanced prosthetics, and Medical Robotics and Human-Machine Interfaces. Graduates will possess the knowledge required to perform these professional activities, both as employees of private or public companies and as independent professionals. Additionally, the solid foundational training in biomaterials, computer science, and electronics will enable potential entry into other general workforce sectors, including consulting and research & development activities.
The specific learning objectives are firmly anchored to the general objectives of class LM21 (in-depth knowledge of mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, and the ability to use this knowledge to interpret and describe interdisciplinary engineering problems; in-depth knowledge of theoretical-scientific aspects of engineering, both general and biomedical, and the ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex problems; ability to design, plan, design, and manage complex and/or innovative systems, processes, and services; contextual knowledge and cross-cutting abilities; knowledge and ability to use at least one European Union language other than Italian, including disciplinary terminology), and are detailed as follows, also in reference to curricula tailored to different orientations, all consistent with the class learning objectives:
- Biomaterials and Biomechanics orientation curriculum for prosthetic and dental applications, to train professionals capable of following rapid changes in the biomaterials and simple prosthetics sectors, with specific learning objectives focused on Biomaterials, Biomechanics, Bioelectronics, Computer Science, Translational Medicine, Drug Delivery, and Artificial Organs.
- Telemedicine, Virtual Hospital, and Rehabilitation orientation curriculum, to train professionals capable of analyzing and optimizing organizational and computer processes underlying the diverse telemedicine and tele-surgery sector, and capable of designing and developing advanced prosthetic systems (sensorized and automated), with specific learning objectives focused on Biomechanics, Bioelectronics, Computer Science, Omics Sciences, Telemedicine, Tele-surgery, and Advanced Prosthetics.
- Medical Robotics and Human-Machine Interfaces orientation curriculum, to train professionals capable of designing and developing complex human-machine interaction systems, and capable of understanding, designing, developing, operating, and maintaining complex medical robotics systems, with specific learning objectives focused on Biomechanics, Bioelectronics, Computer Science, Data Processing, Fundamentals of Robotics, Neuroscience, Neural Modeling, and Human-Machine Interfaces.
The high interdisciplinarity of the course will enable Biomedical Engineering graduates to acquire contextual and cross-cutting knowledge, and develop the ability to analyze and solve known and new problems using known and/or innovative solutions. It will also facilitate the acquisition of specialized terminology from very diverse disciplines, enabling fruitful dialogue with specialists from different fields.
The educational path, both at the basic and applied science levels, is further integrated with extensive laboratory practice sections, allowing students to acquire the knowledge and competencies necessary to achieve the aforementioned specific learning objectives.
From an organizational perspective, training activities primarily consist of lectures, frequently referencing practical case studies, supported by a substantial number of laboratory hours for all disciplines where this teaching method is deemed appropriate.
Seminars by external personnel not part of the course faculty, such as visiting scientists or biomedical sector professionals from public (hospitals, healthcare companies, etc.) and private entities (dental studios, medical IT companies, etc.), will complement the courses.

The Director of DTIMO supported the Master Coordinator's proposals, highlighting the opportunity to eventually develop a dental engineering training path for doctors, even if not immediately.
The Director of the INGEO Department ultimately highlighted the significant opportunity represented by LM21 for the growth of the Chieti-Pescara University and the Abruzzo territory.

Entry, Progression, and Exit Data Cohort 2022-23: 5 students enrolled in the first year
Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam will consist of a Thesis, developed under the guidance of an official course supervisor, possibly in collaboration with external entities (public and private, manufacturing and service companies, research centers, etc.) operating in the relevant field. The thesis must demonstrate mastery of the topics covered, the ability to work independently and originally, as well as the ability to communicate content appropriately even to non-experts.
Final Exam Format The final exam will be conducted through one of the following two alternative methods:
1) Thesis-based graduation exams; compilation theses will result from a student's personal work aimed at deepening one or more topics relevant to the course of study, through a collection of literature data and their critical re-elaboration. Generally, a compilation thesis will include a substantial amount of information, resulting in documents of at least 120 A4 pages, Times New Roman 12, double-spaced. The presentation of such a thesis will be both in written form and as an oral dissertation, accompanied by appropriate audiovisual communication means. The maximum score for a compilation thesis is 3 points.
2) Thesis-based graduation exams; experimental theses will consist of a specific study of literature data related to a well-defined aspect of a discipline within the course, a connected and organized corpus of experimental data related to the study, and a coherent and motivated discussion of the experimental results in light of existing bibliographic resources, with the drafting of one or more conclusions capable of explaining the collected experimental data in light of previous studies in the field. Generally, an experimental thesis will contain approximately 100 A4 pages, Times New Roman 12, double-spaced. The presentation of such a thesis will be both in written form and as an oral dissertation, accompanied by appropriate audiovisual communication means. The maximum score for an experimental thesis is 7 points.
The examination committee will consist of a minimum of 5 faculty members, affiliated with the Department of Engineering and Geology and/or the Department of Technologies in Medicine and Dentistry, belonging to the SSDs present in the Departments.
All faculty members of I, II rank and Researchers, including those on fixed-term contracts, can be appointed as thesis supervisors.
The graduation exam will be conducted through the candidate's presentation to the Graduation Committee of the results achieved during the thesis.
The presentation of results will be in Italian; the thesis can be presented in either Italian or English.
The graduation grade will be expressed in 110/110, determined as the weighted average of the exam grades achieved by the student in the course of their study plan, to which will be added:
- The score assigned by the Graduation Committee for the final thesis, within the maximum scores for compilation or experimental theses as described above;
- A maximum of 2 additional points at the disposal of the Supervisor, which may be awarded in fractional points;
- An additional 1 point for theses completed at foreign research institutions.
The "110/110 with Honors" grade can be awarded in cases where the sum of the weighted average and the additional points available to the Graduation Committee and Supervisor, as well as the optional point for theses completed at foreign research institutions, exceeds 113/110, and the student's curriculum includes at least one exam graded '30 and Honors' in the master's course.

Department DEPARTMENT OF MEDICINE AND AGING SCIENCES  Admission Requirements Required knowledge for access Candidates who hold a degree qualifying for health professions included in class SNT2 (podiatrist, physiotherapist, speech therapist, orthoptist - ophthalmic assistant, neuro and psychomotor therapist for developmental age, psychiatric and psychosocial education and rehabilitation technician, occupational therapist, professional educator) or the corresponding professional training title or university diploma qualifying and equivalent, or another foreign degree recognized as suitable according to current regulations, may be admitted to the Master's Degree in Health Professions of Rehabilitation Sciences.
As this is a Master's Degree program taught in English, another required access title is knowledge of English at B2 level.
The B2 level is the fourth level of English (upper intermediate) established by the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), a system for assessing linguistic knowledge at various levels determined by the European Council.
Knowledge of English (B2 level) will be verified through the entrance test and further improved during the course through the use of scientific English (reading and analysis of scientific texts and articles, use of technical terminology, etc.).
For international students, adequate knowledge of Italian (not lower than B2 level of the CEFR) is also required for access.
Access to the Master's Degree program is limited by number in accordance with Law 264/99 and involves an admission exam in English prepared according to ministerial guidelines, aimed at verifying the student's personal preparation and acquired competencies in the fundamental fields of rehabilitation (physiotherapy, speech therapy, orthoptics and ophthalmic assistance, occupational therapy, etc.).
The date, mode of conduct, and number of available places for the admission exam are defined annually by the Ministry of University and Research (MUR) and published each year in a specific admission notice issued by the University.
Required prerequisites for students wishing to enroll in the program include, in addition to knowledge of English (CEFR B2), good predisposition for human contact, good predisposition for group work, ability to analyze and solve problems.
All knowledge required for access to the program (both basic and specific competencies) will be clearly described and advertised on the website of the DMSI, which is the predominant department.

Admission Procedures The Master's program in Health Professions of Rehabilitation Sciences has quota-controlled access, and admission is contingent upon passing an English test conducted locally and scheduled nationally on a date established annually by the Ministry.
To take the exam, it is necessary to follow the relevant registration procedure and respect the deadlines stated in the Call for Applications for admission to the Master's programs in health professions.
For foreign students, adequate knowledge of the Italian language (at a level not lower than B2 of the QCER) is required for access, which will be verified by a specialized commission through an oral interview. In the presence of certificates, diplomas, or other documents attesting knowledge of the Italian language, the designated commission will decide whether to exempt the individual candidate from the language verification.
Admitted to the admission exam are those who possess the following qualifications:
- A licensing degree in health professions included in the class (podiatrist, physiotherapist, speech therapist, orthoptist - ophthalmic assistant, neuro and psychomotor therapist for developmental age, psychiatric and psychosocial education and rehabilitation technician, occupational therapist, professional educator) or the equivalent professional training qualification or a university diploma with equivalent qualifications, or another foreign degree recognized as suitable under current regulations.
Admitted with reservation are those who will obtain the degree by no later than November 30.
Admitted to the exam are candidates with disabilities and DSA as described in the Call for Applications.
Master's programs may also admit candidates without requiring the admission exam, and in derogation from the national quota, considering that the applicants already perform operational functions:
a. those who have been appointed to a coordination role in accordance with and for the purposes of Article 7 of Law 10 August 2000 No. 251, paragraphs 1 and 2, for at least two years as of the date of Ministerial Decree No. 213 of 12 June 2020;
b. those who hold, with a formal document dated at least two years as of the date of the aforementioned Ministerial Decree No. 213 of 12 June 2020, the position of director or coordinator of one of the Master's programs included in the Master's program of interest.
The date, mode of conducting the admission exam, and the number of eligible candidates are defined annually by the Ministry of University and Research (MUR) and published in a specific admission call issued by the University. All candidates are required to submit an online application according to the University's procedure.
The exam consists of multiple-choice questions presenting five possible answer options, from which the candidate must select only one, discarding incorrect, arbitrary, or less probable conclusions, on the following topics:
- theory/practice relevant to the health professions included in the Master's degree class of interest;
- general culture and logical reasoning;
- regulation of the practice of health professions included in the Master's degree class of interest and health legislation;
- scientific-mathematical culture, statistics, computer science, and English;
- human and social sciences.
The final admission score is the sum of the score obtained in the written exam and the evaluation of the candidate's academic, professional, and educational qualifications. For the evaluation of academic and professional qualifications by the examination committee, the candidate must declare their possession in the registration procedure, providing all necessary data to allow verification of their authenticity.
Candidates who occupy positions immediately following in the ranking may, at the end of the enrollment deadline, access available positions.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
Master's graduates in Health Professions of Rehabilitation Sciences will be able to:
- apply language analysis and communication style skills to provide appropriate information to users of all ages and their families within the rehabilitation process and/or with other healthcare professionals;
- communicate effectively using verbal, non-verbal and written methods to convey assessments and decisions in interdisciplinary rehabilitation teams, while being aware of the specificities of different professional roles and their integration within rehabilitation;
- demonstrate the ability to communicate effectively both orally and in writing;
- demonstrate the basic skills and correct attitudes to carry out training, teaching and instruction activities for the assisted population, healthcare professionals and students at various levels;
- implement educational interventions for individual users, families and groups with the aim of promoting healthy behaviors and motivating them to adhere to the rehabilitation project;
- recognize and respect individual and cultural differences in all professional interaction moments;
- act as a mentor to train and develop competencies in aspiring leaders in clinical and organizational settings;
- adopt supportive managerial styles to support colleagues in conducting projects, teaching and supervision, negotiation, and conflict resolution.
The above-mentioned knowledge and comprehension skills will be acquired through attendance at lectures, exercises, seminars, guided and independent personal study. Written and oral communication skills will be particularly developed during laboratory activities and presentations carried out individually or in groups during classroom activities: i) discussion of case studies and paradigmatic relational situations in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions; ii) internship with supervised experiences by expert tutors in various contexts with debriefing sessions to reflect and reprocess relational experiences with users and the team in simple and complex healthcare settings.
Verification of these skills occurs through seminars via oral presentation in small groups at the end of a professional internship period during which Master's graduates will prepare a written dissertation containing the above-mentioned objectives.

Judgment Autonomy (making judgments)
Master's degree graduates in Health Professions of Rehabilitation Sciences will be able to:
- predict and evaluate the effects resulting from their own decisions and activities, assuming the consequent responsibility;
- demonstrate the ability to make decisions, express functional and rehabilitative judgments through reflective practice;
- participate in researchers' activities to understand or contribute to in-depth studies in the field of rehabilitation;
- formulate autonomous reflections through multidisciplinary scientific, legal, ethical, and deontological discussion.
The teaching tools aimed at acquiring the above-mentioned skills include lectures, small group case discussions with presentations in plenary sessions, seminars, guided and individual study.
These skills will be assessed through written and/or oral certification exams, practical tests, and reports.

Orientation and ongoing tutoring. Ongoing orientation is expressed through various delivery methods: the ongoing tutoring activity is carried out by all faculty members of the Study Course, typically during office hours, and aims to assist students in resolving their issues (e.g., suggesting a correct study method).
Support tutoring and assisted study are composed of training activities aimed at improving the learning of certain courses, generally those of the first year of the study path. Additionally, reference teachers are appointed to whom students can turn in case of need to request a personal tutoring service and to agree on the corresponding methods of execution. The Course will carry out orientation and ongoing tutoring activities through:
• Orientation Committee;
• Reference teachers;
• Teaching tutors available to students for issues related to training and learning;
• Director of Professional Training;
• Clinical tutors responsible for monitoring the professional activities carried out by graduates at affiliated and/or internal university facilities;
• 1 Academic Secretariat Office;
• 1 Student Point of the Biblos Cooperative.
Teaching tutors for entry, ongoing, and exit orientation are coordinated by the Study Course delegate for orientation.
Clinical tutors (1 for every 3 students) will be selected based on the evaluation of the possessed qualifications (including language skills) and the educational background, by a dedicated committee composed of the Study Course President, the Director of Professional Training, and a member of the Steering Committee.
To provide study assistance in specific subjects, reported by students as the most problematic, the tutoring activity carried out by PhD students, selected through specific calls, will be extended to the Study Course.

International mobility section The Master's Degree Course is an international study program as it is entirely delivered in a foreign language (English) (type c, Table A, MUR REGISTRY DECREES.R.0002711.22-11-2021).
Students will be encouraged to engage in international mobility, with orientation and support activities for studying abroad, primarily through opportunities from the "Lifelong Learning Programme" Erasmus of the University. International mobility orientation activities will be carried out in collaboration with the Course Coordinator for the LLP/Erasmus Programme, the Course International Relations Committee, and the Departmental Coordinator for International Relations of DMSI. Furthermore, the Course will be widely promoted abroad to encourage enrollment of international students. The main channel for promoting enrollment of international students will be students attending foreign universities with which the proposing Department has Erasmus agreements.
In line with the University's strategic guidelines, DMSI has recently implemented initiatives supporting the internationalization of research and teaching by increasing the number of research collaboration and cooperation agreements with international partners from 6 initial to the current 77 Erasmus agreements for staff and student mobility and 13 international conventions, and it is expected that LM/SNT2 will further expand these activities.
Finally, Gabriele d'Annunzio University is one of the 10 Universities forming the transnational alliance for implementing the INGENIUM project over the next three years, together with the University of Oviedo (Spain), Université de Rouen Normandie (France), Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (Germany), Munster Technological Institute (Ireland), University of Skövde (Sweden), South-Eastern Finland University of Applied Sciences (Finland), Sofia Medical University (Bulgaria), Gheorghe Asachi Technical University of Iasi (Romania), and University of Crete (Greece). The project, which began with the Kick off Meeting held in Oviedo (Spain) from January 24 to 26, 2023, stems from one of the European Union's priorities for the 2021-2027 period, which foresees the creation of 60 European Universities. The aim of INGENIUM is to consolidate and institutionalize international cooperation among partners in teaching, research, and third mission, including the ecological transition. INGENIUM will be able to issue European degrees, increase research competitiveness in the European space, and enhance synergies between universities and the world of work not only in local contexts but also at an international level.
