UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO STUDIES
COURSE: [A596] PHARMACY
TYPE: Master's Degree
CURRICULUM: Single Cycle 5 Years
SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5111

Autonomy of judgment (making judgments)
Master's degree graduates in Pharmacy must: - correctly advise citizens on over-the-counter medications and health products (dietary supplements, cosmetics, medical devices); - correctly dispense medications; - recommend, where possible, equivalent medications with full autonomy and sense of responsibility, also to optimize National Health Expenditure. Teaching tools include classroom lectures by professors, professional seminars conducted by pharmacists, distributors, health product experts, and pharmaceutical service operators identified in agreement with the professional world, and practical-professional internship in pharmacy under the guidance of a pharmacist (industry tutor) and academic supervision by a professor (academic tutor). The activities carried out in pharmacy are recorded by the pharmacist (industry tutor) in a specific logbook.

Orientation and ongoing tutoring. Orientation is conducted by the Course Director, assisted by the Department of Pharmacy's academic office and a group of faculty members.
The recovery of OFA (Additional Educational Requirements) in the subjects of the admission competition (Biology, Chemistry, Mathematics, and Physics) is provided for students who have acquired them through the methods and schedule established by the Academic Council and published on the Department's website.
Tutoring activities are provided by each faculty member within their own course, and, based on economic availability, by students (ex L.170/2003) and doctoral students on specific subjects (General Chemistry, Physics, Mathematics, Analytical Chemistry, Medicinal Analysis I, Organic Chemistry).

Grants have been awarded to incentivize tutoring, supplementary, prerequisite, and recovery activities.

Annual statistical surveys are conducted to evaluate student satisfaction with tutoring activities, with fully favorable results.
For the year 2023, 44 tutoring evaluation forms were analyzed, with 100% of participating students reporting being very or extremely satisfied with the activity.
For the 2024-25 academic year, tutoring services will presumably be activated in the same courses.
The Thesis Orientation Committee, composed of Professors Giustino Orlando, Luisa Di Marzio, and Alessandra Ammazzalorso, organizes periodic meetings with students to appropriately guide them in choosing thesis paths.
Periodic statistical surveys are conducted via an anonymous online questionnaire to identify issues faced by off-track students.
In the 2019-20 academic year, out of 361 off-track students invited via email, 79 completed forms were received. In the 2020-21 academic year, out of 295 off-track students invited via email, 53 completed forms were received. 18 students reported being 1-2 years off-track, 13 students 3-4 years off-track, and 22 students more than 5 years off-track. In the 2021-22 academic year, out of 282 off-track students invited via email, 43 completed forms were received. 15 students reported being 1-2 years off-track, 12 students 3-4 years off-track, and 16 students more than 5 years off-track.
Among the causes influencing delays in the study path, personal reasons and difficulty passing a specific exam are the two main factors, followed by study and memorization difficulties. Most students do not attribute responsibility to attendance issues or faculty availability during office hours. If the delay is attributed to a specific course, most affected students believe the program is too long and that a tutor assisting with study could be helpful. To improve their position, most students believe it is useful to modify prerequisites. For most courses, students do not believe it is useful to modify their organization. Approximately half of the students believe studying with peers who have the same problem could help them. Only half of the students have significantly utilized the tutoring service, considering it adequate for the purpose.
On December 14, 2023, the Course Director, having obtained from the student office the names of students off-track for at least 2 years, contacted all students via email, inviting them to schedule an appointment with the Director to discuss and address together the problems and difficulties encountered over the years, and to be appropriately guided through a personalized mentoring path.
The consultations are still open, and students who have used them report greatly appreciating the initiative.
(attached Tutoring and Off-Track Surveys.pdf)

2022-23
Interns' and pharmacist/enterprise tutors' satisfaction is very high and evaluated through questionnaires, whose results are summarized in the attached PDF document.
In summary, evaluating both the latest survey (84 student internship forms and 69 pharmacist tutor forms) and the evolution of evaluations over the years, it emerges that pharmacist tutors report high student interest in all training activities (pharmaceutical, pharmaceutical, pharmacological, legislative, economic, information technology, organizational).
Satisfaction percentages for tutors regarding students' university preparation, achieved operational results, willingness to collaborate and learn, and knowledge acquired during training activities are also high.
Interns also show interest in all training activities (pharmaceutical, pharmaceutical, pharmacological, legislative, economic, information technology, organizational), with high satisfaction regarding acquired university preparation, operational results achieved during the internship, and staff availability in the host pharmacy (Tirocini farmacia + stage 17-22.pdf).
Tutors also report maximum satisfaction regarding internship activities at companies within students' chosen activities, evaluated in relation to presence at the company, contact with the enterprise tutor, effort expended, cultural level, technical competence, learning ability, willingness to accept company life, interpersonal skills, and overall judgment (Tirocini farmacia + stage 17-22.pdf).
Update 2022-23:
Regarding student interns' evaluation of the Internship, GAQ examines 111 forms, revealing students' strong interest in all training activities during the internship: pharmaceutical (24.32% very much; 26.14% much), pharmaceutical (44.14% very much; 43.24% much), pharmacological (57.66% very much; 37.84% much), legislative (56.76% very much; 39.64% much), economic (27.03% very much; 38.74% much), information technology (37.84% very much; 39.64% much), organizational (52.25% very much; 39.64% much), with high satisfaction regarding previous university preparation (22% very much, 51% much), operational results achieved during the internship (52% very much, 42% much), and staff availability in the host pharmacy (69% very much, 25% much). Overall, the experience evaluation is extremely positive. Analysis of data from the forms and open-ended comments reveals that many students request more pharmaceutical preparation activity in pharmacies, a point that somewhat aligns with feedback from pharmacist tutors. A certain percentage of students state the need to acquire further information technology skills, particularly regarding management software.

The Department of Pharmacy, through the Thesis Orientation meetings for its Pharmacy and CTF graduates, has involved the Career Guidance and Placement Service representatives to present the details of the service offered.
A Teaching Pharmacy has been established within the Department, for which the Pharmaceutical Legislation course includes the integrated module 'Professional Qualification for Pharmacists'. The Teaching Pharmacy is useful for completing the internship exam, which involves the operations performed by the pharmacist in dispensing SSN and dematerialized prescriptions, dispensing to patients with explanations regarding dosage and administration methods, and activating the management system.
The Department of Pharmacy contributes with the "Pharmaceutical Sciences" curriculum to offer the PhD in 'Biomolecular and Pharmaceutical Sciences', aimed at training researchers in the chemical-pharmaceutical and molecular medicine sectors, with a broad scientific cultural basis and familiarity with scientific methodology. At the end of the training path, researchers will operate in the fields of pharmaceutical chemistry, toxicology, and food, molecular and cellular biology, structural biology, pharmaceutical and medical biotechnology and nanotechnology.
The Department of Pharmacy offers a Second-Level Master in "Pharmaceutical Technology Transfer", with the aim of training specialists who operate or wish to operate in Pharmaceutical Industries developing and producing medicinal products in accordance with Pharmaceutical Quality System concepts. The professional figure trained in the Master naturally finds employment in pharmaceutical production sites or in industries conducting R&D activities, with employment prospects ranging from regulatory aspects related to industrial scale-up in formulation to Quality Assurance or Quality Control departments, up to the regulatory management of production site transfers in Pharmaceutical Companies.
The Department of Pharmacy offers a Second-Level Master in "Science and Communication of Cosmetic and Dermatological Products", with the aim of training professionals who can operate in various roles within the cosmetic sector. The professional figure trained by the Course can find employment as an expert in the formulation of cosmetic and dermatological products, an expert in the industrial production of cosmetic and dermatological preparations; an expert in regulatory aspects related to the use, production, and marketing of cosmetic and dermatological products; an expert in quality control of cosmetic and dermatological preparations, as well as in the safety and efficacy assessment of cosmetic and dermatological preparations; an expert in scientific communication of cosmetics; a cosmetic pharmacist capable of advising customers/patients on the most suitable and personalized use of cosmetic and dermatological products in BtoB and BtoC contexts; a pharmacist operating in territorial pharmacies skilled in preparing cosmetic and dermatological formulations.

Student Opinions The survey of opinions from enrolled students conducted in Academic Year 2022-2023, as of July 31, 2023, concerns 64 courses (54 core and 10 elective), totaling 2,609 processed questionnaires.
For 48 courses (75.00% of the total), the obtained score, evaluated on a scale from 1 to 4, falls within Level A (score from 3.5 to 4 inclusive); for 15 courses (23.44% of the total), the score is within Level B (score from 3 to 3.5 exclusive); for 1 course (1.56% of the total), the score is within Level C (score from 2.5 to 3 exclusive); no course falls within Category D (score from 1 to 2.5 exclusive).
A comprehensive average score of 3.59 is highlighted for the Degree Program, confirming the consistent annual increase in the average score: 3.42 in 15-16, 3.40 in 16-17, 3.44 in 17-18, 3.45 in 18-19, 3.47 in 19-20, 3.50 in 20-21, 3.53 in 21-22, and always exceeding the average scores of health-related Degree Programs at the university surveyed over the triennium 20-23 (average scores of health-related Degree Programs: 3.37 in 20-21, 3.40 in 21-22, 3.40 in 22-23) and always exceeding the university-wide average scores over the triennium 19-22 (average scores of university Degree Programs: 3.35 in 19-20, 3.41 in 20-21, 3.43 in 21-22). This element leads to a very favorable assessment of the teaching activity provided, with a constant objective for further improvement.
Regarding individual core courses, no significant deviations from maximum and minimum values are observed compared to the average of 3.59, with an excellence value of 3.84 in 22-23, 3.82 in 21-22, 3.80 in 20-21, 3.78 in 19-20, and a minimum value of 2.96 in 22-23, 3.11 in 21-22, 3.18 in 20-21, 3.05 in 19-20. However, the minimum value exceeds the attention threshold of 2.8, established in relation to the recommendations of the Joint Student-Teacher Commission.

# Sintesi della Relazione sul Corso di Laurea in Farmacia

## Struttura del Corso
Il Corso di Laurea Magistrale in Farmacia è stato recentemente riformulato per conformarsi ai nuovi decreti (D.I. n.651 del 5-07-2022 e D.M. n.1147 del 10-10-2022). Il programma prevede 5 curricula specializzati:

1. **Pharmaceutical Care**: con insegnamento fondamentale sulle patologie e farmaci di automedicazione
2. **Sperimentale**: per gli studenti interessati alla ricerca, con insegnamento fondamentale sulla valutazione biologica dei farmaci
3. **Cosmesi Funzionale**: con insegnamento fondamentale sulla formulazione e stabilità microbiologica dei prodotti cosmetici
4. **Nutrizione e Alimenti**: con insegnamento fondamentale sulla composizione e sicurezza degli alimenti
5. **Fitoterapia**: con approfondimento sugli aspetti di botanica farmaceutica e farmacologia delle sostanze vegetali

## Statistiche Studentesche
- **Anno accademico 2022-2023**: 781 iscritti totali, 431 in corso
- **Immatricolati**: 173 (in aumento rispetto agli anni precedenti)
- **Provenienza**: 58 studenti fuori regione Abruzzo (indicativo di buona attrattività nazionale)
- **Tasso di abbandono**: Elevato nel passaggio dal primo al secondo anno (da 170 a 99 studenti), probabilmente dovuto alla preferenza per altri corsi sanitari (Medicina, Odontoiatria)

## Tirocinio Professionale
Il corso ha adottato il nuovo Tirocinio Pratico Valutativo (TPV) richiesto dal decreto, con 30 CFU. Il regolamento è stato sviluppato in collaborazione con la Federazione degli Ordini dei Farmacisti Italiani (FOFI) e prevede:

- Commissione di valutazione composta da 4 docenti universitari e 4 farmacisti
- Attivazione di un registro elettronico per il tirocinio
- Inserimento di competenze specifiche richieste dal mercato farmaceutico

## Incontri con le Parti Sociali
Sono stati organizzati diversi incontri con i rappresentanti degli Ordini dei Farmacisti per:
- Definire le competenze necessarie per il tirocinio
- Adeguare il curriculum alle esigenze del mercato
- Discutere la necessità di anticipare l'insegnamento di Legislazione Farmaceutica dal 5° al 4° anno

## Prova Finale
La prova finale comprende:
- Una prova pratica valutativa delle competenze professionali acquisite con il tirocinio
- Una tesi sperimentale o compilativa
- Una discussione pubblica in aula davanti a una commissione

Il corso è ora "abilitante", consentendo agli studenti di esercitare la professione di farmacista dopo il conseguimento del titolo.

## Valutazione
Il corso copre un'area centrale nell'offerta formativa dell'Ateneo, posizionandosi a livelli ottimali in termini di immatricolati, iscritti e laureati. L'ordinamento proposto è stato significativamente migliorato in termini di compattezza, trasparenza ed efficacia, contribuendo agli obiettivi di razionalizzazione e qualificazione dell'offerta formativa dell'Ateneo.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI AND PESCARA

CURRICULUM: Admission Procedure
SECTION: Admission Procedure
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/3105

Admission Procedure To be eligible for enrollment in the Master's Degree in Economics and Behavioral Sciences, students must possess specific curricular requirements and adequate personal preparation, in accordance with Article 6, paragraph 2, of Ministerial Decree No. 270/2004. These requirements are advertised through various information channels (brochures, institutional website, orientation activities for new students).

Verification of Personal Preparation The adequacy of personal preparation is verified through a specific and formalized process. Each enrollment application is examined by the Course's Admission Commission, which reviews individual student records (and, if necessary, through analysis of teaching programs) to verify that the student possesses the necessary skills to successfully complete the study program.

The Admission Commission also assesses the possession of curricular requirements in cases not covered by the specifically admitted categories.

For students meeting the curricular requirements, the Admission Commission proceeds to verify personal preparation.

This verification occurs through a evaluative interview conducted by the Admission Commission, aimed at assessing:
1) Level of motivation and interest
2) Knowledge and skills in the following disciplines: i) general statistics;
ii) political economy/microeconomics; iii) business economics/business and management of enterprises.

Specifically, the following knowledge and skills are evaluated:
i) General Statistics
- Statistical inference: advanced probability calculations
- Main random variables and their distributions - Statistical test theory - Sampling methods - Analysis of linear models - Analysis of variance - Systems of simultaneous equations - Criteria for model identification, estimation, and control
ii) Political Economy/Microeconomics
- Interdependence and benefits of exchange - Competition and the invisible hand - Demand, supply, and elasticity - Efficiency and exchange - Imperfect competition, contestability, and market power - Natural monopoly - The value of information in contracts - Externalities, public goods, and property rights - Regulatory and antitrust policies - Natural resources and environment - Incomes, inequality, and poverty
iii) Business Economics/Business and Management of Enterprises
- Business development: strategies, models, and tools for growth - Analysis for strategic decisions - Crisis management strategies - Business strategies - Organizational design choices - Strategic performance - Social responsibility and sustainability - Production systems and manufacturing - Logistics and supply chain management - Marketing process management - Commercial distribution

No further assessment of the knowledge and skills listed in point 2) is required for graduates of points a), c), d), and e) (box A3.a) who have achieved a graduation grade of at least 99/110, or in cases where graduates of point b) have achieved an average grade of at least 27/30 in the exams taken in the specified scientific areas.

For each candidate, the Admission Commission issues a suitability or unsuitability judgment for enrollment in the Master's Degree in Economics and Behavioral Sciences.

CURRICULUM: Program, texts and objectives
SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/3105

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
At the end of the course, the master's graduate must be able to use the jargon of economic and behavioral sciences. Additionally, they must have acquired the ability to communicate clearly knowledge and ideas about human behavior to both specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Specifically, the graduate will be able to:
- clearly and elaborately present research activities;
- clearly and elaborately present the contribution of neuroscience in business;
- clearly and elaborately present neuro-organizational research activities, the method and results of neuroscience research to a business audience;
- critically discuss the standard assumptions of classical economic theory and the principles of economic experiments necessary to design and conduct an independent experiment; demonstrate how standard economic assumptions translate into predicted behaviors;
- correctly use the technical language of social psychology and organizations, and have acquired the ability to communicate clearly and unambiguously their knowledge and ideas about the functioning of groups and organizations to both specialist and non-specialist audiences;
- correctly use economic terminology;
- rigorously illustrate and discuss the mathematical relationships underlying the studied model.

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgements)
At the end of the course, the master's graduate must be able to integrate knowledge, manage complexity, and form judgments even with partial data. They will be able to critically analyze the contribution of neuroscience in business and will have acquired the ability to evaluate and influence group dynamics in social, commercial, and organizational contexts.

•Adequacy of prior knowledge
•Adequacy of study load relative to assigned credits
•Adequacy of teaching materials

•Respect for teaching schedule
•Clarity of examination procedures

The latest survey published by the PQA through a comprehensive report on student opinions separately considers the 2021-2022 cohort (second-year students in the Economics and Behavioral Sciences Program) and the 2022-2023 cohort (first-year students in the Economics and Behavioral Sciences Program), due to the change in curriculum. Therefore, results for the two Programs are presented separately below.
Regarding the Economics and Behavioral Sciences Program, the report presents a synthesis of 15 evaluation forms received, covering 25% of the teaching activities involved. Data reveal excellent results: the average overall score is 3.85 on a scale from 1 to 4. Analysis of individual questions does not reveal areas of concern (scores equal to or above 3.5).
Regarding the Economics and Behavioral Sciences Program, newly established, the report presents a synthesis of 33 evaluation forms received, covering 33% of the teaching activities involved. Data reveal excellent results: the average overall score is 3.71 on a scale from 1 to 4. Analysis of individual questions does not reveal areas of concern (scores equal to or above 3.5).

The results described here will be subject to analysis and discussion at the first useful Program Council meeting.

In response to the Parity Committee's recommendations, the appointment of the Student Representative for the Program within the Committee itself has been made.
Overall, no specific improvement action is necessary.
Recent results for the 2023/2024 academic year are added. 94 forms were received for 9 courses offered in the first and second terms. Evaluations also consider some students from the previous cohort. Data confirm the trend observed in previous years. Regarding Macro Indicators, overall Program satisfaction is 3.65, exceeding the LM56 Area data (3.39) and the University average (3.36). Similarly, for organizational aspects, the Program achieves an average rating of 3.81 compared to 3.56 and 3.49 for the Area and University, respectively. Finally, in terms of teaching effectiveness, the Program maintains higher values, with an average of 3.87, significantly above the Area (3.54) and University (3.49).

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The graduate must have acquired the ability to apply behavioral sciences methodologies to concrete problems posed by the economic and productive world. They must be able to solve problems in unfamiliar contexts, often within broader frameworks.
Specifically, the graduate:
- Will be able to plan a nudging intervention in various contexts, using different methodologies and knowing how to measure both direct and proximal, indirect, and distal effects;
- Will be able to critically apply learned solutions to interpret and design neuromarketing and 'neuro-organizational' research activities;
- Will understand the tools taught in class and be able to apply them to the analysis of real-world situations;
- Will have acquired the ability to integrate knowledge and manage complexity in studying group and organizational processes, as well as formulate hypotheses on typical and atypical group functioning and organizational behavior;
- Will have developed the ability to analyze the performance of the productive system; identify economic and social aspects of technological progress;
- Will be able to evaluate and discuss ongoing transformations in the economic system;
- Will be able to analyze the trends of international trade;
- Will be able to identify the economic aspects of commercial policies;
- Will be able to evaluate and discuss ongoing transformations in the economic system;
- Will develop a series of competencies related to understanding verbal and non-verbal communication processes and how these processes are influenced by emerging technologies;
- Will be able to design a simple data collection based on observing human behavior in an ecological context;
- Will be able to replicate a behavioral experiment related to financial decisions;
- Will be able to design and conduct behavioral experiments in business environments;
- Will be able to use the different observation techniques learned during the course and apply the most appropriate in professional practice;
- Will be able to evaluate the reliability and validity of data collected through observation and perform descriptive analysis of the collected data;
- Will be able to explain statistical terms and concepts;
- Will be able to identify suitable methods for understanding and predicting data, with particular attention to the experimental framework;
- Will be able to visualize data using specific tools;
- Will be able to translate experimental results into normative implications for business;
- Will be able to write analysis reports.
The abilities to apply knowledge and understanding described above will be acquired through the following teaching activities:
Interactive lectures on core and related courses, seminar activities, practical exercises, simulations, and development of individual and group projects.
The abilities to apply knowledge and understanding described above will be verified through the following methods:
Written and oral exams, exercises, reports, presentations to academic and business audiences, and final exam.

Learning Skills
At the end of the course, the Master's graduate must have acquired the ability to independently deepen topics of interest, both through critical and proactive reading of economic and psychological scientific literature, and through the design, implementation, and interpretation of action-research interventions.

University Communications to CUN Two years after the establishment of the Program, a gap is evident between student satisfaction with the training project and teaching of individual courses (average 3.96 out of 4.00) and inertia in enrollment, especially among local students.
Therefore, starting in June 2021, efforts were made to investigate the causes of this inertia, which results in low enrollment numbers.
First, it was observed that the conversion rate of potential students who specifically expressed interest in enrollment was low. Presentations and orientation meetings, both collective and individual in response to information requests, provided insights into elements that these prospects found more or less attractive regarding the training proposal.
This observation sample was extensive as the Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences was promoted through various channels:
- The blog www.economiacomportamentale.it, managed by doctoral students in Business and Behavioral Sciences, which in 2021 recorded 37,191 users with 119,078 page views, ranking among the most followed resources in Italy for those interested in the discipline;
- The Facebook page of Economics and Behavioral Neuroscience, www.facebook.com/neuroeconomiacomportamentale, with 2,478 followers;
- The newsletter, currently with 600 subscribers, of whom 7% explicitly expressed interest in the Master's program.
These multiple communication initiatives enabled over 90 motivated information requests for enrollment, leading to orientation and program presentation sessions. The conversion rate concluded at only 2.2%, with only two students from these channels pre-enrolling for the admission interview. This rate further decreased by 50% following the admission test, which revealed concerning gaps in English language proficiency for one candidate.
Especially through individual orientation meetings following collective presentations, opportunities arose to explore motivations supporting and hindering enrollment intentions. Among the supporting factors were the innovation and synergistic potential of the path; among the hindering factors was reluctance to face an interdisciplinary path (thus requiring new disciplinary lexicons to learn) entirely delivered in English.
These observations were confirmed by a December 2021 Qualtrics survey that proposed the possibility of obtaining a second degree in Behavioral Economics. On the question of preferred language for course consumption, almost all respondents chose Italian. On the question "If the degree course were entirely delivered in English, how much would this inhibit your enrollment?", on a scale from 0 to 100, the average response was 75.
Further confirmation of the inhibitory impact of full English delivery emerged from end-of-course focus groups organized within the last two editions of both the Master in Behavioral Economics and Neuromarketing and the Advanced Course in Economics and Business Management offered at the University of Chieti-Pescara. At the conclusion of these courses, in addition to collecting teaching evaluations, guidance on career and training opportunities is provided. During these meetings, thanks to the consistency between these courses and the Economics and Behavioral Sciences Program, a high level of interest in deepening the discipline with a Master's degree was recorded. At the same time, the inhibitory effect of the foreign language was again noted.
Consistent with the findings presented, the attractiveness of the Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences, while relatively satisfactory among non-Italian students (the current student body has citizenship from Russia, Canada, Colombia, India, Eritrea, Malta), is hindered for Italian students.
Restructuring the Program by switching to Italian delivery would not hinder the Program's parallel aspiration, supported by the Steering Committee, to also target an international audience, capitalizing on the already consolidated tendency of the teaching staff to produce and make available to foreign students teaching materials and video lessons in English.
Therefore, once the Program consolidates in terms of attractiveness for the Italian student (and professional) population, it could evolve with the establishment of an international curriculum in English, potentially enhanced by developing partnerships with numerous extra-European universities expressing interest in both our country's system and behavioral economics.

Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
At the end of the course, the Master's graduate must have acquired knowledge and understanding related to the domain of economic and behavioral sciences. They will be able to elaborate and apply original ideas in a high-complexity context.
Specifically, the graduate:
- Will become familiar with the most important issues and concepts of behavioral economics, such as understanding behavior governed by habit and cognitive illusions;
- Will learn the fundamentals of Behavioral Finance;
- Will acquire specialized knowledge related to the main scientific literature and be able to discuss its main contributions;
- Will learn the fundamentals of Behavioral Economics;
- Will acquire specialized knowledge of the main scientific references related to Behavioral Economics and Business;
- Will be familiar with the fundamental mechanisms underlying influence and persuasion processes;
- Will be able to recognize environmental, social, communicative, and cognitive components that guide the behavior of individuals and groups;
- Will be able to distinguish between influence processes aimed at empowering goals versus those creating dependency and loss of power;
- Will know the biological bases of cognitive and affective processes with specific reference to organizational and consumption decisions;
- Will know the neurobiological substrate of relational dynamics in commercial and business contexts; knows the main neuroscientific investigation methodologies;
- Will understand the fundamental principles underlying the study of mind/brain relationships in economic actors;
- Will be able to understand the consequences of decisions for both individuals and the collective;
- Will have become familiar with the most important issues and concepts of behavioral and experimental economics, such as deriving expected behavior from classical game theory;
- Will know the typical and atypical dynamics of intragroup processes, with particular reference to the organizational context;
- Will know the main psychosocial processes regulating interdependence within groups;
- Will know the typical and critical aspects of organizational behavior;
- Will have understood theoretical concepts related to innovation, structural change, entrepreneurship, and economic growth of the productive system;
- Will understand theoretical concepts related to trade and organizational models of the international economy;
- Will have basic knowledge and understanding of the characteristics, usage conditions, advantages, and limitations of various qualitative and quantitative techniques based on measuring human behavior in its contexts;
- Will have knowledge of the theoretical foundations of language psychology and communication.

The knowledge and understanding described above will be acquired through the following teaching activities:
Frontal lectures on core and related courses, seminars, exercises, analogical simulations, individual and group projects.
The acquisition of knowledge and understanding described above will be verified through the following methods:
Written and oral exams, reports, public presentations, and final exam.

Brief Description of Related and Integrative Activities The Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences aims to provide knowledge and skills that enable graduates to master not only economic, business, statistical, and legal knowledge and techniques, but also to synergistically value and implement contributions from cognitive, psychosocial, philosophical, and sociological sciences.
The related and integrative activities of the program are consistent with the training path and aimed at acquiring knowledge and skills related to the identified professional profile. They aim to develop a solid and applicable understanding of thinking, reasoning, and decision-making processes, as well as the role of emotions, motivations, and social dynamics in guiding the behavior of individual and collective economic actors.
More specifically, the related and integrative teaching activities include courses aimed at acquiring theoretical and practical knowledge in sociology, philosophy, and public policy, useful for analyzing the social, business, and organizational context, valuing human capital, and promoting innovation and change, both for the company and for the individual and society.
Another area of knowledge and skills concerns the methodological aspects the program aims to transmit. Courses dedicated to this allow developing investigation protocols and cutting-edge research methodologies, drawing on psychophysiological and behavioral investigation techniques from psychology, neuroscience, and cognitive sciences in general. Such knowledge and practices provide graduates with a solid foundation to understand and examine human behavior and consequently implement effective interventions, both in marketing and communication, and in promoting social and public well-being.
Overall, related and integrative activities are allocated a minimum of 12 ECTS credits.

Brief Course Description The Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences aims to train experts in economics and behavioral sciences for innovation, entrepreneurship, marketing, human resource development, and public policy.
Through a markedly interdisciplinary and interactive path, students will learn to synergistically integrate the rigor of theories, methods, and tools characteristic of economic sciences with the sensitivity of theories, methods, and tools characteristic of behavioral sciences.
Students will thus develop an integrated and comprehensive profile, enabling them to develop a deeper, more articulated, and ecological understanding of the behaviors and choices of economic and social actors.
Public and private institutions, organizations, and companies are constantly seeking professionals capable of understanding their stakeholders more effectively to maximize the quality of their predictions and the impact of their interventions.
The behavioral economist is trained to respond to this growing need.

External Effectiveness Not available.

Reasons for Establishing Multiple Courses in the Same Class The motivations for establishing multiple courses in the same LM 56 class are attributable to four groups of arguments:
A. Epistemological motivations;
B. Institutional motivations;
C. Motivations related to labor market opportunities;
D. Motivations related to gaps in the training offer.

A. Epistemological Motivations Over the last 20 years, there has been significant convergence between economics and behavioral sciences – economics and behavioral sciences – manifested in the rise of the discipline known as 'behavioral economics'. Behavioral economics has gained undisputed relevance in economic, social, and political debate, proving particularly fruitful in explaining and predicting an increasing number of economic phenomena. In this way, behavioral economics has become an indispensable complement to more traditional economic disciplines. While traditional economic disciplines are based on the use of sophisticated mathematical apparatus (prioritizing logical-deductive arguments) accompanied by empirical analysis, behavioral economics derives its approach from cognitive and behavioral sciences, relying predominantly on experimental methodology and prioritizing a distinctly inductive approach. This specificity makes behavioral economics a radically different economic discipline from traditional schools (including the neoclassical school), bringing part of its epistemological status closer to the broad domain of cognitive and behavioral disciplines. From this perspective, behavioral economics appears as a more distinctly interdisciplinary domain – certainly closer to hard sciences in its methodological apparatus – than traditional economic disciplines.

This trend, far from being a passing fad, is commonly referred to as the 'behavioral revolution' as it is marking a paradigm shift in economic disciplines, bringing the human being, with their sociality, emotions, instincts, and irrationality, back to the center. It is no coincidence that the Swedish Academy has awarded the Nobel Prize to a significant number of scholars who have embraced the behavioral and experimental approach in economic studies, including Herbert A. Simon, Reinhard Selten, Vernon L. Smith, Daniel Kahneman, Robert Shiller, Richard Thaler, etc.

A distinctive element of this paradigm shift is that it is not confined to mere scientific debate and relegated to the 'ivory towers' of knowledge but is instead spreading more and more into 'everyday life'. Indeed, topics related to behavioral economics are so pervasive that they are continuously covered by widely circulated magazines and newspapers.

It cannot be denied that the emphasis on cognitive and behavioral aspects (and the same use of experimental methodology) contributes to making behavioral economics a discipline particularly 'discernible' without being trivial, making it highly appreciated even by non-specialists. Using an evolutionary metaphor, behavioral economics is proving successful on many fronts, which explains its success and growing diffusion in society.

B. Institutional Motivations The scope of the behavioral revolution in economics is now institutionalized, certainly due to its 'positive' power, as it is capable of explaining or predicting a significant number of economic and social phenomena (including repeated periods of crisis that have characterized advanced economies over the last 20 years).

But its 'positive' scope represents only a fraction of its potential. Indeed, the fusion between economics and behavioral sciences is proving fundamental in the 'normative' dimension as it constitutes a unified body of knowledge capable of providing policy responses appropriate to the reading and management of economic events characterizing complex advanced economies. A characteristic trait of behavioral economics is its applicability to numerous public or private contexts. The debate on behavioral policy solutions is flourishing.

The normative success of behavioral economics is evidenced by precise institutional events in recent years. In 2015, US President Barack Obama signed a document beginning: 'A growing body of evidence demonstrates that behavioral science insights - research findings from fields such as behavioral economics and psychology about how people make decisions and act on them - can be used to design government policies to better serve the American people.' (see Executive Order No. 13707, 'Using Behavioral Science Insights To Better Serve the American People', published in the Federal Register, Vol. 80 N. 181, Friday, September 18, 2015). In the same document, President Obama invites government organizations to hire behavioral science experts, identify policies and develop projects where behavioral science is relevant, create relationships between government bodies and behavioral science research communities, and help citizens' choices and actions using behavioral science contributions. The act sanctions the systematic use of behavioral sciences within the US administrative apparatus through the creation of the so-called Social and Behavioral Sciences Team. Similarly, the UK government led by David Cameron established an organization called the Behavioral Insight Team, also known as the Nudge Unit, with the aim of improving government policies through the use of behavioral economics.

These facts have significantly contributed to the global institutionalization of behavioral economics and are giving rise to imitation processes in other countries. In virtually all advanced economies, professional figures with expertise in behavioral economics are emerging in diverse sectors: from healthcare to schools, from food to transportation, from authorities to pension bodies, etc. The use of behavioral insights is gradually spreading in the administrative apparatus of both private and public advanced economies.

These institutional facts have been received at the Community level with the creation of a dedicated unit - called Behavioral Insights - within the European Commission.

The Community's attitude towards the scope of behavioral economics is absolutely in line with that adopted in more advanced economies and is systematically oriented towards using behavioral insights for societal improvement. The attempt to systematize projects across different countries is clear evidence of the relevance and scope of behavioral policy.

The fusion between economics and behavioral sciences thus represents a field of study with brilliant peculiarities compared to traditional distinctions within economic disciplines, and has its own status of widely recognized and shared institutional legitimacy internationally.

C. Motivations Related to Labor Market Opportunities According to a survey by the renowned consulting firm Gallup, organizations applying behavioral economics outperform competitors by 85% in sales growth and 25% in gross margin. This makes it evident that the fusion between economics and behavioral sciences is representing a paradigmatic revolution within the business world. The growth rate of the sector is making it difficult for companies in Italy to find readily employable skills.

The paradigmatic scope of behavioral economics means its application domains are highly diversified, as application fields are virtually infinite: from manufacturing industry to healthcare, from transportation to schools.

Such heterogeneity is not only sectoral but also inter-company. Graduates will find opportunities in various areas present in both public and private companies, related to typical functional areas - human resources, marketing and sales, production and logistics, research and development, finance and administration.

D. Motivations Related to Gaps in the Training Offer It can be unequivocally stated that behavioral economics represents the main paradigmatic innovation in economic disciplines over the last 50 years. Table 1 presents a brief list of major international universities with similar programs already active. The table does not include national language initiatives, which abound in various countries. Note that the table does not include more advanced study initiatives such as PhDs in Behavioral Economics (predominant in countries like Germany). It also does not include MBAs (Master of Business Administration), which often feature behavioral specializations, as in the case of Cambridge University's MBAs.

Table 1
Country University Course Name Germany University of Kassel MSc in Economic Behaviour and Governance Ireland University College Dublin MSc Behavioural Economics Netherlands Erasmus University Rotterdam Master in Economics and Business (Behavioural Economics specialization) Portugal Universidade Catolica Portuguesa Master in Psychology in Business and Economics UK City University London MSc in Behavioural Economics UK London School of Economics and Political Science Executive MSc in Behavioural Science UK Manchester Metropolitan University MSc in Behavioural and Economic Science UK University of Essex MSc in Behavioural Economics UK University of Exeter MSc in Behavioural Economics and Finance UK University of Nottingham MSc in Behavioural Economics

The courses listed in Table 1, despite different names, are distinctly oriented towards behavioral economics. Indeed, all courses listed in Table 1 have been included by their respective Coordinators in the main Behavioral Economics portal on the Web (www.behavioraleconomics.com). The portal only includes quality initiatives with strong international characteristics. Note that among the few initiatives in Italy listed on the portal is the PhD in Business and Behavioral Sciences, affiliated with the Department of Neuroscience, Imaging, and Clinical Sciences of our University, involving our teachers in the project.

The only second-level degree program in behavioral economics currently present in Italy is the Master's program in Behavioral and Applied Economics (Behavioral Economics and Applied) at the University of Trento.

With this single exception, the absence of second-level study paths in Behavioral Economics appears to be a training gap that must be filled.

The differentiating element compared to other existing degree programs is self-evident when considering that the Master's programs currently active at the University and belonging to class LM 56 (Economics Sciences) have radically different objectives and content compared to a Behavioral Economics Master's program, different disciplinary content, and are all delivered in Italian.

Observing the specific content of the active Master's programs at the same University and their training path, it is possible to note that none of these present cognitive and behavioral connotations. The absence of cognitive and behavioral elements appears to be a substantial factor, capable of strongly distinguishing the content and scope of a Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences.

Specific Educational Objectives and Description of the Training Path The Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences aims to provide knowledge of the foundational elements of behavioral sciences and their economic applications to the business world and institutions. The cultural and professional profile characterizing the pre-study in Economics and Behavioral Sciences, and distinguishing it from all other programs in the same class, can be summarized by the ambition to capitalize on the contributions of the 'behavioral revolution' to enhance the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of graduates in economic disciplines. Through a highly interdisciplinary path, students will be able to synergistically integrate tools, methodologies, and conceptual frameworks typical of the mathematical-normative economic approach with tools, methodologies, and conceptual frameworks of a descriptive-experimental type typical of neuro-cognitive and psychosocial sciences. The final educational objective is to equip graduates to develop a deeper, more articulated, and ecological understanding of the actions of economic and social actors in order to enhance both the predictive power of their analyses and the transformative impact of their intervention proposals.

This cultural and professional project is structured into a series of specific interdisciplinary educational objectives.

The specific educational objectives of the Program and their respective teaching activities are as follows (see attachment for brief course sheets):

Objective A: Provide preparation in statistical-mathematical tools;
Related courses:
- Statistical Data Analysis
- Decisions in Uncertainty Contexts

Objective B: Convey in-depth knowledge of principles and institutions of national, European, international, and comparative law;
Related courses:
- Law and Decision Processes in Public Policies

Objective C: Convey in-depth knowledge of economic analysis and economic policy;
Related courses:
- International Macroeconomics
- Well-being and Development Economics
- Behavioral Finance
- Experimental Economics

Objective D: Convey in-depth knowledge of business analysis and business policy;
Related courses:
- Behavioral Economics for Businesses
- Behavioral Finance
- Group Dynamics and Organizational Behavior

Objective E: Provide knowledge of English and Italian (the latter for foreign students), in written and oral form, with reference also to disciplinary lexicons.

- All courses provide, also to facilitate foreign students' access, audiovisual teaching materials in English;
- Foreign students will acquire adequate Italian language knowledge through the acquisition of a sufficient number of ECTS credits in the 'additional linguistic knowledge' section of the training path.

Objective F: Provide solid knowledge and skills related to experimental methodologies of behavioral sciences;

Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Level - of Goods and Service Production, Professions (Course Establishment)
The consultation regarding the Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences was carried out in four distinct phases, from general to specific, each represented by a specific analysis characterized by distinct objectives, methodologies, and data sources. These phases are: 1) Investigation for defining the course name; 2) Consultation with stakeholders at regional level; 3) Consultation with stakeholders at national and international level; 4) Deepening regarding preferences expressed by stakeholders.

1) Investigation for defining the English course name to attract foreign students.
The course name (and the general orientation regarding its content) was the subject of a specific web investigation. Specifically, an A/B test was conducted on the web promoting courses that, with identical content, differed only in name. The names were:
- Behavioral Economics;
- Economics and Behavioral Sciences.
Analysis determined the choice of the second name, which was clearer and more informative (preference based on the number of views of the course landing page by users who were genuinely and spontaneously interested in the initiative).

2) Consultation with stakeholders at regional level.
Consultation with representative organizations at the local level for production, services, and professions was directed to the organization naturally capable of encompassing the main stakeholders of the initiative. This organization is represented by AIDP - Italian Association for Personnel Management - consisting of a network of over 17,000 members (with 3,000 active members, 16 regional groups, and an international network). AIDP encompasses the variety of subjects responsible for corporate recruitment and thus possesses the best knowledge of labor market trends at regional, national, and international levels. Its members are mostly represented by HR managers of private companies and public institutions representing the main employment market for graduates in Economics and Behavioral Sciences. The Abruzzo and Molise Section of AIDP was consulted during the Assembly on June 28, 2019. Participants were given a questionnaire based on guidelines for stakeholder consultation.
39 respondents participated in the questionnaire, distributed as follows:
- 51% directors or HR staff, HR consultants, and entrepreneurs;
- 28% HR apprentices;
- 8% unspecified.
Results are summarized in the following sections.

Section 1: Course Name
Question 1.1: Do you believe the course name clearly communicates the purpose of the study program? Results: The course name was well-received by 81% of respondents. Specifically, 54% found it somewhat appealing, and 27% fully appealing.

Section 2: Professional Profiles and Labor Market
Question 2.1: To what extent do you believe the professional profiles the course aims to train respond to the needs of the sector/field/industry represented by your company? Results: The appeal for the professional profile Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Marketing was 89% (specifically, 53% somewhat appealing and 36% fully appealing). Following are Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (74%), Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Organization and Human Resources (72%), and at the same level, Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Finance and Control (64%) and Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Public Policies and Social Well-being (64%).

Question 2.2: To what extent do you believe the professional profiles the course aims to train will be in demand in the labor market in the next ten years? Results: The appeal for the professional profile Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Marketing was 97% (specifically, 51% somewhat appealing and 46% fully appealing). Following are Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (92%), Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Organization and Human Resources (82%), Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Finance and Control (73%), and Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Public Policies and Social Well-being (71%).

Question 2.3: Which of the identified professional profiles do you believe best respond to your Organization's needs? (Please indicate the level of response: 1 - Very High, 2 - High, 3 - Medium, 4 - Low) Results: The appeal for the professional profile Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Marketing was Very High and High for 62% of participants (specifically, 54% High and 8% Very High). The result for the professional profile Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Organization and Human Resources was equivalent (62%, specifically 38% Very High and 24% High). Following are Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (57%), Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Public Policies and Social Well-being (49%), and Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Finance and Control (46%).

Section 3: Expected Learning Outcomes
Question 3.1: To what extent (from 1 to 5) do you believe the knowledge and understanding abilities and application skills the course aims to develop in different learning areas respond to the competencies required by the productive world for the specified professional profiles? Results: Regarding the Knowledge and Understanding section, the following average scores were recorded for each Area:
- Innovation and Entrepreneurship: 3.8
- Marketing: 3.9
- Finance and Business Economics: 3.3
- Organization and Human Resources: 4.1
- Public Policies and Social Well-being: 3.6
Regarding the Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding section, the following average scores were recorded for each Area:
- Innovation and Entrepreneurship: 3.8
- Marketing: 4.2
- Finance and Business Economics: 3.3
- Organization and Human Resources: 3.9
- Public Policies and Social Well-being: 3.5
In summary, there is a marked preference for Marketing, Innovation, and Entrepreneurship areas. Equally appealing (though to a lesser degree) are competencies in the Organization and Human Resources area, Finance and Business Economics. The area related to Public Policies and Social Well-being achieved a score that still positions well above the average threshold of 3.

3) Consultation with stakeholders at national and international level.
Consultation with stakeholders at national and international level mirrors that proposed at the regional level. A series of semi-structured audio-recorded interviews were conducted with consultants and managers from numerous multinational companies such as Commerzbank AG, Microsoft, Juntos Finanzas, Nutmeg, Startup Institute, Google, Ebury, Bought By Many, Ford Motor Company, Micron, First West Credit Union, and Jumeirah Group. Common appreciation was expressed for the clarity of the course name, while the attractiveness of the outgoing professional profiles was maximized for the Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Marketing, the Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Organization and Human Resources, and the Expert in Economics and Behavioral Sciences for Public Policies and Social Well-being. Some interviewees highlighted the value of behavioral sciences applied to creative processes, both in terms of product/service innovation and new paradigms for marketing campaigns. Appreciated and encouraged was the synergy between behavioral approaches and statistical skills useful in data mining and pattern detection. The role of the 'nudging' approach in human resource management was also noted, especially in highly dynamic environments requiring constant creation and dissolution of project teams (e.g., Agile Methodology), as well as the need (in both organizations and society) for psychosocial and sociocognitive ergonomics disciplines to help individuals and groups interact effectively with an increasing number of robots and artificial intelligence tools. Some multinational managers in the 'Travel Industry' highlighted the value of an economic-behavioral approach applied to the design of new 'travel products' and generally to new experiential services for a wider, more diverse, and customization-hungry clientele. In the banking sector, managers emphasized the value of the behavioral approach to predict and manage potential 'reputational incidents' with customers and society, even due to seemingly harmless strategic choices and communication and management. In financial contexts, the role of the Innovation Expert was appreciated for designing 'behaviorally inspired' financial products and services. In general, there is a call for experiential and laboratory-oriented teaching approaches, with particular emphasis on a problem-finding approach with organizational realities when defining thesis projects that crown the path. Sharing these suggestions, the teaching regulations will direct students to interact with economic and social actors, both local and international, to define and develop thesis projects aimed at investigating and intervening to produce tangible, albeit marginal, processes of economic, social, and organizational improvement.

4) Deepening regarding preferences expressed by stakeholders.
The deepening concerns preferences expressed by stakeholders and is conducted through telephone interviews and focus groups. From in-depth interviews with HR consultants, personnel directors, and trainers, it was confirmed that interest exists in the possible impact of the Economics and Behavioral Sciences graduate, particularly on the commercial side, even in its most innovative and evolved aspects. A figure both aware and competent in economic and business contexts as well as in cognitive and psychosocial contexts is perceived as highly valuable in marketing, sales, consumer/user/citizen behavior analysis and prediction, and advanced internal and external communication strategies. Some interviewees highlighted the power of this epistemological synergy to form enhanced profiles of product managers, buyers, trend seekers, and data analysts. In summary, enthusiasm was registered for a figure trained to understand the logic and approaches of business, organizational, and administrative contexts while simultaneously bringing innovative tools to understand and influence the neurosociocognitive processes that often underlie their effectiveness and success.

On the side of industrial relations management, interviews revealed some pessimism regarding the future strategic role of this function, while interest was registered for an emerging professional figure capable of building and negotiating motivating and engaging growth paths for organizational talents.

On the side of innovation skills, interviewees emphasized that, based on their experience, deep innovation processes, both in content and process, require the fortunate combination of evolved competencies and students with other potential. Some interviewees therefore suggested strategies on how the Master's program could attract 'outstanding' students through the development of solid partnerships with primary international training poles, with the most important sector associations, and with the most renowned consulting multinational companies. Finally, several interviewees expressed the hope that the Program could be characterized by a strong school/work alternation and that teaching schedules and methods could be structured to facilitate access for already active professionals.

Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Level - of Goods and Service Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
Periodic evaluation of the Master's program's educational objectives includes consultation with organizations recognized as interested social parties. Specifically, there is a Steering Committee for the activities included in the Behavioral Economics and Neuroeconomics section (http://www.ecne.unich.it/comitato-dindirizzo/), to which the Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences belongs. Consultations, prepared annually, use questionnaires to identify training needs and employment prospects of the Program's graduates.

Proposals for remodulating the training offer from teachers and students are collected through formal, informal meetings, and ad hoc questionnaires. Exam results are considered indicators of the training path's effectiveness.

Additionally, the University has established a permanent consultation table with representatives of the productive system and professional sectors, enabling the identification of training and professional needs of the territory and remodulating the Program's curriculum accordingly (https://pqa.unich.it/attivita-ava-2020/consultazione-delle-parti-sociali).

In preparation for the 2024/2025 academic year, annual consultation was conducted with the Steering Committee of the ECNE section to which the Program refers. The meeting was held in mixed mode on April 4, 2023. For the Program, the Chair, Prof. Davide Pietroni (in office until October; from November 1, Prof. Claudio Di Berardino assumed the role), participated, along with the Rector, Prof. Liborio Stuppia.

Among the points raised, the positive judgment from managers and entrepreneurs regarding the training path of the Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences was emphasized. The Program was appreciated for its innovative character and alignment with current market needs.

Reflections touched on themes of internationalization, involvement of local small and medium enterprises, and the interdisciplinary nature characterizing the Program. In particular, the parties appreciated the increase in enrollments, the geographical breadth of the student population's attractiveness, the improvement in students' academic careers, and the satisfaction with courses.

A new Steering Committee meeting is scheduled for September to plan for 2025/2026.

Additionally, since June 2021, various surveys have been conducted to investigate the level of satisfaction and potential issues with the training offer. Presentations and orientation meetings, both collective and individual in response to information requests, provided insights into elements potential candidates found more or less attractive regarding the training proposal.

This observation sample was extensive as the Master's program in Economics and Behavioral Sciences was promoted through various channels:
- The blog www.economiacomportamentale.it, managed by doctoral students in Business and Behavioral Sciences, which in 2022 recorded 9,000 new users with 31,433 page views, ranking among the most followed resources in Italy for those interested in the discipline;
- The Facebook page of Economics and Behavioral Neuroscience, www.facebook.com/neuroeconomiacomportamentale, with 2,708 followers;
- The newsletter, currently with 1,153 subscribers, of whom 46.7% explicitly expressed interest in the Master's program;
- The LinkedIn page https://www.linkedin.com/company/15815167/ with 1,966 followers.

These multiple communication initiatives enabled channeling a hundred motivated information requests for enrollment, leading to orientation and program presentation sessions.

Especially through individual orientation meetings, opportunities arose to explore motivations supporting and hindering enrollment intentions. Among the supporting factors were innovation and the synergistic potential of the path; among the hindering factors was the fear of facing an interdisciplinary path often not perceived as a "natural" continuation of the three-year degree path.

Another opportunity for consulting potential students is represented by end-of-course focus groups organized within the last four editions of both the Master in Behavioral Economics and Neuromarketing and the Advanced Course in Economics and Business Management offered at the University of Chieti-Pescara. At the conclusion of these courses, in addition to collecting teaching evaluations, guidance on career and training opportunities is provided. During these meetings, thanks to the consistency between these courses and the Economics and Behavioral Sciences Program, a high level of interest in deepening the discipline with a Master's degree was recorded.

In light of the findings from the consultation with social parties, the increased attractiveness of the Study Program following the switch to Italian delivery has been confirmed. Furthermore, this choice does not appear to have compromised the Program's parallel aspiration, supported by the Steering Committee, to also target an international audience, capitalizing on the already consolidated tendency of the teaching staff to produce and make available to foreign students teaching materials and video lessons in English.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data

ENTRY DATA
Data collected and summarized by the University's Quality Assurance Office (PQA) indicate that the number of enrolled students in the Economics and Behavioral Sciences Program for the 2022/2023 academic year amounts to 21 units - plus one additional student enrolled under the previous curriculum (Economics and Behavioral Sciences), not considered in subsequent statistics. Compared to the previous academic year, the change in curriculum is noted - modification of the Program name and language of course delivery. Overall, there has been a 50% increase in the number of enrolled students.

For the 2022/2023 academic year, an excellent gender balance in enrollments was confirmed (52% males). 57% of the enrolled students reside in Abruzzo and obtained their first-level degree at UdA - a figure perfectly in line with the previous academic year - while the remaining 43% come from other Italian regions and obtained their degree elsewhere. There are no students residing abroad or with foreign degrees.

These data suggest the effectiveness of information, promotion, and orientation strategies, leading to greater awareness of the Program's existence in the regional and national territory. As expected, the change in language of course delivery (from English to Italian) reduced the foreign enrollment rate to zero, compared to 14% under the previous curriculum. However, the number of enrolled students, although exclusively from Italy, has significantly increased, so the overall balance is positive.

PATH DATA
The currently active Program (Economics and Behavioral Sciences) consists only of first-year students. Therefore, statistics on exam progression and moving to the second year are not available.

For the previous curriculum Program (Economics and Behavioral Sciences), of the 14 enrolled in the 2021 academic year, 12 continued to the second year of the same Program (86%). On average, students earned 45% of the required ECTS credits. A data point to monitor is the presence of enrolled students who did not earn any ECTS credits by December 31, 2022 (21%).

EXIT DATA
The currently active Program (Economics and Behavioral Sciences) consists only of first-year students. Therefore, statistics on degree attainment are not available.

For the previous curriculum Program (Economics and Behavioral Sciences), only one graduate has been recorded to date (grade 110 with honors).

Entry, path, and exit data for the 2021-2022 academic year were discussed at the Program Council meeting, as indicated in the minutes of October 6, 2022. Data for the 2022-2023 academic year will be analyzed and discussed at the first useful Program Council meeting.

Characteristics of the Final Exam
The final exam consists of the presentation and discussion, in public before a committee of teachers, of a written work composed of a compilative, methodological, experimental, or applied work developed in original form under the guidance of a supervisor and the supervision of at least one co-supervisor.

Final Exam Execution Method
To obtain the Master's degree in Economics and Behavioral Sciences, the student, after passing all exams required by the study plan, including those related to autonomously chosen training activities, and after acquiring credits for other training activities (additional linguistic knowledge and/or training internships), must pass a final exam whose objective is to evaluate the ability to correctly apply behavioral economics approaches and the methodological and professional tools learned during the study path.

The final exam is worth 18 ECTS credits and consists of the writing, presentation, and discussion, in public before a committee of teachers, of a written work (thesis) composed of a compilative, methodological, experimental, or applied work developed in original form under the guidance of a supervisor (normally a course teacher who will also serve as supervisor during the discussion) and the supervision of at least one co-supervisor (normally appointed by the Program Chair).

The thesis is an organic and complete work developed originally by the student to demonstrate research, elaboration, and synthesis capabilities. The thesis topic must relate to at least one of the courses/subject areas provided by the Master's program, chosen by the student in agreement with the supervisor.

The thesis can be written in Italian or English, or another language upon prior communication from the supervisor to the Master's Program Chair, who reserves the right to evaluate it.

In any case, the thesis must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian.

Additional details on the final exam are available on the dedicated page of the institutional website.

The discussion takes place in the presence of a committee appointed by the competent Department Director, whose composition is regulated by the University's Teaching Regulations (Article 37).

The Graduation Committee consists of at least seven and no more than eleven members, including the Chair.

During the graduation session, the graduate orally presents their thesis, usually accompanied by slides illustrating the fundamental aspects of the work. The Committee listens and discusses the student's work in public session. Subsequently, the Committee meets in private to assign the graduation grade to each candidate, expressed in hundredths according to the following methods and as provided by Article 9 of the Program's Teaching Regulations.

The final grade is expressed in hundredths and consists of the sum of the three determinants listed below:
a. Weighted average of exam grades expressed in hundredths;
b. Grade obtained in the final exam;
c. Optional integration for honors received in exams.

The value of the sum thus obtained is rounded up to the next integer if the first digit after the decimal point is equal to or greater than 5, or rounded down to the previous integer otherwise.

In the case where the sum of the components is equal to or greater than 110/110 and the student achieves the maximum score for the final exam, the Graduation Committee may award the honor unanimously.

The assignment of scores for the three determinants is carried out according to the following criteria.

Determinant a.
The weighted average of exam grades, weighted by the respective credits, expressed in hundredths, is calculated as follows:
- Multiply the grade obtained in each exam by the number of credits for that exam;
- Calculate value A as the sum of the numbers obtained in the previous step;
- Calculate value B as the sum of the credits of the exams included in the average calculation;
- Calculate value C by dividing value A by value B (C=A/B);
- Calculate value D by dividing value C by 30 (D=C/30);
- Obtain the weighted average of grades expressed in hundredths by multiplying value D by 110 (MP=Dx110).

Also included in determining the weighted average of grades (MP) are grades obtained in exams related to autonomously chosen training activities, weighted by their respective credits (CFU), provided they were previously included in the approved study plan and the total number of CFU acquired does not exceed the CFU required by the curriculum for autonomously chosen training activities. Any excess CFU beyond the 120 CFU required for the degree will not contribute to determining the final grade; the deduction will apply to the CFU of autonomously chosen training activities where the student received the lowest grade in the assessment.

Determinant b.
The grade for the final exam, expressed in hundredths, must be formulated considering both the quality of the work done by the candidate and the candidate's ability to present the topics covered using the knowledge and skills acquired during the entire university training path. The Committee may assign a maximum score of 6 points for the final exam.

Determinant c.
The integration for honors, expressed in hundredths, is determined by awarding 0.4 points for each honor received in the exams taken, up to a maximum of 2 points.

Once the graduation grade is assigned, the Committee proceeds with the public proclamation.

Technical Report Summary of the Evaluation Unit - SUA Form
The Program's design was carried out with appropriate methods and attention, albeit with tight timelines. The motivations for establishing the Program appear convincing and outline an innovative training project within the national context. The cultural and professional profiles of the figure the Program aims to train are clearly defined. Direct consultation with stakeholders is adequate at local and national levels and has been extended to consultants and managers of various multinational companies. The cultural and professional profiles, functions, and competencies are consistent with learning outcomes and, with some limited exceptions, with the objectives of teaching activities. Access requirements and verification methods for courses are adequately defined. Program monitoring is consistent with the University's Quality Assurance system.

Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission Curricular requirements: to access the Master's Degree program, a first-cycle degree or equivalent foreign degree must be held. Specifically, those holding a first-cycle degree in one of the following classes: Class 17 and Class 28 under DM 509/99, L18 and L33 under DM 270/04 or an equivalent degree obtained at a foreign university; those holding a second-cycle degree in one of the following classes: Class 64S and Class 84S under DM 509/99, LM-56 and LM-77 under DM 270/04 or an equivalent degree obtained at a foreign university; those holding a four-year degree under the old system (pre-DM 509/99) in Economics, obtained at an Italian university or an equivalent degree obtained at a foreign university. English language knowledge is also required, in addition to Italian. Verification of these requirements is carried out through a formalized verification process. Communication Skills (abilità comunicative)
The master's graduate will be able to communicate problems, ideas, and solutions related to the context in which they operate clearly, accurately, and comprehensively. They will be able to express themselves effectively to non-specialist audiences of users and clients, and will be able to engage in dialogue with experts in an engaging and integrative/generative manner. In particular, the master's graduate in Economics and Management will acquire the ability to communicate business strategies to different stakeholders and to interact with operators belonging to various business functions.
This outcome will be achieved and verified through the discussion of cases and the presentation of results in class and/or in group work, the presentation during knowledge assessment, and through potential study periods abroad. The writing of the thesis also offers an additional opportunity for deepening and verifying the communication skills developed.

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
The master's graduate will have acquired the ability to integrate knowledge, manage complexity, and form judgments even in the presence of partial information, including reflections on the social and ethical responsibilities related to the application of economic and managerial skills; in particular, they will be able to integrate the perspectives of different business functions.
This outcome can be achieved and verified through:
- classroom discussion, in work groups with teachers and students;
- participation in seminars on entrepreneurial values and managerial behavior;
- personal contribution provided in assessment of academic performance;
- critical contribution demonstrated in the writing of the thesis.
