To assess the "sentiment" of cohorts enrolled in the corresponding undergraduate course, the In-Progress Orientation Committee has prepared an orientation questionnaire "towards the Master's" reserved for third-year students. The questionnaire consists of 17 questions and aims to collect the following cohort characteristics: willingness to continue university studies, areas of interest, decision level, and reasons for interest in selected disciplines, expectations regarding Master's course subjects, willingness to continue at DEA, potential willingness to continue at another department/university, and reasons for the choice. The questionnaire, created on the Microsoft Forms platform, allows quick access for participants via QR code scanning and enables immediate response collection. It aims, through analysis of responses, to provide useful indications for the continuous improvement of the educational offer.

As of December 2023, the CDS has over 1,000 active agreements distributed throughout the national territory and some international ones.
Examples of companies and entities include: Cooperative Credit Bank; GLM SPA; Policlinic of Monza; Bluserena Spa; ASL of Teramo; ICCREA; Ecoh Media srl; Maglificio Gran Sasso Spa; Aran Group; Revenue Agency; Unipol Sai; BDO spa; Pomilio Blum; Del Verde Food Industries; De Cecco Spa; Fater Spa; Honda Italia spa; Confindustria Abruzzo; Confcooperative; Allianz Insurance; Seneca Spa; FIRA spa; Walter Tosto Spa; Denso Manufacturing spa; FCA Italy spa; Toto Holding Spa; Valagro. Overseas internships and non-curricular internships are also provided, which are not linked to the acquisition of CFU (e.g., requested by companies for the completion of a thesis or to carry out specific work experiences of interest to the student), with the aim of completing the CDS training process in work-study alternation. Students of Clemam who completed internship activities from January 2023 to December 2023 totaled 56.
The CDS assists students in defining the project work to be developed during the internship through an academic tutor and in collaboration with the company tutor, in the search for host sites, and in the establishment of agreements. The CDS website details the procedures, active agreements, documents, and deadlines for submitting documentation, and proceeds to collect and analyze the evaluation forms completed by the academic tutor, the student, and the company tutor, in order to assess the effectiveness of the internship.
The administrative procedure coordinator is Ms. Maela Venanzi (mvenanzi@unich.it).
The opinions collected from the evaluation questionnaires are analyzed by the Orientation Committee and the AQ Committee, to understand the effectiveness of the training path and the internship itself.
The questionnaire administered to 40 students who completed the internship by December 2023 shows a synthesis score of 4.85, an increase from the previous year's score of 4.72 (scale of 1-5), with particular appreciation for the acquired skills and adherence to assigned tasks in relation to the training project. No dissatisfaction or suggestions are noted. These results were discussed in the AQ Committee and the Study Course Council.

Assistance for International Mobility The assistance and tutoring activities for international student mobility within the Course of Study are carried out by a Commission for International Relations established by the Department of Business Economics, coordinated by Prof. Nicola De Marco (ndemarco@unich.it), who is also the Erasmus Delegate and International Relations Officer of the Department of Business Economics and also participates in the Commission as the Course of Study President.
The activities related to services offered at both the University and Course of Study levels are as follows:
a) Before departure, language preparation courses (40 hours) in English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Russian, and Serbo-Croatian;
b) Support from the Chieti-Pescara Erasmus Students Association, an active member of the International Exchange Erasmus Student Network for students participating in the Program, with annual periodic meetings;
c) Within the Erasmus program, logistical and academic assistance guaranteed by two contact persons appointed by the respective Departments, both from the sending and receiving universities;
d) For extra-European conventions, assistance from a d'Annunzio faculty member tasked with informing the student about the study plan to follow at the host university.
Currently, the Department of Business Economics has signed various agreements with foreign universities for student international mobility, listed in the attached file. Additional bilateral extra-European conventions are active for student and faculty exchange with the UNIVERSITY OF ALABAMA AT BIRMINGHAM (USA), NAZARETH COLLEGE (USA), UNIVERSITY OF BALTIMORE (USA), and UNIVERSITY OF NICOSIA (CYPRUS), the 'John D. Calandra' Italian American Institute, Queens College/CUNY (USA).
Annually, the International Relations Commission organizes ERASMUS DAY orientation meetings to illustrate the Erasmus program, the partner institutions, and effectively guide the study period abroad.
Additionally, the Commission has improved communication on the dedicated web page, including useful documents requested by students for a better understanding of the Erasmus path, developing a student handbook, a grade equivalence table, and a specification of foreign sites dedicated solely to economic and business disciplines.
Overall, the results are satisfactory, as evidenced by the increasing number of outgoing students in 2023, corresponding to 5 units, the same as in 2022, and 7 incoming students for the Erasmus+ project.
During the 2022/23 academic year, the Course of Study recorded the first student to obtain a Double Degree at Cranfield (https://clemam.unich.it/pagina-double-degree-1005), the first in the entire University.
Since the 2022/23 academic year, the international curriculum for the Double Degree with the University of Neu-Ulm (https://clemam.unich.it/pagina-double-degree-neuulm-1330) has been launched, which saw the participation of 2 students in the first year, who are currently completing their second year at Neu-Ulm, while in the 2023/24 academic year, 7 students are enrolled in the program, of whom 1 is part-time.
However, no foreign students were enrolled in the program in 2023. To increase the appeal of the curriculum for students at Neu-Ulm, the curriculum will be redesigned, including a greater presence of courses in management and organization starting from the next academic year.
Additionally, 1 student from the Course of Study completed an internship abroad during 2023 through the Erasmus placement program, always assisted by the Department's Erasmus Delegate.
The internationalization of the Course of Study is also promoted by the teaching contribution of visiting faculty scheduled for 2023, as well as by courses taught in English in the Management and Business Finance curricula.

Student Opinions The definitive statistics provided by the University Quality Assurance Office for the 2021/22 academic year through the platform https://opinionistudenti.unich.it/, highlight for the Course of Study (CdS) a further increase in the satisfaction rating expressed by students regarding the courses compared to the previous academic year (the analyzed data relates to 609 forms completed by students regarding 30 courses – 83.33% coverage of teaching activities). The summary score, on a scale of 1-4, is 3.54, slightly higher than the 2020/21 academic year's score of 3.50.
In particular, the overall satisfaction is 3.41. The value is higher than the area average (3.33) and the University average (3.31), confirming the constant increase in the CdS's satisfaction among students.
67% of the evaluated courses achieved the maximum evaluation threshold, between 3.5 and 4, a value higher than the 58% of 2020/21. The remaining 33% falls within the 3-3.5 range.
Specifically, in the 2021/22 academic year, improvements are noted in the ratings regarding the lecturer's ability to adequately present the topics (3.56), their availability (3.69), the suitability of the teaching materials (3.46), the ratings on the level of interest in the subject content (3.54), the lecturer's ability to stimulate interest in the subject (3.57), and the suitability of the teaching load (3.33). The rating for the consistency between what was covered in class and what was stated on the course websites regarding the content (3.59) remains nearly the same as last year. However, there is a slight decline in the clarity of explaining exam procedures (3.61) and adherence to class schedules (3.69).
These evaluations are supplemented by ratings extractable from the platform, which as of August 31, 2023, shows a partial figure for 2022/23 of an overall rating of 3.45, currently slightly declining compared to 2021/22. Except for the partial data showing an increase in the rating regarding the lecturer's availability during class and/or office hours to clarify the topics covered (3.71), the remaining elements remain nearly the same or are slightly declining compared to the 2021/22 data.
These data are supplemented by opinions gathered from graduates through the University statistics for the 2021/22 academic year: an improvement in the average satisfaction is noted, rising to 3.27 on a scale of 1-4 (3.22 social area; 3.23 University), compared to 3.20 in the previous academic year. Additionally, improvements are observed across all evaluated aspects, which received scores consistently above 3, in line with and often exceeding the University average. Specifically, the average satisfaction for the CdS achieved a rating of 3.44 (compared to 3.31 at the University level), with particularly appreciated aspects being the courses (3.48 at the CdS level versus 3.33 at the University level) and the internship experience (3.61 at the CdS level versus 3.48 at the University level).
Student opinions are presented and discussed within the Department's AQ Group, the Course Council (held on September 13, 2023), and the Teaching Commission, with the aim of identifying appropriate corrective actions and reorganizing the teaching schedule. This discussion also incorporates feedback from the CPDS (Parity Commission of Teachers and Students), which reports to the Department on student feedback, as well as the presence of student representatives in the Councils and the AQ Group, as evidenced by the minutes posted on the Department and CdS websites. These data are also discussed during periodic meetings with the Steering Committee, as shown in Table A1.b.
The CdS finally has easily accessible procedures to handle student complaints, which are directed to the President of the CdS's email address or the dedicated teaching office email: economiaemanagement@unich.it
Graduates' Opinions The Almalaurea survey (updated as of April 2023) and the University's average statistics for the 2022 graduates include 91 graduates, of whom 87 responded (95.6%), highlighting a slight decline in satisfaction. 64% state they graduated on time, a figure declining from the previous year (66%). The percentage of those reporting overall satisfaction decreases slightly to 87.4% (96% in 2021; 90% University average), and 74.7% would enroll again in the same Course of Study (86% in 2021; 78.3% University average). 86.2% of respondents consider the teaching load adequate (93% in 2021; 89% University average), and the same percentage finds the teaching schedule organization satisfactory (82% in 2021; 86% University average). The percentage of graduates rating the overall relationship with lecturers as satisfactory decreases to 89% (98% in 2021; 92.3% University average). 67.2% report overall satisfaction with post-graduation career services, and 64% appreciate support services for entering the workforce. Lower satisfaction is noted for IT equipment and classrooms.
Graduates' opinions are presented and discussed in the Course Council held on September 13, 2023. No critical issues were identified requiring urgent improvement measures, although continuous actions to enhance services for students are planned through the Department's specific committees.
Additionally, satisfaction data from graduates, along with employment statistics, are presented and discussed in the annual Steering Committee meeting, receiving general consensus and appreciation from the participating stakeholders, as demonstrated by the attached minutes for Table A1.b of the current SUA for the previous academic year.
Applying Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The Master's graduate will be able to apply the most suitable managerial logic and tools to specific business problems in an integrated and coherent manner, as well as develop problem-solving skills in new or unfamiliar situations. Specifically, the graduate in Economics and Management will be able to formulate strategies to create value, design, manage, and control business systems, organize information systems using digital technologies in national and international markets and public administration, in functioning or crisis contexts, and analyze data using quantitative methodologies to support business decision-making. This means being able to select the most appropriate methodological and analytical tools and identify the best operational solutions. This can be achieved through: - active participation in classroom sessions and group work involving the resolution of business cases and/or simulations using software applications and foreign languages; - participation in seminars, workshops, and business games often featuring industry professionals.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
The Master's graduate will have acquired learning skills enabling them to independently deepen and proactively develop their knowledge and competencies related to the main functional areas of business in their professional context. These skills will be acquired through participation in classroom teaching, in traditional and/or interactive formats, individual study, and particularly through the research work conducted for the thesis. The acquisition of learning skills is verified by evaluating the quality of individual or group assignments and the quality of the thesis.
University Communication to CUN The Ordinance amendment primarily involves adding a fourth curriculum to the Course of Study linked to a convention with the University of Neu-Ulm (Germany), International Business School, for the MSc in International Enterprise Information Management, with a double degree.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The Master's graduate will have acquired advanced knowledge in the disciplines characterizing the Course of Study in business, economic, legal, and mathematical-statistical areas, developed more extensively and/or in-depth than at the first cycle. This means being able to not only understand diverse and complex study materials in Italian and English but also develop original ideas in a research context. The courses in business, economic, legal, and mathematical-statistical areas characterizing the four proposed curricula enable the Economics and Management graduate to understand the strategic context of the enterprise and the opportunities and threats of the competitive environment in which enterprises (or public administrations) operate, acquire specific knowledge of the functioning models of national and international markets, know the main legal institutions relevant to enterprise operations and crisis contexts, and finally, know the main quantitative financial and/or statistical analysis models supporting business decisions. These results can be achieved and verified through: - regular attendance at classroom activities and active participation in other teaching formats (group work, simulations, case discussions); - consistent and in-depth individual study; - passing knowledge assessment tests. Knowledge and understanding (especially in foreign language) can also be acquired through a study period abroad (optional) and/or through double degree pathways as specified by the Course of Study.
University Organizational Structure and Responsibilities The Quality Assurance Office plays a central role in promoting the quality culture and Quality Assurance (QA), ensuring compliance with the Quality Assurance Requirements outlined in Annex C of Ministerial Decree 30 January 2013, No. 47.
For the QA of study courses, it specifically organizes and verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-CdS of each course; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for teaching activities in line with planned and declared programs; regulates and verifies periodic course reviews; evaluates the effectiveness of improvement actions and their actual consequences; ensures proper information flow to and from the Evaluation Committee and the Parity Teacher-Student Committees.
For the QA of departmental research, it specifically verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-RD of each Department; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for research activities in line with planned and declared programs; ensures proper information flow to and from the Evaluation Committee.
The Quality Assurance Office is composed of the Rector's delegate for 'Quality', a full professor who has opted for full-time work, responsible for overseeing the Office's activities, along with three full professors from the following ERC (European Research Council) fields: Physical Sciences & Engineering; Social Sciences & Humanities; Life Sciences.
Course of Study QA Organization and Responsibilities Responsible for ReAQD-D: Prof. Daniela Di Berardino The Department of Business Economics has established an internal system of bodies and committees involved in the Quality Assurance process for study courses and the management of primary processes for the courses under the Department.
This system is structured into bodies with specific competencies and responsibilities for QA, involved in monitoring primary processes related to teaching. These bodies are listed below:
Course of Study Director – Prof. STEFANO ZA Responsibilities: Coordinates the CdS QA system and oversees compliance with requirements set by regulations, with the collaboration of the QA Commission/Group, the Parity Teacher-Student Committee (CPDS), in line with the guidelines from the University's central bodies on QA and ANVUR's directions. The Director, with the collaboration of the AQ Group, leads the cyclical and annual review of the CdS, drafting the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA) and the Cyclical Review Report (RRC), and proceeds with the SUA-CdS entry, with the collaboration of the AQ Group. According to annual deadlines, it handles teaching coverage and redefines the study path and educational objectives, based on periodic consultations with stakeholders. Finally, it promotes a quality-oriented culture within the Course Council.
QA Commission/Group and Review Group Members: Course Director, QA Coordinator at the Department of Business Economics (Prof. Daniela Di Berardino), Department professors (Prof. Helen Chiappini and Prof. Christian Morbidoni until February 2024), a student representative, and a technical-administrative staff representative (Fabiano Di Muzio).
Responsibilities: The QA and Review Group oversees the quality management policy of the CdS; specifically, the coordinator manages all quality activities and the specific committees established within the Department for monitoring primary CdS processes. The coordinator also maintains direct contact with the PQA and the Parity Committee. The Course Director is regularly updated on the activities of the Department committees. The AQ Group as a whole monitors compliance with quality policies, regulations, and guidelines in line with PQA and ANVUR's directions, conducting periodic monitoring of indicators, analyzing criticalities, evaluating possible improvement actions, and convening active Department committees for updates on AVA 3 requirements. The AQ Group collaborates in drafting the SUA-CdS, SMA, and RRC.
Parity Teacher-Student Committee Composition: Committee Coordinator and Course professor (Prof. Antonio D'Andreamatteo), a Course professor, and a student representative.
Responsibilities: The committee monitors the teaching offer, teaching quality, and contextual services provided to students by teachers and structures, with particular emphasis on criticalities, which are periodically communicated to the Course Director, Course Council, and the Department's Teaching QA Coordinator.
Course Council Composition: Professors teaching courses and student representatives enrolled in the Course, elected according to the University's General Regulations.
Responsibilities: The Council deliberates on the content of the SUA, the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA), and evaluates and deliberates on the improvement proposals identified by the Course Director and the QA Commission; periodically, it deliberates on the content of the Cyclical Review Report (RRC); collaborates in implementing the CdS quality improvement policies.
Quality policy in the CdS is also exercised through decentralized activities within the Department's committees as follows:

- Orientation Committee (divided into entry, in-course, exit, and placement): Evaluates student opinions on tutoring initiatives, monitors career progression, welcomes and guides new students, monitors the effectiveness of curricular internships and placement, plans and evaluates the effectiveness of support services for entering the workforce;
- International Relations Committee: Coordinates mobility services for students, provides support and guidance for Erasmus students;
- Relations with Territory Committee, Steering Committee, and Course Director: Monitors employment effectiveness, consults stakeholders, redefines the teaching offer, activates conventions;
- Communication Committee: Coordinates contextual support services for students, updates information on the CdS (student guide, CdS functioning, e-learning platform, social networks, Department website), manages media relations;
- Credit Recognition Committee: Verifies access and admission requirements for the CdS. The Teaching Office and the Department's Internship Office also collaborate in acquiring information.
Work Planning and Implementation Deadlines The QA Commission meets periodically according to the schedule outlined in the attached model to carry out the following activities:
- Within the deadlines for entering information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), SMA (October-December), and RRC (at least 3 months before internal deadlines), conduct hearings with specific Department committees regarding QA implementation within the CdS;
- Within the deadlines for entering information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), SMA (October-December), and RRC (at least 3 months before internal deadlines), analyze and evaluate improvement actions for continuous enhancement of the CdS in various organizational aspects, monitor teaching indicators, with particular reference to student, graduate, and alumni opinions, contextual services, external effectiveness of the study course, Erasmus path, effectiveness of curricular internships, and results of actions taken.
Reference indicators are drawn from the Department's Strategic Plan (% students out of course contacted; % recovered students, enrolled, internationalization), internal surveys from the Internship Office and Orientation Committee (student opinions; opinions from companies and organizations; career monitoring, quality forum results), and data provided by the University's Applied and Teaching Department (enrolments, career monitoring, student opinions, employment).
- Within the deadlines for entering information into the SUA-CdS (February-April; July-September), final meetings for discussing the sheets and drafting the SUA;
- Between February and May, coordinate with the Course Director to redefine specific educational objectives of the CdS, based on consultations with stakeholders, for defining the requirements for teaching coverage and programming the teaching offer. Based on guidelines from the Evaluation Committee and the Teaching Delegate, the Department's QA Coordinator will liaise with the Course Director before approving the teaching offer to allow timely verification of the CdS's sustainability and alignment of educational objectives with the planned offer, including verification of the effectiveness of elective courses in the CdS, with biennial checks;
- By the annual deadline set by the PQA (October-December), hold at least two meetings to analyze SMA indicators and evaluate causes and improvement proposals;
- Periodically, verify the correctness and proper entry of syllabi, in coordination with the Teaching Committee;
- Periodically, through the QA/Review Group Coordinator and the Course Director, promote a quality culture within the CdS, both within Councils and through periodic communications to Department committees, and participate in training events related to CdS quality requirements.
Improvement initiatives emerging from periodic meetings are periodically highlighted in the Course Council for planning improvement actions, as evidenced by the minutes of the Course Council meetings.
Brief Description of Related and Complementary Activities The inclusion of training activities related to economic-business disciplines is motivated by the goal of further developing specialized competencies required for business functions in the areas of administration, finance, and control; the inclusion of such activities is also motivated by the goal of further developing specialized competencies required for business functions in the areas of marketing, business networks, innovation management, and entrepreneurship; the inclusion of activities within corporate finance is motivated by the goal of further developing specialized competencies required for business functions in the financial area and analysis of enterprise financial needs, in line with the specified CdS profile; additionally, the inclusion of specific business and organizational activities is motivated by the goal of further developing specialized competencies required for business functions related to the economic-organizational implications of digital transformation processes, human resource management, and complexity.
However, the Course's Didactic Regulations and planned teaching offer will allow students who wish to follow paths with an adequate amount of credits in related and complementary fields that are not already characteristic.
The inclusion of training activities related to the English language is motivated by the possibility of offering courses to further enhance knowledge of this language.
No mandatory foreign language or computer-related complementary activities are provided.
The inclusion of training activities related to psycho-sociological disciplines is important as it grants multidisciplinarity to the training and pertains to the study of the relationship between organizational, psychological, social, and communication processes in business, i.e., the sphere of organizational and business communication.
Finally, the inclusion of legal-related training activities is motivated by the goal of providing students with additional instruction valid for complying with the MIUR-CNDCEC Framework Convention.
Brief Course Description The Master's Course in Economics and Management is designed for students seeking advanced knowledge and skills in both main business functional areas and the operational context in which they will operate.
The Course is structured into 4 distinct curricula:
1) Corporate Finance. This path aims to train graduates with high technical and professional skills, particularly in the areas of economic-financial analysis, performance measurement, corporate finance, business valuation, crisis recovery, and strategic management for value creation within companies;
2) Management. This path aims to train graduates with high technical and professional skills, particularly in the areas of innovation (including digital) process management, entrepreneurship, sustainability, marketing, complex system management, and human resource management;
3) Business Profession and Consulting. This path aims to train graduates with high technical and professional skills, particularly in the areas of management control, administrative direction, legal audit, performance evaluation, and business consulting;
4) International Enterprise Information Management. This path, in a Double Degree convention with the University of Neu-Ulm in Germany, offers skills in managing internal and external business information within a digital transformation context.
To facilitate learning processes, balance lecture periods with exam periods, and internationalization, each academic year is divided into three terms, with courses also offered in English in each of the four curricula. Study abroad experiences of varying duration (one month to one year, including the 2022 Double Degree convention with The Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences (HNU), International Enterprise Information Management (MSc)) are encouraged, as is the completion of business internships. The CdS also offers the possibility of obtaining a Double Degree with Cranfield University (UK) - School of Management through a convention established in 2019. The involvement of business world operators (enterprise, professions, public administration) and interactive teaching methods are encouraged.
Course characteristics can be summarized as: a) Strong economic-business content; b) Professionalizing content and teaching methods; c) Interactive teaching; d) Course structure divided into three terms; e) Inclusion of English-language courses / IEIM curriculum in English; f) Integration between lectures and interventions by business operators and privileged witnesses; g) Option to take part-time teaching, completing the study path in four years with proportional reduction of enrollment fees; h) CFU related to the internship option obtainable through internships at partner companies (including professional offices). For meritorious students, an excellence path is provided to ensure updating of the most advanced disciplinary knowledge, also in view of subsequent study cycles such as the Research Doctorate.
External Effectiveness The statistics elaborated by Almalaurea on the employment status of graduates in 2022 (updated as of April 2022) refer to a group of 41 respondents out of a total of 53 graduates (77.4%). The data show that, one year after obtaining the degree, 78% are employed (compared to 67% in the previous survey), while 9.8% are not employed and not seeking work.
Among the employed, 62.5% found work after graduation, while 25% continued work started before graduation, and the remaining part did not continue work started before graduation.
On average, graduates find employment within three months of graduation, in line with previous surveys.
Of the employed, 18.8% have an indefinite contract one year after graduation, 15.6% are self-employed, 28.1% have fixed-term contracts, 28.1% have training contracts, and 3.1% have research grants or scholarships.
The employed are predominantly (87.5%) in the private sector, with 71.9% working in the services sector, consistent with the career paths identified by the CdS: specifically, 12.5% in credit and insurance, 9.4% in consulting, 25% in commerce, and 12% in education and research.
75% of the employed work in Southern regions, 12.6% in the North, and the remainder in the Center.
25% of the employed who were already working before graduation report an improvement in professional skills due to the study path. Of these, 100% report an improvement in professional skills after graduation, while 46.9% state they use the acquired skills to a very high extent in their work.
Among all employed, 56.3% consider the degree very effective, and 34.4% consider it fairly effective. The data show a general trend of improvement compared to previous surveys, except for the type of employment contract, which is affected by the general economic situation. Opportunities for interaction with the business world through projects and seminars will be increased.
The statistics on the employment status of graduates in 2022 are presented and discussed in the Course Council held on September 13, 2023.
Reasons for Establishing Multiple Courses in Class I The three Master's Courses activated by the Gabriele d'Annunzio University in class LM-77 are:
- Business Economics
- Economics and Management
- Digital Marketing (recently activated, starting 2019-2020).
The reasons for establishing these Courses within the same class can be attributed to the following aspects:
a) The Courses pursue substantially different educational objectives:
- The Master's Course in Business Economics adopts the 'company perspective' systemically considering the company and is oriented towards studying the institutional aspects of business management, with particular attention to production cycle technology, industrial ecology, and eco-compatible management of production systems;
- The Master's Course in Economics and Management adopts the 'business management perspective' and is oriented towards studying business economics and administrative and financial management of public and private companies, with particular reference to human capital aspects. It is aimed at students with business economics and management skills who wish to deepen management, administrative direction, corporate finance, planning, and control topics, and develop the competencies necessary to operate in administrative and financial functions of industrial, commercial, service, and financial intermediary companies, as well as in autonomous professions and business consulting. It is distinguished by greater emphasis on the SSDs of business economics, business organization, business economics and management, and financial intermediaries economics.
- The Master's Course in Digital Marketing differs significantly from the above courses in both objectives and planned training activities. The main objective is to train professional figures with deep market knowledge (particularly marketing) and specific technical skills to operate in the new digital environment in line with the new needs expressed by companies. It also differs from the first two courses in the same class because it is not generalist but has a strong external focus on the customer and growth, not just the product or brand.
b) Ease of coordination: the first two Courses originally belonged to two different Faculties and now belong to two distinct Departments. The Digital Marketing Course was activated by the same Department as the Economics and Management Course but, as stated, with substantially different educational objectives.
c) The number of enrolled students in each of the two already activated Courses (Business Economics and Economics and Management) has consistently aligned with the reference number for the class; merging two of the Courses would exceed the maximum number allowed for Courses in the Class.
Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description The Master's Course in Economics and Management aims to provide students with advanced knowledge and skills in both main business functional areas (accounting, management control, marketing, finance, work organization, strategic management, communication, information systems, digital transition) and the main dimensions of the context in which companies operate (legal, macroeconomic, and quantitative knowledge). It seeks to provide students with an integrated and articulated vision of the above areas and related business issues. The Course is aimed at students with business economics and management skills who wish to deepen management, administrative direction, corporate finance, planning, and control topics, and develop the competencies necessary to operate in administrative and financial functions of industrial, commercial, service, and financial intermediary companies, as well as in autonomous professions and business consulting, and finally in public administration. The Course is structured into 4 distinct curricula with a focus respectively on 1) administration, control, and corporate finance, 2) management and business organization, 3) business consulting of a managerial and/or professional type, and 4) management of information systems of local, international, and public administration companies, fully taught in English. The Master's Course is developed over 6 terms (quadrimesters):
- In the first 5 terms, mandatory and optional courses (including advanced English language courses in curricula 1, 2, and 3) are taught according to the curricula students can join (in compliance with the Course Regulations) to ensure greater coherence of their training with specific employment opportunities; within these courses, differentiated teaching methodologies are used (lectures, exercises, business testimonials, business games, project work, analysis and presentation of business cases, role-playing, teaching laboratories); some courses in curricula 1, 2, and 3 are also taught in English to enhance students' professional skills and encourage enrollment of foreign students for exchange programs.
- The sixth and final term is dedicated to internship activities, laboratory sessions, seminars, business expert testimonials for developing relational skills (project management, professional interview simulations, placement channels, project work, role-playing, interpersonal skills, strategy and performance management), and any other activities useful for training and entering the workforce, as well as thesis writing. Study abroad experiences of varying duration from one month to one year (Campus abroad, Exchange Programs, Free-Mover Semester Programs, Master CEMS-MIM, Double Degree Programs) are provided and encouraged; in particular, teaching is organized to facilitate completing the entire sixth term abroad (no exams for characteristic or complementary courses are scheduled during this period). Curriculum 4, dedicated to the Double Degree agreement with the University of Neu-Ulm in Germany, requires 30 CFU at that university in the first term of the second year.
Opinions of Companies and Organizations with Internship/Traineeship Agreements For several years, the Master's Course in Economics and Management has prepared an evaluation questionnaire administered to companies and organizations where students have completed curricular or extracurricular internships. Currently, the number of active agreements for the CdS is 671 (see attached PDF). Information regarding students' training and competencies relative to the business context where they completed internships was obtained by asking company supervisors to rate various variables on a scale of 1 to 5 (with 1 insufficient and 5 excellent).
Between July 2022 and July 2023, 28 students completed internships. Respondents reported a moderate level of appreciation regarding the intern's ability to achieve internship objectives, with an average score of 2.89.
The suitability of the intern's training for business needs was rated on average at 4.3.
The level of technical knowledge acquired was 4.57, substantially in line with previous years: specifically, 57% received an excellent rating, 42% a good rating of 4, and the remainder a rating of 3.
The degree of autonomy in performing assigned tasks was 4.57 on average, with 57% of excellent ratings and 42% of good ratings.
Regarding the evaluation of behavioral and relational aspects of students, teamwork ability was rated at an average of 4.6, while problem-solving ability was 4.53, showing 57% excellent and 39% excellent ratings.
Work ethic and sense of responsibility scored an average of 4.85, with 78% excellent ratings and the remainder good.
The overall rating expressed by host companies was 4.78, with 50% excellent ratings and 45% good ratings.
Despite the excellent ratings from companies, no company expressed willingness to extend the internship or hire the intern.
The results of the opinions gathered from companies and organizations that hosted students for internships are presented and discussed in the Course Council held on September 13, 2023.
Consultation with National and International Organizations Representing Goods and Services Production and Professions (Course Establishment)
The CdS has activated a Steering Committee and a Relations with Territory Committee since 2013 to establish various and continuous relationships with companies, the professional world, and innovation hubs, aiming to stimulate dialogue with the labor market, identify professional and training needs and their evolution, and verify the attractiveness of the offered training in terms of recruitment. To ensure international consultation, multinational companies and/or those operating stably abroad also participate in the Committee. Since 2020, a representative from Cranfield School of Management, with which the CdS has a Double Degree agreement, has been included in the Committee.
Minutes of meetings prior to 2019 are available at: https://clemam.unich.it/pagina-documenti-aq-456.
Annually or biennially, during the CdS teaching programming, the Steering Committee initiates consultations with stakeholders, addressing the delicate issue of the effectiveness of the CdS teaching offer to guide the design of an appropriate study path responsive to the needs and professional requirements expressed by the labor market.
At the most recent meeting held on May 5, 2021, important national and international companies with headquarters in the territory (NSG, Aptar, Fater, Zaccagnini srl, GADA Spa, FIRA Spa, Banca del Fucino, etc.), representatives of the Chamber of Commerce and Accountants, FederManager Abruzzo-Molise, Confindustria CH-PE, LegaCoop, etc., the Presidents of the Basic and Master's Courses, a member of the Department's Teaching Committee, a member of the Department's Quality Assurance Committee, and the Coordinator of the Steering Committee and Relations with Territory Committee participated. Useful guidelines for improving the teaching offer and the three curricula were identified, already largely implemented for the 2019/20 and 2020/21 academic years, as evidenced by the attached minutes. During the meeting, the educational and professional effectiveness of the CLEMAM Master's Course was analyzed through the analysis and comment of graduate employment indices and the evaluation of their competencies in the workplace. It emerged that the percentage of LM77 DEA graduates starting work after graduation increased in 2020 compared to 2019. Additionally, the percentage of LM77 DEA graduates with stable employment increased in 2020 compared to 2019, exceeding the national value in 2018. Most graduates work in the private sector. A high level of satisfaction with the professional training received was reported, exceeding the national average.
In general, the CdS periodically evaluates student satisfaction with the CdS, both through course evaluations in line with University procedures and through a questionnaire administered to graduates during the final exam discussion, regarding the organization and quality of the CdS. Additional sources of analysis and guidance are the annual verification of graduate employability conducted in collaboration with the Department's Exit and Placement Orientation Committee, through Almalaurea statistics, and the evaluation of trainee knowledge and competencies by host companies.

The President of the Master's Course in Economics and Management, Stefano Za, presented the modifications to the Course Ordinance.
The Master's Course in Economics and Management, starting from the 2022/2023 academic year, is structured into four curricula to better meet the specialization needs expressed by students and especially by companies during periodic consultations.
In the Corporate Finance Curriculum, particular attention is paid to more quantitative aspects. The goal is to train graduates with high technical and professional skills, particularly in the areas of accounting and financial statements, economic-financial analysis, performance measurement, finance, and strategic management for value creation within companies. Some courses will be taught in English (Corporate Finance, Impact Banking and Sustainable Finance, Project Financing).
The Management Curriculum is a more qualitative path, featuring courses in marketing, entrepreneurship and venture capital, innovation management, internationalization strategies, sustainability, reporting, labor law, complexity management, organizational design, and complexity management. Some courses will also be taught in English (Entrepreneurship and Venture Capital and Innovation Management).
The Profession and Business Consulting Curriculum offers skills in the areas of management control, administrative direction, business valuation, and performance management. It is oriented towards the accounting profession and business consulting. This path also meets the requirements specified in the convention with the Chamber of Commerce for exemption from the first of the three exams required for professional qualification.
The fourth Curriculum, International Enterprise Information Management, is new and entirely in English. In a Double Degree convention with the University of Neu-Ulm in Germany, it offers skills in managing internal and external business information within a digital transformation context. The first year includes courses taught in Pescara with a more managerial focus, while the second year places greater emphasis on IT management. Some of these courses are already present in the current curricula, while others are specific, such as Enterprise Modeling and International Corporate Law and Digital Law, enabling operation in international contexts. The expected profile includes figures dealing with IT project management, consulting, and all organizational-managerial areas subject to digitalization processes.
Following the presentations, Prof. De Luca invited the Steering Committee to express an opinion on the proposed changes.
Prof. Za thanked the participants for their interest and valuable contributions. He fully shared the outcomes of the discussion. Regarding Dr. Corneli's (FederManager) question about the importance of the consultant figure, the CdS conducts intensive orientation activities at various times, including the Student Fair, Open Days, Career Day, summer "booth," Night of Researchers, and remote meetings. Regarding the importance of the consultant figure mentioned by Dr. De Grandis (Apra) and Dr. Milczarek (Tangoo Media), Prof. Za emphasized that the third and fourth curricula are dedicated to training business consultants capable of addressing the complex challenges of the labor market in a differentiated manner. Regarding auditing and soft skills, mentioned by Dr. Campana (Ecohmedia) and Dr. Ficca (KPMG), Prof. Za acknowledged their importance but noted that related topics are already included in the planned courses, though they will be further enhanced to follow the suggestions. No evening courses are planned, but the part-time path is available, spreading the courses over four years.
The Committee, after thorough examination, unanimously expressed a positive opinion. In particular, it was noted that having a fully English-language path with joint activities with a foreign university and focused on market demands subject to strong digitalization is a great opportunity.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data The data useful for these evaluations were acquired from the Statistics provided by the University Quality Assurance Office, extracted as of August 28, 2023, integrated with the Sicas system indicators updated to June 2023.
The data below will be presented and discussed in the Course Council on September 13, 2023.
ENTRY The data acquired as of August 28, 2023, from the Statistics provided by the University Quality Assurance Office, show fluctuating enrollment trends with a recent increase: 82 in 2020/21; 64 in 2021/22; 72 in 2022/23.
Total enrolled students reach 182, of which the percentage is on track. For two years, the CdS has conducted an analysis of study continuation preferences among third-year students of the L-18 Bachelor's Course in Economics and Management. The anonymous online questionnaires administered by the Orientation Committee to third-year students of the Bachelor's Course highlighted various reasons for not preferring the same Master's Course. The 114 responses collected as of August 28, 2023, indicate that 84% are considering continuing their studies, but only 38.5% intend to pursue the Master's in DEA, mainly choosing CLEMAM, while 56% wish to change universities, citing La Sapienza, University of Bologna, Bocconi, Luiss, Cattolica di Milano, Bicocca as preferences. The primary reasons for choosing other universities or departments are: seeking greater job and personal opportunities, new life experiences (44%); seeking better and more prestigious infrastructure (24%); interest in specific study paths (28%); disinterest in the DEA's teaching offer (4%). Those who choose to stay at DEA appreciate the possibility of Double Degree and the structure of the study plan. These findings are analyzed and discussed in the Course Councils, leading to the need to enhance information, orientation, and support initiatives for future study path choices by the Bachelor's students.
Sicas shows 1 transfer and 1 withdrawal for the 2022/23 enrollees, but no transfers or incoming transfers. The four curricula of the CdS receive equitable preference from students: 36% enrolled in the Management curriculum, 32% in Business Profession and Consulting, 33% in Corporate Finance. The fourth curriculum, INTERNATIONAL ENTERPRISE INFORMATION MANAGEMENT, in Double Degree with the University of Neu-Ulm in Germany, has only 2 enrollees.
Regarding origins, the Course maintains strong domestic attraction, although the percentage of enrollees from outside the region rises to 27% (24% in 2021/22). Integrating this information with Sicas data, 85% hold a degree from the same University (89% in 2021/22), and only 1 student holds a degree from a foreign university. Considering the access degree origin, 84% of the 2022/23 enrollees obtained their degree at the same University in class L18, of which 88% at the same University. 14% hold degrees in other economic-legal-business classes (L-33; L-28), 80% obtained at the same University. The percentage of enrollees with a Bachelor's degree grade of 110 or higher rises to 15% (11% in the previous year), but a high incidence remains of enrollees who obtained their Bachelor's degree with a grade of 100 or lower (57%).
PATH The statistics from the PQA allow reconstructing the trends of the 2021/22 cohort and the partial 2022/23 cohort as of June 30, 2023. These were integrated with Sicas platform data for the 2021/2022 cohort updated to August 2023.
Internal PQA data for the 2021 cohort show a slight decline in the continuation rate to the second year for full-time students, corresponding to 86% (96% in 2020). There are 3 explicit withdrawals and 6 non-renewals between the first and second year. The percentage of students continuing with more than 40 CFU at the first year decreases from 63% to 55%. The percentage of students who did not earn credits increases from 3.6% to 10% in 2021/22, and inactive students increase from 4.8% (2020/21) to 16.6% (2021/22). On average, 60.3% of the required CFU are earned. Regarding productivity, Sicas reports an average of about 7 exams per year; 48% of students achieve a grade between 28-30, and 36% in the 24-27 range.
EXIT The statistics from the PQA for graduates in the calendar year 2022 show 92 graduates, of which 65% on track, 19.5% graduated in the first year out of time, and the remainder in the second year. 26% achieved a grade between 110 and honors, while 34% achieved a grade between 109-105, with the remainder below 105.
However, there is a decline in the grade achieved compared to 2021 graduates.
These findings will be analyzed by the Course Council to identify possible causes.
Final Exam Characteristics The final exam consists of a discussion of a thesis written by the student under the guidance of a supervisor according to the rules set forth in the 'Final Exam Regulation', approved by the DEA Council, on a topic related to the disciplines characterizing the student's curriculum. The ability to select the most appropriate theoretical frameworks and analytical tools is an integral part of the final assessment.
Final Exam Procedure After passing all exams specified in the study plan, including those related to independently chosen training activities, and after earning credits for other training activities (laboratories and/or training internships) if required for the specific curriculum, the student may take the final exam according to the annual schedule set by the Department Council. The final exam consists of a discussion of a personally and originally written thesis under the guidance of a supervisor, including: 1. an accurate description of the chosen topic; 2. a bibliographic research; 3. a critical review of relevant literature; 4. an application of theoretical knowledge and/or empirical analysis techniques.
The student is admitted to take the final exam when the thesis has been approved by the supervisor, who is chosen when the student has earned at least 60 CFU. The final exam can be taken in English, previously agreed with the Course Director, with the supervisor's consent. In this case, an extended Italian summary must also be prepared. The ability to select the most appropriate theoretical frameworks and analytical tools is an integral part of the final assessment. The CLEMAM Director, in consultation with the supervisor, may authorize partial completion of the thesis work at companies, professional offices, public administrations, public and private research institutions, based on specific agreements. The graduation exam is public and conducted according to a predetermined program, with each candidate having an average of up to twenty minutes, part dedicated to presentation and part to discussion. The final exam evaluation is defined by the examining committee based on the 'Final Exam Regulation' approved by the CDS.
Finally, it is specified that for Double Degree programs, the final thesis discussion is unified. Specifically, for the convention with Cranfield University, the discussion will take place at the host site, while for the convention with the University of Neu-Ulm, it will be scheduled according to the program.

Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission To be admitted to the Master's Degree Program LM-56 in Economics and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems, specific curricular requirements and adequate personal preparation must be held.
Regarding the first, a three-year bachelor's degree, three-year university diploma or foreign degree recognized as suitable by law is required.

L-14 Law and Justice Services Sciences L-15 Tourism Sciences L-16 Administration and Organization Sciences L-18 Economics and Business Management Sciences L-33 Economic Sciences L-36 Political Sciences and International Relations L-37 Social Sciences for Cooperation, Development and Peace L-41 Statistics

For Italian students holding a degree in a class different from those listed above and for foreign students whose degrees are not explicitly related to the aforementioned degree classes, curricular requirements are assessed based on the overall evaluation of the university transcript and specific CFU obtained in economic, business, statistical-mathematical or legal fields, according to the details provided in the course's didactic regulations and in section A3.b of the SUA form.
For students meeting the curricular requirements, the Course of Study, through a dedicated committee, verifies personal preparation, following the procedures specified in the Course's Didactic Regulations.

Admission Requirements To be eligible for enrollment in the Master's Degree Course in 'Economy and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems', students must possess specific curricular requirements and adequate personal preparation, in accordance with Article 6, Paragraph 2 of Ministerial Decree No. 270/2004.
These requirements are advertised through various information channels (brochures, institutional website, orientation activities).
Curricular Requirements To access the Master's Degree Course LM-56 in Economy and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems, students must possess specific curricular requirements and adequate personal preparation.
Regarding the first, a three-year bachelor's degree, a three-year university diploma, or a foreign degree recognized as equivalent under law is required.
Specifically, curricular requirements are considered automatically satisfied:
– in the case of a three-year bachelor's degree obtained in the following degree classes:
L-14 Juridical Services Sciences L-15 Tourism Sciences L-16 Administration and Organization Sciences L-18 Economics and Business Management Sciences L-33 Economic Sciences L-36 Political Sciences and International Relations L-37 Social Sciences for Cooperation, Development and Peace L-41 Statistics
– or, in one of the degree classes under the previous Ministerial Decree 509/1999 identified as equivalent to those previously indicated by the Interministerial Decree of July 9, 2009 - Equivalences between degree classes under Ministerial Decree 509/1999 and degree classes under Ministerial Decree 270/2004, for participation in public competitions - Published in the Official Gazette on October 7, 2009, No. 233;
– or, under the previous four-year system, in one of the following degrees: Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Commerce, Business Economics, Political Economy, Jurisprudence, Political Sciences and equivalent.
For Italian students holding a degree in a class other than those listed above and for foreign students whose degrees are not explicitly related to the aforementioned degree classes, curricular requirements are assessed based on a comprehensive evaluation of the university transcript and specific CFU obtained in economic, business, mathematical-statistical, or legal fields, as detailed below:
- in economic field: at least 18 CFU in SSD SECS-P/01, SECS-P/02, SECS-P/03, SECS-P/04, SECS-P/05, SECS-P/06, SECS-P/12;
- in mathematical-statistical field: at least 9 CFU in SSD SECS-S/01, SECS-S/03, SECS-S/06;
- in business field: at least 9 CFU in SSD SECS-P/07, SECS-P/08, SECS-P/09, SECS-P/10, SECS-P/11, SECS-P/13
- in legal field: at least 6 CFU in SSD IUS/01, IUS/04, IUS/05, IUS/07, IUS/09, IUS/10, IUS/12, IUS/15, IUS/17, IUS/21.
For students meeting the curricular requirements, the Course of Study, through a dedicated committee, proceeds with the verification of personal preparation.
Verification of Personal Preparation The adequacy of personal preparation is verified through a specific and formalized process. Each enrollment application is examined by a dedicated committee of the Course of Study, which evaluates individual student records (and, if necessary, through an analysis of teaching programs) to verify that the student possesses the necessary competencies to successfully follow the study program.
If the committee determines that the student needs to address gaps in one or more disciplinary areas, a tutor professor will be assigned for each area. The tutor professor will prepare a personalized training path to address the gap and verify the recovery, communicating it to the Committee. The student may attend lectures normally but cannot take exams until the gap recovery has been verified.
Personal preparation is automatically considered possessed in the case of a graduation grade of at least 90/110, provided it was obtained within the training path that satisfies the curricular requirements described above.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The Master's graduate will be able to: a) communicate clearly information, ideas, problems and solutions to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, explaining the underlying rationale; b) present and discuss the results of analyses on specific issues; c) share tacit knowledge and promote forms of collective learning; d) fluently use English (or another European Union language besides Italian) in written and oral form, including disciplinary terminology.
These skills will be acquired through participation in seminars, discussion of cases and presentation of results in class and/or group work, presentation during knowledge assessment, study and/or internship periods abroad through the Erasmus program, training internships carried out at university or externally, writing the thesis, and participation in English language training activities. Verification will occur during the completion of individual course assessments (or suitability for TAF F training activities), the final exam, or during evaluation by tutors for study periods abroad or training internships.

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
The master's graduate will be able to: a) evaluate relevant data and methodological tools, as well as optimal interpretive models, in relation to problems of economic growth, development, market functioning, and strategic business decisions; b) identify alternative strategies and formulate policy proposals aimed at developing and governing global, local, and sectoral socioeconomic growth and development models; c) manage complexities arising from the intersection of relevant dimensions and the ecosystem nature of the reference context. He will have: - a critical interdisciplinary preparation enabling him to integrate fundamental knowledge and manage the complexity of sustainable knowledge-based economic growth and development models; - the ability to form autonomous judgments, even with incomplete information, and to collect and interpret data and information useful for decision-making. These skills may also be acquired through seminars and study groups dedicated to the analysis and interpretation of empirical data: for such training activities, collaboration with qualified experts from national and international institutions and enterprises may be arranged. The verification of these competencies will be carried out by assessing: the student's ability to interact and participate in lectures and in-class work, where applicable; the analytical and critical contribution expressed by the student during assessment in the context of examinations and the final thesis.

Incoming Orientation The incoming orientation activities for the Course are coordinated by the Incoming Orientation Representatives Prof.ssa Natascia Ridolfi, Prof.ssa Fabrizia Fontana and Prof. Gianfranco Giulioni. The Course is presented at all opportunities where it is possible to illustrate the training pathway of the economic-quantitative section of the Department, not least the Open Days and Student Fairs organized annually at the Chieti campus of the University.
The orientation activities for the Course are also carried out within the meetings and orientation activities proposed by the three-year Course in Economics, Businesses and Financial Markets, centrally coordinated by the University's Orientation, Studies and Work Division, which relies on the advice of an University Orientation Committee composed of departmental representatives.
The meetings are conducted by the aforementioned professors and include an overview of the training paths activated within the Disciplinary Areas present at the University (https://orientamento.unich.it). For this purpose, videoconferences are also organized with interested Secondary Schools equipped with appropriate facilities.
Additionally, thanks to the University's membership in the Interuniversity Consortium 'AlmaLaurea', it is possible to access, via the University's website, the online path called 'AlmaOrièntati', which serves as a useful orientation path for university choice developed by the aforementioned Interuniversity Consortium.
Among the specific activities for the Course LM-56 in Economics and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems:
- preparation of a brochure and other promotional materials containing information about the Course;
- setting up an information desk within the Pescara teaching complex (viale Pindaro 42) during July, August and September.
Following the Covid-19 emergency, online orientation activities have been organized through the activation of online help desks, one-to-one meetings and webinars.
For orientation activities, particularly those carried out within structured initiatives (Open Days, Student Fair, information booth during the summer period at the Course's campus), doctoral students and research fellows also contribute.
In the context of welcoming and accessing information about study courses for future enrollees in the three-year and master's degrees of the Department, a tutoring service has been activated, provided by Course professors, doctoral students, and research fellows affiliated with the Pescara section of the Department. This service aims to answer questions from those interested in continuing their university career with the Master's Degree in Economics and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems. Informational materials about courses, university requirements, and especially future students and new enrollees receive guidance through the Course Director or Incoming Orientation Representatives via email or Microsoft Teams. This opportunity, along with all incoming orientation initiatives, is available on the Department and Course websites.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The Master's graduate will be able to use appropriate quantitative approaches and methods:
a) to analyze economic systems, industrial sectors, and their dynamics, as well as to assess the impact on them arising from constraints and opportunities connected to rapidly transforming contexts;
b) to solve policy problems within the dynamics of sustainable economic growth and social well-being;
c) to set up the analysis of economic, managerial, and financial variables to support business decisions;
d) to develop new business projects with a strong innovative content, through plans and documents based on independent analysis.
He will have the ability to apply knowledge and understanding that will allow him:
- to analyze and manage specific economic problems;
- an autonomous professional approach to work, with the ability to identify and manage relevant systemic dimensions;
- to work in a group;
- to develop applied research on predefined socioeconomic themes.
These abilities will be acquired and verified through frontal lectures, workshops, and seminars with privileged witnesses, exercises on current and concrete cases and problems, discussions involving interaction between teachers and students aimed at applying acquired knowledge and skills. Participation in competitions outside the university will also be encouraged, with particular, but not exclusive, reference to those related to the creation of start-ups and knowledge transfer.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
The Master's graduate will have acquired a learning ability that allows him to independently deepen and develop his own knowledge and skills in relation to entering the job market or to subsequent training levels. This ability will be acquired through participation in classroom teaching, in traditional and/or interactive form, individual study, and particularly the research work carried out for the preparation of the thesis. The acquisition of learning ability is verified by evaluating the quality of individual or group assignments and the quality of the thesis.
University Communications to the CUN In light of the revisions of the "specific educational objectives" and the "table of training activities," the new course name in Management, Finance and Development is entirely consistent with the reference class LM-56 – Economics, also in analogy to the numerous other courses authorized and activated under the same class by other Italian universities, which use the noun "Finance" in their names. Indeed, from a brief comparative examination, it appears that the proposals presented here, as a whole, suggest more compelling directions for demonstrating the consistency suggested and/or required.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The Master's graduate in Economy and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems will have: a) advanced knowledge to understand and explain the evolution and functioning mechanisms of the economic system in terms of resource use (with specific reference to historical-cultural, environmental, and financial resources, as well as to ecosystems in which they are relevant); b) knowledge of regulatory and institutional contexts at international, national, and local levels, within which competitive dynamics are determined at the level of macroeconomic and regional aggregates, or at the microeconomic level of the enterprise; c) ability to identify economic policy tools (including economic regulation of markets) and business management in line with models of sustainable socioeconomic growth and development. In particular, the Master's graduate will have advanced knowledge and understanding:
- in the field of economic analysis and applied analysis, with a tendency towards original elaborations in the disciplinary fields of socioeconomic development theory;
- on the real functioning of economic systems and ecosystems, in sectors relevant to the activities of businesses and public bodies, their operating methods, and market regulation issues;
- in the field of quantitative analysis, both mathematical and statistical-econometric, of economic phenomena, with specific regard to those related to finance and digital transformation;
- of the institutional and regulatory environment in which such phenomena occur.
The knowledge and understanding just listed will first be acquired through the curricular teachings, which may be supplemented by testimonies from external speakers representing the world of institutions, businesses, and the professions relevant to the Course of Study and the specific curriculum.
In addition to through the teachings, the student may acquire knowledge and the ability to apply knowledge through:
- the experience of training internships and orientation;
- the preparation of the final exam.
The verification of the acquisition of knowledge and the ability to apply knowledge is carried out through various methods, combined differently depending on the specifics of the topics covered and the choices of the teaching staff: written tests, oral tests, active participation in class, evaluation of reports or written works, individual or group, evaluation of oral presentations of individual or group assignments.
For training internships, verification will be based on the evaluation of the university tutor and the company tutor, if carried out externally.
