Brief Description of Affine and Integrative Activities The affine and integrative activities provided in the Course of Study's educational offer are aimed at allowing students to acquire knowledge and skills functionally related to the cultural and professional profile identified by the Course of Study, with particular reference to its interdisciplinary nature and systemic (and ecosystem) interpretative approach.
In contrast to characteristic activities primarily aimed, both in the economic and business fields, at providing more general competencies and knowledge, affine and integrative activities may focus on more specific and in-depth areas, vertical or horizontal, such as:
– in-depth analysis of specific markets, both from a historical-economic and business perspective;
– in-depth analysis of economic models related to specific levels and territorial structures;
– in-depth study, from an economic perspective, of the evolution of the scientific paradigm and policy towards sustainability and circularity, and, from a business perspective, of the related implications on business models and enterprise management;
– in-depth study of legal reasoning, autonomous and critical judgment, with particular reference to the incisiveness and extent of the impact of Community law on domestic law in the fields of private and commercial law;
– training activities for the development of soft skills, especially those related to – but not necessarily limited to – business philosophy, for which the Course of Study relies on the competencies present in the affiliated Department, that of Philosophical, Pedagogical, and Economic-Quantitative Sciences.
Brief Course Description The Master's Degree Course in Economy and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems aims to provide advanced and strongly interdisciplinary economic training, promoting the acquisition of both vertical and horizontal knowledge and skills, essential for addressing contexts characterized by globalization, ecological transition, and digital transformation.
In the study path, the conceptual and applied approach of the ecosystem is prioritized, more modern, innovative, and more consistent with the most recent strategic policy and management settings.
The Course of Study offers two different curricula to choose from, depending on the knowledge and skills to be acquired, and therefore the desired professional outcome.
PATH IN FINANCE AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT (click to read professional opportunities)
Focused on developing competencies associated with managerial functions in economic and financial policy institutions, international organizations, regulatory authorities, economic and financial research offices of central banks and other entities, in the direction of local and multinational enterprises, in development agencies at various territorial levels. The graduate who completes this path will also be able to perform the role of a freelance professional, especially in the economic-financial area at the highest levels of competence.
PATH IN ECONOMY AND BUSINESS MANAGEMENT (click to read professional opportunities)
Aimed at training professional figures who can operate within contexts where the most significant challenges are launched by ecological and digital transformation. These are functions related to the most innovative modes of reaction and organization of production structures in response to stimuli connected to changes associated with ecological and digital transition, for which particular, although not exclusive, attention is given to the phenomenon of innovative start-ups and the sectors of creative industries, Made in Italy, and tourism.
External Effectiveness See attached PDF file.
Reasons for Establishing Multiple Courses in the Class The overall educational offer of the Chieti-Pescara University in class LM-56 (Economics) includes the course in Management and Socioeconomic Development and that of Economy and Commerce.
The University's choice to establish two LM-56 courses, differentiated from each other in terms of training paths and professional profiles, corresponds to the need to better satisfy the educational and professional demands coming from a reference context characterized by complex and varied needs, fully leveraging the scientific competencies and training vocations of two distinct Faculties: the Faculty of Management Sciences for the LM-56 Management and Socioeconomic Development and the Faculty of Economics for the LM-56 Economy and Commerce course.
The LM in Management and Socioeconomic Development is structured as an innovative second-level economics course (similar to an MSc/MPhil in Economics according to international standards), aiming to offer advanced theoretical and practical preparation, markedly analytical and combined with a broad and general view of micro and macroeconomic issues. Within this LM, the possibility is offered to deepen various specific fields of normative and descriptive economic research (such as, for example: knowledge economy, monetary and financial markets, growth and development models, ethics and sustainable development, policies within public policies for promoting development, welfare, labor policies, and professional competencies related to functional, departmental, and project roles within public and private institutions, oriented locally, nationally, and internationally).
Specific Educational Objectives of the Course and Description of the Study Path The Master's Degree Course in Economy and Finance of Businesses and Ecosystems aims to provide advanced and strongly interdisciplinary economic training, promoting the acquisition of both vertical and horizontal knowledge and skills, essential for addressing evolving contexts with the necessary systemic approach. The main objective is to train an expert in economic sciences who has full awareness of the functioning of economic-financial systems and is able to identify, plan, and manage strategies suitable for addressing rapidly transforming and increasingly complex contexts. In particular, specific reference is made to advanced sectoral, territorial, and global growth and development models, in which relevant dimensions (finance, sustainability, innovation) and their intersections are considered. In the study path, the conceptual and applied approach of the ecosystem is prioritized, more modern, innovative, and more consistent with the most recent strategic policy and management settings. The Master's graduate will have advanced training for the theoretical and empirical analysis of complex economic phenomena and their reflections on local entities, businesses, and other public and private subjects. The Course of Study is designed to train senior economist profiles capable of overseeing managerial professional functions both within the activities of public intervention planning by policymakers, regulatory and supervisory agencies at various territorial levels, and within the processes of birth and competitive development of businesses.
In this context, the acquisition of knowledge for the theoretical and empirical study of the functioning of real and financial markets, public intervention principles for the programming and regulation of macroeconomic and sectoral aggregates, and sustainability and circularity principles is of special importance. Additionally, quantitative discipline training allows the learning of knowledge and skills related to the use of mathematical-statistical tools useful for constructing and analyzing models and problems related to economic policy design, business management, market analysis, and more generally identifying patterns within economic data (e.g., big data).
Business area training activities aim to provide knowledge and skills on tools and techniques for detecting, organizing, and facilitating the sharing of information useful for decision-making and the analytical determination of results, in organizational contexts where attention is also directed towards environmental and social sustainability.
Legal area training activities aim to provide advanced competencies and knowledge regarding financial markets law and, more generally, the regulation of enterprise financing.
The course may be structured into curricula that will include common disciplinary sector teachings aimed at conferring graduates of the Course of Study a common set of competencies and knowledge, but which will differ in application areas, and therefore in professional opportunities, also thanks to teachings in differentiated disciplinary fields.
A first curriculum will be more focused on developing competencies associated with managerial functions in economic and financial policy institutions, international organizations, regulatory authorities, economic and financial research offices of central banks and other entities, in the direction of local and multinational enterprises, in development agencies at various territorial levels. The graduate who completes this path will also be able to perform the role of a freelance professional, especially in the economic-financial area at the highest levels of competence.
A second curriculum is instead aimed at training a professional figure who can operate effectively within contexts where attention is directed towards ecological and digital transformation. These are functions related to the most innovative modes of reaction and organization of production structures in response to stimuli connected to changes associated with ecological and digital transition, for which particular, although not exclusive, attention is given to the phenomenon of innovative start-ups and the sectors of creative industries, Made in Italy, and tourism.

Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission To be admitted to the Master's Degree in Economics and Commerce, one must hold a Bachelor's degree. Admission to the course is also subject to the acquisition of a certain number of CFU in specific SSD groups, possibly through an evaluation of the content.
In particular, all those who have acquired in the Bachelor's Degree the following credits (basic, characterizing, qualifying, or elective) may be admitted to the Master's Degree in Economics and Commerce:
a) SECS-P/01; SECS-P/02; SECS-P/03; SECS-P/06; SECS-P/12; M-GGR/02 minimum 18 CFU b) SECS-P/07, SECS-P/08; SECS-P/09; SECS-P/10; SECS-P/11; SECS-P/13 minimum 18 CFU c) MAT/02; MAT/05; MAT/06; MAT/09 SECS-S/01; SECS-S/03; SECS S/06 minimum 18 CFU d) IUS/01; IUS/04; IUS/05; IUS 07; IUS/09; IUS/10, IUS/14; IUS/12; minimum 18 CFU A tolerance of up to a maximum of 10% (i.e., 9 CFU) is permitted. This tolerance margin may be applied to one or more of the above SSD groups. Additionally, knowledge of at least one European Union language, in written and oral form, beyond Italian, is required. Verification of these requirements is carried out through a specific formalized process. In particular, each enrollment application is examined by a dedicated committee of the Course Council, which evaluates individual student records (if necessary, also through a verification of teaching programs) to confirm the existence of admission requirements. Transfers, course changes, and admission to single exams are subject to approval by the Council. The Council may grant full or partial recognition of the student's academic record to date, including validation of passed exams and acquired credits, and indicate the academic year at which the student is enrolled.

Admission Requirements To be admitted to the Master's Degree Program in Economics and Commerce, one must hold a bachelor's degree.
Admission to the program is also subject to the acquisition of a specific number of CFUs in designated SSD sets, possibly including a content evaluation.
In particular, all candidates who have acquired the following credits in their Bachelor's Degree (basic, characterizing, qualifying, or student choice) may be admitted to the Master's Degree Program in Economics and Commerce:
a) SECS-P/01; SECS-P/02; SECS-P/03; SECS-P/06; SECS-P/12; M-GGR/02 minimum 18 CFU
b) SECS-P/07, SECS-P/08; SECS-P/09; SECS-P/10; SECS-P/11; SECS-P/13 minimum 18 CFU
c) MAT/02; MAT/05; MAT/06; MAT/09 SECS-S/01; SECS-S/03; SECS-S/06 minimum 18 CFU
d) IUS/01; IUS/04; IUS/05; IUS/07; IUS/09; IUS/10, IUS/14; IUS/12; minimum 18 CFU
A tolerance of up to 10% (i.e., 9 CFU) is permitted. This tolerance may be applied to one or more of the above SSD sets.
Knowledge of at least one European Union language, in written and oral form, in addition to Italian, is also required.
The adequacy of personal preparation is verified through a specific and formalized pre-admission assessment process. Each enrollment application is reviewed by a dedicated study course committee that evaluates the individual academic records of applicants (possibly through an analysis of teaching programs) to ensure they possess the necessary competencies to successfully complete the study program.
The committee also assesses the possession of curricular requirements in cases not covered by the specifically admitted types through an individual interview aimed at verifying the required competencies.
In cases where the above requirements are not met, the applicant is advised on forms of curricular integration that ensure the overcoming of identified deficiencies.

SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/572

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The Master's graduate in Economy and Commerce is able to communicate and transfer to others, with mastery of technical language and in written and oral form, information, value judgments and proposals regarding the specific activity they are called to carry out in various institutional and business contexts.
The development of specialized knowledge, multidisciplinary activities and active student participation are factors that tend to enhance communication skills. Group work, seminars and laboratory activities can stimulate not only communication skills and discussion with students but also the ability to express acquired knowledge to operators in various sectors.
The programming and organization of teaching activities involve the use of seminars (also in foreign language), discussion of case studies and reports, and the writing of articles or "short papers" on specific aspects of the training program. The verification of the acquisition of communication skills, in summary and/or analytical form - understood as the ability to identify and describe the elements constituting an economic phenomenon and the relationships established between them - is entrusted to written and oral exams and may also require knowledge of multimedia tools. The final exam represents the definitive moment of deepening and verification of the abilities achieved in this area.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [839M] ECONOMICS AND TRADE
TYPE: Master's Degree
CURRICULUM: Autonomy of judgment
SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/572

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
The Master's graduate in Economics and Trade acquires the ability to rework knowledge and know-how in their own way through observation, study, and practice. The educational activity is structured to systematically stimulate the ability to observe, construct, and critically read interpretive and regulatory models related to the functioning of the economic system and its complexities.
The acquisition of appropriate analytical tools in the fields of business economics, law, and mathematical-statistics must raise the level of critical capacity and judgment regarding major economic events. In this context, the judgment activity can also be stimulated through meetings with external representatives from outside the academic world and through in-depth study of the issues addressed.
The student's ability to develop adequate judgment autonomy is verified during in-course assessments and final exams, through case analysis, critical discussion during company testimonies, and the identification of critical variables related to phenomena relevant to managerial activities. The verification of judgment capacity is primarily carried out through the oral examination, as well as the writing and discussion of the final thesis.

This academic year, the complaint management procedure has been activated, aiming to define a process suitable for ensuring the reception, analysis, and handling of: suggestions (intended as advice for the overall improvement of the Master's Degree Course); reports (intended as discrepancies between what is defined in the general documents of the Master's Degree Course and what is detected by the student, as a service user); complaints (intended as requests to modify a decision or act deemed unjust); originating from students, faculty, technical-administrative staff, and stakeholders of the Degree Course.
Suggestions, reports, and complaints can be submitted by sending an email to the President of the Degree Course (clecm@unich.it) with a specific indication of the type of suggestion, report, or complaint in the email subject line.
Suggestions, reports, or complaints must be relevant and not manifestly unfounded to be admitted to the management procedure. The President evaluates relevance and foundation, verifying that they are specific, justified, and within the competence of the CdS Council. Communications indicating generic, confused facts and/or outside the Council's competence will not be considered. The submitter will be notified of the evaluation of manifest unfoundedness and irrelevance, indicating in a concise, clear, and comprehensive manner the reasons for rejection. Suggestions, reports, or complaints deemed relevant will be managed by the President, who will adopt appropriate corrective or improvement actions, involving the faculty of the Degree Course and the secretariats as soon as possible. Major relevance reports will be brought to the attention of the CdS Council, which will receive a list of managed complaints periodically, at least annually. The President will also share these reports with the CdS representative in the joint faculty-student committee. The President also guarantees to the submitter a prompt response regarding the outcome of the report, via email to the address provided by the submitter.

The Department of Economics, referring to the Erasmus 2023-2024 call, at the Department Council meeting of February 23, 2023, decided – following a proposal from all Courses of Study affiliated with it – to provide a one-time incentive to increase Erasmus mobility grants for all students of the Courses of Study affiliated with DEc who were successful in the aforementioned call and actually participated with success in the project (i.e., earning at least 12 curricular CFU abroad for a period of not less than three months).
The total amount allocated for the incentive is 7,000 euros, to be equally distributed among all eligible DEc students (with a maximum of 1,000 euros per student).

Student Opinions The "Student Opinion Survey" for 2022 concerns data collected through questionnaires administered until 31.07.2023 on all courses of the CLECM for the 2021/22 academic year (See Attachment).
This questionnaire was administered to both attending and non-attending students.
The following course dimensions were considered:
• Are the topics of this course interesting according to your judgment?
• Were the preliminary knowledge you possessed sufficient for understanding the topics covered in the exam program?
• Is the required study load proportional to the assigned credits?
• Is the teaching material (indicated and available) adequate for studying the subject?
• Was the course delivered consistently with what was stated on the study course website?
• Are the scheduled times for lectures, exercises, and other teaching activities respected?
• Were the examination methods clearly defined?
• Are these activities useful for learning the subject?
• Does the professor stimulate/motivate interest in the discipline?
• Does the professor present the topics appropriately according to the complexity of the subject?
• Is the professor available during lectures and/or office hours to clarify the topics covered?
The overall average score given by students is 3.39 (on a scale from 1 to 4); this score is perfectly aligned with previous academic years (3.25 in 2017/18; 3.29 in 2018/19; 3.42 in 2019/2020; 3.49 in 2021/2022).
The values are perfectly aligned with the average of social science courses (3.49) and the university average (3.44).
Detailed analysis shows students rated logistical-organizational aspects with a score of 3.46, while teaching effectiveness was rated 3.45.
Notable aspects (with higher scores) include: respect for lecture times (3.61); availability and accessibility of teaching staff (3.61); and consistency of the course with what was stated on the study course website (3.51). The relatively lower scores concern the adequacy of preliminary knowledge for understanding classroom topics (3.13) and the proportionality of the teaching load to assigned credits (3.20).
The overall course average, considering both attending and non-attending students, exceeds the sector CUN Economic and Statistical Sciences university average (3.29).
It should be noted that the greatest differences compared to CUN scores relate to the adequacy of preliminary knowledge for understanding classroom topics and the availability of adequate teaching materials.
In December, the 2022 Parity Report for courses of the School was prepared. Analysis of the document reveals several critical issues affecting all courses. The main critical issues concern:
• Enhancement of tutoring services;
• Updating of teaching programs;
• Strengthening of connections with the world of work;
• Enhancement of language skills;
• Incentivizing internationalization activities.
For the Master's Degree course, specific critical issues were identified:
1) Mismatch between students' knowledge and the knowledge required to understand the topics covered;
2) Partial overlap between the educational offer of the Economics and Statistics track and the educational offer of the Economics and Business Analytics degree program;
3) Improvement of some parts of the course website;
4) Need to increase exit placement activities.
The Council takes note of the points reported in the Parity Report. The President emphasizes that some observations (website improvement, complaint management, etc.) are ready for immediate implementation and will be integrated in the coming months. Regarding more structurally related issues concerning aspects of the educational offer, the reorganization of teaching regulations must be awaited, a process currently being implemented in the department. This academic year, a complaint management procedure has been activated, aiming to define a process to ensure the reception, analysis, and handling of: suggestions (intended as advice for general improvement of the Master's Degree course); reports (intended as discrepancies between what is defined in the general documents of the Master's Degree course and what is reported by the student as a service user); complaints (intended as requests to modify a decision or act deemed unjust); originating from students, faculty, technical-administrative staff, and stakeholders of the course.
The PQA has also established a centralized complaint management system at the university level, accessible at https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi.

Graduate Opinions According to the results of the Almalaurea questionnaire, which had a response rate of 21.7%, in 2022, there were 46 graduates of the degree program, of whom 39.1% were male and 60.9% female.
The average age at graduation is 26.9 years.
Foreign citizens account for 6.5%.
Most graduates are from Abruzzo, and of these, 50% come from another province in the same region, while 17.4% come from another region.
Graduates hold a high school diploma (liceo) in 50% of cases, followed by 47.8% from technical institutes, while the percentages for other school types are significantly lower.
Among high schools, the most represented is the Scientific High School (34.8%).
The majority of students have no parent with a degree (80%).
46.9% chose the degree program for cultural and professional reasons.
Enrollment in the degree program occurs regularly or within one year of completing the Bachelor's degree in 71% of cases.
The average graduation grade is 108.9, while the average exam grade is 27.4.
68.1% of graduates are currently employed.
The average study duration is 3 years, meaning the graduation delay is one year. 90% of respondents followed more than 75% of the required courses.
10% received scholarships during the Master's program.
10% completed study periods abroad recognized by the program.
100% completed curricular internships or activities later recognized by the program.
40% of graduates had work experience during their studies, of whom 25% performed work consistent with their degree.
The average time spent preparing the thesis is 4.2 months.
10% of respondents intend to pursue a Master's degree.
All respondents state that acquiring professional skills is a key factor in job searching; 80% see career opportunities, stability, and security as important, while 70% consider earning potential and workplace relationships decisive.
60% of respondents are interested in working in the private sector.
The data in this section are derived from the Almalaurea Survey on Graduates' Employment Situation (2022 survey year).
One year after graduation, 55.6% of graduates are employed, followed by 22.2% who are not working but seeking employment, and 22.2% who are neither working nor seeking employment.
Among those employed, 80% began working after graduation, while the remaining 20% started before graduation.
30% of employed individuals report working in technical professions, while the remaining 70% are evenly split between intellectual professions, office-based executive roles, and other professions.
Regarding work type, 60% hold a training contract, 5% work independently, 15% have indefinite contracts, 15% have fixed-term contracts, and 5% receive scholarships or research grants.
The average weekly working hours are 37.8.
Smart working is practiced by 25%, while part-time work accounts for 10%.
85% of employed graduates work in the private sector, 10% in the public sector, and 5% in the non-profit sector.
The predominant sector is services (75%), followed by industry (20%).
80% of employed graduates work in the South, 10% in the Northwest, and 10% in the Center.
55% of respondents report using their degree-acquired skills extensively, followed by 35% who use them to a limited extent, and only 10% who do not use them at all.
55% consider the professional training acquired through the degree highly appropriate.
63.2% find the degree very effective in performing their job, followed by 26.43% who consider it somewhat ineffective, and 10.5% who find it ineffective or barely effective.
Graduate opinions will be discussed in a future Course Council meeting.

Learning Skills
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce gradually develops learning in each of the abilities and skills (learning to know, to do, to communicate, to understand reality) closely aligned with economic, business, statistical-mathematical, and legal themes as specified in the curriculum and its educational objectives. Given that the development of learning ability is strongly influenced by motivation level and the ability to recognize value and meaning in studied phenomena and topics, teaching tools extensively use the logical inductive process and related methods (case analysis, commentary on phenomena linked to real data, testimonies, reports on phenomena within students' experience and perception).

The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce will have acquired specialized training that enhances their learning ability and a higher level of analytical knowledge of the topics addressed. This means being able to select and deepen topics, prepare appropriate bibliographic references, and identify a comprehensive theoretical framework for the topics to be analyzed.

The assessment of learning ability is carried out during the teaching activities conducted by faculty members, enhanced by the widespread use of participatory teaching tools. Formal assessment of the learning level is instead entrusted to in-course and final exams. The related procedure (exams, sessions, schedule, registration for evaluation, thesis), which is regulated by the course's regulations, is consistent with the teaching approach adopted by the faculty.

Organizational Structure and Responsibilities at University Level
The Quality Assurance Office plays a central role in promoting the Quality culture and Quality Assurance (QA), ensuring compliance with the Quality Assurance Requirements set forth in Annex C of Ministerial Decree 30 January 2013, No. 47.

For QA purposes of the degree programs, it specifically organizes and verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-CdS of each degree program at the University; oversees the proper conduct of QA procedures for teaching activities in accordance with planned and declared actions; regulates and verifies periodic Review activities for degree programs; evaluates the effectiveness of improvement interventions and their actual consequences; ensures proper information flow to and from the Evaluation Committee and the Joint Faculty-Student Committees.

For QA purposes of departmental research, it specifically verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-RD of each Department; oversees the proper conduct of QA procedures for research activities in accordance with planned and declared actions; ensures proper information flow to and from the Evaluation Committee.

The Quality Assurance Office is composed of the Rector's delegate for 'Quality', a full professor who has opted for full-time work, responsible for overseeing the Office's activities, along with three full-time faculty members from the following ERC (European Research Council) fields: Physical Sciences & Engineering; Social Sciences & Humanities; Life Sciences.

Brief Course Description
The Master's Degree in Economics and Commerce aims to provide advanced training in economic-business, legal, and mathematical-statistical fields. The course seeks to equip graduates with high-level professional skills applicable in both private and public enterprises, requiring advanced knowledge to develop strategies for increasingly competitive contexts.

Within this framework, CLEC/M favors an interdisciplinary study path to provide graduates with key analytical and management tools for business functions, professional activities, and economic operations.

To this end, the Master's Degree in Economics and Commerce is structured into three curricular paths:
a) Economics and Commerce;
b) Economics and Statistics;
c) Economics and Finance.

The Economics and Commerce path emphasizes in-depth study of economic, business, legal, and quantitative disciplines within the context of enterprise management, public and private. It aims to train a 'generalist' figure in economics, making decisions closely related to organizational economic functions, with particular attention to international, national, and territorial economics. Business areas propose interpretive models of entrepreneurial strategies. Legal and quantitative areas complete the profile of an economist who approaches the surrounding reality with a multidisciplinary approach.

Upon completion, the Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce, Economics and Commerce path:
- Can interpret, describe, and measure major economic phenomena in relation to national and international dynamics;
- Possesses specific skills for analyzing and managing territory;
- Has mastery of theories and techniques for qualitative-quantitative data analysis to forecast economic phenomena;
- Uses accounting and financial reporting methodologies;
- Examines key legal institutions connected to the economic process;
- Can share information with both specialists and non-specialists.

The Economics and Statistics path aims to train graduates with adequate methodological and applied knowledge in statistics, capable of operating autonomously and competently in various economic and business management contexts. The goal is to form a professional figure with solid knowledge of economic sciences and the ability to effectively combine quantitative methods with economic reality. Additional business knowledge will form a complete analyst profile.

Upon completion, the Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce, Economics and Statistics path:
- Possesses adequate knowledge of economic, statistical, and econometric disciplines;
- Has good mastery of research methods and statistical methodology;
- Possesses practical skills related to measuring, collecting, and processing data for economic phenomenon analysis;
- Applies sampling theories and methods to conduct micro and macroeconomic investigations to study company and major economic operator behaviors;
- Possesses cognitive tools for developing and updating acquired knowledge.

The Economics and Finance path aims to train graduates with adequate methodological and applied knowledge in finance, capable of operating autonomously and competently in various economic and business management contexts. The goal is to form a professional figure with solid knowledge of quantitative economic data analysis and the ability to effectively combine mathematical-probabilistic methods with finance. Additional business knowledge will form a complete analyst profile.

Upon completion, the Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce, Economics and Finance path:
- Possesses adequate knowledge of economic, statistical, and mathematical-probabilistic disciplines;
- Has good mastery of research methods and mathematical modeling;
- Possesses practical skills related to financial data analysis, modeling, and forecasting;
- Applies mathematical-probabilistic theories to calculate financial risk and optimize investment portfolio choices;
- Possesses cognitive tools for developing and updating acquired knowledge.

For each of the three paths, teaching activities fall into the following four learning areas, identified based on scientific-disciplinary homogeneity criteria:
- Business Area;
- Economic Area;
- Legal Area;
- Mathematical-Statistical Area.

Within each learning area, each curricular path includes a certain number of courses common to other paths, while all others are specific and characteristic of the path itself.

External Effectiveness
The data in this section are derived from the Almalaurea Annual Sheet - Satisfaction with the Completed Degree Program and Graduates' Employment Status.

Analysis of the sheet shows that approximately 90% are overall satisfied with the Master's degree program.
Approximately 90% of students express a positive judgment on the teaching workload.
The organization of exams is considered always satisfactory by 50%, while 30% find it satisfactory for more than half of the exams.
100% of respondents are satisfied with their relationships with faculty members (“definitely yes” for 60% and “more yes than no” for 40%).
70% of respondents describe the classrooms used as “often adequate,” while 10% consider them “often adequate.”
80% of respondents used computer workstations and found them insufficient in 37.5% of cases.
80% of students used library services and expressed a positive evaluation in 75% of cases.
Respondents stated that they would re-enroll in the same degree program in 50% of cases.
Employment rate is 55.6% one year after graduation and reaches 90.6% three years after graduation.
Use of degree-acquired skills for Master's graduates in Economics and Commerce is 55.6% one year after graduation, decreasing to 44.8% three years later, and stabilizing at 55% five years later.
Average salary is €1,237 in the first year and reaches approximately €1,500 in the third year.
Job satisfaction, rated on a scale from 1 to 10, is 7.4 in the first year and reaches 8.1 in the third year.

Reasons for Multiple Courses in the Class
The Master's degree in Economics and Commerce, together with the Master's degree in Management and Socioeconomic Development offered by the Faculty of Management Sciences, covers class LM-56 (Economics Sciences). Although both courses belong to the same class, they respond to the need to train professional figures with different scientific competencies.

The Master's degree in Economics and Commerce consolidates the positive relationship established in previous academic years with numerous companies and business organizations, offering students the opportunity to acquire, in addition to scientific competencies characteristic of public administration and private enterprise management, specific skills required for professions such as accounting and financial specialists, business consultants with broad and interconnected economic, legal, and business knowledge, and other highly qualified, complex, and interdisciplinary professional profiles such as customs officers or international trade consultants.

Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description
For each of the two paths, teaching activities fall into the following four learning areas, identified based on scientific-disciplinary homogeneity criteria:
• Business Area;
• Economic Area;
• Legal Area;
• Mathematical-Statistical Area.

Within each learning area, each curricular path includes a certain number of courses common to other paths, while all others are specific and characteristic of the path itself.

The Master's Degree in Economics and Commerce is generally aimed at training a graduate with the following knowledge, skills, and abilities:

a) Expected Learning Outcomes (by learning area):

Business Area
Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce must possess, upon completion of the program, appropriate knowledge to address economic issues from a business perspective and must have acquired the methodologies, knowledge, and skills necessary to hold responsible roles (directly or through consulting activities) in the administration and management of public bodies and institutions as well as enterprises.

The business area courses in the two curricular paths aim to integrate a foundational knowledge base to make it more solid and evolved. The teaching methodology is primarily represented by frontal teaching (lectures and exercises), considering the temporal progression of the program and the nature of the courses. The effectiveness of business area courses is formally assessed through intermediate checks during the teaching activity (in-course assessment) and at the end of the lecture and exercise cycle (post-course assessment).

Applying Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce must be able to apply the conceptual and analytical tools of business disciplines and understand how to adapt them to various types of enterprises and the reference economic context. High-level competence and the ability to apply acquired knowledge to real situations are gradually achieved through critical analysis, contextualization of knowledge, and the use of professional business language.

Teaching is therefore aimed at acquiring operational conceptual and analytical tools of business disciplines, guiding their study and analysis with the support of appropriate technological tools. The appropriate and widespread use of simulations, data banks, business and professional testimonies, report discussions, case analysis, and dedicated software, both during teaching activities and in in-course and final exams, are verification methods for the student's receptivity and achieved ability in 'knowing how to do'.

Knowledge and skills are acquired and verified in the following teaching activities:
- Business Strategies and Policies
- Accounting II
- Customs Merchandising

Economic Area
Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce must possess a deep understanding of microeconomic and macroeconomic issues; understands the functioning of economic systems to cover, with a specific and quantitative approach, responsible roles (directly or through consulting activities) in the administration and management of public bodies and institutions as well as enterprises.

The economic area courses in the program aim to create a high level of economic knowledge. The teaching methodology is primarily represented by frontal lectures and exercises. The effectiveness of economic area courses is formally assessed through intermediate checks during the teaching activity (in-course assessment) and at the end of the lecture and exercise cycle (post-course assessment).

Applying Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce must be able to apply the conceptual, empirical, and analytical tools of economic disciplines and understand how to adapt them to interpret and evaluate the contexts in which public bodies, institutions, and enterprises operate. High-level competence and the ability to apply acquired knowledge to real situations are gradually achieved through critical analysis, contextualization of knowledge even at the territorial level, and the use of the language specific to economic disciplines.

Teaching is therefore aimed at acquiring operational conceptual and analytical tools of economic disciplines. Discussion of reports and case studies, both during teaching activities and in in-course and final exams, are some of the possible verification methods for the student's receptivity and achieved ability in 'knowing how to do'.

Knowledge and skills are acquired and verified in the following teaching activities:
- Advanced Microeconomics
- Innovation Economics
- Territorial Planning
- Tourism Geography
- Individual and Collective Choice Theory
- Agricultural Economics

Legal Area
Knowledge and Understanding
The content of disciplines in this area aims to form in the graduate a general knowledge of the legal-normative sector, potentially useful for building a managerial profile.

The teaching methodology is primarily represented by frontal lectures. The effectiveness of legal area courses is formally assessed through intermediate checks during the teaching activity (in-course assessment) and at the end of the lecture cycle (post-course assessment).

Applying Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce must know the foundations of legal disciplines and understand how to use them to address economic phenomena from a legal and tax perspective. High-level competence and the ability to apply acquired knowledge to real situations are gradually achieved through critical analysis, contextualization of knowledge, and the use of legal language.

Teaching is therefore aimed at acquiring operational conceptual and analytical tools of legal disciplines. In-course and final exams are structured to verify the student's receptivity and achieved ability in 'knowing how to do'.

Knowledge and skills are acquired and verified in the following teaching activities:
- Labor Law
- International Tax Law
- Contract Law
- Bankruptcy Law

Mathematical-Statistical Area
Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce must possess the necessary knowledge of mathematical-statistical tools and methodologies to hold responsible roles (directly or through consulting activities) in the administration and management of public bodies and institutions as well as enterprises.

The sole mathematical-statistical course in the two curricular paths aims to create a deep understanding of quantitative methods for economic information analysis. The teaching methodology is primarily represented by frontal teaching (lectures and exercises). The effectiveness of courses in this area is formally assessed through intermediate checks during the teaching activity (in-course assessment) and at the end of the lecture and exercise cycle (post-course assessment).

Applying Knowledge and Understanding
The Master's graduate in Economics and Commerce must be able to apply the methods and techniques acquired in mathematical-statistical fields and understand how to use and adapt them to a specific economic context. High-level competence and the ability to apply acquired knowledge to real situations are gradually achieved through critical analysis, contextualization of knowledge, and the use of mathematical-statistical language.

Teaching is therefore aimed at providing operational tools, also supported by technological tools. For example, the use of statistical software, both during teaching activities and in in-course and final exams, represents a verification method for the student's receptivity and achieved ability in 'knowing how to do'.

Knowledge and skills are acquired and verified in the following teaching activities:
- Statistical Models
- Survey Techniques
- Statistical Data Analysis
- Statistical Methods for Economic Analysis
- Economic Statistics
- Computer Science
- Geometry
- Complements of Mathematical Analysis
- Operations Research

Opinions from Organizations and Companies with Internship/Traineeship Agreements
Since 2013, CLECM (via the Internship Service of the School of Economic, Business, Legal, and Social Sciences), has administered a questionnaire to companies, organizations, and professional offices where students complete curricular internships (mandatory).

At the end of the internship period, the company tutor, usually holding a responsible role within the host organization, responds to the questionnaire. This consultation allows respondents to evaluate the overall internship experience through specific questions, verifying the correspondence between the knowledge and skills provided by the Course and the needs/expectations of companies. Specifically, respondents are asked to evaluate the adequacy of academic preparation to business needs; provide a synthetic judgment on acquired skills and observed issues during the internship; evaluate the internship service and suggest improvements and issues regarding the service itself.

This questionnaire is particularly important as it helps understand the actual occupational needs and expectations of potentially interested companies.

Specifically, the following dimensions are investigated:
• ACHIEVEMENT OF FORMATIVE OBJECTIVES SET AT THE START OF THE INTERNSHIP
• INTERNSHIP STUDENT'S MOTIVATION AND COMMITMENT
• ADEQUACY OF ACADEMIC PREPARATION TO BUSINESS NEEDS
• ANALYSIS/SYNTHESIS ABILITY AND CRITICAL THINKING
• PROBLEM-SOLVING ABILITY
• TEAMWORK ABILITY
• COLLABORATION PROPENSITY
• AUTONOMY IN PERFORMING ASSIGNED TASKS
• PUNCTUALITY AND RELIABILITY
• RESPONSIBILITY TAKING ABILITY
• WHETHER A EXTENSION OF THE INITIAL PERIOD WAS PROPOSED
• WHETHER A JOB OFFER WAS MADE
• OVERALL EVALUATION OF THE INTERNSHIP EXPERIENCE
• SKILLS ACQUIRED BY THE INTERNSHIP STUDENT DURING THE INTERNSHIP
• SATISFACTION LEVEL WITH THE ACTIVATION AND MANAGEMENT OF INTERNSHIPS BY THE SCHOOL
• WILLINGNESS TO NEW INTERNSHIPS WITH THE ECONOMICS SCHOOL.

Overall, regarding formative and professional aspects (motivation and commitment, achievement of formative objectives, adequacy of academic preparation to business needs) and relational and management aspects (ability to work in a team, collaboration, and autonomy), the average evaluation of interns is very positive.

The highest average score relates to motivation and commitment (4.84), while the lowest average score (4.65), autonomy in performing assigned tasks, still remains at an extremely appreciable level.

The intern's collaboration propensity is evaluated positively (4.82), while the adequacy of academic preparation to business needs is slightly lower (4.65).

Finally, regarding satisfaction with the activation and management of internships, a very positive judgment is expressed (4.70), and 80% of companies express willingness to new collaborations with the University.

From March 2019 to date, over 100 students have completed internships at 92 organizations, companies, and/or professional offices.

The data collected in the questionnaires will be discussed in a future Course Council meeting.

Consultation with Representative Organizations - National and International Level - of Goods and Services Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
Regarding specific activities of the Course, one of its objectives is to periodically organize, in agreement with the President of the Bachelor's Degree in Economics and Commerce, meetings with representatives of business organizations and associations/professional orders to effectively align graduates' learning outcomes and acquired knowledge with the active labor market on the territory.

It should be noted that, to achieve greater coordination between the educational offerings of CLEC (Bachelor's) and CLEC/M (Master's), the 2016-2017 Educational Regulations for both Courses were revised. This revision, in addition to considering more advanced disciplinary knowledge, led to the creation of a new Economics and Finance path in CLEC/M, offering students from the corresponding Bachelor's path the opportunity to continue their studies in line with their initial training.

Following this revision of the Educational Regulations, on October 27, 2016, a consultation meeting with the labor market and professions was held at the Department of Economics, organized by the Presidents of CLEC and CLEC/M.

- Confindustria Chieti-Pescara;
- Pescara Chamber of Commerce;
- National Association of Financial Consultants (ANASF).

To facilitate periodic consultation with represented professions, the Presidents of the Economics and Commerce Bachelor's and Master's Courses subsequently established an Advisory Committee, a working group formed by recognized stakeholder organizations, Presidents, some members of the Quality Assurance Groups of the Courses, and student representatives.

The Advisory Committee met annually.

From the issues raised by participants, the following interventions from social partners emerged:

Dr. De Ninis, teacher of Law and Economics at ITC Acerbo of Pescara, reiterated the opportunity to strengthen synergy between the Courses and Acerbo through joint orientation activities, targeting students from the third year of the five-year high school program, and emphasized the importance of maintaining high standards in university study programs, with particular attention to STEM disciplines.

Dr. D'Onofrio, Vice-President of the Chieti Chamber of Commerce, confirmed the Chamber's willingness to host students and graduates for internships and to provide the Courses with the experience of its members.

Other issues emerging from the discussion with social partners include:
- The need to improve communication and promotion of the Courses
- Introduction of courses or seminars to educate students in soft skills and problem-solving
- Greater synergy between CLEC and social partners in orientation activities at schools.

It is noted that during the March 16, 2023 meeting, Prof. Valentini and Prof. Nissi informed social partners that a reflection within the Department of Economics has begun on the possibility of revising the entire departmental educational offer (see Department of Economics Council Minutes No. 11/2023 of September 19, 2023). Additionally, in early 2024, the University's bodies expressed the need to rationalize the entire economic area educational offer of the University of Chieti-Pescara (meeting of January 26, 2024, of the Presidents of economic area Courses and Department Directors with the Rector's delegate for teaching, Prof. Angela Di Baldassarre). Pending clarification of the scope of this rationalization process and its extent of impact on current Courses in classes L33 and LM56, the Presidents of CLEC and CLEC/M have postponed the convocation of the next annual meeting of the Advisory Committee (which in recent years was held in the first months of each calendar year) and are considering expanding the scope of social partners to identify the most representative interlocutors for an effective revision of the current educational offer.

Entry, Progression, and Exit Data
The number of new enrollments over the last four academic years has followed a fluctuating trend, decreasing from 60 units in the 2018/19 academic year to 52 in 2019/2020, reaching 32 in 2020/2021, stabilizing at 25 in 2021/2022, and dropping to 22 in the last academic year.

Regarding gender composition of enrollments, parity is observed, contrary to previous years that showed a predominance of female students.

Regarding age group composition, as in previous years, over 80% of new enrollments are between 20 and 24 years old. Abruzzo students account for approximately 70% of the total over the three-year reference period.

Only two students come from other Italian universities, while the remaining new enrollments are Bachelor's graduates from the same university.

Regarding geographical origin, 54.55% of new enrollments come from another municipality in the province, 27.27% from other regions, 13.64% from the same municipality, while only 4.55% come from other provinces in the region.

The average number of CFUs earned is 31.21, the average grade is 25.98, and the average number of exams is 6.

Analyzing the number of credits earned in detail, 40% earned between 21 and 40 credits; 32% earned more than 40 credits, while 24% earned between 6 and 20 credits.

100% of students enrolled in the 2021/22 academic year re-enrolled for the second year.

For this cohort, 32.00% of enrollments continued to the second year with more than 40 CFUs, while only 4% of enrollments had 0 CFUs.

Enrollment trends closely mirror those of new enrollments.

For the 2022/2023 academic year, the number of enrollments is 70 compared to 167 in 2017/2018.

The percentage of graduates still enrolled is 62.50%, dropping to 31.25% one year after graduation, and stabilizing at a much lower percentage (6.25%) two years or more after graduation.

Regarding graduation grades, 87.5% graduate with a grade above 100, of whom 56% achieve 110 with honors.

The decline in new enrollments is one of the Course's weaknesses.

To reverse this negative trend, several improvement actions have been implemented, including:
- Intensification of entrance orientation activities;
- Greater promotion of course activities through social media and the web.

These topics were discussed in the Course Council meetings on December 14, 2022, and February 22, 2023.

Final Exam Characteristics
The final exam consists of a written thesis in Italian or a foreign language on a topic related to a discipline in which the student has taken a final exam. The topic is assigned by a faculty member who serves as the thesis advisor.

Once approved by the advisor, the thesis is evaluated by a committee of seven faculty members. The committee includes the advisor and six other faculty members, preferably from the same scientific-disciplinary group as the advisor or related fields, or as determined by the Department Director or the Course President, who appoints a co-advisor.

The graduate publicly defends their thesis before the entire committee, which then formulates a judgment on the thesis and the candidate's presentation, assigning a score not exceeding six points. A comprehensive judgment is also formulated by the committee based on the candidate's academic career, awarding an additional merit score not exceeding four points for enrolled students and two points for non-enrolled students. The final grade is calculated by summing the points assigned to the thesis and the academic record, plus the average (on a scale of 110, weighted by CFUs for each course) of the grades achieved in passed final exams, rounded up to the nearest integer. The committee may award the honor (lode) unanimously if the final grade is equal to or above 110.

Participation in the Erasmus program will be considered significant in qualifying the study path and will result in the student receiving 2 points toward the academic record's point total.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate will be able to interpret economic phenomena and data, and communicate with mastery of technical language the information and knowledge produced, both to specialist and non-specialist interlocutors. They will also be able to effectively present, using computer tools, the methodologies employed and the results obtained.
These skills will be acquired, in addition to attending lectures and individual study, through the realization and presentation of individual or group projects and during the internship. The programming and organization of teaching activities also include seminars (also in foreign language) and discussion of case studies and reports. Students are also encouraged to take part in overseas stays through the Erasmus program.
The verification of communication skills will occur through written or oral examination, as well as during the evaluation of the final project.

TYPE: Master's Degree
CURRICULUM: Autonomy of Judgment
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1583

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgments)
The master's graduate achieves a high level of autonomy of judgment in the economic-business field, thanks to the ability to analyze and interpret data and information, and to the interdisciplinary knowledge and skills acquired. They are able to assess the information needs of organizations, evaluate existing solutions, and propose innovative solutions with the aid of modern statistical and information technologies. Furthermore, the master's graduate is able to assess the economic and legal implications of their work, and is aware of the issues associated with data processing and its impact on society and the individual.
Autonomy of Judgment is developed through the analysis of concrete cases, meetings with external representatives from outside the academic world, and internship activities.
The verification of Autonomy of Judgment occurs through final written or oral exams, as well as the preparation and discussion of the final thesis.

Student Opinions This document analyzes the University's data from the Academic Year 2022-2023 Student Opinion Survey.
The University's data on the Student Opinion Survey for the Academic Year 2022-2023 comes from questionnaires administered across all courses of the Economics and Business Analytics (CLEBA) Master's Degree program.
It is specified that:
- Students are required to accept completing the questionnaire, but it is optional to answer one or more questions. Therefore, it may occur that a questionnaire is filled without answers: in practice, the only mandatory response is whether classes were attended or not, which determines the type of questionnaire completed;
- Results were obtained by averaging responses, with a score ranging from 1 to 4 (1 strongly disagree, 2 more disagree than agree, 3 more agree than disagree, 4 strongly agree);
In the attachment, it is possible to see that the average score recorded across all questionnaires administered to students in the Academic Year 2022-2023 for CLEBA is 3.54.
The questions receiving very positive evaluations (with a score above the average response) are as follows:
- D13, The course was taught consistently with what was declared on the study program's website (3.68 versus 3.53 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D14, The schedule for lectures, exercises, and other teaching activities is respected (3.67 versus 3.62 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D16, Exam methods were clearly defined (3.64 versus 3.49 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D21, The instructor presents topics appropriately according to the complexity of the subject (3.58 versus 3.49 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D22, The instructor is available during lectures and/or office hours to clarify topics covered (3.73 versus 3.63 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
Student responses with a score equal to or below the average concerned, in particular:
- D0, The topics of this course are interesting to you (3.52 versus 3.48 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D1, Prior knowledge was sufficient for understanding the exam program (3.33 versus 3.29 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D3, The study load required by the course is proportional to the assigned credits (3.31 versus 3.22 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D9, Teaching materials (provided and available) are adequate for studying the subject (3.40 versus 3.32 of the Academic Year 2021-2022);
- D20, The instructor stimulates/motivates interest in the discipline (3.51 versus 3.45 of the Academic Year 2021-2022).

Graduate Opinions The Master's Degree course in Economics and Business Analytics is at the end of its fifth year of establishment.
The first graduates were awarded in October 2020, and AlmaLaurea source data on this topic is not yet available.
Applying Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
At the end of the training path, the Master's graduate in Economics and Business Analytics will have acquired economic, computer, statistical, and legal skills to analyze and interpret economic and business dynamics at the microeconomic and macroeconomic levels, with the aim of optimizing the quality of decision-making and operational processes of organizations, particularly those active in digital markets. The graduate will be able to apply statistical techniques, information technologies, and application programs for the acquisition, management, analysis, and visualization of datasets, even of large size. The graduate will also have acquired the ability to critically interpret competitive dynamics, including international ones, in sectors related to economics and business analytics.
The didactic tools for achieving application skills are both seminar activities and the development of individual or group projects within the curricular courses, as well as the internship and thesis preparation. The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is assessed through written/oral exams, seminars, and the final exam.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
Graduates develop interdisciplinary skills and learning abilities that allow them to continue studying and adapt to rapid changes in the sectors of the economy connected with new technologies and data usage, which are still rapidly evolving. They are able to learn new methodologies and choose the most suitable technological tools for problem resolution. Learning skills are developed in lectures, interaction with professors, analysis of cases with real data, and during the internship. Learning skills are verified in exam tests and thesis preparation, which must present innovative content.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The Master's graduate in Economics and Business Analytics must possess, at the conclusion of the training path, knowledge of the functioning and underlying mechanisms of the knowledge and information economy, electronic and telecommunication markets, and digital marketing, as well as statistical-economic methods and information technologies for business analysis. Additionally, the graduate must be able to fully understand economic, strategic, and business dynamics in digital economy markets to contribute to increasing the quality of decision-making processes of organizations.
Knowledge and understanding of the topics covered are achieved through both core and related activities, as well as through the internship and thesis preparation, and are verified through written and oral exams and the final presentation.
Organization and Responsibilities of the Quality Assurance (AQ) at the Course Level CLEBA carries out the activities of the quality assurance process by relying on the following bodies:
1) Course Director (CdS) The Course Director coordinates the CdS quality assurance system and oversees compliance with the requirements set by specific regulations, with the collaboration of the Parity Committee of Teachers-Students (CPDS) and the Quality Assurance Group (GAQ) of the CdS, in line with the guidelines provided by the University's central bodies on quality assurance. The Course Director annually completes the SUA CdS with the support of the CdS Quality Assurance Manager (GAQ Manager), and leads the annual and cyclical review of the CdS, resulting in the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA) and the Cyclical Review Report (RRC).
2) School Parity Committee It is composed of a representative of the teaching staff for each CdS (Prof. Francesco ACCETTELLA for CLEBA), coordinated by the School of Economic, Business, Legal, and Sociological Sciences, designated by the School Board among the course professors, and a student representative for each CdS coordinated by the School.
The School Parity Committee carries out monitoring activities of the educational offer, teaching quality, and services provided to students by teachers and structures.
3) CdS Quality Assurance Group (GAQ) The CdS Quality Assurance Group (GAQ) is currently composed of:
Prof. Alessandro MARRA, Responsible; Prof. Luigi IPPOLITI, Member; Prof. Fabio FIORAVANTI, Member; Dr. Silvano PAGLIUCA, Member - President of Confindustria Chieti-Pescara and Fastweb Manager;
Ms. Erika MALANDRA, Member (technical-administrative)
and a student representative.
This group is tasked with supervising the implementation of the quality assurance system and related processes within the CdS. It collaborates in the preparation of the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA) and the Cyclical Review Report (RRC), analyzing the current situation of the CdS, highlighting strengths and improvement opportunities, and proposing corresponding objectives, indicators, and target goals. The GAQ Manager supports the Course Director in all quality assurance system activities, including the preparation of the CdS SUA.
During the Cyclical Review Report, the Course Director, as the review manager, joins the GAQ members to form the 'Review Group'.
4) CdS Council It is composed of professors responsible for the courses and representatives of enrolled students, elected according to the procedures set by the University's General Regulations.
The Council annually deliberates on the content of the SUA and the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA); periodically deliberates on the content of the Cyclical Review Report (RRC); and collaborates in the smooth operation of the CdS quality assurance.
5) Department Quality Assurance Reference Teacher (ReAQD)
Prof. Luigi IPPOLITI (ReAQD) serves as the coordinator of the Department's quality assurance policy and the periodic review of departmental research.
Prof. Laura BERARDI (ReAQD_D) serves as the reference teacher for teaching quality assurance at DEC. Prof. BERARDI ensures the connection between PQA and peripheral structures (Department, CdS, CPDS), as well as providing support and consultancy to the Department Director.
Work Planning and Implementation Deadlines for Initiatives
The works for improving the CdS quality assurance system include periodic meetings of the GAQ and the Course Council.
Periodic GAQ meetings may address:
- analysis of training demand, possible proposal to the CdS Council for redefining educational objectives, redesigning and/or modifying the educational offer;
- harmonization of course programs and updating of course sheets;

- quinquennial RRC preparation;
- proposal of improvement initiatives/actions and subsequent monitoring of results.
The Course Director, with the support of the GAQ, plans the works for the annual compilation of the SUA and SMA of the CdS based on the deadlines set by the PQA.
Brief Course Description The Economics and Business Analytics Course aims to contribute to meeting the increased demand for professional figures characterized by skills and abilities in analyzing and managing dynamics related to the digitalization and internationalization process of economic activity.
The training activities aim to develop the ability to use statistical-economic techniques, information technologies, and advanced application programs for the acquisition, management, analysis, and visualization of datasets, even of large size. They also aim to provide the necessary economic, business, statistical, computer, and legal skills to analyze and interpret economic and business dynamics at the microeconomic and macroeconomic levels, with the aim of optimizing the quality of decision-making and operational processes of organizations, particularly those involved in digitalization.
Such knowledge is useful for interpreting roles of direct or indirect responsibility (consulting), as well as for entrepreneurial paths through innovative start-ups.
Further information on the CdS can be found on the website: http://cleba.unich.it
External Effectiveness The Master's Degree course in Economics and Business Analytics is at the end of its fifth year of establishment, and the first graduates were awarded in the autumn session of October 2020.
In this context, some statistics provided by the Course Presidency are presented.
Reasons for the Establishment of Multiple Courses in the Class The active courses (CdS) in the LM-56 degree class at the Chieti-Pescara University are:
- Economics and Business Analytics;
- Management, Finance and Development;
- Economics and Commerce.
The Master's course in Management, Finance and Development aims to provide advanced training in the economic and financial field, with specific reference to current models of sectoral, territorial, and global growth and development, as well as their sustainability, with particular attention to the role of finance and money markets.
The Master's course in Economics and Commerce, structured into multiple pathways, is aimed at training a generalist figure in the economic field, making choices closely related to the functions of economic organizations, with particular attention to the fields of international, national, and territorial economics, classic statistical methodologies, and adequate methodological and applied knowledge in the field of finance.
The Master's course in Economics and Business Analytics differs significantly from the other two courses in terms of objectives and training activities, proposing training activities related to the knowledge and information economy, electronic and telecommunication markets, digital marketing, statistical methods, and information technologies for data science. The Master's graduate in Economics and Business Analytics integrates solid economic knowledge with the ability to analyze and interpret economic and business data, even in large quantities, with skills not only economic but also statistical, computer, and legal.
Specific Educational Objectives of the Course and Description of the Training Path
The educational objectives of the Master's degree course in Economics and Business Analytics are characterized by a multidisciplinary educational offer capable of addressing innovation challenges, even in light of the Industry 4.0 paradigm, using economic-business, technical-scientific (statistical-mathematical and computer), and legal skills.
The educational offer, leveraging all multidisciplinary skills provided by the Department of Economics and, more generally, by the School of Economic, Business, Legal, and Sociological Sciences, responds to significant scientific and technological challenges related to the need to process large amounts of data and produce fundamental information for the knowledge and decision-making process within the innovative sectors of digital economy and business.
In particular, the Master's training path in Economics and Business Analytics provides the appropriate scientific and professional knowledge to: i) understand the economic, strategic, business, and legal dynamics of organizations operating in the economy markets to contribute to increasing the efficiency of analysis and decision-making processes of organizations active in the private and public sectors; ii) use statistical techniques, information technologies, and application programs for the acquisition, management, analysis, and visualization of datasets, even of large size.
The Master's graduate in Economics and Business Analytics will also have an appropriate level of preparation for placement in both basic and applied research contexts, both at universities and research centers, and in business research and development sectors, at national and international levels.
The training activities of the CdS fall under the following learning areas:
- economic area;
- business area;
- statistical-mathematical area;
- computer area;
- legal area.
The economic area training activities are included in SSD SECS-P/01 (Political Economy) and SECS-P/06 (Applied Economics).
They provide the conceptual and applied foundations for studying the Information and Communication Technology economy and analyzing the sectors and markets of the digital economy, aimed at fully understanding the competitive and innovative dynamics peculiar to these areas. Such knowledge is useful for interpreting roles of direct or indirect responsibility (consulting), as well as for entrepreneurial paths through innovative start-ups.
The business area training activities are included in SSD SECS-P/07 (Business Economics) and SECS-P/08 (Economics and Management of Enterprises).
They are aimed at providing knowledge and skills on the application and use of information, big data, and data analytics in company governance and management processes, such as: strategic analysis, strategic planning, business decision information systems, performance measurement, and management of marketing activities on digital channels.
The statistical-mathematical area training activities are included in SSD SECS-S/01 (Statistics), SECS-S/03 (Economic Statistics), and MAT/06 (Probability and Mathematical Statistics).
They provide the methodological and applied foundations for the acquisition and statistical-mathematical analysis of economic and business data (e.g., data analytics, data mining, machine learning, visual analytics, text analytics, time series analysis, spatial series analysis), with particular reference to big data studies.
The computer area training activities are included in SSD INF/01 (Computer Science).
They concern the acquisition and organization of databases, the foundations of big data (non-relational databases, map/reduce paradigm, and data analysis software), and the principles of information security applied to networks and data.
The legal area training activities are included in SSD IUS/05 (Economic Law) and IUS/01 (Private Law).
They provide the foundations for studying the discipline of information processes governing transactions on financial markets, innovative enterprise financing techniques, and knowledge for understanding legal issues posed by the collection, interconnection, and use of large amounts of data, with particular regard to privacy, data legal nature and ownership, service supply contracts, and telecommunication civil liability.
Within the courses, great attention will be given to applications through exercises and/or presentations of concrete case studies.
The training path is oriented to maintain a close connection with the labor market. The studies are therefore completed with a mandatory internship and the final exam.
The internship and final exam offer students the opportunity to deepen the topics addressed in the courses within the working world.
The strategic choice inherent in the outlined training path is to strongly involve students in applying techniques and technologies to real cases.
The aim is to foster a university-work transition path that is actually implemented during the training path itself.
The organization of the training path allows achieving the following specific educational objectives:
1. provide the necessary skills to analyze and interpret economic phenomena related to ICT sectors and markets;
2. provide tools for understanding the peculiar competitive dynamics of the digital economy and conducting sector and market analysis;
3. provide methods and techniques usable in interdisciplinary groups where experts in economics, business analytics, and data science work alongside experts in specific application domains;
4. provide advanced knowledge on the use of information technologies for storing, managing, and transforming data derived from the digital process;
5. provide advanced knowledge on the use of statistical techniques and information technologies to improve the quality of decision-making and operational processes based on digital data related to organizations active in the private and public sectors;
6. provide advanced knowledge on the use of statistical techniques and information technologies to clearly communicate results and the most appropriate strategic lines resulting from data analysis, even through appropriate result visualizations;
7. create professionals capable of operating and competing in the national and international context.
