Orientation in Entry is coordinated by an orientation coordinator appointed by the Chair of the Course. The specific orientation activities planned by the Course for Eco Inclusive Design differ in:
- online, through a dedicated section on the Course's website (http://www.architettura.unich.it). Based on various online orientation methods (synchronous and asynchronous webinars, individual meetings, video presentations, interviews), candidates are assisted in understanding the conceptual, methodological and professional approach characterizing the eco inclusive designer profile, and can receive information on organizational aspects of the Course, as well as be guided in self-assessing initial knowledge through case studies and multimedia materials.
- in person, through organizing activities related to Open Days and dedicated desks for consultation and information on themes and approaches of eco inclusive design.
- participating in the University's orientation activities, reported on the specific web portal page (https://orientamento.unich.it/uda-orienta).
Additionally, for third-year students of the Course in L-4, as well as for students in the final years of University's L-21 and L-23 Degrees, specific meetings with professors of LM-12 are organized to illustrate the Eco Inclusive Design Course.
Data on orientation activities organized directly by the Course is collected in a report prepared by the Chair of the Degree Programme, in collaboration with the Course's orientation and tutoring referents.
Tutoring in Progress The Department of Architecture provides students of all Courses under its jurisdiction with services for academic management, support in formulating study plans, and tutoring for exam access and resolution of administrative issues regarding academic records.
The Eco Inclusive Design Course has also identified a tutor professor (Prof. Rossana Gaddi), who performs several functions: support for the study path (both regarding the selection of elective courses and the Final Synthesis Laboratory), monitoring of academic progress; orientation towards integration programs for emerging gaps; promotion of each student's integration into study groups and the student community; verification of the effectiveness of the training path; facilitation of the teaching relationship between students and teaching staff.
Additional specific tutoring activities planned by the Course include:
- preparation of detailed course sheets describing objectives, teaching content, and assessment methods. During the first semester of each year, collective meetings are also organized to illustrate how teaching activities are structured;
- organization of seminars dedicated to the informed choice of the Final Synthesis Laboratory in System Design for Sustainability or System Design for Social Inclusion, and related internship opportunities at accredited and contracted entities, professional studios, and companies in the territory.
Course professors will also use the Microsoft Teams platform to provide students with teaching materials (presentations, recordings, videos, formats, etc.).
Finally, in relation to inclusion-related topics, the Course pays particular attention to the needs of students with disabilities and DSA. For them, reference is made to the services provided by the University and reported in the 'Service Charter for Support of Students with Disabilities, DSA, and Temporary Specific Needs', downloadable at: https://www.unich.it/sites/default/files/carta_dei_servizi_disabilita_dsa_e_bisogni_specifici_temp.pdf
Curricular Training Periods In the second year of the Master's Degree in Eco Inclusive Design, and subject to the organization of their teaching activities, students complete a mandatory curricular internship at companies, professional studios, research centers, public and private entities and organizations, as a formative experience for integration and comparison with the production world. Host sites are 'contracted' with the Department of Architecture according to the procedures defined by current legislation on internships and traineeships, which require a formal agreement between the Department and the host structures and an adequate training project for each intern.
Students may complete the curricular internship in Italy or abroad (Europe/Extra Europe).
The Department has a technical-administrative staff with specific expertise (and adequate language preparation for international internships) to support students and host sites.
For evaluating the progress, experience, and outcomes of internships, the Course uses appropriate questionnaires to be completed by host site Tutors and intern students, and a dedicated database for collecting, interpreting, and processing the data.

Student Opinions General Considerations The Course of Study in Eco Inclusive Design (LM12) was activated in the academic year 2021-2022. For this reason, the first data regarding the second-year courses are available.
Student opinions are systematically collected through the use of questionnaires administered to evaluate the level of satisfaction regarding individual courses, analyzing the results in an aggregated form. In particular, the activation of the evaluation procedure, to be carried out before the examination sessions, allows for precise indications on the teaching methods, useful also for horizontal and vertical coordination of training activities and teaching loads.
In total, results from 94 evaluations involving 10 courses out of 15 total courses were collected.
Analytical Summary of Evaluations The evaluation results for the academic year 2022/2023 are critically analyzed in an aggregated form (Appendix 1) and will be made public during the Eco Inclusive Design Degree Course Council meeting in September 2023.
The first data emerging from the aggregated data of the Eco Inclusive Design Degree Course shows a strong positioning of student satisfaction in the high range: the macro-indicators indicate that the overall satisfaction rating is 3.44/4.00 and the teaching effectiveness is 3.62/4.00, values higher than both the average of the university's scientific area (respectively 3.32 and 3.47) and the overall university average (respectively 3.35 and 3.47). The data regarding logistical-organizational aspects is essentially aligned with those of the scientific area and the university.
Looking at the detailed responses, all obtained values fall within the highest range (above 3 out of a maximum of 4 points).
The question with the lowest average score (although still a very positive value, equal to 3.18 out of 4) refers to the suitability of prior knowledge for understanding the topics covered in the exam program (Question D1).
The question with the highest score (equal to 3.79 out of 4) emphasizes the availability of the teaching staff to provide clarifications on the topics covered during lectures and office hours (Question D22). This value has improved compared to the same value from the previous year, which was 3.70.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The Master's Degree Course in Eco Inclusive Design enables students to acquire specific disciplinary skills related to 'doing'. In summary, in the various learning areas, the graduate has the ability to:
- Design, develop, and manage complex projects, applying design thinking, applying knowledge acquired in the field of sustainability-oriented Design process and inclusive quality of industrial products, using methods, strategies, and guidelines of Life Cycle Design (LCD) and Design for Inclusion, biodegradable, recyclable materials, and new low-impact materials, tools for functional, structural, and environmental product improvement and evaluation (Sustainable and Inclusive Product Design area).
- Apply knowledge acquired in sustainability-oriented Design processes and inclusive quality of services, following the Design Thinking approach and the Double-Diamond Service Design process, contextualize models of urban and territorial interaction, exchange, and use related to smart networks and ICT development, introduce new languages and techniques of animated audiovisual (Sustainable and Inclusive Service Design area).
- Apply knowledge acquired in Eco-Social Communication Design processes, ideate, design, and develop innovative artifacts, analog, digital, multimedia, or transmedia for inclusive and sustainable services, introduce new languages of animated audiovisual (Eco-Social Communication Design area).
- Apply knowledge acquired in sustainability and inclusion-oriented System-Product Design processes, use new efficient and sustainable business models under economic, social, and environmental aspects (triple bottom line), visualize data, information, and scenarios through Digital and Interaction Design tools for public utility graphics, understand intercultural and demo-anthropological dynamics related to social groups (System Design for Sustainability and Inclusion area).
Students' ability to apply knowledge is achieved through project laboratories, through the ideation, elaboration, and development of innovative solutions for products, services, communication, and systems, and the finalization of knowledge acquired in the various teaching modules. Additional specific disciplinary skills will be acquired by each student or by work groups in specialized thematic workshops.
The overall assessment of the ability to apply acquired knowledge occurs through the preparation and writing of the Master's thesis, which consists of an original research project elaborated under the guidance of a supervisor and presented to the Degree Committee for discussion.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
The Master's graduate is able to: acquire new knowledge autonomously in the fields of sustainable and inclusive product and service design, as well as in the sector of digital techniques for graphical representation and product-service communication; use the learning tools acquired during the study to deepen and independently initiate research and experimentation activities; consult and understand the technical and scientific literature of the rapidly evolving sector, as well as independently select the most suitable methodological and technological tools for solving new problems; consult online databases and organize and process personalized and updatable digital archives; independently pursue higher-level study paths such as a PhD or second-level Master's degrees.
The study course aims to develop students' learning abilities aimed at continuously updating their skills and knowledge in response to technological, methodological, and instrumental advancements in design applied to various sectors of material and immaterial goods production. The acquisition of learning abilities is verified through examination evaluation, via oral or written tests, critical discussion of projects and results achieved.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The core of the Master's Degree Course in Eco Inclusive Design is constituted by specific disciplinary knowledge acquired in the four learning areas and possessed by the graduate to critically understand:
- Cultural, socio-economic, and technological aspects related to environmental and inclusive industrial product themes, the approach, methods, strategies, and guidelines of Life Cycle Design, Life Cycle Assessment, Design for Inclusion, methods for analyzing user tasks, product certifications, digital manufacturing technologies, tools for product quality, safety, and reliability control (Sustainable and Inclusive Product Design area).
- New service needs for businesses and processes for valorizing territorial resources based on sustainability and social inclusion criteria, methods and tools for developing sustainable and inclusive service solutions, blueprint methods, digital tools for designing, representing, and communicating service processes, performances, interfaces, and service performance, innovative models of digital networks for intelligent urban and territorial services (Sustainable and Inclusive Service Design area).
- New communication needs for cultural enterprises, public and private territorial bodies, companies, and non-profit organizations related to environmental and inclusive communication, advanced visual communication tools, User Experience (UXD) logic, research methodologies, and tools for interpreting and evaluating territorial values and resources, communication toolkits (Eco-Social Communication Design area).
- The development and innovation process of the system-product, understood as the integrated and coherent set of product, service, and communication, criteria and guidelines of System Design, the Method for Product-Service System methodology, toolkits for system design, principles of User Experience design for web interfaces, data visualization, virtual prototyping, VR/AR, methods and tools of Integrated Reporting and interface design (System Design for Sustainability and Inclusion area).
Knowledge is acquired by students through frontal lessons, thematic seminars, project exercises, individual and collective reviews. Group work is alternated with individual study. Activities are carried out in close synergy between discipline-specific occasions managed autonomously by teaching modules and moments of sharing and critical discussion at the project laboratory level.
Verification of knowledge and critical understanding is carried out through written and/or oral tests on theoretical and methodological aspects covered by individual teaching modules, and through laboratory exams based on graphical and multimedia project outputs that contextualize and finalize knowledge acquired in the various teaching modules.

Brief Description of Affine and Integrative Activities Affine activities, inserted as integrated teaching modules in the first-year laboratories, aim to complete their theoretical dimension. In particular:
- The affine activity named "Smart cities", inserted as an integrated teaching module of Laboratory 3 "Service Design", is aimed at describing theories and issues useful for designing digital services for cities and intelligent territories: from shared mobility to more efficient management of urban equipment and infrastructure, passing through digital interaction between citizens and public administration. The teaching module thus provides strategic approaches to the digital transformation of cities and territories through digital and information technologies for the benefit of residents, relating urban material infrastructure to human, social, and intellectual capital.
- The affine activity "Cultural heritage", inserted as an integrated teaching module of Laboratory 4 "Communication Design", is aimed at studying material (from objects to built environment) and immaterial cultural heritage for protection and conservation. The module therefore presents an overview of the main recent theoretical tools and orientations, with appropriate extensions to the European and international context, with the aim of identifying a method for analyzing, cataloging, and valorizing local identities, in line with the innovative approach of the Communication Design Laboratory.
Programming of Work and Implementation Deadlines The overall update of the Degree Course is entrusted to the Orientation and Study Plan Commission, which operates primarily based on indications received from the Steering Committee. The Commission relates with the Degree Course Chair and the Parity Commission and periodically reports to the Degree Course Council and Department Council. These bodies are tasked with implementing strategies deemed appropriate to address any critical elements that may arise.
Degree Course themes may converge into the research programs of the PhD in 'Project Cultures: Creativity, Heritage, Environment' with a curriculum in Design and Architecture Technology (focused also on product and process innovation for industrial production and industrial product eco-design). They may also converge into the National Interest PhD in 'Design for Made in Italy' with a curriculum in Design for Inclusion.
Brief Description of the Course The Master's Degree Course in Eco Inclusive Design responds to the requests of new generations seeking to access new experimental paths and innovative professional profiles capable of addressing emerging sectors of Eco-Design and Design for Inclusion.
Within the framework of the European Green Deal strategies for sustainable development and inclusive growth, the Master's Degree Course aims to train a professional with a cultural profile sensitive to the aesthetic, socio-ethical, and economic values of a sustainable, more inclusive, and fair society, and simultaneously a professional profile capable of managing advanced design methods and tools to address, coordinate, and manage applied research and experimentation activities in the fields of product, service, communication artifacts, and systems for environmental sustainability and human diversity valorization.
Consistent with the general objective, the training model is interdisciplinary and structured in project laboratories and workshops, aiming to synergistically integrate tools, methods, and conceptual frameworks of the Life Cycle Design approach, Design for All, Design Thinking, and at a higher complexity level, System Design for Sustainability and System Design for Inclusion. The training path is structured over four Project Laboratories, one optional Final Synthesis Laboratory, three professional workshops, two elective courses, and a final internship at institutions, companies, and professional studios.
Specifically, the study path in Eco Inclusive Design promotes cultural, scientific, and professional profiles consistently united by the conceptual, methodological, and practical synergy between design disciplines of different product, service, and communication fields, and disciplines of human, social, economic, technological, drawing, and digital design. Based on these synergies and intersections, the Course aims to valorize the professional figure of Eco Inclusive Designer in four declinations: Eco-Design and Inclusive Design for product innovation - Design for sustainable and inclusive service innovation - Design for eco-social visual artifact innovation - System Design for sustainability and inclusion.
Graduates in Eco Inclusive Design have a wide range of professional opportunities to enter the workforce as freelancers or within associated studios, design companies, companies, private or university research centers, territorial bodies, institutions, and public or private sector organizations.
The Course allows access to third-cycle studies (PhD and Master's programs).
External Effectiveness The Master's Degree Course was activated in the academic year 2021-2022. Therefore, no statistical data on graduate employment are currently available.
Specific Educational Objectives and Description of the Training Path SPECIFIC EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES The Master's Degree Course in Eco Inclusive Design aims to train experts in the innovation processes of products, services, communication artifacts, and systems oriented towards environmental sustainability and social inclusion. The Degree Course aims to train a designer with a cultural profile sensitive to the aesthetic, socio-ethical, and economic values of a sustainable, more inclusive, and fair society, and a professional profile capable of managing advanced design methods and tools to address and coordinate applied research and experimentation activities in the emerging fields of Eco-Design, Inclusive Design, and Design for All.
The final educational objective is to support graduates in acquiring in-depth skills and knowledge to develop a deeper understanding of environmental and social changes in our era, as well as the ability to identify strategic opportunities at European, national, and regional levels connected to the Green Economy and social inclusion, with a focus on sustainability, inclusivity, and aesthetics to support company competitiveness and improve people's lives in an attractive, innovative, and human-centered way.
Through a distinctly project-based and interdisciplinary path, structured in project laboratories and professional workshops, students have the opportunity to synergistically integrate tools, methodologies, and conceptual frameworks typical of the Life Cycle Design (LCD) approach, Design for Inclusion, Design Thinking, and at a higher complexity level, System Design for Sustainability or System Design for Inclusion.
Specifically, the study path in Eco Inclusive Design promotes cultural, scientific, and professional profiles consistently united by the conceptual, methodological, and practical synergy between design disciplines of different product, service, and communication conceptual and application fields, and disciplines of human, social, economic, technological, drawing, and digital design. Based on these synergies and intersections, the Degree Course aims to valorize the professional figure of Eco Inclusive Designer in four declinations: Eco-Design and Inclusive Design for product innovation - Design for sustainable and inclusive service innovation - Design for eco-social visual artifact innovation - System Design for sustainability and inclusion.
TRAINING PATH The Eco Inclusive Design Degree Course is structured over four Project Laboratories, one optional Final Synthesis Laboratory, three professional workshops, and two elective courses.
In the first year, the training path is structured over four different project laboratories (Eco Product Design, Inclusive Design, Service Design, Communication Design), enabling students to reflect (theories and methods related to 'knowing') and simultaneously invent (experimental design practice related to 'doing') innovative solutions applied to the product, service, and communication dimensions, according to sustainability and social inclusion criteria. Each of the four project laboratories is organized with two integrated modules. The first module is a characteristic Design teaching (ICAR/13) to facilitate advanced project application and experimentation. The second module courses belong to economic (SECS-P/07), technical-design (ICAR/13), urban (ICAR/21), and cultural heritage (ICAR/19) disciplines, tasked with enriching multidisciplinary knowledge and providing critical and operational tools to support project activities. Theoretical training concludes in the first year with the selection of the first elective course to allow students to build and orient their training path in line with their interests and aptitudes.
In the second year, the degree path, to form the exploratory and experimental character of the Master's graduate, offers the possibility of choosing one of two final synthesis laboratories centered on the system-product dimension (product, service, communication), focusing on the complex and interdisciplinary dimension of System Design for Sustainability or, alternatively, System Design for Inclusion. To nourish the ability to understand socio-cultural, economic, and technological contexts, and to form skills in systemic thinking, team work, problem finding, problem setting, and problem solving, the two laboratories integrate modules of project disciplines (ICAR/13), economic (SECS-P/07), digital drawing (ICAR/17), and anthropological sciences (M-DEA/01), and are oriented towards the in-depth study of environmental or inclusive themes, respectively. They also form the basis for the cultural and specialist orientation for the final elaboration of the Master's research project.
At the conclusion of the training path, the Degree Course structure, organized according to the predominant laboratory model, is complemented by three transversal and monodisciplinary courses delivered as workshops to deepen the most current and updated methods and tools of the profession related to testing and digital manufacturing (ICAR/09), eco-certifications (ICAR/12), and motion design (ICAR/13), serving to reinforce profiles in the various project laboratories. Theoretical training concludes in the second year with the selection of the second elective course.
The final semester includes, in addition to the Master's thesis, seminars conducted with companies and professionals to facilitate professional choices and knowledge of working sectors, and a final internship at institutions, companies, and professional studios.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Placement Agreements The Master's Degree Course was activated in the academic year 2021-2022. Therefore, no opinions regarding internship experiences at entities or companies are currently available.

3. Proposal to activate new study courses
- The Master's Degree Course in Eco Inclusive Design aims to train experts in the innovation processes of products, services, communication artifacts, and systems for environmental sustainability and social inclusion. The Degree Course aims to train a professional with a cultural profile sensitive to the aesthetic, socio-ethical, and economic values of a sustainable, more inclusive, and fair society, and simultaneously a professional profile capable of managing advanced design methods and tools to address and coordinate applied research and experimentation activities in the fields of Eco-Design and Inclusive Design.
- Consistent with the general objective, the main characteristic of the Degree Course is the markedly project-based and interdisciplinary path that enables Master's graduates to acquire skills and knowledge to:
- Identify strategic opportunities at European, national, and regional levels connected to the Green Economy and social inclusion.
- Explore the various possibilities related to products, services, and communication artifacts in relation to the sustainable and inclusive evolution of different social, cultural, and economic contexts.
- Support company competitiveness and improve people's lives in an attractive, innovative, and human-centered way.
- Analyze behaviors, needs, and desires of people to go beyond existing users and traditional product categories characterized by high environmental impact and low inclusive quality.
- Study applications related to materials and technologies defining the environmental and inclusive qualities of products.
- Develop innovative solutions for sustainable products and equitable-solidarity services with high social and territorial value.
The training model is interdisciplinary and structured in project laboratories and workshops to synergistically integrate tools, methodologies, and conceptual frameworks typical of the Life Cycle Design (LCD) approach, Design for Inclusion, Design Thinking, and at a higher complexity level, System Design for Sustainability and System Design for Inclusion.
Graduates in Eco Inclusive Design have a wide range of professional opportunities to enter the workforce as Eco-Designers, Inclusive Designers, Service and Communication Designers within companies, associated studios, design companies, private or university research centers, territorial bodies, institutions, and public or private sector organizations.
The Degree Course allows access to third-cycle studies (PhD and Master's programs).
In Italy, among Master's Degree Courses in Design, class LM-12, with training profiles in some way related to the themes and expert profiles defined by the Eco Inclusive Design Degree Course, the following Degree Courses have been identified:
- Eco-Social Design (Free University of Bolzano).
- Planet Life Design, to be activated soon (University of Perugia).
- Design for Innovation – Product Eco-Design Curriculum (University of Campania 'Luigi Vanvitelli' in Aversa).
The specific objectives, training paths, teaching plans, and course programs of the above Degree Courses have been collected and examined. Comparing the Eco Inclusive Design Degree Course with the identified competitor Degree Courses, it can be deduced that they present innovative features, but only partially consistent with the cultural and professional profiles related to Eco-Design and Inclusive Design in the system-product, service, and communication dimension as described by the Eco Inclusive Design Degree Course. Specifically, the Eco-Social Design Degree Course addresses only the environmental aspect with a specialization in product design and interaction design, excluding the service and system dimension. The Planet Life Design Degree Course addresses only the environmental aspect in one of its four areas, Climate and Energy, with exclusive specialization in product design. The Design for Innovation Degree Course addresses only the environmental aspect in the Product Eco-Design curriculum.
In the national landscape, given these unique educational offerings that are only partially similar and substantially different in specialization, thematic scope, and methodological and instrumental approach, the absence of second-level study paths in the fields of Eco-Design and Inclusive Design appears to be a gap that needs to be filled.

the activation of the following Degree Courses is approved unanimously:

CONSULTATIONS The consultation of the above-identified stakeholders was conducted through two distinct online meetings on the Microsoft Teams platform, both on October 30, 2020: the first consultation, from 11:00 AM to 1:20 PM, involved organizations representing service production, as well as associations and territorial bodies (see Appendix: consultation minutes PS1_30ott2020); the second consultation, from 3:00 PM to 5:00 PM, involved organizations representing production and professions (see Appendix: consultation minutes PS2_30ott2020).
METHOD AND TIMING OF STUDIES AND CONSULTATIONS Consultations were conducted through online meetings on the Teams platform on October 30, 2020.
From the first consultation, several considerations and requests emerged, including:
- Appreciation of the combination of sustainability and inclusion themes, capable of intercepting international political, economic, and cultural issues congruent with contemporary emerging problems;
- Hope for direct collaboration between the Degree Course and entities and associations to strengthen university-territory relations, also through applied didactic experimentation addressing specific requests from local administrations;
- Appreciation of the professional profiles the project aims to train, with sensitivity to environmental sustainability and social inclusion themes, which can assume a new role as designers for the valorization of cultural identities and territorial excellences, with holistic and inclusive design approaches.
From the second consultation, several considerations and requests emerged, including:
- Appreciation of the choice of reference theme, combination of sustainability and inclusion, also in relation to recent national surveys reaffirming its central and strategic value for company competitiveness;
- Emphasis on the international relevance of the themes addressed, and the importance of connecting attention to the needs expressed by local productive fabrics to international approaches and experiences;
- Highlighting the need for specialized professionals on inclusion and sustainability themes, emphasizing that Inclusive Design brings ethical and competitive benefits for companies across the entire product-service-communication mix;
- Appreciation of the didactic plan structured in laboratories, positively evaluating the inclusion of certain strategic courses to foster systemic innovation, such as behavioral economics, sustainable materials, and service design;
- Hope for the Degree Course to open up to themes related to territorial contexts and local productive fabrics, also through didactic experimentation conducted in close relation with companies and innovation parks.

Meetings were recorded on Teams, and the responsible interlocutor drafted a summary document preserved in the Department's archive. A minutes document was prepared for each of the two meetings.

Characteristics of the Final Exam
- The final exam for the Master's Degree constitutes the completion and verification of knowledge acquired by the student during the Course. The graduate must demonstrate cultural maturity, critical ability, and independent in-depth understanding in the project areas and in the various supporting disciplines.
- The final exam consists of writing and publicly discussing an original written-graphic Master's thesis on a topic consistent with the course objectives, under the guidance of a Supervisor.
- The thesis is individual. Coordinated theses may be allowed. However, the Committee must always be able to identify each candidate's contribution.
- The sole Supervisor must be a teacher or a contract teacher of the Degree Course. It may be supported by one or more Co-Supervisors.
- The thesis may also be developed in interaction with external companies and entities.
Final Exam Procedure To be admitted to the Master's exam, the graduate must have earned all the required credits, excluding those related to the final exam.
The thesis discussion is public and takes place before the Master's Degree Committee.
Master's Degree Committees are appointed by the Department Director and consist of seven to eleven members selected from regular and contract teachers of the Degree Course.
The Master's Degree Committee's judgment is based on the student's academic record and the thesis discussion outcome.
The Master's Degree grade is expressed out of 110.
The Committee has a maximum of 10 points to assign according to the following criteria:
- Up to 3 points for theses with low scientific-cultural content;
- Up to 5 points for theses with moderate scientific-cultural content;
- Up to 8 points for theses with high scientific-cultural content.
- Additional 2 points for theses deemed exceptional by the Committee's unanimous decision.
If the final grade is 110, the Committee may award the Honors (Lode) unanimously.
Summary of the Technical Report of the Evaluation Unit - SUA Form The motivations leading to the declaration of the Degree Course's characteristics, in its cultural and professional aspects, are thoroughly discussed and convincing. The proposed Master's Degree Course completes the first two training cycles within the design field, constituting the next cycle after the L-4 Degree Course active at the University for four years, whose high attractiveness expresses a strong training demand in the sector and potentially similar Degree Courses at neighboring universities. The cultural and professional profiles of the figure the Degree Course aims to train are clearly defined.
Consultations involved a wide range of stakeholders and provided useful information for the design.
The proposed training path is innovative and strongly focused on laboratory activities.
Four professional profiles are identified, each with adequately defined functions and competencies.
Regarding the disciplinary competencies of the Evaluation Unit members, the path appears sufficiently consistent with the trained professional profiles.
The course provides a programmed number with a comparative evaluation process of individual candidates' skills and knowledge.
The structural resources and teaching staff appear adequate. The Degree Course monitoring is consistent with the University's AQ system.

Access requirements Required knowledge for admission The required knowledge for admission to the Master's Degree in Digital Marketing concerns the following three areas:
1. Minimum academic requirements
2. Adequate personal preparation
3. Adequate knowledge of English
1. Minimum academic requirements.
For admission to the degree course, it is necessary to have obtained a first-level degree or an equivalent foreign degree.
Admission to the Master's Degree in Digital Marketing is open to:
- Holders of a first-level degree in one of the following classes (ex DM 270/04 or equivalent under the old system or an equivalent degree obtained at a foreign university):
L-08 - Degrees in Information Engineering L-09 - Degrees in Industrial Engineering L-11 - Degrees in Foreign Languages and Literatures L-12 - Degrees in Linguistic Mediation L-15 - Degrees in Tourism Sciences L-16 - Degrees in Administration and Organization Sciences L-18 - Degrees in Economics and Business Management Sciences L-20 - Degrees in Communication Sciences L-33 - Degrees in Economic Sciences L-41 - Degrees in Statistics
- Holders of a second-level degree in one of the following classes: Class 64S and Class 84S ex DM 509/99, LM-56 and LM-77 ex DM 270/04 or an equivalent degree obtained at a foreign university;
- Holders of a four-year degree under the old system (pre-DM 509/99) in Economics, obtained at an Italian university or an equivalent degree obtained at a foreign university;
- Holders of a degree different from those listed above, provided they hold at least 48 CFU distributed as follows:
Business area: 24 CFU (SECS-P/07, SECS-P/08, SECS-P/09, SECS-P/10, SECS-P/11)
Economic area: 12 CFU (SECS-P/01, SECS-P/02, SECS-P/03, SECS-P/05, SECS-P/06)
Quantitative-computer area: 12 CFU (from SECS-S/01 to SECS-S/06, from MAT/01 to MAT/09, INF/01 and ING-INF/05)
2. Adequate personal preparation.
Personal preparation is considered adequate if based on knowledge of the fundamental topics included in the following learning areas: economic, business, statistical-mathematical and legal. The adequacy of personal preparation will be verified according to the procedures specified in the study program's didactic regulations.
3. Adequate knowledge of English.
English language knowledge, both written and oral, at least B2 level is required for admission. The adequacy of English language knowledge will be verified according to the procedures specified in the study program's didactic regulations.

Admission Procedures Application requests for enrollment in the Digital Marketing Master's Program must be submitted electronically and will be reviewed by the Pre-evaluation Committee appointed by the Department of Business Economics, which assesses individual student academic records (and may conduct an analysis of teaching programs if necessary) to verify the possession of curricular requirements, adequate personal preparation, and adequate knowledge of English. It is specified that the assessment of adequate personal preparation is mandatory in all cases and can only be accessed by students who meet the curricular requirements; in particular, the possession of curricular requirements cannot be considered as fulfillment of the personal preparation assessment. These are distinct evaluations.
Students enrolled in degrees other than those listed in Table A3.a (minimum curricular requirements) or students who have completed their three-year program and wish to enroll in the Digital Marketing Master's Program but do not possess all 48 CFU previously indicated (24 CFU for the Business Area, 12 CFU for the Economic Area, and 12 CFU for the Quantitative Area) before submitting an enrollment application for the Digital Marketing Master's Program may fill academic debts by enrolling at their home university or at D'Annunzio University to take individual exams, in accordance with the respective academic regulations. It is not possible to enroll with academic debts.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The master's graduate will be able to communicate problems, ideas and solutions related to the context in which they operate clearly, correctly and comprehensively, will be able to express themselves effectively to a non-specialized audience of users and clients, and will be able to dialogue appropriately with experts. In particular, the master's graduate in Digital Marketing will acquire the ability to communicate marketing strategies and plans to different stakeholders, as well as to interact with actors belonging to different business functions.
This outcome will be achieved and verified through case discussions and the presentation of results in class and/or in group work, the presentation during knowledge assessment, and through potential study periods abroad. The writing of the thesis also offers an additional opportunity for deepening and verifying the communication skills developed.

This outcome can be achieved and verified through:
- classroom discussions, in work groups with teachers and students;
- participation in seminars on entrepreneurial values and managerial behavior;

To assess the "sentiment" of cohorts enrolled in the corresponding undergraduate course, the Midway Orientation Commission has prepared an orientation questionnaire "toward the Master's" reserved for third-year students. The questionnaire consists of 17 questions and aims to gather the following cohort characteristics: propensity to continue the university path, areas of interest, decision level, and reasons for interest regarding selected disciplines, expectations regarding the Master's course subjects, propensity to continue at DEA, potential propensity to continue at another department/university, and reasons for the choice. The questionnaire, created on the Microsoft Forms platform, allows quick access for participants via QR code scanning and enables immediate response collection. It aims, through the analysis of responses, to provide useful indications for the continuous improvement of the educational offer.

Training Periods Section B5 – Internship and Placement The Course of Study provides for the completion of a curricular internship (worth 6 CFU) to be carried out at companies, professional offices, banks and insurance companies, public bodies and sector associations, based on specific agreements made with the host organization. By December 2023, the Course of Study can count on over 1000 active agreements distributed throughout the national territory and some international ones.
Examples include the following companies and organizations: Banca di Credito Cooperativo; GLM SPA; Policlinico di Monza; Bluserena Spa, ASL di Teramo; ICCREA; Ecoh Media srl; Maglificio Gran Sasso Spa, Gruppo Aran; Agenzia delle Entrate; Unipol Sai; BDO spa; Pomilio Blum; Del Verde Industrie alimentari; De Cecco Spa; Fater Spa; Honda Italia spa; Confindustria Abruzzo; Confcooperative; Allianz Assicurazioni; Seneca Spa; FIRA spa; Walter Tosto Spa; Denso Manufactoring spa; FCA Italy spa, Toto Holding Spa; Valagro. International internships and non-curricular internships are also provided, which are not linked to the acquisition of CFU (e.g., required by companies for the completion of a thesis or to carry out specific work experiences of interest to the student), with the aim of completing the Course of Study's training process in alternating study/work.
Students of DIMA who completed internship activities from January 2023 to December 2023 were 25.
The Course of Study provides assistance to students in defining the project work to be developed during the internship through an academic tutor and in collaboration with the company tutor, in the search for host sites and in the signing of agreements. The Course of Study's website details the procedures, active agreements, documents, and deadlines for submitting documentation, and proceeds to collect and analyze the evaluation forms completed by the academic tutor, the student, and the company tutor, in order to assess the effectiveness of the internship. The administrative procedure coordinator is Ms. Maela Venanzi (mvenanzi@unich.it).
The opinions collected from the evaluation questionnaires are analyzed by the Orientation Committee and the AQ Committee, to understand the effectiveness of the training path and the internship itself. The questionnaire administered to 22 interns of the Course of Study shows, for internships completed by December 2023, a high level of satisfaction with the experience, with a summary score of 4.77 (scale 1-5). Particularly appreciated were the alignment between the training project's objectives and the tasks performed, the availability of the company tutor, and the opportunity to acquire new professional knowledge, consistent with one's training path, and the adequacy of one's skills in performing the assigned tasks. No dissatisfaction is noted, but among the suggestions, it is highlighted that the list of agreements needs to be revised by removing companies that are no longer available to host students. These results were discussed in the AQ Committee and the Course of Study Council.

Student Opinions STUDENT OPINIONS The data available as of July 31, 2023, relates to 12 courses from the CDs based on 342 completed questionnaires. The courses evaluated must have received at least 6 valid questionnaires as of the update date. Student opinion surveys are provided by the University Quality Assurance Office and, starting this year, all University CDs' evaluations from the academic year 2015-2016 to date are publicly visible at the linked address. Regarding the Dima CD, the average rating for courses in 2022-2023 is 3.50, which is higher than the 3.29 recorded in the academic year 2021-2022. Out of 12 evaluated courses, 7 achieved a satisfaction level in the 3.5-4 range, which is Band A (the highest), compared to 3 courses the previous year. Courses in Band B (ranging from 3 to 3.49) number 5, compared to 9 in the previous year. This indicates a significant improvement in the overall appreciation of the teaching activities provided. Specifically, the availability and accessibility of professors has improved (3.68 CD average vs. 3.57 university average) compared to the previous year (3.5 CD average vs. 3.59 university average). The evaluation regarding adherence to scheduled teaching times has also improved (3.63 CD average vs. 3.5 university average) compared to the previous year (3.44 CD average vs. 3.55 university average). The score for alignment between web communications about course content and actual classroom delivery has also improved (3.55 CD average vs. 3.5 university average) compared to the previous year (3.38 CD average vs. 3.5 university average). The level of interest generated by course content has also improved (3.49 CD average vs. 3.43 university average) compared to the previous year (3.31 CD average vs. 3.43 university average). The same applies to the professor's ability to adequately explain content (3.49 CD average vs. 3.44 university average) compared to the previous year (3.25 CD average vs. 3.46 university average). Compared to 2021/22, there has been improvement in ratings for the professor's ability to stimulate interest (3.47 vs. 3.28), the proportionality of the teaching load required by disciplines (3.38 vs. 3.12), the adequacy of teaching materials used (3.45 vs. 3.22), and clarity regarding exam procedures (3.47 vs. 3.34). The data shows an ongoing process of continuous improvement. Among student suggestions, the most prominent are greater coordination between courses, reduced teaching load, and earlier availability of teaching materials.

Graduate Opinions The data regarding the opinions of the first graduates of the Cds, collected by Almalaurea (updated as of April 2023) and integrated by PQA with average university values, concern 90% of the 30 graduates in 2022. 96.3% report overall satisfaction with the course workload (96.7% last year; 89% average university value) and 92.6% appreciate the overall organization of the academic calendar (90% in 2021; 86% average university value). The relationship with professors is considered overall satisfactory by all students (96.7% in 2021; 92.3% average university value). Less favorable opinions are expressed regarding classrooms and teaching equipment, while 74% consider computer workstations adequate, compared to 53% of the average university value.
75% of respondents consider post-graduation orientation services generally satisfactory and 73% evaluate positively the support services for entering the workforce.
In summary, 92.6% consider the Cds generally satisfactory (100% last year; 89.9% average university value) and 78% would enroll in the same Cds again (90% last year, 73.7% average university value).
Overall, these data, which will be discussed in the September 2023 Course Council meeting, largely reward the CdS.
Ability to apply knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
At the end of the training path, the Master's graduate in Digital Marketing will have acquired managerial, economic, quantitative, and legal skills to analyze and interpret competitive dynamics in the sector, consumer behavior, and related decision-making processes, in order to optimize strategic and operational processes of companies operating in digital markets. They will be able to solve governance and management problems with a marketing orientation in both traditional and digital spheres. The graduate will be able to apply theoretical models and empirical tools and develop a problem-solving and decision-making approach through the use of reports, business plans, and briefings required during the studies. The development of these skills is supported by solving practical cases assigned during the study path, with the aim of analyzing real economic phenomena and business processes, or conducting independent research for which a critical evaluation of results is provided.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is assessed through written/oral exams, seminars, and the final exam.

Learning skills (learning skills)
The Master's graduate will have acquired learning skills enabling them to independently deepen and proactively develop their knowledge and skills related to the main techniques, functions, and roles in the digital marketing context. This ability will be acquired through participation in classroom teaching activities, in traditional and/or interactive form, individual study, and particularly through the research work carried out for the thesis. The acquisition of learning skills is verified by evaluating the quality of individual or group assignments and the quality of the thesis.

University Communications to CUN Below, for each point raised by CUN, the modifications made to the proposal are detailed.
CUN: It is requested to insert the course name in Italian in the space reserved for it, replacing the English course name that should be written in the space designated for it.
Response: The course name has been inserted in Italian (Digital Marketing) in the space reserved for it.
CUN: Required knowledge for admission: it is necessary to specify, possibly referring to the course's didactic regulations, the methods for verifying the adequacy of personal preparation. For graduates from classes other than those indicated, possessing 24 CFU obtained across a wide range of SSD is insufficient to ensure the effective use of the course and must be significantly increased and possibly divided among different areas.
Response: The number of CFU required for admission has been increased from 24 CFU to 78 CFU, divided among different areas as follows:
Business area: 36 CFU (SECS-P/07, SECS-P/08, SECS-P/09, SECS-P/10, SECS-P/11)
Economic area: 18 CFU (SECS-P/01, SECS-P/02, SECS-P/03, SECS-P/05, SECS-P/06)
Quantitative-computer area: 24 CFU (from SECS-S/01 to SECS-S/06, from MAT/01 to MAT/09, and INF/01).
CUN: Additionally, the period 'Candidates who do not possess such curricular requirements (...) and disciplinary sectors with those indicated by the CdS/M.' must be removed as it is not of statutory competence.
Response: The paragraph has been removed.
CUN: Regarding language skills, there is a contradiction between the explicit reference to 'adequate knowledge of English' and the phrase 'For admission purposes, knowledge in written and oral form of at least one European Union language, besides Italian, is also required,' which does not specify a particular language. Moreover, since the training objectives of the class state that 'Graduates in Master's degree courses in the class must be able to effectively use, in written and oral form, at least one European Union language besides Italian, with reference also to disciplinary lexicons,' it is necessary to provide a sufficient number of CFU to acquire such language skills during the Master's degree or, alternatively, declare that such skills (at least B2 level) are required among the admission requirements. Since language credits are in related activities, it is necessary to use the possibility offered by the database entry mask that allows dividing activities into groups of sectors to which CFU can be attributed, in order to highlight their mandatory nature. It is also noted that the appropriate SSD for acquiring language skills is L-LIN/12 and not L-LIN/10.
Response: The modifications made are as follows: the requirement for English language knowledge for admission has been explicitly stated, indicating the required level B2; the SSD has been changed, indicating L-Lin/12. The mandatory nature has been indicated in the mask.
CUN: The emphasis placed on computer knowledge and skills in both specific training objectives and in the description of professional opportunities (starting from the very name of the figures the course intends to train) does not find adequate reflection in the training activities provided in the computer area. It is therefore necessary to significantly increase the CFU reserved for computer training or, alternatively, revise the specific training objectives and professional figures.
Response: Following the suggestions, it was chosen to revise the specific training objectives and professional figures. Therefore, the professional figures and specific training objectives have been reformulated to respect the managerial vocation of the proposed CdS.

Knowledge and understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The Master's graduate in Digital Marketing possesses, at the conclusion of the training path, knowledge of theories and methods for developing scenario analysis and understanding the mechanisms underlying the digital world. The effective use of strategic marketing principles will be fundamental to analyze, understand, and act within the hyper-competitive current market; adopting a customer-oriented approach, they will be able to formulate a balanced and measurable value proposition, in an omnichannel integration logic that includes both online and offline channels. Furthermore, the graduate is able to fully understand economic, strategic, and business dynamics and will be able to develop value for the customer in digital economy markets in order to contribute to increasing the value proposition, consumer satisfaction, stakeholder value, and the quality of organizational decision-making processes.

Knowledge and understanding of the topics covered are achieved both in characteristic and related activities, as well as in the internship and thesis preparation, and are verified through written and oral exams and the discussion of the final exam.

Organizational structure and responsibilities at university level The Quality Assurance Office plays a central role in promoting the culture of Quality and Quality Assurance (QA), ensuring compliance with the Quality Assurance Requirements set forth in Annex C of Ministerial Decree 30 January 2013, n. 47. For the QA of study courses, in particular, it organizes and verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-CdS of each study course of the University; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for teaching activities in accordance with what is planned and declared; regulates and verifies periodic review activities of study courses; evaluates the effectiveness of improvement interventions and their actual consequences; ensures the correct information flow from and to the Evaluation Committee and the Joint Teacher-Student Committees.

For the QA of departmental research, in particular, it verifies the continuous updating of information contained in the SUA-RD of each Department; oversees the regular conduct of QA procedures for research activities in accordance with what is planned and declared; ensures the correct information flow from and to the Evaluation Committee.

The Quality Assurance Office is composed of the Rector's delegate for 'Quality,' a full professor who has opted for full-time work, with the task of overseeing the activities of the Office, as well as three full professors belonging to the following ERC (European Research Council) domains: Physical Sciences & Engineering; Social Sciences & Humanities; Life Sciences.

The Department of Business Economics has activated within itself a system of bodies and committees involved in the Quality Assurance process of Study Courses and in the management of primary processes of the CdS affiliated with the Department.

Course Director – prof. ARMANDO DELLA PORTA
Responsibility: Coordinates the QA system of the CdS and oversees compliance with obligations set forth by regulations, with the collaboration of the Quality Assurance Committee, the Joint Teacher-Student Committee (CPDS), in accordance with what is indicated by the University's central bodies on QA and the guidelines of ANVUR. The Director, with the collaboration of the QA Group, leads the cyclical and annual review of the CdS, drafting the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA) and the Cyclical Review Report (RRC), and proceeds with the insertion of the SUA-CdS, with the collaboration of the QA Group. QA Committee and Review Group

Responsibility: The Committee monitors the training offer, teaching quality, and contextual services provided to students by teachers and structures, with particular emphasis on criticalities, which are periodically communicated to the Course Director, the Course Council, and the Department's Teaching QA Representative.

Course Council
Composition: professors responsible for courses and student representatives enrolled in the Course, elected according to the procedures set forth in the General University Regulation.
Responsibility: The Council deliberates on the content of the SUA, the Annual Monitoring Sheet (SMA), and evaluates and deliberates on the related improvement proposals identified by the Course Director and the QA Committee; periodically, it deliberates on the content of the Cyclical Review Report (RRC); collaborates in implementing the quality improvement policies of the CdS.

The quality policy in the CdS is also exercised through decentralized activities within the committees activated in the Department as follows:

- International Relations Committee: coordinates services for student mobility, provides support and orientation to Erasmus students;
- Relations with Territory Committee, Steering Committee, and Course Director: monitors employment effectiveness, social partner consultations, redefines training offer, activates agreements;
- Communication Committee: coordinates contextual services supporting students, updates information documentation on the CdS (student guide, CdS functioning, e-learning platform, social networks, department website), manages relations with media;

Brief description of related and complementary activities Among the related and complementary activities carried out during the Master's degree in Digital Marketing, activities are provided to develop computer skills and foreign language (English) competencies, which contribute to strengthening both soft and hard skills as well as multidisciplinary teaching functional to achieving the CdS objectives.

Computer-oriented training activities aim to provide methodological and software tools for conducting predictive and descriptive analyses, supporting marketing decision-making processes, designing and implementing data analysis processes, and creating reports and dashboards to highlight and communicate results. These activities strengthen the "hard skills" in quantitative-computer areas specified in the course objectives. For these activities, 9 CFU are provided. Foreign language (English) training activities aim to provide linguistic and narrative storytelling knowledge and skills, which are fundamental in marketing activities. These activities strengthen the "soft skills" in communication areas specified in the course objectives. For these activities, 6 CFU are provided.

Brief course description The objective of the Master's degree in Digital Marketing is to train professional figures with managerial knowledge (particularly in marketing) and digital skills adequate to the new needs of companies operating in a space that is no longer solely physical but digital. The CdS is characterized by a multidisciplinary teaching offer aimed at facilitating the understanding of dynamics and the use of tools necessary to operate effectively in the digital marketing ecosystem. The main objective is therefore to train professional figures not only with deep knowledge of the market and the specific characteristics of activities and processes related to marketing, but also with specific technical skills to operate successfully. For this reason, in the training path, economic, legal, and business disciplines are accompanied by quantitative-computer disciplines, in order to provide students with a comprehensive and integrated vision of the aforementioned areas in line with the needs expressed by companies.

External effectiveness The first statistics collected by AlmaLaurea on the employment situation of graduates in the Digital Marketing course have recently become available and are updated to 2022.

Out of a total of 36 graduates, 28 were interviewed, with an overall response rate of 77.8%. Gender distribution is almost balanced, with a slight female predominance. The average age at graduation is 25.5 years, and the average graduation grade is 109.5 out of 110. The study duration averages 2.1 years, with almost no delay index.

More than two-thirds of graduates have pursued post-graduation training, with a clear preference for company internships, chosen by 57.1% of respondents. Active unemployment is low, set at 8%, and the overall employment rate is 82.1%. A significant gap is observed between men and women, with women showing an employment rate of 92.9% compared to 71.4% for men.

Regarding entry into the labor market, the majority of graduates, 65.2%, began working after obtaining their degree. The transition from graduation to first employment is relatively rapid, with an average time of 3.7 months.

In summary, the Master's degree in Digital Marketing at the University of Pescara appears to provide excellent preparation for the labor market, ensuring a high employment rate and short times for entering employment. Post-graduation training emerges as a key element, with a strong inclination towards practical experiences in companies.

Reasons for establishing multiple courses in the class Within the G. D'Annunzio University Chieti-Pescara, there are two Master's courses in class LM77 (Economics and Management and Business Economics) and one Master's course in class LM56 (Economics and Business Analytics).

The Master's course in Economics and Management, structured into multiple paths, aims to train a generalist figure in economic-business fields. In particular, it aims to "provide students with advanced knowledge and skills in the main functional areas of companies... as well as regarding the main dimensions of the context in which companies operate. It seeks to provide students with a comprehensive and integrated vision of the aforementioned areas and related business issues... It targets students with business economics and management skills who wish to deepen management, administrative direction, corporate finance, planning and control topics, and develop the necessary skills to operate in administrative and financial functions of industrial, commercial, service, and financial intermediary companies, as well as in the field of independent professions and business consulting, and finally in the context of public administrations." There are no courses qualifying as 'digital'.

The Master's course in Business Economics, structured into multiple paths, also aims to train a generalist figure in economic business fields. In particular, "it is characterized by training objectives related to company management, achieved also based on a full and correct evaluation of aspects related to environmental sustainability of economic activities, as well as to accounting profession and business consulting." There are no courses qualifying as 'digital'.

Remaining within the local context, a similar course but of a different class (LM56), active at the same university, is the following:
-Economics and Business Analytics
The Master's course in Economics and Business Analytics aims to train a specialist figure in the technical field of data analysis. In particular, "the training activities aim to develop the ability to use economic-statistical techniques, information technologies, and advanced application programs for the acquisition, management, analysis, and visualization of datasets, even of large size." Only one course is dedicated to marketing (web marketing) for 6 CFU. In this course, there is a substantial prevalence of technical courses over managerial and business courses, which represent a minority (21/120 CFU total).

The Master's course in Digital Marketing differs significantly from the aforementioned courses both in objectives and in the training activities provided. The main objective is to train professional figures not only with deep knowledge of the market (particularly marketing) but also with specific technical skills to operate in the new digital environment in line with the new needs expressed by companies.

It differs from the courses of the same class because it is not generalist but has a strong external focus, on the customer and growth, not only on the product or brand. It differs from the course of a different class because it aims to train managerial and executive figures (42 CFU business area/120 CFU) and not only technical ones.

Specific training objectives of the course and description of the training path The specific training objectives of the Master's degree in Digital Marketing are characterized by a multidisciplinary teaching offer aimed at facilitating the understanding of dynamics and the use of tools necessary to operate effectively in the digital ecosystem, specifically in the marketing field. The main objective is therefore to train managerial figures with deep knowledge of the market and the specific characteristics of activities and processes related to digital marketing. For this reason, in the training path, economic, legal, and business disciplines are accompanied by mathematical-statistical and computer disciplines, in order to provide students with an integrated vision of the aforementioned areas.

Consequently, the courses of the Digital Marketing study program, in addition to providing solid theoretical foundations of a managerial type, further refine them through the integration of case studies and best practices necessary to effectively master the opportunities offered by digital marketing. The courses will be attentive to current trends and all innovative insights necessary to strengthen students' soft and hard skills. The aim is to enable graduates to begin their professional activity in harmony with the requirements of a market that moves in a space that is no longer solely physical but digital.

The training activities of the study program are attributable to the following learning areas:
-economic area;
-business area;
-quantitative-computer area;
-legal area.

Training activities in the economic area are included in the SSD SECS-P/01 (Political Economy).
They include basic knowledge of industrial economics regarding both the functioning of digital and traditional markets (competitive and non-competitive) combined with the use of telematic sales channels, as well as understanding the strategic behavior of companies operating in the digital ecosystem.

Training activities in the business area are included in the SSD SECS-P/07 (Business Economics), SECS-P/08 (Economics and Management of Enterprises), and SSD SECS-P/10 (Business Organization).
They are aimed at acquiring knowledge regarding the understanding of strategic, organizational, and operational dimensions of innovative and change processes, with particular attention to companies operating in the digital ecosystem, emphasizing not only benefits but also main criticalities, with targeted insights regarding strategic marketing planning in the digital context, governance of integrated digital communication systems, and monitoring of performance indicators.

Training activities in the quantitative-computer area are included in the SSD SECS-S/01 (Statistics) and SSD INF/01 (Computer Science).
They provide methodological and applied foundations for processing market data, in order to conduct predictive and descriptive analyses, present and interpret results related to brand reputation, and support decision-making processes regarding marketing strategies to pursue. They also provide basic knowledge regarding the use of different data sources, with particular reference to the use of specific data mining tools useful for those operating in the digital marketing context.

Training activities in the legal area are included in the SSD IUS/05 (Economic Law).
They provide legal knowledge and skills regarding new technologies and economic innovation processes, completing the purely economic/business training of the student with the necessary understanding of the main regulatory sources regarding the issues in question.

The training path is oriented to maintain a close connection with the working environment. The study is completed with an obligatory internship or training internship and the final exam. The internship and final exam offer students the opportunity to deepen in the workplace the topics addressed in the courses. The strategic choice inherent in the training path is to involve students intensively in applying techniques and technologies to real cases. The aim is to foster a University-work transition that actually occurs during the training path itself.

The organization of the training path allows achieving the following main training objectives:
1. provide the necessary skills to analyze and interpret the dynamics governing digital sectors and markets;
2. provide the tools for understanding specific digital economy marketing strategies;
3. provide methods and tools to facilitate interaction and collaboration in interdisciplinary groups where marketing experts work alongside other actors such as economics and management experts, data scientists, and experts in specific application domains;
4. provide knowledge and techniques for interpreting data from sector analyses and performance indicator monitoring, market trends, and insights from digital activities;
5. provide knowledge for conducting sentiment and brand reputation analysis, developing and conducting online advertising campaigns, managing and coordinating both creative and technological, operational, and budget aspects to implement business strategy;
6. provide technological, operational, economic, and business skills to plan and manage sales activities through digital tools.

Opinions of companies and organizations with internship/curricular or extracurricular agreements From the academic year 2020/21, the first year of curricular internships, the CdS provides for the distribution of questionnaires to host companies and organizations to collect their opinions regarding the adequacy of the competencies and abilities of the interns relative to the workplace context. The questionnaire uses a rating scale from 1 (insufficient) to 5 (excellent). The judgment on the overall achievement of objectives is measured on a four-point scale (1=sufficient, 2=good, 3=excellent, 4=unsatisfactory). For the purposes of this report, when calculating the average of the above score, we assign the value 0 to any internships considered unsatisfactory.

In the academic year 2022/2023, the Teaching Secretariat collected and provided to the Course Director and the Quality Assurance Committee the judgments expressed by company tutors on students who completed the curricular internship within the agreed structures.

The data analyzed in this sheet cover the period from July 31, 2022 to July 31, 2023 and include 22 internships. In the analyzed period, the overall evaluation regarding the achievement of objectives by the student registers an average value of 2.54 (out of 3). Specifically, 82% of companies rated the internship as excellent.

The average values of judgments regarding organizational aspects generally provide good results. For example, the item "ability to integrate into the workplace context" registers 4.81 (previously 4.74).

The autonomy of interns is also evaluated positively (4.77, compared to 4.74 of the previous year).

The average judgment on "level of efficiency/effectiveness achieved in pursuing training objectives" is 4.64, substantially in line with previous years (4.70 in 2022 and 4.66 in 2021).

The adequacy of academic training was evaluated with an average value of 4.64 (4.2 in 2022 and 4.6 in 2021), with over 90% of respondents assigning good or excellent.

The average evaluation of the level of technical knowledge acquired is 4.82, increasing from the previous 4.42.

All average indicator values are above 4 (out of 5) and in almost all cases the assigned scores do not fall below 4.

Regarding the evaluation of behavioral and relational aspects of students, all indicators provide an encouraging picture regarding the transversal skills of students graduating from the study program, such as motivation, commitment, and problem-solving ability. The average value of various judgments in this category ranges between 4.77 and 4.9, always showing an increase compared to the previous period, which ranged between 4.2 and 4.7.

On average, over 80% of companies rate each of these aspects as excellent (5 points) and the remainder as good (4 points); no evaluations below 3 are recorded.

Finally, the average synthetic judgment of tutors, regarding the level of satisfaction with the overall internship experience conducted in agreement with the CdS, is in line with the previous year (4.86 in 2023 and 4.82 in 2022). Approximately 83% of respondents rated the experience as excellent (82% in the previous period).

The CdS has continued to intensify, even remotely, during the current academic year the involvement of companies within individual courses through company testimonials, fostering continuous moments of meeting and discussion, training seminars, and in some cases, student support for companies in finding solutions to concrete operational problems.

During the Career Day 2023 (May 17, 2023), feedback was collected from 29 companies out of a total of 33 participants. Companies expressed a high degree of appreciation for the initiative (average rating 5.8 on a scale from 1 to 7). Furthermore, on average, companies rated the likelihood of hiring students after the Career Day as very high (score of 4.9 on a scale from 1 to 7).

Some general considerations emerging from the questionnaire responses, not attributable to specific degree courses, are the importance of improving English language knowledge and practical experiences. All data will be discussed in the first useful Course Council meeting.
