Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and service production, professions (Course establishment)
The idea of establishing a Master's Degree in Digital Marketing arises from the analysis of new training needs expressed by private and public companies to respond to market changes induced by the development of the Internet, digital technologies, and related platforms. For its design, an incremental approach was followed, aimed at defining the teaching offer and the architecture of the CdS by integrating all feedback that would emerge during consultations with interested parties. In a preliminary phase (January 2018-June 2018), the proposing working group, composed of 6 professors from the Department of Business Economics, focused on two aspects: (a) the evaluation of the interest of the world of work in a Digital Marketing Study Course and (b) the evaluation of the availability of internal and external resources for organizing the same. This analysis was guided by a review of sector studies and available information sources supported by the opinion and advice of experts in Digital Marketing. From sector studies, it emerged that digital skills, beyond characterizing diverse work activities, whose weight is quantified by the Skill Digital Rate, also have an actual demand in the market. The list of most requested (and paid) professions includes not only traditional figures, such as IT manager, possessing high digital skills purely technical, but also roles that only a few years ago did not exist or were not clearly defined, which combine technical knowledge with more pronounced managerial knowledge, particularly in marketing, such as multichannel expert, mobile sales manager, e-commerce manager, digital marketing manager, market data analyst, etc. The centrality of professional figures possessing not only deep knowledge of the market (marketing) but also the techniques to operate in the new digital environment is confirmed also by the Ricerca Inapp report, Technological Change, Tasks and Employment (2017), edited by Roberto Quaranta, Valentina Gualtieri, and Dario Guarascio. Among the most requested professions, those capable of merging managerial knowledge with digital skills stand out, which are able to interface with the market (marketing) in a new way thanks to the opportunities offered by digital technologies. Between 2011 and 2016, the professions that grew the most are attributable to activities characterized by high technological intensity and organizational innovation. Specialists in market relations, production technicians, software designers are some of the most requested jobs by the market. According to this report, the combination of managerial knowledge, particularly in marketing, with digital knowledge is the mix that characterizes the profession with the highest growth rate in the period 2011-2016.

Main sources consulted:
1. Digital Skills Observatory (OCD) (2018). Annual Report of the Digital Skills Observatory: Scenarios, gaps, new professional profiles and training paths. Produced by AICA, Assinform, AssinteL, Assinteritalia. Collaboration of MIUR and the Digital Italy Agency.
2. European Commission (2017). ICT for work: Digital skills in the workplace. Report and study produced by Ecorys and the Danish Technological Institute, European Union. doi:10.2759/823113. ISBN 978-92-79-67763-2
3. European Commission (2018). Makes_me: Digital Skills: New Professions, New Educational Methods, New Jobs (SMART/2016/1006).
4. Quaranta R., Gualtieri V., Guarascio D. (eds.) (2017), Technological Change, Tasks and Employment. Inapp Report. https://oa.inapp.org/handle/123456789/82
5. P4I-Partners4Innovation (2018), The most profitable professions in the digital world. https://www.digital4.biz/hr/professioni-piu-richieste-e-piu-pagate-nel-digitale-2018/

After this preliminary phase, the project was shared more broadly, in accordance with D.M. 270/2004, art. 11, comma 4, with the interested social partners as well as with additional experts, through discussion within the Steering Committee and further Interviews with experts (phase 1) and Online and Paper Questionnaires (phase 2).

Below is a summary of the consultations of the two subsequent phases (June 2018-October 2018).

Phase 1: Consultation of Social Partners and Interviews with Experts
A first important sharing with social partners took place on June 29, 2018, when within the meeting of the Steering Committee of the Department of Business Economics, the proposal for the new Master's Degree was presented. The members of the Steering Committee are the following: POLO INNOVAZIONE ARTIGIANATO ARTISTICO E DI PREGIO; POLO INNOVAZIONE SERVIZI AVANZATI; ORDINE DEI DOTTORI COMMERCIALISTI E DEGLI ESPERTI CONTABILI DI CHIETI; ORDINE DEI DOTTORI COMMERCIALISTI E DEGLI ESPERTI CONTABILI DI PESCARA; ORDINE DEI DOTTORI COMMERCIALISTI E DEGLI ESPERTI CONTABILI DI LANCIANO; POLO PER L'INTERNAZIONALIZZAZIONE DELLE IMPRESE ABRUZZESI; F.LLI DE CECCO DI FILIPPO FARA S. MARTINO S.p.a.; CONFINDUSTRIA PESCARA; POLO INNOVAZIONE ABRUZZO INNOVATUR; CONSORZIO CAPITANK; POLO AGIRE; PILKINGTON NSG; APTAR ITALIA; TECNOMATIC SpA; CONSORZIOPANGEA; PRICEWATERHOUSECOOPERS; GRAN GUIZZA; FEDERMANAGER; FIRA; VALAGRO; MARSH; HERTZ; SGB HOLDING; WALTER TOSTO; KLINDEX; BLU SERENA; FATERGROUP. The present members unanimously praised the initiative, considering it certainly current and in line with the needs of companies that are increasingly looking for managerial figures with digital skills. They also suggested collecting broader feedback by involving experts.

In order to further improve the course design and thus create a highly qualified training path capable of creating profiles of interest to the world of work, other experts were consulted, who, while confirming the project's design, reiterated the importance of including an experiential and practical component within each course of the identified study program, in the form of exercises or laboratories. They confirmed the enormous interest of companies in managerial figures with high skills focused externally and on the customer (marketing) rather than internally (accounting) combined with solid technical knowledge of digital platforms. Regarding the profiles of graduates and employment opportunities, experts suggested including the figure of 'E-commerce & social commerce manager'. In particular, Dr. Giovanni Marcantonio, Director of the Development Agency at the Chieti-Pescara Chamber of Commerce, as well as co-author of the research report 'Web-marketing for Internationalization. Reasons, Research, Results' published in 2018 by Meta Editore, while noting, on one hand, the delay of companies in seizing opportunities offered by digitalization, and on the other hand, the absolute importance of a dedicated Master's Degree in Digital Marketing, suggested 'a vertical deepening on different sectors that could concern tourism, food, and SMEs. Such deepening could be organized within the different subjects present in the study plan. In a broader sense, the objective of the Digital Marketing Study Course should be to offer a panorama and knowledge of existing digital tools and train future managers able to choose and implement the most appropriate ones to achieve business objectives.' Dr. Marcantonio confirmed the validity of the project and reiterated, like other experts consulted, the importance of practice, suggesting to include within each course a practical/experiential component (laboratorial type) capable of offering a practical insight into the theories to be addressed in class. Finally, he emphasized that with the enhancement of marketing through digital techniques, the link between various functional areas of the company has strengthened. 'Thanks to the enhancement of Marketing, planning, programming, and control are areas that will be increasingly interconnected in the future.'

In conclusion, all expert comments were communicated to the professors who took them into account in formulating the syllabus content.

Furthermore, Dr. Sorchiotti, consultant and expert in digital marketing, consulted in December 2018, reiterated that the profile of 'Digital Marketing Manager' 'is the most current and sought-after profile. Probably because it is the most flexible, spendable, and easy to adapt to various needs. To further strengthen the path and preparation, I would try to integrate the study of online marketing dynamics in relation to traditional marketing. This latter aspect is particularly underestimated by Business Schools that offer Master's and Digital paths. Yet understanding how to manage online activities and objectives is fundamental to successfully enter a company.'

Before, value creation passed through printing, radio, television, newspapers, and magazines; now it passes through the web, social media, and emails. The profile the Course intends to train is that of the Digital Marketing Manager, a figure currently very sought after by companies. The training strategy is to merge managerial aspects with more technical-quantitative ones. Managerial aspects take shape in courses such as Digital Marketing Principles, Digital Business Organization, Management of Innovation, Business and Social Media Strategies, and Performance Management. More technical-quantitative aspects take shape in courses such as Applied Data Analytics, Marketing Statistics and Metrics, Technology and Business Intelligence, and Digital Marketing User Experience. Completing the training offer are courses in Economics of Online Markets, Economics of Strategic Competition, Digital Law, and Advanced English.

To summarize, the course aims to provide students with logics and tools to read change in order to enable them to develop appropriate marketing strategies. To make the courses more effective, the case method is widely used to make training even more laboratory-based and operational.

Data on entry, path, and exit
ENTRY The data acquired in August 2023 by the Statistics Section provided by the University's Quality Assurance Office confirm the growing trend of enrollments in the CdS, increasing from 41 the previous year to 56 for the 2022/2023 academic year, for a total of 96 enrolled (76 the previous year). It is interesting to note that almost 60% of enrollments (33 out of 56) are women, recording a growth in the course's attractiveness towards the female sex, which represented 45% of new enrollments in the previous year. Enrollments from other regions also increase both numerically (from 22 to 34) and in percentage (from 53.6% to 60%), suggesting excellent visibility of the course and its progressive affirmation in central and southern Italy regions, such as Molise, Marche, Lazio, and Puglia. The percentage of students from other universities remains constant (at 50%), confirming previous observations.

However, for the first time in 2022/2023, a non-zero rate of enrollments from foreign universities (3 students) is recorded. The data thus show a good and growing attractiveness of the CdS.

The course, which proposes a multidisciplinary path open to various degree classes, confirms a prevalence of enrollments from class L-18 (Business Economics), practically constant (26 students in 2022/2023 against 27 the previous year). However, the opening to new degree classes has attracted enrollments mainly from classes L-11 and L-12 (Linguistic Mediation, Modern Languages and Cultures), for a total of 12 new students, but also from Communication Sciences (L-20), Economic Sciences (L-33), Tourism (L-15), and Industrial Engineering (L-9).

Regarding higher education, new students, who mainly came from high schools and technical institutes in 2021/2022, in 2022/2023 count several units from Magistral and Professional Institutes (6), Classical High Schools (3), and others. The prevalence of Technical Institutes remains constant at 10 units.

IN ITINERE The percentage of students progressing to the second year slightly decreases, passing from 91.43% for the 2020/2021 cohort to 88.10% for the 2021/2022 cohort, and the number of exams taken per student decreases (from 6.49 to 5.93). However, the percentage of students who have earned all the required CFU increases (81% in 2021/2022 against 77% the previous year), as do the average CFU per student (48.62 in 2021/2022 against 46.39 the previous year).

The situation is clearer when looking at the details of acquired CFU: while the number of students who have acquired more than 40 CFU increases, in the 2021/2022 cohort, 6 inactive students (0 CFU) emerge.

The percentage indicator of average grades shows an increase in students in the 28-40 range, rising to 54.76% from 48.5% the previous year, while the number of students with an average below 23 drops to zero.

In conclusion, the data confirm a good progression of students' careers, who generally successfully face exam challenges in terms of regularity of acquired CFU and obtaining good evaluations. However, an increase in inactive students is observed, which will be discussed and monitored within the CdS for the current academic year.

EXIT Out of a total of 22 registered in the SICAS system, over 95% graduated on time and 60% received honors. The relatively low number of graduates reflects the decline in the number of enrollments of the 2020/2021 academic year. As observed in previous sections, enrollments are increasing, and the high number of students in course suggests that the indicator will rise in future monitoring. The data on the number of graduates in 2023 has not yet been recorded today.

The indicators show that students graduate on time and generally achieve excellent results in their study path.

All data will be discussed in the first useful Course Council meeting.

Characteristics of the final exam
The final exam consists of the presentation of a written thesis, also in digital form, elaborated personally by the student under the guidance of a supervisor, the result of personal and original work, written in Italian or a foreign language, according to the rules established in the 'Final Exam Regulation', approved by the DEA Council. The work will address a topic related to a discipline in which the student has taken a course exam present in the degree course. The topic is assigned by a professor who assumes the role of supervisor. The assessment of the ability to select the most appropriate theoretical frameworks and analytical tools is an integral part of the final evaluation of the student.

Mode of conducting the final exam
The final exam requires the student to present and discuss a written work on paper or digital support, elaborated personally under the guidance of a supervisor. The student must develop the thesis in a manner consistent with the chosen topic, demonstrating knowledge of the relevant literature attested by an adequate bibliographic research. The thesis constitutes an important individual training opportunity to complete the path. The thesis must be written according to the rules established in the 'Final Exam Regulation' on a topic related to the disciplines characterizing the student's curriculum. The assessment of the ability to select the most appropriate theoretical frameworks and analytical tools is an integral part of the final evaluation of the student.

Program, texts and objectives Communication Skills
The graduate in Computational Cognitive Science must be able to express themselves correctly and with scientific rigor, also in a foreign language (English), both for drafting reports in an industrial context and, more generally, for communicating the results of their analyses and the resulting operational proposals. They must therefore know how to use the appropriate computer-based methods and tools for effective communication. These objectives will be pursued in lectures and laboratory activities, requiring students to present their work and contribute, also using audiovisual means. The graduate must also have acquired good relational skills, knowing how to work in groups, even in international contexts. Communication skills will be assessed through written and/or oral examinations and during the final thesis discussion.

SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/2306

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
The graduate in Computational Cognitive Science must possess, at the end of the study course, an autonomous capacity for judgment regarding the decisions to be made in the registration, analysis, and storage of large amounts of data in the field of neuroscience and, more generally, in clinical and socio-health contexts. To achieve such judgment autonomy, the degree course will provide both technical-scientific tools and socio-cultural foundations in order to stimulate the individual capacity for critical analysis on scientific topics and the connected ethical aspects. The analytical capacity must also be directed towards resolving criticalities, intervening in the optimization of reasoning processes, individual and group, and decision-making processes. The evaluation of the achieved capacity and judgment autonomy will be carried out through written and/or oral exams.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
In the first training path, the student will learn to apply the conceptual tools and theoretical models acquired in both neuroscience research and various applied contexts where neuroscience and its techniques constitute a particularly appreciated added value, such as the research and scientific dissemination field, project management, and advanced training.
In the second training path, the student will develop the necessary skills to analyze how the integration of large volumes of multifactorial data and the ability to process them efficiently can constitute a resource in decision-making within scientific and business contexts, with particular attention to the prevention and management of clinical risk and the selection of diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic processes in a healthcare setting.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding will also be assessed during the exam, primarily through written tests, possibly accompanied by an oral test.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
It will be the responsibility of the degree course to provide the student not only with adequate skills and knowledge for obtaining the degree, but also with work and learning methods appropriate for continuous updating and advancement of their skills to progress to higher levels of knowledge, through a high degree of operational autonomy. This objective will be pursued through the structuring of the training process into different phases and types (lectures, autonomous analysis and research activities, applied experimentation activities, internships, etc.), alternating moments of knowledge acquisition with those of personal re-elaboration and experimental application of acquired knowledge. Assessments will be conducted through pass/fail exams (written and/or oral).
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The courses of the degree program aim to provide students with adequate preparation in the fields of mind and behavior sciences, cognitive neuroscience, imaging technologies, and artificial intelligence, in order to develop knowledge and skills focused on multifactorial data processing. The student is guided toward advanced study of the mathematical, statistical, and technological tools used for the analysis of large volumes of data, such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, as indispensable tools for developing a scientific problem-solving mindset, even in relation to complex systems.
In particular, the first training path provides the student with advanced preparation on the central nervous system and the neural bases of mental activity, from both a physiological and neuropsychological perspective, to enable them to acquire the language and research methods of neuroscience.
In the second training path, the student will acquire knowledge related to tools for managing information and relational flows concerning therapeutic and prognostic aspects, in order to develop interpretive models for specific decision-making contexts and/or create intervention strategies in the field of precision medicine and, therefore, personalized medicine.
The assessment methods for knowledge and understanding are differentiated based on the characteristics of each course: both written tests, possibly in multiple-choice format, and oral tests, to verify reasoning ability.

Brief Description of Related and Complementary Activities The related and complementary activities carried out during the Computational Cognitive Science program include mathematical, physical, and social disciplines necessary to complete the educational activity for students coming from three-year courses lacking these disciplines. In particular, these activities will provide students with the necessary mathematical tools for a methodologically rigorous data analysis. Additionally, methods and techniques used in imaging and neuroscience fields, based on physics topics, will be introduced. Finally, in relation to training aimed at decision-making in healthcare, students will be provided with necessary knowledge in decision-making processes, including ethical aspects.
Course Summary The Master's Degree in Computational Cognitive Sciences aims to train experts in data analysis (data scientists) with adequate psychological, technical-scientific, and programming training capable of managing data of various types acquired through different methodologies. The proposal targets a national and international audience, and therefore some courses will be taught in English.
The common foundation for graduates in Computational Cognitive Sciences will be the ability to effectively manage and analyze large quantities of data, such as those obtained from the analysis of complex systems. Paradigmatic examples are neuroimaging and epidemiology. Graduates will have a multi- and interdisciplinary training that will open multiple occupational and professional opportunities. The course will also provide specialized training aimed at pursuing further research doctorates.
The Master's Degree course is added to the three existing Master's courses in the Cognitive Sciences class currently present in Italy, two at the University of Trento and one at the State University of Milan. Therefore, this Master's Degree aims to represent a unique educational offer for the entire central-south region, proposing training paths in sectors of greatest interest to students and to the world of work and advanced training.
The Master's Degree in Computational Cognitive Sciences is open access and requires an interview to assess the level of knowledge in the disciplines of the course and English language proficiency for admission eligibility according to the specific procedures outlined in the course's teaching regulation. The two-year course is structured into a common first year for all training paths and a differentiated second year with two distinct training paths.
The first year will provide students with basic and advanced training in data statistical analysis and programming, artificial intelligence methods, psychology, and cognitive neuroscience. The second year includes specific courses, laboratory activities, a professionalizing curricular internship, and a final exam. The training paths are:
A) Big-data Analyst in Cognitive Neuroscience (Big-data scientist in cognitive neuroscience), aiming to train a professional capable of understanding and executing all phases of experimental research using behavioral methods and in vivo brain activity analysis. This professional finds employment as a data analyst in neuroscience or as a researcher/technician in public (universities, ASL, research centers) or private (company research departments) settings. Additionally, the training path allows for pursuing further advanced training goals (e.g., research doctorate).
B) Decision-Making in Healthcare Settings, aiming to train a professional capable of applying new knowledge on cognitive processes and new data analysis technologies to provide responsible medical staff with data-based evidence to best guide decisions in healthcare, both at the individual patient level and population level. This professional finds employment as a data analyst in healthcare or as a researcher/technician in public (healthcare companies) or private (clinics, private care facilities) settings.
External Effectiveness No data is available as the course was activated in the Academic Year 2022-23 and therefore the training cycle has not been completed.
Specific Course Learning Objectives and Training Path Description Consistent with the objectives of the LM-55 Cognitive Sciences class, the Master's Degree in Computational Cognitive Sciences aims to provide graduates with advanced and multidisciplinary training (psychological, statistical-methodological, computer science, neuroscience).
Given this multidisciplinary nature, it is likely that enrolled students have acquired a non-homogeneous set of knowledge and skills, as they come from different three-year bachelor's programs. Therefore, initially, the training path will develop from the courses necessary to provide students with the information needed to harmonize their knowledge and skills. By the end of the first year, students will have acquired fundamental psychological, mathematical, statistical, and computer science knowledge to address the more specific part of the course.
In the second year, students will choose one of two specific training paths, both emphasizing the analysis of large volumes of multifactorial data. The first specific training path will focus on the close link between cognitive sciences and technologies, addressing aspects of artificial intelligence, brain imaging techniques, and cognitive neuroscience. The second specific training path will focus instead on the analysis of complex systems and in particular on decision-making mechanisms and clinical risk management in healthcare. The distinction into two specific training paths is the cause of the rather wide range of characteristic sectors that distinguish the course.

Consultation with Representative Organizations of Goods and Service Production and Professions (Course Establishment)
The degree course responds to the growing demand for a professional profile capable of guiding the acquisition, analyzing, and effectively utilizing the large volume of data (big-data) generated by new technologies. In particular, within cognitive sciences, there has been a significant increase in the complexity of topics related to the discipline, which now requires professionals to have ever greater confidence in processing large quantities of data, often related to multifactorial aspects.
Training Path A (Big-data Analyst in Cognitive Neuroscience) specifically addresses the need to enrich the neuroscientist's training with computer science competencies. Although the Italian educational landscape already includes various Master's courses in strictly computer science fields related to the storage and processing of large volumes of data of various types, none are specifically oriented toward neuroscientific data.
Training Path B (Decision-Making in Healthcare Settings) responds to the need for specialized professionals in using data provided by new technologies for analyzing decision-making processes, managing relational and organizational dynamics, and minimizing clinical risk in healthcare.
Currently, only three study courses are active within the LM-55 class in Italy. Two are at the University of Trento and one at the State University of Milan. An analysis of AlmaLaurea training demand data has shown an employment rate exceeding 90% one year after graduation (with 90% of employees working in technical, intellectual, scientific, and highly specialized roles) and above 95% five years after graduation.
On October 13, 2021, a consultation was held with representative organizations of goods and service production and professions (attached minutes), attended by delegates from various central-south companies, contacted also by the University's placement service. Prof. Pizzella participated as an academic representative.
Specifically, the following organizations were consulted: S.Anna Institute (Crotone), FIEGE Logistics Italy, Bluserena, Acea, Verindplast srl, Mecenate Institute; Igefi srl.
Prof. Pizzella presented the proposal, describing the training path and expected learning outcomes. Following the presentation of the training plan, an in-depth discussion highlighted the innovative aspects of the project and the potential professional impacts for future Master's graduates. The parties expressed a favorable opinion on the establishment of the proposed Master's course, identifying it as an opportunity to fill a need in the interdisciplinary analysis of Big Data, not exclusively focused on computer science aspects. The critical issues raised relate to excessive interdisciplinarity, which can be a weakness if objectives are overly broad. Therefore, the educational offer has been structured into two paths with differentiated and therefore more focused objectives, eliminating courses whose content is less relevant to the professional profiles being trained, such as aspects related to human-machine interaction. The Stakeholders also expressed interest in participating in future consultations for the progressive alignment between the educational offer and the demands of the labor market. To this end, an initial guidance committee will be formed, consisting of reference teachers and representatives from the S.Anna Institute and Mecenate Institute.

Final Exam Characteristics For the completion of the degree in Computational Cognitive Science, the final exam consists of a written thesis and an oral presentation in Italian or English. The thesis must be developed originally by the student under the guidance of a supervisor.
Final Exam Procedure The final exam consists of the discussion of the Thesis before a Committee composed of at least five faculty members of the degree course. The final grade is determined by the Committee. The final grade, expressed out of 110, is determined by the sum of the following parameters:
• The weighted average of the grades obtained in the curricular exams, expressed out of 110;
• The quality and originality of the thesis, as well as the autonomy demonstrated by the candidate in preparing and writing the final thesis, up to a maximum of 6 points;
• The evaluation of the quality of the thesis presentation during the discussion, up to a maximum of 2 points;
The procedures for Committee proceedings are established by the Session Chair. The discussion includes a 15-minute presentation of the thesis work by the candidate; the supervisor may intervene during or after the candidate's presentation. The Committee Chair, after the candidate's presentation, invites the co-supervisor to ask one or more questions. The thesis, its presentation, and discussion may be conducted in English, at the student's request.

Enrollment in the five-year Master's Degree in Architecture is subject to passing an entrance test according to current regulations. The test, in addition to knowledge of general culture and logical reasoning, includes verification of basic knowledge in the following disciplines: history of architecture, drawing, physics, and mathematics. The merit ranking of the admission test also serves as verification of the required knowledge for assigning any Additional Educational Requirements (OFA). OFA are categorized by the same thematic areas (Mathematics and Physics, Drawing and Representation, History of Architecture), consist of individual training activities, and are assigned based on not meeting the minimum score threshold for each area set by the Course of Study Teaching Regulations in the entrance test.

SECTION: Admission Procedures

Admission Procedures Admission to the Single Cycle Master's Degree in Architecture is subject to passing an entrance test according to current national regulations.
As in the previous academic year, for the 2023-24 academic year, the maximum number of available places is 120 for EU students and 5 for non-EU students residing abroad.
The test was held on July 28 and September 12, 2023, following the procedures specified in the University's call, published in the Official Bulletin, on the University and Department websites.
ENTRY PREREQUISITES AND ATTENDANCE The required or recommended entry knowledge, particularly regarding passing the admission test, is described and promoted through numerous orientation presentations conducted by the Course Director and the Course Delegate (schools, Open Days, individual online and in-person meetings, etc.), as well as explicitly stated in the relevant Call.
Considering the extreme diversity of origin of new Architecture Course students (scientific, classical, artistic, linguistic high schools; technical and surveying institutes; hospitality schools, etc.), the recommended procedure for teachers with first-year courses is to organize their courses without relying on any preliminary student knowledge, which would inevitably be heterogeneous, to avoid learning difficulties and educational imbalances among students.
OFA The admission test score also serves as verification of the required knowledge for assigning any Additional Educational Obligations (OFA).
The Architecture Course requires passing preliminary knowledge in three distinct areas: Mathematics and Physics (CPA10), Drawing and Representation (CPA12), History of Architecture (CPA11).
As detailed later, OFAs consist of individual training activities assigned based on not meeting the minimum score threshold set by the Didactic Regulations for each area.
For the Architecture Course, OFAs are communicated promptly to affected students, who must fulfill them by attending mandatory (with attendance recording) supplementary teaching courses conducted by faculty members responsible for the OFA subjects.
Following observations from the CV during the relevant visit, OFA assignment has been subject to a more rigorous review process since the 2021/2022 academic year, introducing a minimum threshold of correct answers not below 30% of the total score for each thematic area. This criterion has been maintained for subsequent academic years 2022/2023 and 2023/2024.
Therefore, a first criterion for passing is achieving, in the admission test, a minimum threshold of correct answers exceeding 30% of the total score for each area.
If the threshold is not met, the passing path occurs through mandatory participation (with attendance recording) in recovery courses, assigning individual training activities (as stated in the current regulations) for each technical area.
For the aforementioned academic years, supplementary lessons were held by the History of Architecture faculty and the Mathematics faculty between the end of the semester lectures and the first exam session (December 2022-January 2023; December 2023-January 2024). The Drawing (Descriptive Geometry) faculty conducted an additional verification specifically for students with OFA debt.
OFA debt may also be overcome by taking the corresponding exam for the three areas:
a) Mathematics (AI0022) - 10 CFU for the Mathematics and Physics area;
b) Descriptive Geometry (AI634) - 10 CFU for the Drawing and Representation area;
c) History of Architecture 1 (AI635) - 8 CFU - for the History of Architecture area.
THIS MEANS THAT IF A STUDENT DOES NOT MEET AT LEAST ONE CRITERION PER AREA, THEY CANNOT ENROLL IN SECOND-YEAR EXAMS UNTIL ALL THREE CRITERIA ARE MET.
Enrollment in the second year is always permitted, provided that second-year exams cannot be taken before fulfilling the assigned OFAs.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The Master's degree graduate must acquire the ability to adequately communicate to the client, professionals and the public the meaning, content and effects of proposed projects, with particular reference to objectives, formal and functional solutions, realization and management methods of works. The Master's degree course will provide the knowledge and methodological and operational tools to develop students' communication skills in written, graphic and oral form. Teaching activities are organized to ensure group work and interaction with the teacher and external guests. The traditional lecture model is complemented by the workshop model, which involves active student participation in working groups and the potential contribution of external expert interlocutors. Moreover, digital representation and communication methods and techniques are adopted in various courses, emphasizing the use of multimedia communication systems. Communication skills are also developed through opportunities for cultural exchange via international mobility at partner overseas locations.

CURRICULUM: 5-Year Single Cycle
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/8

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgements)
The master's degree graduate must develop awareness of their work as an architect by cultivating a reflective attitude regarding the effects of their design proposals on the existing context. To this end, the master's degree program will provide both technical-scientific tools and socio-cultural knowledge to stimulate the capacity for critical elaboration at an individual level. In this direction, the master's degree graduate must possess, at the end of the studies, their own personal autonomy of judgment regarding decisions to be made in the governance of territorial transformation processes in interdisciplinary contexts.
The development of autonomy of judgment will be encouraged through the elaboration of projects in which the student will be stimulated to develop their critical spirit and make decisions, both individually and in work groups, simulating the multidisciplinary operational methods present in professional practice.
The assessment of the achieved capacity and autonomy of judgment will be conducted progressively through the examinations of the courses and in the preparation and discussion of the final thesis.

Assistance for Training Periods Curricular Internship The external training activity, which is part of the mandatory training activities of the Architecture Degree Course totaling 11 CFU (275 hours), is aimed at enabling students to gain professional practice experience and career orientation.
The internship is carried out during the fifth year of the course of study.
The training objectives of the internship period are agreed upon with the university tutor, to be identified among the faculty members of the Department of Architecture.
The internship takes place at the designated sites, belonging to the following categories, operating within the fields of architecture and/or architecture services:
- Professional studio;
- Company;
- Public or private body, particularly research institutions;
- Third-sector organization;
- Foreign institution or organization.
The student typically selects the host site and the university tutor, and submits the corresponding internship proposal by presenting the appropriate forms. The agreement with the host organization is signed by the Chair of the Course Council (CdS), while the training project is signed by the university tutor.
At the end of the internship, the student submits the following documents to the Secretariat, prepared according to the appropriate forms:
1. Internship certificate, reproduced on letterhead and bearing the signature and stamp of the tutor from the host organization;
2. Report on the work performed, containing the achieved training objectives, signed by both parties, the promoter and the host.
Additionally:
3. Evaluation/feedback forms regarding the intern (from the host organization's director) and vice versa (see below).
The recognition of CFU for internship activities is attested by the university tutor through the approval, with their signature, of the internship report.
MONITORING The Course Council (CdS) has implemented 'Customer Satisfaction' questionnaires to evaluate the effectiveness of the internship, for both the student and the host organization.
Starting from the academic year 2021/2022, the preparation of each of the two questionnaires has been made mutually independent through the introduction of separate forms, to ensure the necessary independence of judgment.
The questionnaires are collected by the Academic Secretariat (Ms. W. Cilli) and annually reviewed by the Chair of the CdS and the CdS Quality Delegate (Prof. P. Rovigatti), with the aim of obtaining as comprehensive a picture as possible regarding trends, strengths, and potential issues.
The purpose and detailed structure of the questionnaires allow students to constructively and proactively evaluate their internship experience (customer satisfaction), understood as integration into a complex and structured work organization, and allow the host organization to assess the student intern's level of preparation.
From the conducted checks, it has emerged that over 150 internship sites are active, with a clear predominance of professional studios, some public bodies, especially municipalities, and a certain number of companies, research organizations, etc.
As reported in the CdS Council, the questionnaire verification has not revealed any critical issues, but a general level of satisfaction from both interns and host organizations.
ASSISTANCE A specific administrative assistance service for tutoring is active at the CdS, dedicated to managing internship procedures and providing information on them, entrusted to the Student Tutor, Dr. Prosperi.
To coordinate all activities in the 'Internships and Placement' sector, the Department of Architecture has also established a specific delegated position, held by Prof. Filippo Angelucci.
OVERSEAS TRAINING (Internships) The CdS, and more generally the Department of Architecture, encourage the performance of internships at foreign sites, which have been carried out by several students enrolled in the fifth year: in particular through the numerous contacts of faculty members with foreign counterparts and utilizing the active international agreements.
Regarding the Erasmus+/Traineeship Programme, specifically related to the internship activity, the corresponding call was published in April 2023 (deadline May 14).
In line with the approach taken during the 2022 call, an information meeting for students was held by the Erasmus delegate for the CdS (Prof. D. Potenza) (May 9, 2023).
Additionally, awareness-raising activities were conducted for students (particularly those in the fourth year of the course) by the Chair of the CdS through specific meetings for each academic year.
Monitoring Subsequently to the completion of the Erasmus+/Traineeship call procedure (June 2022), a meeting was held between the Chair of the CdS and the Erasmus Delegate of the CdS (Prof. D. Potenza) aimed at monitoring the call's outcomes.
For 2023 (mid-May 2023), a monitoring review of the outcomes was also conducted, in agreement with the CdS Erasmus Delegate.

International Mobility Section INTERNATIONAL MOBILITY: GENERALITIES
The Department of Architecture, and in particular the Study Course in Architecture, promotes international mobility for study and research activities at conventioned sites located in countries outside the European Union.
The academic/educational validity of projects concerning students is subject to approval by the Study Course Council for the purpose of credit recognition, following a positive evaluation by the Convention Coordinator, who may optionally seek the opinion of the teaching staff member responsible for the subject.
The Department has identified a specific figure of 'International Mobility Delegate', also to assist colleagues in organizing activities (Prof. Domenico Potenza).
ERASMUS MOBILITY Erasmus+/Overseas is a European program that allows students to spend a study period at conventioned universities and to complete an internship at organizations in one of the European Union member states (and, for Overseas, also at an extra-European level).
Each year, two types of selection are announced to compete for the allocation of study mobility scholarships and for the execution of internships, with notices published in the official bulletin and on the University website.
Students benefiting from financial support for international mobility must earn at least 12 ECTS credits.
The Study Course in Architecture offers a wide range of destinations with important European universities. For the year 2023 (see Erasmus Call), the Study Course in Architecture has activated bilateral agreements with universities present in 17 countries (cities of the universities in parentheses, number of available places):
Albania (Tirana: 2)
Belgium (Hasselt, Liège, Mons: 7)
Bosnia (Birč: 2)
Brazil (Bahia, São Paulo: 4)
Chile (Santiago: 2)
Colombia (Bogotá: 16)
Czech Republic (Prague: 3)
Croatia (Split: 3)
France (Rouen: 3)
Germany (Kaiserslautern, Coblenz, Mainz, Potsdam/Berlin: 11)
Poland (Katowice: 2)
Portugal (Coimbra, Porto: 6)
Romania (Timișoara: 3)
Slovakia (Bratislava: 3)

Turkey (various: 21)
Data related to the Erasmus+/Overseas Call (2023/2024: deadline March 19, 2023) records a slight increase in the number of students from the Study Course in Architecture. The picture was completed with the second Erasmus+/Traineeship Call, concerning international internships.

At the end of the mobility period, incoming students are provided with a 'customer satisfaction' questionnaire to be completed, evaluating their educational, study, and stay experience.

EXIT ORIENTATION AND WORK GUIDANCE (CdS)
In 2023, consistently with strategies developed in previous months and discussed in various Councils, the CdS's actions to guide students into the world of work were structured essentially in three directions:
1) Adaptation of the CdS training path. Starting from the 2022/2023 academic year, six new elective courses were introduced in the fifth year ('Organization, Management and Safety of Construction Sites', 'Advanced BIM'; 'Professional Training, Regulations and Procedures', 'Advanced Digital Drawing', 'Consolidation of Historic Structures/Design in Seismic Areas', 'Advanced English Language') aimed at facilitating a smoother entry of CdS graduates into the job market. The number of fourth and fifth-year CdS students participating in the event (via prior registration) approached a hundred.
In the following weeks, through direct contact with students and their representatives, the level of satisfaction with the initiative was verified: based on the overall results, it was decided to organize the Career Day also in 2024.

Student Opinions SOURCES The data regarding the annual survey of student opinions concerning the University, the four Areas (Health, Scientific, Social, Humanistic) and the CdS are derived from the 'Student Opinions Survey' framework prepared by the PQA. The results for the academic year 2022/23 have been analyzed, along with those from previous years for comparative purposes.
OVERALL EVALUATION In previous academic years (2016/17; 2017/18; 2018/19; 2019/20; 2021/22), a consistent improvement in the average score of the CdS courses was recorded, rising from 3,12 (2016/17) to 3,27 (2018/19) and then to 3,41 (2019/20).
Already above the University average (3,35) and the Scientific Area average (3,27), this value further increased in the academic year 2020/21, reaching 3,46, the same value recorded in the subsequent academic year 2021/22.
For the academic year 2022/23, an additional increase was recorded, reaching 3,48 (update: September 2023).
This value is higher than both the University average (3,44) and the Scientific Area average (to which Architecture belongs) of 3,43.
Overall, the trend of increasing the average value of the CdS is confirmed, as well as the consistent achievement of values above the University and Area averages. In conclusion, the positive perception of the courses offered within the CdS by students is reinforced.
DATA ANALYSIS Regarding the data updated as of September 4, 2023, it can be noted that 59,57% of the 47 Teaching Activities within the CdS fall under Level A of evaluation, the highest level (values between 3,5 and 4). 34,04% belong to Level B (values between 3 and 3,5). This means that, on a scale from 0 to 4, 93,61% of the CdS activities received evaluations between 3 and 4. Of the remaining 6,39%, Level C (between 2,5 and 3) includes 4,26% (corresponding to 2 Teaching Activities, with values of 2,91 and 2,92, thus close to 3), while only 2,13% (one single Teaching Activity) is slightly below 2,5 (2,43).
Significantly above the CdS average are the values related to the punctuality of teachers in conducting lessons and other teaching activities, and secondly, their availability during office hours for students.
Although with varying degrees (reflected in the average values), the evaluation average is also quite homogeneous across the 11 scientific-disciplinary sectors.
Particularly interesting is the progression of the evaluation for individual courses under survey. While in the academic year 2018/19 only 6 courses had the maximum evaluation (between 3,5 and 4), in the academic year 2022/23 this number rose to 28.
The 2022/23 survey thus reveals very few criticalities: as mentioned, only for 2 courses out of 47 are values slightly below 3 (2,91 and 2,92), and only for one course a value slightly below 2,5 (2,43) was recorded.
PRESENTATION/ANALYSIS BY COLLEGE/INTERVENTIONS As customary, the monitoring results will be presented in detail to the teachers and student representatives for collegial analysis at the CdS Council meeting in October 2023 (i.e., after the summer exam session appeals period (June-September 2023), together with the final data on new enrollments recorded at the end of the procedures related to the two admission tests in July and September 2023.
Acknowledging the positive results achieved, the CdS Chair, as in the previous year, commits to personally contacting the teachers for whom evaluations below the average were recorded, in order to resolve any criticalities, with the aim of further improving the overall evaluation outcomes of the CdS. In particular, this applies to the two Teaching Activities with evaluations slightly below 3, and especially to the single Teaching Activity that recorded a 2022/23 evaluation slightly below 2,5.
JOINT TEACHER-STUDENT COMMISSION Regarding the Joint Teacher-Student Commission (CPDS), the analysis of the latest annual report indicates that the observations raised essentially concern the level of facilities and IT equipment. Concerning the first parameter, during the academic year 2022/23, the opening of the new exhibition room and the start of the bureaucratic procedure for setting up two student-only study rooms located in the Laboratory wing were recorded. The report does not highlight specific criticalities regarding the CdS courses. Nevertheless, as in the previous year, a continuous dialogue/conversation between the CdS Chair and the CPDS Chair (Prof. Angelucci) and the student representatives is planned.
CUSTOMER SATISFACTION For managing student complaints, the CdS relies on the University-wide centralized complaint management system (https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi), but especially on continuous dialogue with the CdS student representatives, both within the Joint Commission and at the level of frequent contacts and periodic meetings between the Chair and the representatives, particularly ahead of CdS Council meetings.
Additionally, following a procedure introduced the previous year (see CdS Council minutes), direct meetings are scheduled between the CdS Chair and all students of each academic year, aimed at an open and constructive discussion regarding issues related to the student experience.

Graduate Opinions SOURCES: Data from the 2022 calendar year, updated in April 2022 and April 2023, regarding graduate satisfaction levels from the CdS, derived from the AlmaLaurea survey (see attached PDF for April 2022 data). Additionally, reference was also made to: pqa.unich.it/archivio-aq/aq-della-didattica, particularly for previous years. For the examined calendar year (2022), a total of 121 graduates out of 144 provided an overall evaluation.

FREQUENCY: 89.7% of graduates regularly attended more than 75% of courses, while the remaining attended between 50% and 75%. The values are largely in line with the university's average, and considering the 'physiological' percentage of authorized non-attending students based on university regulations (health, work, young children, participation in the 'PA 110 e lode' program, etc.), there are no particular issues. In the April 2023 update, changes are minimal (88.4% regularly attended, while 5% attended between 50% and 75%).

CDS EVALUATION: The overall evaluation of graduates' experience within the CdS (April 2022 update) is highly positive, also showing a significant improvement compared to the previous year. In fact, 100% expressed a positive evaluation (details: 47.5% 'definitely yes'; 52.5% 'more yes than no'), compared to 87.7% the previous year (41.1% 'definitely yes'; 46.6% 'more yes than no'). The overall value exceeded the university average. The April 2023 update, including the entire 2022 calendar year, substantially confirmed the previous partial data, as the overall positive evaluation reached 98.2%: details include 53.4% 'definitely yes', 44.8% 'more yes than no', with only 1.7% 'more no than yes' and no 'definitely no'. In both cases, the values exceed the university average.

TEACHER EVALUATION: Broad appreciation is expressed regarding interactions with teachers, translating into a satisfaction rate of 94.9% (combining 'definitely yes' and 'more yes than no'), while the remaining 5.1% falls under 'more no than yes' (with no 'definitely no'). The positive value shows a significant increase compared to 78.1% the previous year. A notable comparison with the university average for overall positive evaluation (80.8%) is evident. The April 2023 update, covering the entire 2022 calendar year, reinforces the overall positive evaluation reaching 98.2%: details include 24.1% 'definitely yes', 74.1% 'more yes than no', and only 1.7% 'more no than yes' with no 'definitely no'. In both cases, the values exceed the university average.

EVALUATION OF CLASSROOMS/SPACES: Despite these satisfactory results, only 42.4% of surveyed students express satisfaction with classrooms, resulting in a dissatisfaction rate of 57.6%, slightly lower than the previous year (58.9%). The situation improved in the second half of 2022, as the April 2023 update shows this value rising to 65.5% (details: 12.1% 'always adequate', 53.4% 'often adequate'). Significantly more satisfactory is the evaluation regarding library services, although these were obviously influenced by pandemic-related restrictions. It is noted that maintenance and improvement initiatives for common spaces, particularly classrooms, do not fall under the direct responsibility of the CdS, which can only exert pressure on the Department's management and university offices, as has been largely done. In this regard, it is worth noting that future improvements to the identified issues should be addressed through recent measures on structures (ongoing renovation of the Pindaro Campus) and common spaces (particularly rooms/study areas), following repeated contacts and meetings promoted by the CdS President with the university's technical department (responsible: Eng. E. Simone). The inauguration of the large exhibition hall (July 2023) has significantly increased the availability of spaces for students. Important will also be the implementation of the organic plan for external space organization, whose project, drafted by Prof. V. Calabrese and Prof. A. Basti of the Department of Architecture, was presented at the university.

NEW ENROLLMENT: A significant improvement is recorded in the percentage of graduates who would re-enroll in the same course at the same university, at 71.2% (previous year: 60.3%): a figure substantially confirmed in the April 2023 update (69%), yet decisively higher than the university average (63.3%). It is interesting to note that during 2022, the percentage of graduates who would re-enroll in the same course at another university decreased significantly (from 25.4% to 17.2%). Comparing this value regarding willingness to re-enroll in the CdS with the high satisfaction index of the CdS, it is possible to hypothesize that the difference between the two percentages may largely stem from the negative evaluation regarding the overall structures, spaces, and some associated services.

PRESENTATION/ANALYSIS: As usual, the updated monitoring data will be presented, analyzed, and discussed with faculty and student representatives in the first useful Council after the summer break of 2023, alongside data related to course evaluations and new enrollments (admission tests: July 27, September 12, 2023).

Ability to apply knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding of the Master's graduate assumes specific characteristics in the context of different learning areas. Regarding architectural design disciplines, the Master's graduate uses acquired theoretical-practical tools to synthesize functional and technological-constructive aspects, visual quality, spatial relationships, regulatory frameworks, and financial constraints. In urban planning and territorial disciplines, the Master's graduate has acquired knowledge of techniques and policies for cities filtered through the concept of sustainability from environmental, socio-economic, and legal-administrative perspectives. Knowledge related to the conservation and restoration of architectural heritage allows for deeper historical competencies and sensitivity to static and construction issues, promoting the Master's graduate's ability to critically understand the values of existing structures, with the aim of transmitting them to the future. For architectural drawing disciplines, two aspects are particularly decisive for developing the Master's graduate's ability to apply knowledge and understanding: the first relates to theoretical knowledge of the history of representation; the second concerns scientific competencies in drawing, namely mastery of representation methods and the ability to use analog and digital representation tools. The evaluation theme requires knowledge of the theoretical aspects characterizing the valuation discipline and the ability to apply numerous procedures, direct and indirect, necessary for determining market and cost values in conflictual and non-conflictual contexts; for verifying the economic-financial feasibility of projects; for estimates in cadastral contexts and for tax valuation of properties. For disciplines related to architectural history, the learning process is based on students acquiring basic cognitive and critical tools for a reasoned understanding of architectural evolution, particularly their ability to conduct personal reflection on historical architecture as a tool for understanding current architectural reality and a valid basis for concrete project implementation. Finally, knowledge and skills acquired in technological disciplines enable the Master's graduate to control the analysis of construction systems oriented according to sustainability principles, particularly environmental.

Learning skills (learning skills)
The Master's course will provide students with a methodological approach to study that will enable future professionals to exercise subsequent autonomous learning processes necessary for critically updating their knowledge in architecture. This will be achieved through the alternation of traditional teaching moments (lectures) with dedicated exercises aimed at stimulating the student's self-organization capacity. In particular, in the fifth year, planned activities are predominantly oriented toward applied training experiences, including external internships, guiding students in choosing the disciplinary area for the Thesis Preparation Laboratory. The choice can be made among five different scientific areas, thus ensuring students access to a wide range of training paths. The 'continuous learning' objective is also pursued through the encouragement and development of personal study and research moments, to be carried out through free-choice training activities. To this end, the Department of Architecture encourages numerous cultural initiatives and events, allowing students of the courses affiliated with the Department to access them freely and without charge, according to their own autonomous decision.

Knowledge and understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Students in the Architecture degree course must acquire specialized levels of knowledge of the methodological and procedural tools of the various disciplines that constitute architectural knowledge, with the perspective of contributing to the quality of processes for conserving, transforming, and managing built heritage, environment, and landscape. The Master's graduate must particularly be able to interpret reality and the meaning of the context in which architectural intervention takes place, define objectives and project approaches aimed at the sustainability of interventions, understand their possible effects on environmental and landscape quality, and verify the economic and social feasibility of anthropogenic transformation processes. These capabilities can also be usefully applied within research paths aimed at developing innovative and original ideas. These objectives are primarily pursued through characteristic teaching courses, project laboratories, and thesis laboratories, where the culture of the atelier is revived and renewed, fundamental for transmitting architectural knowledge. The achievement of the stated objectives is monitored through intermediate tests and verified through written and oral exams, using thematic research, project elaborations, and technical reports, allowing evaluation of theoretical and practical preparation as well as project elaboration capacity.

Organizational structure and responsibilities at the university level
The University of Chieti-Pescara "G. d'Annunzio" states its institutional purposes in Article 2 of the Statute: to promote "the development and dissemination of knowledge and critical knowledge free from any ideological, political, or economic conditioning" and to organize "higher education and training with the responsible collaboration of teachers, students, and administrative and technical staff, guaranteeing professors and researchers, as well as scientific and teaching structures, freedom of research and teaching, and full autonomy in organizing work, choosing content and methods"; to promote "the transfer of scientific knowledge to foster cultural, civic, and economic progress of society, also in the perspective of interaction between cultures and the generation of spin-offs."

In line with the statutory statement, its guiding values, and strategic directions, the Chieti-Pescara University has adopted the provisions of Ministerial Decree No. 47 of January 30, 2013, regarding Self-Evaluation, Initial and Periodic Accreditation of Sites and Study Courses, and Periodic Evaluation, and has structured the organization of its Quality Assurance System (AQ): see external link provided.

PROCEDURE
Based on the definition of new educational objectives to be achieved, an integrated update of the training path was carried out during 2022, activated starting from the 2021/22 and 2022/23 academic years. Considering the positive feedback (see previous tables), for the 2023/24 academic year, the structure of the updated training path developed over the previous two years was confirmed.

Brief course description ORGANIZATION (summary)
The Master's degree course in Architecture at the University of Chieti-Pescara has a duration of 5 years, totaling 300 CFU. Teaching is organized in semesters through lectures and practical activities in laboratories, totaling 28 exams in subjects: mathematics, structural science, construction technology, technical physics, technology, design, architectural composition, drawing and survey, architectural history, restoration, urban planning, and building law. In the final year, where flexibility is encouraged, an internship activity of 11 CFU (total: 275 hours) is provided, aimed at enabling students to gain concrete professional practice experience, administrative procedures, site management, etc. In the fifth year, students can also choose a course (8 CFU) within the Thesis Laboratory among six thematic paths introduced starting from the 2022/23 academic year, with possibilities of interdisciplinary connections between paths, partial or total. This distribution stems from the opportunity to diversify training paths more broadly than in the past, following observations made during the CEV visit. The paths, characterized by research and/or project experiences directly connected to activities in the respective disciplinary areas, are:
- Architectural Design and Construction
- Urban Planning and Development
- Technological Design and Design
- Restoration and Conservation of Architectural and Landscape Heritage
- Representation of Architecture and Environment
- History, Themes, and Problems of Modern and Contemporary Architecture
Additionally, starting from the 2022/23 academic year, six new professionalizing courses have been introduced and activated in the fifth year, aimed at facilitating students' entry into the job market and enhancing their preparation. These courses, defined based on stakeholder comparisons and verified in the meeting of the Steering Committee on March 23, 2023, and the Career Day meeting with companies on November 24, 2023, are:
- Advanced BIM
- Training, Regulations, and Professional Procedures
- Advanced Digital Drawing
- Site Organization, Management, and Safety
- English Language (Advanced Level)
- Structural Consolidation/Design in Seismic Areas
In addition to improving their training path, certified attendance at these courses allows students to acquire additional CFU within the remaining 12 CFU of the Thesis Laboratory.

APPROACH (summary)
The Architecture Study Course in Pescara is oriented towards the needs expressed by contemporary globalized society and, at the same time, by the territorial context within which our University operates. Today, the market for technical professions requires an architect figure reinterpreted in a broader and more articulated way than in the past. Consolidated knowledge of the national study tradition (also recognized internationally), aimed at conserving and valorizing architectural and landscape heritage as part of the architect's professional responsibilities, represents an integral part of the training path, being the basis of the cultural sensitivity and technical aptitude that characterize the architect's multidisciplinary approach to transformations of the built environment. Current evolution of social and industrial needs regarding housing themes—from sustainability of anthropogenic transformations to energy savings; from land consumption to the revitalization of built heritage; from technological innovations in the construction sector to the use of information tools at different design scales—requires new skills and a necessary integration of knowledge. Referring to the specific geographical context, it becomes evident that themes related to design in 'fragile' territories (seismic, hydrogeological, social risks; securing obsolete built heritage, etc.) assume particular relevance, which will absorb a significant market share in the short to medium term, also due to normative measures—some of Community origin—that push in this direction. In this context, the Master's graduate in Architecture from the Chieti-Pescara Course is called upon to manage processes of building transformation and territorial regeneration of renewed complexity compared to the past, projecting the architect's figure into an interdisciplinary dimension where knowledge and use of 'common languages' (e.g., BIM technology) are fundamental, along with the ability to interact with other technical figures, performing coordination and project management functions for complex sites, including 'reconstruction sites' after earthquakes, widely present in our territory. Finally, through participation in specific university calls, access to merit-based international mobility conditions is provided for didactic training programs at European and international sites (Erasmus+, BIP, etc.), encouraged within the Degree Course through various informative actions, as a valuable opportunity for student development and entry into an international professional context.

PRESENTATION/ANALYSIS/IMPROVEMENT: As usual, the results presented here are subject to presentation and analysis in the CdS Councils, particularly on December 22, 2022, and April 20, 2023 (Steering Committee and issues related to graduates and their entry into the job market).
