These courses have already been activated starting from the 2022/23 academic year, recording significant student enrollment from fifth-year students.

Specific educational objectives of the course and description of the training path
The specific educational objectives of the Architecture Study Course in Pescara, in line with the declarations in the Degree Class Decree, are updated considering the needs expressed by contemporary society and the territorial context within which our University operates. The market for technical professions today requires an architect figure reinterpreted in a broader and more articulated way than the historical disciplinary themes related to building and urban design, architectural history, restoration, representation, technology, and valuation of built heritage. Consolidated knowledge of this study tradition should not be lost, as it forms the basis of the cultural sensitivity and technical aptitude that characterize the architect's multidisciplinary approach to transformations of the built environment. However, the current evolution of social and industrial needs regarding housing themes (from sustainability of anthropogenic transformations to energy savings; from land consumption to the revitalization of built heritage; from technological innovations in the construction sector to the use of information tools at different design scales) requires new skills and a necessary integration of knowledge. Referring to the geographical context of our Degree Course, it becomes evident that themes related to design in 'fragile' territories (seismic, hydrogeological, social risks; securing obsolete built heritage, etc.) assume particular relevance, which will absorb a significant market share in the short to medium term, also due to normative measures—some of Community origin—that push in this direction. Therefore, the Master's graduate in Architecture from our Degree Course is called upon to manage processes of building transformation and territorial regeneration of renewed complexity compared to the past, projecting the architect's figure into an interdisciplinary dimension where knowledge and use of 'common languages' (e.g., BIM technology) are fundamental, along with the ability to interact with other technical figures, performing—when necessary—coordination and project management functions for complex sites, including 'reconstruction sites' after earthquakes, widely present in our territory.

The training path of our Architecture Study Course implements the described professional qualification objectives through a learning methodology that makes extensive use of project workshops (to refine the ability to interact within work groups on specific topics) and an organization of courses into five disciplinary areas, two of which are composed of basic disciplines and three of which are characteristic of the study class. In the first two years, the student dedicates their training to basic and characteristic courses, the latter marked by a strong project expression. In the third year, an important phase of basic theoretical and technical-engineering training takes place. The fourth year involves a predominantly project-oriented commitment, aimed at verifying learning in all main disciplines for the continuation and completion of the study path. In the fifth year, planned activities are predominantly oriented toward applied training experiences, including external internships, culminating in the choice of the thesis area and attendance of the related thesis laboratory. Through participation in specific calls, access to merit-based international mobility conditions is also provided for didactic training programs at European (Erasmus) and international sites.

Opinions of entities and companies with internship/curricular or extracurricular agreements
INTERNSHIP: The internship activity, corresponding to 11 CFU (a value significantly higher than the national average for Architecture CdS and the minimum recommendations from the recent Rector Presidents' Consulta), is aimed at enabling students to gain professional practice experience, collaboration on innovative research projects, administrative procedures, site management, etc. The internship period can be carried out at public or private Research Entities, Italian or foreign architecture/engineering studios, specialized laboratories within production structures, etc. Before starting the internship activity, the "Training Project" must be defined, agreed upon with the chosen university tutor, and countersigned by the host entity's tutor. At the end of the activity, the student must produce an adequate report on the work performed, containing the achieved training objectives, signed by the student and countersigned by both tutors, plus a 'Customer satisfaction' questionnaire: this must be drafted by the host entity's tutor based on their expertise.

NUMBER OF INTERNSHIP STUDENTS: From the survey conducted, it resulted that the number of internship students for the 2021 calendar year (specifically: February 5–December 31) was 114. For the following year, the value should be slightly lower.

NUMBER OF HOST ENTITIES: Within the CdS, numerous agreements are active for the purpose of conducting training and orientation internships, opening the teaching path to professional work insertion. Their number is continuously increased, initiated by teachers and/or students, also to foster a broad relationship between graduates and local professional/production realities, since approximately 60% of CdS students, being of non-regional origin, are oriented to carry out their internship experience in their area of origin. From the survey, it is possible to indicate a number of host entities slightly lower than the number of internship students, confirming the extreme diffusion and territorial distribution of these entities.

IMPROVEMENT ACTIONS 2021/2022
During 2021, the following improvement actions were introduced, following presentation in the Council (see minutes of the June 14 and July 20 Councils):
a) It was decided that the two 'Customer satisfaction' questionnaires (internship student - host entity) be completed in entirely autonomous form to avoid mutual conditioning during evaluation. The previous single module was thus divided into two distinct modules.
b) It was decided that all questionnaires, both from students and host entities, be systematically collected and organized by the CdS Teaching Secretariat.
c) It was decided that the 'Customer satisfaction' questionnaires be analyzed by the CdS President and the GAQ/Review Group Quality Delegate (Prof. P. Rovigatti), to arrive at as comprehensive a picture as possible regarding trends, strengths, and potential issues.
The results related to 2020 and the first half of 2021 were presented and discussed in the CdS Council meeting of June 14, 2021 (see minutes). Based on the systematic collection of documentation, particularly the 'Customer satisfaction' modules, corrective actions for the internship experience model will be developed if necessary.

STUDENT EVALUATION OF HOST ENTITIES
Starting from 2020 (CdS Council of January 30, 2020), an obligatory 'Customer satisfaction' questionnaire was activated to evaluate the effectiveness of the internship from both the student's and the host entity's perspective. The purpose of the questionnaire is to allow students to constructively and proactively evaluate their internship experience, understood as integration into a complex and articulated work organization. At the same time, the host entity is called upon to express its evaluation of the intern's experience, highlighting positive aspects or potential issues. The analysis of the 'Customer satisfaction' modules completed by students—already mentioned as conducted by the CdS President and the GAQ Quality Delegate—did not reveal any issues but a generalized degree of satisfaction with the internship experience.

HOST ENTITY EVALUATION OF STUDENTS
Generally, opinions and evaluations regarding the internship activity are collected and subsequently analyzed through meetings with stakeholders (representatives of Orders and professional studios, business world, production, associative groups, secondary education institutions, etc.), resumed starting from 2021 after the forced interruption due to the pandemic emergency. Specifically, the evaluation of the activities carried out by internship students by professional studios, research entities, and host companies is deducible from reading/analyzing the respective obligatory 'Customer satisfaction' modules completed by the host entity's responsible for each intern. The module/type does not provide a numerical average but a choice between: 'excellent', 'good', 'sufficient', 'poor', and, secondly, the 'Overall evaluation of the internship's progress and results' written in analytical-discursive form. From the absolute predominance of the 'excellent' parameter (value close to 100%) and the reading/analysis of the second part, a high and generalized degree of satisfaction from host entities emerged.

RESULTS/CONCLUSION
The joint analysis of internship questionnaires—conducted, as stated, by the CdS President and the GAQ Quality Delegate—did not reveal any issues (except partially for 2021, in some cases, related to the pandemic emergency and consequent difficulties in direct contact) but, as stated, an explicit degree of satisfaction from both students and host entity owners. Considering this, no specific corrective actions were planned. Useful indications were, however, provided by the discussion with the Steering Committee, whose activation was already decided by the CdS Council and whose composition, defined after a thoughtful discussion within the CdS Councils, allowed for a first fruitful meeting held on March 23, 2023.

Consultation with representative organizations of goods and service production, professions (Establishment of the course)
Extract from the minutes of the meeting with stakeholders held on August 20, 2008, on the occasion of the establishment of the five-year single-cycle Master's Degree Course:
"The President invites Prof. Paolo Fusero—delegate of the Dean of the Faculty of Architecture—to illustrate the Master's Degree Course modified according to the didactic reform under Ministerial Decree No. 270 of October 22, 2004. Prof. Fusero proceeds to illustrate the objectives and purposes of the Course, focusing also on the related professional opportunities. In particular, he notes that graduates in the aforementioned course can practice free profession, as well as hold high-responsibility positions in institutions, public and private entities, professional studios, and design companies operating in the fields of construction, management, transformation, and restoration of buildings, cities, and territory. Having taken note of what was reported by Prof. Fusero, the consultation provided for in Article 11, Paragraph 4 of Ministerial Decree No. 270 of October 22, 2004, is carried out. Following a broad examination, this consultation proved positive."

On February 28, 2018, new consultations with stakeholders were held. Below is an extract from the minutes:
"With regard to consultation with stakeholders from the business world, it should be noted that in the past, operational meetings were organized within the Faculty of Architecture. The Department of Architecture then consolidated the relationship by establishing a direct line with representative organizations of the business world in the reference geographical area (central-southern Adriatic belt) to communicate the proposed training offer and at the same time establish a productive collaboration in identifying knowledge, skills, and professional abilities to be achieved with the Master's Degree Course in Architecture that can be utilized in the job market. From the discussion with social partners, interesting evaluative considerations emerged, useful for updating the training program of the Architecture Degree Course. The consultation with stakeholders is coordinated by the Department Director with the assistance of the Course President and the Department Delegate for Quality Assurance and takes place mainly through direct meetings with stakeholders. The work is organized in the form of a technical table, allowing all participating stakeholders to intervene within established timeframes. The consultation primarily focuses on the following topics:
- Graduates' employment potential;
- Need for updating training profiles;
- Expected and observed learning outcomes in the field;
- Possible continuation of studies in post-graduate cycles.
The consultation is directed at the following stakeholders:
- Professional Orders and Associations;
- Small and medium enterprises and their associations;
- Public and private entities operating in the territory in architecture-related fields;
- Secondary education institutions.
The consultation takes place annually, followed by restricted meetings with specific stakeholders for specific needs and purposes, such as training internships, integrated teaching, placement, etc. Each meeting is documented in a specific minute, and at the end of the meeting, stakeholders are invited, through the completion of specific forms, to develop discussion topics, detail specific needs, report issues, or other observations useful for updating the Degree Course's training offer. Parallelly, the Department's Quality Assurance Working Group follows sector investigations on the labor market trend and graduates' employment results, referring to available data and surveys (AlmaLaurea). Important in this regard are also the contextual analyses of the training offer and labor market of other universities in the same reference geographical area (Osservatorio Professione Architetto CRESME-CNA 2015). Stakeholder requests are annually evaluated by the teaching committee entrusted by the Department with verifying the external and internal coherence of the Degree Course's educational objectives and the possible updating of the teaching offer."

A new meeting with stakeholders is scheduled for February 27, 2019.

Consultation with representative organizations of goods and service production, professions (Subsequent consultations)
GENERAL APPROACH: Consultations with stakeholders from the business world, professions, local administration, and category associations are carried out regularly over time and according to a consolidated method, which may be modified based on specific needs for updating derived from context analysis. Stakeholders are numerous and belong to the following categories: Professional Orders, Economic-Financial Sector Entities, Construction Sector Associations, Companies, Institutional Figures and Local Authorities (Municipalities, etc.), representatives of the associative world. The process is oriented according to the following sequence:
- Information on changes introduced in the training offer following the previous year's consultation activities;
- Identification of new possible training paths related to the needs expressed by stakeholders in the reference geographical area. The work is organized in the form of a technical table (Steering Committee, Career Day, etc.), allowing all participating stakeholders to intervene and directly interact with CdS teachers/students. The outcomes of initiatives/events are presented and analyzed in detail in the first useful CdS Council meeting. Based on the results, subsequent more focused initiatives are planned for developing projects, collaboration actions, partnerships, and targeted interventions.

PROCEDURE (2022-2023)
The basic objective remains increasing and improving the relationship between the CdS (teachers/students) and the business world, both to explicitly communicate the purposes of the proposed training offer to stakeholders and to establish a regular and active collaboration in identifying knowledge, skills, and professional abilities that can be utilized in the workplace. Also based on the indications and requests expressed by stakeholders during the meeting with stakeholders (December 21, 2021), the following improvement actions were planned and implemented during the 2022-2023 biennium:
1) Updating the CdS training path, particularly regarding a closer and more targeted relationship with professional and productive realities.
2) Establishment and activation of the CdS Steering Committee, with consultative and propositional functions, tasked with first verifying the validity of the updated training path and advancing any new improvement suggestions.
3) Organization and conduct of the CdS Career Day for fourth and fifth-year students.

1) TRAINING PATH UPDATE (2022-2023)
Following the meeting with stakeholders on December 6, 2021, a detailed 'Training Path Update' was elaborated in early 2022, presented and discussed in multiple Council meetings with CdS Council members. After making the necessary modifications and integrations concerning the teaching planned for the first four years, final approval was achieved in the first half of 2022, with activation starting from the 2022/23 academic year and confirmed for 2023/24. The main modifications and integrations were:
- Expansion of the flexibility of the training offer through the reform of the single-discipline courses of the Thesis Laboratories, increasing their number to six and better specifying their content;
- Introduction in the fifth year of a series of courses explicitly oriented toward future professional activity, named AFO (Oriented Training Activities), activated in the 2022/23 academic year and, considering the positive outcomes, confirmed for 2023/24. These are six new professionalizing courses, aimed at facilitating students' entry into the job market and enhancing their preparation. The courses, defined primarily based on stakeholder comparison, are:
- Advanced BIM
- Training, Regulations, and Professional Procedures
- Advanced Digital Drawing
- Site Organization, Management, and Safety
- English Language (Advanced Level)
- Structural Consolidation/Design in Seismic Areas
Both in the 2022/23 and 2023/24 academic years, student reception of the AFOs has been extremely positive, with over 80 enrollments across various courses by fifth-year students.

2) ESTABLISHMENT AND ACTIVATION OF THE STEERING COMMITTEE (2022-2023)
In addition to the mentioned training path update, it was decided to establish a permanent 'Steering Committee' with consultative, propositional, and verification functions regarding the outcomes of the updated training path, particularly concerning concrete employment opportunities, with the possibility of advancing specific suggestions. By unanimous agreement of the CdS Council, the initial composition of the Committee was established with a limited number of members, though subject to possible future additions, including:
- CdS President
- CdS teacher with external professional experience
- Representative of the Architects' Professional Order (specifically, the President of the Architects' Order of the Province of Pescara)
- Technical municipal administration representative with proven specific experience (specifically, the Head of the Single Activity Production Office SUAP/Single Building Office SUE)
- Expert in sustainability environmental themes (specifically, the head of the Environmental Sustainability and Ecological Transition Sector)
- Representative of recognized prominence in the Pescara architectural professional world
The composition of the 'Steering Committee' was officially approved in the CdS Council meeting of December 22, 2022. After necessary agreements, the first meeting was held on March 23, 2023, at the Pescara university headquarters. In the introductory report, the CdS President illustrated the updated training path, which was shared by external interlocutors, particularly regarding the six AFOs. It was also emphasized the opportunity to further apply Advanced BIM in previous academic years beyond the fifth year. The outcomes of the meeting were presented in the first useful CdS Council meeting (April 20, 2023). A new meeting is scheduled for spring/summer 2024.

3) ORGANIZATION AND CONDUCT OF THE CAREER DAY (2023)
Following an elaborate organizational phase led by the delegate Prof. F. Angelucci, the first Career Day of the CdS was held on November 24, 2023, at the Pescara university campus, attended by institutional figures (mayor or deputy mayor of Pescara, Montesilvano, Spoltore) and 12 pre-selected companies/professional studios. Student attendance (limited to fourth and fifth-year students for the event's purpose) was very high (approximately 100 participants). The meeting was structured into a presentation phase of each company and professional studio, a discussion phase, and finally, direct discussion tables between students and company/studio managers. The objective of the Career Day was to increase students' knowledge of the various activity areas of the invited subjects but, above all, to foster mutual relationships between students and productive/professional realities for the purpose of conducting the mandatory fifth-year internship (11 CFU for a total of 275 hours) and for potential employment opportunities. The outcomes of the Career Day were presented, analyzed, and discussed in the CdS Council meeting of December 7, 2023. The positive evaluation of the event by companies, professional studios, teachers, and students determined a shared opinion to organize the second Career Day during 2024.

EXIT
The total number of graduates from the CdS in the 2021 calendar year was 150, of which 35 were in progress, 35 with one year out of cycle, 5 ahead of schedule, and 75 with more than one year out of cycle. From the surveys conducted, more than half of the graduates (52.5%, with a slight increase from 51.5% in 2021) intend to continue their studies, participating in master's programs and/or PhDs, training internships, and forms of professional qualification supported by scholarships or grants. The remaining quota (47.5%) is exclusively interested in work, both private (starting an autonomous activity or on a self-employed basis) and public. Most graduates declare availability to work outside their residence. For the 2022 calendar year, the total number of graduates was 144. Characteristics of the final exam
The final exam consists of developing an original thesis on topics related to the Master's degree course subjects, under the guidance of a supervisor. The student can choose between two different modes of thesis work:
- Project-based, expressed through studies, research, and graphic project elaborations, generally involving a sufficient number of printed and/or digital elaborations to fully develop the project.
- Compilation-based, consisting of an original critical reading on disciplinary topics of significant scientific interest.

Mode of conducting the final exam
Students who have completed their studies with the recognition of 285 CFU out of 300 are admitted to the Final Exam. The application for admission to the graduation exam is completed by the student through an online form. The graduation committee consists of a minimum of 7 faculty members, affiliated with the Architecture Degree Course, belonging to the SSD present in the Degree Course. All I and II rank teachers and research staff holding courses at the Architecture Degree Course can be appointed as thesis supervisors. The final exam consists of developing an original thesis, expressed through studies, research, graphic project elaborations, on topics related to the Master's degree course subjects, to be developed under the guidance of a supervisor but always with the aim of encouraging and promoting the development of individual student orientations and choices, starting from the identification of the thesis topic. The topics covered in the theses vary based on the chosen area: from complex architectural projects to urban interventions related to the city or territory, from the study/analysis/interpretation of a historical artifact to the investigation of degradation in an architectural structure with a detailed proposal for its restoration and functional reuse (hospital, cultural, productive, etc.), from digital representation experimentation to applied research on current technological issues. The elaborations and presentation formats of the final exam are defined by the supervisor, and possibly together with the co-supervisor, in agreement with the student following the thesis. Generally, this involves a sufficient number of printed and/or digital elaborations to fully develop the thesis project. It is very common to combine boards with the so-called 'book', i.e., an elaboration composed of text and images similar to a bound volume. The graduation grade is expressed in 110/110 and consists of the weighted average of the exam grades reported by the student during their study path, plus the score assigned by the graduation committee for the final thesis work. The additional score adheres to the following criteria, aimed at ensuring on one hand (in line with regulations) a number of CFU significantly higher than that required for the final exam of a non-Master's degree (i.e., 3 CFU) and on the other hand, a uniform evaluation among different committees to avoid penalizing the free choice of the thesis area by each student:
- A maximum of 10 additional points for the majority of the committee (with the supervisor's opinion) over the average/exams;
- An additional 3 points for unanimous committee decision for cases considered of exceptional merit;
- '110/110 with Honors' only if the average/exams is equal to or greater than 97/110, by unanimous committee decision.

Summary of the technical report of the evaluation nucleus
The course covers a scientifically and professionally significant area, unique at the regional level, and consistently positioned at optimal levels, in reference to its class, in terms of enrollments and students. The degree course has adequate, appropriate, and effective facilities, and following an advanced restructuring program of the Pescara Campus, new teaching and scientific spaces will be acquired in the short term, fully commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The degree course can rely on a specific teaching staff for basic and characteristic disciplines, widely adequate to the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The proposed organization, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the university's training offer.

Admission Procedure The Study Course is quota-controlled. To access the admission test for this Study Course, it is necessary to have a five-year upper secondary school diploma, and an entrance test is required for student selection. The admission test, prepared by CISIA (https://www.cisiaonline.it/area-tematica-tolc-farmacia/struttura-della-prova-e-syllabus/), will be conducted online. The 50 questions cover Mathematics (7 questions), Physics (7 questions), Chemistry (15 questions), Biology (15 questions), and Logic (5 questions). The test includes 30 optional English questions that do not contribute to the final score. Test dates will be advertised on the Study Course website (http://www.farmacia.unich.it), the University website (https://www.unich.it/percorsi/futuri-studenti), and the CISIA website (https://tolc.cisiaonline.it/calendario.php?tolc=farmacia). More details about the CISIA test are available at: https://www.cisiaonline.it/area-tematica-tolc-farmacia/struttura-della-prova-e-syllabus/
By May 15th of each year, the Course Council proposes to the Department Council the maximum number of students to enroll in the first year, the admission test procedures, and the enrollment and transfer deadlines to be included in the annual Study Plan.
For the 2024-25 academic year, the programmed student enrollment is 100 units, of which 98 for EU and non-EU citizens as per Article 26 of Law 189/2002 + 2 reserved for foreign residents abroad.
Enrollment and transfer deadlines are determined by the Study Plan.
Additional Educational Obligations (OFA):
Criteria for determination and recovery methods Verification of required knowledge Beyond serving as a selection tool for entry into the first year of the course, the entrance test also fulfills the obligation to verify the basic preparation of all students enrolling for the first time in the Chemistry and Pharmaceutical Technology (CTF) degree course. Therefore, the entrance test also functions as an initial knowledge verification test. This mandatory verification (per DM 270/04) is conducted to identify any educational gaps among new students and to organize necessary recovery activities (additional to the regular course teaching), ensuring academic support for students assigned Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) based on gaps identified through the entrance test/initial knowledge verification.
For the purpose of initial knowledge verification, students transferring from other courses, changing courses, reactivating careers, or enrolling in a subsequent year with career abbreviation will be excluded. Only responses to entrance test questions related to the following disciplines will be considered:
- Biology
- Chemistry
- Physics
- Mathematics All information regarding the entrance test/initial knowledge verification (date, time, location, number of questions, test duration, registration procedures, scoring method for correct, incorrect, or unanswered questions, etc.) is published on the CISIA website (https://tolc.cisiaonline.it/calendario.php?tolc=farmacia).
Any communications regarding the test will be published on the Study Course website (http://www.farmacia.unich.it/) and the University website (https://www.unich.it/percorsi/futuri-studenti).
How Additional Educational Obligations are determined Based on the entrance test results for initial knowledge verification, in disciplinary areas where recovery activities are required for students who answered less than 50% of the questions correctly, Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) will be assigned after enrollment. These must be fulfilled obligatorily within the first year using the recovery methods established by the Course Council President and the instructors of the relevant disciplines.
Completing OFA by October 31st of the year following enrollment is mandatory to access official exam sessions for corresponding courses as per the Study Plan.
Recovery methods Based on the entrance test results, which serve both as an entry selection and initial knowledge verification, if necessary, the Study Course will activate additional recovery courses beyond the official course lectures in each disciplinary area where students have educational deficits. In this regard, instructors of the disciplines involved will establish 1 or 2 weekly hours dedicated to recovery. Attendance at the recovery course is mandatory. Students attending recovery courses are not exempt from attending official course lectures. The educational deficit is considered resolved upon passing a written verification test.
Failure to complete OFA by October 31st of the year following enrollment will prevent students from taking exams for subsequent years unless they have passed at least 18 CFU in the first-year courses within the basic and characterizing course types (University Academic Regulations Article 28, D.R. 863 of December 16, 2013).

Program, texts and objectives Reasons for use in related activities of sectors already provided for in the decree for the class
(CHIM/06 CHIM/08 CHIM/09)
The sectors CHIM/06, CHIM/08 and CHIM/09 have been included to deepen specific and specialized aspects of individual disciplines that cannot be covered in basic courses.
In particular: Organic Chemistry (CHIM/06) to provide knowledge necessary to address, on molecular bases, disciplines such as biochemistry and pharmaceutical science as well as drug synthesis strategy and structure-activity relationships;
Pharmaceutical Chemistry (CHIM/08) and Applied Chemistry (CHIM/09) to provide students with advanced knowledge respectively in drug design, industrial technological formulation, and the development of innovative formulations for drug release, thereby consolidating skills in indispensable disciplines for compliance with European regulations.

Communication Skills (communication skills)
Master's degree graduates in Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Technology must have acquired the ability to communicate within the industrial context with colleagues in biology and medicine for effective group work, also using information technologies learned during the training path and through professionalizing seminars; they must be able to effectively dialogue with experts in specific application fields, understanding the needs of the areas in which they will operate to suggest effective solutions. In particular, they must be able to appropriately suggest project solutions relevant to the professional context, also using scientific English acquired through language tutoring specifically oriented towards professional topics. These skills are verified through oral interviews and/or written assignments for academic activities, as well as through the evaluation of documented training activities by qualified external subjects.
At the same time, by acquiring the qualification for the profession of pharmacist, they must be able to work towards public health goals, also through personalized patient counseling, including chronic patients, to promote adherence to pharmacological therapies, and to ensure appropriate advice for healthy individuals for disease prevention purposes.

SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5110

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
Master's graduates in Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Technology must be able to operate professionally within various aspects of the pharmaceutical world, intervening autonomously and responsibly in decision-making moments. This is particularly important in the context of drug-focused activities aimed at health and well-being, which involve broad ethical, social, and economic aspects. In particular, they must be able to independently develop quality control protocols for health products; collect and interpret data to derive solutions for setting up innovative research strategies and topics; operate in interdisciplinary teams composed of experts from different fields; and be able to develop synergies with other healthcare professions.
Additionally, Master's graduates in Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Technology must be able to correctly advise citizens on self-medication medicines and health products (dietary, cosmetic, medical-surgical devices, cosmetics, and food supplements); dispense medications correctly; and autonomously and responsibly advise patients, where possible, on "equivalent" medications, also with the aim of optimizing National Health Expenditure.
Master's graduates in Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Technology must be able to develop suitable analytical, pharmaceutical, technological, and design solutions when required in pharmaceutical companies.
To acquire these competencies, the preferred teaching tools are classroom lectures by professors, professional seminars conducted by pharmacists, distributors, health product experts, and pharmaceutical service operators identified in agreement with the professional world, and a practical, evaluative professional internship in pharmacy under the guidance of a pharmacist (company tutor) and the supervision of a professor (academic tutor). The assessment method includes oral interviews and/or written assignments. The pharmacy activity is recorded by the pharmacist (company tutor) in a dedicated diary. The assessment of acquired professional competencies involves a practical evaluation test preceding the thesis discussion and covering the areas specified in Article 2, paragraph of Legislative Decree 651 of July 5, 2022. The PPV assessment committee is the Internship Committee, appointed by the Department Council, with a balanced composition of six members, including professors of pharmacological, technological, and pharmaceutical chemistry disciplines, and Presidents or their delegates of the Chieti, Pescara, and Teramo Pharmacists' Orders.

Orientation and In-Process Tutoring
1) In-process orientation is conducted by the Course Director, assisted by the Department of Pharmacy's academic office and all faculty members of the Course (CdS). Tutoring activities are provided by each instructor within their respective courses.
2) Since the 2016-17 academic year, recovery courses for OFA (Additional Educational Obligations) in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology have been activated, aiming to address any educational deficiencies identified in new students through the entrance test/initial knowledge assessment. These recovery courses have been offered every year.
3) Based on the Department's available budget, which receives funding from the University for this purpose, tutoring, supplementary, preparatory, and recovery activities are provided by students/doctoral students (ex L.170/2003) for specific subjects. For the 2020/21 academic year, tutoring sessions were activated in Mathematics and Elements of Statistics (Liana Zito), General and Inorganic Chemistry (Giulia Colacicco), Organic Chemistry I-II (Pierpaolo Rocci), and Analytical Chemistry (Vanessa Perrone). For laboratory-based disciplines, doctoral student tutoring was activated in the following subjects: Drug Analysis I (Annalisa Di Rienzo) and II (Balaha Marwa), Galenic Development Methods (Alice della Valle), and Pharmaceutical Technology, Socioeconomics, and Legislation with Pharmaceutical Laboratory (Giuseppe Scioli). For the 2021/22 academic year, using 2020 funds, tutoring sessions were activated in Mathematics and Elements of Statistics (Liana Zito), General and Inorganic Chemistry (Cesidio Cambise), Organic Chemistry I-II (Eleonora Chiara Toto), and Analytical Chemistry (Greta Di Nardo). For laboratory-based disciplines, doctoral student tutoring was activated in the following subjects: Drug Analysis (Maria Loreta Libero), Microbiology (Paola Di Fermo). For the 2022/23 academic year, using 2021 funds, tutoring sessions were activated in Mathematics and Elements of Statistics (Martina Di Gregorio), General and Inorganic Chemistry (Benedetta Cantoli), Organic Chemistry I-II (Alessia Savini), Analytical Chemistry (Francesco Raspa, Cesidio Cambise), and Drug Analysis I (Alessia Pugliese). For laboratory-based disciplines, doctoral student tutoring was activated in the following subjects: Drug Analysis (Beatrice Marinacci and Francesco Melfi), Drug Analysis I (Nadia Barbacane), Drug Analysis II (Alice Della Valle), Microbiology (Sara D'Arcangelo), Pharmaceutical Technology and Legislation with Laboratory (Annalisa Di Rienzo), and Galenic Development Methods (Rafal Damian Wolicki). For the 2023/24 academic year, using 2022 funds, tutoring sessions were activated in General and Inorganic Chemistry (Francesco Gabriele Chiarelli), Organic Chemistry I (Alba Colaci), and Drug Analysis I (Giuliana Verzino). For laboratory-based disciplines, doctoral student tutoring was activated in the following subjects: Drug Analysis II (Giuseppe Scioli) and Galenic Development Methods (Eleonora Chiara Toto). Student evaluations are available at: https://www.farmacia.unich.it/ctf/assicurazione-di-qualita/valutazione-tutor-studenti. The 26 evaluations collected in 2018/2019 expressed a clearly favorable opinion regarding the tutoring received, including adherence to schedules, clarity of the tutor's explanations, and usefulness. Evaluations from 7 tutors by 29 students in 2020 highlighted excellent results. The 126 evaluations collected for the 2021/22 academic year showed a clearly favorable opinion regarding the tutoring received, including adherence to schedules, clarity of the tutor's explanations, and usefulness, with 98% of students' expectations met. The 75 evaluations collected for the 2022/23 academic year showed a clearly favorable opinion regarding the tutoring received, including adherence to schedules, clarity of the tutor's explanations, and usefulness, with 97% of students' expectations met. The 34 evaluations collected for the 2023/24 academic year showed a clearly favorable opinion regarding the tutoring received, including adherence to schedules, clarity of the tutor's explanations, and usefulness, with 100% of students' expectations met.
4) Selections have been announced for roles supporting digital and departmental orientation, requiring a total commitment of 150 hours. Orientation activities were supported by five students ("150 hours") for each academic year in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 academic years (Student Administrative Collaboration for University Services).
5) For the 2019/2020 academic year, a questionnaire was provided to off-track students before the summer break via Microsoft Forms, to present their personal situation, assess issues, and propose solutions. A high number of students (122 from both study programs) responded. The results were discussed at the Course Council meeting on March 24, 2021. For the 2020/2021 academic year, based on the success of the previous year's questionnaire, off-track students were offered a detailed questionnaire via Microsoft Forms, including specific discipline-related feedback. Twenty-one students responded, with only one revealing their identity and being summoned by the Course Director. Of these, 9 out of 21 were off-track for 1-2 years, 5 for 3-4 years, and 6 for more than 5 years. The main causes of delay were personal reasons and difficulties passing specific exams. The results were included in the attachment and discussed at the Course Council meeting on December 14, 2021. For the 2021/2022 academic year, 30 students responded, with three revealing their identities. One attended the Course Director's summons. Of these, 19 out of 30 were off-track for 1-2 years, 8 for 3-4 years, and 3 for more than 5 years. The numbers have significantly improved compared to the previous year. The main causes of delay were personal reasons and difficulties passing specific exams, with the primary reason for difficulty being an overly long curriculum. The results were included in the attachment and discussed at the Course Council meeting on March 22, 2023. In 2023, the Course Director, accompanied by psychological counseling professor Daniela Marchetti, convened several off-track students who had passed a limited number of exams. Meetings were held on October 30 and November 13, 2023. Of the eight students summoned, two attended the first day and three the second. The meetings highlighted issues including two working students, two students with psychological challenges (which they are addressing with psychological support), and one student who had health issues preventing university attendance for an extended period. Students are addressing these challenges independently but consciously.
6) For several years, the Department has maintained a thesis committee to guide students in selecting their thesis project. Four times a year, a meeting is organized with graduating students, attended by a placement office representative and relevant professional order presidents. The committee currently includes Professors Giustino Orlando, Luisa Di Marzio, and Alessandra Ammazzalorso.

MANDATORY SEMESTER INTERNSHIP For their mandatory semester internship, all students must complete at least six months at pharmacies or hospital pharmacies. Pharmacies welcoming students are contracted with the pharmacists' order. Pharmacies of hospitals in the provinces of Chieti and Pescara have offered their availability to welcome students from the Course. The results of the evaluation questionnaires for 2020/2021, 2022, and 2023 are collected in diagrams in the attachment. It can be highlighted that both interns and pharmacists expressed "very good" satisfaction across all areas (data presented at the CTF Course Council meeting on March 21, 2024, during discussion of the SUA-CdS). It is noteworthy that pharmacists highlight that interns' preparation and knowledge exceed what the interns themselves consider.
TRAINING STAGES AT LABORATORIES AND COMPANIES As mentioned, students may, at their discretion, include training stages at local and national pharmaceutical and food companies, public or private laboratories in their study plan to acquire additional credits. These optional credits can be completed after approval by the Course Council. At the end of the stage, the company tutor provides a judgment on the student. To date, the tutor has always provided a favorable judgment, considering the student's usually high commitment, adequate technical competence, high learning ability, high willingness to adapt to company life, and high ability to establish human relationships (see attachment regarding stages completed in 2023 and the Course's quality assurance link). Interns report being very satisfied with the experience.

International Mobility Office Subject to the requirements set by individual bilateral agreements, students in the Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Technology program can participate in the Erasmus+ program, allowing them to spend a period at partner universities in the EU after passing selection, to carry out study activities equivalent to those conducted at our university. For the 2023/2024 academic year, the student mobility call has been unified and includes all European and extra-European designated destinations (EU and Overseas mobility). The mobility opportunities for the 2024-2025 academic year are listed in the table.
The contact person for Inter Institutional Agreements with partner universities is Professor Luigi Menghini.
Academic Year 2020-21
For student mobility, 33 Erasmus agreements are active, offering the possibility of outgoing mobility for 84 students with a total of 752 months of overseas mobility. Initially, 50 scholarships (awarded to CTF and Pharmacy students) were allocated, totaling 307 monthly stipends, fully or partially utilizing the available slots on 25 active bilateral agreements. The actual number of participants was significantly and dynamically adjusted due to the onset of the COVID-19 health emergency.
Academic Year 2021-22
For the 2021-2022 mobility, 38 scholarships (awarded to CTF and Pharmacy students) were initially allocated, fully or partially utilizing the available slots on 18 active bilateral agreements. The number of mobility applications submitted and actually utilized is significantly lower than previous years but justifiable due to planning uncertainties related to the ongoing COVID-19 health emergency.
Academic Year 2022-23
For the 2022-2023 academic year, 46 active bilateral agreements offer outgoing mobility for 119 students with a total of 1,099 months of overseas mobility, though 47 scholarships were allocated across 24 different bilateral agreements. For the 2022/2023 academic year, the student mobility call has been unified and includes all European and extra-European designated destinations (EU and Overseas mobility). The number of applications submitted and actually utilized is slightly higher than the previous year but remains influenced by planning uncertainties related to the COVID-19 health emergency.
Academic Year 2023-24
For the 2023-2024 academic year, 58 active bilateral agreements offer outgoing mobility for 153 students with a total of 1,288 months of overseas mobility. A total of 37 applications were submitted, and initially, 33 scholarships (awarded to CTF and Pharmacy students) were allocated, only partially utilizing the available slots. The number of applications submitted is lower than the previous year, though the percentage of non-acceptances and rejections has decreased.

Career Guidance
The University has established a centralized Orientation and Placement Service to support the employment and employability of its students, graduates, and postgraduates through assisted career guidance pathways.
During thesis orientation, the University Placement Service has been involved at least three times a year, presenting its potential and offering support to graduates in CV preparation and contact with sector companies.
In December 2022, the Department appointed Professor Claudio Ferrante as the Department Placement Manager.
TEACHING PHARMACY
A Teaching Pharmacy has been established within the Department, for which the Pharmaceutical Legislation course includes the integrated module 'Professional Qualification for Pharmacists'. The Teaching Pharmacy is useful for completing the internship exam, which involves the pharmacist's activities in sending SSN and dematerialized prescriptions, dispensing to patients with explanations on dosage and administration methods, and activating the management system.
RESEARCH DOCTORATE
The Department of Pharmacy participates with the 'Pharmaceutical Sciences' curriculum in offering the Research Doctorate in 'Biomolecular and Pharmaceutical Sciences', aimed at training researchers in the chemical-pharmaceutical and molecular medicine fields, with a broad scientific background and familiarity with scientific methodology. Upon completion, researchers will work in the fields of pharmaceutical, toxicological, and food chemistry, molecular and cellular biology, structural biology, pharmaceutical and medical biotechnology and nanotechnology.
SECOND-LEVEL MASTER'S DEGREE
The Second-Level Master's Degree in Pharmaceutical Technology Transfer was activated for 2022/2023, aiming to train specialists who operate or wish to operate in pharmaceutical industries developing and producing medicinal products in accordance with Pharmaceutical Quality System concepts. The trained professional naturally finds employment in production sites, R&D departments, with career prospects ranging from regulatory aspects of industrial scale-up in formulation to Quality Assurance or Quality Control departments, up to the regulatory management of production site transfers in pharmaceutical companies.
In 2022/2023, the Department of Pharmacy offered for the first time the Second-Level Master's Degree in 'Science and Communication of Cosmetic and Dermatological Products', aiming to train professionals who can operate in various roles within the cosmetic sector. The trained professional can find employment as a specialist in cosmetic and dermatological product formulation, industrial production of cosmetic and dermatological preparations, regulatory aspects related to product use, production, and marketing, quality control of cosmetic and dermatological preparations, safety and efficacy assessment of cosmetic and dermatological preparations, scientific communication of cosmetics, cosmetic pharmacist capable of advising customers/patients on the most suitable and personalized use of cosmetic and dermatological products in B2B and B2C settings, and pharmacist operating in territorial pharmacies specializing in the preparation of cosmetic and dermatological formulations. In 2023/2024, this Master became inter-university with the University of Camerino.
COMPANY VISITS
Collaborations with regional and interregional pharmaceutical companies have been strengthened annually, including guided visits for students in the final years of study. In particular, visits were conducted with the R&D/Quality departments of Pfizer (AP) (January 18 and 25, 2019; January 24 and 31, 2020) and BSP Pharmaceuticals (Latina) in 2019. Previously, visits were organized with Dompé Farmaceutici (AQ) and Liofilchem (TE).
Due to the pandemic, these visits were suspended as companies significantly restricted access to their facilities.
ACTIVITIES 2019
a) In 2019, collaborations with the same companies were intensified, including Janssen-Johnson & Johnson Spa and GRUNENTHAL ITALIA, to facilitate the professional integration of young graduates.
b) On January 16, 2019, the 'Employer Branding' project was presented in collaboration with BSP Pharmaceuticals, featuring a day titled 'Contract Development & Manufacturing in the Pharmaceutical Sector: The BSP Pharmaceuticals Experience'. The event focused on presenting the company, its core business, and the employment reality described from the perspective of recruitment managers, with significant implications for recruitment.
c) On April 1, 2019, the 'JOBS DAY' Lloyds Pharmacies was held in Bettoni Hall. Company pharmacists and the HR Director participated, conducting over 50 interviews for selecting young pharmacists for Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna pharmacies.
d) On December 5, 2019, the 'University-Company Network: New Skills in the Pharmaceutical Industry' event was held in Bettoni Hall, featuring recruitment day for pharmaceutical companies Johnson & Johnson and Janssen Spa. During the event, R&D and HR managers conducted over 30 interviews for temporary employment of our Pharmacy and CTF graduates.
e) In December 2019, the Department joined a partnership with five other Italian universities for a project organized by the Parenteral Drug Association (responsible: Antonio Di Stefano and Lisa Marinelli). The association, established in 2000 as the Italian section of PDA and now operating also in Canton Ticino (Switzerland), aims to create a forum for technical information exchange among professionals in the pharmaceutical field (production, quality, and regulatory). The interaction aims to enhance the research activities of our thesis students, doctoral candidates, assignees, and scholarship holders to facilitate their industrialization through partnerships with companies via internships within pharmaceutical companies producing parenteral drugs exclusively.
f) In December 2019, the spin-off 'Algo Biotech' was authorized. The company aims to develop pharmaceutical/nutraceutical/medical device products requiring industrial partnerships for production scale-up. In the medium term (three years), it is expected to offer fixed-term contracts for Pharmacy and CTF graduates interested in developing individual projects within partner companies.
g) In 2019, new collaborations were established with additional companies for recruiting young graduates in Pharmacy and CTF: Janssen-Johnson & Johnson Spa, GRUNENTHAL ITALIA.
ACTIVITIES 2020
a) In 2020, the Pharmacology group established a convention with Veridia Italia Srl Agricultural Company, which provided equipment on loan and the possibility of hosting students at their premises for experimental theses.
b) On February 4, 2020, a presentation by the Abruzzo representative of the Interregional Order of Chemists and Physicists (Lazio, Umbria, Abruzzo, and Molise) was held to illustrate professional opportunities for students enrolled in the Chemists' Order (see event flyer).
c) On May 28, 2020, and June 4 and 8, three 'recruiting day' events titled 'Contract Development & Manufacturing in the Pharmaceutical Sector – BSP Pharmaceutical Experience', 'Quality Assurance at BSP Pharmaceutical', and 'BSP Pharmaceutical Services and Capabilities' were organized remotely via Teams. Additional Initiatives During the health emergency in the second semester of the 2019/2020 academic year, except for a brief two-week pause, teaching resumed in the form of distance learning using the Teams platform. The only courses affected by the emergency were those requiring a laboratory. Some instructors prepared by providing laboratory exercises available online on specialized websites (e.g., for the chemistry area: American Chemical Society – Chemical Education or Jove, which made resources freely available) or by recording short laboratory experiences they conducted themselves. Some instructors instead postponed their laboratory sessions to the period when students will be admitted to the university, to be conducted in small groups while maintaining social distancing (microbiology). The link to access distance learning is: https://zeus.unich.it/teledidattica/#insegnamenti.
In the 2020/2021 academic year, teaching, except for a brief initial period of a few weeks in person for 50% of students, continued remotely. The only in-person activities were laboratory sessions, with the number of students admitted to the laboratory reduced to ensure social distancing.
Exams were also conducted via Teams through Teams meetings managed by the instructors themselves, respecting the institutional calendar. The only difference was the variation in written and/or oral exams, with only oral exams in March, April, and May. (https://zeus.unich.it/teledidattica/#esami). From June 2020, instructors who deemed it appropriate could also conduct written exams online (https://zeus.unich.it/teledidattica/#scritti).
For graduation sessions, the Teams platform was also used (https://zeus.unich.it/teledidattica/#lauree), and the link was published on the university platform (https://www.unich.it/sedute_online).
In the 2021/22 academic year, teaching was mixed (in-person and live online lectures), and exams were predominantly in person (except for confirmed cases related to the pandemic).
In the 2022/23 academic year, teaching, exams, and graduation sessions have returned completely to in-person.
Disability Service: Ensures the well-being of disabled students at the university, starting from the individual differences of each student. The service aims to implement interventions and offer services to people with disabilities for better integration into the university's educational and social activities.
The Department's Disability Contact is Professor Luigina Cellini (luigina.cellini@unich.it)
The university's Disability and Handicap Service provides information and clarifications to students regarding access to online services, teaching methods, and administrative procedures related to their academic careers, etc. In cases of specific and particular needs, it directs students to the most suitable contact for resolving the issue.
Student Opinions In light of the new methods of administering questionnaires regarding students' opinions on the teaching activities they attend, it is noted that the number of collected evaluation forms is sufficient and significant. This allows us to consider the expressed judgments increasingly accurate. In particular, the number of courses evaluated approaches completeness, thus fully describing the situation of the Study Program.
The analysis presented relates to the five-year period 2017/2018-2022/2023.
The number of completed forms is high and has returned almost to optimal values. It ranges from 1,845 forms in 2016/2017 with 36 courses evaluated, to 2,578 forms with 36 courses evaluated in the 2017/18 academic year, to 1,975 forms in 2018/2019 with 34 courses evaluated, and finally to 2,308 forms in 2019/2020 with 34 courses evaluated, 2,136 in 2020/2021 with 38 courses evaluated, 43 out of 48 courses evaluated in 2021/22 with 1,562 forms, and 41 courses evaluated with 1,904 forms in 2022/23.
In 2017/18, the overall course evaluation improved slightly, reaching a value of 3.36 and remaining higher than the university's health area average, which also improved (3.29). The strengths remain the consistency between the program presented on the website / the program delivered (3.46), the correct definition of exam methods (3.53), instructor availability (3.54), and adherence to the schedule of teaching activities (3.58). The lower evaluations, despite a slight improvement compared to the previous year, concern the proportionality between study load and credits (3.12), the adequacy of teaching materials (3.17), the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics (3.11), and the study load not perfectly proportional to credits (3.12). Regarding satisfaction, 90% of respondents expressed a positive evaluation (yes, more than no), slightly lower than previous years.
It is particularly interesting that the evaluations for the chemistry, biology, and medical science areas are practically identical (3.36, 3.45, and 3.40, respectively), as well as for the different sectors.
In 2018/19, the overall course evaluation remained largely unchanged at 3.34 ± 0.18, with individual course evaluations fluctuating within a narrow range, with a maximum of 3.88 and a minimum of 2.76. Students rated instructor availability (3.57), instructor punctuality (3.51), and clarity in exam procedures (3.54) highly. The lower evaluations concern the proportionality between study load and credits (3.06), which has decreased compared to the previous year, and the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics (3.14). The adequacy of teaching materials (3.22) and the interest stimulated by the instructor in the subject (3.19) have practically reached or surpassed the threshold of 3.2. It is particularly interesting that the evaluations for the chemistry, biology, and medical science areas are practically identical (3.35, 3.44, and 3.32, respectively). For individual courses, values below 2.5 are found only in questions regarding the proportionality between study load and credits and the usefulness of supplementary activities for learning subjects that do not require them.
In 2019/2020, the overall course evaluation remained largely unchanged at 3.35 ± 0.15, with individual course evaluations (3.36 ± 0.18) fluctuating within a narrow range, with a maximum of 3.74 and a minimum of 2.84. Students rated instructor availability (3.56), instructor punctuality (3.51), and clarity in exam procedures (3.47) highly. The lower evaluations concern the proportionality between study load and credits (3.16) and the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics (3.17), which have increased compared to the previous year. Regarding the proportionality between study load and credits, only General Pathology falls below the passing threshold of 2.4. For this course, it would be advisable to partially reduce the program. The adequacy of teaching materials (3.23) and the interest stimulated by the instructor in the subject (3.25) have reached and surpassed the threshold of 3.2. It is particularly interesting that the evaluations for the chemistry, biology, and medical science areas are practically identical (3.34, 3.32, and 3.50, respectively). For individual courses, values below 2.5 are found only in questions regarding the usefulness of supplementary activities for learning subjects that do not require them.
In the 2020/2021 academic year, the overall course evaluation improved significantly to 3.45 ± 0.16, with individual course evaluations (3.44 ± 0.20) fluctuating within a narrow range, with a maximum of 3.95 and a minimum of 2.87, thus showing a significant increase even in these extreme values. Students rated instructor availability (3.68), instructor punctuality (3.65), and clarity in exam procedures (3.53) very highly. The lower evaluations concern the proportionality between study load and credits (3.22) and the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics (3.21), which have increased compared to the previous year and reversed in absolute evaluation terms. Regarding the proportionality between study load and credits, only General Pathology and Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Toxicology II fall below the passing threshold of 2.4. For these courses, it would be advisable to partially reduce the program or provide exemptions, as discussed in the Academic Council meeting on September 1, 2021. Evidently, compared to the previous year, the teaching materials provided by instructors have improved significantly (3.35), as has the interest stimulated by the instructor in the subject (3.37). The evaluations for the chemistry, biology, and medical science areas (3.47, 3.55, and 3.42, respectively) are very similar and significantly improved compared to the previous year. For individual courses, values below 2.5 are found only in questions regarding the proportionality between study load and credits and the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics in two courses.
In the 2021/22 academic year, the overall course evaluation improved significantly to 3.46 ± 0.15, with individual course evaluations (3.45 ± 0.22) fluctuating within a narrow range, with a maximum of 4 and a minimum of 3.05, thus showing a significant increase even in these extreme values. Students rated instructor punctuality (3.69), instructor availability (3.64), and clarity in exam procedures (3.53) very highly. The lower evaluations concern the proportionality between study load and credits (3.23) and the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics (3.27), which have increased compared to the previous year. Regarding the proportionality between study load and credits, only General Pathology and Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Toxicology II fall below the passing threshold of 2.4. For these courses, it would be advisable to partially reduce the program or provide exemptions, as discussed in the Academic Council meeting on December 14, 2021. Evidently, compared to the previous year, the interest stimulated by the instructor in the subject has slightly improved (3.38). It is particularly interesting that the evaluations for the chemistry, biology, and medical science areas (3.5, 3.53, and 3.53, respectively) are practically identical, all slightly better than the previous year. For individual courses, values below 2.5 are found only in questions regarding the proportionality between study load and credits and the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics in two courses.
In the 2022/23 academic year, the overall course evaluation, as the average of individual courses, improved significantly to 3.51 ± 0.20, fluctuating within a narrow range with a maximum of 3.96 and a minimum of 2.97. Students rated instructor punctuality (3.71), instructor availability (3.71), and clarity in exam procedures (3.63) very highly, all increased compared to the previous year. The lower evaluations concern the proportionality between study load and credits (3.32) and the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics (3.35), which have increased compared to the previous year. Only in one course does the adequacy of teaching materials fall below 2.8, and in two courses, the motivation provided by the instructor regarding the subject falls below 2.8. The evaluations regarding the proportionality between study load and credits have significantly increased, possibly because instructors intervened to reduce the program or provided exemptions, as discussed in the Academic Council meeting on January 25, 2023, and suggested by the Joint Committee. All evaluations regarding the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding course topics are above 2.8. Evidently, compared to the previous year, the interest stimulated by the instructor in the subject has slightly improved (3.41). The average evaluation of the Study Program significantly exceeds the average evaluation of the university's Health Area courses (3.41).
Regarding the evaluation of graduates, the 2021/2022 analysis, based on 48 valid forms, shows a maintenance of the evaluation from the previous year. Indeed, the average score, on a scale from 1 to 4, moves from 3.09 in 2018/2019 to 3.07 in 2019/2020 and reaches 3.29 in 2020/2021 and 2021/2022. This value reaches the average of the health areas (3.28) and is higher than the university average (3.23).
Significantly high values are found for the study abroad experience (4.00) and the internship (3.57). The lowest evaluations, but still well above the passing grade, are for computer equipment (2.98) and the adequacy of the study load to the duration of the study program (2.94), in line with last year's results. Graduates also appreciate the university support for study abroad (3.40), library services (3.48), equipment for other teaching activities (laboratories, etc.) (3.29), courses in general (3.25), and the service provided by the secretariat (3.25), although satisfaction with courses in general and the equipment for other teaching activities (laboratories) has slightly decreased compared to last year. For this year, thanks to student contributions to teaching laboratories, it is planned to renew many of the outdated equipment (balances, spectrophotometers) and purchase new equipment such as HPLC, an ultraturrax, a Karl-Fischer titrator, and an automatic titrator.
Graduate satisfaction is maintained at 3.25, thus keeping the good evaluation of the previous year (3.08 in 2018/2019 and 3.21 in 2019/2020). This value is slightly higher than the university average (2.99).
The President recalls that the Joint Committee did not highlight major issues. For the six courses where the score for question D1 (sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding exam program topics) is slightly above the passing threshold of 2.4, it is proposed to schedule meetings between instructors of prerequisite or similar courses to harmonize programs and pay particular attention to basic topics necessary for subsequent courses. Additionally, it is proposed that instructors spend the first hours of their course reviewing concepts essential for understanding the topics to be covered in the course itself.

# Summary: Master's Program in Pharmaceutical Chemistry and Technology (CTF)

## Program Structure
- 5-year Master's program (ciclo unico) with a maximum of 100 students per year
- Includes a mandatory practical training period (tirocinio) with 6-8 months of professional experience
- Features a "prova pratica valutativa" (practical assessment) before the final thesis
- Offers differentiated curriculum paths for students to specialize in:
  * Chemistry-focused path (CTF)
  * Biomedical-focused path (Farmacia)

## Student Profile & Progression
- 62.9% female students (2022/23)
- 77.3% regional students (from Abruzzo), with 22.7% from outside the region
- Increasing academic performance: 8.2% of students graduated with 100/100 (vs. 4.8% in 2021)
- Graduation rate improving: 43.3% graduate within normal program duration (2021/22)
- 94% of students are very satisfied with their internship experience
- 94% of industry partners are very satisfied with student results

## Industry & Professional Engagement
- Regular consultations with pharmaceutical companies (Pfizer, Thermo Fisher, Fater, Valagro-Syngenta)
- Development of "eccellenza" program for high-performing students (300-560 hours of additional training)
- Strong partnerships with professional organizations (FOFI - Federazione Ordini Farmacisti Italiani)
- Curriculum updated based on industry feedback to include:
  * Food chemistry
  * Marketing
  * Regulatory affairs
  * Advanced analytical techniques

## Program Outcomes
- 94% of industry partners rate student knowledge as "very adequate" for pharmacy practice
- 65-69% of students rate their university preparation as "very adequate" for pharmacy practice
- 61.9% of students find their internship experience "very satisfactory"
- 64.9% of students graduate within the normal program duration (2021/22)
- 94% of students are very satisfied with their internship results

## Curriculum Improvements
- Added courses in food chemistry, marketing, and regulatory affairs
- Increased focus on practical skills and industry needs
- Differentiated curriculum paths to better prepare students for their intended career paths
- Enhanced laboratory components to improve practical skills

The program demonstrates strong alignment with industry needs, with continuous improvements based on feedback from pharmaceutical companies and professional organizations. The program has successfully reduced dropout rates and improved graduation rates while maintaining high standards of academic and professional preparation.

Admission procedures Those who hold a Three-Year Degree in Cultural Heritage (class L-1 ex DM 270), class Cl.13 (Cultural Heritage Sciences ex DM 509), University Diploma in Cultural Heritage Operator (ex L. 341/90), class Cl. 41 (Technologies for Conservation and Restoration of Cultural Heritage ex DM 509), class L-43 (Technologies for Conservation and Restoration of Cultural Heritage ex DM 270) and graduates in class Cl.23 (Sciences and Technologies of Visual Arts, Music, Performance and Fashion ex DM 509), class L-3 (Sciences and Technologies of Visual Arts, Music, Performance and Fashion ex DM 270 and equivalent diplomas from Accademia di Belle Arti) and class L-10 (Letters ex DM 270), class Cl. 5 (Letters ex DM 509) may access the Master's Degree. Additionally, graduates from other study programs, including those under the old system, may access the Master's Degree provided they have earned at least 54 CFU in total within the scientific-disciplinary sectors specified for the Three-Year Degree in Cultural Heritage (all L-ART*, all L-ANT*, all L-FIL LET*, L-OR from /01 to /06, L-LIN/01, M-GGR/01, all M-STO*, IUS/10, IUS/18, ICAR/06, ICAR/15, ICAR 18 and ICAR 19, ICAR/21, GEO/01, GEO/07, GEO/02, GEO/10, BIO/08, MDEA/01, FIS/07, SPS/08, SPS/10, CHIM/12). Furthermore, the ability to fluently use at least one European Union language in written and oral form, including disciplinary terminology, must be demonstrated through appropriate certification (language proficiency acquired during the Three-Year Degree or European certificate at B1 level in English). Admission requirements are assessed by a dedicated committee according to the procedures outlined in the regulations. All students must submit a pre-evaluation application via the platform provided by the Student Secretariat, accompanied by a detailed curriculum and all documents attesting to the training activities completed during their previous academic career. The documentation will be reviewed by the dedicated committee, which will issue the suitability assessment for enrollment in the Master's program. For further details, see Articles 4, 7, and 8 of the Study Program Regulations.

COURSE: [BASA] ARCHAEOLOGICAL AND HISTORICAL-ARTISTIC HERITAGE
TYPE: Master's Degree
CURRICULUM: Master's Degree
SECTION: Program, texts, and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/547

Program, texts, and objectives Motivations for the establishment of the interdisciplinary course In the field of Cultural Heritage, there is now a growing need for specialized scientific preparation, enriched by practical experiences in addition to purely theoretical ones. Often, professional and scientific opportunities in this sector require as a necessary condition having followed post-graduate courses and obtained specific qualifications such as specializations or master's degrees. This leads to the need to propose highly specialized, formative courses capable of providing theoretical, methodological, and practical knowledge and skills in the fields of study, research, conservation, and valorization of Cultural Heritage. The reason for establishing a degree course belonging to both classes LM-2 and LM-89 is solidly motivated by the need to structure a path that fully values the common aspects related to the methodology for studying and valorizing Cultural Heritage, although within the specificities of archaeology and art history. The characteristics of Cultural Heritage in Italy, its widespread presence across the territory in significant quantitative but highly interconnected ways (movable and immovable, archaeological, intangible, landscape heritage), necessitates the figure of a high-level operator, capable of moving with the necessary competencies across these different sectors.
Note regarding the sectors and credits selected for characteristic activities The choice of characteristic courses has been made for both paths based on the ministerial tables to ensure, through an adequate and controlled structuring of study plans, the achievement of specific training objectives, namely the ability to address the multiple and varied aspects related to Archaeological and Historical-Artistic Heritage, from cataloging to historical interpretation and valorization, in a thorough, holistic, and integrated manner, while maintaining a solid connection to the common humanistic matrix and opening up to technical-scientific aspects, thanks to characteristic courses together with related courses. In particular, the breadth of Group 6 is determined by the fact that the courses included here, which are characteristic in the ministerial table for LM89, are not characteristic for the ministerial table of LM2. However, the cultural weight of these courses is considerable, as they are fundamental components of the path, from which students must draw for integrated training, to the extent appropriate to their own training path. Three groups of courses (4, 9, and 11) have a range of 0-6: these are courses whose sectors are characteristic only for LM-2 (9), or for LM-89 (4 and 11), therefore they are included among the characteristic courses for students whose study plan includes them, while they are included among the related and integrative courses for all those who wish to deepen one of these specific disciplines.
Overall, the chosen selection corresponds to what is currently required by the labor market, as stated in verification meetings: Master's graduates in the Cultural Heritage sector are employed in a variety of activities, not only related to archaeological and historical-artistic specifics, but globally and more generally to developments in cultural tourism and heritage communication, which requires a wide range of integrated skills that constitute a common element.
PDF inserted: view PDF description: laboratories activated academic year 2016-17
Note regarding credits for other activities The degree course, in addition to characteristic and related activities, allows students to choose an elective course to complete their preparation in a specific direction. It also includes technical-practical training activities (internships and laboratories), which are considered absolutely essential for preparation to successfully enter the workforce. In the final exam, students will apply what they have learned critically through the elaboration of an original written work, integrated with an English abstract and a verification of acquired language skills.

Communication skills
Graduates will acquire in their cultural background a high level of ability in the management, conservation, and restoration of cultural heritage; the capacity to appropriately use the main computer tools and telematic communication instruments within their field of competence. All this in order to enable a graduate of the Master's Degree Program in Archaeological and Historical-Artistic Heritage to operate, work, and collaborate with institutions, bodies, and working groups, both national and international, successfully communicating the results of their studies clearly to both specialist and non-specialist audiences in the field. In this sense, some of the seminar and laboratory activities will be specifically dedicated to teaching and communication training related to the identified study areas.
