Judgment Autonomy (making judgments)
Graduates, developing the research techniques learned in the previous study path, must be able to manage and integrate complex cultural data, inserting them into broad reference fields with a deep critical spirit; such abilities can be achieved through the assignment during studies of in-depth topics which students must report in written or oral form to the reference teacher. The objective is to train personnel capable of providing original contributions in the field of research, of which a fundamental development moment will be the thesis work.

Entry Orientation The Study Course, although a Master's program, traditionally supports activities promoted by the three-year Study Course in Cultural Heritage, starting from activities aimed at the final years of Secondary School, in order to provide comprehensive information about the entire educational path, allowing interested parties to plan their study path across both educational levels, an aspect that is very important from a teaching perspective. For this year, an intensive specific orientation program for Cultural Heritage has been prepared, thanks also to the Transversal Skills and Orientation PCTO pathways activated with local institutions. The Study Course also participates in initiatives organized by the University for this purpose, such as the one scheduled for 18.04.2024, or aimed at a broader audience like the "Night of Researchers" held on 29.09.2023 and the initiative promoted by the Mur "University Unveiled" on 20.03.2024, and has presented two projects within the PNNR Orientation framework. The Study Course coordinates with the dedicated commission of Dilass (coord. prof. M. Cimini) for the organization of such activities, and this year has also established an internal commission composed of Prof. S. Antonelli, C. D'Alberto, and Dr. P. Staffilani. Since the 2020-2021 academic year, an orientation page has been prepared on the Dilass website, containing numerous resources related to the Study Course, including information, testimonials from teachers, students, and alumni. An informative leaflet for Dilass Study Courses has also been prepared, downloadable from the Dilass website in the orientation section. A comprehensive guide to the Study Courses related to Cultural Heritage (three-year Cultural Heritage and Master's in Archaeological and Historical-Artistic Heritage) is compiled each academic year, which, besides being a useful tool for enrolled students, especially when facing the initial phase of the educational path, also serves as an effective orientation tool. The Study Course has also strengthened its presence on social media (FB, Twitter, Instagram), with dedicated pages aimed at direct contact and engagement with interested young people, presenting updates on research conducted and continuous updates on activities carried out within the Study Course's teachings. These channels significantly contribute to promoting the Study Course and bringing potential users closer. The Study Course provides orientation services, carried out by teacher tutors, both before enrollment and at the beginning of courses. All teachers are available through institutional communication channels to answer information requests. Additionally, each year, during September and October, the BASA Study Course organizes and publicizes two or three general orientation meetings to illustrate the course and answer shared questions, and at the end of August, an online calendar is published containing dates, times, and teachers available for individual orientation. These initiatives, starting from those aimed at schools, are usually well-attended and appreciated, as are the social media contacts, which in some cases manage to reach potential interested parties who would otherwise be difficult to engage through other means. Data on pre-enrollment requests and an increase in enrollments demonstrate the effectiveness of the actions implemented in recent years, but there is awareness of the need to further enhance this activity, especially by targeting potential interested parties through specific initiatives. Entry orientation is one of the aspects related to the management of the Study Course that receives constant attention, with a precise monitoring of the results achieved.

Ongoing orientation and tutoring The activity of ongoing orientation and tutoring takes place in person by all involved teachers and occasionally in a remote manner.

- Assistance for completing external training periods (internships and placements)
- Assistance in compiling the study plan;
- Information on teaching organization (teachers, schedules, classrooms, lessons);
- Support in planning studies;
- Information on transfers/moves.
- Final exam (subject selection).

Students who already hold a master's degree or are employed tend to prioritize the relationship with their reference tutor, with whom they usually also interact for thesis work. Only during the initial phase of the course do they frequently utilize the actions implemented by the CdS for orientation and tutoring.

Internship periods The internship activity is chosen by the student for a minimum of 75 hours, equivalent to 3 CFU, at selected and contracted public and private entities (see attachment) related to the study course focus, or by participating in national or international excavation campaigns conducted by archaeology professors in Italy and abroad; finally, within the university at the Fototeca of DiLASS, the University Museum, the Archaeology Laboratory, and the Archaeology Fototeca. These activities can be counted towards the fieldwork experience required by the Ministry of Culture to be included in the lists of Cultural Heritage Professionals (Archaeologists, Art Historians) (D.M. 244 of May 20, 2019). Students can increase the total hours of these activities, acquiring additional CFU that are counted within the off-plan CFU up to a maximum of 18 CFU. The reference tutor is Prof. Maria Giulia Aurigemma, the administrative reference is Dr. Maria Cristina Ricciardi; lists, regulations, forms, and procedures at the DiLASS internship link. Since 2021, a dedicated Internship Team has been created, both to have a direct channel with students and to use it for relations with stakeholders. The possibility of interaction between the different parties involved in internship and placement activities through this channel has made the exchange of information, discussion, and resolution of any issues more straightforward and faster. Thanks to numerous agreements with public and private entities operating in various sectors (archaeological parks, museums, research laboratories, art galleries), students are offered a wide range of training opportunities during and after their studies. Such activities, in their variety, allow students to directly engage with different forms of work related to Archaeological and Historical-Artistic Cultural Heritage and represent an extremely important part of the training project that students undertake with enthusiasm, acquiring excellent skills applicable in the subsequent professional world. The end of health restrictions has allowed a full resumption of these activities, although due to logistical difficulties, some students (6/7 students) had chosen to complete external internships even in reduced numbers. In 2023, four new agreements were added with external entities for curricular internships (Fondazione Musei Civici di Loreto Aprutino, Archivio di Stato di Chieti, Arcidiocesi di Pescara-Penne, Convitto Nazionale G.B. Vico and affiliated schools), contributing to updating and expanding the students' experience opportunities. The administrative reference, Dr. Maria Cristina Ricciardi, carries out constant monitoring throughout the internship process, providing periodic summaries of the internship trends with consistently positive results, considering the satisfaction expressed by both students and representatives of the host entities. The University also has an office that provides assistance for carrying out training periods outside the University (internships and placements).

International Mobility Office The University has an International Relations Office that provides assistance regarding agreements for student international mobility within the framework of ERASMUS and ERASMUS PLUS agreements, whose activities are illustrated in the dedicated section of the website (https://www.unich.it/percorsi/international). Additionally, specific bilateral agreements are in place with other European universities for the development of exchanges and joint research in the field of valorizing archaeological and historical-artistic cultural heritage. For the University's international mobility, see the 'Erasmus' project and the 'Leonardo' project. The Course coordinates on these matters with the Tutor for International Activities of Dilass, Prof. Del Fuoco, and with the International Relations Delegate of Dilass, Prof. Caccamo. Within the Course, Professors Vasco La Salvia and Francesco Caccamo are the points of contact for international relations and internationalization. The aforementioned points of contact are responsible for promoting and carrying out activities for incoming and outgoing students, both within the Erasmus+ project and within the agreements for student and faculty mobility and Summer Schools. During November and December 2022, several meetings were held during class hours to introduce mobility programs to students. The President of the Course also urged the points of contact to direct third-year students to apply for mobility to be carried out during the Master's program, so that they could potentially spend the period abroad already during the first year of the Master's. Already from the current academic year, positive signals are being observed regarding outgoing requests under the Erasmus agreements, while enrollments in the Course have been registered from non-EU students. Incoming students can contact the dedicated address: incoming@unich.it The agreements currently primarily concern training programs and thesis development (see the list of agreements in the attachment). To encourage student participation in international mobility, the Course has provided (Article 9 of the Academic Regulations) since the 2019 cohort that for the final exam: 'Students who have completed a study experience within the ERASMUS project or the international agreements activated by the reference Department (DILASS) and the involved Department (DISPUTER) will be awarded an additional point in the final grade.' Since 2021, an additional support has been established for the scholarship funded by Dilass. The Course also seeks to increase the forms and methods of carrying out study and research activities abroad by leveraging the numerous existing relationships with foreign universities and research institutions, thereby allowing even short-term mobility and specific technical-scientific purposes for students of the degree program, and ensuring the proper recognition of such activities as international training activities. In this context, efforts are also made to promote incoming activities by foreign students. Following this line, action was taken as early as 2018-2019 when the EuroTeCH project (European Technologies and Strategies for Cultural Heritage at Risk (Erasmus Plus)), led by Prof. Menozzi, who won the 2018 KA203 Erasmus Plus-Strategic Partnerships for Higher Education call, was initiated. The project involved BASA students and doctoral students, leveraging the CAAM (University Center for Archaeometry and Microanalysis), with a consortium of academic and private partners that included, among its multiple objectives, the creation of a training path for a new competitive professional figure in the current job market: the archaeologist expert in managing crises of archaeological heritage (natural disasters, conflicts, black market for archaeological goods), thanks to the application of ICT, featuring integrated training modules combining practical training with theoretical courses, laboratory activities, applied technology, and advanced diagnostic protocols (Project link: https://eurotech.udanet.it/mcode=home&cmpcode=schoolrooms&cmd=publiList&id_ctx=52). Regarding the incoming foreign student quota established by the Course for the 2023-2024 academic year, it is 15 units.

Student Opinions From the comparison of the data provided by the PQA, students' opinions are positive with an overall evaluation of 3.62, slightly above the previous year's evaluation (2022 3.61), higher than the area average (3.60) and the university average (3.48). Of the 16 courses evaluated, 87.50% fall under level A and 12.50% under level B, confirming students' overall satisfaction with the teaching provided. The number of courses evaluated remains constant compared to those offered, indicating that the incentive to complete the evaluation forms has been effective, although some courses with a small number of students remain unassessed, as students who delay their exams tend to complete the evaluation forms after the system's data collection period, despite repeated requests to do so before the end of the course or immediately after. In such cases, it will be necessary for the instructor to allocate a specific time during their lessons to conduct the evaluation.

Analyzing in detail the responses to the evaluated questions, small fluctuations in the average score are noted for all questions compared to the 2020-2021 academic year. Clearly positive, with upward trends compared to the previous year, are the evaluations on:
• Consistent implementation of the course as declared on the website with 3.79 (3.75 in 2022)
• Adherence to the teaching schedule with 3.75 (3.74 in 2022)
• The topics covered by the course are interesting with 3.75 (3.61 in 2022)

These data confirm the validity of the teaching choices made at the course level, the quality of teaching, and the overall good organization in the implementation of the teaching path. The updated data from the evaluations will be discussed in the CdS Council meeting in October 2023.

SECTION: Graduate Opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/547

Graduate Opinions According to Alma Laurea data updated as of April 2023, graduates' opinion of the Course of Study is very positive. The overall satisfaction index of the Course of Study is positive at 90.5% with a slight decline compared to the previous year (90.9%), but with a significant increase in graduates who declare themselves highly satisfied with the Course of Study (from 36.4% in 2022 to 42.9% this year). In 2022, 9.1% had not responded, while this year, 4.8% declare themselves more dissatisfied than satisfied and 4.8% are highly dissatisfied; overall, the percentages are better than those of the university. 76.2% of graduates would enroll again in the same course and at the same university. 90.5% of graduates consider the relationship with professors positive, with an increase in the percentage of those expressing a highly positive judgment from 45.5% in 2022 to 52.4% in 2023, while the percentage of graduates dissatisfied with the relationship with professors is 4.8% for those who consider it partially negative and an equal percentage who consider it entirely negative. Regarding computer workstations, there is a decrease in users compared to the previous year (from 72.7% to 57.1%) and a deterioration in evaluation, with only 16.7% of students considering them adequate (62.5% in 2022), despite recent enhancements to both the network and computer equipment in classrooms. The evaluation of classrooms and teaching equipment has improved significantly, with 94.5% of students considering them adequate (81.9% in 2022). Graduates' opinion of library services remains fairly positive (72.2%), but compared to last year, 28% of graduates consider the service fairly inadequate. The average graduation age has slightly decreased compared to 2022 to 28.5 for LM2 (30.8 previously), and 29.3 for LM89 (29.4 previously). This relates to the average duration of the course, which has decreased with a delay index of 0.84 for LM2 and 0.57 for LM89. These data are partly influenced by the fact that a significant number of students enrolled in this Course of Study are pursuing it as a second or third degree, or are already working, with 62-69% of students reporting work experience during their studies, of which 12.5% work full-time, with very different schedules and needs compared to a first-time Master's student. On the other hand, the delay is attributed to the health emergency, which in many cases prevented thesis work due to library, museum, and superintendent warehouse closures, as well as general movement restrictions during lockdowns. This gap, as shown by the data, is gradually being absorbed. The percentage of graduates intending to continue their education with post-graduation experiences is declining for both pathways (50% for LM2; 38.5% for LM89), with 15.4% of LM89 aiming for specialization, 7.7% for a master's or other professional experience. In LM2, 12.5% aim for a PhD, 25% for specialization, while 12.5% for a master's. In recent years, efforts have been made to create opportunities for third-level training in Cultural Heritage, such as the second-level Master in 'Sciences and Technologies for Risk Archaeological Heritage' (StArch) and two doctoral programs in Cultural Heritage Studies, Texts, Writings, Images, and Geosciences. Updated data will be discussed at the Course of Study Council meeting in October 2023.

Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Graduates must demonstrate organizational and managerial skills to operate with defined levels of autonomy and integrate quickly into the workplace; ability to produce written texts and use main computer tools for data management and telematic communication in their specific fields; a high-level education in complementary sectors of Cultural Heritage; adequate language knowledge to integrate into research and work environments on a broad scale. To this end, both guided study hours within each discipline and specially organized laboratories will be dedicated, where students can directly test their learning level.

Learning Skills (learning skills)
The Course also aims to provide adequate training to access PhD programs and various Specialization Schools, offering the necessary tools to access such post-graduation courses, both nationally and internationally. Graduates of this Master's Degree will possess, at the end of their studies, advanced scientific, theoretical, methodological, and operational competencies in the field of Cultural Heritage for all chronological periods related to archaeological and historical-artistic sectors, acquired through diverse teaching methods (lectures, seminars, internships, placements at public and private entities), forming the basis on which students will build their final thesis, expressing both the acquired competencies and their critical and speculative abilities.

Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The Master's Degree in Archaeological and Historical-Artistic Heritage aims to expand and deepen knowledge in various sectors related to the study of archaeological and historical-artistic research methodologies in theoretical, practical, and experimental aspects, as well as the ability to use the most up-to-date and comprehensive tools for research, source reading, and knowledge of archaeological and artistic artifacts, reaching adequate and in-depth operational competencies in field research, laboratory material investigations, and various forms of heritage valorization. Such knowledge and skills will be verified through end-of-module exams, oral assessments, and written tests to gradually evaluate learning phases. To further enrich the training process, in addition to frontal lectures, regular theoretical-practical seminars of varying duration and practical internship placements will be organized.

The President also maintains direct relations with the University Quality Office, the Evaluation Unit, the Parity Committee of Teachers and Students, and the Humanities School.

These activities aim to design corrective and preventive actions for identified issues and implement improvement plans. Members: Prof. M. C. Brief Description of Related and Complementary Activities
For both pathways, a range of courses is provided that integrates or allows for deeper exploration of aspects beyond the core disciplines or represents their completion. Each student is free to choose individually, in line with their scientific interests and potential future professional fields (e.g., disciplines useful for subsequent teaching engagement or subjects that complement specific research aspects). Some core SSDs are reiterated for both classes to allow students who wish to deepen specific aspects of core disciplines, particularly in archaeological and historical-artistic fields. These activities contribute to achieving the Course of Study's educational goals by enabling students to deepen specific disciplinary areas to further enhance educational objectives, while also contextualizing core disciplines and opening to methodologically and culturally adjacent fields.

Brief Course Description
The BASA Master's Degree Course aims to train highly qualified intellectual personnel in the fields of research, conservation, and valorization of archaeological and historical-artistic heritage, capable of being effectively employed in senior and coordinating roles in the study, cataloging, and information processing of Cultural Heritage management, thanks to a solid specialist preparation provided by the course. The courses focus on disciplines related to archaeology and art history, understood in the broadest sense regarding techniques and production sectors from ancient to contemporary times, with broad openings toward European and extra-European art. Historical-critical and research methodology disciplines form the foundational training of the graduate, enabling them, at the end of their studies, to conduct high-level research, participate independently in scientific and critical debates, and operate at a planning level in companies and public and private entities managing, valorizing, and communicating cultural heritage globally. The Course also aims to provide adequate preparation to access teaching training courses for secondary schools, PhD programs, and various Specialization Schools, which are essential for advancing in the career of direction in the Ministry of Culture, public and private research institutions, and academic research and teaching careers.

External Effectiveness
According to Alma Laurea data updated as of April 2023 regarding the employment situation of our graduates, there is a recovery in the employment rate, especially in the first year after graduation, with an average employment rate of 72.7% across both pathways, exceeding the university average. Data on the time required to secure a job have also improved, at 5 years with 3.1 months, compared to 7.4 months in 2022. However, the percentage of graduates using their acquired skills in their work in the first year has decreased, from 75% in 2022 to 12.5% in 2023, reaching a maximum of 44.4% at three years after graduation. This data necessitates continued improvement in student preparation for the evolving challenges of the job market. Job satisfaction is good and increases proportionally with time, at 5.8 one year after graduation, rising to 7.9 at three years and reaching 8.3 at five years. Salary data are largely similar to the previous year, with values not particularly high but reflecting the salary framework for workers in the Cultural Heritage sector. To further facilitate the integration of our graduates into the Cultural Heritage job market, the Course of Study annually expands curricular internship activities and organizes structured meetings with sector operators (freelancers, ministry officials) and experts in cultural economics and management (economists, marketing and cultural tourism experts), bringing students closer to real work issues and diverse employment opportunities in both public and private sectors. It is noteworthy that this aspect has been particularly emphasized in the last year, with initiatives such as the May 25, 2023 event "I am an Archaeologist and Now What? The Job Market in Archaeology After Graduation," a discussion day organized by archaeology professors in collaboration with the CIA (Italian Archaeologists Confederation). Updated data will be discussed at the Course of Study Council meeting in October 2023.

Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description
The BASA Master's Degree Course aims to train highly qualified intellectual personnel in the fields of research, conservation, and valorization of archaeological and historical-artistic heritage, capable of being effectively employed in the study, cataloging, and information processing of Cultural Heritage management, thanks to a solid specialist preparation provided by the course. The courses focus on disciplines related to archaeology and art history, understood in the broadest sense regarding techniques and production sectors from ancient to contemporary times, with broad openings toward European and extra-European art. Historical-critical and research methodology disciplines form the foundational training of the graduate, enabling them, at the end of their studies, to conduct high-level research, participate independently in critical debates, and operate at a planning level in companies and public entities managing, valorizing, and communicating cultural heritage globally. The Course also aims to provide adequate preparation to access teaching training courses for secondary schools, PhD programs, and various Specialization Schools, which are essential for advancing in the career of direction in Archaeological Superintendencies, public and private research institutions, and academic research and teaching careers. The educational path is structured over two years, with the first year dedicated to core disciplines of the course, including ancient and medieval history, archaeology, and art history; the second year is dedicated to technical-scientific and methodological disciplines, from legislation to archaeometric disciplines, alongside some strictly humanistic sectors to complete the reference cultural framework.

Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Placement Agreements
Since 2018, the internship office, on the indication of the responsible Dr. Ricciardi, has prepared a final internship evaluation form (by the host organization's tutor), which was updated last year (see attachment). The form, intended for the host organization, consists of eight multiple-choice questions and two open-ended questions to illustrate any shortcomings detected during the internship and propose improvement suggestions. The multiple-choice questions aim to evaluate the intern's preparation in both basic and transversal skills, the achievement of the training project's goals, the relationship between the organization and the intern, and between the organization and the university. The responses received are positive, predominantly from external internships, but also from internal ones. In 2022, eight students completed external internships. The company tutors' evaluations were very positive, all project goals were achieved, the relationship with the intern was excellent, and the relationship with the university was excellent.

The host organization considers the internship activity very useful and overall highly satisfactory, and the competencies provided by the Course of Study are very appropriate. In 2022, three additional agreements were activated (Arte e Fede Association, Agreement No. 102 dated 05/04/2022; Museum of the 19th Century of Pescara, Agreement No. 103 dated 13/12/2022; State Archives of L'Aquila, Agreement No. 104 dated 05/04/2022), and three more in 2023 (Loreto Aprutino Civic Museums Foundation, Agreement No. 106 dated 10/01/2023; State Archives of Chieti, Agreement No. 107 dated 21/03/2023; Diocese of Pescara-Penne, Agreement No. 109 dated 21/03/2023). Students completing external curricular internships must submit, along with their internship transcript, a report on the activity performed and an evaluation form from the host organization. Students have expressed great enthusiasm in their final reports for the work done, which allowed them to engage with stimulating work environments where they actively participated, encountering new educational contexts. In all activities, the presence of company tutors was significant, who closely followed students, completing very positive evaluation forms, including for relations with the Department and the Course of Study Tutor. The Course of Study intends to continue its actions, strengthen relations with already involved entities, and further expand agreements, especially with entities operating in the territory to improve synergies with the university and facilitate future job opportunities for our graduates. Updated data on these activities will be discussed at the Course of Study Council meeting in October 2023.

Entry, Pathway, and Exit Data
Data provided by the University regarding enrollments for the 2022-2023 academic year, after a decline in the 2021-2022 academic year (34 enrollments), show a rebound to 2020-2021 levels (45 enrollments) with 42 enrollments, for a total of 111 students in the Course of Study, of which 71 are in course and 41 are out of course. Data demonstrate the continued positive trend in the regularity of the study path, with an increase in the average number of exams passed (3.39 in 2021, compared to 3.18 in 2020) and the percentage of acquired CFU relative to required CFU (45% in 2021, 43% in 2020), although there appears to be a slight decline in these values for 2022, though data are not yet final. This result is due to both the general improvement in course structuring (minor changes in the distribution of courses across the two years and semesters, updating the educational offer) and the increase in students coming from a specific three-year degree, enrolling in the Master's as a natural continuation of their education. Monitoring will continue, especially through in-course tutoring. The number of students who manage to acquire between 45 and 60 CFU in the first year and between 90 and 120 CFU in the second remains low, with most students achieving between 18 and 45 CFU in the first year and between 36 and 60 CFU in the second, without significant fluctuations compared to the previous cohort. It has been repeatedly noted in various settings (Course of Study Councils, GAQ meetings) that a non-negligible number of enrolled students are pursuing their second or third degree and are working, making their study schedule very different from that of a regular first-time Master's student. Within the GAQ, it was proposed to incentivize part-time enrollment for this student category, but it remains an option chosen by a limited number of students. In light of the CFU data, as will be discussed later based on graduate data, a constant number of graduates obtain their degree on time (6 in course), 11 within one year, and 5 two years or more, indicating that student careers are gradually improving, although a significant portion of students remain inactive. The main motivation for choosing this course remains cultural (76.9% for LM89, 37.5% for LM2), but professional factors are also added, with 62% of LM2 students stating they chose the course for cultural and professional reasons, indicating that students are increasingly aware that completing the full educational cycle (3+2) is necessary to acquire the competencies required to enter the Cultural Heritage job market. Most graduates in 2022 obtained their degree with the highest marks (14), as in previous years, with an average exam score close to 29. The absolute negative data remain the lack of study periods abroad, with none of the graduates having undertaken this experience. The Course of Study is working to improve this, both by enhancing existing agreements under the Erasmus program and by accrediting study periods abroad through international agreements formalized by various faculty members in recent years. Some recent requests to the Course of Study Council give hope for improvement. Regarding student geographical origin, the regional pool remains stable (with a peak of 92.3% for LM89), with nearly 34% of students coming from outside the region (7.7% for LM2, 28% for LM89), indicating the course's good attractiveness and geographical positioning as a preferred reference for neighboring regions. The social background of students is medium, with 15.4% high for LM89, while the percentage of students for whom neither parent is a graduate remains very high (100% for LM2; 84.6% for LM89). Updated data will be discussed at the Course of Study Council meeting in October 2023.

Final Exam Characteristics
The final exam consists of the elaboration and discussion of a thesis in which the candidate must demonstrate the ability to express original research content, showing knowledge and application of the most advanced sector-specific scientific research methods. The thesis will be supervised by a faculty member and a co-supervisor and must focus on one of the core disciplinary areas of the chosen curriculum. The thesis must include an abstract in English of 700 words.

Final Exam Execution
The thesis elaboration will be supervised by a faculty member (supervisor) and another faculty member with relevant scientific interests (co-supervisor), focusing on one of the core disciplinary areas of the chosen curriculum. The thesis must include an English abstract of 700 words and a development consistent with the topics covered, including all necessary graphical, photographic, and documentary material for understanding. The final exam requires a public discussion before a committee composed of a minimum of seven faculty members of the course and/or external co-supervisors. The discussion of the thesis is conducted in Italian, but it is possible, with the supervisor's agreement, to conduct it in English. The judging committee assigns the final grade in hundredths and may, unanimously, award the highest grade with honors. The minimum grade is 66/110. The committee awards up to a maximum of 6 points for the final exam based on the scientific quality and originality of the thesis, the candidate's scientific maturity, and the ability to synthesize and communicate clearly during the exam. Students who have completed a study period within the Erasmus project or international agreements activated by the reference Department (DILASS) and the involved Department (DISPUTER) receive an additional point in the final grade.

To clarify the type of theses required for the final exam, some titles of theses discussed in recent graduation sessions are listed:
For Archaeology
- Civil medieval architecture of Sulmona from the 13th to 15th century.
- Textile production in the Middle Ages: iconographic and archaeological data compared.
For Art History
- The painted decoration of Santa Maria Maggiore in Lanciano
- The iconography of Tarot cards
- The funerary sculpture of Antonio Baboccio
- Monte Cassino and the Bestiary
- The hermitages of Val Roveto
- The Madonna with Child of Santa Maria Maggiore in Florence

Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission Candidates who hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as suitable according to current regulations (art. 6, paragraph 2, D.M. 270/04) and possess adequate preparation and qualifications suitable for the admission exam may be admitted to the first-level Bachelor's Degree in Occupational Therapy (class L/SNT2).
Admission to the Study Program is quota-driven in accordance with law 264/99. The University, in implementing the annual decrees issued for admission purposes, verifies the adequacy of general culture and logical reasoning knowledge, as well as theoretical/practical knowledge and current regulations specific to the discipline and functional to subsequent professional application, and knowledge of scientific-mathematical culture, statistics, computer science, English, and human and social sciences.
Admission to the Bachelor's Degree in Occupational Therapy (class L/SNT2) following transfer from a different Bachelor's Degree program (not Occupational Therapy, even if belonging to the same class or another program at the same University) is possible within available places. Recognition of studies completed at other Italian Universities, as well as credits earned there, may be granted after review of the curriculum transmitted by the originating University and the accredited course programs at that University.
The admission test used to verify the possession of adequate knowledge and skills will be used for compiling the merit ranking and assigning additional educational obligations (OFA). Specifically, admitted students who score below 25% of the maximum score in Biology and Physics in the entrance test will be assigned additional educational obligations (OFA) to be fulfilled during the first year of the course with the relevant verification methods.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L644] OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY
TYPE:
CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Admission procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/618

Admission procedures Article 4 excerpt from the study program regulations for Occupational Therapy.
Required knowledge for admission Candidates who possess a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as suitable according to current regulations (Article 6, paragraph 2, Ministerial Decree 270/04) and who have adequate preparation and are qualified for the admission exam may be admitted to the first-level Bachelor's Degree in Occupational Therapy (class L/SNT2).
Admission to the study program is quota-based in accordance with Law 264/99. The University, in implementing the annual decrees issued for admission purposes, verifies the adequacy of general culture and logical reasoning knowledge, as well as theoretical/practical knowledge and current regulations specific to the discipline and functional to subsequent professional application, and knowledge of scientific-mathematical culture, statistics, computer science, English, and human and social sciences.
The admission test used to verify the possession of adequate knowledge and skills will be used for the preparation of the merit ranking and for the assignment of additional educational requirements (OFA). Admission to the Occupational Therapy Bachelor's Degree (enabling the health profession of Occupational Therapist) is granted to candidates who rank favorably in the merit ranking, within the programmed number of students. Students admitted to the program who score below 25% of the maximum score in Biology and Physics on the entrance test will be assigned additional educational requirements (OFA) to be completed during the first year of study with the relevant verification methods. Fulfillment of OFA involves the assignment of training activities for each discipline in which the student has shown deficiency. Evaluation will be conducted through the successful completion of a final exam, requiring qualification to be taken within the first year of study and no later than the deadline for renewal of enrollment in the second year, with methods established by the Course Director and the instructors of the relevant courses. It is mandatory to complete the activities necessary for OFA recovery, which is a prerequisite for passing the verification exam. Failure to fulfill OFA within the specified deadlines will result in automatic enrollment in the first year out of sequence. Completion of additional educational requirements does not grant additional credit points beyond those in the curriculum, and the related activities are not part of the study plan. For current regulations on additional educational requirements (OFA), refer to Article 28 of the University Academic Regulations.
Admission to the Occupational Therapy Bachelor's Degree (class L/SNT2) following transfer from a different Bachelor's Degree not in Occupational Therapy (class L/SNT2), even if belonging to the same class or another study program at the same University, is possible within available spots. Recognition of studies completed at Bachelor's Degrees of other Italian Universities, as well as credits earned there, may be granted after review of the curriculum transmitted by the originating University and the course programs accredited at that University.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L644] OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY
SECTION: Admission Procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/618

Admission Procedures: Candidates who possess the high school diploma or another foreign degree recognized as suitable according to current regulations (art. 6, paragraph 2, DM 270/04) and who possess adequate preparation and are qualified for the admission exam can be admitted to the first-level Degree Course in Occupational Therapy (class L/SNT2).
The available places for the Occupational Therapy Degree Course (class L/SNT2) are determined annually by a decree of the Ministry of Education, University, and Research, hereinafter referred to as MIUR, in relation to the actual availability of teaching staff, suitable teaching and scientific facilities (classrooms, laboratories for practical exercises and biomedical research), and services operating in the local structures contracted with the National Health Service, and in relation to the University's proposal, taking into account sustainability at the level of human and instrumental resources.
Access to the Study Course requires a national admission exam prepared by MIUR, consisting of a multiple-choice test on topics of general culture, logic, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology.
For admission to the courses, a general culture is required, with particular relevance to literary, historical-philosophical, social, and institutional fields, as well as the ability to analyze written texts of various types and aptitude for logical-mathematical reasoning, as indicated annually in the call.
Moreover, the required knowledge and skills still refer to the preparation promoted by educational institutions that organize educational and teaching activities consistent with the Ministry's Programs, especially in view of the State Exams, and also relate to the scientific disciplines of Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics.
The content and format of the test are normally established annually by MIUR through a decree and indicated each year in the University's competitive call.
Finally, the University establishes preparatory courses for admission competitions to Health Professions, based on theoretical foundations, exercises, and simulations on the subjects specified in the call.
Admission to the Occupational Therapy Degree Course (class L/SNT2) following a transfer from a different Degree Course (not Occupational Therapy, class L/SNT2), even if belonging to the same class, is subject to passing the admission exam and is possible within the available places.
Information on administrative procedures and required fees for registration to the admission test, if applicable, and for the recognition of acquired credits is available on the University's website at the following link: www.unich.it
Program, Texts, and Objectives Communication Skills (communication skills)
At the end of the study program, Occupational Therapy graduates will be able to manage communication in the following ways:
- Establish a meaningful therapeutic relationship with the person, their family, and caregivers
- Establish effective collaborative relationships with other members of the healthcare team
- Use professional tools such as the rehabilitation record, clinical report, and rehabilitation project, drafting them clearly, concisely, and professionally
- Translate technical language in a way that is understandable even to those not in the professional field
- Use appropriate tools for scientific communication, also in English.
Communication skills will be developed throughout the entire educational path, particularly through the courses characteristic of the profession, seminars, laboratories, and clinical internship.
Teaching tools: classroom activities, teaching laboratories, practical lessons in laboratories and/or equipped classrooms, Clinical Internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.
Assessment methods (which can be conducted in person or exceptionally in virtual form): written reports on the communication aspects of the rehabilitation setting; briefings with tutors and the coordinator; oral and written presentation of projects; Clinical Internship.

Judgment Autonomy (making judgments)
At the end of the training path, graduates in Occupational Therapy will be able to exercise decision-making and operational judgment autonomy in conducting the therapeutic process, using clinical reasoning as a method and reflecting on the social and ethical implications related to the application of knowledge and operational norms.
This autonomy will be realized in all phases of the Occupational Therapy rehabilitation process, particularly through the ability to:
- identify, through the evaluation of clinical data in the psychomotor, cognitive, functional and relational fields, the health needs of the subject in different life stages, also in relation to the presented psychological conditions;
- define functional prognosis and therapeutic goals
- choose and plan strategies, methodologies and techniques to promote health and well-being through the use of occupation and the involvement of the patient or caregiver,
- integrate the resources of the assisted person and the environment with individual and/or collective health needs,
- evaluate using appropriate outcome measures as the result of the intervention,
- compare and use the best scientific evidence, international guidelines, best practices and expert experience in the discipline.
- judgment autonomy will be achieved through the entire training path, particularly through the teaching specific to the profession, seminars and laboratories as well as through the clinical internship.
Verification methods (to be carried out in person or exceptionally in virtual form): written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, clinical case discussions, definition of the Rehabilitation Plan/Program and completion of the clinical record.

Orientation in Entry The 'G. d'Annunzio' University, through its Orientation, Placement, Right to Study and Disability Sector, provides support to Upper Secondary School students in making the challenging choice of the most suitable academic course for their abilities, assisting them in university studies to prevent initial evaluation errors from causing delays or abandonment of the chosen path, and ultimately facilitating their entry into the job market and professions. Orientation encompasses a set of services offered by the University of Chieti-Pescara "Gabriele d'Annunzio" to improve students' relationship with the University, accompanying them throughout their academic journey from the choice of educational path to entry into the workforce through specific and targeted activities for prospective students, enrolled students, and graduates.
The service is coordinated by a Deputy Rector for Orientation, appointed by the School of Medicine and Health Sciences (Prof. Giustino Orlando), assisted by the interim Sector Manager (Mr. Marco Costantini) and a Department Representative for the Program, appointed by the Department Director (Prof. Mirco Fasolo). Entry-level orientation services include periodic public presentations of the educational offer, to which Upper Secondary School students from the territory and from out-of-region schools that request it are invited, along with participation in orientation fairs organized by various national entities.
Orientation services are provided by organizing presentations of the Educational Offer, coordinating University orientation with Department orientation, and involving Upper Secondary School students in meetings and seminars at school institutions:
- Open Days: Annual event held at the Chieti and Pescara campuses, inviting all Upper Secondary Schools in the Abruzzo region and neighboring regions. During this event, the University presents its wide range of study paths within an Educational Offer structured into 4 main academic areas (Health, Scientific, Social, and Humanities) and organized into 68 Programs offered by 14 Departments.
- Student Fairs and Exhibitions: Events where direct meetings with Department and Program professors are possible to deepen knowledge of the University and understand its opportunities. The University organizes its own Student Fair but also actively participates in Student Fairs organized by other cities throughout the academic year (e.g., Macerata, Fermo, Ascoli Piceno, Bari, etc.), as well as abroad (e.g., University of Tirana).
- School Visits: Presentations of Programs and seminars organized by Departments or the Program itself to guide Upper Secondary School students in transitioning from graduation to university studies.
- Urban Box: The "d'Annunzio" University has signed an agreement with the City of Pescara for the use of the Urban Box in Piazza della Rinascita as a meeting point with young people and citizens. The Urban Box serves as a showcase facing the city of Pescara where the University's Educational Offer is presented interactively through videos, brochures, and staff.
- PNRR 2026 Orientation: Following requests from Upper Secondary Schools to activate PNRR School-University Orientation agreements, orientation courses are offered at the University. From the start of the academic year until May, 15-hour orientation courses for different schools are scheduled, held in person and following two modalities: one day of course held at the Chieti campus, featuring a module explaining the university system and TOLC tests, and two separate modules presenting all Health and Scientific area Programs. The second day of course, held at the Pescara campus, involves courses aimed at presenting Social-Humanistic area Programs and all tools for choosing a university path. At the end of the course, the AlmaOrientati questionnaire is administered to better understand each student's profile. Based on the results, students can further explore their test outcomes with the support of experts from each of the four areas present at the Pescara campus.
- Unveiled Universities: CRUI has decided to establish the National University Day on March 20, coinciding with International Happiness Day and within the Minerva Week, a period dedicated to celebrating knowledge and education. For this occasion, the University participated with meetings, workshops, and debates organized on campus open to all citizens.
Through collaboration with a group of professors, the orientation service is also responsible for producing both printed and online versions of the Student Guide, an invaluable information tool and first moment of self-orientation, as well as supporting Upper Secondary School students transitioning to university and new enrollees.
The Program Representatives, who participate in various orientation events held across the territory, invite graduating students and students in their fourth year of Upper Secondary School to complete the AlmaOrientati questionnaire available on the University's Orientation portal, a useful tool to help future enrollees monitor their knowledge of the university world and reflect on self-orientation.
The University provides for free a mobile application specifically developed to more easily access the Orientation Services offered by the University of Chieti-Pescara "Gabriele d'Annunzio". Through this application (App Ud'A Orienta), it is possible to learn about the Educational Offer, discover services, inquire about fees, receive updated information on Open Days and all the numerous Orientation initiatives offered by the University.
To support the activities carried out by the University, the Program has sought to identify additional initiatives to provide clear, simple, and immediate answers to information requests from families and prospective students. In particular, the University and the Program publish specific content on the official Program pages (website, Facebook, Instagram), constantly updated with the help of student tutors for orientation, specifically selected through a dedicated call. On the website of the Department of affiliation, demonstrative materials in .pdf format and informative videos about the Program's professional opportunities have also been added.

Ongoing orientation and in-course tutoring Ongoing orientation is implemented through various actions. Firstly, in-course tutoring is conducted by all faculty members of the Study Course, typically during office hours, and is directed at managing student requests regarding study difficulties, program clarifications, and thesis work.
Additionally, designated faculty members of the Study Course are available for student consultation when needed. This Faculty Tutor role is required to coordinate with the teaching activities of the Courses of Instruction that share the same educational objectives.
The Faculty Tutor is involved in resolving issues related to
- ongoing orientation and monitoring of academic progress
- coordination of didactic-integrative and recovery activities where necessary.
The Study Course also offers a psychological counseling service, provided by Dr. Pieramico Valentina, to which students can turn in case of difficulties and distress, and to address any other obstacles to their university life not necessarily related to the educational aspect.
All these activities align with the cultural and professional profile designed by the Study Course.
Within the Study Course, a practical training tutor is appointed for each academic year, selected by the Teaching Coordination Committee from faculty members who have won external calls for teaching assignments in the context of practical training activities. The practical training tutor handles organizational tasks and supports problem resolution related to professional practical training activities.
For the 2023/2024 academic year, the practical training tutor for the Study Course, coordinated by the Professional Teaching Director Dr. Christian Parone, is Dr. Valentina Pieramico.
For ongoing orientation, two 150-hour scholarship holders support students in organizational and planning matters, particularly concerning exams they must take, as well as assisting faculty and practical training tutors in Study Course-related activities.
A 150-hour scholarship holder student was responsible for orientation, supporting activities during the University's orientation days and for practical training activities. The orientation scholarship holder managed the social networks for promoting the Study Course. The service proved effective and impactful for students.
For ongoing orientation strictly focused on student training, non-contracted entities were invited to hold thematic seminars within the Study Course's teaching activities. Specifically, a series of seminars were organized by the MOVI Study and Research Group to present the Vivaio model to first and second-year students, and its application in developmental age to third-year students. Additional specialized seminars on posture systems and aids for low vision, as well as on issues addressed in the schizophrenia patient approach, were offered to students.

Practical training periods The Occupational Therapy Bachelor's Degree Course, like all three-year health-related courses, has a strong practical focus expressed through internship activities. The practical internship is a form of teaching activity that allows the acquisition of professional competencies through the execution of practical activities with varying degrees of autonomy that gradually increase as the student gains experience.
Three-year health degrees require 60 credits of practical internship (professional training in a clinical setting) to be completed from the first to the third year. The Study Course in TO organizes these activities across all relevant areas for the training of an Occupational Therapist, based on the competencies expressed in the professional profile. All internship activities are carried out at specialized health and rehabilitation services, as well as other scientifically significant structures, which meet the specific educational objectives for the professional figure for each academic year. The progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy acquired during the course enables students to develop the correct ability to observe, assess, and intervene in various rehabilitation issues related to pediatric and adult age groups.
Internship agreements are established after careful collection of information to verify the quality of the structure and, if necessary, a preparatory visit to the host site. All practical internship activities are carried out within accredited structures and supervised by clinical/professional tutors, specifically designated by each structure in agreement with the Study Course body responsible, who assist students in acquiring professional competencies. Tutors work closely with the Occupational Therapist Reference for Internships.
The Study Course's internal Internship Tutors serve as the point of reference for students, supporting the tutors present in the structures to improve the training experiences.
The Director of Professional Training, Dr. Christian Parone, in collaboration with the appointed Tutors, identifies the accredited internship sites to enable students to acquire the competencies specified in the professional profile. For each activated internship, a specific training project and an internship agreement are established in agreement with the host site and respecting the prerequisites useful for educational purposes.
During the periods of professional training in a clinical setting, internship tutors conduct periodic formative evaluations to verify progress toward the established goals as well as a certification evaluation at the end of the training period. Throughout the training process, to facilitate the acquisition of professional competencies in the spheres of knowledge, knowing how to be, and knowing how to do, Tutors or Study Course instructors carry out tutoring activities to support the learning process with individual students (if necessary) and the class group.
At the end of each academic year, a commission composed of the Study Course Tutors verifies the professional competencies acquired by the student in the reference year.
The Study Course in Occupational Therapy, through the Internship Tutors, maintains constant contact with public and private specialized structures that host students in the territory.
Starting from the 2022/2023 academic year, the revision of the curriculum and consequently the training offer plan, aimed at meeting the requests of stakeholders in the workplace, and the constant feedback before and during the internship, will involve administering evaluation questionnaires to both structure tutors and students completing the internship, in order to allow an evaluation of the professional training experiences and to understand the opinions of the host organizations and students regarding strengths and weaknesses of the structures on one hand and each student on the other.
The student evaluation criteria consider the level of preparation and training, accuracy in performing assigned tasks, regularity in personal commitment, engagement in observation activities, interest in deepening knowledge of work tools, ability to reflect on work experience, ability to connect theoretical aspects with practical activities, and willingness to interact with the tutor. The professional training experiences offered by the accredited host structures are monitored and evaluated by assessing: the significance of the activities and the type of activities performed, the welcome by the tutor, the relationship with the tutor and their working method according to the Study Course operational guidelines, the theoretical-practical correspondence of the TO content, the stimulation received in the structure, and the evaluation of the experience for the purpose of orientation in the workplace.
All students enrolled in the Study Course must, starting from the second semester of the first year, compulsorily complete internship activities at structures outside the Study Course. The number of students varies depending on enrollments in different academic years. For the 2022/2023 academic year, 60 students completed their experience at structures of different types, addressing different Occupational Therapy themes. Over 95% of these students consider the experience satisfactory, thanks also to the presence of an occupational therapist tutor in all chosen structures, unlike previous years.

INTERNATIONAL MOBILITY OFFICE The Department of Neuroscience, Imaging and Clinical Sciences, with the support of the International Relations Office (URI), manages student mobility within bilateral agreements that provide for incoming and outgoing student exchanges within community-funded programs such as the Erasmus+ program. Mobility is encouraged and promoted through the provision of scholarships as well as support in administrative procedures: from contacting the foreign institution, to developing the study plan for international mobility, to recognition of exams taken abroad.
The Department maintains several collaboration agreements with various foreign universities and research laboratories. The main goal is to acquaint students of the Course of Study (CdS) with the importance of international training. This involves sensitizing students to an international perspective on occupational therapy.
Currently, three agreements are active with the University of Coimbra (School of Health Technology, Coimbra, Portugal), with the University of Krakow (University of Physical Education in Krakow, Poland), and with the University of Plzen in the Czech Republic (Zapadoceska Univerzita V Plzni).
Within the call issued during the Academic Year 2022/2023, valid for the Erasmus+ Student project for the Academic Year 2023/2024, four female students were selected, with destinations at the three different partner institutions.
Additionally, calls for international mobility for internship activities only are available: Erasmus+ for Traineeship call. The call aims to promote the activation of internships at companies or training and research centers in one of the European countries participating in the Program. Erasmus students have the opportunity, in this way, to acquire specific skills and a better understanding of the socio-economic culture of the host country, with the support of preparatory or updating courses in the language of the host country (or the working language), with the ultimate goal of promoting the mobility of young workers throughout Europe.
Within the call issued during the Academic Year 2022/2023, valid for the Erasmus+ for Traineeship project for the Academic Year 2023/2024, two applications were submitted, but the rankings are not yet known.
The Department of the Course of Study, represented by the Erasmus relations delegate, in collaboration with the Erasmus coordinator for the Course of Study, organizes annual presentation days for the two Erasmus+ pathways, following the release of the call, to facilitate students in submitting their applications. During these meeting days, students who previously completed a study period abroad are also present to share their experience and assist students in choosing the destination and study methods abroad.

Career Guidance The Program in Occupational Therapy promotes activation and plans extra-curricular training internship projects upon request from new graduates. The Program encourages and implements initiatives to improve interactions with public and private specialized host facilities. Annually, for students approaching their graduation exam, the Program organizes meetings and seminars (open to students and tutors) with local Occupational Therapists to better address training needs. These meetings typically occur in the month preceding the two graduation sessions established by the Course Regulations, during March and October, under the supervision of the annually appointed Internship Tutors.

The University promotes the employability of its students, graduates, and alumni through the activation of an effective network of relationships between University, Enterprises, and Research Systems aimed at developing and consolidating a virtuous cycle of relationships and services, oriented to facilitating the 'communication' between enterprise needs, employment integration processes, and educational impacts, and to providing substance and continuity to the transition phase to work for knowledge resources. The University Placement Service manages orientation and mediation activities introduced by the University through the intervention lines provided by the START Program. All information is available at the Services for Graduates, Alumni (and Students) | Orientation & Placement (unich.it) website.
The Occupational Therapy Program at the University of Chieti currently boasts 100% employability of its graduates who are able to work as occupational therapists within healthcare facilities, predominantly in the private sector, within one year of obtaining their degree. This facilitates the Program's career guidance activities, which do not require specific initiatives due to the high demand for the professional figure.

Student opinions The Bachelor's Degree Course is subject to annual evaluation to monitor overall satisfaction, satisfaction regarding organizational logistics, and satisfaction with teaching effectiveness.
Specifically, the assessment of perceived educational process effectiveness by students is presented by considering some questions from the mandatory evaluation questionnaire under Law 370/99, particularly: interest in the topics covered (D0), adequacy of prior knowledge (D1), adequacy of study load to credits assigned to the course of interest (D3), adequacy of teaching materials (D9), coherence of the taught content (D13), respect for teaching schedule (D14), examination procedures (D16), satisfaction with professors (D20), their clarity of exposition (D21), and their availability to provide clarifications (D22). These questionnaires do not investigate the quality of clinical internship training, which represents 1/3 of the total teaching activities of the entire course. The average score in the student opinion survey indicates that the Degree Course maintains a rating above the average over the years, reaching a score of 3.49 for the 2022/23 academic year. Specifically, all evaluated macro-indicators show scores above the university average and even more so above the entire Health Area average, particularly regarding organizational logistics, confirming that the new internal organization of the Degree Course and the new educational offer plan are effective. The Degree Course has improved from a rating of 3.25 to 3.49 over the last 8 years. The percentage of professors rated in Grade A (3.5 to 4 inclusive) remains high, while less than 2% fall into the lowest rating category. The assessment of professor opinions over the last three cohorts has significantly increased, especially regarding: professors' preparation on the actual role of occupational therapists; full availability of professors from different courses to clarify topics covered in lectures; competence and ability of individual professors to deliver their courses as specified on the Course website, stimulating adequate student interest. Better also the evaluation of the study load required based on the CFU assigned to the course, the organization of lectures and exercises, and the definition of examination methods, confirming the validity of the new Degree Course organization following the modification of the educational offer plan. Over the years, professors have aligned their courses with what is presented on institutional websites, encouraging students to follow a training path aligned with their expectations, as confirmed by the evaluation of question D21, which scores 3.54, significantly exceeding the university averages for health professions.
The assessment of professors' commitment and teaching activities is communicated to individual professors, discussed in the Teaching Committee and the Degree Course Council, and considered for resource allocation. In this regard, the Degree Course Council meeting of September 20, 2022, was dedicated to discussing evaluations received from the University Quality Assurance Office and individual professor evaluations for the latest cohort, as well as discussing and resolving criticalities emerging during the compilation of annual evaluation documents for the Degree Course to meet required parameters and ensure students an adequate training path. Each year, the Degree Course allocates an agenda item in the Degree Course Council meeting for discussing and approving the SUA-CdS tables dedicated to student opinions.
During the compilation of the annual report of the Joint Committee of Professors and Students (CPDS), some criticalities emerged and were discussed. Some have been resolved, others are still under evaluation. A methodological limitation in collecting information/evaluations regarding individual courses was identified, but this issue was effectively resolved by the University Quality Assurance Office during the year.
The collected and analyzed data unfortunately also reveal some chronic criticalities primarily related to logistical and infrastructural issues. Criticalities with scores below the university average concern: a) perceived low adequacy of computer workstations and equipment for non-lectural teaching activities; b) presence of inadequate and insufficiently equipped classrooms and laboratories; c) inadequacy of libraries available to students. These criticalities stem from the fact that the Occupational Therapy Degree Course is based at CUMS, which is far from the Campus and thus from the services it provides (library, computer classrooms, etc.).
Some criticalities identified in the previous academic year have significantly improved, but others, outside the Degree Course's responsibility, will be managed at the university level.
Over the years, the University has activated a service (i.e., "Talk to Us to Grow Together") aimed at improving the quality of services offered, allowing various categories (such as: prospective student, student, families, graduate, professor, administrative staff, companies, others) to submit complaints, suggestions, or praise in different areas (teaching, facilities, services, and internationalization) via an online form.
