ALUMNI OPINIONS The survey of graduate opinions is constantly and significantly increasing. The analysis of graduate opinions, conducted by the University Quality Assurance Office for the year 2023, reveals an improvement in the course performance in all three areas defined by the macro-indicators: logistical-organizational aspects, teaching facilities, and overall satisfaction. The areas of greatest criticality, but which have also seen a clear improvement from the latest cohort, concern the course organization in terms of class and exam schedules and the secretariat service. A clearly positive judgment, exceeding even the average of the University's health area, was obtained for the support provided to carry out the internship activity. The absence of evaluation for potential study experiences abroad is due to the recent activation of agreements with foreign universities for Erasmus Plus projects. It is hoped that evaluations will improve in future academic years following the changes made and the new reorganization of the Study Course itself.

A decidedly positive response was given by graduates regarding the courses and the overall study load compared to the course duration (3.47 and 3.53 respectively vs. 3.33 and 3.21 averages in the University's health area), as it has been improving over time.

Finally, the overall judgment on internship experiences and the course of study confirms the adequacy of the work done by the Study Course to improve the quality of the educational offer in recent years. The internship experience received a rating of 3.58 from graduates (vs 3.48 average in the University's health area), while the overall course rating was 3.42 (vs 3.31 as the University's health area average).

The analysis of results from the graduate profile survey and the survey on the perceived effectiveness of the educational process by students again shows that the Study Course continues its process of improving the educational offer over the last three cohorts, with a course organization more aligned with student needs. The training received is extremely adequate for the purpose of using acquired competencies in the workplace: over 93% of students consider themselves extremely satisfied, but especially the number of students who, for their current job, consider the professional training acquired and the degree obtained very effective has increased (60%).

The AlmaLaurea data analysis regarding the graduate profile (referring to all satisfaction evaluations for the completed study course, for the latest cohort considered, i.e., students graduating during the calendar year 2022) reveals that the reasons for choosing the Study Course are mostly cultural and professionalizing factors. Almost 80% of enrolled students graduate on time with an average graduation grade of 104.6, and over 83% of graduates are employed and not enrolled in a second-level degree.

Over 90% of students (more than 20% more than the University average) regularly attended more than 75% of the required courses.

Some criticalities remain regarding the perceived adequacy of computer workstations and teaching equipment (laboratories, practical experiences).

Over 85% of graduates would re-enroll in the same study course at the University.

The opinions of graduates, as well as those of students, were widely discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 20, 2022, for the latest cohort considered last year, using the suggestions and criticisms raised during evaluation to improve the organization of the Study Course and the educational offer proposed. The results of the annual discussion are evident in the continuous growth in terms of Study Course evaluation. Every year, the Study Course dedicates a point on the agenda in the Course Council meeting in September/October for the discussion and approval of the SUA-CdS tables related to graduate opinions.

Applying Knowledge and Understanding
Apply knowledge and understanding in a way that demonstrates a professional approach to work, designing and supporting arguments to solve problems in basic and characteristic disciplines. Teaching tools: classroom activities, laboratory sessions, practical lessons in laboratories or equipped classrooms, internship, reading and interpreting international literature, interactive teaching with e-learning tools and methodologies.

The evaluation of such knowledge and understanding capabilities will be carried out through the following verification methods (which can be conducted in person or exceptionally in virtual form): theoretical/practical exams, written reports on technical aspects (compilation of functional diagnosis and rehabilitation program, and verification of the rehabilitation chart), oral and written presentation of projects and practical tests.

Learning Skills
At the end of the study path, the graduate will be able to know and apply, independently, the appropriate rehabilitative therapeutic intervention using clinical reasoning as a guide for selecting options within the various phases of the rehabilitation process. This autonomy will be achieved through the ability to effectively respond to individual and/or collective health needs, as a single operator or in a multidisciplinary team, choosing the best therapeutic strategies, identifying appropriate approaches and tools, collecting data (including social context analysis), functional evaluation/diagnosis, defining prognosis and therapeutic goals in the short, medium, and long term, developing the therapeutic program, selecting and applying appropriate methodologies for the clinical case (including intensity, time, and type of therapeutic approach) according to the best possible scientific evidence and international guidelines and best practices; ethically, it will be manifested through respect for reference regulations, professional, legal, health, and ethical standards.

At the end of the study path, the Occupational Therapy graduate will:
- be aware of the need for continuous knowledge updating,
- be able to design self-education paths and plan the updating of their knowledge through Continuing Medical Education,
- have acquired an effective study methodology allowing, with a high degree of autonomy, further university education,
- be able to consult databases and online information on specific topics, as well as scientific literature, even in English.

This capability will be developed and verified through exam preparation, internship attendance and evaluation, which combines theory with practice, through critical use of scientific literature and bibliography for final exam preparation.

Teaching tools: classroom activities, seminars, simulation laboratories (also in e-learning), internship.

The evaluation of learning skills will be carried out through the following verification methods (which can be conducted in person or exceptionally in virtual form): theoretical-practical exams, written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, clinical case discussions, definition of the Rehabilitation Plan/Program and compilation of the clinical chart for their area of competence.

Knowledge and Understanding
Occupational Therapy graduates, at the end of the training path, will have acquired good mastery of knowledge in both basic and characteristic disciplines, as well as in social/relational and professional practice aspects.

In particular, they will have acquired the necessary cultural and scientific foundations to:
- understand biological phenomena, organ and apparatus functioning mechanisms, motor and psychomotor development, and correlate them with psychological, social, and environmental health dimensions;
- know and understand the principles of elementary physics and their applications in healthcare, biomechanics, and assistive devices;
- know the biochemical bases and regulatory mechanisms of pathophysiological processes, with particular attention to muscles and the Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems;
- know and understand the functioning and structure of the cell, the specificity of eukaryotic cellular structures, bacteria, and viruses, and basic concepts of current biological topics of scientific interest;
- know the essential morphological characteristics and functional mechanisms of systems, apparatuses, and organs in humans and their interactions, particularly regarding sensory organs, Central and Peripheral Nervous Systems, skeletal, muscular, visual, auditory, and respiratory systems in pediatric and adult age;
- know the histological characteristics of tissues: bone, striated muscle, and nervous tissue;
- know the main causes of disease and their pathogenetic mechanisms, fundamental pathophysiological mechanisms of major apparatuses and systems, main human pathogenic microorganisms, and host defense mechanisms;
- know the basics of general sociology with particular attention to socio-cultural aspects within intercultural contexts;
- understand the physio-pathological elements of different clinical situations;
- understand the elements underlying the rehabilitation intervention process;
- know the meaning of occupation, its influence on a person's health status, the relationship between occupation and human development throughout life, including reference to the conceptual components of the ICF;
- know the main models underlying Occupational Therapy practice;
- know the relationship between occupation and environment understood as sociocultural context, environmental resources, urbanistic environment, and institutional environment to promote the elimination of physical and human barriers to enhance participation;
- recognize and understand how changes, psychophysical alterations in development, socio-cultural disorders, and the personal meaning attributed to occupation can affect quality of life;
- know the characteristics of the therapeutic relationship and elements of interpersonal communication;
- know the scientific foundations of general and specific rehabilitation methodologies guiding the Occupational Therapist's actions in various intervention areas as defined by the professional profile;
- know the regulations governing the practice of Occupational Therapy, civil and criminal responsibilities, and related medical-legal implications;
- know the correct methods for consulting international scientific literature;
- know the principles underlying evidence-based medicine;
- know the statistical tools useful for planning research and managing the profession;
- know the organizational characteristics of rehabilitation activities respecting appropriateness, effectiveness, and efficiency criteria;
- know at least one European Union language besides Italian, within their specific area of competence, for general information exchange.

The teaching methods provided to achieve this specific training objective (application of knowledge) include lectures (in-person or virtual), conferences, seminars, working groups, and discussions. The teaching process will utilize modern teaching tools.

The ability to apply acquired knowledge will be acquired through guided activities in university laboratories, in accredited internship sites, and in the territory, especially through multiprofessional and multidisciplinary approaches.

The evaluation of such knowledge and understanding capabilities will be carried out through the following verification methods: oral, written exams, simulated practical tests, written reports, and rehabilitation chart compilations.

Brief Description of Related and Complementary Activities The training cycle focuses on knowledge and understanding of the main criteria for accessibility and full usability of public and private structures and environments by an expanded user base. Basic notions related to architecture works will also be deepened, both in their historical, logical-formal, compositional, typological-distributive, structural, constructive, and technological aspects, as well as their relationships with historical, physical, and environmental contexts.

The general educational objectives aim at acquiring specific competencies related to:
- universal design,
- design for need,
- correct interaction between man and environment.

The main knowledge will be provided to carry out actions for improving the patient's living environment at home, school, workplace, and primary leisure places to implement all daily activities, productive activities, and those qualifying social and relational life.

Frontal teaching is also dedicated to social structures, meaning environments for healthcare and assistance activities, such as hospitals, care homes, rehabilitation centers, nursing homes, etc.; environments for cultural activities, such as libraries, museums, temporary exhibition halls; environments for any other social activity; finally, all other public buildings, including judicial buildings (courts, magistrates' offices, police stations) and administrative buildings (previdential, welfare organizations, etc.).

The training process is structured around frontal teaching hours, where discussion of internship experiences related to specific teaching knowledge becomes central.

Brief Course Description The Occupational Therapy Degree Course falls under the Class of Degrees in Rehabilitation Health Professions (L/SNT2) as defined by the Ministry of University and Research Decree of March 16, 2007. It is structured over three years and is established within the School of Medicine and Health Sciences. The Occupational Therapy Degree Course is qualifying and allows registration in the Professional Register.

Pursuant to Law 10 August 2000, No. 251, Article 2, Paragraph 1, Occupational Therapy graduates are identified as healthcare professionals in the rehabilitation area who, in professional autonomy, perform prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation tasks, as well as functional evaluation procedures to fulfill the competencies specified in the professional profile, in subjects affected by physical, mental, temporary, or permanent disabilities.

The graduate identifies the health needs of the patient, with particular attention to the subject's, family's, and socio-environmental expectations; evaluates difficulties and resources regarding functionality, autonomy, and integration into the living environment; selects appropriate interventions to achieve the maximum possible recovery of abilities and competencies in motor, cognitive, motivational, and occupational areas. They also implement specific interventions and educate families and caregivers on promoting the person's autonomy, propose the selection and implementation of assistive devices and environmental modifications to facilitate occupations, verify the achievement of predefined goals for the best possible quality of life in daily patient life, in domestic, school/work, social environments, and evaluate the quality of rehabilitation results and processes.

Graduates in this class must acquire adequate preparation in basic disciplines, aimed at the best understanding of fundamental physiological and pathological phenomena related to their preventive and curative activities, as well as the maximum capacity for integration with other healthcare professions.

Additionally, knowledge of at least one European Union language besides Italian is required, aimed at both their specific area of competence and the possibility of exchanging general information.

The academic year is organized into annual courses starting in October and ending in the first week of June.

The Occupational Therapy graduate is a Health Area Professional who provides services under a dependent regime:
- in rehabilitation services within the National and Regional Health Service,
- in accredited and contracted private structures,
- in clinical structures,
- in rehabilitation structures and centers,
- in healthcare residential facilities,
- at the patient's home,
- in medical and/or multi-specialty clinics.

Occupational Therapists work in various medical fields, addressing all life stages whenever autonomy is needed.

Occupational Therapy graduates may also provide self-employed activities:
- in prevention,
- in social settings in schools and kindergartens, laboratories, and residential facilities for disabled individuals, as rehabilitation consultants, specialists in therapeutic materials and assistive devices, and in consultancy services.

External Effectiveness The confirmation that the Study Course's objectives provide training with occupational prospects comes from the National Conference of Health Professions Study Courses and AlmaLaurea surveys. AlmaLaurea external effectiveness data report an average employment rate of over 83% for the latest cohort, in line with national averages for the same class. All graduates work as professionals in healthcare structures, predominantly in the private sector, and found employment shortly after graduation. 11% of students chose to enroll in a second-level degree. Nearly 6% are not working but have not pursued further education and are seeking employment. Over 93% of employed graduates consider the competencies acquired during the study course extremely useful and adequate for professional training and are satisfied with their current job, a value close to national averages for the same class. The satisfaction rating for the job performed reflects the national average value (7.5/10).

Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description The educational path aims at acquiring competencies related to the professional profile through the development of knowledge (knowing), practical skills (knowing how), and attitude (being).

Pursuant to current legislation, the Occupational Therapy graduate must possess:
- a good knowledge of the foundations of prerequisite disciplines [Basic Biological Sciences (human anatomy, applied biology, histology); Basic Prerequisite Sciences (biochemistry, physics applied to biomechanics and assistive devices, informatics and information processing); Morpho-genetic Sciences for Occupational Therapy Prevention (physiology, medical genetics, neurophysiology, pharmacology); Neuropsychiatric Sciences in Occupational Therapy (neurology, fundamentals of neuroimaging, psychiatry)];
- a deep knowledge of the characteristic disciplines of the occupational profession [General Foundations of Occupational Therapy I (theoretical foundations of occupational therapy, prerequisites for occupational therapy); General Foundations of Occupational Therapy II (tools in occupational therapy, evaluations in occupational therapy, approaches in occupational therapy: application of models, nursing sciences, assistive sciences)];
- understanding and relationship capabilities with the user [Psychology and Sociology (clinical psychology, general psychology, disability psychology, sociology of cultural and communication processes); Occupational Therapy in Developmental Age (pediatrics, occupational therapy in pediatric age, speech therapy and cognitive processes, occupational therapy in childhood, child psychiatry); Accessibility and Assistive Technologies in Occupational Therapy (autonomy aids, electronic and computer bioengineering, architecture and accessibility); Occupational Therapy in Adult Age (diseases of the locomotor system, physical medicine and rehabilitation and spinal cord injuries, occupational therapy in adult neurological conditions); Occupational Therapy in School Settings (therapeutic aids in developmental age, occupational therapy in school age, developmental psychology and educational psychology, general and social pedagogy); Occupational Therapy in Work Settings (work organization and ergonomics in occupational therapy, general hygiene and applied hygiene, occupational medicine, business organization, medical law, work psychology and organizational psychology); Applied Medical and Surgical Sciences in Occupational Therapy (oncology, internal medicine, rheumatology, occupational therapy in clinical settings, diseases of the visual apparatus, otorhinolaryngology and diseases of the auditory apparatus); Occupational Therapy in Geriatric Age (fundamentals of neuropsychiatry in geriatric age, geriatrics, prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation for chronic conditions, occupational therapy in geriatric age)];
- practical application of Occupational Science (Training internship in neuro-cognitive, psychosocial, and rehabilitation settings; Professional laboratories; Seminars);
- competencies to participate in various forms of professional updating and to engage in research activities in different application areas [Scientific English; Research Methodology (research methodology, medical statistics, psychometrics, research methodology in occupational therapy)].

In formulating the Educational Project, priority is given to the theoretical/practical study of Occupational Science, implemented through lectures and laboratory sessions serving as a bridge to the Professional Training Internship in the qualifying areas of Occupational Therapy. Courses are structured into modules delivered through lectures and laboratory activities.

Learning outcomes are evaluated through optional in-process self-assessment tests for students and a final oral, practical, or written exam (evaluation expressed as pass/fail or out of thirty), aimed at verifying the achievement of the set objectives for each course and necessary for acquiring educational credits. Regarding professional and internship activities, objectives refer to the Professional Profile and are reported on the Internship Sheet and approved by the Course Council.

The final exam of the Course allows the acquisition of 6 educational credits.

Professional Responsibility This area refers to the Occupational Therapist professional assuming responsibility in all professional actions through the achievement of the following competencies:
- in professional conduct, learns to act respecting the professional profile, code of ethics, regulations, and laws related to the profession, develops specific competencies regarding the person and their caregivers.
- acts in the interest of the user, recognizing their abilities, resources, interests, and reference contexts.
- develops a careful awareness of their internal setting, making it available to the user.
- exercises professional autonomy in clinical practice while respecting the user's interests.

Care and Rehabilitation This area refers to the competencies the student must possess to define the therapeutic-occupational project based on the user's emotional, cognitive, motor, and functional abilities. The student develops competencies to identify strategies in the context of temporary or permanent physical and psychological disorders, considering individual resources, specific occupations, and living environments to improve quality of life, autonomy, and occupational performance.

Therapeutic Education This area refers to the competencies the student must possess to define educational projects for both the user and caregivers.

Prevention This area refers to the competencies the student must possess to define occupational projects for primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.

Management This area includes all essential management tools for the correct daily implementation of the Occupational Therapist's actions through the following actions:
- identify the nature of the problem
- analyze
- choose and interpret
- identify the problem resolution, possibly through collaborations.

Training/Self-Training This area encompasses the context in which the Occupational Therapist develops and consolidates their knowledge and competencies:
- identify learning and training objectives with the coordinator and tutor
- evaluate the achievement of objectives
- assume responsibility for their own training and professional development
- self-assess the achievement of objectives
- reflect and self-assess in the implementation of their knowledge and skills.

Communication and Relationship This area defines the relational substrate through which the Occupational Therapy graduate will apply their professional practice within the overall context through:
- professional communication and relationship skills with the user
- knowledge and management of relational dynamics with other professionals, coordinators, and tutors
- acquisition of the ability to interact with colleagues in multidisciplinary teams and operators from other structures
- negotiate objectives with other professionals
- recognize the need for support.

Educational Path The educational path constitutes the necessary cultural, scientific, and relational background to acquire full professional competence and to understand, address, and manage pathological events requiring rehabilitation and/or therapeutic intervention. Such competencies will be acquired through participation in the entire educational path. In particular, through prerequisite disciplines, the student will achieve a solid foundation of knowledge of bodily functions and structures. The professional construct will be guaranteed by the characteristic disciplines of Occupational Therapy. Practical courses will ensure the translation of Occupational Science into clinical practice, experienced through the training internships related to the aforementioned areas. Training in research methodology will enable the acquisition of competencies for professional updating and participation in research activities in various application areas.

The teaching methods provided include lectures, seminars, working groups, and discussions on relevant topics and simulations aimed at achieving the educational path objectives. Traditional teaching activities are complemented by guided internship activities at specialized healthcare services and other scientifically relevant structures, located in Italy or abroad and linked by specific agreements. This training allows for progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy, within which students acquire the ability to observe, evaluate, and intervene in various rehabilitation-related issues across all life stages, with particular attention to ensuring the person's autonomy, integration, and participation, integrating into a team and cooperating with the various figures involved in the rehabilitation project.

Laboratory and internship activities are conducted under the supervision and guidance of professional tutors specifically designated based on communication skills, specifically trained for this role, and assigned for each class.

The learning assessment is evaluated through exam tests, articulated beyond traditional oral or written exams, also including a sequence of in-process tests (self-assessment tests and intermediate discussions), useful for verifying acquired knowledge and competencies.

The educational path is structured, monitored, validated, and optimized in a continuum to acquire the competencies, knowledge, and skills specified in the curriculum profile established by current regulations and the specific objectives of the Course. These specific educational objectives are supported by a faculty aware of the need to use all institutional tools activated by competent bodies for the accreditation of teaching quality. Through these tools, it is possible to measure the improvement of teaching performance in all different phases contributing to the achievement of the first-level degree, in terms of educational path, exams, perceived quality evaluation by students, and acquisition of professional competencies specified in the educational path's specific objectives.

Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements The structuring of the professional internship, even for the previous academic year, remains a complex criticality due to the number of Occupational Therapists available to facilitate student rotation across various sites. However, the situation compared to previous academic years has significantly improved, as many professionals have been hired and immediately available to assume the role of tutor. We anticipate that the situation may further improve in the future, as recent competitive procedures have been conducted in one of the four ASLs in the region.

Internship activities are safeguarded and improved thanks to the consolidated structure of the Internship Office. The presence of the Course's Internship Office, supporting tutors in the structures, greatly enhances the training experiences. A tutor supports the Teaching Director each year to personalize solutions to the needs of different career paths. In synergy with AITO Abruzzo, suppliers of materials related to the profession (wheelchairs and assistive devices), and other sector associations, training events and practical workshops are regularly organized at the Course. New agreements have been established with high-quality structures in the Abruzzo region, expanding the internship experiential offer, and existing agreements with national excellence structures have been renewed, allowing students to complete internship periods when not engaged in teaching activities or in preparation for specific thesis projects.

All internship activities conducted at specialized healthcare services and other scientifically relevant structures satisfy the specific educational objectives for the professional figure. This training allows for progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy, within which students acquire the ability to observe, evaluate, and intervene in various rehabilitation-related issues in pediatric and adult age, to develop the rehabilitation project and individualized rehabilitation program in a team. Students learn to integrate into a work group, cooperating with the various figures involved in the rehabilitation project. Laboratory and internship activities are conducted under the supervision and guidance of professional tutors specifically designated by each structure in agreement with the University. Tutors work closely with the Course's Internship Office representatives.

During the 2022/2023 academic year, with the improvement of the COVID-19 pandemic situation, students from all three cohorts were able to complete their internships regularly.

The comparison with host structures is conducted regularly, with 24 structures involved in the previous academic year.

We have structured a questionnaire regarding the structure's experience, which we sent to structure managers and tutors in July 2023, allowing us to collect their opinions on the first semester and a large part of the second semester.

The questionnaire consists of 12 closed questions followed by a free space for comments. The questions investigate the tutor's experience with interns and the University structure, the tutor's satisfaction with their role, and the impact of interns' presence within their structure.

All structures involved in the internship were contacted via a first email request and a second reminder, with about half of the internship sites responding.

The structures' responses were generally positive regarding questions about the tutor's experience with interns, with all tutors considering the internship very useful for students' interaction with the structure, the team, and other interns. Some criticalities were noted regarding students' preparation, particularly in structures hosting first-year students. We consider these criticalities normal but will use them as a stimulus to improve student preparation upon entering structures. Positive interpersonal relationships developed during the internship experience were noted, with very positive relationships with the University structure, for which "no criticalities" were reported. Tutors also reported positive presence of interns regarding their professional "know-how" and the services offered by the structure.

With the introduction of this new monitoring system for internship activities, the Study Course will dedicate a point on the agenda in the Course Council meeting in September/October for the discussion and approval of the SUA-CdS tables related to opinions of structures and students on the internship experience.

Representatives of social partners express:
• Full agreement with the revised and updated educational objectives for the Occupational Therapy Degree Course, as they are relevant to the professional profile;
• Positive opinion on the presented teaching plan, as it aligns with professional evolution and healthcare organizations' needs, updated to current professional objectives and made competitive at the national level;
• Full satisfaction with the valorization given to professional internship and professional training, in line with the multiple aspects of the profession and thus preparatory for the workplace, further integrated with basic and characteristic courses.

Consultation with National and International Representative Organizations of Goods and Services Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
Consultation with organizations representing goods and services production, professions, and social partners was conducted through meetings of social partners and documentation of meeting outcomes.

Meetings were held by the Steering Committee, previously established and approved in the CCL of February 7, 2017, aimed at identifying periodicity and methods of consultation with recognized organizations as interested parties.

Following the reorganization of the Study Course and the election of the new Study Course Chair, the Steering Committee members are:
- Prof. Stefania Della Penna, Chair of the Occupational Therapy Degree Course;
- Dr. Cecilia Paolini, Vice-Chair of the Course, SUA-CdS Responsible;
- Dr. Christian Parone, President of AITO (Italian Association of Occupational Therapists), Occupational Therapist, winner of the first-year Internship competition;
- Dr. Valentina Pieramico, Occupational Therapist, winner of the first-year Internship competition.

The Steering Committee carefully evaluated the current educational path in light of training needs and professional objectives to ensure adequate, multidisciplinary preparation and competitiveness achieved through the acquisition of competencies covering all areas of the profession, especially considering new advances in technology applied to individualized assistance.

From the consultation between the Chair and Vice-Chair of the Study Course, the AITO representative, Dr. Sara Cavicchia, the representative of the TSRM PSTRP Abruzzo Order, Dr. Christian Parone, occupational therapists representing the workplace, Dr. Valentina Pieramico and Dr. Giuseppe Matera, the occupational therapist representing the Oltre Le Parole Onlus Foundation, Dr. Lorenza D'Arcangelo, and the representative of the Chieti-Lanciano-Vasto ASL, Dr. Prof. Valentina Tomassini, held on January 29, 2024, the educational objectives were revised based on the real needs of Civil Society and the best definition of necessary professional profiles and their placement, following an analytical analysis of the educational offer plan. In particular, the need to provide training enabling future Occupational Therapists to identify temporary and permanent rehabilitation paths for patients across different age groups was considered, with the new educational offer characterizing this Study Course, making it more current than the previous version and thus more attractive at the national level. The new educational proposal derived from consultations with social partners in previous years has introduced new SSDs useful for the Occupational Therapist's knowledge base, structured as a basic path in the first year and characteristic and applied paths in the second and third years, divided into phases focused on different age groups, starting from Occupational Therapy applied to pediatric age, education, adult, work, up to geriatric age. Thanks to the Professional Training Internship carried out in numerous accredited structures of various characteristics, hosting different patient types, students will have the opportunity to apply the knowledge acquired in their educational path to internship activities, which will be aligned with specific phases of the educational path. In this way, the internship activity will be more effective, stimulating students' personal growth.

From the satisfaction data of graduates and employed individuals, extracted from AlmaLaurea, almost 90% of students rate the study course positively, and student evaluations of the internship experience, both in public and private structures, are above the University average. The Study Course boasts a 100% post-graduation employability rate, and the degree obtained is considered effective in the work performed. This course is the only one present in the Abruzzo Region, but graduates work throughout the national territory. Most students would like to complete longer internships in the same place, while currently, multiple experiences in different locations are proposed. The Study Course has organized a series of questionnaires to be submitted to internship structures to evaluate criticalities and strengths of practical activities. Each year, questionnaires are collected from most structures, and the common finding across all questionnaires is the issues regarding the preparation and motivation of first-year students, while interviews with final-year students indicate that the course adequately prepares students for the workplace.

Based on the findings from various contexts, the Study Course proposes to implement improvement actions based on analyses developed and proposals from different monitoring system representatives, monitoring their implementation and evaluating their effectiveness over the years.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data The Study Course has 62 enrolled students. The course has established itself as an attraction pole for the center-south, with almost 40% of students from outside the region. Over the last three cohorts, the number of students from the same municipality as the Study Course or another municipality in the same province continues to increase. The most represented regions remain Campania, Puglia, and Abruzzo, with a significant increase in students from Campania. The course seems to attract students due to the excellent scientific reputation built by the discipline's faculty in recent years. The type of higher education background of new students indicates a prevalence of graduates from professional, technical, and magistral institutes.

Over the last cohorts, after the pandemic, student performance in terms of students in course and graduates remains penalized. The number of students who are off-track/retaking courses remains significant, while the number of graduates has returned to rise, toward a normal course progression. In the latest cohort, the course has returned to having almost 60% of enrolled students graduating on time.

The confirmation of the positive course evaluation is directly reflected in the analysis of productivity data of the Study Course in the first year of study (Student Career Indicator Systems), measured in terms of CFU earned and average exam grades. In the latest cohort, the percentage of CFU acquired based on required effort has further increased, reaching almost 72%.

Student evaluations of exam modalities remain medium-high even in the latest cohort (3.56 out of 4).

Entry, path, and exit data of students were thoroughly discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 20, 2022, for the latest cohort considered last year, to implement improvements in the educational path. The most critical results are analyzed, and improvement proposals are made. Currently, the Study Course needs greater external promotion, with an orientation program targeting full knowledge of the profession in secondary schools and within private structures. Through the Department's orientation delegate, the Study Course plans to implement a targeted orientation path in the next academic year, including not only on-campus days but also materials, demonstrations, and orientation days at school sites. The program will aim to involve not only regional sites but also, as far as possible, extraregional sites through the channels of the National Conference of Occupational Therapy of the Permanent Conference of Health Professions, of which the Study Course Chair and Teaching Director are members.

Every year, the Study Course dedicates a point on the agenda in the Course Council meeting in September/October for the discussion and approval of the SUA-CdS tables dedicated to entry, path, and exit data.

Final Exam Characteristics Pursuant to Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, considering the Guidelines for the Final Exam of Degree Courses in Health Professions Classes, and based on Article 10 of the Study Course Regulations 'FINAL EXAM CHARACTERISTICS', the final exam is recorded with a pass/fail evaluation by the Supervisor with whom the Student prepared the Thesis.

At the end of their educational path, the student accesses the Degree Exam, which the Course Council (CCS) prepares pursuant to Ministerial Decree/MURST No. 136 of June 5, 2001, Article 6.

The final exam is conducted in the presence of a Degree Committee, composed of not less than 5 and not more than 7 members, appointed by the Chair of the School of Medicine and Health Sciences upon recommendation of the Study Course Chair, ensuring representation of University faculty and faculty of the specific profession's SSD (MED/48). Representatives of the Italian Association of Occupational Therapists and a Ministry representative are also part of the committee.

The final exam consists of:
a) State Exam: a practical test in which the student must demonstrate acquisition of theoretical-practical and technical-operative knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile. The candidate, before the designated committee, randomly draws envelope 'A' or 'B' containing a written task to be completed, identical for all candidates. The test consists of evaluating a clinical case, describing the occupational therapy rehabilitation path, within 40 minutes. After the committee corrects the written work, if deemed necessary, candidates will be called individually to take the oral exam.
b) Thesis preparation and presentation. The thesis is written during the third year under the supervision of a faculty member (supervisor) chosen by the student, and the presentation occurs in the presence of the Degree Committee and the thesis supervisor. The committee may ask questions to the candidate at the end of the presentation for the purpose of final grade evaluation. After the presentation, the committee meets to evaluate the thesis and produce the final exam and degree grade.

The final exam is annually scheduled in two sessions defined at the national level: the first, typically in October-November; the second, in March-April.

To be admitted to take the Degree Exam, the Student must:
1. attend all Integrated Courses of the Offered Educational Plan for the academic year of enrollment and pass the related exams;
2. obtain, in total, 180 CFU structured over the three years of the Study Course;
3. pass the mandatory professional training internship, evaluated and certified annually with a properly recorded exam;
4. submit to the Student Secretariat, within the specified time, the Degree Application along with a copy of the Thesis.

To discuss the Thesis, the Student must have passed (minimum grade of 18 out of 30) the Practical Exam scheduled in the same session as the Thesis presentation, but not on the same day.

The final exam grade, expressed in hundredths, is determined by summing the following parameters:
1. the average in thirtieths (converted to hundredths) obtained by summing the grades in hundredths achieved in the required curricular exams of: a) Integrated Training Activities, b) Mandatory Internship, c) Single-Discipline Training Activities;
2. points assigned by the Committee to the Practical Exam (from 18/30 to 21/30 = 1 point; from 22/30 to 24/30 = 2 points; from 25/30 to 27/30 = 3 points; from 28/30 to 30/30 = 4 points; 30/30 and summa cum laude = 5 points);
3. points assigned by the Committee to the Thesis discussion can be: from 0 to a maximum of 4 for a compilation thesis, from 0 to a maximum of 6 for an experimental thesis. The indicators used to evaluate the final work and assign the score are: a) originality; b) internal coherence; c) quality of work; d) relevance of work; e) appropriateness between objectives and context in which the work was carried out; f) recognition of criticalities; g) clarity of writing; h) relevance of bibliography; i) effort. Summa cum laude can be awarded, with unanimous committee opinion, to graduates who achieve a final score greater than 110;
4. if the Student completes the Study Course within three academic years, they receive an additional point on the final degree grade;
5. if the Student participates in an Erasmus+ program during their study path, they receive an additional point on the final degree grade.

Final Exam Execution Methods Final Exam Execution Methods Pursuant to Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, considering the Guidelines for the Final Exam of Degree Courses in Health Professions Classes, and based on Article 10 of the Study Course Regulations 'FINAL EXAM CHARACTERISTICS', the final exam is recorded with a pass/fail evaluation by the Supervisor with whom the Student prepared the Thesis.

At the end of their educational path, the student accesses the Degree Exam, which the Course Council (CCS) prepares pursuant to Ministerial Decree/MURST No. 136 of June 5, 2001, Article 6.

The final exam is conducted in the presence of a Degree Committee, composed of not less than 5 and not more than 7 members, appointed by the Chair of the School of Medicine and Health Sciences upon recommendation of the Study Course Chair, ensuring representation of University faculty and faculty of the specific profession's SSD (MED/48). Representatives of the Italian Association of Occupational Therapists and a Ministry representative are also part of the committee.

The final exam consists of:
a) State Exam: a practical test in which the student must demonstrate acquisition of theoretical-practical and technical-operative knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile. The test consists of evaluating a clinical case, describing the occupational therapy rehabilitation path, and subsequent discussion in front of the committee or through a written work within 40-60 minutes. If the committee decides to opt for a written work, after correction by the committee, candidates may be called individually for an oral exam if deemed necessary.
b) Thesis preparation and presentation. The thesis presentation occurs in the presence of the Degree Committee and the thesis supervisor. For the purpose of final grade evaluation, the committee may ask questions to the candidate at the end of the presentation. After the presentations for the session, the committee meets to evaluate each candidate's thesis and produce the final exam and degree grade.

To be admitted to take the Degree Exam, the Student must:
1. attend all Integrated Courses of the Offered Educational Plan for the academic year of enrollment and pass the related exams;
2. obtain, in total, 180 CFU structured over the three years of the Study Course;
3. pass the mandatory professional training internship, evaluated and certified annually with a properly recorded exam;
4. upload the Degree Application and the thesis copy to the Study Course website within the specified time: https://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-studio/terapia-occupazionale-l644/tesi

Admission Requirements Candidates may be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree Program in Medical Radiology, Imaging and Radiotherapy Techniques if they hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent.
The required prerequisites for students enrolling in the program should include good interpersonal skills, good teamwork abilities, and problem analysis and resolution skills.
Admission to the Bachelor's Degree Program is quota-controlled under Law 264/99 and requires an admission exam consisting of a multiple-choice test.
A sufficient preparation in physics and mathematics is required for admission to the Bachelor's Degree Program in Medical Radiology, Imaging and Radiotherapy Techniques.
Students admitted to the program who score below 25% of the maximum score in Mathematics, Physics, Biology and Chemistry will be assigned Additional Educational Obligations (OFA).
For students admitted with OFA, who have been duly informed of the deficiencies, attendance at the additional training activities specifically designed to facilitate recovery within the first year of the program is mandatory.
OFA will be considered fulfilled upon passing the exams related to the disciplinary areas subject to OFA.
Students who fail to fulfill the Additional Educational Obligations, as per Article 28 of the University Regulations, by the date set by the University Bodies and within the first year of the program, may enroll in the second year but will not be permitted to take second-year exams until the individual OFA are fulfilled.

The graduate in Medical Radiology, Imaging and Radiotherapy Techniques:

Evaluation tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes
- Observation of film or written frames, dialogues with structured grids;

Brief Course Description. The Bachelor's Degree in Medical Radiology Techniques, for Imaging and Radiotherapy aims to train healthcare operators (pursuant to Article 3, paragraph 1 of Law August 10, 2000, No. 251) responsible for their actions and authorized to perform radiological investigations and procedures, in compliance with European Union radiation protection standards. Graduates are authorized to perform (in accordance with Law January 31, 1983, No. 25) independently or in collaboration with other healthcare professionals, on medical prescription, all interventions requiring the use of ionizing radiation sources, artificial and natural, thermal, ultrasonic, and nuclear magnetic resonance, as well as interventions for physical or dosimetric protection, to fulfill the competencies specified in their professional profile (Ministry of Health Decree September 26, 1994, No. 746 and subsequent amendments). Additionally, graduates are responsible for controlling the correct operation of assigned equipment, addressing minor issues, and implementing verification and control programs to ensure quality according to predefined indicators and standards; they perform their activities in public or private healthcare facilities, under employment or as independent professionals; contribute to the training of support staff and directly participate in updating their professional profile and research.
Graduates in Medical Radiology Techniques, for Imaging and Radiotherapy must have acquired knowledge, skills, and attitudes to practice the profession of Medical Radiology Healthcare Technician.
To achieve this goal, the graduate in Medical Radiology Techniques, for Imaging and Radiotherapy must demonstrate the ability to:
- manage technical-diagnostic procedures for acquisition and processing of imaging according to scientific evidence and guidelines, including functional imaging procedures in Nuclear Medicine;
- evaluate the quality of the produced iconographic document and whether it meets the specifications in the investigation proposal;
- manage technical diagnostic procedures for transmission and storage of imaging;
- deliver radiotherapy treatments;
- use methodologies and tools for quality control, evaluation, and revision;
- implement radiation protection and safety regulations and use individual protection devices;
- establish professional communication with users and colleagues;
- ensure comfort, safety, and privacy of users during diagnostic investigations and radiotherapy treatments;
- act responsibly towards users and the Service by adopting professional behaviors in line with ethical and deontological principles;
- receive and manage patient preparation for diagnostic investigations or radiotherapy treatments, obtaining informed consent where applicable;
- collaborate with doctors, colleagues, and all staff to ensure optimal Service operation and contribute to solving organizational problems;
- use information systems for data collection, analysis, and information management;
- seek the best scientific evidence to explore areas of uncertainty or improvement in their professional practice;
- know English for exchanging instructions and information within their specific field;
- acquire competencies in Health Physics for supporting the Physics Director in quality controls of radiological, radiotherapy, and nuclear medicine equipment, as well as for supporting the Physics Director in developing radiotherapy treatment plans.
Therefore, the prerequisites required for students enrolling in the course should include good interpersonal skills, good teamwork ability, and skills in analyzing and solving problems.
To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree in Medical Radiology Techniques, for Imaging and Radiotherapy, a sufficient preparation in physics and mathematics is required.

TRAINING PATH. The development of the training path aims to involve three aspects of the Medical Radiology Healthcare Technician professional considered essential:
- motivation and aptitude;
- professional skills;
- scientific culture.
1st Year. Focused on providing a good understanding of essential theoretical disciplines derived from basic sciences, with the perspective of their subsequent professional application. Students will also learn the foundations of disciplines characterizing the Medical Radiology Healthcare Technician profession and concepts of radiation protection and safety as prerequisites for the first internship experience, aimed at orienting students to relevant professional fields and acquiring basic competencies.
2nd Year. Focused on deepening specific sectors, procedures, and techniques of Imaging Diagnostics, such as the Senology field, Computed Tomography, and Magnetic Resonance, as well as Oncology and Radiotherapy.
Additionally, relational and communication skills will be acquired.
Multiple internship experiences are planned in contexts where students can apply the acquired knowledge, methodologies, and techniques.
3rd Year. Specialist deepening with particular reference to Interventional Radiology, Neuroradiology, Nuclear Medicine, and Radiotherapy.
The second semester focuses on acquiring knowledge and methodologies related to professional practice, healthcare legislation, and Service organization, as well as legal, bioethical, and deontological principles inspiring the profession.
The importance assigned to internship experiences increases, where students can gradually assume autonomy and responsibility under expert supervision. This curricular logic is also reflected in the selection of credits assigned to internship experiences, which gradually increase from the 1st to the 3rd year.

More tutors and tutoring collaborations with private structures to avoid overcrowded student days.
Personally, I would propose checking the division of students among respective diagnostics because shifts are often not respected, resulting in 3-4 students in the same room.
I greatly appreciated how my internship has been conducted so far in Vasto. I found a department composed of highly competent technicians, doctors, and nurses who were very available to me. I was guided carefully and precisely, while still feeling autonomous in performing tasks: I am satisfied because I believe I have learned a lot. Beyond the assigned tutors, I noticed that all technicians in the department (not only them, but also doctors and nurses) were eager to teach me and were always available to answer my questions and clarify my doubts. For this reason, I felt very comfortable and integrated from the start. The only suggestion I would make is to start a bit earlier in terms of timing: if I had started a month earlier, I would have been able to complete all the required hours during the year, although I fully understand the organizational difficulties in providing a satisfactory training activity for 38 students. Apart from that, nothing special, and thank you for the opportunity to do my internship in the city where I live.
By setting weekly objectives for students, the internship is overall excellent and well conducted; I would only improve the teaching approach of some tutors.
Allow students to continue a path starting with the most difficult diagnostics.

The Academic Curriculum Consultation Committee, after detailed discussion, expressed a favorable opinion on modifying the Academic Curriculum of the Study Course mentioned above.

Entry, Progression, and Exit Data. Compared to the 2021/2022 cohort (26 enrolled, 16 pure enrollments), in the 2022/2023 academic year, there were 31 enrollments, of which 22 pure enrollments, out of a total of 88 students, 84 in progress, one out of course (regular 75).
The 2022 cohort performance shows an average of 2.86 exams passed per student compared to an average of 5 in 2021, with a CFU acquired/CFU due ratio of 21.7, compared to 55 in 2021. The data shows a further decline compared to previous years.
Regarding 2022 exit data, out of a total of 12 graduates (previous academic year 11 graduates), 8 received a final grade of 110 with honors (9 previous year), 2 received a grade between 105 and 110/110 (2 previous year), and 2 received 110/110. 1 student graduated out of course (previous year 4).
The results will be discussed on the agenda at the next CdS Council meeting to implement appropriate improvement measures.
Final Exam Characteristics. Pursuant to Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, the final exam consists of:
a) a practical exam during which the student must demonstrate having acquired the theoretical-practical and technical-professional knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) preparation of a thesis and its defense.
The final exam is organized, by decree of the Minister of Education, University, and Research in concert with the Minister of Health, in two sessions defined at the national level.
Final Exam Execution. The student has access to 6 CFU (Training Activity 'Final Exam') for preparing the Thesis at facilities designated for training. This student activity is defined as 'Thesis Internship'. The student intending to complete the Thesis Internship must, after contacting the Supervisor Professor, submit a formal request to the Study Course Council President within 12 months for the experimental thesis and 6 months for the compilation thesis from the period in which they intend to obtain the final degree, accompanied by their curriculum (list of exams taken and ADO followed with respective grades, list of laboratories where the mandatory internship was performed, any other activity completed for training purposes) and indicating the Supervisor Professor, the discipline within the Integrated Course for developing the Thesis, and the period they intend to take the final exam. The Study Course Council President, after consulting the relevant professors and confirming their availability, assigns the student to the Supervisor, who will be responsible for controlling and certifying the activities performed by the student in preparing the thesis. It is the student's responsibility to fulfill the obligations imposed by the University Student General Secretariat for the graduation exam.
At the end of their training path, the student accesses the final exam prepared by the Study Course Council in accordance with Decree MURST No. 136 of June 5, 2001, Article 6.
The graduation exam, consisting of practical skill demonstration (Practical Exam – Simulation of radiological investigations) and preparation of a report (Thesis), is organized in two sessions, typically in March and October. The graduation exam Commission is composed of at least 7 and no more than 11 members, appointed by the Rector on the proposal of the Study Course Council.
To be admitted to take the graduation exam, the student must:
a. have attended all Integrated Courses and passed the respective exams;
b. have obtained, in total, 180 CFU distributed over the three years of the Study Course;
c. have passed (minimum grade 18/30) the mandatory professionalizing internship, evaluated with an exam and certified annually through a written report;
d. have submitted to the Student Secretariat the request to the Rector 90 days before the graduation exam, and a copy of the thesis at least 30 days before the graduation exam.
e. have passed (minimum grade 18/30) the Practical Exam scheduled in the same session as the thesis defense.
The graduation exam grade, expressed in centesimal, is determined by the sum of the following parameters:
a. the average in thirtieths (then converted to centesimal) obtained by summing the thirtieths grades from Integrated Course exams and the evaluation of the mandatory professionalizing internship;
b. points assigned by the Commission to the Practical Exam (18/30 to 21/30 = 1 point; 22/30 to 24/30 = 2 points; 25/30 to 27/30 = 3 points; 28/30 to 29/30 = 4 points; 30/30 to 30/30 with honors = 5);
c. The Commission has a maximum of 3 points for the compilation thesis and 4 points for the experimental thesis in evaluating the method, presentation, and discussion. Honors (Lode) can be awarded with the Commission's unanimous opinion to candidates who achieve a final score of 112 or higher. The Academic Mention, in addition to Honors, can only be awarded with the Commission's unanimous consent and exclusively to candidates who graduate on time with a base score of at least 106/110 and have completed an experimental thesis of particular scientific relevance.
Bonus Scores: A maximum of 4 points total, with the following criteria: 1 point for study duration (1 point for students in course); 1 point for number of honors (0.2 points per honor in exams, up to 1 point); 1 point for participation in the Erasmus project with at least 3 months' stay; 1 point for completing the thesis in English.
Summary of the Technical Report of the Evaluation Committee. The Study Course has teaching and structural resources commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The course covers an area of clear professional relevance. The proposed curriculum appears significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, contributing to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the university's training offer.

STUDY PLANS INFORMATION General information related to the current academic year Duration
3 years Regulation
2020
status Open Credits
180 CFU Language Italian Type Normative Degree Course Reform 270/04
Degree Class L-29 - Class of Degrees in Pharmaceutical Sciences and Technologies Joint Course No Programmed Access (120 Places)
Location CHIETI (Sustainable Capacity: 120)
Department DEPARTMENT OF PHARMACY Website https://www.farmacia.unich.it/testa Teaching Method Conventional Admission Requirements Verification of knowledge required for admission Yes Course Teachers View List Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission Students must hold a secondary school diploma obtained in Italy or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent under current regulations.
Basic knowledge is required to successfully follow the degree course. Such knowledge includes satisfactory familiarity with basic mathematical calculation, mastery of fundamental laws of mechanical physics, and basic knowledge of cell biology and general chemistry, logical reasoning skills, ability to express oneself orally and in writing without hesitation or errors, and a good general culture.
The methods for verifying such knowledge and skills will be determined in the course's didactic regulations. If the verification of the required knowledge for admission is not positive, the didactic regulations will specify additional educational obligations to be acquired in the first year of the course.
Admission Methods The Degree Course is subject to a quota. Admission requires a five-year secondary school diploma.
By the 15th of May each year, the Degree Course Council proposes to the Department Council the maximum number of students to enroll in the first year, along with the enrollment and transfer deadlines to be included in the annual study plan.
For the 2024-25 academic year, the programmed student capacity is 120 units, of which 118 for Italian, EU, and non-EU citizens residing in Italy, and two for non-EU citizens residing abroad (Article 26, Law 189 of 30.07.02). In case of exceeding 120 units, a merit ranking will be established based on the secondary school diploma grade, also considering the chronological order of enrollment (in case of equal grades, the chronological order of application submission prevails).
Admission procedures will be adequately advertised on the University website (https://www.unich.it) and on the teaching structure noticeboards.
Enrollment and transfer deadlines are published in the Study Plan and in the admission notice for the Degree Course in TESTA.
Additional Educational Obligations (OFA): criteria for determination and recovery methods Following enrollment, Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) will be defined through multiple-choice questions developed by teachers, containing 80 questions on Chemistry, Biology, Physics, Mathematics, and Logic.
The minimum diploma grade threshold for enrollment without OFA is 80/100. Students with a diploma grade below 80/100 will take the initial knowledge verification test. The recovery of OFA must be completed within the first year of the course and covers the subjects of Mathematics, Physics, Biology, and Chemistry.
Verification of Required Knowledge The initial knowledge verification test (mandatory per DM 270/04) is conducted to identify any educational gaps among new students and to organize necessary recovery activities (additional to the regular teaching activities of the Degree Course), ensuring didactic support for students assigned OFA based on the gaps identified through the initial knowledge verification test.
Students transferring from other institutions, changing degree courses, resuming studies, or enrolling in a subsequent year with career abbreviation will be excluded from the initial knowledge verification. All information regarding the initial knowledge verification test (date, time, location, number of questions, test duration, enrollment methods, scoring criteria for correct, incorrect, or unanswered responses, etc.) will be published in the Admission Notice, on the University website (https://www.unich.it), and on the teaching structure noticeboards.
Specifically, the questions for OFA assignment relate to the following disciplines:
- Physics:
Direct and indirect measurements. Fundamental and derived quantities. Physical dimensions of quantities. Decimal metric system. International System of Units (SI). Units of measurement (names and relationships between fundamental and derived units). Multiples and submultiples. Kinematic quantities. Uniform linear motion. Uniformly accelerated linear motion. Uniform circular motion. Harmonic motion. Vectors and vector operations. Forces, moments of forces. Vector composition of forces. Definitions of mass and weight. Acceleration due to gravity. Density and specific weight. Law of universal gravitation. Work. Kinetic energy. Potential energy. Pressure and its units of measurement. Archimedes' principle. Heat propagation mechanisms. Laws of ideal gases. State changes. Basic concepts on acoustic and optical phenomena (reflection, refraction, dispersion). Electrostatics and electrodynamics. Electric field and potential. Electrical resistance and resistivity. Electrical work and power. Effects of electric currents.
- Mathematics:
Natural, integer, rational, and real numbers and their ordering and comparison. Algebraic operations and their properties. Proportions and percentages. Powers and their properties. Scientific notation. Radicals and their properties. Logarithms (base 10 and base e) and their properties. Algebraic expressions. Algebraic equations of first and second degree. Inequalities. Fundamental concepts on functions and their graphical representation. Measurement of lengths, surfaces, and volumes. Measurement of angles in degrees and radians. Sine, cosine, tangent of an angle and their notable values. Cartesian coordinate system in the plane. Equation of a line. Conditions of parallelism and perpendicularity. Distance of a point from a line. Equation of a circle, parabola, hyperbola, ellipse and their representation in the Cartesian plane.
- Chemistry:
States of matter aggregation. Heterogeneous and homogeneous systems. Compounds and elements. Ionic and molecular compounds. Atomic composition (electrons, neutrons, protons). Atomic number and mass number. Atomic weight and molecular weight. Chemical reactions and stoichiometry (balancing and elementary stoichiometric calculations). Concept of mole. Avogadro's number. Solutions. Solution concentration. Concepts of acid and base. Acidity, neutrality, basicity of aqueous solutions. pH. Carbohydrates. Lipids. Amino acids and proteins. Nucleic acids.
- Biology:
Organic molecules present in living organisms and their functions. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Animal and plant cells. Cell membrane and its functions. Cellular structures and their functions. Cell division: mitosis and meiosis. Chromosomal complement. Animal and plant tissues. Photosynthesis. Glycolysis. Aerobic respiration. Fermentation. Sexual and asexual reproduction. Genes and DNA. Genetic code and its translation. Protein synthesis. Anatomy of main systems and their functions and interactions. General knowledge on viruses, bacteria, and fungi. Main organs and systems of plants and their functions.
Specifically, regarding the verification method for possessing such knowledge, the test, with a maximum time of 120 minutes, consists of 80 multiple-choice questions (4 answers) and is structured as follows:
-20 Chemistry questions
-20 Physics questions
-20 Mathematics questions
-20 Biology questions How Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) are determined The initial knowledge verification test will be conducted after enrollment. Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) will be assigned exclusively to students who answer correctly less than 50% of the questions in the disciplinary areas where recovery activities are provided (Chemistry, Physics, Mathematics, Biology). OFA must be completed within the first year through the recovery methods established by the Course Director and the teachers of the relevant disciplines.
Completing OFA by October 31 of the year following enrollment is mandatory to access official exam sessions for the corresponding courses in the Study Plan.
Recovery Methods Based on the initial knowledge verification, if necessary, the Degree Course will activate additional recovery courses beyond the official course lectures in each disciplinary area where students have educational gaps. In this regard, teachers of the disciplines subject to OFA will establish 1 or 2 weekly hours dedicated to recovery. Attendance at the recovery course is mandatory. Students attending recovery courses are not exempt from the obligation to attend official courses. The educational gap is considered filled upon passing a written verification test.
Failure to complete OFA by October 31 of the year following enrollment will prevent students from taking exams for subsequent years unless they have passed at least 18 CFU related to the courses in the first year of the course within the basic and characteristic types.

Program, texts and objectives Note regarding credits for other activities The CFU window reserved for the final exam, between 3 and 9 CFU, depends on the type of thesis the student intends to pursue (compilatory or experimental). When the student chooses to follow a compilatory thesis path, it will be worth 3 CFU and the student must complete a 150-hour training internship equivalent to 6 CFU. If the student is oriented towards an experimental thesis, it will carry a weight of 9 CFU, with exemption from completing the training internship.
Communication skills
In terms of acquiring adequate knowledge and tools for communication, the graduate must acquire:
- Good scientific communication in Italian and English;
- IT skills, data processing, presentation and discussion of experimental data;
- Ability to work in groups.
- Ability to communicate with non-specialist interlocutors in order to implement prevention and health education interventions for the population in relation to toxicological-environmental aspects.
Written and oral communication skills will be developed during seminars, exercises and internship, which also include the preparation of reports and written documents and oral presentation of the same. The acquisition and assessment of the aforementioned communication skills will also be provided through the preparation of the final exam and its discussion. English (B1 level) is acquired and verified through seminars and e-learning training activities and the corresponding assessment tests.
Both acquisition of the four language skills (reading, writing, listening, and dialogue) and mandatory attendance of lectures may be required, according to criteria to be specified during the course, in line with the requirements of the academic bodies.

SECTION: Judgment autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1865

Judgment autonomy (making judgements)
In terms of acquiring conscious judgment autonomy, graduates in Eco-sustainable Technologies and Environmental Toxicology will be able to:
- evaluate and interpret experimental and process data;
- assess process economics;
- implement a scientific approach to chemical-toxicological issues;
- acquire awareness of environmental risk assessment, toxic compounds, and/or their effects on environmental/food matrices;
- develop evaluations regarding chemical and industrial processes, particularly focusing on monitoring pollutants in the environment and contaminants in food;
- capacity for reflection on social, scientific, or ethical issues related to environmental topics.
These skills will be acquired through foundational, related, and professional training activities, both through attending lectures and practical exercises. Judgment autonomy will be particularly developed through practical exercises, organized seminars, preparation of reports, especially in areas related to toxicological-environmental risk assessment, as well as during internship and training activities and through assignments given by the supervisor for the final exam preparation.
The acquisition of judgment autonomy is verified through the evaluation of laboratory reports, the assessment of the degree of autonomy and ability to work, also in groups, during the assignment prepared for the final exam, as well as the internship.

Ongoing orientation and tutoring Ongoing orientation is conducted by the Dean of the Degree Course, assisted by tutors Prof. Amelia Catladi, Giustino Orlando, and Marcello Locatelli, and the academic office of the Department of Pharmacy. Students may approach the identified teachers/tutors for clarifications regarding courses, internship, and traineeship. Tutors are also appointed for international students, students with disabilities, working students, and student representatives.
For students engaged in documented work activities, a personalized study path may be arranged with individual teachers, including partial exemptions from attending lectures. If students work in laboratories using techniques covered by the laboratory courses of the Degree Course, a partial or total exemption from laboratory attendance may be granted upon prior agreement with the teacher.
The Degree Course promotes accessibility in the facilities hosting the course and in teaching materials for students with disabilities, ensuring the right to education for all enrolled students. Each year, teachers responsible for optional courses make themselves available to inform students about the content of the courses, enabling them to compile a personalized study plan. An annual meeting is organized primarily for second and third-year students to provide necessary information for activating the internship period, both in academic settings and external structures. Upon internship activation, each student is assigned an academic tutor who will follow them throughout the internship period.

International mobility Assistance and agreements for student international mobility ERASMUS PROGRAM Compatible with the requirements specified in the individual agreements and considering the TESTA degree program's affiliation with the Department of Pharmacy, TESTA degree program students can participate in the Erasmus+ program, allowing them to spend a period at the cooperating European universities after passing the selection process, for equivalent study activities to those carried out at our University.
In February 2021, a working group was established at the Department of Pharmacy for the Erasmus project, structured as follows:
Erasmus delegates for the Pharmacy degree program: Alessandra Ammazzalorso and Simone Carradori Erasmus delegates for the CTF degree program: Claudio Ferrante and Cristina Maccallini Erasmus delegate for the TESTA degree program: Simone Carradori and Luigi Menghini Within the working group, activities related to Erasmus agreements were distributed geographically among the agreement referents, as specified below:
ERASMUS agreement referent:
Alessandra Ammazzalorso: Spain Simone Carradori France: Romania Celia Christian: Estonia and Lithuania Viviana di Giacomo: Malta, Poland, Iceland Claudio Ferrante: Croatia, Macedonia, Turkey Cristina Maccallini: Germany, Portugal Luigi Menghini: all other destinations.

For the 2020-2021 academic year, 33 Erasmus agreements are active, offering the possibility of outgoing mobility for 84 students with a total of 752 months of international mobility.
For the 2020-2021 mobility, 50 scholarships were initially allocated (for CTF and Pharmacy students), totaling 307 months, fully or partially utilizing the availability on 25 active bilateral agreements. The actual number of beneficiaries was significantly and dynamically adjusted due to the emergence of the COVID-19 health emergency.
A.A.2021-22
For the 2021-2022 mobility, 38 scholarships were initially allocated (for CTF and Pharmacy students), fully or partially utilizing the availability on 18 active bilateral agreements. The number of mobility applications submitted and actually utilized is significantly lower than previous years but justifiable due to planning uncertainties related to the ongoing COVID-19 health emergency.
A.A.2022-23
For the 2022-2023 academic year, 46 active bilateral agreements offer the possibility of outgoing mobility for 119 students with a total of 1099 months of international mobility. For the 2022/2023 academic year, the student mobility call was unified, covering all European and extra-European cooperating destinations (EU and Overseas mobility).
A.A. 2023-24
No TESTA degree program student utilized international mobility in the 2023/24 academic year, likely due to the specificity of the courses offered in the curriculum, which do not have a counterpart abroad.
