COURSE DESCRIPTION BRIEFLY
The Geological Sciences Degree Course has a duration of three years, has open access, and allows the attainment of the degree in Geological Sciences (Ministerial Degree Class L-34 Geological Sciences). To obtain the degree, 180 credit units (CFUs) must be acquired. The Course guarantees students the acquisition of all basic knowledge for the formation of a modern Geologist, with adequate preparation in basic chemical, physical, mathematical, and computer science disciplines, and a solid training in Earth Sciences disciplines, in their theoretical, experimental, and applied aspects (Physical Geography, Paleontology, Geochemistry, Mineralogy, Petrology, Earth Physics, Geomorphology, Geology, Applied Geology, Geotechnics, Geological Survey and Mapping, GIS - Geographic Information System). The geographical context of the Chieti Pescara University, located between the Apennines and the Adriatic coast, represents an ideal natural laboratory to observe and understand geological processes, the resources derived from them (water, mineral, geo-environmental), and related risks (earthquakes, landslides, floods, coastal dynamics). Therefore, a significant percentage of CFUs is acquired through field training activities, in the form of both daily outings and multi-day field courses. Theoretical lessons will also be integrated with practical laboratory activities (microscopy, rock and fossil recognition, geochemistry, soil mechanics, geological maps and sections, GIS computer laboratory). The Course offers the possibility to acquire CFUs abroad through six Erasmus agreements with six European Universities. After the three-year degree in Geological Sciences, graduates can: - continue studies with a Master's Degree; - access First-Level Master's programs; - access the free profession as 'Junior Geologist' (Section B of the Geologists' Professional Register), after passing the state exam; - be employed as an unqualified geologist (technical functions) in public bodies, institutions, companies, and professional offices. The University of Chieti - Pescara offers direct access to the Master's Degrees of Class LM-74 Geological Sciences and Technologies.

EXTERNAL EFFECTIVENESS
The number of satisfied three-year graduates with the study course is confirmed at 100% for 2022. The number of graduates seeking employment is relatively low since approximately 87% enrolled in a Master's Degree and 20% work while studying. The number of graduates not enrolled in a Master's Degree who are employed or seeking employment is extremely low. Clearly, the three-year program provides good cultural preparation that encourages students to continue, deepening geological topics. At the national level, it is still being discussed to eliminate the professional figure of the Junior Geologist, Section A of the Professional Geologists' Order reserved for three-year graduates in Earth Sciences. Graduates participating in the qualification exam for Section A of the Geologists' Order are very low, practically negligible nationwide. The data confirm that the vast majority of graduates are directed towards enrollment in Master's Degree courses. The data are generally discussed and analyzed in the Annual Monitoring Sheet, the last analysis in the CdS on 12/14/2022, and will be discussed again in December 2023 during the preparation of the 2023 SMA. To improve external effectiveness, the CdS proposes internal orientation activities aimed at improving the attractiveness of the LM-74 Master's Degree course, the main focus of employment for three-year graduates.

SPECIFIC EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES OF THE COURSE AND DESCRIPTION OF THE TRAINING PATH
The increasingly widespread demand for the active presence on the territory of the cultural and professional figure of the geologist imposes the formation of a subject who is equipped with: ° high competence ° broad and qualified preparation ° ability to understand various territorial issues and collaborate in their management. To satisfy these training needs, the degree course aims to confer graduates, in addition to the indispensable 'qualifying knowledge' required by the class, the following specific attributes: ° broad knowledge of the characteristics, processes, history, and materials of the Earth system, even through the autonomous use of textbooks; ° necessary foundations for approaching cutting-edge topics in Earth Sciences; ° ability to identify, collect, analyze, and process geological data from laboratory and field; ° ability to communicate in detail, to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors, geological issues and their resolution procedures; ° training for insertion into work activities, through the acquisition of appropriate technical and scientific skills and methodologies. To achieve the listed objectives, the training path is structured in courses for basic subjects and different sectors of Earth Sciences, delivered through frontal lessons and classroom and laboratory exercises. Additionally, in accordance with the European Descriptors for 'Earth Science', it is considered necessary, to develop a satisfactory understanding of Earth Sciences, to have a significant 'learning experience' and internship in the field (field activities). It is believed that this learning through experience constitutes a particularly valuable aspect of training. Indeed, field studies allow students to develop and enhance many key skills (e.g., work timing, problem-solving ability, self-management, interpersonal relationships), which are valuable elements for employers and lifelong training. Through these guided experiences, students address real geological aspects, conducting specific surveys both in groups and individually; thus, they acquire the following abilities: - reasoning in the spatiotemporal context; - using quantitative methods; - applying theoretical knowledge to real cases; - using thematic mapping methods and synthesis restoration. The final exam consists of the elaboration and presentation of results obtained through the in-depth study of aspects related to 'field' activities. To complete the student's training, internships, traineeships (at public or private bodies, companies, professional orders, etc.), and courses aimed at English language knowledge are provided. Finally, the quality of the activities carried out is also monitored, both through the collection of student opinions and through the acquisition of evaluations from recent graduates regarding the adequacy of the professional preparation achieved. The Degree Course is structured in accordance with the indications (Syllabus) of the College of Presidents of Geological Sciences Study Courses: this ensures the appropriate level of homogeneity of the educational offer and promotes the mobility of students in the Class.

OPINIONS OF ENTITIES AND COMPANIES WITH CURRICULAR OR EXTRA-CURRICULAR INTERNSHIP AGREEMENTS
The three-year degree course does not provide for internships or traineeships at entities or companies; this opportunity has been successfully expanded and generally satisfied in the Master's Degree in Geological Sciences and Technologies as a natural continuation of the three-year degree course.

CONSULTATION WITH REPRESENTATIVE ORGANIZATIONS - AT NATIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL LEVELS - OF GOODS AND SERVICES PRODUCTION, PROFESSIONS (COURSE ESTABLISHMENT)
The three-year Geological Sciences Course underwent a reorganization of the curriculum in the 2008/09 Academic Year. The President, Professor Leandro D'Alessandro, reorganized the course, keeping in mind that Geological Sciences graduates will possess knowledge suitable for practicing the profession in various occupational fields, particularly contributing to activities such as: thematic mapping, assessment of geological hazards, geological risk analysis, geological interventions during prevention and emergency phases for safety, geognostic investigations and subsoil exploration with direct investigations, mechanical methods and simple geophysical methods, recovery of geological resources, assessment and prevention of degradation of cultural and environmental assets, analysis and certification of geological materials, environmental impact assessment regarding geological aspects, geodetic and topographic surveys, execution of geotechnical laboratory tests and analyses, cultural tourism. These professional skills can be applied in public administrations, private institutions, companies, and professional offices. Having taken note of what was reported by Professor D'Alessandro, the consultation provided for in Article 11, paragraph 4 of Ministerial Decree No. 270 of October 22, 2004, is carried out. Following a thorough examination, this consultation proves positive.

SUBSEQUENT CONSULTATION WITH REPRESENTATIVE ORGANIZATIONS - AT NATIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL LEVELS - OF GOODS AND SERVICES PRODUCTION, PROFESSIONS
The Study Course bases its consultations with stakeholders on two advisory committees, one national and one local. National Advisory Committee of the National College of Presidents of Geology and Geophysics Study Courses (Degree Classes L-34, LM-74, and LM-79), composed of a coordination group of the College itself and representatives of interest-bearing parties, including ISPRA, CNR, INGV, INOGS, ENEA, National Civil Protection, ENI, AssoMineraria, Basin Authorities, Regions, National Council of Geologists, Professional Geologists, National Association of Natural Sciences Teachers, Natural Sciences Museums, National Conference of Presidents and Directors of University Structures of Sciences and Technologies. The National Advisory Committee is tasked with interacting with national interest bearers, acquiring opinions and indications through questionnaires on the university training of Geologists, identifying potential deficiencies and critical issues in the university path, and the most promising development lines. The results of the surveys are then processed and transferred to the Presidents of the CdS through documents containing suggestions to guide integration, improvement, and modernization strategies of the CdS courses and Syllabus to refer to, in order to graduate Geologists in line with the demands of the world of work. The National Advisory Committee, presented during the National College of CdS Presidents' Assembly on May 23, 2017, highlighted the need to consolidate/reinforce skills in the fields of applied geology to engineering and hydrogeology, numerical modeling, geological and geomorphological survey, with particular attention to modern numerical techniques and GIS, applied geophysics, as well as in basic physical, chemical, and mathematical disciplines. The most promising employment fields are those of evaluation and management of geological and environmental risks, applied geology and hydrogeology, geothermal energy and renewable energies, research and exploitation of hydrocarbons.

On June 16, 2016, the Study Course Council established a Local Advisory Committee, composed of: Dr. Silvano Agostini (Abruzzo Archaeological Superintendency), Dr. Fabrizio Galadini (National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology), Dr. Geol. Nicola Tullo (President of the Abruzzo Geologists' Order), Professor Marco Ferretti (National Association of Natural Sciences Teachers), Dr. Ing. Iris Flacco (Head of the Energy Policy, Air Quality, and SINA Service, Abruzzo Region), Dr. Stefano Portigliotti (Head of Thales Alenia Space), Professor Pascal Allemand (Laboratory of Geology, University of Lyon 1). On March 28, 2022, the Study Course Council modified the composition of the aforementioned Advisory Committee, which now consists of: Dr. Nicola Labbrozzi – President of the Abruzzo Region Geologists' Order Dr. Barba Salvatore – National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology Dr. Elena Romano – ISPRA, CONS-ANTR (area for integrated assessment of marine-coastal and brackish environmental quality, physical, chemical, and biological, and impacts in the coastal zone in relation to anthropogenic pressures) Dr. Maurizio D'Orefice – ISPRA, GEO-CAR (Service for structural and marine geology, survey, and geological mapping) Dr. Roberto Gambini – Former Head of Global Geothermal Technological Line Enel Green Power, Founder and Chairman RE&E non-profit association (Rethinking Energy & Environment) Ing. Ylenia Mascarucci – Geotechnical Engineer - PROGER spa Ing. Mauro Contestabile – Head of the "Soil Defense" Service, Abruzzo Region (pursuant to Article 3 of the Abruzzo Region Resolution of December 22, 2020) Dr. Cristina Salciccia – President of the Regional Section of the National Association of Natural Sciences Teachers Dr. Lino Olivastri – Confindustria, Vice President of CNCT Dr. Luciano Di Martino – Director of Maiella National Park To the Local Advisory Committee of the first establishment, in December 2020, an opinion was requested on the reform of the CdS prepared by the Council. During the meeting, held remotely, it was noted that the three-year study title does not produce a professional form that can be utilized in the job market, but is simply the first step to proceed to the Master's Degree. It was also noted that Junior Geologists (professionals with a three-year degree) have difficulty finding work, but that, on the other hand, suitable positions are also lacking. Evidently, it should be investigated which aspects could be included in the three-year degree to make the Junior Geologist more 'attractive' to the job market, perhaps by establishing a closer link with the job chains, such as by offering a choice of internships. The committee then proceeded to discuss the reform, considering it well-structured and organized. Finally, the Committee notes that in recent years, we have witnessed significant changes in the behavior of young students. They can easily distance themselves from traditional teaching and feel more secure when learning through alternative teaching methods, such as project-based teaching. The course offers numerous hours of exercises, but many relate to the macro and microscopic description of rocks. It is necessary to analyze the quantity and quality of the practical parts of the courses.

The committee, after a new evaluation of the Study Course's educational offer, conducted through the previously submitted material, further discussed possible development themes, focusing on the importance of developing/updating an educational offer capable of making geologists competitive in the job market and up to date.

ENTRY, PATH, AND EXIT DATA
The negative trend in the number of enrollments has been interrupted, increasing from 24 units to 32 units, to which are added another 4 units of new enrollments from transfers and reactivation of previous careers. The data is even more positive when considering that the trend continues to be negative not only in Italy but throughout Europe. The transition from the first to the second year remains critical, with approximately 58% of students passing to the second year, in line with the previous year, but above the regional average and in line with the national average. More than 20% of first-year students come from other regions compared to approximately 7% of the regional average and 19% of the national average. The percentage of graduates within the normal course duration continues to show a positive trend, reaching approximately 60%, significantly higher than the regional and national averages. The main criticalities such as the number of enrollments, internationalization, and the transition from the first to the second year had already been addressed within the CdS, which has initiated a series of ongoing initiatives reported in the attached PDF. Their effectiveness will be subsequently analyzed and evaluated. The data is generally discussed and analyzed in the Annual Monitoring Sheet in the CdS on 12/14/2022 and will be discussed again in December 2023 during the preparation of the 2023 SMA.

FINAL EXAM CHARACTERISTICS
In the final exam, the student presents the results of an independent in-depth study of the aspects covered with the 'field' training activities. The presentation of the results obtained is evaluated by a dedicated Commission of Professors.

FINAL EXAM EXECUTION METHOD
The final exam consists of the elaboration and presentation of a report, experimental or compilative, related to the content of one of the disciplines of the degree course and is held before an examination commission composed of three professors of the Degree Course, specifically appointed by the President of the Study Course Council. The commission convenes about 20 days before the Degree Proclamation and proposes a grade from 0 to 4. The Graduation Commission on the day of the Proclamation assigns the final score, taking into account the grade of the Examination Commission.

The Faculty can rely on specific teaching for basic and characteristic disciplines, widely adequate to the new programming and prospects for its complete implementation. The proposed organization, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the university's educational offer.

Admission procedures The required qualification for enrollment in the Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques is a Secondary school diploma issued upon completion of a five-year or four-year course of study that grants access to the Italian university system according to current regulations, or another secondary school diploma of the second level obtained abroad and recognized as equivalent. Enrollment is permitted for holders of four-year diplomas issued by institutions where the integrated year is not offered; in such cases, a specific educational debt will be assigned to be recovered according to the procedures set forth in the current University Academic Regulations.
Extra-EU candidates not regularly residing in Italy, except in cases exempted by current regulations, must also take a test of Italian language knowledge organized by the Study Course.
Additionally, enrollment in the Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques requires taking the TOLC-PSI test provided by CISIA.
Admission criteria, procedures, and deadlines for the Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques, including the validity criteria for the TOLC-PSI, are regulated by a specific selection notice.
The TOLC-PSI score will also be considered to assess the initial preparation of candidates who complete enrollment and to determine the fulfillment of Additional Educational Obligations (OFA). Possession of adequate initial preparation in the following areas is considered a facilitating factor for successfully undertaking the proposed training path: a) Italian language; b) logical-mathematical area; c) humanities and social sciences area; d) physical-chemical-biological sciences area.
If one or more OFAs are assigned to a student, the student must fulfill these obligations within the first year of study, otherwise they will be unable to take exams in subsequent years, except as provided in Article 8 of this Regulation.
OFA recovery methods may include individually assigned training activities, attendance at university courses (including seminar-style courses), or other training activities indicated by the Study Course. To facilitate OFA fulfillment, the Study Course may organize additional training activities.
OFA recovery procedures, deadlines, and activities are established by the Study Course and communicated to students via a dedicated notice published on the Course's dedicated page.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The degree course requires students to take assessment tests involving oral interviews, written assignments on topics or open questions. It also requires presenting reports on experiences gained during internship activities, relating to research articles, and comparing their arguments with those of the working group. Finally, the final exam involves writing an individual assignment to be presented to a committee. All these assessment and deepening opportunities develop the graduate's ability to communicate effectively to an audience of peers and experts and to decode and encode psychological content.

SECTION: Judgment Autonomy

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
Each course in the psychological field illustrates the phenomena under study from various theoretical perspectives, highlighting similarities and differences and proposing possible integrations as well as the most recent developments; it also emphasizes the most important open issues.
The methodological teachings and the internship provide the foundation for handling data in a way that is useful for interpretation, hypothesis formulation, identifying ways to verify them, and evaluating the solution found.
All teachings serve to ground knowledge on criteria of scientific rigor and promote reflection on the development of thought and the canons governing the formation of knowledge. The internship activities train students to test their knowledge and verify its solidity. Therefore, the student learns to interpret data and provide autonomous, scientifically grounded judgments throughout the entire educational process. Each teaching includes an examination that particularly requires the use of critical thinking.

Orientation for New Students The orientation for new students is coordinated by a departmental orientation delegate (Department of Psychological, Health and Territory Sciences), appointed by the Department Director (for this academic year, Professor Michela Cortini, supported by Dr. Teresa Galanti) and the CdS orientation committee, established upon request of the University orientation delegate and composed of Professors Stefano Pagliaro, Irene Ceccato, and Pasquale La Malva. The orientation services for new students include periodic public presentations of the educational offer, inviting high school graduates from the territory and from out-of-region schools that request it, along with participation in orientation fairs (such as the recent orientation fair at the Chieti Chamber of Commerce), organized by various national entities.
CdS representatives, who participate in numerous orientation events across the territory, invite high school graduates and students in their fourth year of Secondary Schools to complete the AlmaOrientati questionnaire available on the University Orientation portal, a useful tool to help future students monitor their knowledge of the university world and reflect on self-orientation.
For some years, research-action has been conducted on the role played by family influences, with main findings presented at symposia dedicated to orientation at various congresses of the Italian Psychological Association (AIP) (the first in chronological order being the Sawitri-Cortini presentation, see https://www.aipass.org/sites/default/files/programma_definitivo_cesena14.pdf).
Based on these results, an intervention by Professor Cortini has been initiated on the territory, in coordination with the Orientation Division, regarding errors to avoid in university path choices.
The orientation service for new students also offers the possibility of individual meetings between students and/or families (by appointment). The aim of individual counseling is to support a conscious choice of the university path, fully addressing the interests and aptitudes of potential new students.
Through collaboration with a group of professors, the orientation service is also responsible for producing both printed and online versions of the student guide, an extremely useful information tool and the first step in self-orientation, as well as supporting secondary school students transitioning to university and newly enrolled students.
These services are offered in coordination with the University Orientation Division, whose service offerings can be consulted at the following link.
Additionally, orientation activities are advertised on the CdS online bulletin board and reported on the CdS page.
Since spring 2020, concurrently with the COVID-19 emergency, the CdS, in line with the University Orientation Division's provisions, has prepared additional online consultation materials beyond those already available on the university website to support remote orientation activities: https://www.disputer.unich.it/didattica/orientamento. Since September 2021, an innovative entry orientation laboratory has been established, developed with the support of 2 Lego Serious Play Facilitators, scheduled at least once a year and aimed at students undecided between different courses.
After the winter holidays, the CdS orientation committee monitors the quality of the entry orientation with new students.

Ongoing Orientation and Tutoring The ongoing orientation is explicitly carried out through various actions. Finally, at least one outgoing orientation event is always guaranteed, designed to increase students' awareness regarding the choice of the most suitable master's degree course based on their interests and potential.

International Mobility Office The Department of Psychological, Health and Territory Sciences, with the support of the International Relations Office (URI), manages student mobility within bilateral agreements that provide for incoming and outgoing student exchanges within community-funded programs such as the Erasmus program. Mobility is encouraged and promoted through the provision of scholarships and support in administrative procedures: from contacting the foreign institution, to preparing the study plan for international mobility, to recognition of exams taken abroad.
The Department maintains various collaboration agreements with foreign universities and research laboratories. The main objective is to acquaint undergraduate students with the importance of sharing research results and international training. This involves sensitizing students to an international perspective on psychological sciences, for example by asking faculty to promote their relationships with foreign laboratories so that students can engage with internationally shared topics for their final project. To increase opportunities available to students, the Department has established new bilateral agreements for student mobility with the following universities: Heinrich-Heine University Düsseldorf (D); Stockholm University (SE); University of Nis (RS); University of Würzburg (D); University of Primorska (SI); Jagiellonian University (PL); Private University of Health Sciences (A); University of Murcia (SP). Thanks to these new agreements, the Department can guarantee mobility for 61 students compared to the previous 17 available.
Additionally, the Department's Erasmus and International Mobility Coordinator, Prof. Marcello Costantini, is the local coordinator (PI) of the INGENIUM consortium, funded by the European community: an interuniversity consortium with nine other partners aimed at increasing the internationalization of the university and the Course of Study.
The Department also maintains dialogue with the ERASMUS STUDENT NETWORK association (Pescara and Chieti branches), composed of volunteers supporting incoming Erasmus students and D'Annunzio students departing for study stays abroad. In collaboration with this association, information/education opportunities regarding Erasmus pathways have been offered, detailed on the Course of Study's website, with high satisfaction among both incoming and outgoing students.

CURRICULUM: CAREER GUIDANCE
SECTION: Career Guidance
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/4

Career Guidance In a vertically structured university education system, characterized by the 3+2 cycle, with the three-year degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques as foundational education, career guidance is primarily expressed through the transition to a master's degree program. However, although the Course is characterized by a low level of employability, employment opportunities in both public and private sectors are not negligible: for example, elderly care facilities, family homes, etc.
For these reasons, career guidance is implemented through two main sets of initiatives:
a) continuous monitoring of the skills expressed by students, to support them in choosing suitable master's degree programs, with periodic information on the internal educational offerings as well as those across the entire national territory;
b) annual organization of one-day events featuring activities designed to foster interaction between students, the Professional Order, and local companies.
For example, annually the Psychologists' Professional Order organizes the Psychology Open Day, which also involves students from the Course. This annual event allows students to learn about various professional fields and connect with local structures (cooperatives, family homes, associations) that have been working for years on different psychological topics.
Career guidance is guaranteed through constant dialogue with the University Placement Service, which assists graduates and graduates of the Course in searching for scholarships, work placements, internships, and more generally in entering the workforce, with various initiatives that facilitate the meeting between job demand and supply, also serving as opportunities to connect with the broader job market (see, for example, the 'START' initiative with its website, which supports the meeting between job demand and supply).

UNIVERSITY: GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA

SECTION: STUDENT OPINIONS

Student Opinions The data regarding student opinions for the academic year 2021/2022, provided by PQA, were collected through an online questionnaire administered via the student career management software (ESSE3).
For students of the Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques, the data refer to 11,404 processed forms, related to 72 training activities out of 71, evaluated through multiple-choice questions on a scale from 1 to 4 (where 1 = definitely no, 2 = more no than yes, 3 = more yes than no, 4 = definitely yes).
The obtained scores were distributed into 4 evaluation levels, i.e.: Level D (from 1 to 2.5 not included), Level C (from 2.5 to 3 not included), Level B (from 3 to 3.5 not included), Level A (from 3.5 to 4).
The evaluations of individual courses are more than satisfactory and improving compared to the 2020/2021 academic year: none of the courses are at Level D (vs. one course in the previous academic year); one course is at Level C (as in the previous academic year); 36 (50.7%) courses are at Level B (vs. 40 in the previous academic year); 35 (47.89%) at Level A (vs. 26 in the previous academic year).
With regard to the course that received evaluations below 3, the relevant instructor has already been encouraged to implement initiatives aimed at improving its critical aspects.
The overall average judgment is fully positive, positioned at Level B, with a score of 3.46, slightly higher than the previous year (3.45 in 2020/2021), in line with the average score of bachelor's degree courses in the reference area, i.e., the social area (3.46), and slightly higher than the university's average (3.43).
The macro-indicator "teaching effectiveness" achieves an average score of 3.52 (3.52 social area, 3.49 entire university). The aspects that define it show slight improvement or stability compared to the previous year: indeed, scores increase regarding the instructor's ability to stimulate interest in the discipline (3.44 vs. 3.42) and the adequacy of the subject exposition in relation to its complexity (3.49 vs. 3.47), while the evaluation of instructors' availability to provide clarifications on the topics covered remains constant (3.62 vs. 3.62).
The macro-indicator "logistical-organizational aspects" shows a similar pattern to the previous one, with an average evaluation of 3.52, equal to that of the reference area and higher than the entire university's (3.47), and also showing slight improvement or stability compared to the previous academic year; indeed, there is an increase in scores regarding the adequacy of teaching materials (3.45 vs. 3.43) and the consistency between the course delivery and what is stated on the CdS website (3.55 vs. 3.52), while scores regarding adherence to teaching activity schedules (3.61 vs. 3.60) and clarity in defining exam modalities (3.47 vs. 3.48) remain approximately stable.
Finally, the macro-indicator "overall satisfaction" achieves an average score of 3.33 (3.33 social area, 3.31 university). Topics are considered mostly interesting with a score of 3.42 (vs. 3.43 previous year), preliminary knowledge is considered mostly sufficient for understanding the topics covered in the exam program with a score of 3.23 (vs. 3.20 previous year), and the required study load is considered mostly proportional to CFU with a score of 3.33 (vs. 3.28 previous year). These last two aspects represent once again "critical points" (understood as aspects that received lower evaluations compared to others, but still positive as they are always above the score of 3). They are, however, improving, indicating that the interventions proposed by the CdS Council (spending more time on the introduction of foundational concepts in courses with a more scientific approach and, during orientation, focusing on setting expectations regarding content and study load) have been effective. The CdS Council will be sensitized again on these aspects to improve corrective actions.
With regard to the evaluations by graduating students, the online questionnaire was completed at the time of submitting the graduation application. The processed data relate to questionnaires completed from the start of the survey until its closure, a period corresponding to the time frame defined by student secretariats for submitting graduation applications; in the survey reported here, the survey period was March 1, 2022 – January 30, 2023 (PQA report 2023, academic year 2021/2022).
The surveys investigated the adequacy of facilities and the effectiveness of the overall educational process. The data related to the Bachelor's Degree in Psychological Sciences and Techniques for the 2021/2022 academic year refer to 429 valid forms. The evaluation range and response options are similar to those of the student opinions mentioned above.
For the academic year 2021/2022, the Bachelor's Degree program achieves an average score of 3.31; the value remains nearly stable compared to the previous year (3.32) and is higher than the university's average (3.23).
Regarding logistical-organizational aspects, the score for the overall organization of courses (schedule, exams) is 3.12, equal to the previous academic year and close to the university's average (3.14).
The evaluation of support provided by the home university during the study abroad period remains stable at a score of 3.22, as in the previous academic year; however, the evaluation is lower than the university's average (3.31).
The score for secretariat services remains constant at 3.01 compared to the previous academic year (3.01) and in line with the university's average (2.99).
Stability is also observed, compared to the previous academic year, in the evaluations of teaching facilities, as shown by the judgment on classrooms (3.35 vs. 3.35, university 3.12), on equipment for other teaching activities (3.09 vs. 3.08, university 3.02), and on computer equipment (2.90 vs. 2.91, university 2.89).
Regarding these last ones, which continue to receive evaluations below 3, it is again noted that students are increasingly equipped with personal portable electronic devices, making the use of university or course computer equipment almost unnecessary.
It is also noted that the Study Course has software (e.g., Qualtrics, E-Prime) useful for completing final projects and conducting some activities for laboratories, practical experiences, etc. It is hoped that, in the future, the evaluation of IT services can distinguish between hardware and software components for greater accuracy in the survey.
Finally, regarding overall satisfaction, there are no significant changes compared to the previous year, and the scores are close to, or even higher than, those of the university, as can be seen in the evaluations regarding the acceptability of the study load during the period (3.27 vs. 3.28; 3.29 university) and the study abroad experience (3.78 vs. 3.80; 3.87 university), as well as in the overall satisfaction with courses (3.43 vs. 3.43; 3.33 university) and overall satisfaction with the Study Course (3.43 vs. 3.42; university 3.31).
From the overview of student and graduating student opinions, a generally positive and stable evaluation of the CdS emerges, with an increase in some scores related to aspects considered critical, which, although in some cases of modest magnitude, suggest further room for improvement by continuing and refining the initiatives already implemented, which will be further discussed at the CdS Council meeting.
For aspects not directly related to the bachelor's degree program, the relevant university bodies will be sensitized.
With regard to the possibility of receiving complaints and suggestions, the CdS has not established an internal Customer Satisfaction system, also considering the facilitating role of student representatives in this regard; however, it is noted that PQA has established a centralized complaint management system at the university level, to which students can easily turn.
Finally, from meetings of the CPDS, the issue of classroom availability for CdS courses repeatedly emerges, forcing an often suboptimal lesson schedule; students also express concern regarding the delivery of TPV credits, which will be managed internally and for which, starting from the third year of the new curriculum, dedicated spaces will be needed.

GRADUATE OPINIONS The data regarding graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques from the University "G. d'Annunzio" of Chieti-Pescara for the calendar year 2022, provided by AlmaLaurea (updated as of April 2023) and reported here, will be observed following three comparison guidelines: comparatively to previous years (2021 and 2020), tracking their trend over the three-year period; compared to the overall graduate data of the University; and compared to the data of graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques from other Italian universities (overall graduates of the degree class). It is noted that, to more accurately observe the trend of the Degree Course in recent years, only graduates enrolled in recent years were considered. In the group considered for the year 2022, the response rate was 95.8% (343 respondents out of 358 graduates). The percentage of 2022 graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques at the University who attended at least half of the required courses increases, after a decline in the previous year, reaching 90.1% (86.5% in 2021, 88.9% in 2020). This percentage, slightly lower than that reported for the entire University (91.6%), is higher than the national average for the degree class (87.2%). It is worth noting that the usually higher percentage of attendance reported for the entire University may be due to the mandatory attendance requirement in some degree courses. Regarding the evaluation of the study load of courses in relation to the duration of the degree course, the data show that it is considered predominantly and decidedly adequate by 93.9% of respondents, a percentage that has increased compared to previous years (92.2% in 2020, 90.7% in 2021) and is higher than the value reported for the entire University (89.4%) and the national average for the degree class (92.3%). The evaluation of the relationship with faculty is confirmed as excellent, with a gradual increase over the three-year period in the already high percentage of graduates who found the relationship generally predominantly and decidedly satisfactory (92.2% in 2020, 93.4% in 2021, 94.2% in 2022). The percentage remains higher than the figure reported for the University (90.5%) and the national average for the degree class (90.8%). The positive evaluations above are confirmed by the high level of overall satisfaction with the degree course, as shown by the percentage of graduates predominantly and decidedly satisfied with the Degree Course (CdS) in 2022, which stands at 98.5%, an increase compared to previous years (94.7% in 2020, 93.7% in 2021) and higher than the percentage reported for the entire University (91%) and Italian degree courses in Psychological Sciences and Techniques (95%). The percentage of 2022 graduates who found the exam organization (appeals, schedules, information, reservations, etc.) satisfactory for at least "more than half of the exams" is 80.5%. The value decreases compared to previous years (82.3% in 2020, 85.8% in 2021), is close to the figure reported for the University (79.7%), and lower than the national average (84.7%). The evaluation of classrooms continues to improve, with 98.5% of the considered group having used them: classrooms are considered "often adequate" and "always or almost always adequate" by 93.5 out of 100 graduates from 2022 (87.3 in 2020, 89.5 in 2021), and the value is higher than that reported for the entire University (85.6 out of 100) and other Italian degree courses in Psychological Sciences and Techniques (85.2 out of 100). The percentage of 2022 graduates in the degree course in question who report having used computer workstations is 36.7% (38.1% in 2020, 35% in 2021). At the University, 50.7% have used them, and nationally, 61.6%. Out of 100 users, 60.3 graduates of the Degree Course in question, 57.1 graduates of the University, and 61.5 graduates of the national degree class find them adequately numerous. Regarding the adequacy of equipment for other teaching activities (laboratories, practical activities, etc.), out of 100 graduates from the degree course analyzed in 2022, 70.8 consider them adequate, decidedly and predominantly, compared to 76.2 in 2020 and 79.3 in 2021. The value is also lower than that of graduates from other degree courses at the University (73.1 out of 100) and other Italian degree courses in Psychological Sciences and Techniques (78.1 out of 100). Additionally, the percentage of users of the degree course's equipment (52.8%) is lower than both the figure reported for the University (68.1%) and the national average (63.5%). The percentage of 2022 graduates in the Degree Course who reported using library services is 70.3%, a decrease compared to previous years (84.6% in 2020, 77.3% in 2021), close to the figure reported for the University (70%) and the national average (72.1%). These services are positively evaluated ("often adequate" and "always or almost always adequate") by 94.2 out of 100 graduates from 2022, a value that has decreased over the three-year period (98.2 in 2020, 99.1 in 2021), higher than the entire University (89.5 out of 100) and close to the national average for the degree class (94.9 out of 100). Finally, the percentage of graduates who would enroll again in the same degree course at the same University increases to 82.5% (79.8% in 2020, 77.5% in 2021); the value is higher than that of other courses at the University (70%) and the national average (79.4%). Overall, the data considered here indicate general satisfaction among graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques from the University "G. d'Annunzio" in the calendar year 2022. Observing the trend over the three-year period of interest, there is further improvement in the already high evaluations regarding the relationship with faculty and overall satisfaction with the degree course; the number of positive evaluations regarding classroom adequacy also increases, but other structural and logistical aspects that, although satisfactory in some cases, have experienced a negative decline in evaluations remain to be improved. The strengths emerging from the high and satisfactory evaluations above are also expressed comparatively against other degree courses at the University and against other Italian degree courses in Psychological Sciences and Techniques, which they mostly align with, if not surpass, and are reflected in the high percentage of graduates who would enroll again in the Psychological Sciences and Techniques degree course at the University "G. d'Annunzio". The Degree Course Council will discuss the logistical and structural aspects that require improvement, evaluating appropriate interventions within the Council's direct competence.

Ability to apply knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Ten CFU are required through the completion of an assessed practical internship (TPV), in line with Law 8 November 2021, No. 163. This opportunity involves all areas of psychology and allows students to apply their knowledge to a specific situation and verify their mastery. It also enables the elaboration of the experience through a targeted report that promotes awareness of the learning process. Such an activity trains students to approach studies in terms of problem-solving and is fundamental for both a responsible approach to work and for continuing studies at a higher level. Practical skills acquired during the internship are evaluated.

Learning skills (learning skills)
The course develops in students the ability to reflect on study topics and to meta-reflect on their own abilities and learning processes. Exams for each discipline aim primarily to monitor and verify students' learning ability through examinations designed to assess not only disciplinary knowledge but also the ability to learn, which is essential for continuous professional updating required by all professions today. The study program also aims to provide adequate training to continue studies and research independently, with a high level of responsibility in identifying goals and learning strategies, and with good critical evaluation skills, thus laying the foundation for access to Master's degrees, particularly in psychology.

University communications to CUN A minor adjustment to the organizational structure has been made to ensure the presence of the necessary CFU for the European validity of the degree (EuroPsy). Both the CFU range for the Base-Interdisciplinary Table (changed from 18min-18max to 10min-18max) and the CFU range for the Characterizing-Psychology General and Physiological Table (changed from 24min-24max to 24min-32max) have been adjusted to allow an increase in CFU in the methodological area (M-PSI/03) sufficient to meet the EuroPsy requirement (at least 30 CFU in the methodological area).

Knowledge and understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques acquire foundational knowledge on the fundamental topics of all psychology areas as well as related humanities and biomedical fields. These knowledge areas cover mental processes and their development, the neural correlates of psychological functioning and their biogenetic bases, psychological measurement methods, and references provided by humanities for the study of the psyche. They also introduce more applied and clinical areas that can be further explored in Master's programs. For areas requiring more than one academic year, knowledge of advanced texts and research articles related to both classical and cutting-edge topics is required. The level of learning is assessed through exams conducted in both written and oral formats, depending on the specific course characteristics.

Organization and responsibility of AQ at the Degree Course level The organization and responsibility of Quality Assurance (AQ) at the Degree Course level are structured as follows:
Course Director: The Director, Professor Cortini, coordinates the AQ system of the Degree Course and oversees compliance with requirements set by regulations, supported by the Parity Commission and the review group, in line with the central University bodies' guidelines on AQ;
Parity Commission of the School: Monitors the educational offer and the quality of teaching and services provided by faculty and structures to students;
AQ and Review Commission: Monitors and ensures the quality of the Degree Course, prepares the review report, analyzes the current situation of the Degree Course, highlights strengths and improvement opportunities, and proposes concrete actions; it consists of the Degree Course Director, Professor Michela Cortini, Professor Alessandra Babore, Professor Rocco Palumbo, Professor Teresa Galanti, and student representatives.
Degree Course Council: Discusses and approves the review report and collaborates in the smooth operation of the Degree Course's AQ. Since the academic year 2018/19, a specific point on Quality Assurance has been included in the agenda of all Council meetings.
In line with Quality Assurance policies and the Department's Improvement Plan (which has appointed a Quality Assurance Department Representative: Professor Di Domenico), the Degree Course in Psychological Sciences and Techniques has established a specific Steering Committee in addition to the annual meeting with stakeholders for the entire educational offer. The Steering Committee, composed of the Degree Course Director, a representative of the Abruzzo Region Psychologists' Order, and qualified representatives from various organizational fields, meets at least once a year.
In February 2019, the table of coordinators of the psychological area Degree Courses at the University was established, with the task of supporting the connection between the first-cycle degree path and guidance toward a Master's program.

Program of work and deadlines for implementing initiatives The Degree Course's organizational cycle involves continuous decision-making and verification activities, in compliance with accreditation regulations, requiring an annual comparison between defined goals and achieved targets. This activity, carried out by the Quality Assurance Group, also benefits from external verification by the Parity Commission of Faculty-Students. These bodies define the standard and exceptional operational characteristics of the Degree Course for the following academic year during the winter period. Standard decisions include the composition of the teaching staff (reference teachers), the planned number of students, modifications to the teaching regulations, the academic calendar, and all annual initiatives and actions. During the spring period, these decisions are concretized in the complete preparation of the annual Unified Course Sheet (SUA). Standard systematic decisions may be supplemented by extraordinary decisions (e.g., modifications to the teaching structure, new initiatives, etc.), which are decided by the Council and/or other control and verification bodies during the winter period.

In the autumn period, the evaluation of student feedback is of fundamental importance, together with statistical data on student inflow and outflow, informing the Committee's assessment for the Annual Review Report.

Compared to the last Review Report, the Degree Course in Psychological Sciences and Techniques has already implemented and planned the improvement activities identified, and has also provided training for developing teaching skills and supporting innovative teaching through the INGENIUM network.

The responsibility for this objective lies with the Degree Course's Quality Assurance Group.

All activities are reported on the Degree Course's website.

Annual Review With the introduction of the new ANVUR AVA 2.0 Guidelines, the Degree Course self-assessment system has been partially modified. The Degree Course self-assessment activity is now structured as follows:
- Annual Monitoring Sheet (AMS), replacing the Annual Review Report, consisting of a concise critical comment on the quantitative indicators calculated by ANVUR on student careers, attractiveness, internationalization, graduate employability, quantity and qualification of teaching staff, and graduate satisfaction (to be centrally provided by ANVUR);
- Cyclic Review, with a partially revised format compared to the previous version; it contains a thorough self-assessment of the overall Degree Course trend based on all relevant analysis elements.

Below is the AMS for the year 2017:

I. Enrolment Section: Enrolments are decreasing (approximately -50% over the three-year reference period) due to the implementation of local enrollment planning.
II. Group A - Teaching Indicators: The percentage of graduates within the standard course duration shows a slight decline but is in line with the regional and national averages. The percentage of students from other regions is higher than the regional average, demonstrating the broad reach of the Degree Course's student base. The percentage of employed graduates one year after graduation averages around 8%, primarily because most graduates continue to a Master's program. The percentage of permanent faculty members belonging to basic and characterizing SSDs is approximately 80% and slightly lower than the regional and national averages.
III. Group B - Internationalization Indicators: The percentage of graduates who have earned at least 12 CFU abroad within the standard course duration is increasing (from 3% in 2013 to 12% in 2015). However, a low number of students are on mobility compared to regional and national averages.
IV. Group E - Additional indicators for teaching evaluation: Teaching indicators show a slightly lower position in some cases (e.g., percentage of CFU earned in the first year) compared to regional and national averages, but in other cases, they are more in line. However, all indicators show a positive upward trend.
V. Indicators for experimental deepening:
- Study paths and career regularity: The dropout rate averages around 33% and is slightly higher than the regional and national averages.
- Staff size and qualification: The values of these indicators show a negative trend, significantly deviating from the reference value calculated following ANVUR guidelines (33.3 for the humanities-social area) since the number of faculty is considerably lower than the number of students enrolled in the Degree Course.

Brief comment The teaching, career, and internationalization indicators generally show a lower position compared to national averages, although in line with the regional reference area. However, between 2013 and 2015, these indicators have shown significant improvement, certainly due to the progressive reduction in available places through local planning. For 2015, the comparison with the national average shows a slight disadvantage, but compared to the southern and island regions, many indicators show a better position. Given the still relatively high number of enrollments, a high dropout rate should not be considered entirely negative, testifying to the 'in itinere' selective nature of the Degree Course. The Degree Course Council has, however, planned measures to 1) better recognize the effort of meritorious students, facilitating their path (e.g., allowing advanced exams for particularly outstanding students), and 2) redirect students who are not keeping up with the study plan. Regarding internationalization, the position is particularly unsatisfactory compared to national and regional averages, but improvement is expected through the University's policies encouraging students to take advantage of the numerous opportunities for study abroad in exchange and mobility programs. In this regard, a specific review of Erasmus agreements applicable to the three-year Degree Course will be conducted. While the local enrollment planning has been a strength demonstrating its results, the Degree Course's critical position regarding indicators expressing the ratio between student numbers and faculty numbers (pure or weighted by teaching hours) has been noted, progressively improving between 2013 and 2015 but still significantly distant from national and regional averages. Therefore, the Degree Course, in consultation with political bodies, must carefully consider its enrollment policy in relation to the possibilities of recruiting new faculty, as, despite compliance with AVA regulations, the positioning of these indicators on the national comparison plane is strategically delicate. Consequently, the following actions must be taken: A) targeted recruitment policies for teaching staff to improve the quality sustainability of the Degree Course, B) downward adjustment of enrollment quotas, or C) a reasonable combination of A and B.

Brief description of related and complementary activities Related and complementary activities, provided as part of the Degree Course's educational offerings in Psychological Sciences and Techniques, aim to acquire knowledge that contributes to defining the interdisciplinary nature of psychology, which is completed with contributions from philosophical and biomedical disciplines. These activities thus contribute to the educational goal of adequately situating psychological knowledge within the context of natural, human, and social sciences, incorporating disciplines that, through reflection on the human being, explanations of biomedical nature for behavior and pathologies, and the study of mind-body-behavior connections, have enabled psychology to become a science.

Brief description of the course The Psychological Sciences and Techniques study program (Class L 24) requires the acquisition of 180 credits over three years and aims to acquire foundational psychological knowledge and skills (in terms of theories, methodologies, research data, and intervention forms) through interdisciplinary comparison. Specifically, the educational offer includes, in the first two years, the acquisition of key knowledge and skills in various psychology areas; in the third year, more professional-oriented psychology areas (e.g., developmental and organizational) are deepened to complete the basic training and guide the choice of Master's degree. This Degree Course includes both frontal teaching courses and training activities conducted with experiential methodologies; specifically, 10 CFU are dedicated to the assessed practical internship (TPV), in line with the provisions of Legislative Decree No. 163/2021 on qualifying degrees. Admission to the degree course is quota-based, and upon completion, students may continue their university education with a Master's degree or take the state exam for 'Psychological Techniques Specialist for Social, Organizational, and Work Contexts' or 'Psychological Techniques Specialist for Personal and Community Services' (B Register).

External effectiveness Based on data provided by AlmaLaurea regarding the year 2022 (employment status of 2021 graduates one year after graduation), considering the group "graduates who did not enroll in another degree course" (48 out of 390 interviewed and 526 graduates), the employment rate of graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques from the University "G. d'Annunzio" is 45.8% (vs. 69.4% University, 55.1% degree class). The value increases compared to the previous year, when it was 40%. The percentage of employed individuals who extensively use the skills acquired through the degree is 27.3% (vs. 56.8% University, 30.6% degree class), and job satisfaction, rated on a scale from 1 to 10, is 7.6 (vs. 8 University, 7.6 degree class). Finally, the average net monthly salary (in euros) for graduates of the Degree Course is 1248 (vs. 1333 University, 1174 degree class). The lower employment rate, lower salary, and lower use of skills by graduates of the Degree Course and the national degree class, compared to other University degree courses, can be attributed to the presence of more professionalizing degree courses at the University (which allow more immediate and adequate entry into the job market) and, simultaneously, the need for graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques to complete their training, making them less employable with only a three-year degree. To confirm this, note that 86.2% of total graduates (a percentage corresponding to that of the degree class), compared to 68% of the entire University, continue their studies by enrolling in a second-level degree course.

These data were presented and discussed during the Degree Course Council meeting on September 4, 2023.

Specific educational objectives and description of the educational path The Three-Year Degree Course in Psychological Sciences and Techniques offers a unique study path aimed at providing the theoretical and methodological foundations of scientific training in psychology, supported by adequate training in the most relevant interdisciplinary fields, such as humanities, social sciences, and biomedical sciences. According to Article 1, Paragraph 3, of Law 8 November 2021, No. 163, part of the assessed practical internship activities required for qualification to practice as a psychologist, amounting to 10 CFU, are carried out during the study program. The specific arrangement of these professional training activities, defined by the University's teaching regulations for Class L-24 degree courses, concerns: a) activities for acquiring basic professional skills related to empirical methods characterizing all psychology areas and techniques for assessing mental and behavioral functioning processes, including their psychobiological correlates, in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts; b) activities for acquiring basic professional skills related to psychological assessment and the main forms of intervention on interpersonal, intragroup, and intergroup relationships in various social contexts, at the level of dyads, families, small groups, and organizations; c) analysis of the main forms of alteration of psychological processes and human behavior in relation to different age groups and social and life contexts. Graduates of the degree course must have acquired: - the theoretical foundations of psychological knowledge, developed in the basic areas of general, developmental, and social psychology, psychobiology, and psychometrics; - the characteristic knowledge of each psychology area, connected both to advancements in basic areas and to knowledge of applied aspects in the fields of work psychology, dynamic psychology, and clinical psychology; - an adequate situating of psychological knowledge within the context of natural, human, and social sciences; - mastery of the fundamental elements of experimental research techniques, behavioral observation, and statistical analysis of psychological data, as well as the basics of investigation and intervention methodologies; - the ability to critically address issues related to psychology's study objects and effectively communicate reflections on them. The Psychological Sciences and Techniques study program aims to train qualified professionals in social reintegration and integration activities, school and career orientation processes, and entry into the job market, as well as in the provision of services aimed at preventing adult distress and social marginalization of children and adolescents, cognitive and functional rehabilitation for adults and minors, and management of growth and development processes, both individual and group. An additional educational objective of the course is also the exercise of comprehension skills, beyond Italian, in English, and the acquisition of computer skills, indispensable tools for the training of psychologists.

Opinions of organizations and companies with internship/curricular or extracurricular agreements The L-24 path is characterized by a predominance of theoretical training regarding the foundational areas of psychology and limited operational applicability of the degree from a professional standpoint; this aspect is instead the primary objective of Master's programs. Following Law No. 163 of November 8, 2021, regarding qualifying degrees, and the consequent structural modification effective from the 2023/2024 academic year, assessed practical internships "internal" totaling 10 CFU are provided for the various applied psychology areas in the three-year degree course, to be completed in the third year. Since the internship is "internal," students do not go to organizations and companies, but rather the Degree Course hosts representatives from various organizations and entities that employ psychologists in different capacities. With these professionals, dialogue is active, as evidenced by the reports from the Degree Course's stakeholder table, from which general satisfaction with the training provided emerges.

Consultation with national and international organizations representing goods and service production, and professions (Establishment of the course)
The Psychological Sciences and Techniques study program at the University G. d'Annunzio of Chieti-Pescara has been revised in response to Ministerial Decree 163/2021 to align with the required standards, primarily regarding the Assessed Practical Internship (TPV). In consultation with the Degree Course's Quality Assurance Group, alongside students and coordinators of LM51 paths, representatives of various social organizations and organizations representing goods and service production and professions were consulted: from RetexLavorare and Honda Italia to CNOP, the Regional Psychologists' Order, and the Student and Academic Secretariat coordinators of the University G. d'Annunzio of Chieti-Pescara, among others. The coordinator, Professor Michela Cortini, also attended meetings organized jointly by CPA and AIP (Italian Psychological Association) regarding how to implement Law 163/2021 and was one of the promoters of the coordination table of Presidents of Psychological Area Degree Courses at the University G. d'Annunzio of Chieti-Pescara. The Degree Course Council also established an internal commission tasked with evaluating all modifications requested by Ministerial Decree 163/2021, representing all major concursus sectors in the psychological area. Considering the limited number of graduates registered with the Regional Psychologists' Order (13 for 2022), consultations revealed a characterization of the Degree Course in terms of preparatory for the Master's degree LM51. All the re-design activities of the educational path were functional to achieving this primary objective, without neglecting an evaluation with the socio-economic system regarding possible employment outcomes for graduates in Psychological Sciences and Techniques. Regarding the latter, consultation with Retexlavorare.com suggested a greater emphasis on the possible employment outcome related to school and career orientation, which was taken into account. From various interlocutors, the need to maintain an adequate planned number, in relation to both improving student preparation and the excessive number of psychology graduates currently in Italy and persistent difficulties in employment for psychology graduates, emerged.

OUTCOMES Overall, general satisfaction with the Degree Course's educational offer is evident, which has been renewed with the implementation of the decrees implementing Law 163/2021. In detail, Retexlavorare highlights the expansion of the Degree Course's professional opportunities, which has also expanded to the "Employment Services Technician" profile with the implementation of the qualifying degree; this change is expected to impact employment statistics for the Degree Course graduates. In particular, from the Psychological Area Degree Course Coordinators' Table, satisfaction is expressed for the ongoing and exit orientation paths, for which the Degree Course is requested to maintain constant commitment. From the Abruzzo Region Psychologists' Order, some concern is expressed regarding the organization of the assessed practical internship (TPV), with a request to design the TPV content and verification methods optimally.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data From the Student Career Indicators System (S.I.Ca.S.), prepared by the PQA, it appears that the number of students enrolled in the 2022/2023 cohort of the Psychological Sciences and Techniques Degree Course is 603 (of which 580 enrolled, of whom 479 are pure enrollments). Regarding the geographical origin of students enrolled in the cohort, the percentage from Abruzzo increases, rising from 28% in the 2021/2022 cohort to 37% in the 2022/2023 cohort. Only one student resides abroad. Among Italian regions, the highest influx comes from Puglia (107 students, 18% of the total), followed by Campania (72 students, 12%) and Basilicata (49 students, 8%). Regarding the type of diploma obtained, 38% of the 2022/2023 cohort students come from high schools (with scientific high school leading at 18%), 31% from magistral institutes, 12% from technical institutes, 8% from professional institutes, and the remaining 10% from other school types. The diploma grade of 10% of the 2022/2023 cohort students is excellent (100/100 and 100/100 with honors); the percentage shows a slight decrease compared to the previous cohort (11%), but the percentage in the intermediate range increases (51% vs. 46% previous cohort), and correspondingly, the percentage with a low score (below 80/100) decreases to 39% (vs. 43% previous cohort). Considering full-time students in the first year of the 2021/2022 cohort, the percentage of students who earned more than 40 CFU when moving to the second year decreases to 50% (vs. 58% the previous year). Correspondingly, the percentages of students who earned between 21 and 40 CFU increase (25% for the 2021/2022 cohort vs. 23% for the 2020/2021 cohort) and those with fewer than 20 CFU increase (24% for the 2021/2022 cohort vs. 18% for the 2020/2021 cohort). Regarding the average grade, the percentage of students with an average between 28/30 and 30/30 decreases, from 19% in the 2020/2021 cohort to 10% in the 2021/2022 cohort, as does the percentage with an average between 24/30 and 27/30, which drops from 53% in the 2020/2021 cohort to 51% in the 2021/2022 cohort. Correspondingly, the percentage with an average between 18/30 and 23/30 increases from 17% in the 2020/2021 cohort to 27% in the 2021/2022 cohort. The grades for graduation improve in the 2021/2022 academic year compared to the previous year: of the 456 graduates in 2021/2022, 55% (vs. 69% the previous year) obtained a degree with a grade below 100, 40% (vs. 28% the previous year) with a grade between 100 and 109, and the remaining 5% with a grade of 110 and 110/summa cum laude (vs. 3% the previous year). Regarding study duration, the percentage of graduates in progress increases to 78% for the 2021/2022 academic year (vs. 69% the previous year). The percentage of regularly enrolled students who earned at least 9 CFU abroad increases during the 2021/2022 academic year, reaching 1.4% (compared to 0.6% the previous year). This data reflects the significant effort of the Degree Course in promoting internationalization, achieving results above the regional average and approaching national levels. Finally, of the 1932 students enrolled in the 2022/2023 academic year, 303 students (15.68%) are out of course in the final year, a percentage nearly stable compared to the previous academic year (15.27%).

These data were presented and discussed during the Degree Course Council meeting on September 4, 2023.

Characteristics of the final exam The final exam requires the preparation of an individual paper, to be written in Italian or English, on a topic chosen by the student. This paper consists of an analysis of some research articles or theoretical contributions. The paper is presented to a graduation committee that evaluates it.

Method of conducting the final exam The final exam consists of preparing a short paper in Italian or English (usually not exceeding 30/40 pages) of a compilative or experimental nature, supervised by a faculty member of the Psychological Area Degree Course, the supervisor, who is responsible for agreeing on the topic, providing guidance for bibliographic research, following the writing stages, and conducting a final review. The topics of the final exam cover all disciplinary areas derived from all Psychological Area Degree Course courses. The purpose is to encourage reflection on mind and behavior using different approaches and levels of analysis. There is no public discussion, but the student must present the work to their supervisor and a designated committee that evaluates the paper. The Graduation Committee, appointed by the Dean of the School of Medicine and Health Sciences, consists of at least five and no more than seven members, with a majority being permanent faculty members of the University. Criteria and methods for evaluating the final paper are regulated by the Degree Course Council and available on the Degree Course's dedicated webpage. At least once a year, the Degree Course's Quality Assurance Group proposes to students a seminar on preparing the final exam, with the aim of conveying all essential information regarding administrative deadlines to meet for taking the final exam, as well as guidelines on how to choose the discipline for the final exam, conduct bibliographic research, create an index, and prepare the reference bibliography. A PowerPoint presentation summarizing these suggestions is also available on the Degree Course's portal. As a mere example, among the latest final exams discussed are the following titles: "Psychological-emotional consequences of parental grief in childhood," "Neurobiological bases of dreams," "Personality traits and recidivism risk in sex offenders," "New horizons in personnel selection," "Qualifications of technological development," "Memory and emotions: an experimental study on a sample of young and elderly people," "Stereotypes and prejudices towards tattoos," "Work-related stress and visual disability," "Face recognition: a neuropsychological perspective." For deadlines for requesting and submitting forms for the final exam, refer to the dedicated page on the Degree Course's website.

Technical report summary of the evaluation nucleus The course covers a central area between the humanities and life sciences, scientifically and professionally relevant and consistently positioned at optimal levels, in reference to the degree class, in terms of enrollments, students, and graduates. The Faculty has adequate, appropriate, and effective facilities, and following an advanced restructuring program of the Chieti Campus, new teaching and scientific spaces will be acquired in the near future, fully aligned with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The situation regarding faculty is more critical, although it should be noted that at least partially, the basic and characterizing disciplines of the course are represented at the University: with a targeted use of the University's specific faculty, the course could partially adjust its faculty, which should nonetheless be strengthened. The proposed structure, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's educational offer.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI-PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO
