SECTION: Admission Procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/546

Admission Procedures The Study Course provides local numerical planning quantified in 430 places, of which 2 are reserved for non-EU students residing abroad.
Admission to the Study Course occurs without any admission test and until the available places are filled, based on the chronological order of receipt of enrollment applications.
Admission to the Study Course is granted to candidates holding a secondary school diploma or a foreign diploma recognized as equivalent under current regulations.
For initial preparation verification, students must participate in the online Test called TOLC-F identified by the University for the preliminary assessment of knowledge acquired during higher education. Taking the test is mandatory for enrollment: if a student passes the test with a defined score, they will be considered to have fulfilled the Additional Educational Requirements (OFA).
Students participating in the TOLC-F for Motor Sciences will undergo initial knowledge verification in the following areas: Biology (15 questions), Chemistry (15 questions), Mathematics (7 questions), Physics (7 questions), and Logic (6 questions).
The test also includes an English section with 30 questions. The outcome of the English section does not affect the final TOLC-F assessment, but based on the result, it provides self-assessment of English language knowledge for the student and enhances the test's national usability for potential enrollment at other locations.
The test score is calculated automatically by multiplying the score obtained in each TOLC-F section by its respective weight.

SECTIONS NUMBER OF QUESTIONS WEIGHT
BIOLOGY 15 QUESTIONS 1
CHEMISTRY 15 QUESTIONS 1
MATHEMATICS 7 QUESTIONS 1
PHYSICS 7 QUESTIONS 1.5
LOGIC 6 QUESTIONS 1.5
TOTAL 50 QUESTIONS ENGLISH 30 QUESTIONS TOTAL WITH ENGLISH 80 QUESTIONS

The TOLC-F can be taken at any of the convening locations listed on the CISIA website. The result is valid for admission to the degree course at all locations using the CISIA consortium's TOLC-F, regardless of where it was taken.
Students who pass the test with a score equal to or higher than 26.0/56.5 are enrolled without Additional Educational Requirements (OFA).
Students enrolled with OFA are those who:
- did not achieve the minimum TOLC-F score of 26/56.5;
- did not take the TOLC-F test.
Typically, the TOLC-F test can be taken multiple times during CISIA's scheduled macro periods to improve the score, especially if the course's threshold was not met.
The TOLC-F result is valid for two years.

Additional Educational Requirements (OFA)
OFA can be fulfilled no later than December 31 of the year following enrollment (December 31, 2023 for students enrolled in the 2022-23 academic year) through one of the following alternative methods:
a) by passing specific assessments at the end of dedicated integrated training activities;
b) by passing exams in the first year of the study course, for a minimum of 18 CFU in basic and/or characterizing disciplines.
Students with unfulfilled OFA may enroll in the second year but cannot take exams until OFA are completed.
OFA does not affect the number of credits the student must earn in their study path or their average grade; the assessment does not produce a grade.

Transfers and Changes of Course For students coming from other study courses or locations, OFA are considered fulfilled if at least one of the following conditions is met:
- at least 5 CFU were acquired in all scientific-disciplinary sectors activated in the first year of the course during the previous academic career;
- the TOLC-F was taken in the two calendar years preceding the transfer/change date, with a minimum score of 26.
The TOLC @CASA Program can be used. Program, texts, and objectives.

Communication Skills
The graduate must be able to:
• communicate techniques and methodologies to practitioners with confidence and competence.
• use correct and appropriate language when interacting with subjects of different ages, abilities, gender, and socio-cultural conditions;
• motivate, involve, and reassure individual and group users throughout all phases of motor and sports activities;
• use appropriate technical terms for different types of motor activities and sports disciplines.
• have had the opportunity to deepen and consolidate their linguistic and computer knowledge;
• operate within various organizational and sports systems.
The final exam will also provide students with an additional opportunity to deepen and verify their analytical, processing, and communication skills. It involves discussing a written work related to the study path before a commission.

Making Judgments
Thanks to solid competence, especially regarding the biological and technical-scientific aspects of movement, the graduate will be able to evaluate the behaviors and lifestyles of subjects engaging in motor and sports activities in recreational settings, the associated risk factors, and propose the best solutions to meet their needs and goals. They will be able to program specific motor activities based on evaluations of metabolic changes and medical advice. Judgment autonomy, based on solid knowledge and understanding of all culturally connected aspects of movement, will enable the graduate to achieve a higher level of competence and judgment compared to other professional figures regarding the choice of activities to propose and the methodologies and evaluation techniques to adopt to meet the practitioner's needs.
Graduates will also be able to assess the severity of possible injuries or acute pathology signs occurring during activities and the need for timely medical assistance; additionally, they will evaluate the technical and hygienic-sanitary adequacy of sports facilities and equipment for specific motor and sports activity programs.

Entry Orientation
The 'G. d'Annunzio' University, through its Orientation, Tutoring, Placement, Student Rights, and Disability Office, supports high school students in making the challenging choice of the most suitable academic course for their abilities, assisting them in university studies to prevent initial evaluation errors from causing delays or abandonment of the chosen path, and facilitating their entry into the job market and professions.
Entry-level tutoring activities for the Study Course are coordinated by the School of Medicine and Health Sciences to which the Study Course belongs.
To support the University's activities, the Study Course has sought to identify additional initiatives to provide clear, simple, and immediate responses to information requests from families and prospective students.
On April 4, 2024, the University organized an Open Day for high school students.
The University presented its wide range of study paths within a structured Educational Offer divided into 4 main academic areas (Health, Scientific, Social, and Humanistic) and organized into 68 Study Courses offered by 14 Departments.
The Study Course is part of a biennial partnership (POT) in Motor Sciences (L22) involving 5 actions: entry orientation, laboratory activities, recovery of educational deficits, tutoring, and teacher training for high schools.
The Study Course has two proposals in the PCTO initiative catalog: "le ricicliadi" and "la salute a portata di click".
The Study Course is presented during ORIENTAUDA days within the Scientific Courses container.

Orientation and ongoing tutoring The orientation and ongoing tutoring activities are coordinated by the Dean of the Course of Study with the support of the academic office, tutor professors, and when possible, student tutors (students from the Master's program STAMPA selected based on merit), to provide:

SECTION: Training Periods
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/546

Training Periods The internships allow the interaction of theoretical information and knowledge with practical and operational applications characteristic of the specific competencies of the Graduate in Motor Sciences.
The internship activities, which represent the only compulsory attendance activity of the entire educational path, consist of practical training periods to be carried out at structures, internal or external to the University, or at institutions or bodies, public or private (Hosting Entities), identified by the Course of Study and contracted with the University through the Course of Study, or sometimes through the Placement sector.
The Council of the Course of Study annually plans the available internships for students. For each activity, a Training and Orientation Project is prepared, containing the objectives and methods of the internship, indicating its duration and the presence times of the intern at the hosting structures.
The signing of agreements with external structures is subject to the Hosting Entities meeting certain quality requirements, such as having within their staff graduates in Motor Sciences.
The training and orientation activity is followed and verified by an Academic Tutor, appointed by the Council of the Course of Study, and a Company Tutor indicated by the Hosting Entity.
For each activity, a minimum attendance of at least 75% of the hours specified in the Training Project is required, and the attribution of the corresponding CFU is subject to a final positive evaluation, expressed through an assessment of suitability by the Tutors.
The number of CFU for internships is higher in the third year of the course; this choice aims to facilitate entry into the job market after obtaining the degree.
Based on agreements with various Sports Federations, some internship activities provide for the issuance of federal licenses.
The Course of Study, through constant collaboration with CONI (Abruzzo Regional Committee), organizes numerous seminars for both the student population and sector professionals.
These events take place at the teaching facilities of the Course of Study.
The teaching offer related to internships is updated annually, published online, and presented to students at the beginning of each academic year.
Enrollment in the various activities, for several years now, is carried out through a dedicated information system that allows students to choose based on available places.
The Course of Study has developed a system for evaluating and monitoring internship activities and hosting structures; students are required to complete and return to the Academic Secretariat - in order to formalize the acquisition of CFU related to the completed internship - a specially prepared form.

- BASIC AND SPECIALIST CONSULTING FOR STUDENTS, BUSINESSES, AND GRADUATES;
- SERVICES FOR BUSINESSES AND GRADUATES: JOB INTERMEDIATION;
- ORIENTATION FOR STARTING A BUSINESS AND MICROCREDIT.
Regarding exit orientation from Study Courses, the Central Placement Service, in close collaboration with businesses and other partners, organizes workshops for students, graduates, and doctoral candidates. Through these meetings, the University aims to contribute to improving the employability levels of students enrolled in various Study Courses. As indicated in the Cyclical Review, the Course of Study has access to the employment outcomes provided by Almalaurea, which offer a fairly detailed overview of graduates' employment prospects, highlighting that the percentage of graduates enrolled in a Master's degree course is higher than the national average: exit orientation activities should therefore be somehow correlated with the corresponding entrance orientation activities for Master's degree paths. The Course of Study has also initiated a series of initiatives in addition to the University's general activities:
- The Study Course has convention agreements with numerous Italian sports federations (Italian Sailing Federation, Italian Football Federation, Italian Handball Federation, Italian Athletics Federation, Italian Swimming Federation, Italian Volleyball Federation, Italian Basketball Federation, Italian Weightlifting Federation, CAI/Italian Sport Climbing Federation, Italian Boxing Federation, Italian Archery Federation); some of these provide students with certifications and/or qualifications usable in the world free of charge or at subsidized costs.
- Unlike other Courses of Study that identify professionals for whom a Professional Register exists, graduates in Sciences of Motor Activities and Sports are not classified into a specific Professional Register. However, the Course of Study has actively engaged at both local and national levels to clearly define a professional field for its graduates. In this regard, a working group was established at the Abruzzo Region (Prot. 0044859/18) to promote, within prevention and health promotion projects, the professionalism of graduates in motor and sports activities. In fact, among the requirements for certifying 'health clubs' and 'safe clubs', the presence of graduates in Sciences of Motor Activities and Sports and Sciences and Techniques of Preventive and Adapted Motor Activities is required.
- Internship activities, mainly placed in the third year of the course, beyond their educational purpose, represent an opportunity to promote the skills and professionalism of the Course of Study students at the Partner Organizations and can serve as useful contacts for employment purposes after obtaining the degree.
The monitoring of exit orientation is based on Almalaurea data.

Additional initiatives
1. As already reported, the Course of Study has relationships with several Italian sports federations; some of these issue certifications and/or specific titles.
2. The Course of Study is affiliated with EAS (European Athlete as Student): this is a European network established in 2004 under the auspices of the European Commission, with the primary objective of supporting European athletes in combining sports and high-performance education. Some faculty members of the Course of Study were funded for the Erasmus+ project 'More than Gold' (Project n. 603346-EPP-1-2018-1-LV-SPO-SCP), submitted jointly with EAS and four other European partners, for the years 2019-2020. Thanks to this collaboration, the course has promoted a dual career regulation that supports the student-athlete in their academic journey. The regulation was issued in January 2020.
3. Unlike other Courses of Study that identify professionals for whom a professional register exists, graduates in Sciences of Motor Activities and Sport are unfortunately not registered in a specific professional register. However, the Course of Study has actively engaged at both local and national levels to identify a professional field for its graduates.
In particular:
- A working group was established at the Abruzzo Region (Prot. 0044859/18) to promote, within prevention and health promotion projects, the professionalism of graduates in motor and sports fields, leading to the 'Palestre della Salute' and 'Palestre Sicure' projects (https://www.dmsi.unich.it/il-progetto-regionale-palestre-della-salute-e-palestre-sicure). These projects, implemented in 2020, represent the outcome of a long period of discussion and reflection, beginning in 2018, between the Course of Study leadership of UdA and the University of L'Aquila, the Abruzzo Region's Health Department, sector representatives (Italian Committee of Motor Sciences), General Practitioners, and Regional Sports Doctors, regarding the role and competencies that undergraduate and graduate students in motor sciences should possess for the prevention and management of exercise-sensitive pathologies (obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, colon and breast cancer, Alzheimer's disease, etc.). The project entered its implementation phase in 2022 and involves graduates in the region.
It is believed that such projects may influence the future occupational profile of graduates, and therefore the dialogue with these institutions has been (and continues to be) profoundly useful for guiding the Course of Study's educational choices.

UNIVERSITY: GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO UNIVERSITY – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L022] SCIENCES OF MOTOR ACTIVITIES AND SPORT
SECTION: STUDENT OPINIONS
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/546

Student Opinions The collected data show a generally positive picture regarding satisfaction with the Study Program (CdS). Students consistently appreciate the study program, as suggested by the average score of 3.40 out of 4, indicating a high level of satisfaction. It is interesting to note that this score is also increasing compared to previous years, suggesting gradual improvement in the CdS. A particularly reassuring aspect is that all evaluations associated with the courses exceed a score of 3, suggesting that students generally perceive adequate quality in the courses and instructors. This is an important indicator of the overall quality of the study program, as student engagement and interest are often directly correlated with the quality of teaching. It is equally significant that none of the questionnaire questions received a score below 2.5, confirming that the program's weak points appear to be minimal or absent. The lowest evaluation was assigned to the perception of the proportionality between the required study load and the assigned credits, as well as to the sufficiency of preliminary knowledge for understanding the program's topics, both with a score of 3.26. These scores suggest that instructors for each subject need to consider students' initial level. On the other hand, it is encouraging to note that the highest evaluations were assigned to adherence to schedules and instructors' availability to provide clarifications, both with a score of 3.50. These results indicate that the CdS appears to ensure a well-organized time structure and strong interaction between students and instructors. Finally, the fact that the evaluations for the CdS are very similar to the average values of the University and the Scientific Area suggests that the program is cohesively integrated within the institution and the broader disciplinary area. Although some minor differences are present, these do not appear to be statistically significant, suggesting that the CdS is aligned in quality with the general standards of the university and the reference scientific area. In summary, the data indicate a positive evaluation of the CdS by students, with some areas for possible improvement, but overall, the program seems to satisfactorily meet students' expectations. The CdS has repeatedly sensitized instructors to provide teaching materials in advance at the address https://fad.unich.it/. According to the CPDS, the student body does not report any critical issues that differ from the daily student experience as revealed by the questionnaires; simultaneously, the CPDS has reiterated the need to sensitize students on the significance of their opinions being collected; moreover, considering the improvement in student evaluations recorded over the three-year period, it hopes that effective and continuous interaction with the CdS/AQ group and/or the reference instructors will be maintained to identify and resolve any issues related to the overall organization and individual courses. In addition to the possibility of expressing their judgment on the courses offered, students also have access to a centralized customer care and complaint system (see link) and the opportunity to express opinions on the internship offer.

GRADUATE OPINIONS From the analysis of AlmaLaurea data (https://pqa.unich.it/sites/st16/files/allegatiparagrafo/28-04-2022/scienze_delle_attivita_motorie_e_sportive_l-22.pdf), updated as of April 2023, it emerges that graduates' overall judgment is positive and in line with the university's standards ('definitely yes' and 'more yes than no' 89.8% average for the course vs 90% university and 88.8% national).
In particular, the relationship with faculty in general is positive ('definitely yes' and 'more yes than no' 88.4% vs 90.3% university and 87.6% national), as is the organization of exams ('definitely yes' and 'more yes than no' 88.0% vs 79.8% university and 82.8% national). The data are similar to those recorded in the previous academic year.
The percentage of graduates who attended more than 50% of the required courses is similar to last year (81.5% vs 88.4% university and 88.6% national).
Positive also is the evaluation of classrooms, considered often or almost always adequate by 83.9% of students (vs 84.3% university and 84.1% national), and of libraries ('definitely positive' and 'quite positive' 85.2% vs 89.3 university and 93.2% national). Starting from last year, there has been a significant increase in appreciation of laboratory facilities, considered often or always adequate by 73.2% vs 62% two years ago. Regarding this, the course of study (CdS) had invested available teaching funds in setting up two new gyms and enhancing the existing teaching laboratory: unfortunately, the health emergency made it impossible to use these new facilities for the academic years 2019/20 and 2020/21, while they were used (and therefore appreciated) during the academic years 2021/22 and 2022/23.
However, despite this important positive trend, the evaluation of computer workstations remains low and similar to the university's (59.6% vs 56.3 university and 49.1% national). This criticality has always been reported, even by the parity commissions of previous years. Therefore, a joint action with CPDS is necessary to sensitize the medical school to the problem of the facilities.
The data regarding graduates' opinions will be discussed in the next CdS councils.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is achieved through practical exercises conducted by course instructors during the semester, and subsequently, at the end of the academic period, through oral or written assessments. Additionally, this ability is acquired through mandatory participation in Training Internships, whose suitability assessment is obtained only after the student effectively demonstrates understanding of the course content and the ability to apply the related knowledge.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is verified through a specific questionnaire administered to the referents—internal or external to the CdS—of the Training Internship activities that students must complete over the three years of the course. The collected data are extremely useful for verifying to what extent students can apply, in a professional context, the knowledge acquired in the classroom.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
The course structure, based on theoretical lectures, small-group sessions, practical lessons, and exercises conducted in small groups, combined with internships at affiliated facilities where content, methods, and objectives have been defined, will enable students to acquire learning and transfer skills to the workplace. Graduates must possess the ability to integrate into various work environments, assume responsibilities, and work both individually and in groups.
The learning skills developed during the course will serve as a tool for continuous cultural and professional post-graduation updating.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
Knowledge is acquired through conventional teaching (classroom lectures) supplemented by meetings and practical exercises, also in groups, at laboratories and gyms. Studying motor and sports techniques and functional measurement and evaluation systems is necessary for effectively understanding the practical differences of various motor and sports activities and the effects of physical exercise on motor preparation and health. Knowledge is further acquired through the mandatory attendance of Curricular and Training Internships, which complete the student's academic path and represent an important phase for developing understanding through the application of knowledge gained through conventional teaching.
Knowledge and understanding are verified not only through mandatory assessments but also increasingly through in-course assessments conducted in classrooms or laboratories with student groups. These in-course assessments allow instructors to evaluate the degree of understanding of topics covered during the course, track progressive knowledge acquisition relative to the planned curriculum, and introduce corrective actions if necessary before the final assessment of the course.

Brief Course Description CHARACTERISTICS AND OBJECTIVES
The Course provides a general preparation for the professional in physical activity, understood as body movement for educational, recreational, sports, or health maintenance/recovery purposes.
The Course is three years long, totaling 180 university credits (CFU). Teaching is organized in semesters and includes frontal and laboratory activities followed by assessments.
The Course aims to transmit adequate technical-scientific knowledge and skills for designing, conducting, and managing motor and sports activities in public and private facilities and sports organizations (Societies and Federations).
To this end, it requires that the learning of basic disciplines precede and be aimed at building operational and applied skills.
In particular, basic disciplines (Physics, Chemistry, Anatomy, Physiology, Anthropometry, etc.) form the foundation for understanding and studying the effects of physical exercise, which in turn constitute the cultural basis for the more specific Course content regarding the technical-training and methodological aspects of motor and sports activities.
The Course also provides solid knowledge in biomedical fields, necessary for forming a competent professional in health maintenance and improvement.
Similarly, psycho-pedagogical aspects are developed in relation to motor and sports disciplines to provide the cultural basis for the instructor profession.
Practical skills are acquired through field exercises and internships activated at motor and sports facilities within the University or at numerous external affiliated facilities.
The Course has also introduced part-time enrollment, primarily for working students; for this purpose, the Course has prepared a specific study plan organized over six years.
WORKING AREAS Graduates acquire the theoretical and practical abilities necessary to design, conduct, teach, and evaluate physical activity in its various forms; autonomous in their professional field, they are able to base their activities on scientific foundations and update professionally.
Graduates find employment in public and private facilities, sports organizations, recreational and social associations, and centers promoting and conducting motor and sports activities in various environments.
FROM SCHOOL TO UNIVERSITY The Course has local quota-based access. Graduates with a high school diploma grade below 75/100 will be assigned additional educational obligations (OFA). The methods for fulfilling these obligations are detailed in the Didactic Regulation.

Specific Course Objectives and Course Path Description The specific objective of the Bachelor's degree in Science of Motor Activities and Sports is to provide adequate cultural and operational skills for:
a) Conducting and evaluating individual and group motor activities with educational, recreational, and sports purposes aimed at maintaining physical and psychological well-being through promoting active lifestyles;
b) Conducting, managing, and evaluating individual and group fitness activities.
It is necessary to develop reference professional profiles equipped with the culture and technical-scientific skills required to take charge of guiding practitioners through motor activity paths that align with their goals and abilities, while minimizing common issues associated with incorrect sports practice and various physical activities. These can be carried out in organized forms, in public and private locations, within social sports, competitive sports, and tourist-recreational services, with the goals of achieving, maintaining, or restoring physical and psychological well-being, expressing and improving active lifestyles, developing social relationships, and achieving satisfying or competitive performances.
Graduates will be able to immediately enter the workforce, as well as access master's degree courses or qualification master's programs for specific professional activities.
To this end, the Bachelor's degree aims to develop knowledge and skills in motor-sports and biomedical fields related to sports and various forms of physical activity necessary for:
- Conducting motor and sports activity programs in forms and ways that best respond to the needs and abilities of practitioners and the territorial and cultural context in which they are conducted;
- Taking autonomous judgment and developing skills related to evaluation and analysis procedures of the practitioner and context, necessary for a correct proposal of motor and sports activities;
- Acquiring a scientific work method that leads to continuous development and updating of cultural and operational skills, enabling comparison with the international professional world, and developing the ability and propensity to progress in their educational process.
The Bachelor's degree is structured into teaching courses, elective activities, and internships partially organized in collaboration with CUS Chieti, the Superior Schools of the Chieti and Pescara provinces, and other selected sports societies, integrated with course teachings and aimed at developing specific practical and operational skills in motor and sports activities.
The course, structured in semesters for a progressive didactic path, requires that courses follow in the three years so that the learning of basic disciplines precedes and is aimed at building operational and applied skills.
In particular, knowledge provided by basic disciplines forms the foundation for understanding and studying physiological effects of exercise, which in turn provide the cultural basis for the more specific course content regarding the execution of movement and its trainability. Biomedical knowledge ensures the formation of a competent professional in the fields of human health maintenance and improvement.
Similarly, psycho-pedagogical aspects are addressed in relation to motor and sports disciplines to provide the cultural basis for the instructor profession.
The analysis and study of various forms of motor and sports activities are conducted without predefined division into sports disciplines; this approach allows addressing the scientific and cultural aspects of different disciplines with a unique didactic and analytical methodology. Within these teachings, selective training paths for selected sports disciplines are further developed, also with the collaboration and intervention of CONI Sports Federations. It is expected that these teaching activities conducted in collaboration with Federations may lead to recognition of the university training path for access to federal technical staff.
In the preventive area, knowledge is acquired for maintaining optimal physical efficiency throughout life in normal subjects aiming to prevent sedentary-related pathologies through active and healthy lifestyles. Additionally, knowledge of legal-administrative and managerial aspects regulating motor activities is transmitted. Knowledge of English, provided through a dedicated course not only covering basic language but also specifically addressing the world of sports and motor activities, will enable proper access to international scientific and technical knowledge.
The Bachelor's degree allows a portion of CFUs to be acquired through Erasmus experiences at European universities. Other fundamental skills for updating, such as the ability to conduct bibliographic research and critically analyze scientific literature, can be developed through specific interventions and preparation for the final exam, which concludes the studies.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements The CdS has chosen to allocate most internship hours to the third year and at external entities to facilitate students' relationship with the labor market.
The opinion of external entities hosting students annually is generally evaluated through an online questionnaire. This tool serves as continuous consultation to gather information on the cultural and professional level of interns, as well as observations and requests for new or different skills deemed relevant. Both internship activities and annual meetings with hosting entities allow the CdS to obtain significant information to effectively guide educational curricula.
Activities have been developed in-house or in collaboration with external partners, such as sports societies, sports federations, regional sports committees, sports associations, independent professionals, private studios, and provincial school offices. In total, 36 internships were organized across the first, second, and third years. Seven agreements provided for the issuance of a certificate, recognized by the relevant sports federation or a certified regional training center, at a subsidized or free cost.
Compared to previous years, all activities were conducted in person except for the FIGC Grassroots Soccer Instructor Level E course, conducted in collaboration with FIGC. This course included an online theoretical component, adhering to FIGC's post-pandemic requirements. Nevertheless, the federation committed to switching to in-person delivery for the following academic year.
Companies were asked to evaluate, beyond attendance, proactivity, punctuality, professionalism, learning, and preparation. Unfortunately, the number of received forms is insufficient to form a judgment on students. Therefore, companies were further encouraged to provide a detailed evaluation of hosted interns.
The CdS could not proceed with the project proposed by the school office during the steering committee meeting, which aimed to organize joint training activities between the Course and the school office to enhance graduates' educational skills. This project had enabled CdS students to complete their training internships at eight Comprehensive Schools.
The questionnaire prepared by the CdS for internship evaluation generally received positive feedback from students. Students were asked to respond to the following questions using a scale from one to five, where one indicated low satisfaction and five indicated high satisfaction:
1. Do you consider this activity useful from an educational perspective?
2. Is the required effort adequate for the assigned CFUs?
3. Does the activity have professionalizing value?
4. Are the facilities where the activity was conducted adequate?
5. Was the tutor available to support the activity?
6. Was the meeting schedule respected?
7. Were you directly involved in the internship activities?
First-year activities received an average rating of 4.7. Second-year activities received an average rating of 4.7. Third-year activities received an average rating of 4.6 with a minimum of 3.3. Overall, all questionnaire items were rated positively or more than positively, with few exceptions.
From the described situation, several improvement proposals can be considered, such as:
- Further encouraging companies to provide detailed evaluations of hosted interns;
- Expanding the variety of entities involved in internships;
- Carefully analyzing questionnaire results to identify specific areas for improvement and implementing corrective actions;
- Collaborating with the school office to offer students broader learning opportunities and integrate internship skills with relevant educational sector competencies;
- Collecting student experiences after completing internships and evaluating their suggestions.
Data related to this framework will be discussed in the next CdS councils.
Consultation with National and International Organizations Representing Goods and Service Production, Professions (Course Establishment)
Consultation was conducted at the university level on February 13, 2014. During this meeting, no specific criticalities regarding the CdS were identified.
Consultation with National and International Organizations Representing Goods and Service Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
The CdS had previously established a Steering Committee (SUA 2017 A1b); however, this committee never became operational due to limited availability of involved entities to participate in structured meetings (SUA-CdS 2018 A1b). Therefore, the CdS re-established a joint Steering Committee (CI) for CL-SAMS and CLM-STAMPA (SUA-CdS 2019 A1b [1]), composed of:
- The Chair of the L-22 Course
- The Chair of the LM-67 Course
- The Chair of CONI Abruzzo and some Federations (Regional Offices)
- The Regional School of Sport – CONI Abruzzo
- Representation of the Italian Committee of Motor Sciences
- Representation of the National Union of Kinesiologists
- Representation of the Regional School Office and/or some primary and secondary schools;
- Representation of the Department for Health and Prevention, Abruzzo Region Health Assessorate;
- Representation of Sports Doctors of Chieti and Pescara;
- Representation of General Practitioners;
- Representation of ASDs and gyms;
- Student representation from L-22 and LM-67.
This new CI first met on February 25, 2020, thanks to sustained efforts over time and in various contexts to sensitize stakeholders about the importance of dialogue to improve the educational project of the two Courses in line with labor market demands. During the meeting, significant interest from the school world was registered, which expressed willingness to collaborate closely with the CdS to outline educational content relevant to the primary school graduate. Discussions also focused on the various professional fields of the three-year and master's graduates. The table was reconvened on April 4, 2024, to jointly analyze the regulations on non-regulated professions, particularly the report on non-organized professions including the kinesiologist profession under Legislative Decree No. 36 of February 28, 2021, Article 41, regarding the reorganization and reform of provisions on professional and amateur sports entities and sports work (see regulations https://www.gazzettaufficiale.it/eli/id/2021/03/18/21G00043/sg).
The CdS has continued to engage informally with accredited internship entities and institutions interested in sports, prevention, adapted physical activity, fitness, motor education, and research to obtain significant information for effectively guiding educational curricula and to stimulate institutional interest in the professional figure of the Graduate in Motor Sciences and the development of appropriate professional opportunities.
Specifically:
- Thanks to Prof. Claudio Robazza, member of the internal PQ and Director of the Regional School of Sport, the dialogue with CONI has strengthened over time and has materialized in joint organization of practical internships, highly professionalizing seminar activities within curricular courses, and roundtables open to teachers, instructors, and students;
- The dialogue with the school world and motor education has been maintained through internship activities at schools and the "School in Motion" project, aimed at primary school children (approximately 23,000 children/year), promoting correct lifestyles. This project, active from 2015 to 2020, involved three-year graduates in primary school classes, allowed CdS students to complete internships at schools, and involved the CdS in research on the school population and the development of work protocols. This project verified the technical, scientific, and operational qualities of young graduates. The judgment of School Directors and reference teachers, gathered during specific meetings and via a questionnaire, highlighted strong appreciation for CdS graduates by teachers, who also emphasized the need to consolidate the presence of specialist educators in motor sciences within primary schools;
- The regional projects 'Health Gyms' and 'Safe Gyms' (https://www.dmsi.unich.it/il-progetto-regionale-palestre-della-salute-e-palestre-sicure), implemented since 2020, represent the outcome of a long period of dialogue and reflection, initiated in 2018, between the Chairs of the UdA and University of L'Aquila Courses, the Abruzzo Region Health Assessorate, category representatives (Italian Committee of Motor Sciences), General Practitioners, and Sports Doctors, regarding the role and skills that three-year and master's graduates in motor sciences should have for preventing and managing exercise-sensitive pathologies (obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, colon and breast cancer, Alzheimer's disease, etc.). It is believed that these projects, together with 'School in Motion,' may influence the occupational profile of graduates in the near future, making the dialogue with these institutions profoundly useful for guiding the CdS educational choices;
- Activities in 'Sports Journalism' and the permanent 'Press Office Lab' (with the endorsement of the order and highly applied content) allow the CdS to engage with professional journalists and ensure continuous adaptation to new and different skill requirements from the press, television, and web. The experimentation of new communication methods, involving the contamination of 'classic' journalism with social media use, has materialized in practical experiences, such as managing the Lab's social media pages (https://www.facebook.com/LAB-Ufficio-Stampa-508883656133417/), and successful projects (winners of the One Mile Minds award, 2018 and 2019);
- Simultaneously, the CdS has continued to monitor the demand for skills in the labor market and professional sectors (amateur sports associations, private entities, gyms, etc.) through a stakeholder survey. This is a data collection system based on evaluation forms completed by hosting entities and affiliated parties for student internships. This tool serves as a 'continuous consultation' to gather information on the cultural and professional level of interns, as well as observations and requests for new or different skills deemed relevant. The questionnaire is administered to all facilities hosting CL-SAMS students for curricular internships starting from 2015, by the Course Chair, but only from 2018 have the data been reprocessed and formally discussed by the internal PQ and the Course Council. It is noted, however, that only a limited number of facilities complete the questionnaire; additionally, administrative issues in 2019 (leave, first temporary and then definitive, of the staff member responsible for organizing internships) made data collection even more difficult. The outcomes of dialogues with institutions, analysis of internship questionnaires, and contextual evolution (particularly the projects with the Region) have been presented and discussed in the CdS over time (CdS Meeting Minutes of September 19, 2018, October 25, 2018, September 25, 2019).
The offered training is particularly suitable for the well-being, health, and leisure sectors, while greater efforts should be dedicated to training operators in the sports sector. Strong appreciation of CdS students by primary school teachers, while secondary school teachers and ASD operators have highlighted the need for a greater practical-application component in student preparation.
The actions identified by the CdS to address criticalities and suggestions from the labor market, already detailed in the 2019 RCC, are briefly reported here:
a) Revision of the elective course offerings and curricular internships;
b) Control of Syllabi to ensure consistency with the Course of Study;
c) Sensitizing faculty to support the development of soft skills;
d) Modification of content in 'Principles and Techniques for Physical Preparation', 'Individual Sports', and 'Team Sports' courses to favor the practical component;
e) Establishment of a Training and Student Careers Committee to evaluate the educational plan and quality of external internships.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data Regarding the last five academic years, the data recorded in previous SUA reports and those from the 2022/2023 report (see https://pqa.unich.it/dati-statistici) are as follows:
2018/19 - Enrolled: 423 (pure: 374) - Total enrolled: 1578 (ongoing: 1090);
2019/20 - Enrolled: 422 (pure: 379) - Total enrolled: 1505 (ongoing: 1038);
2020/21 - Enrolled: 432 (pure: 375) - Total enrolled: 1460 (ongoing: 1066);
2021/22 - Enrolled: 345 (pure: 298) - Total enrolled: 1322 (ongoing: 981);
2022/23 - Enrolled: 348 (pure: 306) - Total enrolled: 1211 (ongoing: 903).
The course appears to maintain its attractiveness over time (the closed enrollment was set at 420 units from 2018/19). The decline in enrolled students for the academic years 2021/22 and 2022/23 may be attributed to the introduction of the mandatory TOLC-F test.
The positive trend regarding the number of ongoing students is confirmed, increasing from 64% in 2016/17 to 69% in 2018/19 and 2019/20, and from 73% in 2020/21 to 74% in 2021/22 and 75% in 2022/23.
Regarding the origin of first-year students, it remains nearly constant with approximately 74% of students from the Abruzzo region (258) and the remainder from other regions (90).
Approximately 74% of students obtained their high school diploma with a grade below 80/100.
The origin of enrolled students is approximately 48% (vs 52% of the previous year) from high schools and 52% from technical, professional, and other institutes.
The number of graduates in the last five years is as follows:
2018/19 – 132 ongoing, 42 one year late, 82 two years late;
2019/20 – 51 ongoing, 43 one year late, 99 two years late;
2020/21 – 133 ongoing, 58 one year late, 93 two years late;
2021/22 – 173 ongoing, 56 one year late, 65 two years late;
2022/23 – 195 ongoing, 27 one year late, 55 two years late.
This trend shows an increase in ongoing graduates and a reduction in late graduates.
The distribution of graduation grades has remained relatively stable:
2018/19 – 9 grades of 110-110L, 17 grades of 105-109, 230 grades below 105;
2019/20 – 1 grade of 110-110L, 7 grades of 105-109, 286 grades below 105;
2020/21 – 2 grades of 110-110L, 10 grades of 105-109, 272 grades below 105;
2021/22 – 0 grades of 110-110L, 16 grades of 105-109, 280 grades below 105;
2022/23 – 6 grades of 110-110L, 34 grades of 105-109, 237 grades below 105.
In summary, the data on graduate trends over the last five years show a picture characterized by an increase in ongoing graduates and a reduction in late graduates. This suggests that the CdS is making positive progress in optimizing academic efficiency. However, it is important to continue working to ensure even greater student success through continuous monitoring of trends over the years to identify potential emerging trends or issues. This can help pinpoint specific areas requiring targeted interventions. Entry activities should also be supported by offering new students comprehensive orientation aimed at helping them organize and optimize their study path. Finally, it is important to continue collecting student feedback and using this information to improve the study path.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data will be discussed in the next CdS councils.
Final Exam Characteristics Four credits are reserved for the final exam.
In the final exam, the candidate presents to the Commission, possibly using multimedia tools, their own compiled or experimental work, or a brief synthesis of a scientific publication, textbook chapter, or other agreed-upon publication.
The work or synthesis is prepared under the supervision of a Course instructor, the supervisor, and possibly external co-supervisors.
Final Exam Execution The student must:
- Have passed all exams related to the courses in the study plan;
- Have obtained suitability in internship activities;
- Have fulfilled administrative obligations as per the Student Secretariat.
The final exam, which constitutes an important individual educational opportunity to complete the path, aims to engage the student in formalization, planning, and development work. The thesis content must relate to the Course's educational objectives.
The final exam work may be a literature review with critical data analysis in the case of a compiled thesis, or an illustration of materials, methods, and results of a student-conducted research under the supervisor's guidance in the case of an experimental thesis. Three graduation sessions are scheduled (summer, autumn, and extraordinary).
Two weeks before the graduation session, the candidate presents their work, possibly using multimedia tools, to a pre-evaluation committee composed of the supervisor and two other Course instructors, appointed by the Course Chair; additional members beyond the instructors may include thesis co-supervisors or those who have significantly contributed to the research without formal roles in the Course.
The evaluation of the work will be based on the depth of the work, critical engagement, cultural maturity, personal elaboration ability, accuracy of execution, synthesis ability, and clarity of exposition. The supervisor then transmits a copy of the student's work and the pre-evaluation committee minutes to the Evaluation Committee and the Course's Academic Secretariat.
On the graduation session day, the Evaluation Committee, composed of at least five and no more than seven instructors, evaluates the work, assigning a score not exceeding six points, and also evaluates the candidate's entire academic path.
The final exam score is expressed in hundredths with possible honors, whose attribution, in case of a score of at least 110/110, is at the discretion of the Graduation Committee and is decided without specific automatic calculation mechanisms, granted only if all committee members unanimously agree.
The graduation grade is determined by:
- The weighted average of grades obtained in curricular exams, expressed in hundredths;
- Honors obtained in profit exams (0.1 point per honor);
- Study completion time within the legal duration of the degree course (3 points for those graduating on time);
- Student participation in international exchange projects (1 point);
- Points assigned by the committee for the final exam (maximum 6).
Below are the different evaluation criteria.
COMPILED THESIS
-Quality of selected documentation
0: Theoretical references regarding the thesis topic are missing or irrelevant;
1-2: The theoretical framework of references is outlined broadly;
3-4: The theoretical framework of references is indicated with sufficient precision to draw conclusions;
5-6: The theoretical framework of references is indicated in depth, considering national and international scientific literature.
-Quality of the synthesis performed
0: No synthesis is performed; sources are listed sequentially without integration effort;
1-2: Sources are presented with minimal integration;
3-4: Sources are presented with good integration;
5-6: Sources are integrated excellently and systematically, providing a complete and updated overview of the current state of the art regarding the topic.
-Quality of exposition and communication effectiveness
0: Poor quality of exposition and communication effectiveness;
1-2: Sufficient quality of exposition and communication effectiveness;
3-4: Good quality of exposition and communication effectiveness in presenting the work;
5-6: Excellent quality of exposition and communication effectiveness.
EXPERIMENTAL THESIS
-Importance of the work hypothesis or fundamental question
0: The hypothesis/fundamental question is not formulated and presented;
1-2: The hypothesis/fundamental question is formulated and presented in general terms;
3-4: The hypothesis/fundamental question is formulated and presented clearly, with references to the current state of the art;
5-6: The hypothesis/fundamental question is formulated and presented excellently, with systematic references to the current state of the art.
-Quality of selected documentation
0: Theoretical references regarding the thesis topic are missing or irrelevant;
1-2: The theoretical framework of references is outlined broadly;
3-4: The theoretical framework of references is indicated with sufficient precision to draw conclusions;
5-6: The theoretical framework of references is indicated in depth, considering national and international scientific literature.
-Quality of data collection methodology
0: Work methodology and data collection are absent;
1-2: Work methodology and data collection are described generally;
3-4: Work methodology and data collection are described clearly;
5-6: Work methodology and data collection are described excellently.
-Quality of data interpretation
0: No interpretation of empirical data is present;
1-2: Empirical data present minimal interpretation;
3-4: Empirical data present good interpretation;
5-6: Empirical data are interpreted excellently and systematically, providing a complete overview and thorough analysis of the theoretical framework regarding the selected topic.
-Quality of conclusion
0: Conclusions are absent;
1-2: Conclusions are present but consist of inconsistent observations relative to the rest of the work;
3-4: Conclusions refer to the fundamental hypothesis/question presented and summarize results sufficiently;
5-6: Conclusions refer to the fundamental hypothesis/question presented and summarize results meticulously and elaborately, linking these to the current state of the art regarding the topic.
-Quality of exposition and communication effectiveness
0: Poor quality of exposition and communication effectiveness;
1-2: Sufficient quality of exposition and communication effectiveness;
3-4: Good quality of exposition and communication effectiveness in presenting the work;
5-6: Excellent quality of exposition and communication effectiveness.
After assigning scores for each evaluation criterion, the arithmetic mean of the scores is calculated to obtain the final score (maximum 6 points) to be assigned to the candidate.
The minimum passing score for the final exam is 66/110.
Once the graduation grade is determined, the Committee proceeds with the proclamation.

The Faculty has adequate, appropriate, and effective facilities. Admission Procedures For the 2024-25 academic year, enrollment in the Bachelor's Degree in Sustainable Habitat Sciences is open.
After enrollment, basic knowledge will be verified through a test that also serves for the assignment of any Additional Educational Requirements (OFA).
OFA, categorized by thematic areas (Mathematics and Physics, Drawing and Representation, History of Architecture), consist of additional individual training activities assigned based on not achieving a minimum threshold of correct answers (at least 30% of the total score) in each thematic area during the verification test.
1) OFA can be fulfilled by participating in individual training activities assigned directly by the responsible instructor or by attending integrated teaching courses led by tutors specializing in the OFA subjects.
2) OFA can also be fulfilled by passing the corresponding exams for the three thematic areas:
a) HISTORY OF LANDSCAPE AND COMMON GOODS - 12 cfu for the History of Architecture thematic area;
b) HABITAT DRAWING - 12 cfu for the Drawing and Representation thematic area;
c) ELEMENTS OF CLIMATOLOGY - 12 cfu for the Mathematics and Physics thematic area.
3) OFA debts can also be cleared by earning at least 24 cfu from first-year exams in TAF type A and B.
This means that a student with OFA debts cannot enroll in second-year exams if they do not meet at least one of the three criteria.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate must acquire the ability to adequately communicate to the client, operators and the public the meaning, content and effects of the proposed technical solutions, with particular reference to objectives, formal and functional options, implementation and management methods of anthropic interventions.
The degree course will provide the knowledge and methodological and operational tools to develop students' communication skills, in written, graphic and oral form. Teaching activities are organized to ensure group work and interaction with the teacher and external guests. The traditional lecture model is complemented by the workshop model, which involves active student participation in working groups and the potential contribution of expert external speakers. Moreover, digital representation and communication methods and techniques are adopted in various courses, emphasizing the use of multimedia communication systems. Communication skills are also developed through cultural exchange opportunities within international mobility programs at the designated foreign sites.
Communication skills, presentation ability and mastery of technical/specialist terminology are verified through:
- the final exams of each training activity, in oral and/or written form.

UNIVERSITY: GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO UNIVERSITY - CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [910T] SUSTAINABLE HABITAT SCIENCES
SECTION: JUDGMENT AUTONOMY
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1864

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
The graduate must develop a reflective attitude regarding the effects of plans, measures, and anthropic interventions in the existing context. To this end, the degree course will provide both technical-scientific tools and socio-cultural knowledge to stimulate the capacity for critical elaboration at an individual level. In this direction, the graduate must possess, at the end of the study course, their own personal judgment autonomy regarding methodological choices in territorial governance processes in interdisciplinary contexts.
The development of judgment autonomy will be encouraged through the elaboration of plans and applied solutions in which the student will be stimulated to develop their critical spirit and make decisions, both individually and in work groups, simulating the multidisciplinary operational methods present in professional activity.
The assessment of the achieved judgment capacity and autonomy will be carried out progressively in the profit exams of the courses and in the preparation and discussion of the final degree thesis.

Entrance Orientation The entrance orientation activities for the Degree Program in Sustainable Habitat Sciences are promoted by both the University (Orientation Office, Tutoring, Placement, etc.) and directly by the Degree Program in Sustainable Habitat Sciences in coordination with the Department of Architecture.
University entrance orientation activities, within the Uda Orienta program (https://orientamento.unich.it/uda-orienta), aim to provide high school students with integrated services to improve their relationship with the University.
In particular, the University coordinates the following entrance orientation activities:

- Student fairs and exhibitions where direct meetings with department and course professors are possible to deepen knowledge of the University and understand its opportunities (e.g., Student Fair).

Entrance orientation is also carried out through the provision and distribution of printed informational materials and the availability of numerous online services, ranging from pre-enrollment and matriculation to administrative procedures and exam booking.

Information on entrance orientation is available on the Department's dedicated website (http://www.architettura.unich.it/habitat/), including details about the Degree Program characteristics, professional opportunities and skills, access modalities and teaching methods, calendar and booking forms for individual online meetings, news, and newsletter registration.

International Mobility Office In total, the Department of Architecture and the Habitat Bachelor's program currently have the following agreements for international student mobility:
34 Erasmus agreements;
23 international agreements;
14 agreements with non-European locations.
ERASMUS MOBILITY Erasmus+ is a European program that allows students to spend a study period or complete an internship in an EU country for a duration ranging from 3 to 12 months.
An annual selection is announced for students to compete for Erasmus+ mobility scholarships, with a notice published in the Official Bulletin and on the University website.
The Department of Architecture offers a wide range of destinations with prestigious European universities through agreements in the following countries: Belgium, Germany, Spain, France, Greece, Croatia, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, United Kingdom.
The Course Coordinator for Erasmus (Professor Stefania Gruosso) assists outgoing students in completing Learning Agreements, providing guidance on the partner university's course offerings and other information.
Proposes the validation of exams completed at the foreign location, converting them into grades and credits, for approval by the Course Council.
INTERNATIONAL MOBILITY The Department of Architecture annually funds international student mobility for study and research activities at designated partner locations in countries outside the European Union.
The Coordinator of the International Agreement, Professor Domenico Potenza (selected among Department faculty), organizes a selection procedure with a notice published on the Department website, forming a merit ranking to allocate positions based on annual program availability.
The academic/educational validity of projects involving students is subject to approval by the Course Council for credit recognition, following a positive evaluation by the Agreement Coordinator, who may seek the opinion of the teaching professor.
Students receiving financial support for international mobility must earn at least 12 CFU within the elective CFU category.

DEPARTMENT CAREER GUIDANCE In addition to initiatives promoted by the University through the Job Placement service, the Department organizes specific activities aimed at strengthening relationships with the world of work and businesses, in line with the needs expressed by stakeholders during various consultation sessions.

The program, particularly curated by the Sustainable Habitat Sciences Bachelor's Program, included in the first session meetings with actors (public and private) operating in the fields of urban and territorial planning and environmental design, which updated students on the various opportunities available through extracurricular placements to transfer knowledge acquired during studies to the workplace and develop new professional skills.
In the second session, a debate took place between students, companies, and public bodies on the evolution of the labor market in sustainability fields, particularly Green Jobs.

The overall result is very satisfactory, scoring 3.52, which exceeds both the average score available for study programs in the scientific area (3.43) and the average for all programs across the University (3.43).
Regarding specific questionnaire questions, a positive assessment was noted for interest in the discipline (3.56) and for the coherence of individual courses with both the Bachelor's Program curriculum and the information provided on the website (3.57). Students reported effective course organization in terms of availability to provide support and useful methodological tools for understanding the subjects covered (3.74).
A detailed analysis of the 20 courses offered in the 2022-23 academic year shows excellent performance (Level A) for 10 courses, good performance (Level B) for 6 courses, and satisfactory (Level C) for the remaining 3 courses.
Student opinion data will be presented and discussed at the Bachelor's Program Council meeting scheduled for 27 September 2022.
For managing student complaints (Customer Satisfaction), the Program Committee relies on the centralized University-level complaint management system (https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi).
This system is also accessible via the Departmental website.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI-PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO
COURSE: [600P] TECHNICAL PROFESSIONS FOR CONSTRUCTION AND TERRITORY
SECTION: Admission procedures
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1903

Admission procedures Access to the degree course is locally regulated and a maximum of 50 places is available (of which 10 are reserved for public employees as per the PA 110 and Lode memorandum of understanding between the Minister for Public Administration and the University of Chieti-Pescara Gabriele d'Annunzio).
The numerical quota is ensured through an enrollment procedure based on the chronological order of application submission.
This enrollment procedure consists of three phases: 1) reservation, 2) enrollment, 3) completion. The reservation list is ordered according to the aforementioned criterion, and the completion of enrollment procedures - where the number of places has not been reached - results in a new reservation list. The process repeats until the available places are exhausted.
It is required that enrolled students with a secondary school grade below 70/100 must fulfill Additional Educational Obligations (OFA), which consist of passing at least one exam among the basic subjects (Physics and Fundamentals of Informatics) and the Topography course by February of the academic year following enrollment.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [600P] TECHNICAL PROFESSIONS FOR CONSTRUCTION AND TERRITORY
SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1903

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills (communication skills)
All teaching activities of the professionalizing Bachelor's degree program include both written and oral assessments, in which the student has the opportunity to measure and refine their own effective communication skills for the results of their study activities. The student will therefore be encouraged to learn how to communicate technical topics rigorously, clearly, and coherently. During the training process, the student will be called upon to work individually and as a member of a group. In particular, the comparison with other students in group work will be an incentive to develop discussion and debate skills. Laboratory activities and internships will also constitute essential tools for developing communication skills and will simultaneously promote the student's personal and professional growth. The final exam, which involves discussing the results achieved before a committee, will offer an additional opportunity for in-depth study and verification of the student's analytical, processing, and transfer skills for the content of the work completed.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [600P] PROFESSIONAL TECHNICAL PROFESSIONS FOR CONSTRUCTION AND TERRITORY
SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1903

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
During the course of study, the student will be trained to choose the most appropriate approach to solving basic technical problems, critically analyzing their various aspects in a multidisciplinary manner, and will be able to make operational decisions.
The numerous laboratory activities, the completion of the training internship, and the final application-oriented exam will allow the student to practice the acquired knowledge, by confronting practical cases, and to make well-founded decisions that take into account the various aspects involved.
Among the aims of the proposed training activities is also the ability to work in a group, to select relevant information, to choose and use appropriate tools and analysis methods, to define strategies collectively, to justify, also dialectically, the choices made, and to become aware of the implications, also social, of the actions taken.
In such areas, the graduate will be able to operate with defined levels of autonomy to integrate into various work environments.
The acquisition of the ability to make well-founded decisions autonomously will be verified through oral examination tests and in the evaluation of the internship activity and the final test.

Orientation in entry Activities are centrally coordinated by the Orientation and Disability Committee, which includes representatives from the departments and schools of the 'G. d'Annunzio' University. For the INGEO Department, and specifically for the course of study in Technical Professions for Construction and Territory, the coordinating role is entrusted to Professors Luigi Berardi and Mariano Pierantozzi.
Regarding orientation in entry, visits to schools are carried out during the academic year; in particular, in agreement with the outgoing orientation coordinators of the same schools, meetings are organized to present the educational offer of the three-year and master's courses, and, if requested, introductory lessons illustrating the topics covered in the study path. Parallel to the school meetings, on the central coordination of the University, days of meeting are organized at the university headquarters in Viale Pindaro, where the educational offer is presented (https://orientamento.unich.it).
Additionally, an annual Open Day is organized where course information is enriched with presentations of the research activities of individual professors. The information provided through these direct meetings is also made available via a website (www.ingeo.unich.it/ediliziaeterritorio), which includes a dedicated orientation page among its main sections, gathering all necessary information for understanding the activities, enrollment procedures, and welcome infrastructure. Brochures and posters for the study courses in electronic format are also available on the website.
During the Open Day on 22/04/2022, the intervention of the National Secretary of the Association of Licensed Geometers, Dr. Enrico Rispoli, was scheduled at the Pescara Campus. The purpose was to illustrate the possible professional opportunities enabled by the course of study in Technical Professions for Construction and Territory.
Orientation activities for the Academic Year 2023-24 focused on four main areas:
1. PNRR Orienta-UdA activities
2. University Orientation activities
3. Departmental Orientation activities
4. Departmental PCTO activities These initiatives, all currently ongoing, have involved numerous schools in the regions of Abruzzo, Marche, and Puglia.
Specifically, the Orienta UDA program, a 15-hour PCTO path for mainly schools in the provinces of Chieti and Pescara, is structured over three days (Chieti, Pescara, and Open Day). This path reached approximately 4,000 students, presenting the entire Italian scientific educational offer, with particular focus on that of the University and especially the INGEO Department. The initiative was primarily guided by the engineering delegate, with support from orientation tutors.
University Orientation activities included participation in educational fairs at national and regional levels, such as the Chieti, Bari, and Ascoli Piceno Student Fair, and visits to local classical and scientific high schools. These were coordinated by the engineering delegate and professors from various study courses.
Departmental Orientation provided an overview of the study courses offered by the department, with presentations held at various schools in Abruzzo and Marche.
Departmental PCTO activities included schools participating in lessons on specific engineering topics, contributing to the dissemination of departmental research in secondary schools.
Finally, orientation activities included organizing 'University Unveiled', an initiative by CRUI that featured meetings, workshops, and debates, offering the community a unique opportunity for participation, and organizing Open Days, particularly the one on April 4 in Pescara.

Training periods assignment The internships have been activated starting from the 2023-24 academic year, that is, the third year of the course for the first cohort of enrolled students.

TYPE:
