Final exam characteristics. The final exam of the Degree Program, with the value of a State Exam enabling the profession of Orthotist and Ophthalmological Assistant (D.Lgs 502/1992, art. 6, paragraph 3), aims to verify both the level achieved by the student in acquiring basic and characteristic knowledge of the Degree Program and the specific professional preparation.
The final exam consists of two different assessment moments:
a) a practical test during which the student must demonstrate having acquired the theoretical-practical and technical-professional knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) the preparation of a thesis (short paper) and its defense.
The practical test is structured to allow the candidate to demonstrate having acquired the practical and technical knowledge and skills within the operational context specified by their professional profile.
The final thesis must concern the orthotics and ophthalmology field, and the student must demonstrate the ability to conduct a scientific experimental study by consulting the most recent reference scientific sources (experimental thesis) or prepare a compilative paper (compilative thesis).
The student has access to 7 CFU (Final Exam Training Activity) dedicated to preparing the Thesis at facilities designated for training.
The final exam grade, expressed in hundredths, is determined by the sum of the following parameters: a) the average in thirtieths; b) points assigned by the Commission to the Practical Internship Test; c) points assigned by the Commission to the Thesis Defense.
The highest honors (summa cum laude) may be awarded, with the unanimous opinion of the Commission, to graduates who achieve a final score of 110 or higher.

Final exam execution mode. The final exam of the Degree Program aims to verify both the level achieved by the student in acquiring basic and characteristic knowledge of the Degree Program and the specific professional preparation.
To be admitted to the final exam, the student must have acquired all the required credits specified by the Study Program's curriculum, except for the CFU assigned to the final exam, which are acquired upon the exam.
The Degree Program Council, upon approving the annual Academic Calendar, will propose to the School of Medicine and Surgery the two graduation sessions, with a single exam session for each.
The Degree Exam Commission is composed of at least 7 and no more than 11 members, appointed by the CDS and preferably consisting of faculty from the current academic year.
Considering that the final exam has the value of a State Exam, it enables the exercise of the healthcare profession and consists of two different assessment moments:
a) a practical test during which the student must demonstrate having acquired the theoretical-practical and technical-professional knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) the preparation of a thesis (short paper) and its defense.
The practical test is structured to allow the candidate to demonstrate having acquired the practical and technical knowledge and skills within the operational context specified by their professional profile.
The final thesis must concern the orthotics and ophthalmology field, and the student must demonstrate the ability to conduct a scientific experimental study by consulting the most recent reference scientific sources (experimental thesis) or prepare a compilative paper (compilative thesis).
The student has access to 7 CFU (Final Exam Training Activity) dedicated to preparing the Thesis at facilities designated for training.
The student must present the thesis with a PowerPoint presentation followed by a discussion with the Commission.
It is the student's responsibility to fulfill the obligations imposed by the University Student General Office for the Degree Exam.
The final exam, considered as a qualifying test for acquiring the respective credits, is assessed and documented through a certificate issued by the Supervisor with whom the Student completed the Thesis.
The Student, at the end of their educational path, accesses the final exam prepared by the Academic Council in accordance with D.M./MURST No. 136 of 5/6/2001, Article 6. The Degree Exam is typically organized in two sessions, in October and March, with a Commission composed of at least 7 and no more than 11 members, appointed by the Degree Program.
To be admitted to the Degree Exam, the Student must: a) have attended all Integrated Courses and passed the respective exams; b) have obtained, in total, 180 CFU distributed over the three years of the Study Program; c) have passed the mandatory training-professional internship, evaluated and certified at the end of each academic year through documentation; d) have submitted to the Student Office the application to the Rector, accompanied by the exam transcript, internship transcript, and PDF thesis CD (non-reproducible format).
The final exam grade, expressed in hundredths, is determined by the sum of the following parameters:
a) the average in thirtieths (then converted to hundredths) obtained by summing the thirtieths grades achieved in both the 16 curricular Integrated Course exams and the evaluation of the mandatory training-professional internship;
b) points assigned by the Commission to the Practical Internship Test (from 18/30 to 21/30 = 1 point; from 22/30 to 24/30 = 2 points; from 25/30 to 27/30 = 3 points; from 28/30 to 30/30 = 4 points);
c) points assigned by the Commission to the Thesis Defense (from 0 up to a maximum of 7 points).
The highest honors may be awarded, with the unanimous opinion of the Commission, to graduates who achieve a final score of 110 or higher.

The course covers a clearly relevant professional area. Department DEPARTMENT OF MODERN LANGUAGES, LITERATURES AND CULTURES Website https://www.lingue.unich.it/didattica  Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission Students holding a five-year secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent under current regulations are admitted to the Study Program. Admission to the Study Program is regulated by a verification test whose procedures will be determined in the Teaching Regulations of the Study Program. In case of negative verification results, additional mandatory requirements must be fulfilled during the first year through specific recovery activities established in the Teaching Regulations.
Admission Procedures All students holding a five-year secondary school diploma or an equivalent recognized qualification are admitted to the Course. At enrollment, students must indicate the chosen study languages as LANGUAGE A and LANGUAGE B (one of which must be European) from those listed in the Course Offer. The three-year language (both Language A and B) may be replaced exclusively at the time of enrollment for the second year.
The Ministry of Education, University and Research (Article 6 of D.M. 270/2004) requires all universities to verify the initial preparation of new students, to enable freshmen to assess their preparation against the basic knowledge required for university study and to identify, with the assistance of Tutor professors, individual paths to address any initial gaps, facilitating the student's successful integration into the chosen Study Program. The ministerial provision also stipulates that any additional mandatory requirements must be fulfilled during the first year of the course.
For the L-12 Study Program, the verification test for admission knowledge is mandatory for first-year students. Students transferring from other universities and students enrolling for a second degree are exempt from the test.
The verification test will be held according to a schedule published on the Department of Modern Languages, Literatures and Cultures website. Two sessions are planned: September and February.
The Commission responsible for the test is appointed by the Department Director after consulting the Study Program Chair. This Commission consists of a minimum of three to a maximum of five permanent professors.
The 60-minute verification test consists of thirty multiple-choice questions designed to assess an adequate level of text comprehension, knowledge of morphosyntactic structures and vocabulary in Italian. Each correct answer is awarded one point (1), while no answer or incorrect answer receives zero points (0). The test is passed if the student achieves a score of at least 20/30.
For students who take and pass the test, the additional mandatory requirements are considered fulfilled. A negative test result results in the assignment of an Additional Mandatory Requirement (OFA) to be fulfilled during the first year by attending a mandatory 24-hour Italian language course offered by the Department.
After completing the recovery procedures, the student must retake the test to verify the required competence level. The debt must be fulfilled within the first year of the course. If the debt is not fulfilled, the verification test must be repeated in the following academic year.
As per the University's Teaching Regulations, students who have not fulfilled the OFA by October 31 of the year following enrollment cannot register for second-year courses, unless they have acquired at least eighteen CFU in the first-year basic and characteristic courses.
In addition to the verification test for admission knowledge, a Placement Test will be administered to assess the linguistic competence level in one of the following languages: French, English, Spanish or German. This second test will be used to optimize the organization of courses and will not result in Additional Mandatory Requirements.
Both tests may be conducted remotely if necessary.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [0659] MEDIAZIONE LINGUISTICA E COMUNICAZIONE INTERCULTURALE
SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/563

Program, texts and objectives Note regarding credits for other activities The level of linguistic competence of students is verified through in-course assessments and curriculum examinations; students who have not acquired such skills are not admitted to the final examination.
Communication skills
Graduates of the Mediazione linguistica e comunicazione interculturale course must be able to argue and communicate, in the foreign languages studied as well as in Italian, ideas, problems and solutions. In particular, they must demonstrate: ability to communicate, orally and in writing, based on various text types, information, ideas, issues and/or difficulties to specialist and non-specialist interlocutors; ability to interact as a linguistic intercultural mediator in the languages studied; ability to interact with others and lead collaborative activities; ability to process and present data using basic computer and multimedia tools. These skills are developed through frontal lessons, debates and classroom exercises, seminar activities, use of laboratories and multimedia tools, internship and training experience, linguistic-communicative experience in teaching support activities carried out by CEL/Lecturers and in international exchanges such as Erasmus. The acquisition of these skills will be assessed through oral and/or written assessments, in-course and at the conclusion of each disciplinary course.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [0659] LINGUISTIC MEDIATION AND INTERCULTURAL COMMUNICATION
TYPE:
CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/563

Judgment Autonomy (making judgments)
Graduates of the Linguistic Mediation and Intercultural Communication Course must demonstrate having developed autonomous judgment capabilities regarding the themes of their field of study and the ability to expand the autonomous judgment acquired through socio-cultural and ethical-scientific reflections connected to such themes. In particular, they must demonstrate: ability to describe and interpret, based on the four linguistic skills, sectoral and non-sectoral texts; ability to identify and analytically rephrase issues and propose autonomous solutions; ability to address different work areas and themes, as well as to locate and evaluate information sources related to various fields of knowledge; ability to adopt appropriate translation and mediation strategies. To achieve this autonomy, in addition to frontal lessons and seminars, teaching tools such as debate and exercises, support from laboratories and multimedia tools, attendance at professionalizing seminars, and experience through internships and traineeships are provided. The assessment of acquired judgment autonomy will be carried out through oral and/or written checks, during the course and at the end of each disciplinary course, as well as through the preparation of the final exam.

In the Erasmus+ program, which also includes teacher mobility, students can go to a foreign university for a period ranging from three to twelve months to carry out study activities equivalent to those offered by their home university. Among the types of agreements are training programs, with course attendance and the possibility of taking exams planned in the Learning Agreement, activities for thesis preparation, and internships.
The Erasmus+ program places particular emphasis on students and staff with special needs, whose physical, psychological, or general health conditions would prevent full participation without additional funding to cover further costs related to support, welcome, accessibility to facilities, and pedagogical and technical support services. This ensures that everyone can fully enjoy all aspects of European mobility.
During their stay abroad, L-12 Course of Study students on mobility carry out various training activities based on the Learning Agreement (L.A.), aimed at acquiring a variable number of CFU to be recorded in the Transcript of Record (T.O.R.). In the 2023-2024 academic year, 77 students from the Department received Erasmus funding, an increase from the previous year (34).

At the central level, also in light of the authorization granted by the Ministry of Labour and Social Policies to carry out work mediation activities, targeted interventions are implemented and specific services for entering the workforce are provided, aimed at both young people and companies.
Through a series of meetings, the University, through its Placement Service, contributes to improving the employability levels of students enrolled in various courses. The meetings are open to students, graduates, alumni, and PhD students. For each meeting, regardless of the specific topics discussed and compatible with the commitments related to the educational path, participation is recommended for all enrolled students. Speakers, in their various interventions, will present cross-cutting reflections and insights useful for general orientation.

Method for acquiring cfu:
Professional seminars can be attended starting from the first year of study, and cfu can be acquired as they are completed. If the acquired cfu are insufficient to cover the number required by the student's curriculum, they can be supplemented by other qualifications held by the student (other courses, language certifications, ECDL).
Once the required credits have been acquired according to the student's study plan, the student may request cfu recognition at the Student Secretariat of the Department of Languages, Literatures and Modern Cultures.
cfu will be automatically inserted into the student's record only after approval by the Study Course Council for each student.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [0659] LINGUISTIC MEDIATION AND INTERCULTURAL COMMUNICATION
SECTION: Student opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/563

Student opinions The L-12 Study Course provides an online questionnaire for collecting student opinions, managed by the university offices responsible and administered before exams. The questionnaire concerns the organization of the Study Course, specifically the various courses, teaching activities, as well as student interest and satisfaction. Each individual teacher has access, through a restricted area, to the results of student evaluations regarding their own courses; the Course Director has access to all evaluations of the Study Course. Some aspects of the evaluation are periodically discussed in the Quality Management Group, the Course Council, and the Teaching Commission to highlight positive aspects and critical elements, and implement any improvement measures.
Data analysis Regarding the academic year 2022-2023, the analysis was conducted on data available in the restricted area, which provides information derived from questionnaires administered by the university. In the academic year 2022-2023, the values confirmed those of the previous year. Specifically, for course evaluations at the disciplinary sector level, a decidedly good trend was observed, with an average score of 3.42.
These values suggest the effectiveness of monitoring activities undertaken by the Course Director in recent years, a better distribution of lectures and exams to avoid overlaps, and, in general, greater availability of teachers. Regularly, during the Course Council, the results of course evaluations are discussed and improvement proposals are made regarding the identified critical aspects.
Among the suggestions highlighted by the questionnaire, particular interest is given to those concerning the reduction of the overall teaching load, the increase in support activities for teaching, and greater coordination between courses. The CdS carefully considers the results of student opinion collection for potential improvement measures. For the academic year 2023-24, it is planned to further strengthen monitoring activities for the teaching organization, in order to minimize scheduling overlaps as much as possible, with particular attention to language courses.
Through the strengthening of tutoring activities, it will also be attempted to improve teaching results where critical elements emerge in passing exams. The CdS takes note of observations and improvement proposals from teachers and students through the bodies involved in the Quality Assurance process, the Parity Commission, as well as through other forms of meetings organized by the Course Director (such as meetings between the Course Director and student representatives), where it is also possible to receive observations from the student body and develop effective resolution strategies.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI-PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO
COURSE: [0659] LANGUAGE MEDIATION AND INTERCULTURAL COMMUNICATION
SECTION: Opinions of graduates
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/563

Opinions of graduates The University of Chieti-Pescara documents on the Quality Assurance Unit website the teaching trends and the opinions of graduates made available, for each academic year, through the University's databases based on AlmaLaurea surveys.
The information regarding the 2022 graduates of the L-12 Study Course in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication, based on the AlmaLaurea survey, is accessible via the University's Quality Assurance Unit website through the external link below. The attached data also includes the opinions of graduates from equivalent courses and is compared with the University's total for the same course type.
For the purpose of monitoring the Study Course's progress and potential improvement interventions, the data concerning the "satisfaction with the completed study course" is first considered, compared with the University's data for 2022, AlmaLaurea data updated to April 2023.
Analysis of the PDF "satisfaction with the completed study course" - AlmaLaurea Data (updated to April 2023):
In 2022, 149 students graduated in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication (compared to 183 in 2021), of whom 143 were interviewed. The percentage of students who regularly attended more than 75% of the required courses decreased to 65.7%, compared to 71.7% in 2021 and 80.3% in 2020; this is slightly below the University average of 67.5%.
In evaluating the appropriateness of the course workload relative to the course duration, the two positive responses ("definitely yes" and "more yes than no") show good consistency, totaling 81.9%, slightly below the University trend (88.7%). The percentage of students who would enroll again in the same study course at the same University decreased slightly from 47.5% in 2021 to 43.4% in 2022.
The organization of exams is considered "always/almost always appropriate" by 21.7% of respondents; this represents a significant increase compared to the previous four years: 16.7% in 2021, 13.4% in 2020, and 7.8% in 2019. However, these values are lower than the University average (30.6%).
There is an improvement in the evaluation of classrooms, which are always, almost always, or often appropriate for 64% of respondents, compared to 50% in 2021. The same improvement applies to the evaluation of computer workstations, which decreased from 72% of respondents reporting inadequacy in 2021 to 54.5% in 2022. However, these values remain slightly below the University average (43.7%).
The equipment for other teaching activities is always, almost always, or often appropriate for 56.3% of respondents in 2022, an increase from 48.1% in 2021. However, these figures are significantly lower than the University average (73.2%). The library services are still well evaluated (the "definitely and quite positive" assessment reaches 87.9%). Considering approximately 200 students enrolled in the L-12 Study Course, the low satisfaction percentages regarding infrastructure and equipment usage should be carefully analyzed by the University to implement synergistic improvement interventions.
Regarding satisfaction expressed by respondents about relationships with teachers in general, summing the first two responses ("definitely yes" and "more yes than no") yields a satisfaction rate of 85.3%, slightly below the University figure (90.3%). The same evaluative responses regarding overall satisfaction with the Study Course, when summed, reach 81.1%, also slightly below the University trend (89.8%).
It is also useful to examine some data reported in the graduates' profile, as per the attached PDF.
Regarding the graduates' profile, the following points emerge:
- The average age at graduation in 2022 is 24.4, in line with the previous year;
- The number of foreign citizens has increased (4% in 2022 compared to 3.3% in 2021);
- Significantly, in the selected group, regarding the "social origin" data, 81.8% of graduates have no parent with a degree; 14% have at least one parent with a degree;
- Data on student origin shows a decrease in graduates from other regions, dropping from 36.3% in 2021 to 32.2% in 2022; 40.9% of students come from another province in the same region, while 26.8% reside in the same province as the study location. Therefore, revitalization of communication and promotion through orientation activities is necessary.
- Regarding secondary education, there is a prevalence of students from high schools (linguistic, scientific, classical, humanities, and artistic-musical-coreutic), totaling 69.1%; however, this figure is lower than the previous year (73.1%). The percentage of students from technical and professional institutes has increased (29.6% in 2022 compared to 24.7% in 2021). The L-12 Study Course is attractive to students from diverse backgrounds. Only 1.3% hold a foreign degree.
Regarding academic success, the average exam score is 25.5 out of 30, and the graduation grade is 97.6 out of 110. Both values are in line with previous years. However, the percentage of students still enrolled has significantly decreased to 36.2%, compared to 47.8% the previous year. Regarding study conditions, 37.1% of graduates utilized scholarship services, and only 17.5% completed recognized study periods abroad. These data reflect the pandemic's impact, which slowed student careers and complicated international mobility through Erasmus or agreements.
The pandemic has also reduced the percentage of students who completed curricular or recognized work placements; this figure stands at 34.3%, an increase from 28% in 2021. In place of internships, the Study Course has activated professional seminars to allow students to acquire the necessary CFU. Despite the pandemic, the Study Course has implemented agreements with entities, institutions, and companies to promote internship and placement activities. These training opportunities will be further encouraged to better prepare graduates for the job market.
Ability to apply knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Graduates of the Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication Course have developed the ability to professionally apply acquired knowledge and address issues by identifying appropriate solutions within their field of study and in diverse work contexts, with particular emphasis on environments requiring communication skills. They are able to interact with texts, people, and institutions of other cultures and civilizations in various daily and professional contexts, including migration contexts, and have acquired interdisciplinary knowledge integration skills. They can collect, classify, and synthesize data and information typical of their field, as well as transmit them orally and in writing in the study languages, using new technologies. They are also able to read, listen, interpret, and translate texts of various types, including specialized texts, in Italian and the foreign study languages, using linguistic, translation, and communication methods and tools. They can utilize multimedia and telecommunication tools in specific areas of competence, i.e., for research and processing of information materials. They can also apply acquired interdisciplinary knowledge, particularly economic-legal, to written and oral mediation.
These abilities are developed not only through theoretical- descriptive lectures and seminar activities, but also through debate and exercise tools, supported by laboratories and multimedia tools, through exchanges with native speakers of the study languages, conducted both in collaboration with the University Language Center's lecturers and through international agreements (Erasmus, University agreements, etc.), as well as through internship and placement experiences.
The acquisition of these abilities is assessed through oral and/or written evaluations, both during the course and at the end of each discipline, which evaluate disciplinary knowledge, comprehension, argumentation, and correct presentation of content. Regarding the study languages, lexical and morphosyntactic knowledge, comprehension and production of oral and written texts, as well as the ability to perform linguistic and intercultural mediation, are assessed. The final exam evaluates the ability to analyze and synthesize materials related to the chosen topic.
Learning skills (learning skills)
Graduates of the Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication Course must demonstrate adequate learning abilities and methodologies to address subsequent in-depth study and expansion of studies, as well as the progressive updating required by the job market. In particular, they must demonstrate: acquisition of a study method, ability to work towards goals, and ability for autonomous and group work; acquisition and development of linguistic abilities and mediation strategies appropriate for performing the professional activities planned by the Course and for continuing studies. These abilities are developed through lectures and seminars, debates and classroom exercises, and through in-course tutoring. The acquisition of these abilities is assessed through oral and/or written evaluations, both during the course and at the end of each discipline, as well as through the preparation of the final exam.
Knowledge and understanding (knowledge and understanding)
To obtain the degree, students must demonstrate acquired and consolidated linguistic-communicative competencies in two foreign languages, adequate cultural and interdisciplinary knowledge, and understanding of the issues and epistemological horizon of at least two foreign languages in addition to Italian. Knowledge and understanding extend to linguistic and intercultural mediation in various contexts, based on metalinguistic reasoning. In particular, graduates are able to understand conversations and texts, including specialized ones, in a foreign language, interpreting them from an adequate cultural and interdisciplinary perspective; they know the historical-cultural contexts of the studied foreign languages, especially regarding traditions and customs, and can compare them with their own reality; they know the methodologies and strategies of linguistic mediation necessary for work environments; they possess economic-legal knowledge useful for the professional context and information technology skills that increasingly accompany language study and its application in the job market; they develop transversal competencies of a communicative-relational, organizational-management, and programming nature.
Acquisition of such knowledge and understanding primarily occurs through the didactic tool of theoretical-descriptive lectures and seminar activities, coordinated with classroom exercises, and integrated with the use of language laboratories and other multimedia tools.
Assessment of acquired knowledge and understanding is conducted, in addition to standard end-of-course evaluations, through ongoing evaluations of achieved learning levels. Evaluation forms assess knowledge, ability to organize thoughts, argumentative skills, correctness of oral and/or written presentation, and communication strategies used. Acquired knowledge and understanding are also applied in the preparation of the final exam's written work.

Brief description of related and complementary activities The L-12 Study Course allocates 18 credits to related and complementary training activities, distributed within the study plan across three academic years. Below is a brief description of the planned activities to clarify how these activities contribute to achieving the specific educational objectives of the course:
CRITICAL LITERATURE AND COMPARATIVE LITERATURE (L-FIL-LET/14):
The course aims to provide synchronic and diachronic orientation on literary theories, literary criticism, and comparative literature within an interdisciplinary framework, referring to studies and research on textuality. The inclusion of this course in the L-12 Study Course is functional both to deepen theoretical-practical knowledge related to contextualizing the studied languages and their cultures, and to build a solid theoretical foundation essential for developing advanced communication and written and oral mediation skills.
INTERNATIONAL LAW (IUS/13):
The course aims to acquire fundamental knowledge of international legal systems, while also providing tools for learning the correct methodology of the subject. Knowledge of international law is essential for professionalizing the figure of a linguistic mediator and responds to the occupational needs of the territory.
BUSINESS ECONOMICS (SECS-P/07):
The course aims to indicate the foundations of company study in its multiple aspects, presenting at the same time the basic concepts and language of economic-business disciplines. This discipline intends to provide a unified and synthetic vision of phenomena, operational processes, and company functioning, deepening analytical and quantitative determination issues of their equilibrium conditions in relation to technical, economic, and financial aspects. At the end of the training path, students will possess tools to interact, within the various professions they will undertake as linguistic mediators, with different company realities and especially with the various types of stakeholders.
PHILOSOPHY OF SCIENCE (M-FIL/02):
The course represents an introduction to fundamental topics of contemporary Philosophy of Science; basic notions of logic, reasoning, problem solving are provided, and main authors and theoretical models are considered. The course aims to lead students to critically reflect on the indicated topics (objectivity, truth, analyticity, realism, theorization, experimentation, innovation, models), linking them to issues of contemporary science and technology, particularly in linguistic, translation, and interpretation fields.
GEOGRAPHY OF LANGUAGES (GGR/01): The course aims to deepen the connections between culture, cultural geography, and languages. The discipline thus provides an in-depth understanding of the relationship between space and language from a geographical perspective. Initially, the main themes, concepts, and key words of cultural geography are introduced, followed by highlighting changes in different languages over time and space, acculturation and deculturation processes, and linguistic policies in some European and extra-European contexts.
INTERNATIONAL FILM MOVEMENTS AND AUTHORS (L-ART/06):
The course contributes to achieving the Study Course's educational objectives by introducing students to the main concepts of audiovisual language through the exploration of significant practices in international film production. The course aims to enable students to know the general lines of International New Cinema, common elements among the examined film movements, and the specificities of the proposed films, in light of the most advanced critical and theoretical reflections on cinema and audiovisuals. The acquired skills can be productively applied in students' participation in the Venice and Pesaro International Film Festivals, valuable opportunities to meet scholars, experts, directors, and actors.
GLOBAL COMMUNICATION HISTORY (M-STO/04): The course activities and educational objectives aim to provide students with basic competencies regarding contemporary world history, with particular attention to forms, modes, and languages of communication processes in the globalized dimension of the last two centuries, believing such competencies are necessary to achieve the goals of the Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication course.
MODERN EUROPEAN HISTORY (M-STO/02): Among the educational objectives of the discipline, on one hand, is to lead the student to appropriate the keys to reading the past, and on the other, to educate them to critical exercise, placing them in a position to evaluate European historical reality in its specificity and complexity. At the end of preparation, the student will be able to understand, through acquired historical knowledge, the centrality of long-term changes and persistences in the European story from the 1500s to the 1800s.
Brief course description The Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication L-12 Study Course presents as a highly specialized course in the linguistic field. Beyond linguistic training, with a special focus on translation and mediation, the student receives qualified training in linguistic, glottodidactic, and microlinguistic fields, along with knowledge in multietnic and multicultural contexts, including institutional environments. The Study Course aims to create a professional figure of a linguistic expert capable of performing an interlinguistic and intercultural mediation function. The Course provides for the acquisition of linguistic-cultural mediation knowledge and skills that can be applied in numerous contexts: public and private entities, companies, and educational and training institutions, both at national and international levels.
The Department of affiliation organizes, in collaboration with public and private entities, internships to familiarize students with the various professional contexts provided by the Course.
In the Study Course structure, linguistic courses, which account for the majority of training credits, are complemented by disciplines from different fields such as historical-cultural, literary, and economic-legal. Participation in courses, professional seminars, and other training and cultural experiences that aim to expand and deepen the specific disciplinary characteristics of the study path is also encouraged.
The Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication degree allows access to various master's degrees, particularly the LM38 and LM37 Study Courses.
External effectiveness Based on AlmaLaurea surveys, information regarding the 2022 graduates of the L-12 Study Course in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication is accessible from the University's Quality Assurance Unit website at the following link: https://pqa.unich.it/archivio-aq/aq-della-didattica/l-12-mediazione-linguistica-e-comunicazione-interculturale For the purpose of monitoring the Study Course's progress and potential improvement interventions, the data concerning the graduates' employment status is first considered, AlmaLaurea data updated to April 2023 for the 2022 survey year. Of the 182 graduates of 2021, 128 were interviewed one year after graduation. Additionally, a comparison is made of the L-12 Study Course data (2021) available on the same site under the "AlmaLaurea 2022 (Ud'A Data)" section, both with the University d'Annunzio data and with national data.
Analysis of the PDF data (Ud'A Data):
The employment rate of the interviewed individuals (examined group: 44 graduates who did not enroll in another degree course) is 50%. The L-12 Study Course's employment rate is lower than the University's rate (69.4%) and national data (64.3%).
The monthly salary is €1,139, lower than the University average (€1,333) but in line with national data (€1,157). The percentage of employed individuals who highly utilize the skills acquired with the degree in their work is 22.7%. This is a lower value than the University average (56.8%) and national average (29.7%).
Satisfaction with the work is rated 8 out of 10, in line with the University average and higher than national data (7.4).
The number of those enrolling in a master's degree continues to increase, at 63.3%; however, this is a lower figure than the University average (68%) and national data (66%).
The same AlmaLaurea survey on graduates' employment status, updated to June 2023, provides data on a group of 182 graduates, including those who were working at the time of graduation. The survey considers second-level education and post-graduation, employment status, entry into the job market, characteristics of current work, company characteristics, salary, use and demand for the degree in current work, degree effectiveness, and satisfaction with current work, and finally job search. Of 182 graduates (decreasing from the previous year's 212), 128 were interviewed, with an average age of 24.3 years and an average graduation grade of 98.7. Given the moderate percentage of second-level education in the selected group (64.1%), of which 55.6% at the same University, entry into the job market shows 36% employed.
Regarding current work characteristics, most respondents report performing "other professions" (42.6%). 12.8% perform indefinite-term work (a significant decrease from 30.3% the previous year). The spread of part-time work is 51.1%, increasing from the previous year (45.5%). A new data point to consider is the spread of remote work, which stands at 8.5%.
Compared to the previous year, there is a slight increase in private sector employment (90.9% in 2021 and 91.5% in 2022) and a consequent decrease in public sector (6.4% in 2022 compared to 9.1% in 2021). Greater employment is in commerce (46.8%); the education and research sector has decreased to 4.3% (from 12.1% the previous year). The transport, advertising, and communication sector accounts for 8.5%.
Regarding the geographical area of work, the south prevails with 70.2%, followed by the north with 19.2% and the center with 4.3%. Abroad accounts for 6.4%.
40% of the selected graduates who continued working before graduation report noticing an improvement in their work due to the degree; this is a significant increase from 15.4% the previous year. Similarly, 34% of the selected group states that the professional training acquired at university is very appropriate, compared to 21.2% the previous year. However, it should be noted that the percentage of degree demand for work activities is only 4.3%, while it is not required but useful for 51.1%. The degree is not required and not useful for 19.1%. These are concerning data to monitor, highlighting a significant gap between training and the job market.
A final data point regarding employment status indicates that 45.3% of the unemployed are engaged in continuing studies.

Specific educational objectives and description of the educational path The L-12 Study Course aims to provide adequate knowledge of methods, skills, and cultural and scientific content related to foreign languages, linguistic-cultural mediation, translation, and interpretation. In particular, the Course intends to respond to a dual educational purpose, linguistic and cultural, as the mediator's role, beyond communication and technical-linguistic skills, requires specific intercultural training to facilitate fruitful comparison with foreign countries' realities, even in migration contexts. This training is also accompanied by knowledge of issues related to the work areas for which the Course aims to form professional figures. More specifically, graduates in Language Mediation and Intercultural Communication must have acquired:
- Solid linguistic skills, oral and written, in two foreign languages, one of which European, in addition to Italian;
- Secure skills in the field of translation and interpretation;
- Specific theoretical knowledge on language structures and usage variations in both synchronic and diachronic dimensions;
- Specific knowledge on issues of Italian as a second language, used in all social and institutional contexts of linguistic-cultural mediation;
- Solid knowledge of the cultural heritage of the study languages, including literary heritage, in a comparative perspective;
- Basic notions in historical, geographical, logical-communicative, audiovisual-multimedia, and economic-legal fields;
- Ability to use main information technology and telecommunication tools in communication and technical-linguistic activities;
- Ability to operate with organizational autonomy and integrate into work environments.
Knowledge, skills, and abilities will be acquired through participation in lectures, seminars, and classroom exercises; use of language laboratories and other multimedia tools; linguistic-communicative experiences obtained through international exchanges; training and cultural experiences to facilitate integration into the job market; internships and placements.
The educational path is structured into four correlated learning areas:
1. Language Area. This area includes training activities in the two foreign languages (one of which European) chosen by the student from those indicated in the teaching regulations. Language teaching proceeds in parallel throughout the three years and is organized to foster the formation and progressive consolidation of written, oral, multimedia linguistic-communicative skills suitable for the context of use and the specific cultural reality of the studied languages. The teaching is also aimed at developing technical skills specific to linguistic mediation, i.e., translation and interpretation from and to Italian, in line with the Study Course's educational objectives.
2. Linguistic Area. This area includes training activities in linguistic-theoretical, glottodidactic, and philological fields. It aims to develop knowledge and metalinguistic reflection skills in synchrony and diachrony, and analysis of language usage variations.
3. Literature and Culture Area. This area includes training activities aimed at developing a good awareness of the cultural and literary contexts of the study languages, in an international dimension and from an intercultural perspective.
4. Interdisciplinary Knowledge Area. This area includes training activities in historical, geographical, logical-communicative, and audiovisual-multimedia fields, forming the basis of interdisciplinary training, as well as economic-legal teachings functional to the educational path and linked to the territory's occupational needs.
The path also includes student-selected activities to enrich and complete the interdisciplinary horizon, and the mandatory acquisition of information technology and telecommunication skills aimed at mediation activities necessary for performing more specific communication and information management activities within various courses (internet access, electronic resource consultation, preparation of multimedia texts, etc.). Professional seminars are also organized, aimed at providing knowledge useful for entering the job market (such as European community project design, use of digital tools, international cooperation activities, etc.), as well as internships and placements at companies, entities, and public and private institutions requiring linguistic and intercultural mediation skills.
Opinions of entities and companies with curricular or extracurricular internship agreements As with other Study Courses of the Department of Languages, Literatures, and Modern Cultures, the L-12 Study Course has conducted a survey of opinions from entities, companies, and institutions that have signed curricular or extracurricular internship agreements. The survey activities were carried out by the Study Course Chair, assisted by the Department's Teaching Tutor, Dr. Lorena Savini.
On March 9, 2023, the L-12 Study Course Chair held a meeting with entities and companies that had hosted students for internship or placement activities.
The numerous current agreements stipulated by the Department (list available at the inserted link) include companies, entities, and institutions where L-12 Study Course students can complete internships and placements. So far, most companies, entities, and institutions that have previously hosted our interns and trainees have renewed their collaboration, expressing positive judgments on the students' commitment during their internship/placement periods. In some cases, local companies have employed some more capable, professionally qualified, and geographically mobile graduates, taking advantage of government incentives. The usefulness of the internship/placement experience has been confirmed by all hosting structures.
From the perspective of enhancing the Study Course's educational offer, the meeting with social partners highlighted the following significant points:
- Social partners' appreciation for this annual working table and active involvement in making university paths more aligned with the job market's needs;
- Need to complement linguistic skills with some sector-specific knowledge (economic, legal, tourism techniques, company functioning, etc.), as well as acquisition of transversal skills;
- Opportunity to enhance techniques for using foreign languages in professional contexts: from customer psychology to public communication techniques;
- Need to enhance practical aspects and spontaneous use of foreign languages at all levels;
- Need to enhance information technology (Excel, PowerPoint, cloud usage, etc.) and digital skills (company websites, as well as digital teaching modules).
Representatives of entities, companies, and businesses are regularly asked to complete a questionnaire indicating whether they have hosted L-12 Study Course students/graduates for internship/placement activities, and their overall assessment of them. They are then asked to identify the Study Course's strengths and areas for improvement, providing suggestions and observations. Social partners are asked which foreign languages are most functional in their sector, and finally, they are asked to assess the correspondence between the professional figures the Study Course aims to form and the sector they represent. The questionnaire also focuses on the information technology skills provided by the Study Course, which in the past represented an area to enhance and on which the Study Course is investing. Finally, social partners are asked if, in light of the changed work needs caused by the pandemic, new skills should be sought in a professional figure within their sector.
The results of questionnaires completed by social partners regarding the Study Courses indicate that:
- Half of the involved parties have hosted students and/or graduates of the L-12 Study Course for curricular or extracurricular internships;
- The aforementioned parties are "satisfied" or "very satisfied" with the activities of the hosted students/graduates;
- The aforementioned parties have hired L-12 Study Course graduates in half of the cases;
- English and German are indicated as the first and second most important languages in the sectors represented by social partners;
- The L-12 Study Course's educational objectives are considered "quite" or "fully" adequate in all cases;
- The majority of involved parties consider the professional figures of Linguistic and Intercultural Mediator and Facilitator and Linguistic Expert in International Business Relations, which the Study Course aims to form, to be "definitely" or "quite" responsive to the needs of the represented sector;
- Among the suggestions provided by social partners regarding training activities and skills to insert or enhance in the Study Course, information technology skills and digital skills are highlighted;
- Among the new skills sought in a professional figure emerging from the changed work needs caused by the pandemic, respondents indicated digital skills, workflow and activity management in remote work, and knowledge related to online teaching methodologies;
- Among the Study Course's strengths, the development of social communication skills, possession of flexibility and transversality, possession of linguistic knowledge, and students' cultural preparation are highlighted.

Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international level - of goods and services production, professions (Subsequent consultations)
The Study Course continuously dialogues with the job market through internships and placements, professional seminars (through which students interact with experienced professionals), and consultations with social partners. The Study Course Chair, in agreement with the AQ Group, the Teaching Tutor, and interested teachers, periodically organizes meetings with social partners.
Over the last five years, these meetings have been very useful for modifying the L-12 Study Course's teaching regulations, making the Study Course more effective educationally and more competitive for the job market. During these meetings, the enhancement of certain linguistic disciplines and teaching that provide interdisciplinary knowledge was discussed; the possibility of enhancing activities aimed at conveying knowledge useful for entering the job market, such as professional seminars; and the possibility of transforming the previous four professional profiles of the Study Course into two main figures, namely Linguistic and Intercultural Mediator and Facilitator and Linguistic Expert in International Business Relations of companies and businesses. It also emerged the need to strengthen knowledge of the local company reality and information technology means. Finally, the importance of enhancing linguistic study through linguistic certifications issued by the CLA was emphasized.

Entry, path, and exit data The following data are examined from the University's Quality Assurance Unit website:
Enrollment flow The number of enrolled students for the 2022-2023 academic year is 200; this is a stable figure compared to the previous academic year (198). Total enrolled students are 784, of which 464 are in course and 320 are out of course, 440 regular.
Enrolled students by geographical origin and type of high school diploma From the comparison of data regarding geographical origin, in the 2022-2023 academic year, the figure for students from other regions remains stable compared to the previous year: 56. However, it should be noted that this figure is lower than the 2020-2021 academic year (75) and the 2019-2020 academic year (93). Most students come from another municipality in the province (71); additionally, 32 students come from another province in the same region, and 38 students come from the same municipality. Three students reside abroad.
Regarding the type of high school diploma, it should be noted that the majority of enrolled students come from high schools (69), followed by magistral institutes (54) and then technical and professional institutes (52). Twenty-five enrolled students come from unspecified other training.
Enrolled students by high school diploma grade The majority of enrolled students in the L-12 Study Course achieved a high school diploma grade up to 80 (87) and between 80 and 99 (76). The number of students with a grade of 100 and 100 cum laude is increasing: 29 compared to 27 in the previous academic year, and 25 in the 2020-2021 academic year.
Course progression It should be noted that data for the 2022-2023 academic year are partial as the academic year is not yet completed, so it is not possible to analyze and evaluate the documentation precisely. In the 2021-2022 academic year, the average number of exams passed per student was 4.33, increasing from the 2020-2021 academic year (3.50). Regarding the percentage of CFU acquired, the figure stands at 54% in 2021, also increasing from the previous academic year (43.2%). Additionally, consider the non-renewals of enrollment, which decreased from 36 in the 2020-2021 academic year to 15 in the 2021-2022 academic year. Regarding explicit withdrawals within the cohort, it decreased from 48 in 2020 to 11 in 2021.
Regarding progression to the second year, analyzing the latest available cohort (2021-2022), the percentage of progression to the second year is 57.21, decreasing from the previous cohort (64.57). A nearly stable figure concerns the percentage of progression to the second year with more than 40 CFU (23.38). The percentage of CFU acquired relative to CFU to be taken is 34.55, a value decreasing from the previous cohort (37.95).
Exit data From the analysis of data regarding 2022 graduates, a total of 149 graduates are recorded, decreasing from the previous year (183). 52 students graduate in course; this is a declining figure compared to the previous year (82). 41 students graduate one year beyond the course duration, decreasing from the previous academic year (53), and 54 students graduate two or more years beyond the course duration; this figure is slightly increasing from the previous academic year (41). These are certainly data to monitor, but it is also necessary to consider that these values stem from the complex pandemic period.
Regarding the grade, the total number of graduates who achieved the final grade of 110 and 110 cum laude is 7; 16 students achieved a grade between 105 and 110, and 126 students fall within the grade range up to 105.
Study plan Attached: https://www.unich.it/sites/default/files/ugov_suafiles/149066.pdf
Characteristics of the final exam The final exam requires the preparation of a written work on a topic connected with one of the courses in the Study Course, chosen by the student to verify acquired abilities and competencies during their educational path.
Final exam execution method The final exam requires 6 CFU and consists of preparing and discussing a written work on a topic connected with one of the courses in the Study Course.
The student gains access to the final exam after acquiring all credits specified in the teaching regulations and after demonstrating to have reached a linguistic competence level of B2+ of the CEFR in both study languages. This competence verification occurs simultaneously with the Language, Translation, and Mediation exam of the third year, whose content is structured to achieve the linguistic skills corresponding to the B2+ level.
The final exam consists of preparing a written work (minimum 20, maximum 40 pages, each of 2,000-2,500 characters) belonging to one of the following types: specialist article; brief linguistic analysis essay; translation of a short text; review article of recent publications on a specific topic or disciplinary sector; reasoned bibliography on a scientific theme/question. The final work should be recognized as an important individual training opportunity to complete the study path, without requiring particular originality.
A student who wishes to prepare the final work in a foreign language may request authorization from the Study Course Council. In any case, the work written in a foreign language must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian.
It is possible to write the thesis in a Taf D course (held at another Department) only with prior authorization from the Study Course Council, which will assess the congruence of the chosen course with the student's educational path.
The topic choice, consistent with the Study Course's educational objectives, must be agreed upon with a teacher who teaches a discipline for which the candidate has taken at least one exam and who will serve as the Supervisor. The examining committees, composed of at least five members, evaluate the candidate considering the entire study path. In assigning scores, the committee starts from the weighted average of the scores acquired by the student in the profit exams, to which an additional score for the written work is added. This additional score, ranging from 0 to 5, takes into account the breadth of the work, precision of writing and analysis, effectiveness of argumentation and/or translation. Additionally, the following additional scores are assigned:
1 additional point for students who are not out of course at the time of the graduation exam;
1 additional point for students who have participated in international mobility;
1 additional point for students who have acquired at least three honors in their study path. The acquisition of more than three honors will not yield additional points.
Technical report summary of the evaluation committee The course covers a scientifically and professionally relevant area, unique at the regional level, and consistently positioned at optimal levels, in reference to its class, in terms of enrollments, students, and graduates. The Faculty has adequate, congruent, and effective equipped spaces, and following a program in an advanced phase of deep restructuring of the Pescara Campus, new teaching and scientific spaces will be acquired in the short term, fully commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The Faculty can rely on a specific teaching staff for basic and characteristic disciplines, widely adequate to the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The proposed regulations, significantly improved in terms of compactness, transparency, and effectiveness, can contribute to the goals of rationalization and qualification of the University's educational offer.

Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission Candidates who hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as suitable according to current regulations (art. 6, paragraph 2, D.M. 270/04) and who possess adequate preparation and are qualified for the admission exam may be admitted to the first-level Bachelor's Degree course. The required knowledge for admission are verified by achieving the minimum score in the admission test as specified by current regulations. Candidates who do not reach this score will be assigned additional educational obligations (OFA) to be fulfilled through attendance at recovery courses appropriately indicated by the Competent Academic Board according to the procedures outlined in the Study Program Regulations. Admission Method The Bachelor's Degree in Logopedia is a nationally programmed course, and the number of places, date, and admission procedures are annually determined by the University and established by the MIUR through ministerial decrees, as provided by D.L. 264/99, in coordination with the Ministry of Health and the Regional Health System. Students eligible to take the national test must hold a high school diploma. The admission test consists of multiple-choice questions on general culture, mathematics, physics, biology, chemistry, and logical reasoning. Students required to fulfill OFA will be exempted if they earn 18 CFU in the foundational and core courses of the first year. Otherwise, they must attend recovery courses appropriately indicated by the Study Program Council. Currently, Physics is the only subject subject to OFA.

COURSE: [L610] LOGOPEDICS
SECTION: Syllabus, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1784

Syllabus, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate must be able to manage communication effectively as the ability to establish a meaningful therapeutic relationship with the person and to build an effective relationship with all other professionals from the same or other disciplines; they must also be capable of using communication tools in a healthcare setting, demonstrating the ability to complete the logopedic file, draft a therapeutic report, design a logopedic intervention, etc., communicating clearly, concisely, and professionally in both spoken and written form, technically and grammatically accurate, and able to translate technical language into understandable terms for non-specialists; they must be able to communicate appropriately in international scientific contexts to convey ideas, problems, and related solutions. Teaching tools: classroom activities, internship.
Assessment methods: written reports on communication aspects of the rehabilitation setting; briefings with tutors and the coordinator; oral and written presentation of projects; internship.

-----

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L610] LOGOPEDICS
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1784

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgements)
The graduate, at the end of the study path, will be able to know and know how to apply, in an autonomous manner, the logopedic process using clinical reasoning as a guide tool for the choice criterion within the possible options that compose the various phases of the process itself. Such autonomy will be realized through the ability to effectively respond to the health needs of the individual and/or collective, as a single operator or in a team, opting for the best therapeutic strategies, identifying the appropriate approaches and tools, conducting data collection (including social context analysis), patient examination, appropriate logopedic evaluation/diagnosis, defining prognosis and therapeutic goals, short, medium and long term, developing the therapeutic program, choosing and applying methodologies and techniques to the clinical case (including intensity, time, the type of professional technical approach) according to the best possible and available scientific evidence, according to international guidelines and Evidence Based; in the ethical field, it will manifest in respect for the reference regulations, professional, legal, health and deontological.

The autonomy of judgment of the Logopedist graduate will be fully realized through the habitual and judicious use of communication, knowledge, technical skills, clinical reasoning (diagnostic and evaluative process), emotions, values, and reflection in daily practice for the benefit of the individual or the community.

Teaching tools: classroom activities, practical lessons in the laboratory and/or equipped classrooms, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.

Verification methods: written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, discussion of clinical cases, definition of the Rehabilitation Project/Program and compilation of the logopedic and/or rehabilitative file on real clinical cases.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO
COURSE: [L610] LOGOPEDIA
SECTION: Orientation in Entry
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1784

Orientation in Entry The Orientation in Entry is intended for those who are encountering university life for the first time and for secondary school teachers of the second degree who, by delegation or interest, wish to acquire information about the University's educational offerings and the Orientation in Entry activities organized by individual Study Programs. The implementation of the projects that characterize this initial phase of orientation for university choice within the Study Programs is entrusted to the University's Orientation Sector.
This office, under the direction of the University Commission for Orientation and Tutoring coordinated by the Rector's Representative, develops and implements Orientation in Entry initiatives for various Departments and takes charge of all activities it deems consistent with the University's broader policy of penetration and presence in the territory.
Orientation in Entry takes place through two different modalities:
• General Orientation activities common to all University Departments, decided upon and shared with the Rector's Representative within the University Orientation Commission.
• Departmental Orientation activities, specific and typical of the Study Programs.
During dedicated days, interested students will also be able to visit, guided by tutor students, the clinics, libraries, and departmental facilities.
Since the academic year 2019-20, an online Orientation in Entry has also been introduced.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L610] LOGOPEDIA
TYPE:
CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Orientation and ongoing tutoring
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1784

Orientation and ongoing tutoring The internship and laboratory activities are scheduled throughout all three years of study and correspond to a total of 60 CFU in the study plan. Conventional teaching is complemented by continuous guided clinical internship activities at specialized public and private health services in agreement with the university.
The observational internship required in the first year at school and care facilities, which allows acquisition of knowledge related to physiological development, growth and decline, precedes the clinical internship that instead enables learning and practical knowledge of logopedic activities: the student consolidates theoretical knowledge, observes its application and consequences on the patient; simultaneously develops the ability to evaluate and address various issues related to logopedic rehabilitation in pediatric, adult and geriatric contexts: from preventive aspects, to assessment and specific intervention.
The student learns to integrate into an interdisciplinary context, cooperating with the different figures involved in the rehabilitation process; experiences a progressive assumption of responsibility and professional autonomy, moving from knowing to knowing how to be through doing. Laboratory and internship activities are carried out under the guidance and supervision of professional tutors, identified based on the specific area of intervention, to ensure as complete a training as possible for each student. The internship and laboratory activities are coordinated by the professional teaching coordinator, a teacher belonging to the professional profile corresponding to the degree course and organized with the support and collaboration of the clinical tutors of the degree course.
The clinical tutors support and facilitate the student in their field learning by providing constant indications, corrections and suggestions; for this reason, they are responsible for verifying learning and clinical reasoning abilities, analysis and interpretation of diagnostic-instrumental data through practical patient tests and simulations. They suggest and train the student in the correct use of specific professional assessment tools. All this with the aim of facilitating as much as possible their easy and immediate entry into the professional world as a qualified professional able to manage and apply with patients the knowledge and skills acquired during frontal lessons.
To this end, agreements have been established with entities where the professional figure of the logopedist is defined.
Furthermore, by organizing optional seminars, students will be encouraged to conduct self-managed in-depth sessions, implementing the prerequisites for their autonomy. To foster this, students who are particularly dedicated and motivated will have the opportunity to benefit from support tutoring and in-depth pathways.
The tutor teachers are the reference teachers and the internship tutors are appointed by the agreed-upon structures where students carry out the clinical-practical internship.
Learning assessment will take place through the administration of multiple-choice questionnaires.

Training Periods Assignment The service provides graduates with opportunities for labor market integration through:
information on internship operations, identification of professional goals, and selection of company offers closest to each candidate's specific needs,
assignment of a tutor and support in preparing the training project,
individual/group supervision meetings for the training path and final assessment of learning level, as well as training paths for skill enhancement or deepening.
All teaching structures of the University departments responsible will manage the administrative aspects of internships: they establish conventions with interested entities and companies, design the training path students must follow during the experience, and issue certification confirming the characteristics and actual completion of the internship.
The student will actively participate in planning clinical internships, promoting non-regional internship sites they intend to attend for agreed periods with the professional teaching coordinator: based on conventions between the hosting entity and the Chieti-Pescara University and the individual training project.

Student opinions This academic year, students have the opportunity to evaluate, for the third time, their opinion regarding the three years of the course. The student evaluation was positive with a total score of 3.36 out of 4 and remains consistent with last year's score of 3.56.
It is noted that students continue to appreciate the quality of the teaching implemented by the faculty, despite the introduction of new faculty members in some subjects.
For a detailed analysis, examining the level of educational activities, 54.55% was rated as type A, 36.36% as type B, and 9.09% as type C. No evaluation was given as type D.
The score range for individual subjects varies from 2.66 to 3.80.
This year, the analysis of these four years of the Logopedics course has shown a good score provided by students, indicating that faculty have also made a similar effort to improve the quality of course teaching.
To address a very sensitive issue for the population, where many parents are forced to take their children outside the region to facilitate their learning, this year the teaching of Clinical and Instrumental Semiotics of Dysphonia and Dysphagia has begun. The course does not have a customer satisfaction system. Students can use the University's system via the link below.

"Descrizione sintetica delle attività affini e integrative Si offrirà allo studente una prospettiva sullo sviluppo dell’individuo, approfondendo le principali teorie sull’argomento. Attraverso un approccio trasversale si analizzerà la complessità dei differenti contesti di crescita integrando le classiche teorie con elementi strettamente attuali in merito al tema dell’educazione." → "Synthetic description of related and integrated activities The student will be offered a perspective on individual development, deepening the main theories on the subject. Through a cross-cutting approach, the complexity of different growth contexts will be analyzed, integrating classic theories with strictly current elements regarding the topic of education."

"Inoltre con un’attenta valutazione psicomotoria si provvederà ad avere un quadro evolutivo di partenza del bambino che abbiamo di fronte per poter impostare, se necessario, un progetto educativo/riabilitativo e formulare quindi un programma di lavoro." → "Additionally, with a careful psychomotor evaluation, a starting developmental overview of the child will be obtained to set up, if necessary, an educational/rehabilitation project and formulate a work program."

"Grazie alla valutazione psicomotoria è possibile evidenziare eventuali problematiche evolutive, valutare le competenze del bambino in relazione alla sua età e capire come organizza i suoi movimenti e la comunicazione corporea; per questo motivo diventa importante comunicare agli studenti le informazioni relative alla psicologia dell'educazione e dello sviluppo." → "Thanks to the psychomotor evaluation, it is possible to highlight potential developmental issues, assess the child's skills in relation to their age, and understand how they organize their movements and body communication; for this reason, it becomes important to communicate to students information related to educational and developmental psychology."

"Descrizione del corso in breve Il Corso di laurea in Logopedia è destinato alla formazione di professionisti sanitari deputati alla prevenzione, valutazione e trattamento dei disturbi comunicativo - linguistici e della deglutizione in tutte le fasce di età, ai sensi del D.M. del Ministero della Sanità 14 settembre 1994, n. 742. L'attività professionale può essere spendibile nell'ambito privato convenzionato, pubblico, e libero professionale." → "Brief course description The Bachelor's degree in Logopedics is intended for the training of health professionals dedicated to the prevention, evaluation, and treatment of communicative-linguistic disorders and swallowing in all age groups, in accordance with the Ministry of Health Decree of September 14, 1994, No. 742. Professional activity can be utilized in the private, public, and freelance sectors."

"L'insieme delle conoscenze che saranno acquisite dal laureato, costituiranno il bagaglio culturale, scientifico e relazionale necessario ad acquisire la piena competenza professionale e a comprendere affrontare e gestire gli eventi patologici che richiedono l'intervento logopedico in tutte le fasce d'età. Tali conoscenze saranno conseguite mediante la partecipazione a lezioni frontali, esercitazioni di laboratorio, lezioni pratiche in aule attrezzate, sotto la supervisione di docenti e tutor, che mediante lo studio personale (biblioteca, banche dati) delle materie offerte dal Corso di Studio (CdS)." → "The set of knowledge acquired by the graduate will constitute the necessary cultural, scientific, and relational baggage to acquire full professional competence and to understand, address, and manage pathological events requiring logopedic intervention in all age groups. Such knowledge will be achieved through participation in frontal lessons, laboratory exercises, practical lessons in equipped classrooms, under the supervision of teachers and tutors, through personal study (library, databases) of the subjects offered by the Study Course (CdS)."

"All'attività didattica tradizionale si affianca l'attività di tirocinio guidato presso servizi sanitari specialistici pubblici ed altre strutture di rilievo scientifico e di valenza per il soddisfacimento degli obiettivi formativi." → "Traditional teaching activities are complemented by guided internship activities at public specialized health services and other scientifically significant structures of value for meeting the training objectives."

"Le capacità di apprendimento e le competenze acquisite al termine del percorso consentiranno, inoltre, il proseguimento degli studi attraverso la frequenza di corsi della laurea magistrale di Classe LM/SNT2, corsi di perfezionamento scientifico e di alta formazione permanente e ricorrente (master di 1° e 2° livello, corsi di perfezionamento), corsi di aggiornamento e approfondimento (Educazione Continua in Medicina), con elevato grado di autonomia." → "The learning abilities and competencies acquired at the end of the course will also allow for the continuation of studies through attendance at Master's degree courses of Class LM/SNT2, scientific specialization courses, and permanent and recurring advanced training (1st and 2nd level master's, specialization courses), update and in-depth courses (Continuing Medical Education), with a high degree of autonomy."
