UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L270] LETTERS
SECTION: Student Opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/62

Student Opinions The survey of student opinions on teaching activities conducted electronically in the 2022-2023 academic year produced a relatively high overall score for the Study Course in Letters, equal to 3.62/4 for attending students, with a constant and significant increase compared to previous years (it was 3.44/4 in 2017-2018 and 3.46/4 in 2018-2019, 3.52/4 in 2019-2020, 3.56/4 in 2020-2021, 3.59/4 in 2021-2022). The data appears particularly positive as it is higher not only than the university average (3.44/4) but also than that of humanities study courses (3.54/4). It should also be noted that the number of students who expressed their evaluation is quite high and increasing since the mandatory connection between exam enrollment and teaching evaluations became operational: for the 2022-2023 academic year, 2,636 evaluations were recorded. Moreover, it is certainly a positive circumstance that the scores achieved by individual courses offered by the Study Course are quite homogeneous, without downward peaks (from the survey of attending students, it emerges that no course has a score below 3.23/4). In line with the trends in the humanities area, the highest ratings concern teaching effectiveness (3.69/4), followed by logistical-organizational aspects (3.66/4), and finally overall satisfaction (3.50/4). Regarding the individual questions, the highest results are those related to professors' availability to provide clarifications on topics covered in class (3.77/4), adherence to class and exercise schedules (3.73/4), and the consistency of programs with what is stated in the Syllabus (3.70/4). Excellent results are also obtained regarding the interest in the disciplines (3.67/4), the teacher's ability to present topics appropriately according to the complexity of the disciplines, and their ability to stimulate interest in the discipline (both at 3.65/4), as well as teaching materials (3.60/4). Slightly lower, but still satisfactory, are the results regarding the study load required in relation to the assigned CFUs (3.46/4), explainable by the fact that part of the students are engaged in work activities in addition to studies, and those regarding the preliminary knowledge possessed (3.38/4), which is explained by the heterogeneity of the students' previous schools. The CPDS, while not reporting significant issues, still suggests carefully monitoring the relationship between the required teaching effort and the number of CFUs delivered by individual disciplines, without compromising the quality of the educational standards. In this regard, the AQ Group annually monitors the syllabi of the disciplines and intervenes in cases of clear discrepancies in the relationship between the required teaching effort and CFUs, requesting the appropriate corrections from the relevant professors. The results of the student opinion survey are presented and discussed in the degree course council meeting in September 2023. Regarding the management of potential student complaints, the Study Course has identified a specific role of 'Student Guarantor' who handles them: the name and procedure are advertised on the course website (https://www.dilass.unich.it/node/8700). A listening service is also managed by the PQA (see the external link).

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI-PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO
COURSE: [L270] LETTERS
TYPE:
CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Opinions of graduates
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/62

Opinions of graduates The number of graduates of the degree course for the calendar year 2021 was 93. According to the AlmaLaurea 2022 data, 90.6% of graduates considered the study load of the courses appropriate for the duration of the degree program (42.4% rated it "very appropriate," 48.2% "appropriate"), a percentage that has increased compared to the previous year (in 2021 it was 85.7%). 44.7% of respondents considered the organization of exams (calls, schedules, information, reservations) satisfactory for more than half of the exams, while 32.9% considered it always satisfactory (only 4.7% never or almost never). Similarly, regarding the assessment of the relationship with teachers, the data show an improvement trend: 37.6% rated it "very satisfactory" (it was 34.5% in 2021 and 30.6% in 2020), while 54.1% rated it positively. All data are in line with or slightly above the university averages.
Regarding the evaluation of the classrooms used during the study years, 33.3% found them almost always appropriate, 54.8% often appropriate. Positive evaluation of the number of computer workstations, rated as sufficient by 60.0%, while data on equipment for other teaching activities such as laboratories are slightly lower, rated as sufficient by 79.2% (compared to 83.4% in 2021), and library services rated as sufficient by 81.8% (compared to 88.9% in 2021).
The overall satisfaction rate of graduates is increasing: 76.5% of respondents would enroll in the degree program again (73.8% in 2021). The percentage of students who declare being very satisfied with the course followed remains nearly stable: 50.6% (compared to 51.2% in 2021); however, this figure is about 9 percentage points higher than the university average.
The degree course will continue to work to consolidate and increase student productivity in order to optimize career development and facilitate the completion of the program; in particular, it will pay attention to the organization of teaching activities, seeking to address problems arising from the flexibility and breadth of the educational offer.
The data on AlmaLaurea graduate opinions are presented and discussed in the degree course council meeting in September 2023.
Applying knowledge and understanding
At the end of the program, the student possesses significant flexibility in applying acquired knowledge, based on the development of learning abilities necessary to independently address both work context situations and subsequent studies.
Specifically, the student can conduct comprehensive and up-to-date bibliographic research, both through digital tools and traditional methods, correctly navigating an archive and successfully retrieving and examining sources; can present literary, linguistic, historical, and artistic topics in oral and written form at various levels of depth, from popular to school and specialist; can draft, expand, reduce, or correct a written text for professional use, particularly in journalism, advertising, scientific, institutional, and cultural dissemination contexts; is able to work in the management of archives, libraries, theaters, museums, phonoteques, cinematheques, videoteques for the preservation and dissemination of memory and historical heritage; can address, from a management and organizational perspective, a cultural event, such as an exhibition, theatrical performance, screening, or musical event; can formulate an original critical discourse on a text, engaging with previous readings and interpretations and applying the most up-to-date methodologies, also in a comparative perspective; can appropriately set up the critical edition of a text, even in the face of unpublished material; can linguistically analyze a text, hypothesizing its geographical area and historical period of origin, identifying its characteristics and specificities from a textual perspective and evaluating its communicative adequacy in relation to context and purpose.
The achievement of the above-mentioned applying knowledge and understanding abilities occurs through critical reflection on texts proposed for individual study, stimulated by classroom activities, exercises, and laboratory activities.
The verification of achieving the applying knowledge and understanding abilities occurs primarily through exam tests and/or intermediate and final oral and/or written assessments.
Learning skills
Graduates in Letters must demonstrate the ability to extend and deepen their studies with a high degree of autonomy and methodological awareness (an ability that can be developed through seminar-style lectures within individual disciplines and during the preparation of the final exam).
They also acquire the ability to continuously update their knowledge and expand their training through an effective scientific methodology, using appropriate tools, including digital and telecommunication tools, in a conscious manner.
Learning skills develop through active participation in the teaching activities provided by the degree course, but also and especially through personal study, progressively reinforcing one's study method with the guidance of teachers.
They are verified throughout the study program, especially in individual study activities required to pass each exam, in the preparation of individual and/or group projects, and in activities carried out in preparation for the final exam.
University communications to the CUN The structure of the Letters degree course is based on the idea of a broad educational offer that, starting from a core of foundational disciplines, allows for in-depth study in specific areas aimed at characterizing paths in line with the aptitudes of future graduates and the professional profiles provided for. In light of the presence of four curricula in the framework, the range of basic, characterizing, and related activities has a certain extension, which has been significantly reduced due to the CUN's observations. In line with CUN guidelines (with some limited exceptions), the maximum of a credit range (in an area or educational activity) does not exceed double the minimum, even with specific paths. This approach allows for achieving both the general educational objectives indicated and those more specific to the individual course variations.
Knowledge and understanding
Through attendance and study of basic and characterizing disciplines, the student develops knowledge that is articulated and implemented through related courses, seminars, laboratory activities, internships, and the final written exam. Specifically, at the end of the course, the student acquires solid foundational knowledge regarding the historical phases of literary disciplines offered in the curriculum, being able to navigate between fundamental themes and stylistic traits related to specific eras or specific to individual authors, also in relation to the broader cultural context in which they are inserted; acquires solid foundational knowledge regarding the methods and techniques of philology, starting from the ability to read a critical edition correctly interpreting its apparatus; knows the history and its periodizations and can read and interpret historical sources (narrative, documentary, material, iconographic); knows the historical evolution of Italian artistic, musical, theatrical, and cinematic disciplines, also in their technical aspects; knows the foundations of modern linguistic theories and their main application possibilities and possesses awareness of linguistic variation dynamics, according to the diatopic, diastratic, diafasic, and diamesic axes; knows the main lines of evolution of Romance languages and in more detail those of Italian and Italo-Romance dialects, and can place linguistic traits in their diachronic dimension; knows at a good level the characteristics, both written and oral, of at least one modern language of the European Union.
The above knowledge and understanding abilities are achieved by the student through participation in frontal lectures and seminars, as well as through individual study hours, as provided by the educational activities.
The verification of achieving learning outcomes occurs primarily through oral and/or written exams.

Brief course description The Letters degree course, characterized by a strong interdisciplinarity and complementarity of its courses, aims primarily to train intellectual personnel with a strong humanistic character. It offers four study paths: Classical Letters, Modern Letters, Languages of Music, Theater, and Media, History. The comprehensive set of basic, common courses for all paths allows for orienting the humanistic training, pursued through the progressive consolidation of theoretical knowledge and methodological tools, towards a rigorous in-depth study of the dynamics of languages, texts, and literary traditions (from ancient and medieval to modern and contemporary times), historical phenomena, and contemporary communication. The specific characterization of each path, on the one hand, lays the foundation for a broad training in the respective areas, and on the other, serves as a guide for subsequent educational and professional choices.
Teaching activities include frontal lectures, exercises, seminars, assisted study, as well as spaces dedicated to technical-operational training of students, such as language laboratories, computer laboratories, writing laboratories (also in specific areas such as journalism and the multimedia galaxy), training internships at public and private structures, and stages. The interaction between courses and technical-applicative training activities is aimed at building professional profiles already after the three-year cycle, requiring the implementation of traditional humanistic resources with new knowledge. This broad and flexible multidisciplinary training – always anchored to historical, linguistic, literary, artistic, and philological foundations – can be further tailored to diverse areas through specific specializations more typical of master's courses. In particular, the course allows students to acquire most of the credits required to access, after obtaining a master's degree, the teaching of linguistic-literary and historical disciplines in secondary schools.
External effectiveness Regarding professional opportunities, the primary goal of Letters degree course students is access to the teaching career in schools through the acquisition of a master's degree. The data provided by the AlmaLaurea report for the 2022 survey year confirms this and suggests that the degree course effectively fulfills its role: one year after obtaining the degree, 90.9% of the selected group is enrolled in a master's degree program.
To this end, the degree course ensures, within its competence, that graduates acquire most of the CFU in specific scientific-disciplinary sectors required as current prerequisites for various teaching categories open to graduates with humanistic training. The revision of the course framework has enabled the implementation of study plans with psycho-antropo-pedagogical disciplines necessary to meet the CFU requirements set by current regulations as an additional prerequisite for access to the teaching career.
Regarding other possible occupational areas that the flexibility of humanistic training allows Letters graduates (in particular, access to public administration competitions, publishing, institutional and corporate archiving, business communication, advertising communication, editorial writing, valorization of bibliographic and cultural heritage, activities in theater and performance), they are affected by the ongoing critical situation in youth employment at the national level. In particular, the percentage of graduates who declare working one year after obtaining their degree is low: 20%, a figure that, however, shows a significant increase compared to the previous year (6.9% in 2021).
The degree course, in collaboration with other degree courses under DiLass (in particular with the master's course in Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions, which is the natural continuation of the three-year Letters course), aims to increase and promote student participation in all exit orientation meetings, also promoting their organization.
The data on external effectiveness are presented and discussed in the degree course council meeting in September 2023.
Specific educational objectives and description of the educational path The Letters bachelor's degree aims to provide students with a solid foundational education primarily in literary, linguistic, historical, and historical-artistic disciplines.
Studies are conducted through the acquisition of both theoretical and methodological and applied skills, enabling the three-year graduate to:
- acquire solid, up-to-date bibliographic foundational knowledge regarding the historical phases of Italian literature and literary criticism, also in relation to the broader cultural context in which they are inserted;
- analyze literary texts, ancient and modern, recognizing their constitutive elements and correctly placing them in their era and cultural context;
- interpret documents of various types (written and visual) across very broad chronological spans, from the ancient world to the contemporary age;
- acquire solid foundational knowledge regarding the methods and techniques of classical and/or modern philology, starting from the ability to read a critical edition;
- know the main lines of evolution of Romance languages and in more detail of Italian;
- know history and its periodizations, from the ancient world to the contemporary age, being aware of the main historiographical problems and methodologies of historical sciences;
- examine an artistic, theatrical, musical, and cinematic product, recognizing its constitutive elements and, through appropriate tools, correctly placing it in its era and cultural context.
Starting from a solid common base of knowledge related to Italian literature, history, and the structure of the Italian language, general linguistics, and glottology, classical, Romance, and modern philology, methodological disciplines related to literary text analysis, European literatures, and history, students can then orient their educational path according to different directions: a) a classical orientation aiming to deepen the ancient world, both linguistically-literary and philological, and historically-artistic-archaeological; b) a modern orientation that prioritizes, leveraging always linguistic-literary, philological, and historical-artistic disciplines, study areas from the Middle Ages to the contemporary age; c) an artistic orientation, while maintaining the centrality of linguistic-literary, philological, and historical disciplines, offers the possibility of developing specific knowledge and skills related to musical, theatrical, cinematic, and new communication languages; d) a historical orientation, where the linguistic-literary and philological aspects are complemented by disciplinary deepening in history from antiquity to the contemporary age.
Students can add elective courses to the basic and characterizing activities in each of the indicated areas to build a more defined profile both professionally and in terms of choosing a potential master's study path. The achievement of these objectives is also supported by a wide range of choices among additional educational activities, such as laboratories (linguistic, computer, various forms of writing, or specific to the theater and new media sector) and internships at duly contracted institutions.
The course is also oriented to acquiring good written and oral command of at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian, as well as providing the indispensable knowledge for using the main computer tools and telecommunication in specific areas of competence.
The educational path in the first and second year involves attending basic and characterizing courses, particularly in Italian literature, history of the Italian language, general linguistics, ancient and medieval history, classical or Romance and Italian philology, geography; in the third year, courses in modern and contemporary history, contemporary and comparative Italian literature, archaeological and historical-artistic disciplines that better characterize the individual paths are generally provided.
The graduate's formation is adequate and directed towards continuing studies in a master's degree course. The knowledge and applied abilities acquired are, however, useful - in line with the expected professional profile - for entry into professional sectors requiring full command, both oral and written, of the Italian language in its syntactic and grammatical aspects; good command of linguistic and stylistic forms; a solid foundational humanistic and aesthetic education, necessary to competently frame cultural products and services.
Opinions of organizations and companies with internship/curricular or extra-curricular agreements The Letters degree course has long established a system for monitoring and evaluating the internship experience from the perspective of hosting organizations/companies and interns. The goal is to encourage reflection by interns on the experience, highlight how acquired skills have been utilized, how integration into the work context occurred, which abilities were acquired, and, more generally, to comprehensively monitor internships promoted by the degree course. In particular, students who complete an internship present a report on the experience, which is reviewed by the internship service managers.
In recent years, the degree course has held several consultations with representatives of territorial organizations and stakeholders to better calibrate educational objectives in the perspective of the employability of the degree on the job market. The latest consultation took place on March 28, 2023 (see Table A1.b). Overall, the judgment of these operators regarding the structure of the degree course, the offered training, the teaching objectives, and their alignment with the expected occupational outcomes for graduates is very positive; useful indications emerge for making the professional characteristics of Letters graduates better aligned with the needs of the job market, also through specific laboratory activities and an expansion of the space dedicated to internships and stages, aspects particularly valuable in the communication and human resources management sectors; in particular, the need to strengthen students' training in writing and professional writing uses is emphasized, without neglecting information technology skills and knowledge of at least one foreign language at a good level, to make the degree more employable in the local, national, and international job markets. These suggestions have been received by the degree course, which has adjusted the educational offer in response to the needs of the job market. In particular, new courses have been introduced (Italian Grammar and Linguistics, English Linguistics, Fundamentals of Humanistic Informatics) that not only respond to the need to enrich the profile of graduates but also contribute specifically to a better employability of the university degree, enhancing both disciplinary and transversal skills.
The internship assistance service delegate, Professor Antonella Di Nallo, has recently developed new evaluation questionnaires based on the indications provided by the University Quality Office for monitoring internship activities and their alignment with the expected professional profiles. As illustrated in the meeting of March 28, 2023 (see Table A1.b), the results of the questionnaires have highlighted, from students, a strong interest and positive evaluation of the experience, while some questionnaires returned by the conventioned subjects, such as the one from the State Archives of Pescara, indicate a lack of professional writing skills and knowledge of primary sources (specialized directories) among the student interns. It is also noteworthy that the course in Italian Grammar and Linguistics, established on the request of the Steering Committee and stakeholders, received positive feedback. In the same meeting, stakeholders emphasized the need to develop students' information technology skills for the digitization of archival heritage and strengthen basic skills in cataloging and document management.
Considering that approximately 95% of Letters graduates continue their educational path by enrolling in a master's course to acquire the requirements for entering the teaching career, the degree course has considered as stakeholders students, teachers, and the directing structures of the master's course in Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions, as well as representatives of the school world (specifically, directors). For this reason, these actors were invited to meetings and provided useful contributions to refining some educational strategies of the course.
The degree course established a Steering Committee in 2021 with the aim of ensuring systematic and continuous dialogue with the job market and socioeconomic context, at least at regional and national levels, as well as strengthening and promoting an educational offer consistent with societal needs. It currently includes:
Professor Emiliano (Chair of the Letters degree course); Professor Anna Enrichetta Soccio (Chair of the Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions degree course); Professor Antonella Di Nallo (DILASS delegate for relations with stakeholders); Professor Francesco Berardi (DILASS delegate for placement); Professor Pierluigi Ortolano (Letters degree course delegate for relations with the job market); Professor Mario Cimini; Doctor Nina Celli, head of the online platform ProVersi; Doctor Marilena Staniscia, representative of the Carabba Publishing House of Lanciano; Doctor Pietro Lambertini (newspaper "Il Centro"). The Committee meets on average twice a year (for meeting minutes, see https://www.dilass.unich.it/node/9595).
The data on opinions of organizations and companies are discussed in the September 2023 Council.
Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international levels - of goods and service production, professions (Course establishment)
In order to revise the framework of the Letters degree course (established in 2012, under DM 270/04), the organizational structures of the degree course (Teaching Commission, Quality Assurance Commission, internship and placement delegates) coordinated by the current Chair, Professor Mario Cimini, initiated a consultation in December 2018 with representative organizations at the local level of production, services, and professions. This was to gather indications and opinions regarding the structure and characteristics of the degree course, educational needs, teaching objectives, and occupational opportunities provided by the degree.
On December 10, 2018, at 4:00 PM, at the Department of Letters, Arts, and Social Sciences of the 'G. d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara, a meeting was held under the coordination of the Degree Course Chair, attended by representatives of the following social partners with whom the degree course has had relationships regarding internship and stage management: Etipublica Public Promotion Association (Pescara), Archaeological, Artistic, and Landscape Superintendency of Abruzzo (Chieti), National Center for Dannunzian Studies (Pescara), Rocco Carabba Publishing House (Lanciano), Tiboni Foundation for Culture (Pescara), Marrucino Theater (Chieti), Comprehensive School No. 4 of Chieti, Provincial Voluntary Service Center (Chieti), Spazio MATTA - Artists for the Matta of Pescara (see attached minutes).
This meeting followed a previous meeting on March 7, 2018, attended by representatives of the following entities: National Center for Dannunzian Studies (Pescara), Mediamuseum (Pescara), State Archives (Pescara), 'Eta Beta' Cooperative (Refugee Reception Center, CAS, Pescara), Rocco Carabba Publishing House (Lanciano), State Archives of Chieti, 'Il Messaggero' (Pescara editorial office), Genti d'Abruzzo Foundation (Pescara).
After the Chair presented the characteristics of the Letters course and the project for updating the framework, the following topics were discussed:
1. The founding project of the degree course, its name, framework, and planned revision;
2. Professional profiles identified for graduates of the degree course;
3. Educational objectives of the degree course;
4. Expected learning outcomes and the framework of educational activities;
5. Opinions of companies and territorial entities on internships and occupational opportunities consistent with the educational paths offered by the degree course.
Other territorial entities - Rete 8 Television Station (Pescara), Formoda Foundation (Penne), Brioni Roman Style (Penne), Solfanelli Publisher (Chieti), F.lli De Cecco SPA (Pescara), Regional Social Observatory (Abruzzo), European Center for Rossetti Studies (Vasto), National Tostian Institute (Ortona), Newspaper 'Il Centro' (Pescara), Regional Cultural Services Center (Pescara), Ianieri Publisher (Pescara) - were consulted on the same topics via a questionnaire sent by email (see attached to the meeting minutes).
Cross-referencing the elements emerging from the December 10, 2018 meeting discussion with the data extracted from the questionnaire managed through an information system, the following is evident:
overall, the judgment of these operators regarding the name of the degree course, the offered training, the teaching objectives, and their alignment with the expected occupational outcomes for graduates is very positive;
useful indications emerge for making the professional characteristics of Letters graduates better aligned with the needs of the job market, also through specific laboratory activities and an expansion of the space dedicated to internships and stages – aspects particularly valuable in the communication and human resources management sectors;
in particular, the need to strengthen students' training in writing and professional writing uses is emphasized, without neglecting information technology skills and knowledge of at least one foreign language at a good level, to make the degree more employable in the local, national, and international job markets. These indications are incorporated into the framework revision project through the introduction of scientific-disciplinary sectors related to foreign languages and an increase in credits reserved for language competencies;
particularly appreciated by educational operators is the cultural and educational approach of the degree course, which appropriately lays the foundation, first and foremost for fundamental knowledge and skills, for access to the secondary and higher teaching career (to be completed with a master's degree path), which in reality represents the primary outcome for Letters graduates. In this perspective, the internship carried out in secondary schools represents a valid form of orientation and preparation for the teaching career.
Consultation with representative organizations - at national and international levels - of goods and service production, professions (Course establishment)
The degree course has established a Steering Committee (common to both the three-year and master's degree courses) to intensify and make relations with stakeholders more timely. The Committee, established by the Letters degree course Council resolution of April 9, 2021, consists of:
- Professor Mario Cimini (Chair of the Letters degree course)
- Professor Anna Enrichetta Soccio (Chair of the master's degree course in Philology, Linguistics, and Literary Traditions)
- Professor Francesco Berardi (Placement delegate for Dilass)
- Professor Pierluigi Ortolano (Delegate for relations with the job market, Letters degree course)
- Giammarco Campetta (Student Representative)
- Doctor Marilena Staniscia (Administrative Director of Rocco Carabba Publishing House of Lanciano)
- Doctor Nina Celli (Representative of digital media ProVersi, Etipublica, Maresca Group, Pescara)
- Professor Antonella Sanvitale (Classical High School 'G. d'Annunzio' of Pescara).
The first meeting of the Committee, with the participation of all members, was held on May 25, 2021, and was an opportunity to review the new teaching regulations and gather indications on strengthening educational objectives that better respond to the needs of the job market. In particular, stakeholders positively recognized the degree course's policy of promoting "university education also designed for other employment opportunities beyond teaching, which is traditionally linked to the degree course." The need to modulate and expand the internship opportunities offered to students in light of this objective was also emphasized, once the pandemic emergency was overcome.
On February 23, 2022, the Committee met again (fully attended) to review the positive reception by stakeholders of the introduction of disciplines such as "English linguistics," "Fundamentals of humanistic informatics," and "Italian grammar and linguistics" into the educational path, which broaden students' educational opportunities in the areas of foreign languages, informatics, and expressive-communicative skills in Italian, in line with repeated requests for preparation for the job market. The situation of internships was also reviewed, seeing a restructuring of existing agreements with the elimination of ineffective agreements and the introduction of others better aligned with educational needs. To increase the number of students opting for an internship, it was decided to organize information and promotion meetings for such activities (hoping that the pandemic situation will allow achieving this goal). For details of the meeting, see the attached minutes.
The Committee will continue to play a role in the 'maintenance' of the educational project, allowing stable dialogue with interested parties and thus periodic monitoring of the educational path's alignment with the training needs represented by the interested parties.
A new meeting of the Steering Committee was held on December 15, 2022, via Microsoft Teams. Entry, progression, and exit data The total number of enrollments for the 2022-2023 academic year (221), including transfers and movements, has confirmed a positive growth trend that has characterized recent years: in 2021-22 there were 214 enrollments, in 2020-21 there were 220. The distribution among paths remains stable, with a prevalence of Modern Letters (150) and the remaining enrollments distributed between Languages of Theater (31), Classical Letters (28, increasing from 16 in 2021-22) and History (22, increasing from 17 in 2021-22). The number of pure enrollments remains stable at 171 (170 in 2021-22), indicating good attractiveness of the course not only in the provincial and regional Abruzzo territory but also in neighboring regions (Molise and Puglia, in particular): the percentage of enrollments from outside the region has shown a positive recovery already initiated last year, moving from 12.83% in 2020-2021 to 16.96% in 2021-2022 to 17.78% in 2022-23. The majority of new students come from classical, scientific, and human sciences high schools (80.5%). The number of students who choose the course with a high school diploma grade above 80/100 remains stable (45 enrollments, including 45 who achieved a final grade of 100 or 100 cum laude); this is undoubtedly an index of the trust that the student population and families place in the course's educational offer.
Regarding the trend of the latest cohort observable (2020), data show a slight decrease compared to previous cohorts. The percentage of students who confirmed enrollment in the second year is 76.6% (compared to 87.7% the previous year); no transfers out for the 2020 cohort. It should be noted that often, rather than dropouts, it is about non-re-enrollments that are later recovered after some years.
The percentage of students who continue to the second year in the same degree course having acquired at least 40 CFU is 36.9% (2020 cohort), in line with the previous cohort. Good is the percentage of acquired CFU / required CFU, which is 51.4% (for 2020) and 58.5% (for 2021), figures substantially stable compared to the previous cohort.
Regarding exit data, the number of graduates has decreased to 94 (110 in 2021, while in 2020 there were 127, but this figure should be viewed in relation to the number of enrollments in previous years); the percentage of students graduating within the normal duration of the course (four years) remains nearly stable at 43 out of 94 (61 out of 127 in 2020, 54 out of 110 in 2021). This is undoubtedly an effect of the long-term impact of the pandemic, as students who graduated in 2021 fully experienced the health emergency period during their studies.
The degree course, however, sets as a priority objective to continue on the path already taken in recent years, particularly by intensifying orientation activities at entry, during the course, and at exit, promoting the internationalization of the offered training, and carefully monitoring student productivity to intervene promptly in situations of greater criticality.
The data on student careers are constantly monitored by the Quality Assurance Group of the degree course and then transmitted to the Council, which discusses them in assembly (starting from the September 2023 council).
Characteristics of the final exam The final exam requires the preparation and presentation of a written exposition, whose topic falls within the scope of a discipline included by the student in their study plan and belonging to one of the scientific-disciplinary sectors present in the Letters degree course framework; connected to the final exam is also the verification of knowledge of a modern foreign language.
To access the final exam, the student must have acquired the number of university credits specified by the teaching regulations, minus those reserved for the final exam. The judging commission uses as reference criteria for evaluation the ability to synthesize, scientific accuracy, coherence of argumentation, and expressive clarity demonstrated by the graduate. It expresses the overall grade out of 110, taking into account the curriculum and the final exam.
Mode of conducting the final exam The final exam for the degree is public and consists of the discussion of a written work, in Italian (other languages are not permitted), on a topic related to a discipline included by the student in their study plan and agreed with the supervisor (a teacher belonging to the scientific-disciplinary sector of the discipline requested by the graduate) at least four months before the graduation session. The student may request to take the final exam in a discipline for which they have taken or validated the exam. The text of the written work should be approximately forty pages (the editorial criteria are indicated by the supervisor as needed). To access the discussion, the student must have acquired the number of university credits specified by the Teaching Regulations, minus those reserved for the final exam. In the graduation session, after a brief introduction by the supervisor, the student will present their work before a dedicated judging commission appointed by the Department Director and typically composed of five members chosen among professors and researchers. The commission awards up to a maximum of 4 points for the final exam, with reference criteria being the ability to synthesize, scientific accuracy, coherence of argumentation, and expressive clarity demonstrated by the graduate in the written work and oral presentation. Students who have carried out study experiences within ERASMUS programs or international agreements activated by the reference department are awarded an additional point. The judging commission expresses the overall grade out of 110, taking into account the curriculum and the final exam, and, unanimously, may award the highest grade with honors. The minimum passing grade for the exam is 66 out of 110. Before accessing the graduation session, the candidate must have passed the verification of knowledge of a modern foreign language.

Additionally, a good logical reasoning ability and adequate basic knowledge in scientific disciplines, particularly in mathematics, physics, and materials science, are required.
Students' initial preparation will be verified through an entrance test following the procedures outlined in the Course's Didactic Regulations.
If the verification of the required access knowledge is not successful, additional mandatory coursework will be assigned to be completed in the first year of the course according to the procedures specified in the aforementioned Regulations.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [801T] ENGINEERING OF CONSTRUCTIONS
SECTION: Admission Requirements
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5

Admission Requirements The STUDY PROGRAM has OPEN ACCESS, therefore no selective verification is required that could prevent enrollment in the program.
A MANDATORY VERIFICATION OF MINIMUM KNOWLEDGE is however required, consisting of the TOLC-I (Test OnLine Cisia for Engineering) test provided by CISIA (Consorzio Interuniversitario Sistemi Integrati per l'Accesso).
The TOLC-I consists of 50 questions, including 20 on mathematics, 10 on logic, 10 on sciences, and 10 on verbal comprehension. An English section is also included, which does not contribute to the final score.
The total time available is 125 minutes.
The TOLC-I can be taken in person (TOLC at the university) or remotely (TOLC@CASA), at any university campus that adheres to CISIA.
For future students of the academic year 2024-25, our University will offer the TOLC-I in person.
Based on the result obtained, an indication of the student's initial preparation level is provided, as specified in the CISIA Guide for Engineering TOLC-I Test.
During registration on the CISIA portal's TOLC area, students can declare to be holders of disabilities or affected by specific learning disorders (DSA) to correctly define the test administration method.
Attribution of Additional Training Requirements (OFA)
For the purpose of the Bachelor's degree program in Engineering of Constructions, the TOLC-I is considered fully passed if a score of at least 8/20 is achieved in the Mathematics Section and at least 4/10 in the Sciences Section.
If the threshold scores are not achieved, Additional Training Requirements (OFA) are assigned in the insufficient areas.
OFA may consist of individually assigned training activities or other recovery training activities organized by the Study Program on basic notions of the relevant fields.
OFA will be considered fulfilled upon successful completion of the corresponding assessment.
OFA will also be considered fulfilled once at least 18 ECTS credits are acquired in the first-year exams of Mathematical Analysis, Physics, or Materials Science.
Until OFA are fulfilled, it will not be possible to take exams from subsequent years.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI/PESCARA GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO
COURSE: [801T] CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING
SECTION: Program, texts and objectives
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The ability to communicate information, ideas, problems and solutions to interlocutors who are not specialists is essential for the effective integration of graduates into the building construction world. It is therefore important for graduates to possess appropriate tools for communicating the results of their work. The degree course will therefore provide all the tools to develop students' communication skills, both written and oral, also in a foreign language, and communication through graphic representation, as well as through the use of computer and telecommunication tools.
These objectives will be pursued in lectures and practical exercises by requiring students to present both oral and written, computerized versions of their work and contributions, also using audiovisual means, particularly in preparing the documents for the construction site.
Assessments of communication abilities will take place in final exams and in specific intermediate assessments, also of a seminar nature.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO STUDIES – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [801T] CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING
TYPE:
CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/5

Judgment Autonomy (making judgements)
The graduate must possess, at the end of the study course, their own autonomous capacity for judgment regarding decisions to be made in the management of operations transforming the built environment; they will therefore have the ability to collect and interpret data considered useful for determining autonomous judgments, including reflection on social, scientific or ethical issues related to them. To achieve this judgment autonomy, the degree course will provide both technical-scientific tools and socio-cultural knowledge to stimulate the capacity for critical processing at an individual level.
The objective of fostering the formation and growth of judgment autonomy, and stimulating the capacity for individual critical processing, will be pursued in both theoretical and application-design courses. Judgment autonomy will also be encouraged through the study of projects in which the student will be stimulated to develop critical spirit and make reasoned decisions, both individually and in work groups.
The assessment of the achieved capacity and judgment autonomy will be carried out progressively in the examinations, also through the figure of the Tutor, who will follow the evolution of the individual formation process.

Incoming Orientation. The activities are coordinated by the Orientation, Placement, and Social Working Group, composed of faculty members of the Study Program. Incoming Orientation is conducted throughout the academic year.

The orientation activities for the 2023-24 academic year focused on four main areas:
1. PNRR Orienta-UdA Activities
2. University Orientation Activities
3. Departmental Orientation Activities
4. Departmental PCTO Activities. These initiatives, all currently ongoing, have involved numerous schools in the Abruzzo, Marche, and Puglia regions.

Specifically, the Orienta UDA program, a 15-hour PCTO path for schools primarily in the Chieti and Pescara provinces, is structured over three days (Chieti, Pescara, and Open Day). This path has reached approximately 4,000 students, presenting the entire Italian scientific educational offer, with a particular focus on that of the University and especially on the INGEO Department. The initiative was mainly guided by the Engineering Delegate, with the support of Orientation Tutors.

University Orientation activities included participation in educational fairs at both national and regional levels, such as the Chieti Student Fair, Bari, Ascoli Piceno, and visits to local classical and scientific high schools. These were coordinated by the Engineering Delegate and faculty members of various study programs.

Departmental Orientation provided an overview of the study programs offered by the department, with presentations held at various schools in Abruzzo and Marche.

Departmental PCTO activities included schools participating in lectures on specific engineering topics, contributing to the dissemination of departmental research in secondary schools.

Additionally, orientation activities included organizing 'Unveiling the University,' established and sponsored by CRUI (Conference of Italian University Rectors) and MUR (Ministry of University and Research), which featured meetings, workshops, and debates, offering the community a unique opportunity to participate, and organizing Open Days, particularly the one on April 4 in Pescara.

Parallel to school visits, on central coordination by the University, Open Days are organized at both university campuses on Viale Pindaro and Via dei Vestini, where course information is enriched with presentations of individual faculty research activities.

Finally, the Study Program adhered to the 'A Day as a Freshman' initiative on March 18 and 19, 2024, attended by several local high schools. High school students had the opportunity to attend university courses in classrooms for an immersive experience in the university world.

Through direct agreements with outgoing orientation coordinators at secondary schools, in-person meetings are organized at their campuses; these meetings aim to illustrate the study program's educational offer, essential knowledge for entering the educational path, and the career prospects of the three-year degree in Construction Engineering. Schools are offered the possibility to host introductory lectures on topics covered in the study program.

Active also are:
• a Study Program Facebook page https://www.facebook.com/ingegneriadannunzio presenting Study Program activities.
• a Study Program Twitter page https://twitter.com/ingegneriaUdA disseminating Study Program announcements.
• a Study Program Instagram page https://www.instagram.com/ingegneriadannunzio/ presenting Study Program activities.

Systematic monitoring actions are being implemented to evaluate the results of organized initiatives to assess their effectiveness and proceed with potential improvements. In particular, during the initial monitoring phase of our orientation activities, we conducted brief surveys at the end of various events to gather participants' perceptions of the outcomes. This method provided an initial insight into the effectiveness of such activities. Surveys were conducted using the Slido program. Given the importance of data collection, we requested the central administration to purchase the software for further information.

We also plan to implement social media campaigns as part of our monitoring strategy to further assess the actual impact of our initiatives. This will allow us to more comprehensively attest to the real effectiveness of our orientation actions.

Training period arrangements The Study Course, through the coordination of the Guidance Committee, establishes various agreements with private firms and/or public bodies in order to activate the training internships required by the academic curriculum.
The internship activity aims to provide students with professional practice experiences, administrative procedures, site management, etc. The internship period takes place at public or private structures previously agreed upon with the Department hosting the Construction Engineering Study Course.
Before the start of the internship activity, the 'Training Project' must be defined, which will be agreed upon with the academic tutor and countersigned by the tutor of the public/private structure.
At the end of the internship period, the student must prepare a 'Summary Report' of the experience carried out, which must be signed by the student and countersigned by the academic tutor and the tutor of the public/private structure before being submitted to the Study Course Chair.
To ensure an adequate quality standard, at the end of the internship, electronic platform questionnaires are distributed to both students and host entities to evaluate the effectiveness of the internship and any improvement actions to be implemented.

International Mobility Section At the Department of Engineering and Geology, numerous collaboration agreements with various foreign universities are in place to promote and support student mobility for study, internship, and training periods abroad. All agreements, falling under the new program called Erasmus+, are valid for multiple years (septennium 2012/2027). For overseas training, the Study Course refers to the sector coordination of the Department of Engineering and Geology, carried out through the responsible person appointed by the Department Council, Prof. Sara Amoroso, and the University's central offices. Since March 2020, international mobility management activities have been enhanced through the creation of an Erasmus working group, which for the L23 Study Course consists of Prof. Sara Amoroso, Prof. Masciotta, and student representatives of the Study Courses. To promote student participation in overseas training activities, the “Orientation and Placement” working group, together with the “Erasmus” group, has created correspondence tables between courses offered within the Study Course and those available at various Erasmus locations with active exchange agreements. The availability of these correspondences facilitates both the organization of overseas activities by students and the approval of Erasmus study plans by the Study Course Council. The results of these activities, subject to continuous revision to account for changes in course offerings, are available on the following web page: https://www.ingegneriadellecostruzioni.unich.it/erasmus/studiare-allestero. Additionally, to further enhance student mobility supporting study and internship periods abroad, the Study Course has implemented since 2019/20 a series of initiatives aimed at increasing the number of students with Erasmus experience. In particular, a bonus has been introduced in the graduation score for students who have earned CFU abroad, and a semesterly administered Erasmus questionnaire to identify the main reasons hindering students' overseas experiences; additionally, awareness seminars have been organized by students who have already completed the Erasmus experience. An additional economic contribution has also been provided by the INGEO Department to increase the overseas stay scholarships for those intending to undertake the Erasmus experience. Student Feedback STUDENT OPINIONS FROM ATTENDING STUDENTS The analysis of the opinions of attending students is based on the average responses for each evaluated question, which over the last eight academic years has ranged from a minimum of 570 in 2021/23 to a maximum of 1698 in 2016/17, with an overall average of 1054 responses per question. For the 2022/23 academic year, 766 questionnaires were completed.
The historical data of the overall synthetic score shows, for the period 2015-2022, positive values for each analyzed year and also highlights a growth trend in the most recent years of monitoring. The numerical details from the academic year 2015-16 to 2022-23 show the following scores: 3.34, 3.18, 3.29, 3.32, 3.34, 3.42, 3.42, 3.54, and 3.51. It is interesting to note, within the same time period, a clear increase in the percentages of decidedly positive responses, which after an initial reduction from 42% to 40% in 2016-17, saw an increase to 45%, 47%, 51%, 53%, 55.8%, and finally 57.14% in 2022-23.
Detailed analysis shows that the Course of Study has relatively homogeneous evaluations, which range from an initial range of 2.9-3.45 in the 2015-16 academic year to a range of 3.17-3.85 in the 2022-23 academic year for all evaluated topics. It is interesting to note that for each of the last seven analyzed academic years, the highest-scoring responses relate to judgments on the interest of the topics offered in courses, respect for class schedules by professors, and their availability for student meetings; this demonstrates on one hand the effectiveness of the continuous updating of the educational offer that the Course of Study has undertaken in recent years in response to requests from the student body, and on the other hand the qualification and selection of teaching staff.
Finally, a difference is observed between students' evaluations and suggestions regarding teaching loads. In this latter case, the majority of students indicate that "the courses presuppose the appropriate level of foundational knowledge" and that "it is advisable to maintain the current teaching load"; considerations that are joined by the "impracticality" of improving synergy with other courses for a small portion of students.
DISCUSSIONS OF STUDENT OPINION RESULTS IN COUNCIL MEETINGS The results of the student opinions above, given the complete availability of data for both semesters starting from August, were discussed in detail in the November 2023 council meeting, alongside those of graduates and professors. The discussion of the observations from the Parity Commission of Teachers and Students, held in the Course of Study on February 19, 2024, provided positive feedback for areas related to teaching and course organization. It was emphasized that, in response to possible criticalities identified for the integrated courses in the first year of analysis and physics, the revision of the educational offer already active from 2023-24 has planned the elimination of integrated courses.
STUDENT COMPLAINT MANAGEMENT The Course of Study, after internal evaluations regarding the opportunity to implement an internal complaint management system, has opened the email suggerimentiereclami.idc@unich.it to receive student suggestions and complaints. These communications are managed by the Parity Commission of Teachers and Students, which, after an initial review, directs them to discussion in the Course Council.

Graduate Opinions GRADUATE OPINIONS The sample surveyed by Almalaurea, consisting of 20 respondents out of 36 graduates (55.5%), can be considered reasonably representative.
Comparison with other degrees in equivalent courses shows that 80% considered the study load appropriate for the duration of the study program, with a 'definitely yes' percentage of 45%, exceeding the national average of 32.5%.
The organization of exams in terms of calls, schedules, information, etc., is considered consistently satisfactory by 45% of respondents and by 40% for more than half of the exams.
Also excellent are the percentages of respondents who reported being satisfied with their relationships with professors: a decidedly positive judgment is recorded for 20% and a positive judgment for 80%, compared to national averages of 22% and 66%, respectively.
90% of respondents are satisfied with the degree program, in line with the national average.
However, the judgment on classrooms is lower, with a positive rating of 65% compared to a national average of 78.7%. The lower values compared to the national average are attributed to equipment for other teaching activities and library services.
The data showing that 60% would enroll in the same program again is positive.
The employment rate one year after graduation is in line with the national average (66.7% compared to 71.0%); students enrolled in a subsequent degree program, 73.5%, are in line with the national average of 79.4%.
DISCUSSIONS OF GRADUATE OPINION RESULTS IN COUNCIL SESSION The results of the above-mentioned graduate opinions were discussed in detail in the November 2023 council, alongside those of students, graduates, and professors, identifying the main criticalities.
CRITICALITIES HIGHLIGHTED BY GRADUATE OPINIONS: ANALYSIS AND SOLUTIONS The criticalities highlighted by graduates in the Almalaurea report align with those reported in the Parity Commission of Teachers and Students report (Section B) and refer to infrastructure and laboratories.
For the former, the adjustments implemented by the University should be noted first for the plant component (2019/20), then for classroom equipment (2020/21), and finally for the building envelope (2022/23).
For laboratories, in addition to enhancing the didactic equipment of SCAM, the 2023 implementation of lightweight laboratories for teaching should be noted.
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The knowledge provided in the course and the indications on their use must be complemented by achieving the ability to apply the acquired tools. To this end, students will be provided with interpretative keys to move from the identification and understanding of the theoretical profiles of the studied subjects to the application of the mechanisms for using the acquired knowledge. This will occur, in particular, through an interdisciplinary approach as a defining element in building a professional profile capable of analyzing and understanding the complexity of the transformation processes of the built environment.
Verification tests (oral, written, project-based exams) require the application of knowledge at progressively higher levels of difficulty and their successful completion.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
It is the responsibility of the degree program to provide students with, beyond the necessary knowledge in specific disciplinary fields, a study and work method enabling them to autonomously develop their capabilities in a continuous learning process, positioning them to undertake, if necessary, further studies with a high degree of autonomy.
This objective will be pursued through the structuring of the training process into different phases and types (frontal lectures, autonomous analysis and research activities, applied experimentation activities, internships, etc.), alternating moments of knowledge acquisition with those of personal re-elaboration and experimental application of the acquired knowledge.
Verification will occur through intermediate tests during courses, passing exams, and the discussion of the final project.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The degree program aims to provide students with essential knowledge to acquire the technical-methodological tools for understanding issues related to the management of transformations in the built environment. Graduates must be able to understand and interpret the reality of building constructions and the dynamics of their design, transformation, and management; they must also acquire knowledge and understanding of the tools used to control the building process, in its technical-constructive and economic aspects, to provide technical support for controlling its transformations.
These objectives will be primarily pursued through basic and characteristic teaching courses, of both methodological and applied nature. Verification of objective achievement will be carried out through passing the passing exams, where both theoretical preparation and specific technical-applicative and design knowledge will be evaluated.
