Brief Course Description The three-year Construction Engineering course is an open-access program. It does, however, require an entrance verification of basic scientific knowledge.
The three-year Construction Engineering course is designed to train graduates who can contribute to the design, realization, maintenance, and disposal of the built environment; a sector that expresses consistent and continuous demand, especially in the context of necessary retrofitting of existing built heritage and the creation of new building structures with high innovative content, generally ensuring significant responsibility and satisfaction.
The training path initially acquires basic scientific tools, such as mathematics, physics, computer science, drawing, and materials science; subsequently, it provides the knowledge and skills necessary to operate on the built environment throughout all its life phases. In this sense, it provides tools for structural, energy, geotechnical, architectural, economic, and hydraulic analyses. Theoretical activities are complemented, depending on the specific nature of each course, by practical, laboratory, and project-based exercises to develop cross-application skills.
The study program requires the completion of a training internship to be carried out at companies, public or private entities, professional orders, or internal technical structures within the University.
The teaching offer defines a designer figure who, due to their technical-scientific training, is eligible for registration in both the Junior Engineers' Register and the Junior Architects' Register.
At the same time, within the same University, a path for continued advanced study is offered through the Master's degree in Construction Engineering.
External Effectiveness DATA ANALYSIS FROM ALMALAUREA SOURCE The 2022 sample, from Almalaurea data, consists of 36 graduates, of whom 20 responded to the questionnaire: the collected data constitute a relatively representative reference of 55.5%. The gender ratio of the surveyed sample corresponds to 75% men and 25% women. The average age at graduation is 25.4 years, with an average study duration of 5.8 years. The percentage of three-year graduates intending to continue their studies by enrolling in a Master's degree is 80%.
The 2022 surveys of graduates one year after graduation involved a sample of 40 people, with 34 respondents. Of these, 70% are men and 30% women. A significant number, 73.5%, enrolled in a second-level degree program, while 66.7% of those not continuing their studies did so for work reasons. 22% perform technical professions, while 55% work in intellectual roles. The employment sector is private, with a 78% share in industry.
In conclusion, the first-level degree is certainly attractive as a first step toward completing university education through a Master's degree, but a significant portion of graduates also choose to enter the labor market immediately.
DISCUSSIONS IN COUNCIL SESSION The results of the L23 graduates' statistics related to the labor market were discussed, alongside student, graduate, and professor opinions, in the November 2023 council.
IMPROVEMENT ACTIONS The findings from Almalaurea data and communications with student representatives do not currently indicate the need for specific improvement actions, but continuous monitoring is maintained to address any emerging issues immediately.
Specific Course Training Objectives and Description of the Training Path The Construction Engineering degree program is aimed at training a professional figure operating in the fields of architecture, engineering, and construction, who contributes and collaborates in various areas to programming, design, implementation, and management activities for the transformation of the built environment. Graduates have a preparation that allows them to receive and manage innovation, consistently with scientific and technological development within the disciplines of architecture and civil engineering. The training is aimed at understanding and comprehending the issues and characteristics of building structures in relation to the physical-environmental, historical, socio-economic, and productive context of the transformation intervention.
In this field, the specific competencies of the graduate relate to activities connected to the construction sector, with particular emphasis on structural analysis and design, technological and construction choices and their execution, organization and management of construction sites, economic management and evaluation of building processes, technical-administrative direction of industrial production processes for materials and components for construction, as well as maintenance, rehabilitation, and adaptation of building structures.
The Construction Engineering degree is characterized by the deepening of technical-scientific disciplines and construction, execution, and management themes in architecture.
The Construction Engineering degree generally aims to provide the necessary competencies to perform activities such as:
- Supporting programming, design, and implementation of the built environment;
- Analyzing and evaluating the products of architecture and civil engineering in terms of typological-distributive, structural, construction, and technological aspects;
- Managing production and implementation processes in construction;
- Organizing and managing construction sites;
- Analyzing and controlling the environmental impact of materials and components for construction;
- Maintaining, rehabilitating, and recovering building structures;
- Controlling construction site safety, both in prevention and emergency;
- Providing technical-administrative and economic direction for industrial production processes of materials and components for construction.
The training path involves a progression where students initially acquire basic training in understanding the foundations of mathematics, physics, materials science, and drawing; they also gain initial experience in construction fundamentals. Additionally, students expand their knowledge in economic and computer science areas while strengthening their knowledge in the construction sector, both as territory management and hydraulics, and as architectural and structural aspects of construction. Finally, students complete their training by deepening safety themes in construction and integrating their knowledge with disciplines related to geotechnical engineering and technical physics.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements, Curricular or Extra-curricular The L23 Course of Study includes a mandatory training internship to be carried out during the study program with hosting entities that have established agreements with the Course of Study. The internship regulation also allows individual students to propose a hosting entity, with which the Course of Study will establish an appropriate agreement after verifying the minimum requirements.
Since March 2020 (point 4 of the CCdS meeting of March 27, 2020), the Steering Committee Working Group has been integrated, and among its activities is the continuous search for additional hosting entities to be added to the existing database (attached in Section B5: Assistance for External Training Periods).
In the new Course of Study website, expected to be online from April 2024, a dedicated section for curricular internships will be provided.
The Course of Study has established, thanks to the creation of the Steering Committee Working Group, a systematic survey of opinions from hosting entities and interns after their experience. The survey is conducted through the University Moodle system at the following link.
Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Levels - of Goods and Services Production and Professions (Course Establishment)
At the time of establishing the degree program, consultation was conducted as required by Article 11, Paragraph 4 of Ministerial Decree No. 270/2004.
After extensive discussion with representative organizations present in the territory, a generally positive judgment was expressed on the new study program project: in particular, representative organizations expressed a favorable opinion on the realization of a teaching project oriented toward training construction professionals capable of integrating broadly into the labor market and responding adequately to demand in both new construction and existing management sectors, as well as in the industry producing construction products and structures, in line with emerging European trends.
The consultation led to identifying the three-year Construction Engineering graduate as a versatile technician capable of assuming responsibility, even at a high level, on construction sites, simple and complex, in free professions, public and private entities, and throughout the various phases of the building production cycle and the life of the built environment, from design to management.
Through the cyclical repetition of consultations, the initially identified objectives have been verified in practice and the opportunity to make path improvements to give a more distinctive identity to the professional figure to be trained has been recognized. The degree program has been updated through a remodulation of the teaching schedule and a more explicit and immediately understandable name.
The academic body that conducted the initial consultation is identifiable in the Faculty Council Commission, delegated to the procedural documentation for the degree program.
Today, the continuity of contact with territorial organizations will be guaranteed by the Course of Study Chair and the Department Director. Operational and decision-making meetings will be expanded to include the AQ Management Group.
The consulted organizations, directly or through documents and sector studies, are the Engineering and Architects Orders and Industrial Associations, particularly those of Building Contractors in the provinces of Chieti and Pescara.
Systematic and periodic consultations are planned, currently more occasional, to establish an open table for all interested representatives, both to maintain external third-party monitoring and to remain aligned with labor market evolution.
Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Levels - of Goods and Services Production and Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
Based on meetings conducted during the initial accreditation phase and elements emerging over the years, the following institutions are identified as stakeholders for the Construction Engineering L23 degree program: Confindustria (Chieti-Pescara), ANCE (Chieti and Pescara), Ente Scuola Edile (Chieti and Pescara), Engineering and Architects Orders (Chieti and Pescara), College of Surveyors (Chieti and Pescara), Province of Pescara, and schools in the provinces of Chieti, Pescara, and L'Aquila (classical and scientific high schools, surveyor institutes).
On January 12, 2016, a meeting was held with these organizations in Chieti (https://elearning.unich.it/mod/resource/view.php?id=15578). Due to limited attendance compared to invited participants, it was decided to periodically consult these organizations via email questionnaires (attached questionnaire at point C3), trusting that this more streamlined interaction would encourage greater participation.
In March 2019, the lack of responses to the sent questionnaires was noted (Parties Social Minutes of March 12, 2019), so they were sent again and the response was verified in a subsequent meeting. On April 10, 2019, during a new meeting with social parties (Parties Social Minutes of April 10, 2019), no responses were received for the second sending either.
Informal contacts were then initiated with the Engineering Orders and local companies, which generally expressed appreciation for the training of three-year graduates in class L-23. Based on this, the Course of Study Council meeting of June 5, 2019, established a Steering Committee including Course of Study figures and social parties. The objective of the Committee is to maintain continuous contact with periodic in-person meetings at least annually, which was deemed useful to extend to student representation as well.
On December 12, 2019, another meeting with social parties was held, with responses from both Engineering Orders and a representative of local companies; social parties expressed a favorable opinion on the current teaching offer of the L23 Course of Study and suggested, possibly through elective training activities, increasing the number of professionalizing and economic courses.
The open teacher-student meetings have proven very useful for identifying and addressing any criticalities or anomalies reported by students. Previous meetings saw active student participation: 17/11/2015 (approximately 40 students, L23 + LM24), 08/03/2016 (approximately 150 students, L23 + LM24), 16/12/2019 (approximately 80 students, L23 + LM24). Given the positive response from the student body, these collective teacher-student meetings will be repeated at least once a year.
Consultations were also conducted with national bodies to harmonize all L-23 courses across various Italian universities, with meetings at CUN on March 21, 2019, and at La Sapienza University in Rome on April 8, 2019, and May 30, 2019.
In the Course of Study Council meeting of March 27, 2020 (point 4), it was decided to enhance the Steering Committee by establishing a Working Group composed of the following entities: Chairs of L23 and LM24 Courses of Study, Prof. Vincenzo Sepe, Prof. Guido Camata, Prof. Giuseppe Brando, Prof. Gianmichele Panarelli, Student Representatives L23 and LM24, Presidents of Provincial Councils of Engineering and Architecture Orders, President or delegate of Confindustria for the provinces of Chieti and Pescara, and President of ANCE for the provinces of Chieti and Pescara. The Working Group's activities focus on periodic meetings with stakeholders and the continuous management and revision of hosting entities for curricular internships.
On July 20, 2022, an assembly was held in a mixed presence-online format to illustrate the rationale of the training project to the main stakeholders, namely students of the three-year Construction Engineering L23 program. After an initial presentation of the practical implications and potential impacts of the current degree path, an unanimous positive judgment and alignment with the strategic vision of the project were recorded. The assembly was followed by an online questionnaire, which expanded the participant base and fully confirmed the previously expressed judgments.
On October 22, 2022, a meeting was held with the Engineering Orders of the Chieti and Pescara territories, where the University "G. d'Annunzio" is located; the Engineering Order of the Calabria Region; the certification company ABIcert; the Ferrara-based company Archliving; the Pescara-based company Energylab3; ANCE Marche; and the Abruzzo Region's Infrastructure and Transport Department. The selected entities were chosen to cover a national geographical scope and represent a variety of public and private entities adequately representative of the future work environments for Construction Engineering graduates. Stakeholders expressed an extremely positive judgment on the proposed teaching offer, identifying the necessary interdisciplinarity that is currently decisive for success in the labor market.
On November 28, 2023, a Steering Committee meeting was held with the President of the Pescara Engineering Order, a representative of the Reggio Calabria Engineering Order Foundation, and a representative of a local company. The possibility of involving professional categories in selecting thesis topics was discussed. The Pescara Engineering Order President proposed establishing a committee within the Pescara Engineering Order to facilitate dialogue with studios and companies. The CIRT professors welcomed the initiative, seeing it as an opportunity to facilitate post-graduation placement, and offered to collaborate with the Order.
Professors communicated that the procedure to request the inclusion of the University "G. d'Annunzio" - Pescara - among the sites for the State Exams for the qualification to practice as an Engineer has been initiated. The assembly welcomed this communication positively.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data The 2022-23 academic year enrollment data indicate an increase in enrollments compared to the post-COVID period; overall, the enrollment number, totaling 47, is trending toward pre-COVID conditions, with values in line with national and regional reference data.
The geographical origin analysis of students shows a recovery, compared to the post-COVID period, of non-local students, representing 34% of new enrollments.
The academic background of the student body shows approximately 50% coming from high schools, with the remainder from technical and magistral institutes; similarly, the male/female ratio is now balanced.
Regarding student careers, the average number of exams passed per student is 2.05, and the percentage of acquired credits relative to required credits is 24.3%.
Regarding degree completion, 8% are graduates in progress, 25% are one year beyond the program duration, and the remaining percentage is two or more years beyond the normal program duration.
DISCUSSIONS OF ENTRY, PATH, AND EXIT DATA IN COURSE OF STUDY COUNCIL The entry, in-progress, and exit results of the Course of Study are normally analyzed annually in December Course of Study Council meetings to gain a clear and comprehensive view after the closure of regular enrollments scheduled for early November. The latest discussion occurred in the Council meeting of December 15, 2023.
IMPROVEMENT ACTIONS Regarding actions to increase enrollment numbers, which saw a significant decrease during the post-COVID period, the Course of Study has significantly intensified orientation actions, increasing contact with schools in the reference areas to systematically conduct in-person presentations of the teaching offer.
Regarding difficulties in passing first-year basic exams, a supplementary mathematics and physics course has been institutionalized.
The integration between Analysis and Physics courses has also been eliminated, as feedback from the CPDS indicated an excessive workload for students.
Final Project Characteristics The final project consists of a public exam where the candidate presents and discusses an independently compiled report under the supervision of a supervisor. Depending on the candidate's choice, the report may contain a critical synthesis of the training path or an in-depth analysis of a topic related to the course of study, or both.
Final Project Execution Method The candidate is assigned a specific time for presenting their work. The graduation committee forms its judgment after a block of presentations that occupies no more than half a day.
The thesis report must be written under the guidance of a Course of Study professor (supervisor). The co-supervisor, if present, may also be an external expert in the subject.
The thesis committee consists of the supervisors plus other Course of Study professors, up to the minimum number of members required by the University's Teaching Regulation.
The maximum score for the final project is 8 points out of 110. The following guidelines may be considered for these 8 points:
• Up to 5 points for the graduation exam, awarded considering both the presented work and the candidate's presentation.
• Up to 3 points for the curriculum:
  * Maximum 1 point for punctuality in the study path.
  * Maximum 2 points for the average of 'M' exams (out of 110), awarded as follows:
    -- 1 point if the student is in progress or in the first year beyond the program, regardless of the M average.
    -- 0 points otherwise.
    -- 0 points if M ≤ 90;
    -- 1 point if 90 < M ≤ 100;
    -- 2 points if M > 100.
• Up to 2 points for internationalization of the training path through Erasmus courses:
  * 1 point for semester-long;
  * 2 points for annual;
  * For periods shorter than six months, up to a maximum of 0.5 points.
The evaluation of the thesis report may consider the candidate's ability to apply knowledge across disciplines.
The final project is designed to assess the candidate's ability to integrate knowledge and skills acquired throughout the training path.

Admission Procedures The L-9 Biomedical Engineering Bachelor's Degree Course has open access; therefore, no selective verification is required to enroll in the Course. However, a minimum knowledge verification is required, consisting of the TOLC-I (Test OnLine CISIA for Engineering) test provided by CISIA (Consorzio Interuniversitario Sistemi Integrati per l'Accesso). This test can be taken at any CISIA consortium location and is valid nationwide.
The TOLC-I consists of 50 questions: 20 in mathematics, 10 in logic, 10 in sciences, 10 in verbal comprehension. An English section is also included, but its score is not counted toward the final score. Based on the result, an indication of the student's preparation level is provided as per the CISIA Online Test Guide for Engineering TOLC-I.
During registration on the CISIA portal's TOLC area, students may declare to be persons with disabilities or affected by specific learning disorders (DSA) to properly define the test administration method.
For enrollment in the L-9 three-year degree course, the TOLC-I is fully passed if a score of at least 8/20 is achieved in the Mathematics section and at least 4/10 in the Sciences section. If the TOLC-I is passed, it does not result in Additional Educational Requirements (OFA) for the three-year Biomedical Engineering degree courses at the "G. d'Annunzio" University of Chieti-Pescara. If the threshold scores are not met, Additional Educational Requirements (OFA) are assigned in the insufficient areas.
For students with OFA, recovery training activities will be held on basic concepts in the two areas, concluding with a profit verification test (recovery test). If the recovery test is passed, the OFA will be considered fulfilled.
Alternatively, OFA for either area will be considered fulfilled once the student has earned at least 18 credits (CFU) in total across courses in the scientific-disciplinary sectors (SSD) MAT/05 (Mathematical Analysis), FIS/07 (Physics), CHIM/03 (Chemistry).
Students who do not fulfill this obligation may enroll in the second year and attend classes regularly, but cannot take exams for subsequent years until the assigned OFA are completed.

Syllabus, texts and objectives Note regarding the sectors and credits selected for basic activities The presence of sector FIS/07 among basic activities is due to the fact that
- as per the SSD declaration - the competencies of the sector concern the study and development of physical methodologies (theoretical and experimental) necessary for both the description and understanding of living matter in the environmental, biological and medical context, as well as for the development and use of instrumentation required for the control and detection of physical phenomena in the field of prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The competencies of this sector also cover biophysics and biomedical diagnostics.

SECTION: Communication skills
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1863

Communication skills (communication skills)
The graduate in Biomedical Engineering:
- is able to draft technical reports related to the activities carried out and to interpret technical reports written by colleagues, superiors, or subordinates; - is able to interpret and apply (and potentially 'produce/draft') internal company regulations and technical manuals;
- is able to effectively integrate into the design process and manufacture a custom medical device, contributing to identifying optimal solutions for its realization and manufacturing;
- is able to interact with qualified personnel authorized by national law to practice the medical and dental professions to evaluate their technical, instrumental, and organizational needs and to propose the most suitable biomaterials for the structural and design requirements of highly complex custom medical devices;
- is able to collaborate in testing, research, and development activities in the industrial medical, dental, and pharmaceutical fields for clinical-use biomaterials.
Written and oral communication skills are developed during examination assessments, where the instructor must also consider these aspects in the final evaluation. In particular, these skills will be essential during the internship/practice and in training activities preceding the writing of the final thesis. A sufficient knowledge of a foreign language provides the student with additional communication skills.

SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1863

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
Autonomy of judgment is developed through critical reflection on the texts proposed for individual study, exercises, organized seminars, and preparation of reports, especially within characteristic and related courses.
The development of autonomous judgment capabilities aimed at identifying, formulating, and solving problems specifically related to dental materials technology and sciences relies on the characteristic courses of the Biomedical Engineering degree program. Additionally, the planned internship and training activities, as well as the tasks assigned by the supervisor for the final exam preparation, are useful for this purpose.
The verification of acquiring autonomy of judgment occurs through discussion of advanced aspects of the discipline during written and/or oral exams, as well as during the activities assigned for the preparation of the final exam and internship.

Incoming Orientation The orientation activities for the Academic Year 2023-24 focused on four main areas:
1. PNRR Orienta-UdA activities
2. University orientation activities
3. Departmental orientation activities
4. Departmental PCTO activities These initiatives, all currently ongoing, have involved numerous schools in the regions of Abruzzo, Marche, and Puglia.
Specifically, the Orienta UDA program, a 15-hour PCTO pathway for schools primarily in the provinces of Chieti and Pescara, is structured over three days (Chieti, Pescara, and Open Day). This pathway reached approximately 4,000 students, presenting the entire Italian scientific educational offer, with particular focus on that of the University and especially the INGEO Department. The initiative was mainly led by the engineering delegate, with support from orientation tutors.
University orientation activities included participation in educational fairs at both national and regional levels, such as the Chieti, Bari, and Ascoli Piceno Student Salons, as well as visits to local classical and scientific high schools. These were coordinated by the engineering delegate and faculty members from various study programs.
Departmental orientation provided an overview of the study programs offered by the department, with presentations held at various schools in Abruzzo and Marche.
Departmental PCTO activities included schools participating in lectures on specific engineering topics, contributing to the dissemination of departmental research in secondary schools.
Finally, orientation activities included organizing 'Università Svelata', an initiative by CRUI featuring meetings, workshops, and debates, offering the community a unique opportunity for participation, and organizing Open Days, particularly the Pescara Open Day on April 4.

TYPE: COURSE
CURRICULUM: COURSE
SECTION: Training periods arrangement
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1863

Training periods arrangement The Course of Study continues to define agreements with private and/or public entities in order to activate mandatory internships, allowing students to establish preparatory collaborations for entering the workforce.
The internship activity aims to provide students with professional practice experiences and administrative procedures. The internship period will take place at public or private approved structures. Before starting the internship, a 'Training Project' must be defined, agreed upon with the academic tutor, and countersigned by the tutor of the public/private structure. The agreement format between student-academic tutor-structure is approved by the CoS Council on 3/5/2022.
At the end of the internship period, the student must prepare a 'Summary Report' of the experience to be submitted to the Course Director; this report must be signed by the student and countersigned by the academic tutor and the tutor of the public/private structure.
Following the appointment of the 'Working Group: Steering Committee', questionnaires have been prepared to be distributed to both students and host entities upon completion of the internship, in order to evaluate effectiveness and potential improvement actions.
Students are required to attend a mandatory free workplace safety course organized by the University's Safety and Prevention Service and obtain the corresponding certificate before applying for an internship.

International Mobility Office At the Department of Engineering and Geology, numerous collaboration agreements with foreign universities are in place to promote and support student mobility for study, internship, and traineeship periods abroad. All agreements fall under the new program named Erasmus+, valid for the period 2012-2027. For overseas training, the Study Course refers to the sector coordination of the Department of Engineering and Geology, carried out through the responsible appointed by the Department Council, Professor Sara Amoroso, and the University Central Offices. The Erasmus working group for the Study Course L9, composed of Professor Amoroso and Professor Cristina Falcinelli, has developed correspondence tables between courses offered within the Study Course and those available at various Erasmus sites with active exchange agreements. The availability of such correspondences facilitates both the organization of overseas activities by students and the approval of Erasmus study plans by the Study Course Council. The results of these activities, subject to continuous revision to account for changes in training offers, are available on the following web page: https://ibl9.unich.it/pagina-studiare-allestero-1397
Additionally, to further enhance student mobility in support of study and internship periods abroad, the Study Course has introduced a bonus in the graduation score for students who have earned CFU abroad. The Department INGEO has also provided an additional financial contribution to increase the overseas stay scholarships for those intending to undertake the Erasmus experience.

Student Opinions SUMMARY STUDENTS' RESPONSES TO THE PRE-EXAM QUESTIONNAIRE
1) ANALYTICAL SUMMARY OF EVALUATIONS For attending students, the average score is above 3 out of 4, indicating an overall positive result. Only the score related to the question "Were the preliminary knowledge sufficient for understanding the topics covered in the exam program?" is below 3. It will be necessary to meet with students to delve deeper into this point and identify potential corrective actions (which will obviously be specific to individual courses). Teachers will be advised to distribute a questionnaire at the beginning of first-year courses to assess student preparedness. Corrective actions such as reinforcing tutoring and recovery courses can then be identified. Overall, the course workload is rated high. A high score is observed for question 23 regarding the teacher's availability to clarify the topics covered.
For non-attending students, the average is lower (2.96). The trend is similar, with the lowest score related to the basic preparation of incoming students. Similar to attending students, the study load is considered high.
2) SUMMARY OF STUDENTS' RESPONSES TO THE PRE-EXAM QUESTIONNAIRE For attending students, all courses in all CUN areas received scores above 3. For non-attending students, course scores are fairly homogeneous. For non-attending students, courses in the areas of mathematical and computer sciences, biological sciences, and civil engineering and architecture are particularly critical.
3) SUMMARY OF DISCIPLINARY SECTORS For all students, the distribution of scores is fairly homogeneous. It will be important to discuss the lowest scores (for individual questions) with the Academic Committee and individual teachers, and formulate corrective actions. However, it should be noted that some courses will change instructors in the 2022/23 academic year.
4) SUMMARY OF TEACHING The same considerations as in the previous point apply.
5) SUMMARY OF STUDENTS' RESPONSES TO THE PRE-EXAM QUESTIONNAIRE The data from attending students is difficult to interpret and, in particular, contradicts the information provided in the previous sections.
For non-attending students, a high number (108) of students do not attend due to work reasons, although a low number (16) suggest evening courses should be introduced. The high number of students not attending to follow other courses likely reflects that many are second-year students attending first-year courses. The teaching structures are not the cause of non-attendance. Additionally, a significant number (62) of students suggest reducing the workload. 50 students suggest introducing mid-term exams.
6) DISCUSSION OF STUDENT OPINIONS RESULTS IN THE COURSE COUNCIL The results of the student opinions, given the complete availability of data from both semesters starting in August 2022, were discussed in detail at the meeting on 13/09/2022.
7) CRITICITIES IDENTIFIED IN STUDENT OPINIONS: ANALYSIS AND SOLUTIONS No particular structural criticisms are identified. It will be important to thoroughly analyze the results of individual courses at the Academic Committee meeting scheduled for October 2022, keeping in mind that some course instructors will change in the 2022/23 academic year. The issue of the teaching workload will also be discussed collegially.

GRADUATE OPINIONS NO GRADUATES YET
Ability to Apply Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The biomedical engineering graduate must be able to:
- Deepen knowledge and understanding of essential mathematical, statistical, and physical and chemical phenomena, with particular attention to engineering applications in the dental sector, especially for designers and manufacturers of custom medical devices;
- Apply biomechanics knowledge for the development of medical devices for diagnosis and motor rehabilitation;
- Apply basic knowledge of electronics, computer science, digital design, mechanics, chemistry, and physics for the manufacturing of custom medical devices;
- Apply knowledge of the operating principles of high-technology instrumentation for the manufacturing of medical devices;
In summary, at the end of the studies, the student must possess critical thinking, problem analysis skills, and be able to identify relationships between acquired disciplines and recognize their interconnections.
Teaching tools: classroom activities, practical lessons in laboratories and/or equipped classrooms, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.
Assessment of these knowledge and understanding abilities will be conducted through the following verification methods: theoretical/practical exams, oral and written project presentations, computer-simulated practical tests, journal club.
Learning Skills (learning skills)
The biomedical engineering graduate is able to follow the evolution of knowledge on tools and methods aimed at analyzing, quantifying, controlling, and optimizing the impact of technologies in the dental field, as well as to conduct in-depth studies through autonomous research. They are also qualified to undertake, with a high degree of autonomy, advanced studies.
All learning skills development is supported by all training activities of the study course: individual study, preparation of individual and group projects, bibliographic research, activities carried out during exercises and laboratories, learning activities through discussion with academic and industry tutors, during the internship, and in preparation for the final exam.
Learning skills are assessed through verification methods throughout the entire training process.
Knowledge and Understanding (knowledge and understanding)
At the end of the three-year study program, the biomedical engineering graduate will have general knowledge of mathematical analysis, geometry, physics, chemistry, computer science, biomechanics, biology, anatomy, and physiology, and the engineering foundations in the scientific disciplines of Industrial Engineering necessary to develop the ability to understand the technical and functional specifics of systems and methods used for prevention, safety, diagnosis, therapy, and rehabilitation in the biomedical and dental fields.
During the training process, students acquire adequate knowledge and understanding, in written and oral form, of at least one language besides Italian. The aforementioned knowledge and understanding abilities are acquired by students through attending theoretical and practical courses, studying the course materials indicated or provided by instructors, and through discussion and dialogue with instructors.
Assessment of these knowledge and understanding abilities will be conducted through the following verification methods: oral and written exams, simulated practical tests, laboratory practical tests, written reports, Journal club.
Teaching tools: classroom activities, practical lessons in laboratories and/or equipped classrooms, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.

Summary Description of Related and Integrated Activities
Related and integrated activities cover central medical subjects such as physiology, human anatomy, histology, and dental diseases. The purpose of these activities is to provide basic medical knowledge for biomedical engineering students. Complementing the training activities is a computational mechanics course that involves the application of numerical modeling to the study of various parts of the human body.
Cross-disciplinary interest also includes basic knowledge from the computer science course and the English language course.
Course Summary
Biomedical engineering uses engineering methods and technologies to understand issues related to life sciences and assist in the design and development of devices and instruments for diagnosis and therapy.
The biomedical engineering bachelor's degree provides solid training in basic competencies (mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science, statistics), medical-biological competencies (histology, anatomy, physiology), and other engineering competencies (biomechanics, biophysics, biomaterials, imaging, programming, and technological-scientific methodologies).
Graduates of the class will possess advanced professional knowledge to perform the role of custom medical device designers, contributing to research and development activities for their realization. The main occupational opportunities provided by the class's bachelor's degree, beyond that of custom medical device designers and manufacturers, include: biomedical and pharmaceutical industries producing and supplying biomaterials; diagnostic, treatment, and rehabilitation equipment; public and private hospital companies; service companies for managing medical and dental digital systems for telemedicine; research laboratories specialized in biomaterials.
Research fields on medical and dental biomaterials include physical, chemical, and biological aspects, structure-property relationships, synthesis and characterization of the materials themselves, as well as biomimetic aspects and aesthetics. Research techniques used for the study and production of medical devices include analytical and descriptive spectrometry, electronic and analytical microscopy, laser scanning optical microscopy, cell culture, proteomics and transcriptomics, human visual evaluation, mechanical tests, rheology, thermal analysis (including calorimetry and thermomechanical analysis), and X-ray diffraction.
The bachelor's degree offers two curricula: General and MedTech. The General curriculum aims to train biomedical engineers with a solid and broad foundational and methodological preparation, both for access to master's degree courses and for the job market. The MedTech curriculum aims to train biomedical engineers especially skilled in biomaterials, prostheses, and instrumentation for medical and dental sciences.
External Effectiveness Data not yet available as there are no graduates yet.
Specific Course Learning Objectives and Course Path Description
The biomedical engineering graduate will develop the ability to analytically describe, simulate, and analyze the time behavior of materials and biomaterials adopted in the manufacturing of custom medical devices; they will also develop the ability to adopt and apply typical biomedical engineering analysis, investigation, and design methods, aimed at designing algorithms and systems for diagnosis and therapy.
They must:
- Possess basic knowledge of materials, biomaterials, and dental materials used in device manufacturing;
- Develop consolidated technical knowledge of instrumentation for diagnosis, therapy, and rehabilitation;
- Be aware of the organization of healthcare structures and the issues related to the management and use of digital systems.
The biomedical engineering graduate will not be able to interact directly with patients, but only with specialist medical personnel (doctors and dentists or other healthcare figures) in order to arrive at correct design and development of medical devices.
The achievement of these objectives is expressed through four learning areas:
1) Basic training (Mathematics, Chemistry, Applied Physics, Probability and Statistics)
2) Basic interdisciplinary training (biomechanics, computer science, and medical/biological aspects)
3) Basic training in Industrial Engineering
4) Training in Biomedical Engineering, differently distributed across two curricula:
- General
- MedTech
The General curriculum aims to train biomedical engineers with a solid and broad foundational and methodological preparation, both for access to master's degree courses and for the job market.
The MedTech curriculum aims to train biomedical engineers especially skilled in biomaterials, prostheses, and instrumentation for medical and dental sciences.
The acquisition of these knowledge will be verified, at the instructor's discretion, through written and/or oral exams or the integration of practical exams. Learning assessments aim to verify the actual understanding of subjects and the ability to solve specific problems.
Knowledge and skills are acquired and verified in the following training activities:
1) Basic Training MATHEMATICAL ANALYSIS (18 CFU for both curricula)
GEOMETRY (6 CFU)
CHEMISTRY (12 CFU)
COMPUTER SCIENCE (6 CFU)
PHYSICS (18 CFU for both curricula)
PROBABILITY AND MATHEMATICAL STATISTICS (6 CFU for General curriculum; 3 CFU for MedTech curriculum)
2) Basic Interdisciplinary Training HISTOLOGY (6 CFU for both curricula)
ANATOMY (6 CFU for both curricula)
PHYSIOLOGY (6 CFU for both curricula)
SOLID MECHANICS (9 CFU for both curricula)
3) Basic Industrial Engineering TECHNOLOGIES AND WORKING SYSTEMS (9 CFU for both curricula)
COMPUTATIONAL BIOMECHANICS (6 CFU for both curricula)
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY OF MATERIALS (6 CFU for General curriculum)
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY OF BIOMATERIALS (6 CFU for both curricula)
INDUSTRIAL DESIGN (3 CFU for both curricula)
4) Biomedical Engineering TRAINING BIOENGINEERING ELECTRONICS AND COMPUTER SCIENCE (12 CFU)
BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING INDUSTRIAL (12 CFU)
5) Specialized Training in Applied Biomedical Engineering for Dentistry DENTAL MATERIALS (6 CFU for MedTech curriculum)
PROSTHETIC TECHNOLOGIES (6 CFU for MedTech curriculum)
In addition to the courses listed above, biomedical engineering students must take two elective exams (12 CFU). It is also planned to deepen knowledge of ENGLISH LANGUAGE (6 CFU) and to complete the TRAINING INTERNSHIP (6 CFU) at public or private biomedical companies.

Summary of Regional Coordination Committee Opinion
On January 16, 2020 at 11:30 AM, the Regional Coordination Committee of Abruzzo Universities met virtually to discuss and deliberate the following agenda:
1. Communications
2. Approval of previous meeting minutes
3. Proposal to activate new study courses:
The meeting was chaired by the Rector of 'G. d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara, Prof. Sergio Caputi.
Present were:
a) The Rector of 'G. d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara, Prof. Sergio Caputi;
b) Rector of the University of L'Aquila, Prof. Edoardo Alesse;
c) Rector of the University of Teramo, Prof. Dino Mastrocola;
d) Rector of the Gran Sasso Science Institute, Prof. Eugenio Coccia;
e) The delegate of the President of the Abruzzo Region, Marco Marsilio, Dr. Claudio Di Giampietro;
f) Mr. Giuseppe Argentino, student of the University of Chieti-Pescara;
g) Ms. Sofia Cappannari, student of the University of L'Aquila.
Absent:
- Mr. Gianmarco Piovan, student of the University of Teramo
At 12:00 PM, Prof. Sergio Caputi declared the meeting open.
Attendees agreed to provide a brief description of the proposals before proceeding to discuss the agenda items.
The Bachelor's Degree in Dental Technology (class Ing-Ind L09) becomes fundamental in the new dental practice scenario, which involves the use of digital systems (scanners, mills, 3D printers, etc.), considering that quality and customization of products are increasingly important, and current research on biomaterials encompasses physical, chemical, and biological aspects of ceramic, metallic, polymeric, and composite materials. Recent studies have evaluated the reinforcement mechanisms of dental ceramics and the development of new ceramic materials, metallurgy and structure-property relationships for alloys, synthesis and characterization of polymeric materials, aesthetics of dental prosthetic materials, and formulation of dental composite materials based on optimal clinical performance and interactions of fibroblasts and epithelial cells with dental materials. Research techniques have included analytical and descriptive spectrometry, analytical electron microscopy, cell cultures, human visual evaluation, mechanical tests, rheology, thermal analysis (including calorimetry and thermomechanical analysis), and X-ray diffraction.
It should be noted that in the European community (Greece), the Dental Bioengineering course already exists, and similar courses are active in the USA. Graduates of the class will possess advanced professional knowledge to perform the role of custom medical device designers, contributing to research, development, and realization of new medical devices and materials. The main occupational opportunities provided by the class's course, beyond that of custom medical device designers and manufacturers, include: biomedical and pharmaceutical industries producing and supplying dental materials and biomaterials, equipment for diagnosis, treatment, and oral rehabilitation; service companies for managing dental digital systems such as CAD/CAM for telemedicine; research laboratories specialized in dental materials.
The proposal to activate the CDS in DENTAL TECHNOLOGY (L9) was put to a vote.

Course Final Exam Characteristics
The student has access to 3 credits dedicated to preparing the Thesis at university facilities. This student activity is defined as 'Thesis Internship'.
The student who wishes to complete the Thesis Internship in a specific discipline must submit a formal request to the instructor, accompanied by their curriculum (list of exams taken and grades achieved, list of optional activities followed, internships in laboratories or clinics, or any other activity completed for training purposes).
The instructor, upon verifying availability, accepts the request and assigns, if necessary, a Supervisor to oversee and certify the activities carried out by the student in the facility.
Final Exam Execution
The student's work is evaluated by the Graduation Committee. The Graduation Committee consists of the advisors and other instructors of the Course up to the minimum number of members specified in the University's Academic Regulations.
Before the graduation session, a Restricted Committee composed of at least three Course instructors (including the thesis supervisor) meets with the candidate to present the work. The Restricted Committee proposes to the Graduation Committee the score for the thesis alone. The appointment of the Restricted Committee is handled by a delegate of the Course Director.
The maximum score for the final exam is 9 points out of 110. The following guidelines apply to the allocation of these 9 points:
- Up to a maximum of 5 points for an experimental thesis written work, up to a maximum of 3 points for a compilation thesis written work;
- Up to a maximum of 3 points for the curriculum, with a maximum of 1 point for punctuality in the study path and a maximum of 2 points for the average of exam scores 'M' (on a 110-point scale), allocated as follows: 1 point if the student is in the current year or first year outside the curriculum (regardless of the average), and 0 points otherwise; 0 points if M ≤ 90; 1 point if 90 < M ≤ 100; 2 points if M > 100.
- 1 point for the internationalization of the training path with Erasmus courses.
In awarding the 5-point score for thesis quality, the Committee must consider the thesis nature, assigning greater value to theses promoting innovative and original insights in the discipline.
The Committee, unanimously, is free to award the full 9 points even outside the specified allocations.
Summa cum laude may be awarded, by unanimous decision of the Committee, in cases where the total score, sum of the average exam scores and the final exam score, is at least 110/110.
The final thesis may be written in English.

Teaching method Conventional Admission requirements verification Yes Course instructors View list Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission Candidates admitted to the Nursing Studies Course must hold a secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent.
Essential prerequisites and motivational requirements for students wishing to enroll in the Nursing Studies Course must include good interpersonal skills, flexibility, and ability to analyze and solve problems.
Admission to the Nursing Studies Course requires adequate preparation in logic, general culture, and the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics.
Admission to the Studies Course is limited by law 264/99 and involves a national admission exam prepared by MIUR consisting of a multiple-choice test.
Admission method Admission to the Studies Course (CdS) is limited by law 264/99 and involves a national admission exam prepared by MIUR consisting of a multiple-choice test. The competition notice indicates the accredited training poles in Chieti, Pescara, and Vasto for teaching and clinical internship activities. Successful candidates must indicate their preferred training poles in order of preference at enrollment. Assignment to preferred training poles is based on the highest score in the merit ranking. The Ministry of Education, University and Research (Article 6 of D.M. 270/2004) requires all universities to verify the initial preparation of new students to allow freshmen to assess their preparation against the basic knowledge required for university study, and to arrange for any educational deficits to be remedied in the first year of the course. On the online site of the CdS, students view the additional educational obligations verified by the teaching committee based on scores obtained in the merit ranking. Students must fulfill the educational obligation through the following recovery activities: mandatory attendance of 8 hours of physics, 8 hours of biology, and 8 hours of chemistry within the first year of the course. At the end of the recovery procedures, students will undergo a verification test consisting of multiple-choice questions to assess the required competency levels.
Additional educational obligations must be fulfilled by the date set by the University bodies (October 31) and no later than the first year of the course. Information on recovery is available on the online site of the CdS (Link to CdS website). Students with additional educational obligations cannot enroll in second-year course exams until the obligations are met. If the deficit is not fulfilled within the first year, the recovery will be repeated in the following academic year, only once.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
Nursing graduates must develop the following communication skills:
- Use appropriate communication skills with users of all ages and their families within the care process and/or with other healthcare professionals in appropriate verbal, non-verbal and written form:
- Use principles of teaching and learning for specific information or educational interventions directed at individual users, families and groups with the aim of promoting healthy behaviors, reducing risk factors, promoting self-care abilities, particularly for people with chronic diseases:
- Support and encourage users towards health choices, reinforcing coping skills, self-esteem and enhancing available resources;
- Demonstrate effective communication skills with users and in relationships with other professionals;
- Communicate effectively using verbal, non-verbal and written methods the nursing assessments and decisions in interdisciplinary healthcare teams;
- Establish professional relationships and collaborate with other healthcare professionals, being aware of the specificities of different professional roles and their integration with nursing care;
- Assume leadership roles towards support staff and/or students, including delegation and supervision of care activities provided by others, ensuring compliance with quality and safety standards for planning and management of care;
- Facilitate coordination of care to achieve agreed health outcomes;
- Collaborate with the care team to agree on operational methods and implement and develop protocols and guidelines.
Teaching methods and activities, didactic tools to develop expected outcomes:
- Lectures;
- Videos and critical analysis of films, simulations, narratives, testimonies;
- Discussion of cases and paradigmatic relational situations in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions;
- Internship with supervised experiences by tutors in different settings with debriefing sessions to reflect and reprocess relational experiences with users and the team.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- Observation of film or written frames, dialogues with structured grids;
- Evaluation feedback during internship (through portfolio, structured evaluation sheets and clinical reports);
- Structured objective exam with stations featuring simulations on relational competencies.

CURRICULUM:
SECTION: Judgment Autonomy
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/613

Judgment Autonomy (making judgments)
Nursing graduates must demonstrate judgment autonomy through the following competencies:
- Provide nursing care by recognizing and respecting the dignity, culture, values, and rights of individuals and groups;
- Adapt nursing care by identifying similarities and differences among individuals, considering their values, ethnicities, and socio-cultural practices, as well as those of their families;
- Integrate knowledge of cultural diversity, legal aspects, and ethical principles in delivering and managing nursing care across various contexts and healthcare services;
- Analyze directives and operational practices of healthcare services and identify appropriate nursing actions considering legal, political, geographical, economic, ethical, and social influences;
- Utilize critical thinking skills to deliver effective nursing care to users across different age groups;
- Assume responsibility and accountability for professional practice in accordance with the professional profile, code of ethics, and ethical and legal standards;
- Recognize differences in roles and responsibilities between qualified nurses, support staff, and other healthcare professionals.
Teaching methods and activities, didactic tools to develop expected outcomes:
- Lectures;
- Guided reading and application exercises;
- Videos, image demonstrations, diagrams, materials, and charts;
- Case discussions in subgroups with presentations in plenary sessions;
- Internship with supervised experiences in diverse settings and progressive assumption of autonomy and responsibility;
- Debriefing sessions to reflect on and reprocess professional practice experiences.
Assessment tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- Written and oral exams, staged case tests;
- Assessment feedback during internship (through portfolios, structured evaluation forms, and clinical reports on professional practice);
- Structured objective station exam.

Orientation and ongoing tutoring B5-ORIENTAMENTO IN ITINERE APRILE 2024
The Study Course (CdS), through a Course of Perfection (CP) established ad hoc, has trained and continues to train nursing tutors with pedagogical skills. The tutor's role is to accompany the student throughout the training path and guide them in the best acquisition of professional competencies in various nursing areas. The characteristic training activity takes place under agreements activated with Entities and Structures of the National Health Service (SSN) and private entities in the local and national territory. This is also to offer preferential pathways in professional choices applicable in the workplace. Furthermore, ongoing orientation is expressed through multiple delivery methods: all teachers fulfill this role during their office hours, while, as previously mentioned, specific reference figures (nursing tutors) have been trained to whom students can turn in case of need. The names of the nursing tutors are listed in the Administration section, 'Information'.
The nursing tutors, in turn, then report the emerging issues to the Academic Directors who are the reference figures for the characteristic activities: Dr. Daniela Daniele (Chieti teaching pole), Dr. Paola Mosca (Pescara teaching pole), Dr. Luciana Potalivo (Vasto teaching pole).
The CdS in Nursing has promoted the activation of a CP in Clinical Tutoring for all graduates in Health Professions. Indeed, in February 2019, with Decree R. 183/2019, the admission notice for the CP in 'Clinical Tutor for Health Professions' A.Y. 2018/2019 was published. The Course aims to train professionals capable of accompanying and guiding students in the undergraduate courses of health professions. The objective of the Course of Perfection is to: develop the pedagogical approach and learn tutorial methods applicable during the internship.
The Course responds to the Dublin Descriptors' indications, fostering the connection between the University and Health Companies. The trained professional figures can find opportunities in Training and Updating Units, corporate training paths, assistance Units, and within the Health Professions Degree Courses.
The CdS, through the Academic Director of the Chieti teaching pole, Dr. Daniela Daniele, and the nursing tutor, Dr. Antonio Di Paolo, has published the CP via posters on the official website of:
- ASL LANCIANO-VASTO-CHIETI,
- AUSL PESCARA
- OPI PESCARA
- OPI CHIETI 52 applications were received, 22 exceeding the maximum allowed number, demonstrating the CP's attractiveness.
DESCRIPTION OF THE TUTORING SYSTEM The clinical contexts require the student, at the end of the three-year degree course, to have competencies to effectively manage complex care. Therefore, in the training context, the possibility of experimenting with managing dynamic and unpredictable situations must be guaranteed. The tutoring system is aimed at guiding and supporting the student throughout the training path, based on a fundamental principle:
IF THE STUDENT HEARS, HE FORGETS; IF HE SEES, HE REMEMBERS; IF HE DOES, HE UNDERSTANDS.
Simulation is a strategy that allows reproducing real and complex situations, requiring the student to immerse themselves acting 'as themselves' in risk-free situations for patient and operator. Mechanical manikins are used for training exercises to develop skills. In response to simulation, the student demonstrates:
- Applying systematic evaluation learned in lectures
- Acting with critical thinking and decision-making skills
- Implementing technical-management interventions
- Coordinating with other operators
- Managing emotions arising from the situation.
In 3-hour laboratories, a group of 10 students simulates a clinical situation; the scenario reproduces a ward room where the manikin is the patient, two students are nurses, and the laboratory tutor, who adds realistic aspects to the simulation through assistance requests; the remaining students act as observers. In relation to parameter modifications or descriptions, students are called to collect data, assign meaning, and interact in a coordinated manner for the choice and implementation of interventions. At the end of the simulation, the tutor guides reflection on the concluded experience. The laboratory demonstrates a multidimensional learning opportunity because it offers students the possibility to experiment with technical/operational learning while simultaneously developing it in the dimension of clinical evolution (simulated by the manikin) and management/emotional simulation by the tutor/actor. The combination of elements (manikin, tutor, and students) is the most appreciated aspect by students as the simultaneous experience of technical/management activities, management/organizational activities, combined with the tutor's ability to make students feel fully involved, places the student in a situation of realism, challenge to their abilities and knowledge, to verify how tensions and emotions present in certain situations can affect the outcome of care gestures and decisions.
CLINICAL INTERNSHIP The student's tutoring activity is a continuous process involving the definition of internship sites and concludes when the student achieves the predefined objectives. Assigning the student to the internship site is the responsibility of the Academic Director of the CdS in collaboration with the Tutors and is communicated to the interested parties via email within one week before the start of each clinical internship period. The clinical internship programming and assignments are formulated based on the progression of theoretical content, the training objectives set by the academic curriculum, and differentiated by year of study.
In the first year of study, the student completes the internship only in certain Operative Units (Medicine, Surgery, Residential Care Structures, Territorial Services) where, respecting the theoretical concepts learned in lectures and with specific learning objectives, they can acquire the indispensable technical and relational competencies in nursing. Additionally, through this path, they can begin to orient themselves within the complex context of healthcare organization.
First-year students - First placement The placement in the internship is conditional upon participation in activities considered preparatory: laboratories and exercises, as well as training interventions related to risk prevention and safety in internship locations.
A few days before the start of the clinical internship, a meeting is held with students, during which some documents accompanying the student during the internship are presented. In particular, the following are presented and discussed:
- Behavioral norms to adopt during the clinical internship, even in case of injury
- The logbook for certification of internship attendance.
Subsequently, a further meeting is organized per Hospital Pole, in coordination between the CdS Presidency and the Sanitary and Nursing Directorate, where, in the presence of students, tutors, and coordinators, additional information on the methods of execution, organization of the clinical internship, the hospital organizational chart, and its representatives are provided.
Second and third-year students From the second year of study, students, benefiting from a broader knowledge base and experience, are progressively assigned to other Operative Units: Cardiology, Dialysis, Day Hospital, Operating Room, Oncological Day Hospital, Digestive Endoscopy, and Materno-Infant Area. In response to specific situations or learning needs identified during formative evaluations, the Academic Director may consider personalizing clinical internship paths to facilitate achieving the set objectives and performance levels.
The academic curriculum provides for theoretical training in Critical Area and Psychiatric Area in the third year, after which students are assigned to DSM Services and the Intensive Care, Critical Care, Emergency Department, and 118 Services.
Before the end of the training path and during the second or third year, each student is guaranteed the opportunity to repeat the internship in the basic Operative Units attended in the first year (Medicine and/or Surgery). The second placement in these units allows the student, based on greater experience and acquired knowledge, to practice planning care for medical or surgical clinical cases and collaborate in performing complex techniques.
At the end of each internship period, students are invited to attend a meeting with the reference tutor for an open discussion on the experience, any problems encountered, clarifications, and/or proposals to be made.
If the performed path and achieved learning are unsatisfactory, the student is offered to integrate the deficient phases and repeat the field experience.
INJURY DURING INTERNSHIP The student is insured by the 'G. d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara for injuries.
The insurance policy covers students during their stay at internship sites for the period scheduled by the CdS.
In case of injury due to traumatic causes or infectious risk, the student must follow the procedure of the Hospital Enterprise where the internship is conducted.
In any case, the student must go to the Emergency Department of the internship site, after notifying the Nursing Coordinator of the assigned Unit and the reference tutor; the Emergency Department prepares a three-copy report, one copy of which is delivered by the hospital to INAIL, and the remaining two are delivered to the student.
The Academic Director certifies the sequence of events and delivers the report and the certification of the sequence of events to the student.
The student keeps a copy for themselves, delivers one copy to their Laboratory tutor who keeps it in the student's personal file, and finally, it is the student's responsibility to deliver all original documentation to the Competent University Offices. The CdS, to verify the level of satisfaction of tutoring and internship activities, has prepared a customer satisfaction questionnaire for several years, which is completed by graduates before the practical licensing exam. The responses to the questionnaire questions have been analyzed and presented in graphical form (SEE ATTACHED LEVEL OF SATISFACTION OF GRADUATES).
On May 15, 2020, after multiple Skype meetings with the Academic Directors of the three Poles and Dr. Iannone, aimed at evaluating suitable methods for conducting professional laboratory and internship activities during the COVID-19 health emergency, the CdS President published the following document:
NURSING STUDY COURSE: INSTRUCTIONS FOR RESUMING PROFESSIONAL INTERNSHIP AND LABORATORY TRAINING ACTIVITIES Given the health emergency related to Covid-19, to resume the professional internship and laboratory activities as soon as possible, it is necessary to reprogram them to ensure the continuation of the training path for all students.
In particular, in line with the recommendations of the Ministry of University and Research Decrees n.12 of April 9, 2020 and n.58 of April 29, 2020 and the Guidelines of the Permanent Conference of Health Professions Degree Classes, and respecting the University's regulations, a temporary 'alternative' method of conducting the internship and laboratory has been organized. Specifically:
- FIRST YEAR: While frequencies to ADO (which were to be carried out in the second semester) have already been recognized, from next June until the in-person path can resume, sessions on the TEAMS platform will be organized for some of these activities, participation in which will be considered 'distance internship': 8 hours of internship will be counted for each activity carried out.
Additionally, sessions on the TEAMS platform will be held, considered as internship hours, with synchronous and interactive methods, where designated tutors will ensure the achievement of training objectives, using the following tools:
- briefing, debriefing;
- discussion of clinical cases and ethical issues;
- resolution of exercises/problems with guidance/supervision.
For these activities, if the discussion of assigned clinical cases, in the presence of the tutor and Academic Director, receives a positive evaluation, 20 hours of internship will be recognized.
Finally, the laboratory will continue and be completed, with attendance recognized only for 100% participation. The scheduled calendar will be modified.
- SECOND YEAR: While frequencies to ADO and seminars (which were to be carried out in the second semester) have already been recognized, from next June until the in-person path can resume, sessions on the TEAMS platform will be organized for some of these activities, participation in which will be considered 'distance internship': 6 hours for ADO and 8 hours for seminars will be attributed.
The meetings dedicated to the internship will be held via dedicated TEAMS sessions, with the following methods adopted:
- briefing and debriefing sessions
- development of clinical cases, which, once elaborated by the student, will be discussed on the platform in the presence of the tutor and Academic Director.
A positive evaluation of such a clinical case by the tutor and Academic Director will result in the attribution of 40 hours of internship.
Finally, the laboratory will continue and be completed, with attendance recognized only for 100% participation. The scheduled calendar will be modified.
- THIRD YEAR: While frequencies to seminars (which were to be carried out in the second semester) have already been recognized, from next June until the in-person path can resume, sessions on the TEAMS platform will be organized for some of these activities, participation in which will be considered 'distance internship': 8 hours of internship will be attributed.
For the internship, sessions on the TEAMS platform will be planned, including:
- discussion of clinical cases
- briefing, debriefing sessions
- critical analysis of scientific literature
- discussion of ethical issues For internships initiated via telecommunication, 40 hours of internship will be attributed only if the evaluation by the tutor and Academic Director is positive.
Finally, the laboratory will continue and be completed, with attendance recognized only for 100% participation. The scheduled calendar will be modified.
- OUT OF COURSE: Students are required to participate in the activities as scheduled above to reduce the training debt.
The planned activities will be scheduled and communicated shortly by the Academic Directors of the three Teaching Poles to the respective student representatives, clarifying doubts and providing further explanations.
For participation in FAD Courses organized by ISS and made available to students, 20 hours of internship are recognized (recognition is conditional on presenting the participation certificate).
For any voluntary activities carried out in support of healthcare structures (Ministry of University and Research Decree n.12 of April 9, 2020), 4 hours are recognized per day of presence.
Finally, all students are reminded that to enroll in the internship exam, in addition to completing all hours, verification and declaration by the tutor and subsequent declaration by the Academic Director are indispensable.
The student's inability, for any reason, to submit the internship logbook to the tutor will prevent them from taking the exam.
If a student loses their internship logbook, it is essential to report the loss to the competent authorities, immediately informing the tutor and Academic Director.

Suriano Mina GRANTS FOR TUTORING ACTIVITIES The analysis of indicator iC01 of the SMA (Annual Monitoring Sheet) indicates that the percentage of students who have acquired 40CFU has progressively increased from 2018 to 2021. These data, however, must be monitored in subsequent analyses. Additionally, it is noted that the percentage of students who have acquired at least 40CFU is higher than the geographical area values and the non-telecommunication university average. In this sense, the training activity directed at teaching staff on learning processes and the innovation of teaching methodologies, which the CdS has planned and implemented through two seminars/webinars by Prof. Nardi on September 29 and October 22, 2021, followed by six didactic laboratories (three dedicated to MODULE 1 'CONDUCTING A LESSON' in May 2022 and three to MODULE 2 'EVALUATING AND VALUING LEARNING' in June and July 2022), appears very appropriate.
The CdS constantly promotes orientation and tutoring actions aimed at increasing dialogue with students to achieve greater regularity and performance. In this regard, the President requested grants for peer tutoring activities to the main Department (DMSI). Peer tutoring activities refer to activities aimed at guiding and assisting students throughout their studies, as provided for in Article 13 of Law 341/1990; the public selection is open to capable and deserving students of the University of Chieti-Pescara 'G. d'Annunzio', regularly enrolled in the first and second year of the Master's Degree Course in Nursing and Midwifery of the University of Chieti-Pescara 'G. d'Annunzio' for carrying out activities for students enrolled in the Nursing Degree Course. Eight students from the Master's Degree Course in Nursing and Midwifery responded to the notice. The committee responsible for evaluating requirements and qualifications sent the merit ranking to DMSI. Tutors will be assigned students who have difficulties in their study path.
The CdS relies, on the indications of the University Quality Assurance Office, in collaboration with the Information Systems Unit U-Gov Teaching and Research, on the dynamic dashboard called UdA in Numeri accessible at https://ingrid.unich.it to monitor student careers and evaluate the percentage of students with struggling careers.

Training periods B5-ASSISTANCE FOR THE EXECUTION OF EXTERNAL TRAINING PERIODS (INTERNSHIPS AND TRAINING) ACADEMIC YEAR 2023-2024
The execution of external training periods (internships and traineeships) concerns both ongoing training and the preparation of the thesis/final exam when it is experimental, at Conventional Structures (AASSLL, DSB, Hospice, INAIL, Penitentiary Institutes, CIM, SERT, etc.). Assistance is delegated to Tutors, thesis supervisors, and the Course Director with the support of the three Academic Directors of the Pole, who manage institutional relations with conventional and hosting entities.
In addition to ASL 02 Lanciano-Vasto-Chieti and AUSL of Pescara, the healthcare structures where professional internships are carried out are:
- 'Villa Pini D'Abruzzo' Nursing Home Chieti, contact Dr. Annamaria Di Giandomenico
- 'Villa Serena' Nursing Home Città Sant'Angelo, contact Dr. Donatella Candeloro
- 'G. Spatocco' Nursing Home Chieti, contact Dr. Luigi Zappacosta
- 'Pierangeli' Nursing Home Pescara, contact Dr. Luigi Zappacosta
- Assisted Living Residences: United Institutes of Assistance 'S. Giovanni Battista' Chieti, contact Dr. Martina Marini
- Elderly Care Home: 'Compassionist Sisters of Maria' Chieti Scalo, contact Sister Maddalena, Superior, Sister Valentina, and Nurse Daniele Gasbarri
- Rehabilitation Center for Neurological and Motor Disabilities Foundation Institute 'Santa Caterina' Francavilla al Mare, contact Dr. Simonetta Di Nardo The structures must:
- address situations or processes related to the competencies specified in the internship project according to the academic year
- provide internship contacts and guides
- collaborate with the Academic Director in monitoring learning.
In the structures listed above, during the Academic Year 2018/2019, approximately 50 students completed their internship.
In the link http://www.med.unich.it/corsi-di-laurea/infermieristica/sezione-qualita the results of student evaluations of internship sites are reported.
During the Academic Year 2017/2018, the Italian Military Health Service INTERFORZE (A.N.S.M.I.) conducted ADO activities for third-year students, coordinated with Dr. Corrado Picone, Vice-President of the National Commission for Major Risks and Maxiemergencies and Responsible Commissioner for the Interregional Grouping Abruzzo-Marche-Molise:
- 16.03.2018 'Military forces in rescue operations. Prevention and safety in hostile environments: activities of the State Police'.
- 23.03.2018: 'Pediatric/neonatal emergencies outside hospitals. Organization of medical assistance in maxiemergencies'.
- 20.04.2018: 'Communication in emergencies: Aeronautics Military in 'First Line'. Major events: State Police intervention'.
- 04.05.2018: 'Nuclear-biological-chemical-radiological risk. Carabinieri weapon and snow emergency 2017'.
- 18.05.2018: 'Aeronautics Military in managing a maxiemergency. Carabinieri in natural disasters'.
These activities stimulated some students who chose to complete a traineeship period for their final thesis within the Military Health Service.
A thesis titled 'THE COMPETENCIES OF THE MILITARY NURSE' was defended in the April 2019 session by student Miriana Forlano with Dr. Carlo Della Pelle as supervisor and Dr. Corrado Picone as co-supervisor. Notable was the interest shown by some second and third-year students who attended the HATRANUS II conference, Prevention and Safety: Territorial and Health Emergency, held at the Rectorate Auditorium of 'G. d'Annunzio' University, Chieti Campus on May 29, 2019, organized by the Master's Course Director in Medicine and Surgery, Prof. Muraro, with the collaboration of Dr. Picone. Some students of the Nursing Course wished to speak personally with some speakers and establish contacts for potential employment opportunities in the Military Health Service. Attached is the PDF file of the program and photos taken during the conference.
