At the CCdS meeting on May 11, 2020, the President communicated that on February 26, 2020, the School of Medicine and Health Sciences signed a convention with Medicasa Italia, founded in Milan in 1993, specialized in designing and providing Home Care services on behalf of ASL, operating throughout Italy to offer a wide range of services at home. With over 20 years of experience, Medicasa provides competent and qualified personnel to assist patients in their homes. Nursing Course students can: complete internships to acquire knowledge about the professional role in the territory and the techniques and services performed at home; learn the main characteristics of the home care plan; observe and practice the relational aspects peculiar to a successful helping relationship between professional and patient/caregiver.
The President and Academic Directors visited the Pescara office at Via Alcide De Gasperi on January 10, 2020, and highly appreciated the organization of activities carried out by the Cooperative.
Due to the lockdown, activities could not begin in 2020. However, on March 23, 2021, the President confirmed to the Medicasa contact, Dr. Giuseppe Di Maggio, the availability of Academic Directors of the Chieti and Pescara poles to send students for ADI (Integrated Home Care) activities.
ACADEMIC YEAR 2021-2022
The President of the Course received a convention request from Avv. Antonietta Cataldo, Administrative Director of the Social Cooperative Residenza Protetta Fraternitas of Castel Frentano. Academic Directors expressed a favorable opinion, and on April 14, 2022, the signed documentation was received from Avv. Cataldo. The President of the Course had the convention signed by the President of the School of Medicine and Health Sciences, Prof. Liborio Stuppia. Another convention will be signed with the Social Cooperative La Rondine, which provides Integrated Home Care (ADI) services including medical, nursing, rehabilitation, and specialized services at the user's home. Service objectives include: improving quality of life by keeping elderly, disabled, and patients with certain conditions at home, reducing hospitalization rates by promoting discharge (protected discharge), avoiding improper admissions, and qualifying care in the territory. La Rondine has provided services in the Lanciano Vasto territory since 2005; since August 2016, the service has been extended to the Chieti territory.
Additionally, on April 8, the President met with the responsible and a medical director of the Don Orione structure in Pescara to sign a convention enabling Nursing Course students to expand their internship activities. The structure provides services in various fields: rehabilitation, diagnosis and treatment, specialized medicine.

International mobility The University of G. d'Annunzio has obtained the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education (ECHE) 2014-2020, certified by the European Commission (EACEA (Education, Audiovisual and Culture Executive Agency)), based on the Erasmus Policy Statement, a necessary document that grants the right to participate in the new Erasmus+ Program 2014/2020. The goal of the new Program is to encourage international mobility for over four million people (double the previous amount) with European funding (2014/2020) for study and training periods abroad. The International Relations Office of the University organizes student and teacher mobility through meetings aimed at promoting participation and subsequently guiding selected students. ?The link for information on international mobility (Students - Erasmus, Overseas, Visiting students, seminars/training abroad - Traineeship, Non-teaching staff, Teachers) Erasmus+ for study purposes, Erasmus+ Traineeship, Erasmus Incoming Students, International Conventions, Opportunities) is the following:?https://www.unich.it/didattica/international/mobilita.?

outgoing.chieti@unich.it A Bilateral Agreement is a mutual commitment agreement between partner universities, providing for student mobility for specific internship programs at the Course's training poles; this clinical activity is coordinated by the Academic Director of the Pole who assigns a specific tutor to the student. ?The Nursing Course has delegated, for assistance and Erasmus agreements, as well as for managing related documentation, in collaboration with the University's URI service, Dr. Gabriella Mincione (gabriella.mincione@unich.it), who was replaced in the Academic Year 2018/2019 by Dr. Giulia Renda (giulia.renda@unich.it). Each Academic Year, the Erasmus Plus Traineeship call is published at the following link: http://unich.traineeship.it/. Within the Erasmus+ Program, the Erasmus Traineeship Program (only internship) aims to promote the activation of internships at companies or training and research centers in one of the participating European countries.?The Erasmus student has the opportunity to acquire specific skills and a better understanding of the socio-economic culture of the host country, with the support of preparatory or updating courses in the host country's language (or working language), with the ultimate goal of promoting the mobility of young workers throughout Europe. The training internship is intended for students/graduates and doctoral candidates of the University G. d'Annunzio Chieti-Pescara. Candidates must be winners of a mobility internship grant before the thesis or doctoral defense. In no case can the thesis defense take place during the internship period: mobility must be carried out entirely before or entirely after the thesis defense.? During the Academic Year 2016-2017, the Nursing Course welcomed two students from Riga Medical College of the University of Latvia under the Erasmus Plus Traineeship (only internship) program. In the same Academic Year, three students from the Nursing Course of the University G. d'Annunzio Chieti-Pescara completed a 9-month period at the Spanish university of Huelva under the Erasmus Plus study program.? During the Academic Year 2017-18, the Nursing Course, within the Erasmus+ (PLUS) study program, received two students from the Spanish university of Jaen, while one of our students went to the same university. In the same Academic Year, a student from the Nursing Course of the University G. d'Annunzio Chieti Pescara won a mobility period for studies at the University of Huelva.? During the Academic Year 2018/2019, one student won a period at the University of Jaen and one student at the University of Huelva.

Pleyade is part of the Dutch Healthcare System in the Arnhem - Nijmegen region; it has approximately 1,300 employees and includes 12 facilities between nursing homes, hospitals, and educational institutions. Pleyade actively participates in technological research applied to healthcare and nursing care, always placing human contact and patient needs at the center.

The chosen topic has the following title: The multidisciplinary role of Health Care Professionals in integrated care between hospital and territory. Planned activities are: Lectures by experts. Meetings with stakeholders and local actors. Meetings with the local community. Design and processing activities. Expected learning outcomes: At the end of the program, students are expected to: Share issues related to territorial healthcare assistance; Stimulate reflection on new models and paradigms for the concept of Community Health Houses; Develop architectural models based on adaptation to environmental aspects, reduction of anthropic impacts, reuse of existing heritage, etc. Comparison and discussion of topics through seminar activities; Lectures and dialogues with experts; Drafting of a design program starting from comparison with stakeholders and territory actors; Construction of future design scenarios at different scales; Presentation and dissemination of the project idea.

Additional initiatives Since 24 March 2020, due to the Covid-19 emergency, the online teaching method has been activated for the educational offer within the second semester 2019/2020, to which students can connect using the link https://zeus.unich.it/teledidattica. The Study Course has adopted all the indications received from the Teaching Delegate, Prof. Cuculo, since the first communication of 11 March 2020.
Following the first activation of each individual team, the schedule for distance learning corresponds to the originally planned schedule for in-person teaching.
Additionally, guidelines for conducting graduation sessions in a telework format have been adopted and implemented, which were carried out without any issues on the following dates: 15 April (morning and afternoon), 16 and 17 April morning, 20 April (morning and afternoon), 21 and 22 April morning.
Furthermore, the Study Course has sent to all Teachers of the Study Course the communication received on 1 April 2020 from Prof. Cuculo regarding the organization of written exams in collaboration with Dr. Iannone, the UGOV - Teaching representative of the Study Course, and the communication of 4 April regarding curricular internships and tutoring activities.
The President communicates that on 15 September 2020, the Academic Senate and the Board of Directors deliberated on the guidelines regarding the timing and methods for resuming teaching activities related to the so-called Phase 3 of the Covid-19 emergency. Specifically:
LECTURES
- Start of lectures For all Study Courses:
  - Semestral courses: start on Monday, 12 October 2020
  - Annual courses: start on Monday, 3 November 2020
- Method of delivery / live lectures and recordings Lectures for courses delivered to the maximum extent in university classrooms, ensuring that in-person teaching is always accessible remotely. However, on 12 November 2020, due to the increase in infection rates, all in-person lectures were suspended in compliance with Ordinance of the Regional Council President No. 92 of 26 October 2020 and the explanatory note of 30 October 2020.
Lectures were held exclusively in a remote format.
Subsequently, in compliance with the provisions of the DPCM of 14 January 2021, starting from 1 February 2021, lectures for courses were delivered to the maximum extent possible in university classrooms, but always accessible remotely.
Final graduation exams were conducted according to the method chosen by the student - either in person or online - following the application of the currently in-force protocols (PREVIOUS EMAIL TO THE STUDY COURSE SECRETARIAT AND THE SUPERVISOR PROFESSOR AT LEAST FIFTEEN DAYS IN ADVANCE).
Written profit exams were conducted online, applying the operational protocols already in use.
Oral profit exams were conducted according to the method chosen by the student - either in person or online - following the application of the operational protocols already in use (PREVIOUS ANNOTATION OF THE REQUEST ON ESSE3 AND EMAIL TO THE PROFESSOR AT LEAST FIVE DAYS IN ADVANCE).
Finally, the new provisions in compliance with the Ordinance of the President of the Abruzzo Region, No. 7 of 12.02.2021, effective from 12 February 2021 until further notice, indicate the suspension of in-person lectures, profit exams, and final theses.
Therefore, the remote delivery method will be used.
With Decree-Law 6 August 2021, No. 111, new provisions were adopted in view of the start of the 2021/2022 academic year, taking into account the new epidemiological context and the progress of the vaccination plan. Initially, Article 1, Paragraph 1, reaffirmed the principle - which all universities had already followed during the previous academic year - of prioritizing in-person teaching and curricular activities.
To this end, the President of the Nursing Study Course and the teaching representative communicated the new provisions to all teachers and students:
a) Use of respiratory protection devices, except for individuals with medical conditions or disabilities incompatible with their use, and for sports activities;
b) A minimum interpersonal safety distance of at least one meter is recommended, ensuring the widest possible in-person participation of students in teaching and curricular activities, while considering the structural and logistical conditions of the buildings;
c) Access to or remaining in university premises is prohibited for individuals with respiratory symptoms or body temperature above 37.5°C.
It is also noted that the Decree-Law introduced important changes, in particular:
- From 1 September 2021 until 31 December 2021, all university staff, both teaching and administrative, must possess and present the Green Covid-19 certificate;
- Failure to comply with these obligations results in the staff being considered unjustifiably absent, and from the fifth day of absence, depending on the characteristics and specificities of the work performance of teaching staff versus administrative staff, the employment relationship will be suspended without payment of salary or any other compensation;
- From 1 September 2021 until 31 December 2021, university students must also possess the Green Covid-19 certificate to participate in in-person teaching and curricular activities;
- The obligation to possess the Green Covid-19 certificate does not apply to teaching and administrative staff, as well as students, exempt from the vaccination campaign based on a medical certificate issued according to criteria defined in a Ministry of Health circular;
- Universities conduct checks regarding possession of the Green Covid-19 certificate according to modalities to be indicated in a subsequent DPCM and, in any case, according to organizational choices of each university, while respecting privacy regulations and handling data contained in the Green Covid-19 certificate within the scope of the law;
- Checks on university students regarding possession of the Green Covid-19 certificate are conducted on a sample basis and according to modalities determined by each university;
- These checks fall under the responsibility of the "responsible" persons of the universities, meaning, as per Article 2, Paragraph 1, Letter b) of Law No. 240 of 2010, the Rectors and their delegates as determined by each university's organization for control purposes.
On 7 January 2022, following the pandemic evolution, it was decided that exams could be taken in a mixed format.
On 22 March 2022, another provision was issued.
Spread of the Covid-19 epidemic - Extension of current measures until April In the absence of publication of the Decree of 17 March 'Urgent measures for overcoming the measures to counter the spread of the Covid-19 epidemic' and the subsequent indications from the Minister of University and Research, the measures already in place for April are confirmed, and remote teaching delivery is guaranteed without attendance obligation for all individuals falling under the specified reasons.
Additional provisions communicated on 13 April:
'Following the provisions of Decree-Law No. 24 of 24 March 2022 'Urgent measures for overcoming the measures to counter the spread of the Covid-19 epidemic, following the cessation of the emergency status' - which has discontinued the Covid-19 emergency status from 1 April 2022 and indicated a gradual return to normality - and the subsequent indications from the Minister of University and Research, the guidelines approved at the Academic Senate meeting of 16 September 2021 regarding the organization of teaching activities for the first semester of the 2021/2022 academic year are confirmed, with some modifications only regarding profit and graduation exams.'
In brief:
The delivery method for teaching activities in the second semester will remain unchanged from the first semester:
All university teaching activities, whether lectures or practical activities (internships, laboratories, seminars, exercises), are delivered in person, with rotation for larger courses, in compliance with the safety protocols adopted by the university and compatible with the availability of spaces.
Until the end of the second semester lectures, remote access will be guaranteed for students who are unable to attend university premises due to the health emergency or who cannot book a classroom seat.
Regarding exam and graduation sessions, starting from 1 May 2022:
Exam sessions are held in person, with appropriate scheduling if there is a risk of overcrowding incompatible with interpersonal distancing. However, exam sessions can still be conducted remotely for the reasons specified by the Academic Senate at the 16 September 2021 meeting, provided the student makes a documented request via email to the professor at least five days before the exam date.
Final graduation or diploma exams are primarily conducted in person, with appropriate scheduling if there is a risk of overcrowding incompatible with interpersonal distancing.
Up to five accompanying persons, equipped with FFP2 respiratory protection devices, may attend in-person graduation sessions, up to the maximum capacity of the rooms, which must always comply with interpersonal distancing requirements.
However, graduation sessions can still be conducted remotely if the student makes a justified request via email to the Study Course Academic Secretariat at least fifteen days before the start date. Remote access will also be guaranteed to allow family members who could not attend to follow the thesis discussion and the proclamation of graduates.
For more detailed information, refer to the provisions approved at the Academic Senate meeting of 16 September 2021, accessible at the page Latest provisions for conducting teaching, exams, and graduation sessions and MUR Note For information Decree-Law No. 24 of 24 March 2022

SECTION: Student opinions

Student opinions OBJECTIVES OF THE SURVEY The survey of opinions from enrolled students represents:
-the fulfillment of the legal obligation set forth by Law 370 of 1999 and amendments
-an opportunity to acquire the level of student satisfaction regarding the structural and organizational resources provided by the University, the organization of teaching activities, the methods of lesson delivery, the content of courses, as well as the competencies of instructors.
The usefulness of the survey increases with a higher rate of evaluated courses, hence the need to sensitize instructors and students about the importance of evaluation.
SURVEY TOOLS The University's unified questionnaire, used since the academic year 2013/14, is the one proposed in the AVA Document of January 28, 2013, with minor modifications, and consists of 10 questions. The scoring scale adopted for the response options is that proposed by CNVSU and also suggested by ANVUR, ranging from a minimum of 1 (corresponding to 'definitely no') to a maximum of 4 (corresponding to 'definitely yes'), with two intermediate evaluations: 2, equivalent to 'more no than yes', and 3, equivalent to 'more yes than no'. In the online survey, an additional section was added for collecting free student comments.
Details of the data are reported in the attached PDF (ANALYSIS OF STUDENT OPINION DATA, QUADRO B6 2023).
ANALYSIS OF STUDENT OPINION A.A. 2022/2023 VS A.A. 2021/2022
In A.A. 2022-2023, the average value attributed to the Course of Study increased compared to A.A. 2021-2022 (3.42 vs 3.35).
ANALYSIS CONDUCTED BY THE JOINT TEACHER-STUDENT COMMISSION Analysis and proposals on management and use of questionnaires regarding student satisfaction During the past year, it emerged from discussions with students a functional issue with the platform for collecting student opinions, which does not allow disaggregated compilation of integrated courses, i.e., the possibility to express an opinion on each individual instructor composing the integrated course, and provides different compilation options depending on whether access is via fixed computer or smartphone, from the website or through the app. Since the vast majority of students access via smartphone, a method that allows for reduced compilation, there is a concrete risk that judgments cannot be detailed optimally and that certain specific situations may be missed in the survey. These issues were brought to the attention of the PQA during the meeting held on November 11, 2022. Therefore, this report is compiled with the awareness that the results to be analyzed may be less reliable.
The number of completed evaluation forms was only slightly lower than in the 2019-2020 academic year, and significantly lower than the previous year (7,512 vs 11,011), covering however 51% of courses and 80% of instructors. The average score was 3.35, the highest of the three years considered.
Strengths: Compared to the previous two years, a significant increase in the quality of courses was noted, with 22% rated Class A (compared to 5.17% and 2% in 2019-2020 and 2018-2019, respectively), 77% Class B, and only 1 out of 118 courses Class C. No course was rated Class D.
Weaknesses: The questions with the lowest scores were D1 'Were the preliminary knowledge sufficient for understanding the topics covered in the exam program?' and D3 'Is the study load required by the course proportional to the assigned credits?', confirming the initial cultural difficulties noted in previous years and accounting for the necessary effort to address existing gaps and progress in building the cultural background required for nursing practice. In this regard, since these difficulties were also noted in previous years, several initiatives have been implemented; for details, refer to the discussion in Quadro D.
Additionally, following the changed context resulting from the pandemic event, our University has adhered to a request from the Didactic Commission of CRUI to survey Distance Learning, therefore this year, for the first time, the PQA has prepared a new Report dedicated to opinions collected on Distance Learning.
Considering the abrupt change in lifestyle and personal interaction styles, as well as teaching methods, the survey reveals an overall satisfactory management of teaching activities during the pandemic emergency, with 86% of students reporting overall satisfaction.
Indeed, despite the vast majority of lessons being held remotely (78%), and most students (69%) following lessons exclusively remotely, most instructors (57%) opted for synchronous methods to maintain virtual contact with students.
The platform provided by our University for distance learning is Teams, and 90% of lessons were held on this platform, with lessons recorded in 70% of cases. It is also encouraging that students rated instructors as comfortable with the digital tools in 89% of cases.
It is important to note that students' living and study conditions were significantly influenced by the possibility of attending remote lessons: less than half of students (47%) resided in the city of the course and could interact directly with instructors; for others, communication and exchange were primarily through Teams or email.
Despite the comforting fact that 79% of students had a private space to attend lessons and 67% had a personal computer, it stands out that 23% of students, almost a quarter, attended lessons on smartphones, and 15% were unable to satisfactorily access teaching activities due to insufficient digital tools and internet connection.
The opinions of graduates were also examined. The Graduate Opinion Survey collects the opinions of all students who submitted a graduation application in the three sessions (summer, autumn, and extraordinary) of the 2020/21 academic year. The questionnaire used is the one proposed by ANVUR (Form n.5), appropriately remodeled and integrated with additional questions to provide a comprehensive view of the adequacy of facilities (classrooms, equipment, and support services) and the overall experience of their training path.
The evaluation given by graduates of the 2020/2021 academic year can be considered generally positive, with an average score of 3.21, slightly higher than the previous year but slightly lower than the average scores of the Health Area and University (respectively 3.29 and 3.23).
WEAKNESS: The question with the lowest score was D3: 'Was the overall organization (schedule, exams, intermediate and final) of the courses in the reference period acceptable?' which received a rating of 2.98, indicating students' clear request for greater attention to the organizational management of the complex set of activities they are required to undertake.
SOLUTION: This point has been addressed over the past two years by the responsible parties of the various poles, who also had to manage all additional difficulties caused by the pandemic regarding internships, through a reorganization of the lesson and internship calendar. In future questionnaires, we will be able to assess the effectiveness of the changes implemented.
As a pilot this year, a questionnaire for evaluating the Internship experience was also administered to students.
The results were interesting and stimulated new reflections: 100% of students believe the Internship was effective in improving skills, technical and relational abilities, and 70% reported being very or extremely satisfied with the experience, confirming the enormous professionalizing and developmental value always attributed to internships in the context of the Course of Study. New reflections were stimulated by discussions with students about the tutorial model they encountered, the advantages and disadvantages of different situations.
These reflections led to a request from the student body for greater interaction between the Course of Study and the heads of host departments to agree on an organized tutorial model that serves as a clear reference point for students and optimizes the learning process while simplifying the work of structured nurses acting as tutors.
From interaction with the student body, two additional critical points worthy of attention emerged: 1- a high rate of lesson postponements and non-compliance with the didactic calendar issued at the beginning of the semester, postponements and absences that compromise the student's proper preparation; 2- the presence of instructors who have not demonstrated full mastery of the courses assigned to them.
Proposed solution: The joint commission proposes that Professor Mincione take on the task of interacting with the student body and involved instructors to agree on a resolution method for the reported issues.
Analysis and proposals on the validity of assessment methods for knowledge and skills acquired by students in relation to expected learning outcomes.
Programs and examination methods for each course in the study plan are available online (Home page UdA, Teaching, Teaching Activities, Prevalent Department of Medicine and Aging Sciences, Nursing Course of Study, link to Course of Study site: https://scuolamedicina.unich.it/corsi-di-studio/infermieristica-l603). In most individual course sheets, there is consistency between methods, teaching tools described, and expected learning outcomes; others are found to be non-compliant in methods and topics. Instructors have been invited to update syllabi according to new regulations, particularly by completing the Sustainability section. In this section, it is required to verify how course topics relate to the United Nations 2030 Agenda Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
WEAKNESS: However, sample checks have shown that not all syllabi have been inserted, some are incomplete.
PROPOSAL: It is proposed to entrust the Didactic Directors of the Training Poles and the subcommittees that have already analyzed the programs in the three locations and therefore have a precise overview of the situation with a stricter control of syllabus insertion. Regarding this proposal, during 2023, the Didactic Directors of the three poles have carried out a complete revision of the Nursing discipline syllabi and uploaded them to the dedicated platform.
The analysis conducted will be included in the agenda of the October 2023 Course of Study Council.
At the same time, to evaluate potential weaknesses and obtain suggestions for improving our students' training, the proposal to use the link https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi by students themselves will be presented to the Council.

Learning Skills
Nursing graduates must develop the following self-learning skills:
- develop skills for independent study;
- demonstrate the ability to cultivate doubts and tolerate uncertainties arising from study and practical activity as a source of new learning;
- develop the ability to pose questions in relation to the exercise of one's activity, formulating relevant questions at the right time, place, and to the right interlocutors;
- demonstrate the ability to continuously seek opportunities for self-learning;
- demonstrate self-assessment skills of one's own competencies and outline one's own development and learning needs;
- demonstrate collaborative learning skills and sharing of knowledge within work teams;
- demonstrate ability and autonomy in seeking necessary information to solve problems or uncertainties in professional practice, critically selecting secondary and primary sources of research evidence.
Teaching tools, methodologies, and training activities to develop expected outcomes:
- problem-based learning (PBL);
- use of cognitive maps;
- use of contracts and self-learning plans to empower the student in planning their internship path and self-assessment;
- laboratories for bibliographic research methodology, both paper and online;
- guided reading for critical evaluation of scientific and professional literature in Italian and English.
Evaluation tools to verify achievement of expected outcomes:
- project work, report on specific research mandates;
- tutorial supervision on the internship path;
- active participation in work and debriefing sessions;
- punctuality and quality in presenting documents.
Brief course description The Course of Study (CdS) in Nursing aims to ensure students acquire adequate mastery of general scientific knowledge, methods, and content, oriented towards acquiring the most specific knowledge and professional skills, traceable to abilities and comprehension skills, applied in autonomy of judgment, in collaboration with other health professionals, in managing nursing care for the person and the community.
To be admitted to the CdS, one must possess a secondary school diploma or another degree obtained abroad, recognized equivalent according to current regulations. The training potential of the Nursing Course of Study for the academic year 2021/2022 is 245 (two hundred forty-five), plus 5 (five) places, of which 3 (three) for non-EU extracommunity students residing in Italy and 2 (two) for non-EU extracommunity students residing abroad. In the number of places reserved for non-EU extracommunity students residing abroad, none are reserved for Chinese students adhering to the 'Marco Polo' program.
The sustainability of the CdS is related to the actual availability of human resources, teaching staff, and support staff, suitable structures and teaching and scientific equipment (classrooms, laboratories for exercises, simulations, and biomedical research), services, and complex operational units contracted with the National Health Service, as well as private health structures contracted in the territory. Teaching and internship activities are structured at the Chieti, Vasto, and Pescara training poles in the respective Health Agencies, under the responsibility of a teaching director of maximum qualification in the professional sector, appointed based on a curriculum evaluation by the Course of Study Council. Access to the CdS, whose modalities will be indicated year by year on the University website (www.unich.it), is subject to passing a national admission test. For greater teaching effectiveness, possession or acquisition of adequate knowledge of Biology, Chemistry, and Physics is required for access, as defined according to Article 4 (OFA) of the CdS Didactic Regulations. To obtain the degree, the student must have earned 180 CFU, including all theoretical and practical teaching activities and the final qualifying exam. The normal duration of the CdS is three years. Longer durations may be provided for part-time students, as provided in Article 17 of the current CdS Didactic Regulations. Those who obtain the degree are awarded the academic title of Doctor in Nursing.
External Effectiveness C2, 2023
C2 EXTERNAL EFFECTIVENESS The analysis of data on the employment status of 2021 graduates at one year (year of investigation 2022 updated to April 2023, see attached file) indicates that:
the number of graduates is 192, increasing compared to the 2021 survey (173); the percentage of graduates enrolled in a second-level degree increases from 6.9% to 16.4% in 2022; the employment rate slightly decreases from 91.4% to 90.0% in 2022); the percentage of employed individuals who use acquired degree skills to a high extent decreases from 92.4% to 89.8%; the average net monthly salary is comparable (from 1,647.00 to 1,638.00 euros). There is a slight decrease in satisfaction with the work performed (from 8.5 in 2021 to 8.1 in 2022).
In general, the data analysis shows that external effectiveness is significantly higher than for the same type of course at the University.
The data will be discussed at the Course of Study Council meeting in September 2023.
From consultation of AlmaLaurea data (see attached file), referring to the years of investigation 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, and 2020 (where graduates are respectively 180 vs 165 vs 162 vs 212 vs 209), at one year after graduation, the RESPONSE RATE is respectively 72%, 78%, 76.5%, 76.9%, 73.2%; in all years women represent the majority, although in 2018 the gap with male graduates narrows to 66% compared to 73% the previous year.
Nurses graduate during the course, although the average duration in years has slightly increased from 2016 (3.5 vs 3.9), and they are relatively young: 24.3 years. The average degree grade for the three years considered is 105.4/110.
Compared to the post-graduation training context, in the last three years, the percentage of those enrolled in a second-level degree has visibly increased from 0.8% in 2016 to 9% in 2018, then decreased to 5.5% in 2019, and increased again to 9.8% in 2020; the motivation for enrolling in a second-level degree is: in 2016, 100% is driven to improve their cultural training, decreasing to 66.7% in 2017, 54% in 2018, 33% in 2019, and 20% in 2020; simultaneously, the percentage of those choosing the Master's to improve job prospects and because a second-level degree is necessary for this purpose increases over the years.
Considering the section 'Characteristics of current work', permanent employment contracts have further decreased in 2019 compared to 2018: specifically, permanent employment decreased from 14.6% in 2018 to 12.9% in 2019 and to 11.5% in 2020, increasing the non-standard work type from 68.5% in 2018 to 75% in 2019 and to 77.9% in 2020: this data can be explained by the increase in outsourcing of services by healthcare companies, involving cooperatives and temporary agencies.
The average weekly working hours respect the sector CCNL (36).
Our graduates work predominantly in the private sector until 2019 (70.7% in 2019, 73% in 2018 and 2017, 50.5% in 2016) while in 2020 the health emergency due to the Covid-19 pandemic records a trend reversal in favor of the public sector (in 2020 the percentage is 51.9% in public and 44.3% in private). Therefore, in 2019, private sector work decreases from 70.7% to 44.3%.
The geographical area where nurses find employment one year after graduation, with a gradual increase, is Southern Italy, the region of origin of half of the students enrolled in the CdS (Puglia is the leading region).
A data certainly worth highlighting is that Nursing graduates have been appreciated abroad, especially in Great Britain: in 2016 the share was 12%. However, from interviews, the percentage decreased in 2017 to just over 1.0%, increased to 4.2% in 2018, zeroed out in 2019, and slightly increased to 0.8% in 2020.
The net monthly salary of over 1300 euros, despite high professional responsibilities, is still above the national average of 990 euros (ISTAT, 2018). In 2020, the net monthly salary rises to 1595.00 euros.
Additionally, the skills acquired with the degree are used to a high extent by 77.5% in 2018 (comparable to previous years); in 2019 it is 81%, in 2020 85.5%.
The training acquired at university is considered 'very appropriate' and gradually increases from 2016 to 2019 (84 vs 86.5 vs 86.5 vs 90.5) with a decline to 84.7% in 2020: probably the decline recorded in 2020 is due to the effects of implementing distance learning due to the Covid-19 health emergency. Indeed, at the end of February 2020, the Courses of Study for Health Degrees and Master's Degrees underwent important changes in teaching, laboratory, and professional/internship activities due to the emergency situation caused by the Covid-19 pandemic. Immediately, the DPCM of April 10, Article 1, Paragraph k,1 stated that internships for Health Professions could continue. However, while teaching activities resumed almost immediately in distance mode, laboratories and professional/internship activities were suspended throughout Italy, mainly by joint decision of Health Agencies/Universities as emerged from a survey conducted by the Permanent Conference of Health Degree Classes.
The internships of Health Degree Courses and Master's Degrees constitute the indispensable part of the training of future health professionals because they are capable of generating and consolidating the expected competencies at an initial and advanced level and developing a solid professional identity through learning processes from experience, practice, and anticipatory socialization to work. For its indispensability and relevance (=60 CFU for Bachelor's Degrees, 30 CFU for Master's Degrees), the internship has always been carried out 'in person' for the total number of hours scheduled.
Restarting internships in a profoundly changed context and re-proposing, where necessary, a 'congruent part' in distance mode requires a comprehensive vision capable of guiding unprecedented choices to ensure learning experiences of quality generating competencies not inferior to those learned 'in person'. The Permanent Conference has developed guidelines aimed at suggesting a range of opportunities and diversified approaches capable of stimulating different learning styles and student needs, avoiding further isolation. Furthermore, the guidelines were fundamental to ensure, where possible, a unified coordination of the preparatory phase among all CdS of the same University through inter- or intra-departmental systems to guarantee a harmonious approach towards companies, while respecting different specificities.
The last observed variable is 'EFFECTIVENESS OF THE DEGREE AND SATISFACTION WITH CURRENT WORK', where the effectiveness of the degree in the work performed measured with the judgment 'very effective/effective' in 2020 is 97.7%, in 2019 it is 95.7% vs 96.6% in 2018.
SATISFACTION WITH THE WORK PERFORMED, on a scale of 1-10, is above 7.5 in the analyzed years (in 2018: 7.9, in 2019: 7.7, in 2020: 8.4) indicating full alignment between one's study course and the actual work performed.
Specific training objectives and description of the training path The graduate, at the end of the three-year path, must be able to:
- manage with autonomy and responsibility interventions aimed at prevention, care, assistance, and safeguarding the health of the assisted person, family, and community;
- manage nursing care for patients (pediatric, adult, and elderly) with acute and chronic respiratory problems, cardiovascular problems, metabolic and rheumatic problems, acute and chronic renal problems, acute and chronic gastrointestinal problems, liver problems, neurological problems, oncological problems, infectious problems, orthopedic and traumatological problems, obstetric-gynecological problems, hematological problems, behavioral and cognitive alterations, situations of discomfort/disturbance of mental health;
- assess and manage nursing care for chronic patients and disabilities in all ages;
- manage perioperative nursing care;
- ensure safe administration of therapy and monitor its effectiveness;
- perform nursing techniques learned and defined by the Course of Study standards with skill and ability;
- activate decision-making processes based on the general and clinical conditions of the patient, values of altered parameters, reports, and laboratory tests;
- manage diagnostic pathways ensuring adequate preparation of the patient and subsequent monitoring of the procedure;
- integrate nursing care into multidisciplinary care projects;
- assess the problems of the assisted person through structured and systematic techniques and methods, identifying alterations in functional models (activity and exercise, perception and maintenance of health, nutrition and metabolism, elimination model, rest and sleep, cognition and perception, concept of self, role and relationships, coping and stress management, sexuality and reproduction, values and beliefs);
- activate and support, both individually and in collaboration with other health professionals, the residual capabilities of the person to promote adaptation to limitations and alterations produced by illness and changes in lifestyle;
- identify the nursing care needs of the person and their related reactions to illness, treatments in progress, institutionalization, changes in daily activities, and perceived quality of life;
- define the priorities of interventions based on nursing care needs, organizational needs, and optimal use of available resources;
- design and implement, in collaboration with other professionals, information and health education interventions for risk factor control aimed at the individual and the community;
- evaluate the results of the provided care and adapt the nursing planning based on the evolution of the patient's problems;
- manage and organize nursing care (including night shifts) for patients;
- distinguish nursing care needs from other assistance needs, differentiating the contribution of support staff from that of nurses;
- assign and supervise assistance activities to support staff;
- manage paper and computer-based information systems supporting care;
- document nursing care provided in accordance with legal and ethical principles;
- ensure patients and significant persons receive relevant and updated information about their health status;
- prepare conditions for the discharge of the assisted person, in collaboration with team members;
- ensure continuity of care between different shifts and between different services/structures;
- use professional integration tools (meetings, team meetings, case discussions);
- work integrated within the team respecting competence spaces;
- ensure an effective physical and psychosocial environment for patient safety;
- use practices for protection from physical, chemical, and biological risks in the workplace;
- adopt precautions for manual handling of loads;
- adopt strategies for infection risk prevention (standard precautions) in hospitals and community settings;
- monitor and vigil the clinical and psychosocial condition of the patient, identifying early signs of worsening;
- activate necessary interventions to manage acute and/or critical situations;
- identify triggering factors for reactivation in chronic patients;
- activate and manage a therapeutic and supportive relationship with the user, their family, and significant persons;
- manage care processes respecting cultural, ethnic, generational, and gender differences;
- support, in collaboration with the team, the assisted person and family in the terminal phase and grief;
- activate informal assistance networks to support the user and family in long-term care projects.
TRAINING PATH:
1st year - aimed at providing knowledge in basic, biomedical, and preventive hygiene disciplines; foundations of the professional discipline, also in a psychopedagogical context, as indispensable requirements to face the first internship experience aimed at orienting the student to the reference professional areas and acquiring basic prevention and assistance competencies;
2nd year - aimed at clinical knowledge and preventive and assistance interventions, aimed at addressing priority health issues in medical and surgical areas, specialized and integrated areas, maternal-infant area, and oncological area, focused on acute and chronic phases of illness to support educational and psychosocial aspects. Simulation experiences are provided in nursing laboratories and internships in contexts where the student can experiment with acquired knowledge and techniques;
3rd year - aimed at specialized in-depth in neurological and mental health areas and acquisition of knowledge and methodologies related to professional practice and integration skills in work teams and in more complex organizational contexts. The relevance of internship experiences increases, and the student can gradually assume greater autonomy and responsibility under expert supervision. Additional training activities are provided, with internships in excellence structures to support thesis elaboration and develop methodological skills in scientific and nursing research.
This curricular logic has been concretized in the growth of credits assigned to clinical internship from the 1st to the 3rd year of the course.

Characteristics of the final exam According to Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, the final exam, with the value of a qualifying State exam - ex Article 6 of Legislative Decree No. 502/1992 and subsequent amendments - consists of:
a) a practical exam during which the student must demonstrate acquisition of theoretical-practical and technical-operative knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) preparation and defense of a thesis.
The exam is organized nationally in two defined sessions, established by MIUR decree and in the presence of MIUR, Ministry of Health, and IPASVI representatives.
Final exam execution modalities FINAL EXAM MODALITIES The student has 6 CFU available for preparing the final exam and thesis, distributed between the 2nd year (2 CFU)* and the 3rd year (4 CFU) of the course. Exam sessions are established, as per MUR, in the periods of October/November (autumn session) and March/April (extraordinary session), according to a calendar determined within the teaching programming. The student, in the second semester of the second year, contacts the supervisor teacher to carry out a graduation internship, presents to a commission, composed of three teachers and appointed for approval, the title and topic of the thesis and the name of the supervisor teacher. The thesis title deposit form must be submitted to the student office within 12 months for experimental theses and 6 months for compiled theses. The certification of the acquired credits is issued by the Course of Study President and the Teaching Director. The figure of a Correlator Teacher may be provided.
The Correlator figure is provided, a Teacher or Tutor with recognized academic competence, who may, on proposal of the Supervisor, be listed in the work and participate in the Commission's activities, but cannot contribute to the graduation grade.
To be admitted to take the graduation exam, the student must:
a. have passed all exams provided by the study plan, at least 30 days before the graduation session date, and in particular for the extraordinary session, by February 28;
b. have completed and passed the annual clinical internship exams;
c. have submitted the graduation application to the Rector through the student office within the deadlines indicated by the student office;
d. have submitted a copy of the thesis on paper/informational support.
The final exam Commission is composed of not less than 7 and not more than 11 members appointed by the Rector on proposal of the Course of Study Council and includes at least two members designated by professional colleges. A representative of the Ministry of Health is present, with the function of external supervisor.
The structure of the graduation exam includes:
1. a practical qualifying exam to evaluate technical skills in performing nursing procedures, holistic approach in taking care of the person, and global ethical-behavioral aspect both in prevention and care and assistance areas, through the extraction of a clinical case. The verification is based on the verification of knowledge and applied comprehension skills, autonomy of judgment, and communication skills (Dublin Descriptors 2, 3, 4: Knowledge and Applied Comprehension; Autonomy of Judgment; Communication Skills);
2. preparation and discussion of a theoretical-applicative (compiled) or experimental thesis. To discuss the thesis, the student must have passed the final practical exam in the same graduation session.
The final graduation grade, expressed in hundredths, is determined by the average of the grades of the curricular exams, integrated with the following evaluations:
- the score given by the Commission on the method, presentation, and discussion of the thesis with a maximum of 4 points for both compiled and experimental theses.
- a maximum bonus of 4 points from the practical exam, distributed through the following score ranges:
score between 18 and 20, 0 points
score between 21 and 25, 1 point
score between 26 and 28, 2 points
score between 29 and 30, 3 points
Honors, 4 points.
- a bonus of 2 (two) points for participation in the Erasmus Project, with a stay of at least three months.
* The final exam of the Nursing Course of Study, according to Article 7 of the Interministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, has the value of a qualifying exam for the nursing profession and consists of a practical exam and the preparation of a thesis and its defense.
The purpose of the thesis is to engage the student in a design and research or in-depth work on specific nursing areas through the analysis and synthesis of relevant bibliographic sources.
Since the study plan provides 2 CFU in the second semester of the second year for presenting the final work project, all students are dedicated two hours, embedded in the second-year second-semester teaching calendar, during which all indications and information for preparing a thesis meeting criteria of originality and scientific rigor are provided. During the meeting, guidelines (appropriately published on the CdS website, on the page dedicated to the final exam) elaborated by the CdS Quality Group for thesis preparation are proposed and deepened, with explanations and examples, to which students must adhere; all formal steps, also in terms of timing and prerequisites, that the student must respect until the day of the defense are explained; relevant international databases for searching and identifying nursing bibliographic sources are again shared.
Students are met again about two months before the thesis defense, so that, while sharing their work with the supervisor, they can present the state of the art of their work and receive clear indications on how to revise it, especially regarding citation of sources in the text body and construction of the final bibliography. Additionally, suggestions are provided on how to design presentation slides to fully highlight the effort put into the final thesis and meet the Commission's expectations. Finally, since the defense day inevitably brings anxiety and concern, simple advice is given on how to face and manage them in the best way.
FNOPI DOCUMENT - FEBRUARY 3, 2020
The President of the CdS received the document, received on February 3, 2020, proposed by the FNOPI to ensure uniformity in conducting the final exam and the role of representation by the Ordinal Body. The FNOPI (National Federation of Nursing Professional Orders) has drawn up the GUIDELINES FOR CONDUCTING THE FINAL EXAM OF NURSING AND PEDIATRIC NURSING DEGREE COURSES, with the contribution of referents of the Central Committee, members of the FNOPI Observatory on Training and Research, and external experts from the academic world, to highlight the contribution that representatives of OPIs act as Commissioners in conducting the State Exam. The document is based on national guidelines for the final exam of Nursing and Pediatric Nursing Degree Courses and on current regulations.
Below is the text of the document:
'FINAL EXAM COMMISSION The Commission for the final exam is composed of not less than 7 and not more than 11 members with voting rights, appointed by the Rector on proposal of the Course of Study Council.
Two members of the Commission with voting rights are designated by the provincial OPIs of the territorial reference, taking into account possible different territorial locations of the CdS, communicating the names to the University according to the times and methods provided by their respective regulations.
Professional Representatives of the Orders that are part of the Commission must be of the same professional profile (i.e., Nurses for the Nursing Course of Study, Pediatric Nurses for the Pediatric Nursing Course of Study), preferably in active service.
The Ministries of Education, University, and Research and Health may send their experts as representatives to individual sessions.
They oversee the regularity of the exam, signing the minutes. In case of failure to designate the aforementioned ministerial members, the Rector may exercise the substitutive power.
Normally, the Commission includes Directors of Professional Teaching Activities/Professional Teaching Coordinators and University Teachers of SSD MED/45 as provided by the Permanent Conference guidelines.
These guidelines provide that the Commission must be dedicated, stable, and guarantee continuity for the entire final exam.
PRACTICAL EXAM The document of the Permanent Conference provides that in the practical exam, competencies resulting from Dublin Descriptors 2, 3, and 4 are evaluated:
2. knowledge and applied comprehension - applying knowledge and understanding,
3. autonomy of judgment - making judgments,
4. communication skills - communication skills,
and, in particular, the ability to identify problems, make decisions on professional issues, identify priorities for individual patients, groups, or work processes, design and decide interventions based on available evidence and organizational conditions, act safely, consider ethical, deontological, and legal dimensions in one's actions; demonstrate orientation towards interprofessional practice, evaluate effects on patients.
The document also provides that the modalities of conducting the practical exam may include one or more modalities among the following:
- structured, semi-structured, or open-ended written test on paradigmatic cases/situations of professional practice.
- oral interview with discussion of cases or an elaborated project.
- observation of professional skills (e.g., technical, relational, diagnostic, project-oriented) in real clinical contexts, in simulated laboratory contexts, or with video support - structured clinical skills examination (OSCE).
According to the indications provided jointly by MIUR and the Ministry of Health (circular of September 30, 2016), the exam may be conducted in two alternative modalities:
a) practical simulation, structured to allow the graduate to demonstrate acquisition of knowledge and practical, technical, and relational skills;
b) exam with closed and open-ended questions on clinical cases or paradigmatic situations of professional practice.
The above modalities may be integrated with an interview if the Commission deems it appropriate.
Written tests with quiz evaluations of only theoretical knowledge are not considered valid.
The minimum performance level expected in the practical exam to be considered passed is 60%.
The modalities of practical exams are normally indicated in the Course of Study Didactic Regulations and in the SUA Sheet to ensure wide and widespread communication to students, Orders, and stakeholders to reinforce sharing of exam modalities and content.
The exam must:
a) Be based on the selection of 'core' competencies expected from a graduate. Such competencies are normally identified with professional representatives (L.3/2018 art. 3 comma f) and services;
In particular, it is necessary to select nursing competencies ensuring:
? balanced sampling of competencies to be evaluated so that they are exemplary of the expected practice, avoiding emphasis on details;
? high relevance to priority health issues selected based on the following criteria: relevance, prevalence, severity, treatability, pedagogical exemplarity, interdisciplinary contribution;
? adequate contextualization in different practice settings, with particular attention also to territorial, community, and residential services.
b) Be standardized, exposing each student:
? to the same level of complexity;
? to an exam where the outcome measurement is predefined and shared by the Commission to reduce variability of evaluators' judgment.
c) Refer to scientific sources, evidence-based guidelines, updated texts.
d) Be anonymous, when possible.
THESIS The thesis allows verification of the achievement of the competencies indicated in the 5th Dublin Descriptor, i.e., the student's ability to carry out an autonomous and methodologically rigorous learning path. The purpose of the thesis is to engage the student in a design and research or in-depth work on specific nursing areas through the analysis and synthesis of relevant bibliographic sources. The content of the thesis must be related to nursing and disciplines covered in the study plan. Normally, the student will have the supervision of at least one supervisor chosen according to the University regulations.
Evaluation system The final graduation grade is expressed in 110/110 with possible honors and is formed by the arithmetic or weighted average (according to what defined by University regulations) of the grades obtained in the profit exams, including the three Clinical Internship exams, scaled to 110, and the sum of the evaluations obtained in the final exam (practical exam + thesis), which contribute to determining the final grade.
The practical exam with applicative value is a barrier: in case of insufficient evaluation, the candidate cannot proceed with the thesis discussion. Therefore, the exam must be repeated in the next graduation session.
Both parts of the single final exam contribute to determining the final grade. The guidelines of the Permanent Conference of Health Degree Courses recommend valuing the exam with a maximum of 10 points (5 for the practical exam and 5 for the thesis defense).
The Commission may award additional points up to a maximum of 2 in total to candidates who have received honors in the profit exams of the courses, and/or who have participated with positive results in Erasmus/Socrates Programs and are in regular course.
Generally, it is suggested to consider the minimum average of 110/110 of the student's career as the basis for awarding honors.
Recommendations To Nursing Professional Orders It is recommended to:
a) Identify a group of professionals possible Representatives of the Commission,
nurses with an adequate curriculum (preferably holding a Master's Degree in Nursing and Midwifery or a Master's):
not involved as Teachers or Teaching Tutors in the training of students at the site where the qualification exam will be held;
who share the vision expressed by FNOPI regarding Nursing and Pediatric Nursing. For this purpose, specific training initiatives on the role of OPI representative, on the objectives and characteristics of the final exam are recommended.

a) Emphasize the importance of the final exam, its purpose and specificity compared to internship exams, recalling its relevance throughout the entire training path.
b) Offer a preparation path for the final exam making the expected standards transparent and providing guidelines/documents of direction.
c) Promote an adequate distance between the practical exam and the thesis discussion to ensure appropriate information of the outcome that is a prerequisite for continuing the final exam.

Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission Candidates admitted to the Dental Hygiene Bachelor's Degree program must hold a five-year secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent, and must rank favorably in the admission ranking in accordance with current national regulations for quota-based admission to Bachelor's Degree programs. The number of students admitted to the first year is determined annually by the competent national authorities based on available facilities and teaching staff. The admission examination for the Bachelor's Degree program is conducted according to modalities defined by the Ministry of Education, Universities and Research (MIUR) and consists of multiple-choice quizzes covering topics in Logic and General Culture, Biology, Chemistry, Mathematics, and Physics.
For admission to the Bachelor's Degree program, students must possess adequate prior preparation from previous studies, particularly in Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, Physics, Logic, and General Culture.
The required knowledge for admission will be verified through the national quota-based university entrance examination.
The Bachelor's Degree program will also verify the student's adequate preparation according to modalities specified in the Course of Study Teaching Regulations. In case of verified deficiencies, students will be assigned additional training obligations to be fulfilled within the first year.
Admission modalities The number of students admitted to the Bachelor's Degree program is determined annually by the Ministry based on the actual availability of human resources, teaching and support staff, suitable facilities and equipment (classrooms, laboratories for practical exercises and biomedical research simulations), services, and operational units in hospital structures and territories affiliated with the National Health Service, as specified in the Ministry's annual decree. Admission modalities for the Bachelor's Degree program will be indicated in the University's competitive call.
Students admitted to the program who score below 25% of the maximum score in Biology, Chemistry, Mathematics, and Physics in the entrance test will be assigned additional training obligations (OFA). These students will be informed via email and direct meetings about the deficiencies in their preparation and the activities provided to support their recovery.
Completion of OFA involves the assignment of individual seminar-style training activities for each discipline in which the student showed deficiency, to be completed during the first semester of the first year.
Verification of results achieved in the prerequisite training activities will occur within the assessment of integrated courses including the SSDs for which OFA was assigned. Additionally, pursuant to Article 49, paragraph 3, point b of the University Teaching Regulations, students who do not fulfill the additional training obligations as specified in Article 28 of the Course of Study Teaching Regulations cannot enroll in second-year courses. Therefore, while second-year enrollment is permitted, students cannot take second-year exams until the OFA are completed.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate must establish and maintain a relationship with the user, starting from prevention, taking into account the various levels of complexity related to it. This constitutes the foundation of professional practice, which must be centered on the individual, respecting individual differences and considering their influence on eating habits related to oral health, lifestyle, and the individual's own habits.
The dental hygiene graduate:
- will interview patients for needs assessment;
- will carry out their activities in accordance with the principles of patient/user-centered professional practice;
- will build a relationship/partnership as the foundation of oral hygiene intervention;
- will employ a variety of personalized strategies based on the patient's needs;
- will develop education programs and educational materials to meet the learning needs of individuals and groups.
Graduates must be particularly skilled in interpersonal communication, including oral and written communication with professionals and service users, in group work, and within interdisciplinary work groups with health and social professionals.
To achieve this, the dental hygiene graduate must:
- select appropriate communication methods;
- identify and recognize communication barriers (problems reading or writing, misunderstanding, cultural issues, fear, etc.);
- adapt to a communication style suitable to meet the needs and learning capabilities of individual persons and/or groups;
- employ effective verbal communication skills;
- write clearly, concisely, and professionally, technically and grammatically accurately;
- build educational material taking into account the comprehension ability of the target group and/or individuals;
- facilitate two-way communication;
- employ active listening techniques;
- interpret and respond to non-verbal communication;
- apply principles of collaboration and negotiation in group work;
- incorporate the knowledge, experiences, and personal skills of other group members during their activities;
- collaborate with other group members to define objectives;
- adapt their personal approach to group members and situations involving the work group;
- work with other group members to identify and resolve conflicts;
- contribute to decisions made within the work group;
- take responsibility for completing the assigned task.
Communication skills will be acquired through the teachings of human sciences, psychopedagogical, and sociological disciplines to ensure the learning of necessary behavioral and relational competencies to operate in a complex work environment. Additionally, the internship involves close contact between the student and patients under the supervision of tutors, whose task will be to modulate the approach methodology from the initial phase to the completion of professional training.
Communication skills will be verified by tutors during the related teaching activities, during the internship, and through evaluations of teaching activities, up to the final exam.
Graduates must be able to communicate information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialist and non-specialist interlocutors.

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
Graduates must have the ability to collect and interpret data (typically within their field of study) deemed useful for forming independent judgments, including reflection on related social, scientific or ethical issues.
The Dental Hygiene graduate:
- Must be able to independently manage non-surgical periodontal disease treatment and caries prevention, always under the direction of a Dentist or other qualified professionals.
- Must be able to evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment plan, implemented interventions, and achieved results.
- Must be able to recognize their own limitations in patient care and acknowledge the need to refer patients to other competencies for dental-rehabilitative or medical therapies.
Graduates' autonomy of judgment will be expressed through the recognition and ability to independently assess issues related to the patient's condition, in relation to oral hygiene aspects and prevention of dental pathologies, and through developing practical and/or experimental prevention schemes, and selecting optimal methodologies, strategies, and equipment use to achieve expected results, also through critical review of information obtained via bibliographic and/or computer research.
The development of these abilities will occur and be verified during internships, where interaction with diverse people, professionals, structures and methodologies will facilitate the development of independent critical thinking. Equally important will be active participation in lectures, preparation for exams and the final project, further moments of development and verification.
Knowledge of relevant regulations, professional, legal, and health regulations and their application will be aimed at achieving specific professional competencies, i.e., the ability to independently and/or in teams master and manage acts, technologies and procedures.
Acquiring behavior consistent with ethical foundations will be one of the objectives completing the educational path.
Autonomy of judgment will be verified through evaluations by assigned tutors, through internship exams, and through verification related to the final exam.

ALMALAUREA Data Applying Knowledge and Understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
Graduates in Dental Hygiene must be able to independently organize the knowledge and operational techniques acquired for the exercise of the profession of Dental Hygienist.
In particular, graduates must:
-know to recognize, at the level of the oral cavity, clinical signs of local and systemic pathologies as well as morphological-functional aspects typical of oral and maxillofacial health;
-be able to recognize vital signs and perform first aid maneuvers in the workplace;
-be able to perform the full range of operational procedures specific to the professional profile;
-be able to control cross-infection in the exercise of the profession;
-know and apply anti-smoking counseling techniques (brief intervention), techniques for motivating patients to home hygiene, periodic professional check-ups, and rational nutrition aimed at protecting oral health;
-know to interact with other members of the dental team: dentist, dental office assistant, administrative staff.
The teaching tools aimed at achieving the ability to apply knowledge within the characteristic activities include, besides the set of teaching activities directed at the student (frontal lessons, self-learning, etc.), a pre-clinical activity at individual benches and clinical internship on the patient.
Other fundamental tools will be represented by the use of information technology, consultation and/or construction and updating of databases, bibliographic research, use of textbooks, and preparation of the thesis for the final exam.
The evaluation of these skills will be carried out through exams, periodic practical evaluations within the internship activities aimed at verifying the acquisition of manual and technical-operative skills in the different clinical activities specific to the professional profile, and with the final exam itself.
Learning Skills
Graduates in Dental Hygiene must possess the ability to update theoretical knowledge acquired through consultation and analysis of scientific publications in the field of Dental Hygiene, also through the use of online databases.
Graduates must achieve sufficient knowledge and possess methodological skills to enable them to continue their study and cultural growth independently (Master's degree, University specialization courses, University Master's degrees).
Graduates must be able to correctly interpret the legislation concerning the exercise of the profession of Dental Hygienist in the European Union country where they practice and carry out professional activities in compliance with the medical-legal and ethical regulations in force in the country where they practice.
The learning ability is evaluated through continuous verification forms during training activities, integrating knowledge acquired during specific activities with those obtained through personal study, evaluating the critical contribution demonstrated during seminar and clinical internship activities, as well as through the verification of the ability to self-learning developed during the activity related to the final exam (thesis).
Graduates must have developed the learning abilities necessary to pursue further studies with a high degree of autonomy.
Knowledge and Understanding
Graduates in Dental Hygiene must acquire post-secondary level knowledge in the fields of basic biomedical disciplines and clinical disciplines, manual skills, and operational techniques, functional to the exercise of the profession of Dental Hygienist.
In particular, the graduate in Dental Hygiene must:
- possess knowledge of the fundamentals of morphology, physiology, and human pathology;
- know the main disease patterns and therapeutic procedures, medical and surgical, complementary to the profession of Dental Hygienist;
- understand the effects of pharmacological therapy for systemic diseases on oral health and any implications for the therapeutic procedures specified by the professional profile;
- know the demographic aspects, prevention, and treatment of oral and dental diseases in developmental, adult, and geriatric age, also in the medically compromised patient or patient with physical or mental disability.
The aforementioned knowledge is acquired through basic and characteristic activities. The teaching method includes frontal lessons, laboratories, exercises, and clinical internships.
Verification methods are based on oral interviews, written essays, and, for disciplines requiring it, practical tests on simulators and patients.
Graduates must know how to use the specific language of Dental Hygiene Sciences.
