Brief Course Description The CdS in Dental Hygiene (enabling the health profession of Dental Hygienist, class of degree in Health Technical Professions L/SNT 3) aims to train health professionals in the technical-diagnostic and technical-assistive areas who, in accordance with Article 3 of Law 10 August 2000, n. 251, carry out, with professional autonomy, the technical procedures necessary for the execution of diagnostic methods on biological materials or on the person, or technical-assistive activities, in accordance with the regulations concerning the identification of figures and their professional profiles defined by the Minister of Health's decree.
The CdS was activated in the academic year 2008-2009 (Ordinamento 509) with Rector's Decree n. 116 of November 26, 2008, in accordance with Article 6 of Ministerial Decree n. 509 of November 3, 1999. In the academic year 2011-2012, the first year of the course was activated in accordance with Ministerial Decree 270/2004 and subsequent implementing decrees. The CdS lasts three years and is divided into six semesters; the first year is dedicated to basic training activities, the two subsequent years are characterized by characteristic and integrative training activities. The learning of scientific and technical competencies and the acquisition of specific professional abilities are counted in University Training Credits (CFU), for a total of 180 CFU over three years, including 60 CFU of Professional Practical Internship for a total of 1500 hours (supervised by a Tutor, the student works directly on the patient to acquire the manual and technical skills necessary for their profession) and 6 CFU of Optional Teaching Activities. To achieve these training objectives, the three-year course with programmed access (multiple-choice test) includes both the study of basic disciplines (biology, anatomy, chemistry, physics, physiology, etc.) and professional disciplines (periodontology, pediatric dentistry, oral surgery, oral medicine, etc.).
To be admitted to the final exam, which involves acquiring 3 CFU for English language knowledge and 6 CFU for the preparation and discussion of the thesis, the student must have passed all exams specified in their Didactic Ordinance.
The final exam has the value of a state exam, enabling the exercise of the profession.
The degree title allows access to Master's degree courses in the class of Health Technical Professions (LM/SNT 3), without academic debts, to Level I Master's degrees, and to Specialization Courses.
The Dental Hygienist is the health professional trained to work within the dental team. They play a very important role in the care of oral health and the general health of the population. Their main task is to prevent and treat gum diseases, through therapies using instruments that remove bacterial plaque and subgingival calculus, and providing instructions for maintaining good oral hygiene. Additionally, they are able to reduce the frequency of cavities in children by applying special sealants on teeth, and reduce dental sensitivity with appropriate procedures involving the application, in various forms, of fluoride-based products. They also address general health by providing dietary advice not only to reduce sugar consumption to prevent caries but also, for example, to counteract obesity or metabolic diseases such as diabetes. An important aspect is their activity against smoking habits, which, besides being responsible for dental discoloration and mucosal diseases in the mouth, is the main cause of cardiovascular disorders and many tumors.
External Effectiveness The Interuniversity Consortium ALMALAUREA conducted a survey on the employment status of graduates in Dental Hygiene; the relevant data provided are updated to 2022.
13 students were interviewed out of 15 who obtained the academic degree in the calendar year 2022, and the responses highlighted the following situation:
76.9% finds employment within one year of obtaining the degree, 100% of these use the acquired skills to a high degree. The average net monthly salary is €1764.
The data in our possession confirm that the training derived from university studies is highly effective for entering the workforce, which is accessed within the first six months after obtaining the degree.
ALMALAUREA Data Specific Training Objectives and Description of the Training Path Within the health profession of Dental Hygienist, graduates are the health professionals to whom the responsibilities provided by Ministerial Decree n. 137 of March 15, 1999, and subsequent amendments, apply, or they carry out, on the indication of Dentists and Medical Surgeons authorized to practice Dentistry, tasks related to the prevention of oral-dental affections. Graduates in Dental Hygiene carry out dental health education activities and participate in primary prevention projects within the public health system; they collaborate in compiling the dental and maxillofacial clinical record and are responsible for collecting technical-statistical data; they perform scaling and root planing as well as the topical application of various preventive means; they provide instruction on various oral hygiene methods and the use of diagnostic tools to detect bacterial plaque and dental biofilm, motivating the need for periodic clinical checks; they indicate the norms of rational nutrition for the protection of dental health.
Graduates in Dental Hygiene are equipped with adequate preparation in basic disciplines, enabling them to best understand the most relevant elements underlying pathological processes that develop in developmental, adult, and geriatric age, on which their clinical intervention focuses. They must also be able to use at least one European Union language, besides Italian, within their specific area of competence and for general information exchange.
The teaching structures identify, through the appropriate selection of disciplinary fields of characteristic training activities, with particular attention to professionalizing scientific-disciplinary sectors, the specific training paths for the aforementioned health profession.
The achievement of professional competencies is carried out through a structured theoretical and practical training in a path that, in the first three semesters, acquires the basic knowledge necessary and preparatory for the acquisition of specific professional competencies, which will occur in the following three semesters.
It is specified that specific professional competencies will be acquired both through traditional classroom lessons and through specific activities carried out within the professional internship, which thus assumes an equal role to theoretical training.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Practical Training Agreements The Review Group aims to establish contacts with local public bodies, professional associations, and school districts to integrate these figures into public oral hygiene prevention.
Additionally, the CdS will propose to the Department of Medical, Oral, and Biotechnological Sciences in which it is based the activation of post-graduate courses, particularly courses for updating and specialization aimed at deepening knowledge and innovative technologies for both new graduates and those graduated in previous years, but especially for holders of the professional diploma of the previous ordinance, which allows them to practice the profession.

Consultation with Representative Organizations - at National and International Level - of Goods and Services Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
Regarding consultation with organizations representing goods and services production and professions, at the national level, structures (interest holders) of the Dental Hygiene Course have been identified, including: the University Dental Clinic and ASL 02 Lanciano Vasto Chieti.
In this specific area, for the Dental Hygiene Course, a constant objective is the organization of periodic meetings and discussion tables with the professional association, UNID (National Union of Dental Hygienists) and AIDI (Italian Association of Dental Hygienists).
The association has continuous consultations with the members of the Course Council thanks to the presence in the teaching staff of Regional AIDI ABRUZZO Council Members, who are present as teachers but also as Coordinator of Professional Internships (as per C.C.d.S. minutes of November 14, 2017), and also as tutors (as per C.C.d.S. minutes of November 14, 2017), enrolled in professional associations, who constantly support the student, participate in meetings with the teaching staff, and are responsible for the correct and continuous flow of information between the university world and the workplace.
Consultations with interested parties have always had an informal character. For this purpose, a steering committee was established (Ref. CdS Council Minutes of March 15, 2018), composed of members of the CdS Council, tasked with conducting discussions with representative professional associations.
Following negotiations with social partners on February 16, 2018, within the National Commission for Dental Hygiene Courses, the following decisions were reached and approved as follows.
- February 16, 2018: Following email agreements (February 9, 2018) between Dr. Michela Rossini, Vice-President of the CNCdSID, and the Presidents of AIDI and UNID, the Board of the National Commission for Dental Hygiene Courses and Dr. Antonia Abbinante, President of AIDI, and Dr. Maurizio Luperini, President of UNID, met in Rome during the Listerine Award Congress to evaluate possible proposals to improve professional teaching activities. In particular:
1. Whether the functions and competencies characterizing the professional figure of the Dental Hygienist are adequately described, thus constituting a clear basis for defining the expected learning outcomes;
2. Whether the specific expected learning outcomes and the generic ones provided by the ordinance are consistent with professional needs so that the graduates' preparation responds to the broader needs of society and the labor market (training demand). The two representatives of the Associations confirmed, as in the June 2017 meeting, that the functions and competencies characterizing the professional figure of the Dental Hygienist are adequately described and constitute a clear basis for defining the expected learning outcomes; considering the specific expected learning outcomes and the generic ones provided by the ordinance, they are considered consistent with professional needs and the graduates' preparation responds to the broader needs of society and the labor market.
It is reiterated once again the importance of respecting teaching requirements for Health Professions courses and the need to support the inclusion of the Dental Hygienist figure in territorial health structures. The Presidents of AIDI and UNID agree that the MED/50 subjects and internships must be managed by Dental Hygienists and not by Dentists or other medical figures not belonging to the professional profile. Regarding the June 2017 meeting, where the proposal for participation of category association representatives in annual internship exams was raised, it is agreed that the second-year internship exam is ideal and functional, as the first year is too early for a correct evaluation and the third year is not particularly useful since the period following it includes the professional licensing exams. The proposal remains to be further defined and will be the subject of future consultations.
Consultations with social partners were conducted during the past year aimed at modifying the CdS ordinance. It should be noted that annually, to align training paths at the national level, social partners maintain a constant relationship with the CdS of this and other Universities, generally within the framework of the National Congress of Dental Hygiene Courses.

Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam consists of two sequential phases:
- The first phase involves the execution of specific techniques of intervention typical of the Dental Hygienist profession.
- The second phase consists of the dissertation of the written summary of the didactic path carried out over the three years of study.
The purpose of both phases is to verify the achievement of the specific theoretical-practical professional abilities necessary for the exercise of the profession.
Method of Conducting the Final Exam The final exam has the value of a State Exam enabling the exercise of the profession and is conducted in two sessions, in the periods and ways prescribed by the Ministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, further clarified by the Ministry of Health/MIUR circular (0046319-P-30/09/2016). In particular, the latter note reiterates that the single final exam consists of two different moments: the dissertation of the thesis and a practical test.
The final exam is conducted in two sessions: the first, normally in October/November, called Ordinary; the second in March/April, called Extraordinary. The final exam will cover:
a. a practical test during which the student must demonstrate to have acquired the knowledge and skills, theoretical-practical, and technical-operative specific to the professional profile. This test may consist of performing specific professional techniques on an appropriate patient selected in advance, or, in the absence of suitable patients or at the commission's choice, be replaced by a practical test on a manikin, after prior communication to candidates;
b. the writing and dissertation of a thesis, in the preparation of which the student will have the supervision of a professor of the Degree Course, called Supervisor, and possibly external co-supervisors.
The purpose of the thesis is to engage the student in a formalization, planning, and research work that substantially contributes to completing their professional and scientific training. The thesis content must be related to themes or disciplines closely connected to the professional profile of the Dental Hygienist. The thesis evaluation will be based on the following criteria: level of depth and scientific relevance of the work, critical contribution of the graduate, accuracy of the methodology adopted for developing the topic, mode of presentation/discussion of the work.
The final exam grade, expressed in hundredths, is determined by summing the following parameters:
a) the weighted average in thirtieths of the grades obtained in the curricular exams (Integrated Courses, Training Internships, A.D.O., and other activities specified in the study plan);
b) the points assigned by the Commission to the Laboratory Test: from 18/30 to 21/30 = 0.50 points; from 22/30 to 24/30 = 1 point; from 25/30 to 27/30 = 1.50 points; from 28/30 to 30/30 = 2 points;
c) the points assigned by the Commission to the thesis discussion (from 0 up to a maximum of 5 points, for both experimental and compilative theses).
The highest honor (lode) may be awarded, with the unanimous opinion of the Commission, to graduates who achieve a final score not lower than 110.
The possibility is provided for the student to write the thesis in English. The deadline for submitting the graduation application and related documentation will be indicated in the notices on the CdS website.
The Commission for the final exam is composed of not less than 7 and not more than 11 members, appointed by the Rector on the proposal of the Course Council, of which 2 members are designated by the professional college, i.e., by the professional associations, chosen among their members.
The dates of the sessions are communicated in advance to the Ministries of University and Scientific Research and of Health, which may send experts as their representatives to the individual sessions. In case of failure to designate the aforementioned members, the Rector exercises the substitutive power. The role of President of the Commission is held by the President of the CdS, who may appoint a substitute chosen among the permanent professors of the CdS in case of absence. The composition of the commission cannot change during the two evaluation moments, except in case of serious impediments for which the member will be replaced by a substitute member, previously appointed.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate must be able to manage communication effectively as the ability to establish a meaningful therapeutic relationship with the person and to establish an effective relationship with all other professionals from the same or other disciplines; they must also be able to use communication tools in the healthcare context, demonstrating the ability to complete the physiotherapy record, draft a therapeutic report, design a physiotherapy intervention, etc., communicating clearly, concisely, and professionally in both verbal and written form, technically and grammatically accurate, knowing how to translate technical language in a comprehensible way even for non-specialists; they must be able to communicate appropriately in international scientific contexts to convey ideas, problems and their solutions.
Teaching tools: classroom activities, simulation laboratories, internship.
Assessment methods: written reports on the communication aspects of the rehabilitation setting; briefings with tutors and the coordinator; oral and written presentation of projects; internship.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L602] PHYSIOTHERAPY
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/611

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgements)
The graduate at the end of the study path will be able to:
- use communication skills and meaningful non-verbal therapeutic relationship skills with people of all ages and their families, and establish an effective relationship with other health professionals;
- adapt communication according to the context and respect cultural, ethnic, and value differences of the people assisted; communicate appropriately in national and international scientific contexts to convey ideas, problems, and their solutions;
- communicate in both verbal and written form clearly, concisely, and professionally, technically and grammatically accurately, also knowing how to translate technical language in a comprehensible way with patients and the team;
- listen, inform, and dialogue with patients and families effectively and understandably, communicate, argue, and motivate one's own work and decisions made with colleagues and with different professional figures.
The autonomy of judgment of the physiotherapy graduate will be fully realized through the habitual and judicious use of communication, knowledge, technical skills, clinical reasoning (diagnostic and evaluative process), emotions, values, and reflection in daily practice for the benefit of the individual or the community.
Teaching tools: frontal lectures in the classroom, teaching laboratories, practical lessons in the laboratory and/or equipped classrooms, internship, reading and interpretation of international literature.
Assessment methods: written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, discussion of clinical cases, definition of the rehabilitation project/program and compilation of the physiotherapy and/or rehabilitation file on real clinical cases; practical demonstration of the planning and execution of specific maneuvers and techniques.

Graduate Opinions According to data available on the Alma Laurea website, in 2022, 29 students completed the Physiotherapy Degree at our University, and 86.2% of them responded to the Alma Laurea questions.
2022 graduates are predominantly male (60%) with an average age at graduation of 25.6 years. Over 50% of graduates (52%) reside outside the region, highlighting the consistent strong appeal of the Physiotherapy Degree Course. The high school diploma remains the most commonly held pre-university qualification among graduates (64%), although it has declined compared to 2012 (64% vs 87.8%), while the percentage of technical diplomas has increased (36% vs 12.2%). The choice of the Degree Course is primarily driven by cultural and professional factors (60%). The average exam score (27.6) improves compared to the previous academic year (28.1 vs 26.7); similarly, the average degree grade increases from 111.1 in 2021 to 112.3 in 2022. 88% of graduates completed curricular training internships, but only 36% had work experience during their university studies, indicating a cohort primarily focused on studies, as evidenced by their excellent performance.
84% of the considered cohort attended more than 75% of the required courses, with 68% considering the study load appropriate for the duration of the Degree Course, thus confirming a generally well-organized Physiotherapy Degree Course, although this figure is lower than the University's average (89.4%). 16% of the cohort consistently or almost always found the exam organization (sessions, schedules, information, registrations, etc.) satisfactory; this figure has declined compared to the previous academic year. However, 8% found the exam organization never or almost never satisfactory, indicating an improvement in this parameter.
During the 2021-2022 academic year, the Degree Course, following a proposal by the GAQ, implemented initiatives to improve exam session organization, avoiding overlaps and increasing the number of available sessions for students. These actions produced improvements in exam session organization and scheduling, receiving positive feedback from the student representation: over 90% of the first-year exam sessions were scheduled without date and time overlaps, with slightly lower percentages for the second and third years.
While the majority of graduates (84%) express satisfaction with their relationships with professors in general, it is unfortunately confirmed that there is less favorability towards the Degree Course compared to the University. This data, conflicting with the high appeal of the Degree Course and the high employment rate one year after graduation, merits discussion in the next Degree Course Council to identify improvement strategies after carefully examining the reasons for dissatisfaction. Graduates evaluated library services positively, but, unlike the previous cohort, did not always consider classrooms and teaching equipment adequate for other activities (laboratories, practical activities). The majority of students (62.5%) highlighted the inadequacy of computer workstations. In this regard, the Presidency Office reiterated the request to the School of Medicine for the establishment of computer classrooms and equipped study rooms at the CUMS branch site, securing an 80-seat classroom to accommodate the increased number of first- and second-year students. The cohort also expressed significant criticism towards the job placement office/services, remaining largely dissatisfied with the support services for job searching.
24.1% of the surveyed cohort would enroll in the same Degree Course again, compared to 68% who would enroll in the same Degree Course at another University, showing a negative trend compared to the previous year.
In conclusion, the Degree Course confirms its appeal to students motivated by cultural and professional factors. Moreover, the regularity of studies (demonstrated by the high percentage of students in progress: 80%), the high average exam and degree scores confirm the quality of the Degree Course. The main criticisms concern the availability of classrooms, teaching equipment for educational activities, and computer workstations. These points will be further discussed in upcoming Degree Course Councils and Quality Group meetings to identify collaborative solutions, necessarily involving University Governance.
Learning Skills
Physiotherapy graduates will be able to:
- Conduct self-assessment of their educational level to maintain their knowledge at the highest level required for professional practice;
- Design self-training paths to enhance their competencies, particularly in Evidence-Based Practice within rehabilitation and physiotherapy;
- Develop competent and independent problem-solving abilities, demonstrating the capacity to continuously seek opportunities for self-learning;
- Take responsibility for their professional development and respond to ongoing changes in knowledge and health and social needs.
Over the three years of the course, they will acquire learning skills and competencies enabling, upon completion, the continuation of studies through a Master's Degree in Class LM/SNT/02, scientific specialization courses, and permanent and recurring advanced training (1st and 2nd level master's, specialization courses), update and in-depth courses (Continuing Medical Education) with a high degree of autonomy.
This skill will be developed and verified through exam preparation, attendance and evaluation of the internship, which combines theory with practice, through critical use of scientific literature and bibliography for final exam preparation.
Teaching Tools: Classroom activities, seminars, simulation laboratories, internship.
Assessment of learning skills will be carried out through the following verification methods: theoretical-practical exams, written and oral reports on technical/professional aspects, clinical case discussions, definition of rehabilitation project/program, and completion of physiotherapy/rehabilitation records for simulated and real clinical cases; research and production of teaching materials.

Brief Course Description The Physiotherapy Degree Course is a three-year, limited-enrollment program aiming to train healthcare professionals who, in accordance with the Ministry of Health Decree 14 September 1994, n. 741, independently or in collaboration with other healthcare professionals, carry out prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation interventions in the areas of motor function, cortical functions, and visceral functions following pathological events of various causes, congenital or acquired.
Physiotherapy graduates possess adequate preparation in basic disciplines, enabling them to best understand the key elements underlying pathological processes on which their rehabilitation and/or therapeutic interventions focus across all age groups (pediatric, adult, geriatric), and to collaborate effectively with physicians, physiatrists, and other graduates from the same or other technical-healthcare classes. They must also be able to use at least English, in addition to Italian, within their specific field and for general information exchange.
Physiotherapy graduates, in reference to the physician's diagnosis and prescriptions, within their scope of competence, develop, also in multidisciplinary teams, a rehabilitation protocol aimed at identifying and overcoming the health needs of patients with disabilities; they carry out functional rehabilitation for motor, psychomotor, and cognitive disabilities using physical, manual, and occupational therapies; propose the use of prostheses and aids, train patients in their use, and verify their effectiveness; verify the response of the rehabilitation methodology to the functional recovery goals; conduct research, teaching, and professional consultancy activities in healthcare services and settings requiring their professional competencies.
The achievement of professional competencies is realized through theoretical and practical training, including the acquisition of specific behavioral skills, ensuring full mastery of all necessary competencies and their immediate application in the workplace.
Physiotherapists carry out their professional activities in public or private healthcare facilities, in dependent or self-employed status.
External Effectiveness Regarding those employed one year after graduation, data from the Alma Laurea website indicate that only 15 out of 30 graduates from 2021 were surveyed. The one-year employment rate is 84.6%, a figure that, while high, shows a decline compared to the previous cohort (96.6%) and the same Degree Course at other Universities (91%). The 15.4% who have never worked after graduation include 7.7% of graduates who are not working or seeking work, being engaged in other courses or internships/practicums.
Notably, 90.9% (vs 75% of the previous cohort) of graduates who continued working before graduation noted an improvement in their work due to the degree, attesting to the educational effectiveness of the Physiotherapy Degree Course. Consistent with this, 100% (vs 97.1% of the previous cohort) of graduates consider the degree highly effective in their work, with an average satisfaction score of 7.8 (scale 1-10). The net monthly salary of a physiotherapist one year after graduation is €1,251. No gender differences are evident in the Alma Laurea report.
Overall, it is noted that the improvement strategies implemented by the GAQ have led graduates to a higher level of satisfaction with the Degree Course. Only a small percentage prefers to continue post-graduation education rather than enter the workforce.
Reasons for Establishing Multiple Courses in the Class The establishment of multiple courses in the class was requested by the regional administration.
Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description In line with Article 6, Paragraph 3, of Legislative Decree 30 December 1992, n. 502, as amended, and in accordance with Law 26 February 1999, n. 42, and Law 10 August 2000, n. 251, the specific educational objective of the course is to train graduates suitable for the healthcare profession.
Upon completion of the training path, the Physiotherapy graduate, having acquired knowledge, competencies, and communication skills, will have the following abilities:
a) Define and plan physiotherapy interventions.
This area translates the professional's responsibility in physiotherapy into all professional actions.
The graduate at the end of the three-year course is able to:
- Involve the patient by requesting active participation and informing them of the physiotherapy path sequence;
- Identify problems and related physiotherapy goals, setting them progressively in therapeutic steps;
- Identify possible preventive, educational, and therapeutic interventions;
- Propose physiotherapy interventions to the team for defining the rehabilitation project goals for the patient;
- Participate in planning educational-informative activities suggesting initiatives for managing the person and self-care for patients and families.
b) Manage their work considering goals and priorities.
This area translates the professional's competencies and knowledge in physiotherapy.
The graduate at the end of the three-year course is able to:
- Correctly perform functional assessment;
- Formulate functional diagnosis;
- Define goals and evaluate their achievement by measuring the outcomes of physiotherapy interventions;
- Perform physiotherapy treatment;
- Choose physiotherapy proposals in relation to possible comorbidities;
- Prepare the setting for implementing physiotherapy interventions;
- Use aids/orthoses to facilitate functional abilities;
- Maintain a continuous collaborative process in patient care with the patient and/or family and/or caregivers;
- Verify and evaluate the results achieved;
- Verify interim results of the physiotherapy proposal in collaboration with other professionals;
- Document professional acts and activities carried out.
c) Management.
This area translates the professional's knowledge of resources, information, and economic aspects in physiotherapy.
The graduate at the end of the three-year course is able to:
- Understand essential management tools for correct daily practice in physiotherapy, using appropriate tools such as quality criteria, managing privacy and clinical risk, and making decisions after a correct problem-solving process;
- Ensure a rehabilitation path based on evidence of effectiveness, aiming to provide an effective, useful, and economically sustainable service.
EDUCATIONAL PATH:
Courses (Integrated Courses) are structured into modules and are delivered through frontal lectures, classroom exercises, laboratory activities, and elective student choices.
Learning outcomes are assessed through self-assessment in-course tests for students and a final oral or written exam, verifying the achievement of set objectives, unique and simultaneous for each integrated course, necessary for acquiring credit units.
Laboratory, English, and first-year internship learning outcomes result in a pass/fail status.
The total knowledge acquired by the graduate equals 180 CFU, including 96 frontal teaching hours, 60 clinical professional internships, and 24 teaching activities (other, optional: language, thesis preparation). These are essential to build the necessary cultural, scientific, and relational background for full professional competence and to understand, address, and manage pathological events requiring rehabilitation and/or therapeutic intervention across all age groups.
Specifically, the educational path includes disciplines represented by Basic Scientific Disciplinary Areas:
- BIO/10, BIO/12, BIO/13, MED/03, BIO/09, BIO/16, BIO/17, MDEA/01, MPED/01, MPSI/01, SPS/07, SPS/08, INF/01, MED/01, FIS/07, ING-INF/06, aimed at providing a solid foundation in biological aspects and functions of human organs and systems, statistical methodology for studying individual and social life phenomena, and concepts of emergency and first aid preparation for the characteristic disciplines of the Degree Course.
Professional-specific training is achieved through Characteristic Scientific Disciplinary Areas:
- MED/48, MED/34, MED/33, MED/09, MEDF/01, MED/10, MED/36, MED/38, MED/39, MED/50, MED/12, MED/26, IUS/10, IUS/07, MED/44, enabling the acquisition of specific professional training and fundamental concepts of human sciences and behavior, ethics and professional deontology, pathophysiology of physical activity and locomotor system diseases, physiotherapy methodologies and techniques, etiology and pathogenesis of diseases, pathology and clinical practice, patient treatment, neurological diseases and sensory organs, and reproductive and maternal-child medicine, along with management elements useful for professional development in work contexts.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Training Agreements The Degree Course has established agreements with numerous rehabilitation structures to optimize the professional training of Physiotherapy students across the Abruzzo region and nationally. Current agreements are with the following structures: Pescara and Chieti ASL, Don Orione Institute Pescara, Paolo VI Foundation Pescara, Villa Serena Clinic Pescara, Sant'Agnese Rehabilitation Center Scerne di Pineto, Santa Camilla Clinic Chieti.
To support students throughout their educational path, the Degree Course has a Professional Teaching Coordinator, Clinical Tutors, and Teaching Tutors distributed nationwide based on students' regions of origin. The number of professional Tutors and agreements with structures outside the region has recently increased.
To gather opinions from entities and companies hosting students for internships/training, the Degree Course has established a dedicated Committee (Tutor Committee, Degree Course Council of 14/10/2021) to prepare a student evaluation form for all affiliated structures. The form is currently being distributed.
Overall, despite not yet having objective data, based on positive verbal feedback from Tutors, the continuous renewal of agreements, and the increasing number of new structure requests for agreements, we believe the Degree Course has a strong regional impact and high-quality student training.

In recent years, due to the hiring of faculty from SSD MED/48, there has been a progressive reduction in teaching assignments for specialist figures and physiotherapists, a criticism often raised during formal or informal meetings with social partners. Considering the outcomes of ongoing interactions with stakeholders for periodic updates to the educational profiles, the Degree Course has implemented improvement actions by modifying the teaching regulations and planned educational offerings for the academic years 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25, reducing the number of modules, increasing CFU for basic and characteristic disciplines essential for the professional profile (Human Anatomy, etc.), and organizing external seminars, professional laboratories, ADE, and physiotherapy area courses.

The Degree Course Chair and Secretary maintain excellent relationships with students, facilitating the direct management of student complaints.
Through periodic GAQ meetings (composed of the Chair, Vice-Chair, two clinical area faculty, and the student representative), the Degree Course systematically analyzes identified problems, their causes, and defines improvement actions where necessary. The Degree Course also:
- Systematically analyzes learning assessment results and final exams to improve student career management;
- Systematically analyzes and monitors the employment outcomes (short, medium, and long term) of Degree Course graduates, also in relation to those of the same class nationally, macroregionally, or regionally;
- Defines and implements improvement actions based on developed analyses and proposals from various AQ system actors, monitors their implementation, and evaluates their effectiveness.
All Degree Course activities are reported in the minutes of Degree Course Council meetings, GAQ meeting minutes, SMA, and SUA-CdS.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data In the 2022/23 academic year, the Physiotherapy Degree Course saw an increase in enrolled students compared to the previous year (76 vs 67 students), reaching a total of 221 students, of whom 206 are in progress (93.2% of students), a figure in line with the previous year (94%). Over 85% of new students come from outside the region, confirming the continued appeal of the Degree Course, significantly improving the percentage from previous years (52% and 65.2%). The majority of new students (76%) hold a high school diploma, while 12% come from technical institutes, 5% from magistral institutes, and the remaining 7% from other schools. The diploma grade was 100 with honors for 3 new students and 100 for 16 new students, between 80 and 99 for 60 students, and up to 80 for the remaining 35 students, indicating a good starting cultural level.
In 2022, 29 students completed their degree with a grade of 105/110 or higher. Specifically, 21 students (67.7% of graduates) achieved a grade of 110/110 with honors (a significant increase compared to the previous two years: 54.4% and 39.3%), 3 students achieved 110/110, while the remaining 7 students (22.6%) achieved 105/110, indicating an excellent cultural and educational level at the end of the study path. 71% (slightly lower than the previous cohort) completed the degree within the three years of the course, while 16.1% took one additional year and 12.9% more than two years, slightly higher than the previous cohort.
Overall, there is a slight decrease in the percentage of graduates in progress (81% vs 71%); this data will be discussed by the GAQ and Degree Course to identify solutions with the support of Degree Course faculty, particularly teaching Tutors. A significant increase in enrollments, especially from students outside the region, demonstrates the continued appeal of the Degree Course, particularly among students from high schools.
Characteristics of the Final Exam The final exam, which serves as the State Exam enabling the profession of Physiotherapist (D.Lgs 502/1992, Art. 6, Para. 3), consists of:
a) A practical exam where the student must demonstrate acquisition of theoretical-practical and technical-operational knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) Preparation of an experimental thesis and its defense.
The final grade is expressed out of 110.
If a total grade of 110/110 is achieved, the Chair of the Final Exam Committee will propose the award of honors, which can only be granted unanimously by the committee members.
The final exam awards 5 CFU.
Conduct of the Final Exam To be eligible to take the Final Exam, the student must:
a) Complete all Integrated Courses and pass the respective exams;
b) Earn a total of 180 CFU distributed across the study years;
c) Pass the mandatory professional training internship (minimum grade 18/30);
d) Submit the thesis request and upload the thesis copy online by the specified deadlines.
To defend the thesis, the student must pass (minimum grade 18/30) the mandatory professional practical exam held in the same session as the thesis defense. The thesis assigned by the Supervisor and approved by the Degree Course Chair must relate to topics covered in the Supervisor's course. The Correlator role is provided.
The degree grade, expressed out of 110, is determined by the following parameters:
1) The average in thirtieths (converted to out of 110) obtained from exam grades in Integrated Courses and the evaluation of the mandatory internship;
2) Points awarded by the committee for the practical exam (18/30 to 24/30 = 0 points; 25/30 to 27/30 = 0.5 points; 28/30 to 30/30 = 1 point; 30/30 with honors = 1.5 points);
3) Points awarded by the Degree Committee during thesis defense, corresponding to the average of individual scores by committee members up to a maximum of 7 points:
- Research type (experimental study; compilation study): maximum 4 points;
- Quality of presentation: maximum 1 point;
- Mastery of the topic: maximum 1 point;
- Discussion skills: maximum 1 point.
4) Years of study: 1 point for graduates in progress;
5) Number of honors obtained in profit exams: 0.1 points per honor;
6) Involvement in international programs of minimum duration of three months: yes = 0.5 points; no = 0 points.
Honors may be awarded with unanimous committee approval to candidates achieving a final score > 111.
The use of any teaching tools (slides, projections, PowerPoint presentations, etc.) should serve as a support for better understanding of the presentation, thus not containing purely discursive parts but graphs, figures, and tables, and may be prepared in English.
The thesis defense occurs in the presence of the thesis Supervisor and the Correlator, while the Degree Committee Chair serves as the Counter-Supervisor.
The Degree Committee consists of 2 external category representatives, a minimum of 5 to a maximum of 9 Degree Course faculty members, and the Ministry of University and Research Delegate.
The Final Exam is conducted only in Italian.
Summary of the Technical Report by the Evaluation Committee The Degree Course has resources of teaching and structural capacity commensurate with the new programming and prospects for full implementation. The course covers a clearly relevant professional area. The proposed curriculum appears significantly improved in terms of cohesiveness, transparency, and effectiveness, contributing to the University's goals of rationalizing and qualifying the educational offer.

Admission Requirements Required knowledge for admission For admission to the Bachelor's degree course - Education track - students must possess a sufficient general culture and the basic knowledge required by the secondary school curriculum of any secondary school or other foreign degree recognized as equivalent. The Bachelor's degree includes specific training activities for acquiring the basic knowledge related to education and training sciences, particularly aimed at students who did not complete such activities in secondary school. The verification of the required knowledge for admission will be carried out through a multiple-choice test (and/or other type of assessment) for students enrolled in the Education track, non-selective, covering general culture content, basic disciplinary content required by any secondary school curriculum, and basic knowledge of the characteristic disciplines of the Bachelor's degree course. Negative verification results do not prejudice the possibility of enrolling in the course. Specific additional activities in the characteristic disciplines of the Bachelor's degree course will be provided for the recovery of any educational deficits, to be followed in the first year of the course to support regular training activities. For admission to the Bachelor's degree course - Philosophy track - students must possess a sufficient general culture and the basic knowledge required by the secondary school curriculum and certified by the corresponding Italian degree, or by another foreign degree recognized as equivalent. At the beginning of the study program, the possession and extent of basic philosophical knowledge within the required general culture will be verified, particularly through an interview and/or written test. An unfavorable verification result does not prejudice enrollment in the course. In case of total absence or insufficiency of even minimal basic philosophical culture, specific additional teaching activities on the characteristic disciplines of the Bachelor's degree course will be offered, which the student must follow to support regular training activities.

Admission Procedures A) Required knowledge for entry (DM n. 270 of 2004, art. 6, paragraph 1)
To enter the degree program, students must possess an adequate general culture and basic knowledge as required by any secondary school curriculum or other foreign qualification recognized as suitable. The degree program includes specific training activities for acquiring basic knowledge in philosophy, education sciences, and training, particularly aimed at students who did not cover these topics in secondary school.
B) Verification of entry requirements (DM n. 270 of 2004, art. 6, paragraph 1)
a) Introduction The Ministry of University and Research (art. 6 of D.M. 270/2004, updated by decree of June 6, 2023, n. 96) requires all universities to verify the initial preparation of new enrollees, to enable freshmen to assess their personal preparation against the basic knowledge required for university study, and to identify, with the assistance of tutor teachers, individual paths to address any initial knowledge gaps, thereby facilitating the student's successful integration into the chosen study program.
The ministerial regulation also stipulates that any additional educational obligations resulting from insufficient initial knowledge must be fulfilled in the first year of the program.
The Department of Philosophical, Pedagogical, and Economic-Quantitative Sciences implements the above ministerial regulation by administering a test with the following characteristics.
b) Who must take the test The test is mandatory for students enrolled in the bachelor's degree program who obtained a high school diploma with a grade below 75/100. Students who obtained a high school diploma with a grade of 75/100 or higher are exempt from taking the test.
All students transferring from other universities in the area and students enrolling in a second degree are exempt from the test.
c) Registration, venue, and dates for the test Official test sessions will be held at the Chieti campus. The schedule of sessions will be published on the Department's 'announcements' page. The test is conducted in November of each academic year and repeated in April of the same academic year. Students must register online via reservation up to 3 days before the exam date.
d) Subjects assessed, duration, and procedure For each student, identifying data will be recorded. After the recognition process, students will have 30 minutes to answer 30 multiple-choice questions (three) on philosophical, pedagogical, and historical culture.
e) Evaluation and recording of results To pass the test, students must answer exactly 16 out of 30 questions correctly.
The test result will be recorded with the student's details and the evaluation 'PASSED' or 'NOT PASSED'.
A negative result entails the assignment of an Additional Educational Obligation (OFA).
In case of a negative result ('NOT PASSED'), the student will be assigned a knowledge gap, which (unless otherwise specified in the following point 'f') must be addressed by October 31 of the first year of the program, by defining a recovery path with the relevant disciplines. At the end of this path, the student must take a test on the area or areas found insufficient in the initial test.
f) Additional provisions The fulfillment of the OFA is also verified by passing a minimum of 18 CFU, related to courses in the first year of the study plan, within the basic, characterizing, and related pedagogical and philosophical areas, by the extraordinary exam session of the first academic year (February of the academic year following enrollment).
In case of failure to fulfill the OFA by the deadline, students must still recover the knowledge gap by passing a minimum of 18 CFU in first-year philosophical and pedagogical courses.
Failure to fulfill the OFA or to pass the test prevents students from taking exams for courses offered from the second year of the program onwards.

Program, texts and objectives Motivations for establishing the interclass course The structure of ministerial tables for study courses has always considered the need to build integrated pathways, conveniently broadening the didactic offer within each table, however, there are fields, professional operational contexts, specific needs of the professional market, for which interdisciplinary sensitivity requires much more than what can be ensured by a single table. For this reason, Interclass Courses have been provided, and for the same reason an Interclass Course in Philosophy and Sciences of Education is proposed, intended for both experts in Sciences of Education and Training, as well as for professionals whose expertise centers on philosophical knowledge. Therefore, it targets certain professional profiles destined for the area of social ethics, service management, social communication, non-university post-secondary training, and personnel management, for which both philosophical and pedagogical-educational sensitivity is useful and appropriate. Finally, it targets various professional profiles requiring competencies and knowledge related to training processes in contemporary society, outlining a pathway that provides the necessary tools for research and knowledge, also aimed at future integration into the teaching world.
Note regarding credits for other activities Language skills are ensured through teaching delivered in the form of a teaching laboratory, with a final assessment to verify suitability.

SECTION: Communication skills
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/619

Communication skills (communication skills)
In the Educational Sciences track, all teaching activities, also through the possibility of experimenting with models and techniques aimed at improving the quality and effectiveness of one's communication in relational and professional contexts, generally aim to enhance communication skills.
Students will also be guided through the content of the courses and through the use of appropriate teaching methodologies to understand and acquire knowledge of communication strategies in educational and training contexts.
Graduates in the Educational Sciences track will particularly acquire the ability to:
improve their relational skills;
identify communication techniques operating in texts and authors related to the field of educational research;
critically evaluate the quality and effectiveness of different presentation choices;
develop observation and listening skills towards others;
optimize the effectiveness of their own communication;
understand different communication modalities in interpersonal relationships;
manage, through communication, potential critical situations in their professional context.
They will also acquire functional and interpersonal communication skills aimed at team building and team leadership.
Finally, the course aims to develop students' communication skills through the targeted use of the various communication tools currently available, by educating them to choose the most suitable strategies and channels according to the content to be transmitted.
Expected learning outcomes in terms of communication skills will be periodically verified through traditional assessment methods and through comparisons with professional realities in school, extracurricular, and professional contexts related to education, business, and human capital development, where students will be called upon during their path to communicate theoretical knowledge, address educational issues, and develop possible solutions.
The training path of the Philosophy track aims to develop in students the communication skills necessary to express their knowledge clearly and rigorously, identifying and defining the means and expressive modalities appropriate to the theoretical objective pursued and to the interlocutors addressed.
In this regard, students will be guided to understand and acquire knowledge of philosophical communication strategies, in order to:
- identify communication techniques operating in texts and authors related to the field of philosophical research;
- recognize the relationship connecting different expository strategies to the historical context in which the texts mature and to the nature of the interlocutors they address;
- critically evaluate the quality and effectiveness of different presentation choices.
At the same time, the course aims to introduce students to the various communication tools currently available, educating them to distinguish and choose the tools and expressive modalities that are appropriate and functional to different communication situations and needs.
Specifically, graduates will acquire:
- the ability to communicate their knowledge in written and oral form, organizing their arguments within a coherent and logically structured framework;
- the ability to use appropriate expressive structures and vary them according to the needs of the different communication media adopted.
These objectives will be achieved:
1. by guiding students, in the forms and modes peculiar to each discipline provided for in our curriculum, to present the acquired theoretical data in the form of written or oral reports;
2. by guiding students to design and produce texts on philosophical topics;
3. by guiding students, where possible and according to the peculiarities of each discipline, to read texts in the original language, allowing them to perceive and critically evaluate the specificity of philosophical vocabulary in different languages and traditions.
To verify the competencies acquired by students in the various disciplinary fields, each course or laboratory must identify, in light of the specificity of each discipline or type of laboratory, ongoing assessments, written or oral tests, or final exercises.

SECTION: AUTONOMY OF JUDGMENT
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/619

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgements)
In the Educational Sciences track, all activities will be carried out according to the most consolidated and modern results of educational research and through appropriate teaching methodologies, with the aim of providing graduates with an Autonomy of Judgment that enables them to use appropriate methods to conduct research activities or other complex investigations related to bibliographic research, design, and implementation of interventions. Some specific courses, integrating pedagogical disciplines, will allow graduates to autonomously interpret data, engage in mature reflection on social and ethical issues related to the complex educational landscape, and develop an autonomous ability to consult legal and safety regulations.

Through the study of disciplines and the contextualization of acquired theoretical content, graduates in the Educational Sciences track will particularly acquire:
- the ability to conduct bibliographic research and utilize databases and other information sources;
- the ability to design and implement appropriate interventions, interpret data, and draw conclusions;
- the ability to select and utilize appropriate technologies and methodologies;
- the ability to combine theory and practice to solve educational and relational problems;
- an understanding of applicable educational solutions and their limitations;
- awareness of the potential non-specific implications of educational practices.

Even in the case of Autonomy of Judgment, the expected learning outcomes will be periodically verified through traditional assessment methods and through discussions between teachers, students, and representatives of school, extracurricular, and education-related professional entities, as well as those related to business and, more generally, to the development of human capital.

Graduates of the Philosophy track will be able to define and utilize appropriate methodologies to conduct investigations or carry out research on topics relevant to their area of competence and understanding. Such research may involve the critical analysis of texts and the reconstruction of the cultural context from which they originate.

Specifically, graduates will acquire:
- the ability to conduct bibliographic research, using various information sources judiciously;
- the ability to interpret acquired data with critical acumen and draw the correct conclusions;
- the ability to use acquired knowledge to define and initiate research activities on authors, texts, or issues relevant to their area of competence;
- the ability to use their competencies to address issues related to public discourse.

These objectives will be achieved through the teaching activities provided by the various disciplines, which present distinct tools and methods for analyzing authors and texts, enabling students to identify and apply the most appropriate strategies within the theoretical, logical, moral, and historical-philosophical conceptual framework in which they propose to operate.

To verify the competencies acquired by students in different disciplinary areas, each course or laboratory must identify, in light of the specificity of each discipline or type of laboratory, in-course assessments, written or oral exams, or final exercises. Specifically, the final verification of the Autonomy of Judgment acquired by students will occur through activities related to the final exam, for which each student, under the guidance of the instructor, will be guided to engage with authors, texts, and issues of the philosophical tradition, compile a reasoned and appropriately updated bibliography on their area of competence; analyze primary bibliography and secondary literature to define their main conceptual nodes and recognize the historical and interpretive tradition to which they belong; draw correct conclusions from the acquired and analyzed data, and use these theoretical acquisitions to support a public discussion.

Incoming Orientation The entrance orientation activity is aimed at students in their third, fourth, and fifth years of secondary schools and is connected to the University's PNRR orientation project. It includes 15-hour training courses delivered to student groups, focusing on basic competencies of the disciplines involved in the study plan, soft skills, and logical reasoning. This activity is coordinated by the University's Orientation and Placement Division and the respective Orientation Committee, composed of faculty representatives from various departments and educational programs. The faculty representatives collaborate with all course instructors.

In addition, informative meetings are organized to illustrate the academic structures and educational offerings of the Study Program, in collaboration with regional secondary schools. These meetings are conducted by specialists in both philosophical and pedagogical-didactic areas.

The Course is also presented through informational materials, seminars, and individual and group information desks during the University's Open Day and other regional and national initiatives organized by schools, institutions, and associations.

The reporting of all activities of the Study Program L19-5 is documented in the minutes of the Council for the relevant academic year. Further reference is made to the consultation of the Department's website pages and archives.

To ensure continuous support for high school students and the dissemination of informational materials, a physical information desk is active, managed in collaboration with university students acting as tutors.

The orientation referents for the interclass course L-5+L-19 are Professor Oreste Tolone and Professoress Marianna Liparoti.

Ongoing Orientation and Tutoring Ongoing orientation and tutoring are ensured by the constant presence of faculty members of the Study Program in Philosophy and Educational Sciences at the department. All faculty provide detailed information on their office hours, contact details, and teaching materials, to enable students, including those with specific needs, to make the most appropriate educational choices and continue their academic path effectively. Additionally, all information is published and continuously updated on the Department's website.

This activity, also oriented towards future professional choices and supported by the presence of student tutors, is carried out in relation to various individual situations and issues, providing academic support aimed at achieving educational success. Distance listening and orientation via online information desk has also been implemented for ongoing orientation by individual faculty members.

The Dean of the Degree Program has scheduled two weekly hours of orientation for students of the Study Program (Wednesdays from 12:00 to 14:00) in her office, where she provides information, guides students on direct internship activities, and presents legislative developments regarding the professional roles of educators and pedagogists.

Assigned Training Periods All students of the Study Program are required to complete professionalizing curricular internships at services and work contexts related to the philosophical and pedagogical field, for which the University provides a constantly updated database and contracts and labor market regulations. Additionally, some operational tools are provided to deepen one's competence in terms of self-promotion aimed at employment, also through online checks on the acquired training.

Students may complete the curricular internship at one of the institutions contracted with their Study Program (consultable on the Department's website), or, if wishing to complete the internship at an institution not yet contracted, request the contracting procedure through the forms available on the Department's page. Upon agreement with the identified institution, a training project will be agreed upon, to be formalized using a specific form available on the Department's page.

The project and any agreement must be submitted in person at the Academic Office (after scheduling an appointment by calling 08713555881) or via institutional email (@studenti.unich.it) to Dr. Antonio Appignani at antonio.appignani@unich.it. The project must be approved by the committee and signed by the tutor of the respective Study Program before the internship can begin. Therefore, it must be submitted at least 15 days before the intended start date and will be returned to the sender via email, along with the internship booklet.

The internship activities planned in the project must be carried out in person, under the supervision of the tutor assigned by the institution, for a total of 100 hours. Additionally, two indirect internship meetings, totaling 6 hours, will be organized in January.

At the end of the internship, students must prepare a final report according to the template on the Department's page and submit it, also through a delegate, along with the internship booklet/self-certification of completion, to the Department's secretariat at least 10 days before the date of the qualification exam, on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 9:00 to 13:00. The absence of these documents within the specified time will prevent participation in the exam.

The Dean of Internship Activities is Professor Stefania Maddalena.

The referents for the Study Program L-5 and L-19 are Professors Federica De Felice, Sofia Montecchiani, and Marianna Liparoti.

Activities related to external training periods are accompanied by periodic indirect internship meetings, coordinated by the Dean of the Degree Program, involving colleagues from the four pedagogical scientific-disciplinary sectors, representatives of the Regional School Office, Abruzzo school networks, local authorities, associations, and invited guests periodically for ad hoc seminars (some posters are attached).

The list of contracted sites is available at the link: https://www.disfipeq.unich.it/sites/st10/files/sedi_2023.pdf

International Mobility To improve the internationalization level of the educational path, the Study Program encourages students and graduates to undertake study periods abroad, offering a wide number of agreements with European university sites. Study abroad opportunities are communicated to students through a specific selection call (see link below). Selected students may be granted support in the form of mobility scholarships. Among the most important goals of the stay, which may be focused solely on writing the thesis, is obviously attending and passing training activities whose content is consistent with the Study Program's educational objectives.

The Study Program maintains a fruitful collaboration with numerous foreign universities within the Erasmus+ program, with some of which bilateral meetings, seminars, and workshops are active. The involved countries are: Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, France, Germany, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Spain, Switzerland (see detailed list available at the end and attached). In the last two years, we have also sought to integrate existing agreements to cover both the needs of pedagogists and philosophers.

Erasmus exchange promotion and orientation meetings are documented in the Study Program's minutes for the relevant academic year. Further reference is made to the Department's website pages and archives.

Erasmus and Internationalization Coordinator for the Department of Philosophical, Pedagogical, and Economic-Quantitative Sciences for the philosophical and pedagogical area: Professor Marco Forlivesi, Professoress Stefania Achella

Note. In recent years, there has been a decrease in student participation in Erasmus+ opportunities, particularly after the pandemic, due to economic reasons and broader psychological concerns. However, the projections of applications received over the last three years, from 2021 to 2024, reflect a slight upward trend, increasing from 12 applications in 2021 to 22 in 2022, reaching 26 in 2023. The increase covers both the philosophical and economic areas. However, attention must be paid to prevent a high rate of withdrawals, as unfortunately occurs in other departments. To avoid this phenomenon, a series of meetings with candidates intending to go abroad are planned.

On the internationalization front, the Department has joined two other initiatives proposed by the University: short-term faculty mobility and the invitation of visiting professors. Even in the case of short-term mobility, which was blocked immediately after the pandemic, a constant increase has been observed (for 2023-24, out of the initial 2 available positions granted to the Department, 6 mobility proposals were submitted, 4 accepted, and 2 deemed suitable).

The Chieti section of DiSFiPEQ has also hosted several visiting professors from various foreign universities (Germany, France, Austria, etc.) in recent years. The experience with visiting professors has been particularly positive as it has allowed our students to engage with different teaching and research methods, contributing to the expansion of their education. Furthermore, the continuous exchange between the department and foreign universities has materialized in the organization of scientific events featuring participation by various foreign professors, as well as in the production of scientific articles in collaboration with researchers and professors from other countries.

Career Guidance To facilitate graduates' entry into the job market and professions, the University's Placement Sector offers a range of services structured around four intervention lines: Basic and specialized counseling for students, businesses, and graduates; Job placement; Guidance for starting a business and microcredit; Career orientation workshops. All information is available at the link provided below.
Graduates of the CdS can also access the Curricula service, a search engine implemented by the University to carry out the functions of a labor market operator following accreditation granted by the Ministry of Labor, which authorized its registration in the Electronic Register of Intermediary Agencies from January 2, 2012. This role stems from the desire to complete the support process for graduates entering the job market, initiated in 2004 through the activation of the University Program called Start, and subsequently the Ministry Program FIxO, for a centralized Placement Service aimed at providing services to graduates during the critical transition from study to work.
All students of the CdS also complete professional internships at occupational entities and are continuously supported by a database offering access to some contractual and labor market regulation sheets.
Additionally, operational tools are provided for deepening one's competence in terms of self-promotion aimed at employment, also through online checks on acquired training.
Career orientation activities aim to provide graduates with knowledge elements that facilitate interaction with the job market and can be carried out through various modalities, such as Internships and Tutorials and Project Work.
There is active collaboration with the job market, directly with institutions and companies, which in most cases demonstrate sensitivity and interest in projects presented by universities.
The common goal becomes facilitating students' entry into the job market and contributing, through the dissemination of knowledge and skills, to the socio-economic development of the territory.
The CdS also benefits from opportunities offered by the University of Chieti-Pescara "G. d'Annunzio," which, as promoter and coordinator of the InnovAction project presented under the LLP-Leonardo da Vinci program (People in the Labour Market) and approved by the European Union through the Italian National Agency for Leonardo (ISFOL), provides scholarships for 24-week transnational internships to be carried out in European Union countries.
It should be noted, however, that as a three-year CdS, one of the priority objectives is always the further enhancement of initiatives aimed at guiding CdS students toward master's degree programs.

STUDENT OPINIONS Based on information obtained from questionnaires administered by the University, which constitute the source from which the data commented here are extracted, the evaluation of the Study Program by students is in line with the overall trend derived from previous years' census. The overall score derived from the opinions of attending students is 3.49 out of 4. For non-attending students, almost half indicate work activity as the main reason for non-attendance or reduced attendance. These results stem particularly from the interest in the topics covered in the courses, the ability of the Study Program's faculty to stimulate engagement with various disciplines, and the appreciation of the organization, communication, and conduct of the assessment exams. Good also is the evaluation of the required study load, the teaching materials provided, and the consistency between the frontal teaching delivered and the content previewed on the Study Program's respective web pages. The judgment on the adequacy of preliminary knowledge (acquired through previous academic and training segments) for mastering the exam program remains at the same level as the previous academic year. The commitment to increasing attention to the introductory and preparatory segment of the various courses offered, particularly in the common two-year period, constitutes a distinguishing feature of the Study Program, which must however address the diverse academic background of the student population (see Table C1). Students' judgment is fully in line regarding the faculty's ability to present teaching topics appropriately to the complexity of the respective subjects, as well as their availability (during lectures and office hours) to provide useful and effective clarifications on the topics covered. Among the suggestions highlighted by the questionnaire, particular interest is given to improving the educational synergy between various courses, which already distinguishes the Study Program, both in terms of the gradual nature of the educational offer over the three-year period and from the perspective of numerous cross-references (content and/or methodological) between many of the courses offered. Given the specific nature of the Study Program, which, like every interdisciplinary course, must calibrate the offer not only from the perspective of CFUs delivered in various SSDs but also the coherence of the overall cultural proposal, the point mentioned is constantly under attention. The Coordinator of the Study Program, in collaboration with the AQ Groups and the Review Committee, has continued to implement specific measures—particularly monitoring and coordinating the semester distribution of courses and the weekly allocation of frontal lecture hours (as extensively documented in the Study Program's minutes)—to avoid, where possible, overlaps and/or overcrowding in the course schedule. Particular effort has also been devoted to organizing the tutoring, which takes place, with student collaboration, in defined hours and spaces, thereby more specifically and effectively supporting both the faculty's activities and the University's various information desks. In general, it is positively noteworthy that faculty and students of the Study Program can easily express their observations and improvement proposals in individual and collective settings.

GRADUATE OPINIONS Based on data from the annual AlmaLaurea survey (updated April 2023), 86% of graduates report overall satisfaction with the CDS. Graduate satisfaction is largely confirmed by all evaluation indices, particularly regarding the study load of courses in relation to the effectiveness and duration of the program, exam organization, and computer workstations, with some indices exceeding double (teacher-student relationships, classroom suitability, adherence to schedules) or even triple (humanities library system). To confirm the picture emerging from the data, over 60% of interviewed graduates state they would re-enroll in the CDS in its current configuration. Additionally, students appreciate the Erasmus agreements active between the CDS and several important European universities, the high number of affiliated associations and entities (not only regional) where internships can be carried out, as well as the positive relationship between the CDS and the main educational and cultural entities in the regional territory. Among others, the established relationships between CDS-affiliated faculty and the Abruzzo section of the Italian Philosophical Society, as well as with departments of major educational institutions in the provinces of Chieti and Pescara, can be mentioned. These relationships, as reported by students themselves, enable a valid dialogue and transfer of competencies between secondary school philosophical education and the CDS, also evidenced by the organization of numerous inter-institutional initiatives on philosophical-pedagogical and intercultural themes.
Learning Skills
Through appropriate teaching methodologies and the structure of the entire training plan, the Educational Sciences track aims to progressively develop those abilities (attention, continuity, and consistency in learning) that enable the establishment of self-formation processes, transfer of knowledge across different fields, in the perspective of 'learning to learn'. The course also aims to develop in students the ability to learn in professional updating processes and in the context of personal research to enhance knowledge for practical application.
Expected learning skills outcomes will be periodically verified through traditional assessment methods within individual courses and the training internship activities.
The Philosophy track aims to develop in students the abilities of sustained attention, application, and critical sensitivity that enable the deepening of acquired knowledge at subsequent study levels, particularly fostering the formation of a specific sensitivity for applying and deepening the competencies gained.
This objective will primarily be pursued through supervised study hours within the teaching activities of each discipline. The achievement of this objective will be verified both during the course through systematic interaction activated during lectures, and in the final evaluation related to each discipline.
University Communication to CUN As reported by the CUN, the required consultation has been updated, the number of basic and characterizing CFUs has been reduced, and SSDs have been reduced in areas with limited CFUs.
The data entered do not indicate anomalies in the RAD and the course offering simulator.
