Brief Course Description The Bachelor's Degree in Philosophy and Educational Sciences is structured into two tracks corresponding to the reference classes and simultaneously integrated:
- Philosophy
- Educational Sciences The Philosophy track aims to provide students with a thorough general philosophical education characterized by mastery of the historical trajectory of Western philosophical thought from antiquity to the present, and comprehensive knowledge of the main themes, authors, and fundamental currents that characterize different periods of the philosophical tradition. In this sense, the training path provided within the Study Course aims to introduce students to the analysis, conceptual understanding, and historical contextualization of some of the most relevant works within the individual periods of the philosophical tradition. A specific educational objective of the Study Course is also to achieve general knowledge of the themes and fundamental issues characterizing different fields of philosophical inquiry (theoretical, epistemological, linguistic, aesthetic, ethical, religious), and to acquire a solid critical-argumentative ability in these research areas. Graduates must also achieve knowledge and skills in textual practice, conceptual and terminological deepening, mastery of the historical method and analytical argumentation, as well as possessing the necessary tools for research (at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian, bibliographic research, computer skills, etc.).
The training path aims to provide students with a solid and well-structured basic philosophical education, both historically and thematically-problematically. Additionally, as an integrative support, a balanced range of courses of a historical, literary, and socio-psychopedagogical nature has been introduced, aimed at providing an adequate general humanistic contextualization of the philosophical issues addressed within the Study Course.
The training path also aims to provide students with fundamental prerequisites necessary for a potential future entry into the secondary school teaching circuit, for which, in addition to philosophical courses, it is useful to integrate those of a general historical and socio-psychopedagogical nature.
Graduates in the Educational Sciences track will acquire basic theoretical knowledge and operational skills in pedagogical sciences and methodological-didactic disciplines, integrated with differentiated areas of knowledge and skills in philosophical, sociological, and psychological disciplines. They will also acquire knowledge and skills on educational themes in general, in their various dimensions, including those related to discrimination, integration, and multiculturalism, through training activities aimed at analyzing social, cultural, and territorial realities, enabling the elaboration, implementation, management, and evaluation of educational projects suitable for the current social and professional complexity.
The path thus enables the acquisition of pedagogical-planning, methodological-didactic, communicative-relational, and organizational-institutional skills to intervene in training processes even through modern educational technologies.
The path is finally integrated with teaching activities aimed at acquiring knowledge of at least one foreign language in addition to Italian and adequate computer and communication tools.
The acquisition of specific knowledge and skills in pedagogical, psychological, and sociological sciences will enable our graduates to intervene in the field of prevention of educational discomfort and various forms of marginality and educational-family deviance through network work and inter-institutional collaboration.
Crucial is the acquisition of the ability to interact with users and collaborate with schools and agencies (public and private structures, non-profit organizations, volunteer associations, etc.) present in the territory, which deal with childhood, pre-adolescence, adolescence, and elderly care, in order to counter, in a formative perspective, the effects of educational deficits and marginality with appropriate response strategies. Internship activities, as part of the training path, will take place at cultural, educational, socio-health, territorial, and political-economic agencies.
The path also aims to create knowledge and skills to optimize the valorization of human resources, particularly cultural ones.
Within the integrative training activities of both tracks, students can engage with new cultural scenarios in which philosophical and pedagogical reflection of our era can productively be inserted.
External Effectiveness For graduates who do not opt for enrollment in Master's degree classes or the training paths for teaching in the humanities field, the CDS enables effective entry into a wide range of additional occupational sectors (journalism, publishing, communication, information and human resources management, non-profit activities, cultural promotion) and to apply for roles in public and private entities (particularly museums, archives, libraries), as well as in educational structures and community and social service organizations (with particular regard to the prevention and reduction of discomfort, volunteer organizations, social cooperation, and early childhood educational contexts). Considering the limitations of employment statistics for graduates of a three-year CDS, the following is highlighted. Within the first year after completing the course, approximately 71.4% of graduates in the combined L19-L5 classes are enrolled in a Master's degree program (compared to a University average of 68%): among those enrolled in the second level, the majority combine their chosen path with internship/practicum. The percentage of L5 graduates enrolling in the Master's program is close to 100%. For L19 graduates, considering their specific acquired training competencies and respective occupational fields, the percentage of those enrolling in a Master's program appears substantially in line with the previous academic year. Overall, nearly 55.6% of graduates are employed, two-thirds of whom are working while studying for the second level, with an increase of over 5 percentage points compared to the previous academic year, and in line with the national youth employment situation. Of these, approximately 40% extensively use the skills acquired through the degree, and 90% consider the degree acquisition relevant and effective for their entry into the chosen field.
Specific Educational Objectives and Description of the Training Path The Bachelor's Degree in Philosophy and Educational Sciences is structured into two tracks corresponding to the reference classes and simultaneously integrated:
- Philosophy
- Educational Sciences Graduates in the Educational Sciences track will acquire basic theoretical knowledge and operational skills in pedagogical sciences and methodological-didactic disciplines, integrated with differentiated areas of knowledge and skills in philosophical, sociological, and psychological disciplines, also related to the field of human capital management. They will also acquire knowledge and skills on educational themes in general, in their various dimensions, including those related to discrimination, integration, and multiculturalism, through training activities aimed at analyzing social, cultural, and territorial realities, enabling the elaboration, implementation, management, and evaluation of educational projects suitable for the current social and professional complexity.
The path thus enables the acquisition of pedagogical-planning, methodological-didactic, communicative-relational, and organizational-institutional skills to intervene in training processes even through modern educational technologies.
The path is finally integrated with teaching activities aimed at acquiring knowledge of at least one foreign language in addition to Italian and adequate computer and communication tools.
Indeed, the complexity of today's social, cultural, and productive scenarios and the continuous transformation of knowledge construction and dissemination processes highlight the need for renewed professional figures equipped with knowledge and skills applicable in the field of education and training.
The path aims to form an operator with relational and cultural skills. Foundational competencies for this educational professionalism are the ability to ideate, plan, program, implement, carry out, and verify activities aimed at developing and forming in the fields of play, motor skills, language, growth, and psychophysical well-being. This professionalism aims at valorizing the cognitive, creative, expressive, and relational potential of every individual.
The path is therefore aimed at acquiring knowledge related to child development and the linguistic-expressive, communicative, and logical tools indispensable for valorizing the plurality of learning experiences.
The acquisition of specific knowledge and skills in pedagogical, psychological, and sociological sciences will enable our graduates to intervene in the field of prevention of educational discomfort and various forms of marginality and educational-family deviance through network work and inter-institutional collaboration.
Crucial is the acquisition of the ability to interact with users and collaborate with schools and agencies (public and private structures, non-profit organizations, volunteer associations, etc.) present in the territory, which deal with childhood, pre-adolescence, adolescence, and elderly care, in order to counter, in a formative perspective, the effects of educational deficits and marginality with appropriate response strategies. Internship activities, as part of the training path, will take place at educational and professional institutions.
The path also aims to create knowledge and skills to optimize the valorization of human resources, particularly cultural ones.
Human capital is of fundamental importance for the success of any organized reality, regardless of its size and nature. Any innovation, technology, or organization has the human and cultural factor as its foundational and defining element: thus, creative genius must be enhanced. The challenge for any organization now, especially, lies in the competencies of 'people', who, with their qualities, imagination, and creativity, combined with appropriate skills and knowledge, can help, predict, and manage the complexity of the future.
The course is therefore also aimed at training a professional capable of operating in both the field of professional training and in the management of human and intellectual capital.
The Philosophy track aims to provide students with a thorough general philosophical education characterized by mastery of the historical trajectory of Western philosophical thought from antiquity to the present, and comprehensive knowledge of the main themes, authors, and fundamental currents that characterize different periods of the philosophical tradition. In this sense, the training path provided within the Study Course aims to introduce students to the analysis, conceptual understanding, and historical contextualization of some of the most relevant works within the individual periods of the philosophical tradition. A specific educational objective of the Study Course is also to achieve general knowledge of the themes and fundamental issues characterizing different fields of philosophical inquiry (theoretical, epistemological, linguistic, aesthetic, ethical, religious), and to acquire a solid critical-argumentative ability in these research areas. Graduates must also achieve knowledge and skills in textual practice, conceptual and terminological deepening, mastery of the historical method and analytical argumentation, as well as possessing the necessary tools for research (at least one European Union language, in addition to Italian, bibliographic research, computer skills, etc.).
The training path aims to provide students with a solid and well-structured basic philosophical education, both historically and thematically-problematically. Additionally, as an integrative support, a balanced range of courses of a historical, literary, and socio-psychopedagogical nature has been introduced, aimed at providing an adequate general humanistic contextualization of the philosophical issues addressed within the Study Course.
The training path also aims to provide students with fundamental prerequisites necessary for a potential future entry into the secondary school teaching circuit. To this end, on the solid foundation of philosophical courses, a significantly increased credit quota of general historical and socio-psychopedagogical courses has been integrated.
Within the integrative training activities of both tracks, courses of an economic, political, and medical-anthropological nature have also been included, aiming to present students with new cultural scenarios in which philosophical reflection of our era could productively be inserted. These new scenarios are intended to later connect with the training design of some Master's degree paths.
Students from both tracks must complete internship activities at educational, extracurricular, professional institutions, and the business world.
Opinions of Entities and Companies with Internship/Placement Agreements All CDS graduates must complete professional internships. According to data provided by the CDS Internship Service Manager, in the 2022-23 academic year, 50 students completed internship activities, substantially in line with the previous academic year. In 2022, a total of 29 agreements were activated, of which 9 related to social cooperatives, 8 to schools, 7 to nurseries, 3 to libraries, and 2 to companies. General data provided by the PQA, derived from student surveys, confirm an evaluation of approximately 3 out of 4 regarding the support provided for completing the internship and overall satisfaction with the internship experience. At the final internship examination, a substantially consistent picture was confirmed with previous years' charts, also provided in the attachment, which is summarized here, showing overall very positive data on the student experience and the contribution of the internship to the training path and clarification of potential occupational choices. The data are corroborated on the host entities' side, which highlight as strengths of the interns a good ability to organize individual work and interact in group work, as well as to identify with assigned roles, demonstrating interest and motivation towards assigned tasks. Particular emphasis is placed on a sense of responsibility (punctuality, rigor, regularity, respect for rules), availability towards others, and finally, appreciation of diversity and multiculturalism, which is of great relevance in all contemporary educational contexts. The evaluation of basic skills (oral and written expression) is average, as is the evaluation of critical-planning and management skills (selection of work materials, autonomy in performing assigned tasks, problem resolution). Theoretical preparation useful for the internship and knowledge of the specific sector in which the intern performs their experience are considered improvable.

Consultation with National and International Organizations Representing Goods and Service Production, Professions (Subsequent Consultations)
The President and responsible members of Groups, Committees, and Disciplinary Areas of the CDS have, since its establishment, carried out an intensive exchange and dialogue, both individual and collective, with representatives and realities of the educational (particularly school), productive, professional, and institutional world, at both national and regional levels. To make ongoing consultations more efficient and to track their evolution, the CDS has established two lines of action:
1) On March 8, 2018, it decided to establish an Advisory Committee with entities and organizations that are social partners and stakeholders regarding the CDS's training offer. In accordance with ANVUR Guidelines (August 10, 2017), this Committee serves as a forum for reflection consistent with the cultural profiles of graduates, with the task of reflecting, deepening, and providing elements regarding the actual occupational potential of graduates, as well as planning seminars and workshops. The Committee consists of CDS-affiliated faculty members (representing different disciplinary and learning areas) and representatives from the world of work, culture, and research;
2) To support the Committee's activities, the CDS has also decided to use consultation questionnaires as tools to enhance and broaden the scope of consulted entities. Depending on the CDS's needs, questionnaires may be used in parallel with the Advisory Committee meeting or as an alternative, varying according to specific needs for data collection, type of interlocutors, logistics (in-person/remote), and the timing of the CDS's Quality Assurance processes.
3) Periodic meetings of the CONCLEP (National Coordination of Bachelor's Degree Courses for Professional Socio-Pedagogical Educators and Pedagogists) are held. In particular, in light of the Bill on 'Provisions regarding the ordering of pedagogical and educational professions and establishment of relevant professional registers' (Senate Bill 788/2024), new consultations will be conducted for necessary adjustments to study paths in relation to public and institutional accreditation processes for the professions formed by the Bachelor's Degree Course.
Minutes of the Committee meetings, which will naturally be integrated and enriched over time, as well as the results of questionnaires administered through specific data collection campaigns and time frames established by the CDS, are available as attached documents, up to the 2019/2020 academic year. For the 2022/23 academic year, previous documents are considered valid. The reconvocation of the external component of the Committee will therefore occur at least biennially, also considering the evolution of the regulatory and health framework and the complex dynamics connected to it.
Entry, Path, and Exit Data The cohort of students enrolled in the CDS for the 2022/23 academic year (out of a total of 548 students, 410 in progress) slightly exceeds the reference size indicated by DM 47 of January 30, 2013, for classes L19 and L5. The number of new enrollments, equal to 191 (a value nearly in line with the previous cohort), confirms the balanced development of the CDS. The latest available data on the number of graduates (which should be compared with the AlmaLaurea data presented and commented on in section B7, to which reference is made) relates to the year 2022, showing an increase of approximately 5% compared to the previous three years. Graduates in progress amount to approximately 46.7%. The average age of graduates is about 28 years (27 for the previous cohort), with a student population predominantly female (about 72%). The average grade of 91 graduates is 100.9/110 (higher than the previous year's average). Regarding secondary education, most graduates come from high schools (82.2%), while the remaining percentage comes from technical (15.6%) and professional institutes (2.2%), with an average grade of 76.9/100. The student base is decidedly supra-regional for each reference cohort and remains in line with data already processed in the previous Single Accreditation Sheet: if 61.1% of new enrollments come from the provinces of Chieti and Pescara and other Abruzzo provinces, the remaining percentage (38.9%, slightly higher than the previous year) comes from other regions (predominantly Molise, Puglia, Campania, Basilicata). New enrollments have backgrounds in various types of secondary education, with a prevalence of classical and scientific high school backgrounds, and to a lesser extent socio-psychopedagogical and linguistic. Analysis of previous cohorts shows a relatively consistent distribution. From the students' results, particularly regarding the achievement of minimum access requirements (OFA), a medium-good preparation is evident. Available data do not allow identification of teaching-related critical issues regarding nature, quality, or quantity. The CDS's teaching path is primarily aimed at basic training for enrollment in Master's degree courses. To this end, activities are generally oriented towards this goal, although graduates, particularly those in class L19, may find more immediate employment opportunities in the fields of early childhood and adolescent services.
Characteristics of the Final Exam For the completion of the degree, the Educational Sciences track requires the written elaboration of a research project, either project-oriented or analytical, focused on one of the disciplines characterizing the chosen path and the competencies specific to the educator and expert in training and human resource development.
In the Philosophy track, the final exam requires students to engage with one or more texts by one or more authors, based on the acquisition of some essential lines of secondary literature. The exam will concretely consist of the elaboration, writing, and public discussion of a written text.
Final Exam Execution The final exam must be requested at least four months in advance to a course faculty member (supervisor), by completing a specific form to be submitted to the Student Secretariat. The supervisor will guide the graduate's work by providing scientific and bibliographic guidance, analytical tools, and text revision.
One month before the graduation session date, the graduate will submit to the Student Secretariat a form with the approved title of the final exam.
The final exam is presented within a graduation session (summer, autumn, extraordinary) in oral form, possibly supported by computer tools, in the presence of a commission of five faculty members, including the supervisor. At the end of the session, the commission, based on the candidate's academic record and the presentation and discussion of the final exam, issues a judgment expressed as 110/110, possibly with the addition of 'cum laude'.
Extended Description:
Nature of the Final Exam.
The final exam consists of the following acts:
- Presentation by the student of a written work on a specific topic, called thesis, related to one of the courses in the student's study plan, developed under the supervision of a faculty member, called supervisor;
- Approval of the thesis by the supervisor;
- Discussion and approval of the thesis, called graduation session, before a specific commission, called the graduation exam commission;
- Evaluation by the commission of the entire study path, the thesis, and its discussion.
Thesis Topic and Language.
- The student may write the thesis only in a discipline whose course has been or is being taught within the Study Course, and for which the student has passed the exam or been exempted from it (referred to as the 'affiliated course').
- The language in which the thesis is written and the language of the discussion before the graduation exam commission are governed by Article 35, Paragraph 4, of the University Academic Regulations, which is referred to: "The final exam for a bachelor's or master's degree and the respective thesis may be conducted in a foreign language, upon favorable and motivated opinion of the Course Council, ensuring the possibility of effective evaluation due to sufficient expertise within the faculty body. In any case, the thesis written in a foreign language must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian."
Student Responsibilities.
- The declaration of intent to submit a request for admission to the final exam (denoted as 'Form A' or 'Thesis Request Form') must be submitted to the Student Secretariat at least four months before the start of the week scheduled for the graduation session for which the student is applying. In this form, the thesis topic, not the title, must be indicated.
- The admission request for the final exam (denoted as 'Form C' or 'Thesis Title and Affiliated Course Form') must be submitted to the Student Secretariat at least one month before the start of the week scheduled for the graduation session for which the student is applying. In this form, the thesis title and the affiliated course must be indicated; the formulation of the thesis topic indicated in 'Form A' may differ from the thesis title indicated in 'Form C'; the only person authorized to evaluate and certify the conformity of the thesis title in 'Form C' with the thesis topic in 'Form A' is the supervisor who signs 'Form C'.
- The Student Secretariat may require the student to submit additional documentation or complete further acts necessary for the administrative procedures of the final exam. The student must be aware of the Student Secretariat's regulations and their scheduling and comply with them.
Supervisor Designation and Responsibilities.
- Only a faculty member with a formal relationship with the University of Chieti-Pescara 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' and who teaches or has taught the relevant course may serve as supervisor.
- The supervisor is responsible for guiding the student in preparing the thesis to achieve the specific educational objectives of the Study Course through the acquisition of knowledge, the ability to apply it, independent judgment, communication skills, and learning abilities as described in the Study Course description.
- Approval of the thesis by the supervisor is manifested through the signing of the required documentation that the student must submit to the Student Secretariat.
Graduation Exam Commission Designation and Responsibilities.
- The appointment and composition of the graduation exam commission are governed primarily by Article 37, Paragraphs 1-4, of the University Academic Regulations, which is referred to: "1. Graduation exam commissions for bachelor's, master's, and specialization diplomas are appointed by the Head of the Competent Department or, after consultation with Departments, by the President of the relevant School, if established, who also sets the work schedule. It is possible to operate simultaneously with multiple commissions. 2. Graduation exam commissions consist of at least five and no more than seven members for bachelor's and specialization diplomas; at least seven and no more than eleven members for master's degrees, including the President. 3. The majority of commission members must be permanent professors of the University. 4. The President of the Commission is, among the members, the first-tier professor with the greatest seniority or, in the absence, the associate professor with the greatest seniority, unless otherwise determined by the regulations of the competent teaching structures. The President must ensure the full regularity of the exam and the adherence of final evaluations to the general criteria established by the bodies responsible for the Study Course."
- Pursuant to Article 35, Paragraph 5, Letter d, of the University Academic Regulations, it is specified that, subject to the provisions of Article 37, Paragraph 3, any individual whose scientific qualification in relation to the thesis subject has been verified by the Course Council may serve as a commission member.
- The graduation exam commission evaluates the student's entire study path, the thesis presented, and the student's proficiency in discussing it; at the end of the evaluation, it issues either a judgment of failure to pass the final exam or a judgment of passing the final exam expressed as a final grade; in case of passing, the commission proclaims the student a doctor in the class of the degree to which they are enrolled and declares the final grade awarded.
Final Grade Determination.
- The final grade ranges from 66 to 110 and is composed of the sum, up to a maximum of 110 points, of the weighted average of the exam grades expressed in 110ths and the thesis grade.
- The weighted average of the exam grades expressed in 110ths is obtained by expressing in 110ths the weighted average of the exam grades expressed in 30ths. Grades of a simple declaration of suitability or passing an exam do not contribute to the weighted average calculation, nor do grades from exams taken outside the study plan. All grades from exams passed in the study plan, including those from independently chosen activities (called 'TAF D'), contribute to the weighted average calculation, with the following two clarifications: a grade of '30 and lode' contributes with a value of 30.10; grades associated with excess CFUs from independently chosen activities exceeding the planned CFUs do not contribute to the weighted average calculation.
- Following the thesis discussion, if the graduation commission deems the final exam passed, it assigns a thesis grade ranging from 0 to 6 points. This score will be assigned considering the quality and scope of the thesis and the student's proficiency in presenting the topics clearly and eruditely.
- If the sum of the weighted average expressed in 110ths and the thesis grade exceeds 110, the graduation commission may award 'cum laude'. 'Cum laude' is awarded as an expression of the relevance of the results achieved by the student in the thesis work. The award of 'cum laude' must be proposed by the supervisor and requires unanimous agreement by the thesis commission.
Conduct of the Final Exam.
The modalities for conducting the final exam are governed by Article 35, Paragraphs 9 and 11, of the University Academic Regulations, which is referred to: "9. The student may withdraw from the exam until the moment they are dismissed by the Commission President to proceed with the grading decision, which occurs without the student's or outsiders' presence. 11. The conduct of bachelor's, master's, specialization, and doctoral exams is public, and the proclamation of the final result is public."
Final Exam Schedule.
The definition of the final exam schedule is governed by Article 36 of the University Academic Regulations, which is referred to: "1. The final exam schedule for the bachelor's and master's degrees is set annually by the competent Department or School, if established, and must include at least four sessions distributed across three periods: May to July; October to December; February to April. 2. Final exams for each academic year must be conducted by April 30 of the following academic year; students enrolled in the previous academic year may take them without re-enrollment."
Reference Clause.
For matters not expressly regulated above, refer to the University Academic Regulations (see below, Articles 35-37) and relevant legal provisions.
University Academic Regulations (Articles 35-37):
Article 35 - Final Exam and Awarding of Degrees
1. Degrees are awarded upon passing a final exam. The number of CFUs attributed to it must be commensurate with the time required for preparation. The modalities of conduct and evaluation criteria are regulated by the Study Course's Academic Regulations.
2. The bachelor's final exam typically involves the student presenting a written and/or graphical work on paper or digital support, which does not require particular originality and should constitute an important individual training opportunity to complete the path.
3. For the Master's degree, a written thesis, also in digital form, elaborated personally by the student under the guidance of a supervisor, is required.
4. The bachelor's and Master's final exams and their respective works and theses may be conducted in a foreign language, upon favorable and motivated opinion of the Course Council, ensuring the possibility of effective evaluation due to sufficient expertise within the faculty body. In any case, the work and thesis written in a foreign language must be accompanied by an adequate summary in Italian.
5. It is the responsibility of the Departments or Schools where the Study Courses are based to:
a) regulate the modalities of organizing final exams;
b) ensure uniformity of evaluation criteria for each type of final exam, also in relation to the weight to be assigned to the student's academic record;
c) regulate the modalities of assigning works and theses and designating supervisors and possible co-supervisors, ensuring the broadest use of the Department or School's available competencies and a balanced distribution of related workloads;
d) establish the modalities for the possible assignment of co-supervisor and commission member roles to external experts as subject matter specialists, subject to the verification by the Course Council of their scientific and/or professional qualification in relation to the dissertation or dissertations under examination.
6. The evaluation commissions, appointed under the following Article 37, evaluate the candidate, taking into account the entire study path and the conduct of the final exam.
7. To pass the bachelor's and Master's degree exams, a minimum score of sixty-six is required. The commissions have 110 points; if the final grade is 110, and the relevance of the results achieved by the candidate is confirmed, 'cum laude' may be awarded unanimously.
8. To pass the specialization diploma exam, a minimum score of forty-two is required. The commissions have 70 points; if the final grade is 70, and the excellence of the results achieved by the candidate is confirmed, 'cum laude' may be awarded unanimously.
9. The student may withdraw from the exam until the moment they are dismissed by the Commission President to proceed with the grading decision, which occurs without the student's or outsiders' presence.
10. Department or School Regulations establish the procedures to follow in case the candidate does not achieve the required minimum score.
11. The conduct of bachelor's, master's, specialization, and doctoral exams is public, and the proclamation of the final result is public.
12. The modalities for issuing double, multiple, or joint degrees are regulated by the relevant agreements.
Article 36 - Final Exam Schedule
1. The final exam schedule for the bachelor's and Master's degrees is set annually by the competent Department or School, if established, and must include at least four sessions distributed across three periods: May to July; October to December; February to April.
2. Final exams for each academic year must be conducted by April 30 of the following academic year; students enrolled in the previous academic year may take them without re-enrollment.
University Academic Regulations ex D.M. n. 270/2004.
Article 37 - Evaluation Commissions for Final Exams
1. Commissions for evaluating bachelor's, Master's, and specialization diploma exams are appointed by the Head of the Competent Department or, after consultation with Departments, by the President of the relevant School, if established, who also sets the work schedule. It is possible to operate simultaneously with multiple commissions.
2. Evaluation commissions consist of at least five and no more than seven members for bachelor's and specialization diploma exams; at least seven and no more than eleven members for Master's degrees, including the President.
3. The majority of commission members must be permanent professors of the University.
4. The President of the Commission is, among the members, the first-tier professor with the greatest seniority or, in the absence, the associate professor with the greatest seniority, unless otherwise determined by the regulations of the competent teaching structures. The President must ensure the full regularity of the exam and the adherence of final evaluations to the general criteria established by the bodies responsible for the Study Course.
5. In the case of inter-university Study Courses, the evaluation commission must include at least two faculty members from each participating university.

Admission Requirements To be admitted to the degree course, it is necessary to hold a five-year upper secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent, or a four-year upper secondary school diploma plus the corresponding supplementary year. Additionally, a good general cultural level, logical reasoning ability, competence in understanding Italian texts, and basic mathematical knowledge are required (and verified). These requirements are publicized through various information channels (brochures, institutional website, orientation at secondary schools, and on-site orientation).

Verification of the required knowledge for admission is carried out by a commission (appointed by the Degree Course Council and composed of at least three members of the same Council) through entrance interviews appropriately scheduled and publicized. By decision of 15.02.2021, as amended in the electronic minutes of 25.02.2022, the Degree Course Council decided to exempt students from secondary schools who participated in the agreed lessons within orientation and PCTO activities and passed the final verification tests at an advanced level from the entrance interview.

At the end of the interviews, the commission immediately communicates the verification outcome to the students. The verification outcome does not prevent enrollment, and in case of deficiencies, may result in the assignment of additional mandatory requirements (OFA) to be fulfilled by the end of September of the first year of the course, through ongoing tutoring by a faculty member from the relevant areas, designated by the commission that conducted the interview.

If, at the end of the tutoring period, the faculty member/tutor does not consider the OFA fulfilled, the student may enroll in second-year exams only after acquiring at least 18 CFU in basic or characterizing subjects.

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
The graduate of the Economics, Businesses and Financial Markets Course has the ability to analyze the economic and financial framework; is able to collect and select data and information to support the analyses to be carried out, the decisions to be made, and the activities to be implemented. Possesses skills to solve specific problems in the economic, business and financial fields.
Is able to interpret economically relevant data and knows how to analyze and use them in decision-making processes. The possession of such competencies related to autonomy of judgment is guaranteed within the individual training activities through the specificity of each teaching discipline's role, taking into account also cultural, technological and methodological changes.
The verification of the possession of autonomy of judgment is carried out within the evaluation of the courses in the student's individual study plan and through the assessment of the degree of autonomous and critical processing ability of the topic of the final exam.

Training periods The University promotes the employability and employment of its graduates through the activation of an effective network of relationships between the University, Businesses and the Research system aimed at developing and consolidating a virtuous system of relationships and services, oriented both to facilitate the 'communication' between business needs, employment processes and the impacts on educational plans, and to provide substance and continuity to the transition phase to work for knowledge resources. For this reason, it offers the opportunity to carry out the alternance between study and work in order to facilitate professional choices through direct knowledge of the working world.
Regarding the Course of Study, it is specified that part of the activities listed still refer to the previous Course of Study named "Economy, Markets and Development", which from the academic year 2021/22 adopts the name "Economy, Businesses and Financial Markets".
The activities are coordinated by Prof. Furia in her capacity as President of the Course of Study, with the support of Ms. Elvira Vitiello, Academic-Administrative Manager.
Students enrolled in the Course of Study in Economy, Businesses and Financial Markets may carry out internship activities at conventioned entities with the University, for training purposes that are consistent with the educational path of the Course of Study, whether with entities and companies directly conventioned with the Course of Study.
Based on the individual convention established to date between the Course of Study and the Hosting Entity, the internship is founded on a training project that defines the location, duration, objectives, methods of the internship and the intern's obligations. For each intern, an internal tutor (a Course of Study lecturer) and an enterprise tutor are identified.
At the end of the internship period, the company has always submitted a final report. To enable a more comprehensive assessment of the activities carried out by the student, the Course of Study approved on 27.11.2019 a detailed form that the enterprise tutor must return at the end of the internship; on 28.01.2020, for the same purpose, another form was approved for the interns. Therefore, at the conclusion of the internship, the student submits two evaluation forms, one completed by the student themselves and one by the enterprise tutor. In 2023, 38 training projects were initiated and 32 conventions were activated.

Workplace Guidance The Placement Service is managed by the University's Orientation, Studies and Work Division.
For outgoing orientation, understood as vocational and professional orientation specifically aimed at facilitating the entry of graduates into the job market, the University has established a full-fledged placement structure designed to increase the employment and employability of its students through the implementation of assisted workplace guidance pathways. To this end, the University has developed the online platform S.T.A.R.T. (Stages, Internships, Advanced Training, Research, Territory and Placement) with the aim of strengthening an active network of relationships between the University, businesses and research systems, to develop a virtuous process of relationships and services oriented towards both facilitating the 'communication' between business needs, employment processes and educational outcomes, and providing substance and continuity to the transition phase to work for qualified knowledge resources that enable the economic/production system to meet the ongoing challenges of the market. In particular, for workplace guidance, the computer platform JOB is active, which is linked to the aforementioned post-graduation orientation program S.T.A.R.T. and is the tool used by the University's Placement Service to carry out mediation activities.
The responsibility lies with Prof. Davide Quaglione.
Following the formalization of connections with representatives of the territory (establishment of an advisory committee, to which additional stakeholders have recently been added), from the academic year 2018/19, professionalizing seminars have been activated, held by the stakeholders themselves and other entrepreneurs and experts from the world of work.
Among the Course of Study initiatives, the CAREER DAY 2024 is highlighted, organized by Prof. Fontana in collaboration with AIDP Abruzzo-Molise (Italian Association for Personnel Management) and the Pescara Employment Center. At its first edition, held on May 8, 2024, the Career Day 2024 was dedicated to the meeting between Companies/Institutions and students of the Pescara Department Study Courses. The day began with company presentations, followed by one-to-one interviews between the companies and students.

At the Course Council meeting of 10 March 2023, the student representative reported some criticalities noted by second-year students (especially commuters) regarding the schedule of optional courses. It was noted that these courses are common to the second and third years and sometimes their lecture times coincide with those of mandatory courses. Considering the availability of classrooms and professors, a greater attention to this point was requested, and in extreme cases, the preparation of two separate lists of optional courses for the second and third years.
At the Course Council meeting of 28 March 2023, the point was discussed, and the President, while reiterating that the lecture schedule is strongly influenced by classroom availability, emphasized that the student's proposal to separate courses between the first and second years would be seriously considered for the next academic year (given the deadlines, the improvement could be implemented for the 24.25 academic year).

Applying knowledge and understanding
The graduate of the Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets degree course knows quantitative methods for applied analysis in microeconomic, macroeconomic, and financial fields, enabling them to make forecasts and estimates regarding economic development processes, market dynamics, and business operations. They are able to use mathematical-statistical and economic knowledge in theoretical and applied studies and business activities. They can work in groups, conduct research on predefined topics, and develop empirical analyses of economic phenomena (both micro and macro), combining a solid theoretical foundation with the most up-to-date analytical techniques.
The teaching approach, based on frontal lectures and continuous tutoring activities, provides that training is accompanied by in-depth study and elaboration of knowledge through the student's personal study activities. It is through a sufficient personal re-elaboration of the content acquired during lectures that the student concretely measures their level of ability to apply the knowledge gained. The training path also includes, alongside frontal lectures, computer lab exercises, case discussions, and meetings with entrepreneurs, managers, and professionals.
Learning skills
The graduate of the Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets degree course is able to apply the methods and tools of learning developed with a high degree of autonomy, both in professional contexts and for undertaking subsequent specialized studies.
The ability to learn is assessed through verification methods carried out during training activities, tutoring activities during project execution, and through the completion of the final exam.
Knowledge and understanding
The graduate of the Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets degree course has a diversified and flexible education open to interdisciplinary exchanges; has fundamental knowledge in quantitative analysis as a tool for understanding economic, financial, and business activity phenomena, as well as market regulation. They have a good understanding of the main themes and issues in operating on national and international, real and financial markets, as well as the business economic system.
Knowledge and understanding are achieved through participation in frontal lectures, exercises, seminars, guided personal study, and independent study, as provided by the training activities in the study plan. Verifications, including interim assessments, verify learning and understanding outcomes and, if necessary, activate all tutoring and support mechanisms for optimal learning.

Brief Course Description
The Course of Study provides a training offer aimed at acquiring concrete and solid fundamental knowledge to operate in public and private companies, banks, and national and international financial intermediaries.
Training activities aim primarily at students learning the logic and tools necessary for implementing decisions by different actors operating in business and financial sectors.
Demand for training in the real sector comes particularly from companies, agencies, entities, and free professional activities that decide or support development programs; for the financial sector, it comes from banking and non-banking intermediaries, including insurance companies, leasing companies, confidi, investment funds, hedge funds, and numerous institutional investors whose role is fundamental for every economic growth process in an increasingly complex and globalized world.
Considering turnover dynamics and the growing importance of finance in socio-economic crises at national and international levels, there is a growing need for specific skills, such as those acquired through the training offered by the Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets Bachelor's Degree, to carry out activities supporting economic models.
Each academic year is divided into two semesters, with study loads appropriately distributed for a total of 180 CFU. The courses provided allow students to acquire concrete knowledge and skills in economic, financial, quantitative, business, and legal fields. Additionally, an English language course, an English-language mathematics laboratory for economics, a behavioral economics training laboratory, and external internship activities are provided.
Graduates in Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets are able to:
- Understand business operations, focusing on interactions between decisions made at the company level and the functioning of markets on which companies operate;
- Make rational decisions in different economic contexts, such as production sectors, financial markets, and institutional systems;
- Analyze economic problems from an interdisciplinary perspective, based on economic-financial, managerial, legal, statistical-mathematical, historical, and political-institutional competencies.
The Course of Study was designed to train Strategic Business Consultants and Market Experts. Junior professionals capable of addressing typical issues of economic realities operating in the business and financial sectors, particularly financial. At the same time, the training path provides the foundation for accessing a master's academic path, not only in the same fields as the three-year course but also in global market management, ecological transformation, and sustainable development.

Reasons for establishing multiple courses in the class
The course, compared to others activated in the same class, is able to provide a diversified and flexible training, ensuring mastery of fundamental analysis tools, as well as well-characterized professional skills, especially oriented towards understanding and governing the main issues of growth and development models. Particular attention is paid to the role of markets, regulations, and Agencies and Entities for development promotion, as well as to financial services markets for the functions supporting the real economy; diversification is evidenced by the presence of numerous disciplines not found in other Bachelor's Degree courses related to the same class L-33, exceeding the required differentiation requirement of at least 40 CFU.
Specific Educational Objectives and Course Description
The Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets Bachelor's Degree aims to provide training for understanding the functioning of modern economic systems through the acquisition of methodologies and tools used by decision-makers in different business contexts, as well as to provide the necessary knowledge for understanding the functioning of markets with specific (but not exclusive) reference to financial markets, through the study of methods and processes used by intermediaries, particularly banks and insurance companies.
Training activities aim primarily at students learning the logic and tools necessary for implementing decisions by different actors operating in the real and financial sectors. In particular, the Course of Study provides a training offer aimed at acquiring fundamental knowledge to operate in public and private companies, banks, and other financial intermediaries.
The course offers students a broad training, covering around a core of economic-quantitative disciplines, the essential methodological aspects of business, legal, historical, and political-institutional subjects. This training is aimed at ensuring students acquire all necessary analytical tools for understanding the basic mechanisms regulating the operations of public and private companies, financial intermediaries, and markets on which different economic agents interact.
The Course of Study provides adequate training for those aiming to work in business management and financial management, as well as at financial market intermediaries.
More specifically, the Course of Study:
- Provides tools to understand business operations, focusing on interactions between decisions made at the company level and the functioning of markets on which companies operate;
- Allows acquisition of necessary skills to make rational decisions in different economic contexts, such as production sectors, financial markets, and institutional systems, providing appropriate tools to identify and handle data supporting decisions and measure their impacts;
- Develops the ability to analyze economic problems from an interdisciplinary perspective, based on economic-financial, managerial, legal, statistical-mathematical, historical, and political-institutional competencies.
The Course of Study was designed to train junior professionals capable of addressing typical issues of business realities operating in both the real and financial sectors of the economy, thanks to the use of main explanatory and interpretive models of market functioning and their growth dynamics. The broad training ensures the ability to analyze both macro and micro and sectoral aspects, as well as to understand the role of public and private entities guiding growth and development processes and the role of financial institutions supporting these processes within the rules established by national and international regulators. At the same time, the training path provides the foundation for accessing a master's academic path, not only in the same fields as the three-year course but also in socioeconomic development programming and its management.
The interdisciplinary approach of the Course of Study will also allow addressing the complexity of territorial governance combined with socioeconomic development sustainability. Indeed, to ensure the adequacy of decision-making processes, the Course of Study allows acquisition of indispensable knowledge of organizational structures and legal institutions influencing economic choices and behaviors in general and financial markets in particular.
Opinions of organizations and companies with internship agreements
The data still refers mainly to students enrolled in the Economics, Markets and Development Course who can carry out internships at entities contracted with the University for training purposes consistent with the CdS training path, and with entities and companies directly contracted with the CdS.
Based on the single agreement between the CdS and the Host Entity, the internship is based on a training project defining the location, duration, objectives, methods, and obligations of the intern. Each intern is assigned an internal tutor (a CdS professor) and a company tutor. The duration of the curricular internship is set at 125 hours (5 CFU) for students in the 2020.21 cohort and 150 hours (6 CFU) for students in the 2021.22 cohort.
At the end of the internship period, the company has always submitted a final report. To allow a more comprehensive assessment of the student's activities, the CdS approved on November 27, 2019, an analytical form that the company tutor must return at the end of the internship; on January 28, 2020, the same form was approved for interns.
In the 2022/23 academic year, 30 agreements were activated, 33 training projects with 28 interns.

Consultation with representative organizations of goods and services production, professions (Course establishment)
The new structure of the CdS Didactic Ordinance is the result of a consultation process initiated with stakeholders represented in the Steering Committee, established on October 11, 2018, and was presented and discussed in the same Committee at the meeting on January 14, 2021.
In previous meetings (October 11, 2018, February 11, 2019, and November 6, 2019), stakeholders emphasized the opportunity to include in the training path content directly usable in the workplace, to provide acquisition of IT and/or language skills, to increase laboratory and seminar activities conducted by representatives of the business world and professions, and to increase the CFU allocated to training internships. Among the rationalization interventions suggested during the meetings, the possibility of modifying the course name to make it fully consistent with the training offer content was also proposed.
At the Steering Committee meeting on January 14, 2021, proposals for modifying the Didactic Ordinance to improve the CdS training offer were presented, discussed, and shared. In particular, the modifications concerned, besides expanding some ranges of basic activities, a detailed intervention on related activities and a corrective intervention on other activities.
Regarding the name change, the Committee proposed to submit a name containing, besides the term Economics (which distinguishes class L33), the expression Enterprises from which it can easily be inferred that the business phenomenon is studied from an economic, financial, and managerial perspective, and the term Markets, denoting the objective of providing students with knowledge and tools to analyze and understand different market structures, their functioning, and evolutionary dynamics, and their placement within an institutional framework.
At the Economics, Markets and Development Bachelor's Degree Course Council meeting on January 21, 2021, all proposals for modifying the Ordinance were approved. Regarding the new name, the Council decided to complete it by adding the term Financial to Markets. In this way, emphasis is given, also in the course name, to one of the most relevant profiles in the study of different markets and which in the training offer is the subject of in-depth study, without neglecting other specific production sectors (particularly related to tourism and cultural and creative activities, in line with the Steering Committee's suggestions).
The name Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets replaces the previous name Economics, Markets and Development for which the Consultation Committee on Didactic Ordinances met on March 1, 2013, in the presence of: Prof. Carmine DI ILIO (Rector), Prof. Anna MORGANTE (Dean of Economics Faculty), Prof. Riccardo PALUMBO (Deputy Dean of Management Sciences Faculty), Prof. Ezio SCIARRA (Chair of Social Services Bachelor's Degree, Faculty of Social Sciences), Dott. Ermando BOZZA (Chair of Commercialists' Order LANCIANO), Massimo D'ONOFRIO (Vice Chair of Commercialists' Order), Dott. Silvano PAGLIUCA (Delegate of Industrial Union PE), Dott. Marina DI IORIO (Chair of Social Assistants' Order Reg.), Dott. Paolo PRIMAVERA (Chair of Industrial Union CH), Dott. Domenico DI MICHELE (Chair of Commercialists' Order PE), Dott. Dino Salese (Administrator of DOA Consult), Dott. Enzo Stellabotte (Federmanager Abruzzo and Molise); for student representatives Valentina Pirovano (CdS representative).
Prof. Paola Nardone presented the essential characteristics of the Bachelor's Degree Course and emphasized that the CdL in Economics, Markets and Development, established in the 2013/14 academic year, has a stable number of enrollments, if not slightly increasing (303 enrollments in 2017-2018, of which 271 in course and 32 out of course), compared to the average for CdLs of the same L-33 class in the South of Italy and Italy, which is slightly lower. Therefore, the Economics, Markets and Development CdL does not have an attractiveness problem but must perhaps consider how to differentiate itself from other first-level CdLs of the Economic Sciences class (L33) and how to meet the training needs of a labor market in continuous evolution at global and national levels, tending to stagnate at the local level.
All stakeholders unanimously agreed that it would be appropriate to include in the training offer, possibly as optional courses, courses focused on certain specializations, such as the tourism-hotel sector and the agri-food sector. In any case, it was emphasized that courses, besides offering content, should aim to train students, preparing them for entry into the workforce. For this purpose, it could be useful to organize meetings with operators where students learn to create a CV and face a job interview. Mr. Felizzi, President of FIRA (S.p.A. a public capital company of the Abruzzo Region), hopes for an increase in laboratory and seminar activities conducted by representatives of the business world and professions (ALL. Unico,1/a).
Subsequently, on February 11, 2019, a meeting was held at the initiative of the Chairs of the Bachelor's and Master's Degree Courses to monitor the reference context of the Economics, Markets and Development Course and identify potential sectors of expansion where the professional figure the CdS aims to train could find opportunities, with the following participants: Prof. Paola Nardone, Chair L-33, Prof. Gianfranco Giulioni, Chair LM-56, Prof. Nicola Mattoscio, General Director of Fondazione Pescarabruzzo, Prof. Rita Martella, CdS Teacher, Dott. Dino Salese (Administrator of DOA Consult), Dott. Enzo Stellabotte (Federmanager Abruzzo and Molise).
Mr. Salese proposed conducting a survey on training needs for the tourism-hotel and agri-food sectors of Abruzzo, involving individual companies, consortia, and sector associations, to verify the current state of organizational development of companies in these sectors, the professional figures present, their training methods, and the training needs perceived by the companies themselves to better manage their business strategies. The University can use the collected information to better design and direct its training offer, making it more aligned with specific sector/filiera needs, as well as to play a facilitating role in the development of entire sectors (ALL. UNICO 1/b).
On November 6, 2019, the Committee met again. The Chair spoke to illustrate events since the last meeting and the current state of the CdS, and the intention to propose to the Council for the 2020.21 academic year some modifications to the Didactic Regulation to correct some issues that emerged over the years. In particular, it is considered appropriate to include an English language course, to adjust the placement of some disciplines in the years, and to increase the number of CFU dedicated to internships, following the indications from the previous Steering Committee meeting. During the discussion, the opportunity to create more opportunities to bring students closer to the world of work was highlighted, and the invitation to observe the markets of more developed geographical areas, which can provide guidance for anticipating, in the design of training activities, the changes in the labor market of the reference context (all. 1.c.).
On January 14, 2021, the Steering Committee met to discuss modifications to the Didactic Ordinance and the change of the Course name.
At the Economics, Markets and Development Bachelor's Degree Course Council meeting on January 21, 2021, the Steering Committee was integrated with the following stakeholders:
Dott. Felice Simonelli, Senior Research Fellow and Head of Policy Evaluation and Project Development at CEPS (Centre for European Policy Studies)
Dott. Domenico Scamuffa, Assistant at Bank of Italy
Dott. Alessandro Massolo, National Expert Distaccato (END) at European Commission-DG Competition and Official at the Competition and Market Authority
Dott. Carlo Piretti, General Manager of the Fantini Group Wines
Subsequently, the Steering Committee met on December 22, 2021, jointly for the Bachelor's and Master's Degree Courses to discuss proposals for revising the Master's Degree Ordinance through a comprehensive evaluation of both paths.
On March 28, 2023, the Committee met jointly again; the CdS Chair presented some modifications to the training offer following the arrival of some business area teachers in the department. Numerous reflections emerged during the discussion regarding a comprehensive evaluation of both paths. Among these, Mr. Massolo emphasized the need for practice to support the good theoretical training offer and to give more publicity to our CdS; Mr. Scamuffa highlighted that the path is well projected towards the future as it opens to digital transition and even if we want green/ecological, which are priorities in Bank of Italy policies and international monetary policies; Mr. Salese emphasized the importance of intercepting the demand from the change in organization of public institutions (municipalities, etc.) that face huge difficulties in finding graduates capable of handling and managing public accounting; and Mr. Stellabotte invited to develop the necessary skills to manage EU PNRR funds, as many funds return because Italy lacks the skills to organize their use.

The following information derives from data prepared by the University's Quality Office and relates to the CdS in Economics, Markets and Development.

From data provided by the Quality Office regarding 'Co-hort Trend', the following is evident:
- Of the 53 enrolled in 2020, 32 students renewed their enrollment in 2021 (6 explicit withdrawals, 14 non-renewals, and 1 transfer out) and 25 in 2022 (with a transfer, 2 withdrawals, and 4 non-renewals).

Finally, it results that students have acquired 45.95% (previous year 44.41%) of CFU, compared to required CFU.

Final Exam Characteristics
The final exam, considering its role in training, consists of verifying knowledge and skills within one or more disciplinary fields provided in the Course of Study Ordinance. The Didactic Regulation will specify its modalities.
Final Exam Execution
To obtain the three-year Economics, Enterprises and Financial Markets Bachelor's Degree, the student, after passing all exams provided in the study plan, including those related to autonomously chosen training activities, and after acquiring credits for other training activities (laboratories and/or training internships), must also cover the credits assigned to the final exam, whose objective is to evaluate the ability to correctly apply economic reasoning and methodological and professional tools acquired during the study path.
The final exam, which provides for the attribution of 3 CFU, consists of the approval by the supervisor of a written work on a specific topic related to one of the course's teachings. The topic of the work must be agreed upon by the student with the professor designated as supervisor.
The evaluation of the work, which can, upon favorable opinion of the Course Council, be written in a foreign language, is carried out by a Commission appointed by the Head of the Competent Department, whose composition is regulated in the University's Didactic Regulation (Article 37).
The Graduation Commission is normally composed of seven members, but at least five, appointed by the Department Head. The Graduation Commission, after acquiring the documentation related to the candidates' curricula and assigning the graduation grade in hundredths, proceeds to the proclamation.
The details regarding the form and consistency of the work, the modalities of the final exam, the scores assigned and related criteria, the Commission composition, and the admissibility of languages other than Italian are described in the Course's Didactic Regulation.

Admission requirements Required knowledge for admission To be admitted to the Bachelor's Degree course, one must hold a five-year secondary school diploma or another foreign qualification recognized as equivalent, or a four-year secondary school diploma plus the corresponding supplementary year.
Additionally, for admission to the Economics and Management Bachelor's Degree:
- Verbal and linguistic skills for understanding, processing, and presenting texts in Italian;
- Basic knowledge of English;
- General culture enabling understanding of socio-economic phenomena;
- Logical and deductive skills;
- Basic mathematical and computer science knowledge.
As provided in Article 6 of Ministerial Decree 270/2004, verification of these knowledge and skills is conducted through an entrance test, carried out according to criteria established annually by the University and indicated on the Course website. The test aims to assess students' initial preparation in the following areas: ability to understand written texts; mathematics; logic.
In case of failure or non-attendance at the test, the student is assigned an Additional Mandatory Training (OFA), to be completed within the first year of the course, according to the procedures set forth in the Course's Academic Regulations.

URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/573

Admission Procedures All students who pass the entrance test, written, typically held by September 30 according to the criteria defined by the University, are admitted to the first year of the Economics and Management degree course. The test requires achieving a minimum score of 10 to pass. Students can practice the test in the "Practice" section of the website www.cisiaonline.it.
In case of failure to pass or not taking the test, students may enroll but will be assigned an Additional Educational Obligation (OFA), in accordance with Article 28 of the current Academic Regulations. The verification of OFA fulfillment occurs through the acquisition, by September 30 of the following calendar year, of at least 18 CFU related to exams for basic or characterizing courses of the first year of the study plan. Failure to fulfill the OFA by the deadline will prevent students from taking exams in the second and third years unless they have earned the required 18 CFU. Therefore, for students assigned an OFA, it constitutes a prerequisite for all exams in the second and third years.
Transfers, course changes, and single exam admissions are subject to approval by the Course Council. The Council may grant full or partial recognition of the student's previous academic record, including validation of completed exams and acquired credits, and specify the year of study at which the student is enrolled and any OFA to be fulfilled.

SECTION: Communication Skills

Communication Skills
The activities contributing to the educational path are designed to encourage active student participation and the development of appropriate communication skills. Graduates in Economy and Management acquire the following general and specific skills in the business context, as well as interdisciplinary skills in the economic, legal, and quantitative fields:
- ability to express concepts and argue both generally and in reference to business situations;
- ability to communicate effectively and comprehensively, particularly in business situations and problems, using appropriate communication and representation technologies;
- ability to express main concepts in a second language (English) acquired through specific training activities and verified through the relevant exam.
To this end, in addition to the internship report and final exam, discussions, seminars, and presentations of business cases, empirical investigations, and documents produced by domestic and international economic and financial institutions are scheduled within some courses, either individually or in groups. The Study Course also promotes and encourages student participation in mobility programs to foster the development of appropriate communication skills in an international context. Communication skills are assessed through various methods:
- exams are organized using different modalities, requiring students to develop a wide range of communication skills;
- students are invited to participate actively by asking questions and engaging in class discussions.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [L018] ECONOMY AND MANAGEMENT
SECTION: Autonomy of judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/573

Autonomy of judgment (making judgements)
Mastery of appropriate technical skills and the genuinely interdisciplinary nature of the training path enable the graduate in Economy and Management to develop the ability to identify and solve decision-making problems of an economic management nature, applying an appropriate combination of qualitative and quantitative approaches while fully aware of the ethical and social responsibilities underlying their actions and the ethical-professional principles forming the basis of economic and business activities. The training offer aims to provide theoretical education supported by empirical analysis, enabling the Economy and Management graduate to evaluate economic-financial data acquired from the market or internally processed within business contexts, necessary to support strategic and operational decisions of companies. The development of an autonomous judgment capacity is contributed to by both participation in internship and/or placement activities and frequent meetings with external experts, organized in a way that allows active student participation, with students called upon to express their viewpoint on the topics discussed. This outcome will also be achieved through:
- classroom discussion in working groups with teachers and students;
- personal contribution provided in assessment of learning;
- critical contribution demonstrated in the preparation of the final work.

International internships and non-curricular internships are also provided, not linked to CFU acquisition (e.g., required by companies for thesis work or to carry out specific work experiences of interest to the student), aimed at completing the Study Course's training process in alternating study/work. Students of the CLEM who completed internship activities during January-December 2023 totaled 227. No curricular international internships were carried out in 2023, unlike the previous year.
The Study Course assists students in defining project work to be developed during the internship, in searching for host sites through specific initiatives, including the Career Day, where participating companies, in addition to introductory interviews with students, present their internship and/or traineeship opportunities. The Study Course assists students in carrying out external training periods through a dedicated service that presents host companies, handles the signing of new agreements, and collects and analyzes evaluation forms completed by the academic tutor, the student, and the company tutor, to assess the effectiveness of the internship carried out.
The administrative procedure contact is Ms. Maela Venanzi (mvenanzi@unich.it). To support the procedure, all information and necessary documentation to activate and manage the internship or traineeship experience are provided through a specific section dedicated to the Study Course on the Department website. Feedback collected from evaluation questionnaires is analyzed by the Orientation Commission and the AQ Commission to understand the effectiveness of the training path and the internship itself.
The questionnaire was administered to 163 CLEM interns (internships completed in 2023) and indicates a satisfaction level of 4.72 (scale 1-5). The congruence between the training project objectives and tasks performed, the availability of the company tutor, and the opportunity to acquire new professional knowledge, consistent with their training path, are appreciated. Among the suggestions provided, there is a request to increase the hours allocated for the internship and revise the agreements to select only organizations available at present.

INTERNATIONAL MOBILITY ASSISTANCE The assistance and tutoring activities for international mobility of students within the Course of Study are carried out by a Commission for International Relations established by the Department of Business Economics, coordinated by Prof. Nicola De Marco (ndemarco@unich.it), who also serves as Erasmus and International Relations Delegate for the Department of Business Economics.
Activities related to services offered at both the University and Course of Study levels include:
a) Pre-departure language preparation courses (40 hours) in English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Russian, and Serbo-Croatian;
b) Support from the Chieti-Pescara Erasmus Students Association, an active member of the International Exchange Erasmus Student Network, for students participating in the Program, with annual periodic meetings;
c) Within the Erasmus program, logistical and academic assistance guaranteed by two contact persons appointed by the respective Departments, both from the sending and receiving universities;
d) For Extra-European agreements, assistance from a faculty member of d'Annunzio University to inform the student about the study plan to follow at the host university.
The Department of Business Economics has signed various agreements with foreign universities for student international mobility, listed in the attached file and valid for Erasmus+ agreements, in addition to bilateral agreements for student and faculty exchange with the University of Alabama at Birmingham (USA), Nazareth College (USA), University of Baltimore (USA), University of Nicosia (Cyprus), the 'John D. Calandra' Italian American Institute, and Queens College/CUNY (USA).
Annually, the International Relations Commission organizes ERASMUS DAYS, which are orientation and support meetings to understand the Erasmus program, the partner locations, similar Courses of Study, and the procedures required by the call, aiming to effectively guide the study period abroad and the subsequent recognition of the 12 CFU required by the program.
Additional support information is available on the Course of Study dedicated web page, which includes useful documents requested by students for a better understanding of the Erasmus path, an operational guidebook, a grade equivalence table, and a specific list of overseas locations dedicated solely to business economics disciplines. To encourage participation in the program, the Final Exam Regulation includes a score bonus on the final grade for students who earn all 12 CFU abroad.
Overall results are satisfactory: outgoing students (departing), 34 in 2023 compared to 36 in 2022; incoming students, 24 in 2023.
No students participated in Erasmus placement.
