Brief Course Description
The Healthcare Assistance Course of Study was established by Ministerial Decree of April 2, 2001.
The Course requires a total of 180 CFU, structured over three academic years, with at least 60 CFU to be acquired through training activities aimed at developing specific professional skills (internship).
Each CFU corresponds to 25 hours of student work, including lecture hours, tutorial activity hours, seminar hours, hours spent by the student in other training activities specified in the curriculum, and hours of independent study necessary to complete their education.
The Healthcare Assistance Course concludes with a licensing exam and the award of the Healthcare Assistant diploma, a professional profile identified as the prevention, promotion, and health education specialist. Their activity is directed towards the individual, family, and community, identifying health needs and priority preventive, educational, and recovery interventions. They primarily operate at the territorial level within social medicine, public hygiene and environmental health, epidemiological research, healthcare, prevention, and health education. They also intervene in situations requiring constant health monitoring and the development of targeted, comprehensive, and continuous prevention and health education programs.
The Healthcare Assistant carries out their activities in public and private structures, in dependent or freelance capacity.
External Effectiveness
Employment data relate to 11 of the 14 2021 graduates interviewed one year after graduation. 90.9% of respondents reported working. 80% found employment in the "Health" economic sector and work in the public sector. Regarding time to enter the workforce, an average of 3.6 months passed since graduation. 60% have an indefinite-term contract, and the average working hours are 38. 90% of working graduates reported using their degree-acquired skills to a high extent, and 90% rated their professional training acquired at the University as very appropriate. 90% evaluated the degree as very effective/effective in their work, and the satisfaction score (on a scale from 1 to 10) was 9.
External effectiveness data will be presented and discussed within the Course Council.
Specific Course Objectives and Training Path Description
The Healthcare Assistance Course of Study aims to train operators with scientific and technical knowledge necessary to responsibly perform the functions of Healthcare Assistant according to the principles and methods of prevention, promotion, and health education as per Ministerial Decree 17.01.1997, n. 69.
The Course aims to provide students with an integrated health-social culture, a basic prerequisite for learning the content and methods of preventive, educational, recovery, and support interventions for individual and community health.
In particular, graduates must possess competencies to:
- Carry out prevention, promotion, and health education activities and use specific methods, techniques, and tools;
- Identify health needs and priority preventive, educational, and recovery intervention areas for the individual, family, and community;
- Identify health needs based on epidemiological and socio-cultural data;
- Identify biological and social risk factors;
- Plan, program, implement, and evaluate health education interventions in all life stages;
- Collaborate in defining communication methodologies, programs, and campaigns for health promotion and education;
- Contribute to the training and updating of health and school operators regarding health education methodology;
- Intervene in family planning and health, sexual, and socio-affective education programs;
- Implement specific support interventions for families;
- Activate network resources in collaboration with general practitioners and other territorial operators;
- Participate in family therapy programs;
- Monitor, to the extent of their competence, hygienic-sanitary conditions in families, schools, and assisted communities;
- Control environmental hygiene and infectious risk;
- Report and verbalize to competent authorities and propose operational solutions;
- Operate within centers jointly or alternatively with health education services, in public relations offices;
- Collaborate, to the extent of their competence, in health promotion and education initiatives in schools;
- Participate in initiatives for evaluating and improving the quality of health services, particularly focusing on user satisfaction levels;
- Contribute to initiatives aimed at protecting citizens' rights, with particular reference to health promotion;
- Participate in departmental activities, both district and hospital, with interprofessional coordination functions, especially in departments implementing national, regional, and local health programming objectives;
- Perform their functions with professional autonomy using specific techniques and tools;
- Carry out teaching and consulting activities in services where their professional competence is required;
- Act both individually and in collaboration with other health, social, and school operators, utilizing support staff when necessary;
- Contribute to the training of support staff and directly participate in updating related to their professional profile;
- Work in teams and integrate with health and social professions.
Training Path
The first year is aimed at providing knowledge related to the somato-psychic development of the individual and the study of the community to understand factors influencing individual and community health production. The training path, oriented towards health study, places the knowledge of the bio-psychosocial development of the individual in relation to historical, cultural, and social context. The development of methodological and instrumental competencies relates to the field of research and observation in health, social, and psychological contexts to guide the identification of health needs and the methodology for identifying biological and social risk factors, essential and preliminary steps for planning preventive, promotional, educational, and support interventions.
In the second year, the etiopathogenesis of infectious and mental diseases of greater health-social relevance is addressed, along with some clinical-assistive and environmental aspects of considerable importance for management and preventive purposes. The concept of individual and community psycho-physical risk in relation to the environmental context is deepened, and knowledge and skills regarding individual and collective operational methods and tools for implementing prevention, promotion, and health education interventions are acquired. Additionally, knowledge regarding the areas of preventive, educational, promotional, and recovery interventions, such as family, school, work, and daily life, is deepened, where the methodological approach becomes specific to each context.
In the third year, the etiopathogenesis of chronic-degenerative diseases with greater health and social impact is addressed, and knowledge of emergency medicine is deepened. Additionally, competencies for safeguarding citizens' rights, public relations, and the quality process of health services are acquired. Finally, the study of managerial and health economics aspects is aimed at understanding how resources can be best managed in the socio-health field, particularly in the areas of prevention and health promotion.

Entry, Path, and Exit Data
The analyzed data relate to students enrolled in Academic Years 2020/2021 (cohort 2020), 2021/2022 (cohort 2021), and 2022/2023 (cohort 2022), extracted from statistical data available on the University Quality Office website.
Regarding Cohort 2020, there were 36 enrolled students (69.4% female), of which 29 were pure enrollments. 38.9% are aged 19 or younger, 41.7% between 20 and 22 years, 8.3% between 23 and 24 years, and 11.1% aged 25 or older. Regarding geographical origin, Abruzzo accounts for 69.4%, followed by Puglia at 11%, and Sicily and Basilicata at 5.6%, with Marche, Campania, and Molise at 2.8%, showing an active interregional mobility of 30.6%. Regarding educational background, the high school diploma and technical-oriented diploma are predominant at 35.1%, followed by the magisterial diploma (16.2%), professional-oriented diploma (8.2%), and foreign diploma or others (2.7%). Of the 36 enrolled students, 21 (58.3%) obtained a high school diploma grade up to 80/100, 13 (36.1%) between 80 and 99, and 2 (5.6%) with a grade of 100 and honors. In terms of academic outcomes, the average CFU earned in the first year was 24 per student. Regarding the exams taken, with available data, the average grades range from a minimum of 20.1 to a maximum of 27.1. 13.9% earned more than 40 CFU.
Regarding Cohort 2021, there were 35 enrolled students (71.4% female), of which 23 were pure enrollments. 42.9% are aged 19 or younger, 31.4% between 20 and 22 years, 17.1% between 23 and 24 years, and 8.6% aged 25 or older. Regarding geographical origin, Abruzzo accounts for 45.7%, followed by Puglia at 34.2%, Basilicata at 8.5%, and Calabria, Marche, Molise, and Sicily at 2.9%, with active interregional mobility at 54.3%. Regarding educational background, the high school diploma is predominant at 34.3%, followed by technical-oriented diploma (25.7%), magisterial diploma (17.1%), professional-oriented diploma (14.3%), and foreign diploma (8.6%). Of the 35 enrolled students, 18 (51.4%) obtained a high school diploma grade up to 80/100, 16 (45.7%) between 80 and 99, and one student with a grade of 100. In terms of academic outcomes, the average CFU earned was 37.6 per student. Regarding the exams taken, with available data, the average grades range from a minimum of 23.8 to a maximum of 30. 48.6% earned more than 40 CFU.
Regarding Cohort 2022, there were 26 enrolled students (73.1% female), of which 18 were pure enrollments. 38.5% are aged 19 or younger, 23.1% between 20 and 22 years, 3.8% between 23 and 24 years, and 34.6% aged 25 or older. Regarding geographical origin, Abruzzo accounts for 84.7%, followed by Puglia at 7.7%, and Molise and Sicily at 3.8%, with active interregional mobility at 15.3%. Regarding educational background, the technical-oriented diploma is predominant at 34.6%, followed by high school diploma (30.8%), magisterial diploma (23.1%), foreign diploma (7.7%), and professional diploma (3.8%). Of the 26 enrolled students, 25 (96.2%) obtained a high school diploma grade below 80/100, and 1 (3.8%) between 80 and 99.
The analyzed data show a decline in the number of enrollments in the last year, alongside an increase in the proportion of students residing in the Abruzzo region. This trend aligns with the decline in enrollments recorded by the University and the reduction in interregional mobility, likely attributable to the post-Covid economic crisis negatively impacting families' ability to invest in tertiary education.
Final Exam Characteristics
To be admitted to the final exam, the student must have passed all exams specified in the Course's curriculum, including those related to professional training and internship activities, and acquired the relevant credits.
The final exam has the value of a state licensing exam for the exercise of the profession.
The final exam consists of:
a) A practical test during which the student must demonstrate the acquisition of theoretical-practical and technical-operational knowledge and skills specific to the professional profile;
b) Preparation and defense of a thesis.
The final exam is organized, by Decree of the Minister of Education, University, and Research in coordination with the Minister of Labor, Health, and Social Policies, into two national sessions.
Final Exam Procedure
The final exam aims to assess the achievement of expected competencies as expressed by the Dublin Descriptors and the Course-specific Learning Outcome Descriptors (RAD). In accordance with the Bologna Process and subsequent harmonization documents for European training paths, the following areas are evaluated in the final exam:
- Applied knowledge and understanding – Applying knowledge and understanding,
- Judgment autonomy – Making judgments,
- Communication skills – Communication skills,
- Learning skills – Learning skills,
corresponding respectively to the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th Dublin Descriptor.
Therefore, final licensing is granted to students capable of:
- Applying their knowledge with a professional approach and adequate skills to solve problems in their field of study;
- Making decisions to effectively resolve complex problems/situations in their field of study;
- Collecting and interpreting data to formulate autonomous professional judgments, even on social, scientific, or ethical issues;
- Activating effective communication on clinical, social, scientific, or ethical topics related to their profile;
- Learning independently.
In accordance with current regulations, the final exam consists of:
1. A practical test (applied value) where the candidate must demonstrate acquisition of competencies specific to the professional profile;
2. Preparation and defense of a written thesis.
The tests are normally conducted on two separate days.
The final exam is held, pursuant to Article 7 of Ministerial Decree of February 19, 2009, in two sessions defined nationally: the first, typically in October/November, and the second in March/April. Session dates are communicated to the Ministries of University and Research and Health, which may send experts as their representatives to individual sessions. In case of failure to designate the aforementioned members, the Rector exercises the substitutive power.
The practical test consists of a written report with open-ended questions on cases, with 90 minutes allocated.
It aims to assess the achievement of the professional profile's required competencies. In this test, the following Dublin Descriptors are evaluated:
2. Applied knowledge and understanding,
3. Judgment autonomy,
4. Communication skills.
Specifically, the ability to identify problems, make decisions, prioritize for individual patients, patient groups, or work processes; plan and decide interventions based on available evidence and given organizational conditions; act safely, considering ethical, deontological, and legal dimensions in their actions; demonstrate orientation towards interprofessional practice and risk assessment and effects on patients.
Written reports are evaluated anonymously, with grades expressed in thirtieths, which are then converted to scores according to the following parameters:
- 18/30 to 21/30: 1 point
- 22/30 to 24/30: 2 points
- 25/30 to 27/30: 3 points
- 28/30 to 30/30: 4 points
- 30/30 and honors: 5 points.
After this procedure, the candidate's identity is assigned to the respective task.
The thesis allows verification of the achievement of the 5th Dublin Descriptor, i.e., the student's ability to conduct an autonomous and methodologically rigorous learning process. The purpose of the thesis is to engage the student in a design and research work that contributes to completing their professional and scientific training. The thesis content must be closely related to themes strictly connected to the professional profile.
Normally, the student will have supervision from a Course instructor, called the Supervisor, and possibly Co-supervisors, also external to the Course.
The graduation grade is expressed in hundredths and is determined by the following parameters:
a. The average of grades obtained in curricular exams, elective activities, and internship, expressed in hundredths;
b. The score achieved in the practical test, maximum 5 points based on collegial evaluation;
c. The points awarded by the Graduation Committee during the thesis defense, obtained by summing individual points awarded by committee members up to a maximum of 7 (in relation to the thesis value, the clarity and effectiveness of the candidate's presentation, and the quality of the slides presented).
The total grade, determined by combining the scores from the above parameters, is rounded to the nearest whole number. The honors proposed by the Graduation Committee Chair may be awarded with unanimous committee agreement to candidates achieving a final score > 110.
The Final Exam Committee consists of at least 7 and no more than 11 members, appointed by the Rector on proposal from the Course Council, including at least 2 members designated by the Order of Medical Radiology and Health Technical Professions, Rehabilitation, and Prevention Technicians (TSRM-PSTRP). The Professional Representatives on the Committee must be of the same profile, in active service, and must not hold the role of University Instructor or Teaching Tutor in the same Course to ensure an external and independent quality and relevance control of students' professional preparation. The Committee composition cannot change during the two evaluation sessions unless the aforementioned Rectorial decree is amended.

Teaching method Conventional Access requirements verification Yes Course instructors View list Access requirements Required knowledge For enrollment in the Design Bachelor's Degree, a secondary school diploma obtained in Italy or another foreign degree recognized as equivalent is required.
Additionally, a good knowledge of spoken and written Italian, good logical reasoning ability, and adequate basic knowledge in mathematics, art history, architecture, and design, drawing and representation, and English are required.
The methods for verifying these knowledge and abilities will be determined in the course's didactic regulations. If the verification of the required knowledge is not successful, the didactic regulations will specify any additional educational requirements to be acquired in the first year of the course.
Admission method The Design Bachelor's Degree has programmed access and requires a mandatory online admission test conducted via the 'Cineca QUID' platform from home.
For the 2024/2025 academic year, 80 places are available for admission to the Design Bachelor's Degree, consisting of:
- 75 places reserved for Community students, as well as non-Community students residing in Italy.
- 5 places reserved for Extra-Community students residing abroad, with the possibility of reallocating Community and Italian students if no eligible Extra-Community student is found.
The selection of candidates and the merit ranking are based on the following evaluation criteria:
- Test result
- Academic record (high school diploma grade)
The test consists of multiple-choice questions with four possible answers, one of which is correct. The test comprises 40 questions divided into 5 sections to assess knowledge in the following thematic areas:
- Mathematics and Geometry (5 questions)
- Drawing and Representation (5 questions)
- Art and Design History (10 questions)
- Logic (5 questions)
- General Culture and Verbal Comprehension (15 questions)
Points assigned per answer:
- Correct answer: 1
- No answer or multiple answers: 0
- Incorrect answer: -0.25
The academic record evaluation, added to the test score, considers the grade obtained in the high school diploma. The conversion of the high school diploma grade (obtained by July 2024 and valid for enrollment in a first-cycle degree course) is calculated as follows:
- Grades from 70 to 74: 1 point
- Grades from 75 to 79: 2 points
- Grades from 80 to 84: 4 points
- Grades from 85 to 89: 6 points
- Grades from 90 to 94: 8 points
- Grades from 95 to 100: 10 points
- Grade of 100 with honors: 12 points
The admission test merit score also serves as the verification of the required knowledge for access and for assigning any additional educational requirements (OFA).
OFA are assigned based on not achieving a minimum score in the following thematic areas:
Mathematics and Geometry: minimum score of 1.5 out of 5 points Drawing and Representation: minimum score of 1.5 out of 5 points Art and Design History: minimum score of 3 out of 10 points
OFA are fulfilled by participating in individual training activities assigned directly by the reference instructor, or by attending integrated teaching courses led by tutors specialized in the thematic areas of the OFA, or through in-depth one-to-one tutoring (instructor-student) within the reference courses. In all cases, a final assessment via test or interview with the reference instructor is required.
The deadline for fulfilling OFA in the thematic areas of Geometry, Drawing and Representation, and Art and Design History is set for October 31, 2025.
OFA assigned in one or more thematic areas are considered fulfilled upon passing the first-year exams for:
- Geometry for Design for the Mathematics and Geometry thematic area
- Drawing for Design for the Drawing and Representation thematic area
- History of Design for the Art and Design History thematic area.
Enrollment in the second year is permitted, but it is not possible to take second-year exams before fulfilling any assigned OFA.
For students directly admitted to the second year, OFA are considered fulfilled upon earning at least 36 CFU in TAF A and B courses.

Program, texts and objectives Communication skills
The graduate is able to work in multidisciplinary teams and interact, in at least one European Union language besides Italian, with other professionals and the various operators in marketing, research and development, production, communication, sales and distribution present in companies and the reference business structure. They are able to communicate in written and oral form to transmit and promote the exchange of relevant information and data, problems to be addressed, ideas and project solutions, with the support of the most effective graphic and computer tools.
The acquisition of communication skills is achieved through attendance at the various training activities provided by the study course, which promote specific and differentiated teaching methods for organizing seminars, workshops and presentation of students' project research results. The verification of the acquisition of communication skills is achieved through evaluation, during exams and Final synthesis laboratory, of traditional graphic works and physical and/or virtual models, and of digital and multimedia presentations produced by the student.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITÀ DEGLI STUDI GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [707T] DESIGN
SECTION: Autonomy of Judgment
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1083

Autonomy of Judgment (making judgments)
The graduate is capable of independently identifying and analyzing design-related problems in the fields of industrial product and visual communication, through observation, interpretation, and evaluation of information related to different production sectors and economic, social, and technological contexts, necessary to initiate a metaprojective research aimed at developing product and process innovation.
Specifically, to effectively and efficiently achieve the expected outcomes in terms of autonomy of judgment, specific teaching activities and laboratory sessions are provided concerning reasoned bibliographic research (traditional and computer-based) and the critical collection and processing of data and information, in desk and field research modes. Additionally, specific tools supporting different teaching methods are used, mainly consisting of the ability to independently manage digital presentations, and the ability to organize small educational exhibitions, seminars, and in-depth reading sessions.
Autonomy of Judgment is achieved through attendance at the training activities provided by the study course and the mandatory internship activity. Verification is obtained through the faculty's assessment of the student's level of critical and constructive autonomy, as well as the depth and validity of theoretical arguments and the originality and completeness of the design solutions developed in the study course.

Training periods The internship at companies, public or private entities, totaling 6 CFU, is part of the mandatory training activities of the Design Degree Course. It is aimed at acquiring professional practice experience and occupational orientation.
The training objectives must be agreed upon with the university tutor.
The tutors are indicated by the Program and selected from the professors responsible for the Final Year Project Laboratories in Product Design, Interior Design, and Communication Design.
The internship can be carried out at any accredited site belonging to the following categories, provided it operates in the fields of Design (product design, interior design, or communication design) and/or Design services:
- Professional studio;
- Company;
- Public or private entity;
- Third sector entity;
- Foreign institution or organization.
Only students enrolled from the third year of the three-year degree, in compliance with university fee payments, can carry out the internship activity.
The total hours to be completed are calculated by multiplying the number of training credits specified in the study plan by 25 (1 CFU = 25 hours).
The student selects the host site using the models provided by the academic regulations of the study course, submits to the Department the documents containing the internship proposal agreed upon with the host site tutor and the university tutor.
The organization and execution of internships are coordinated by the Chair of the Program. The accreditation process is followed and validated by Prof. Emilio Rossi. Meanwhile, the consistency and appropriateness of the internship objectives and methods are verified by the heads of the three LSF and the tutors of the host entities.
To monitor internship results, two questionnaires are used by the Program:
- Host Site Satisfaction Questionnaire: evaluation of IT knowledge, creative skills, market knowledge, and the intern's level of autonomy (MOD. 4.1).
- Intern Satisfaction Questionnaire: evaluation of welcome, tutor relationship, and overall internship experience (MOD. 4.2).
All students in the Design Program carry out an external internship from the third year at one of the accredited host sites (currently over 160). To make internships more effective, a dedicated web space has been created on the Program's website, where information about internship offers and access procedures is collected.
Internship and laboratory activities are primarily conducted in person, with appropriate scheduling adjustments if necessary to avoid gatherings incompatible with interpersonal distancing requirements.
However, such activities can also be carried out remotely when insurmountable logistical and/or organizational obstacles prevent in-person execution, as assessed by the Course Chair in consultation with the Department Director.
Students may request remote internship and laboratory activities only in cases specified by the University's guidelines.
International mobility Erasmus Erasmus+ is a European program that allows students to spend a study period at partner universities and complete an internship at entities in one of the European Union member states or Extra EU countries.
Each year, two types of selection are announced for study mobility and internship placements, with notices published in the official bulletin and on the University's website.
The Department of Architecture offers a wide range of destinations with prestigious European universities in the following countries: Albania, Belgium, Bosnia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Croatia, France, Germany, Mexico, Czech Republic, Romania, Portugal, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Turkey.

International mobility The Department of Architecture participates in blended intensive programs, Blended Intensive Programmes (BIP), with online learning and cooperation activities, allowing joint groups of students, teaching staff, and administrative personnel from different countries to collaborate on specific tasks collectively and simultaneously.
Traineeship For international internships, Design Program students can benefit from the Traineeship program to complete internships at companies, firms, professional studios, and training and research centers in one of the countries participating in the Erasmus program, recognized by the home university as part of the study program. International internship activities are recognized as curricular internships for current students; extra-plan credits for students who have already completed the 6 CFU curricular internship; extra-curricular credits for recent graduates who applied for the Traineeship before obtaining their degree and thus also benefit from the stipend for post-graduation internships.

Student opinions In this section, the data from the annual survey conducted by the University Quality Assurance Office are reported, referring to the opinions of students enrolled in the Design Degree Course. In the latest survey for the academic year 2022-23, the anonymous evaluation expressed by students relates to the courses offered in the Design Degree Course for the first, second, and third years.

For the academic year 2022-23, the overall score for the Degree Course is 3.34, slightly below the average score of the Scientific Area (3.43) and slightly below the University average (3.44).

The scores of courses grouped by evaluation bands (A from 3.5 to 4, B from 3 to 3.5, C from 2.5 to 3, D from 1 to 2.5), referring to the academic year 2022-23 and updated as of 4/09/23, show significant values in band A and contained values in band C. There are no courses in band D. Specifically: 34% of courses are in level A, 50% in level B, and only 15% in level C.

The macro-indicators for the academic year 2022-23 are slightly below the University and Scientific Area averages: overall satisfaction is lower (3.18 compared to 3.35 for the University and 3.32 for the Scientific Area; however, values related to logistical organization (3.42 vs. 3.48) and teaching effectiveness (3.40 vs. 3.47) are in line with the Scientific Area).

Regarding specific questionnaire questions, the trend of average scores is favorable.

In the academic year 2022-23, the alignment of courses with declared program content (D13, 3.45), adherence to schedules (D14, 3.57), clarity of exam procedures (D16, 3.39), and lecturers' ability to clarify topics covered (D22, 3.58) achieved scores above the Degree Course average (3.34).

Scores slightly below the Degree Course average include responses to questions about interest in course topics (D0, 3.28), study load (D3, 3.19), course teaching materials (D9, 3.26), lecturers' ability to stimulate (D20, 3.31), and their ability to present topics appropriately (D21, 3.32). Only the question regarding prior knowledge relative to exam programs (D1, 3.09) received a lower evaluation.

Additionally, from the 2021 Parity Commission (lecturers-students) report, some issues emerged concerning requests for organizing recurring meetings with companies, design studios, organizations, and institutions, extracurricular activities (TOEFL courses, software courses, company visits), and teaching activities to address initial educational gaps for students.

The Degree Course Chair acknowledges the data from the annual survey conducted by the University Quality Assurance Office and commits to continuing analysis of outcomes and raising lecturer awareness to share and implement improvement initiatives suggested by students, particularly to enhance synergies between courses, teaching material quality, and alignment between exam topics and prior knowledge. This includes organizing meetings with the business world, arranging supplementary teaching activities and in-depth tutoring for students required to complete OFAs assigned through the entrance test. The results of the annual survey conducted by the University Quality Assurance Office, regarding Design students' opinions, were discussed at the Degree Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

For managing student complaints, the Degree Course relies on the centralized University-level complaint management system: https://www.unich.it/parla-con-noi This system is also accessible via the Departmental website.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF CHIETI-PESCARA
COURSE: [707T] DESIGN
SECTION: Graduate Opinions
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/1083

Graduate Opinions In this section, the data from the AlmaLaurea survey, updated as of April 2023, regarding satisfaction with the completed study course are reported. The data specifically concern graduates of the calendar year 2022: 74 (interviewed 64).
The overall judgment of the study course is favorable: 87.5% of graduates consider it very positive or at least positive, slightly below the university average of 89.8% and the total class average of 88.4%, but significantly higher for satisfaction with teacher relationships (93.8%), compared to the university average (90.3%) and the national average (86.7%). The positive judgment is confirmed by the 2023 data of graduates who would enroll in the same Design course at the university (76.6%), strongly increasing from 2022 (63.4%) and 2021 (59.8%), exceeding the university average of 67.4% and the total class average of 65.8%.
Regularly attended the study course, considering more than 75% of the courses, 90.6%, significantly higher than the university average of 67.5% and the total class average of 84.9%. The evaluation of classrooms is improving: 87.1% of graduates, compared to 70.5% in 2022 and 65.3% in 2021, consider classrooms always or often adequate, exceeding the university value (84.3%) and the Italian universities value (82.0%). More problematic is the evaluation of computer workstations, considered adequate in number by only 52.6% of graduates compared to 56.3% of the university and 50.1% of Italian universities. Similarly, the data on equipment for other teaching activities (69.5%) is below the university average (73.2%) and Italian universities (69.9%). Conversely, encouraging and improving are the data regarding library services (94.5%). Similarly, 90.6% of respondents consider the teaching load adequate for the duration of the study course, exceeding the university average (88.7%) and the average of other universities (89.5%). It is relevant that 93.7% of graduates considered the exam organization satisfactory, exceeding the university average (79.8%) and the total class average (85.6%). Similarly, library services received a rating of 94.5%, exceeding the university (89.3%) and national data (91.8%).
The survey results indicate that improvement actions should primarily focus on strengthening the structures supporting the study course (classrooms, laboratories, computer workstations, considered by students not always adequate for teaching activities). In this regard, the study course constantly urges the Department and the university for a rapid intervention in the structures of the Pindaro Campus, to close the gap with other national sites.
The results of the AlmaLaurea 2022 survey on graduate opinions were discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Ability to apply knowledge and understanding (applying knowledge and understanding)
The graduate is able to apply the knowledge acquired during the training path and in relation to the different fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. Specifically, they are capable of using theoretical-critical tools, methodological tools, and technical-economic evaluation methods learned to carry out the various professional activities required by the production system. They are prepared to apply the acquired knowledge through problem setting (structuring knowledge), problem solving (concretizing solutions), and continuous orientation of the company towards innovation.
The ability to apply knowledge and understanding is achieved through attendance at the planned training activities, particularly through the activities programmed by the design courses and the Final Synthesis Laboratory. Verification of these abilities is carried out through interviews and the presentation of written/graphic, multimedia, and physical/virtual product models. During exams and the final thesis, the abilities of exposition, communication, and critical argumentation of the design choices made are also evaluated.

Learning skills
The graduate is able, autonomously, to use the learning tools acquired to deepen the studied content in technical, economic, and humanistic fields, to undertake further studies after the three-year degree, and for continuous professional updating, especially in the field of material, technology, and new production process innovation.
The acquisition of learning skills is realized through the use of computer tools to support the drafting of research reports, the development of design syntheses, and the formalization of graphic interpretation of critical data. Verification of the acquisition of learning skills is achieved through evaluation, during exams, Final Synthesis Laboratory, and Internship, of the student's elaborations produced in constructing information that also involves the use of online databases, in graphic and communicative representation of identified issues, and in specific design applications oriented towards innovation.

Knowledge and understanding (knowledge and understanding)
The graduate is able to reach knowledge of the most updated methods, tools, and themes of innovation in the study fields of design. They are capable of critically addressing the phases of pre-competitive analysis, project brief definition, generation and selection of new product ideas, elaboration and development of concept design, using more advanced design innovation methodologies and new digital representation, modeling, and interactive and multimedia communication technologies. They are prepared to understand the complexity of phenomena characterizing the socio-cultural, economic, and technological macro-trends in the different reference contexts where companies operate.

Such knowledge and skills are achieved through attendance at the training activities provided by the study course and the mandatory internship activity. Verification is carried out through in-course learning tests, exam tests, and the graduation exam.

Brief course description The three-year Design degree course aims to train a professional profile of designer with technical skills in the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. The activities provided by the study course are aimed at acquiring knowledge, skills, methods, and tools to operate in all phases of the industrial product and communication artifact design process, from pre-competitive analysis to the brief, from idea generation and evaluation to concept design, from concept development to pre-engineering, production, and distribution phases.

The thread running through the degree course is the concept of innovation related to value creation processes in the different application fields of the project. The training model is interdisciplinary and is expressed through theoretical-critical lectures, multidisciplinary laboratories, workshops, an internship in companies and professional studios, and the graduation thesis. Students, after a common two-year theoretical, methodological, and instrumental training in various disciplines of the humanistic, economic, scientific-technological, and drawing areas, as well as project areas, at the third year have the opportunity to characterize their path by choosing the Final Synthesis Laboratory in product design, interior design, or communication design. This results in a learning method capable of fostering students' creative processes through direct interactions, both with teachers and with nationally and internationally renowned designers, and with important manufacturing companies and research networks operating internationally on design themes.

The training path of the Design degree course defines the competencies associated with different professional profiles in the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. Design graduates have a wide range of professional opportunities to enter the workforce within companies, studios, and design societies, cultural institutions, public bodies, editorial offices, and service agencies. The course trains the following professional profiles: product designer, interior designer, communication designer, graphic designer, web designer, product ergonomist. The obtained title allows access to master's degree and first-level master's courses.

External effectiveness In this section, the summary of data on the employment status of Design graduates is reported, referring only to graduates who did not enroll in another degree course. The data are extracted from the AlmaLaurea 2022 survey one year after graduation (data updated as of April 2023). Among a total of 98 graduates, 69 interviewed, and a sample of 29 (58.6% women and 41.4% men), the survey reveals an average age at graduation of 24 years, an average graduation grade of 105.6, an average study duration of 4.1 years with a delay index of 0.37.

Currently enrolled in a second-level degree course are 52.2% of graduates (51.9% total universities - 68% university), mostly to improve their cultural training (35.1%) or to improve job prospects (37.8%). 39.1% of respondents participated in at least one post-graduation training. Among the reasons for not enrolling in another degree course, the main reasons are work-related (31%) and economic (6.9%). Graduates not interested because intending to pursue further post-graduation training account for 20.7%.

The employment rate, considering data only for graduates who did not enroll in another degree course, is 55.2%, below the university value (69.4%) and the total class average (64.4%). Only 24.1% are not working, not enrolled in a second-level degree, and not seeking. 20.7% of the selected sample are seeking work. On average, from graduation to finding the first job takes 4.5 months.

Regarding the characteristics of current work, the predominant profession is technical with 21.7% of the selected sample, followed by intellectual, scientific, and highly specialized professions (17.4%) and other professions (21.7%), while the percentage of executive professions in office work is reduced (13.0%). Part-time work is widespread in 34.8% of cases with an average of 33.1 hours per week. 87.0% work in the private sector. Predominantly in industry (26.1%), including manufacturing industry (4.3%) and construction (21.7%). 73.9% in commerce, consulting, and other business services. Predominantly in the South (73.9%). Only 4.3% in the Center. The average monthly net salary (average 1 year) is €954, below the national average (€1,121) and the university (€1,333).

37.5% of employed graduates use the competencies acquired with the degree to a high extent in their work, below the total class average (49.7%) and the university (56.8%). Even more encouraging is the percentage of 50.0% of graduates who consider the degree very effective and effective in their work, with 37.5% considering it fairly effective. Only 12.5% consider it little effective. Job satisfaction is rated 8.2 out of 10, exceeding the total class average (7.8) and the university (8.0).

To encourage graduates to enroll in a second-level degree course, starting from the 2021-2022 academic year, the Master's degree in Eco Inclusive Design has been activated at our campus.

The results of the AlmaLaurea survey on the employment status of graduates were discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Specific training objectives of the course and description of the training path The three-year Design degree course aims to train a professional profile of a "project technician" with operational skills in the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design.

The specific objective is the acquisition of knowledge, skills, methods, and tools to operate in all phases of the project of material and digital industrial artifacts, from pre-competitive analysis activities to the project brief, from idea generation and evaluation to concept design development, from product development to pre-engineering phases.

The training path aims to prepare a designer who possesses both knowledge of methods and tools to guide and manage incremental and radical product innovation processes, as well as cultural sensitivities and critical skills to act consciously in the socio-cultural, technological, productive, and economic context where companies in the visual, multimedia, and interactive communication sectors, and industrial products sectors operate.

The training model is interdisciplinary and involves the fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. The thread running through the degree course is the concept of innovation related to value creation processes in the different application project fields, as a result of the intersection between the technical potential field and the social potential field. Indeed, the encounter between the possible and the desired requires a particular ability to move between different disciplinary universes, from technical and economic knowledge to artistic and socio-cultural sensitivities, from environmental awareness to linguistic and communicative analysis.

Alongside individual theoretical study and applied investigations of methods and tools related to industrial design, students, also through group work, are prompted to reflect closely related to the project's different dimensions and degrees of complexity. In particular, the project activity follows an inductive form that produces knowledge through continuous ideative and logical-interpretative processes of hypothesis formulation, solution experimentation, and result evaluation.

Training is expressed through theoretical-critical lectures, multidisciplinary laboratories, workshops, an obligatory internship in the third year at companies and professional studios, and the graduation thesis. Specifically, students, after a common two-year theoretical-methodological and instrumental training (humanistic, economic, scientific-technological areas, drawing), and applied (product design, interior design, and communication design fields), at the third year have the opportunity to characterize their path by emphasizing preparation in one of the three project areas through the choice of the Final Synthesis Laboratory in Product design, Interior design, or Design of Communication.

This results in a learning method capable of fostering creative processes of mutual enrichment between project, cultural, productive, and economic fields, through direct interactions with teachers and nationally and internationally renowned designers, relationships with important manufacturing companies at the internship level, and with research networks operating internationally on Innovation Design driven themes.

The training project is structured around four spheres of knowledge:
- Basic humanistic and scientific knowledge. These are information technology, logical-mathematical, economic, historical-critical, artistic, and aesthetic-communicative knowledge, capable of supporting the various application fields of product design, interior design, and communication design. They do not directly concern professional activity but are fundamental to combining technical knowledge with the humanistic dimension and the designer's ability to imagine.
- Specific technical-professional knowledge in the field of production of a technical, project, and engineering nature specific to the exercise of professional activity. These are, in particular, competencies aimed at technological innovation, structural verification, and economic evaluation of projects and products, methods and tools of production, ergonomic approach and eco-design, chemical, physical, and mechanical properties of materials, execution design, and product realization techniques, prototype development, and use of modeling and rapid prototyping techniques.
- Characterizing knowledge of the communication field of a theoretical and technical nature in the fields of visual communication, graphic, and motion design. These are, in particular, knowledge of linguistic and communicative analysis, methodologies, strategies, and techniques of design and realization of interactive interfaces of material products and digital communication artifacts.
- Transversal knowledge related to the development of communicative (in written and oral form in at least one European Union language, besides Italian), relational, and decision-making skills of designers with the professional and business world, and the growth of aptitudes for problem setting and problem solving, to structure and concretize the solution to the design problem in a way consistent with the given and identified constraints, which are essential to improve the efficiency and value of professional activity.

Opinions of organizations and companies with internship / traineeship agreements (curricular or extra-curricular) During the period from September 1, 2022 to July 31, 2023, a survey was conducted to collect both the opinions of companies and professional studios accredited with the Design study course for traineeship activities, and the opinions of trainees. The sites are mostly present in Abruzzo and southern regions, from which most enrolled students originate. The list, available on the Department website, is divided by each of the three thesis areas (Product, Interior, Communication) to ensure coherence with the specificities of the different training profiles.

The survey of opinions involved 90 trainees and over 80 host sites, as each hosted more than one trainee.

The survey method was based on the completion of questionnaires: Form 1 to be completed by the host organization's Tutor for evaluating the trainee's activity and overall judgment on the traineeship's progress and results; Form 2 to be completed by the Trainee on the traineeship experience.

The survey results show that almost all host organization tutors (company or studio) expressed a positive judgment with an excellent rating (83.5%) for the trainee's activity, 15.5% a good judgment, and only 1.0% a sufficient judgment. None were insufficient.

In the overall judgments provided by tutors on the traineeship's progress and results, particular emphasis is placed on: the trainee's design ability and learning capacity; the ability to carry out assigned work with attention and precision; skills in problem solving and teamwork; knowledge of graphic programs and main 2D and 3D software; creative aptitude, responsibility, and decision-making autonomy; determination and reliability in achieving set goals; good methodological, theoretical, and technical preparation.

Regarding traineeship satisfaction, 91.0% of trainees gave a positive evaluation. Among the positive aspects reported by trainees, the reception received and the quality of the work environment, the good relationship with the tutor and the work staff, appreciation for the practical and concrete nature of the work experience, successful integration into the company organization, the opportunity to learn new design software, and the professional and relational opportunity, the acquisition of new technical and professional skills are highlighted.

Among the negative aspects, some trainees reported difficulty balancing traineeship activities with class and exam schedules, the limited duration of the traineeship (125 hours) not allowing a complete and satisfactory experience, and distance or sometimes difficulty reaching the host site. Some trainees suggested that the study course should include more hours of design practice, streamline the activation and conclusion of traineeships through an online procedure. In response to these suggestions, the study course has: increased traineeship hours to 150 hours; repeatedly urged university offices to activate a digital system for managing the entire traineeship procedure, which would also make monitoring and evaluation of final results and traineeship experience more accurate.

The results of the internal survey on the opinions of companies and design studios that hosted the Design study course trainees were discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Summary of the regional coordination committee opinion THE REGIONAL COORDINATION COMMITTEE OF ABRUZZO UNIVERSITIES, on December 10, 2015, expressed a favorable opinion on the proposal to establish the Design for Innovation Study Course (L-4).

During the meeting, the following intervened:
- The Rector of the Chieti-Pescara University, who noted that in the three Abruzzo universities there is no study course in the Industrial Design class and thus it is a strategic choice to recover in Abruzzo the demand for design training;
- The Rector of the University of Teramo, who, in expressing a favorable opinion on the activation of the course, emphasized that within the five priority domains of the Abruzzo region, design is also included;
- The Rector of the University of L'Aquila communicated the university's willingness to collaborate, involving teachers with supplementary contracts, and expressed the intention, in the future, to collaborate on an inter-university master's course.

After extensive discussion, unanimously approved the activation of the Design for Innovation study course at the University of Chieti-Pescara.

- absence of a study course in class L-4 in the regional territory;
- request from the regional socio-economic and business context for "Project Technicians" capable of operating in the design field;
- from data on the degree of industrialization, presented at a recent meeting held at the Abruzzo Region, it emerges the need to combine instrumental training aspects with reflective research aspects.

Taking inspiration from the above motivations, Prof. Marano noted that in Abruzzo there is a significant demand for professional profiles capable of performing a technical-design role for innovation in the fields of:
Product design: the Innovation Hubs require project operators capable of fostering Design innovation processes from the perspective of typological, technological, functional, and aesthetic innovation, with particular attention to the development of new materials and the ergonomic and environmental characteristics of products.
Interior design: the sector of temporary installations in cultural, museum, and commercial spaces and the furnishing of private and public internal spaces such as residences, offices, shops, restaurants, and entertainment venues is a field of professional practice requiring a specific profile of Interior Design technician.
Communication design: communication design is a continuously expanding professional sector. Its presence is transversal and active in companies for brand, product, and service communication, as well as in retail where the consumer encounters merchandise. In publishing, advertising, tourism, transportation, sports events, entertainment, and wherever content and information dissemination in analog and/or digital form is fundamental.

Subsequently, the following professional profiles were analyzed:
Product design technician: capable of conceiving and articulating all characteristics determining the quality aspects of an industrial product in relation to use and technological and production possibilities.
Interior design technician: able to define the systems of installation and furnishing, and the range of components that allow internal spaces to be inhabited from a cultural and functional point of view.
Communication design technician: expert in designing analog and digital communication artifacts, in the fields of electronic publishing, advertising graphics, digital interfaces, multimedia, and web design.

Aspects related to:
- training objectives;
- graduate profiles;
- training activities plan;
- interdisciplinary teaching model;
were further discussed.

Entry, path, and exit data In this section, the summary data of the annual survey elaborated by the University Quality Office are presented, referring to entry, path, and exit data of the three-year Design L-4 degree course.

Entry data The enrollment flow is stable. After the 2020/2021 cohort with free access and 204 enrollments, the number of enrollments for the 2021/2022 and 2022/2023 cohorts has been constant due to the introduction of programmed access for a maximum of 80 students. Also for the 2023-24 academic year, the study course has programmed access for 80 students. In the 2022/23 academic year, total enrollments were 325, of which 284 in course and 41 out of course. Geographic origin analysis of enrollments for the 2022/23 academic year indicates that 55.7% of enrolled students come from Abruzzo and 44.3% from other regions. Regarding origin by type of secondary school, 70% of enrolled students in the 2022/22 academic year come from High Schools, 17.2% from technical and professional institutes, 10% from magistrali, and other (2.8%). Regarding the diploma grade, it is important to note that 54.3% of students reported a diploma grade between 80 and 100. 24.3% of students enrolled with a grade of 100 or 100 and Lode. 21.4% with a grade up to 80.

Path data Compared to the 2020 cohort (data extraction: June 30, 2023), the enrolled students: in 2020 academic year 193 with 80.5% of the ratio between acquired CFU and required CFU and an average of 5.28 exams passed per student; in 2021 academic year 160 with 68.4% of the ratio between acquired CFU and required CFU and an average of 6.14 exams passed per student; in 2022 academic year 149 with 58.1% of the ratio between acquired CFU and required CFU and an average of 6.26 exams passed per student (2022 data are partial as the 2022/23 academic year is not yet didactically concluded). Withdrawals and non-renewal of enrollments are contained.

Path data demonstrate good efficiency of the study course. Indeed, in the analysis of the 2021/22 cohort with 77 enrolled students, 77.92% of students continued to the second year and 64.94% of students acquired more than 40 CFU, while inactive students accounted for 6.49%. Only 5.19% of enrolled students had zero CFU acquired.

Exit data Exit data also express good study efficiency. Indeed, in the calendar year 2022, 72.97% of students graduated on time, 12.16% after one year, 13.51% after two years or more. Early graduates were 1 out of 74. In the same year, among 74 graduates, 33 obtained a graduation grade of 110 and Lode, 2 obtained a grade of 110, 16 obtained a grade between 105 and 109, and 23 graduated with a grade below 105.

Improvement actions can be directed mainly in exit orientation to strengthen opportunities for comparison and networking between graduates and the business world. The study course plans to organize specific JOB DAY events to support Design study course graduates and alumni in the transition phase from university studies to work activities in close collaboration with companies, entities, and design studios.

The results of the annual survey elaborated by the University Quality Office, referring to entry, path, and exit data of the Design study course, were discussed in the Course Council meeting on September 14, 2023.

Characteristics of the final exam The final exam consists of a critical reflection and in-depth study of the project developed in one of the Final Synthesis Laboratories (LSF in Product design, LSF in Interior design, LSF in Communication design). The thesis is carried out under the guidance of a supervisor and evaluated by a graduation committee.

Final exam execution modalities - operational guidelines In the Design degree course, the preparation of the graduation thesis is structured in two successive phases:
- The first is carried out by the student within one of the three Final Synthesis Laboratories (LSF) of choice (third year, second semester) in Product design, Interior design, or Communication design. The LSFs are composed of a characteristic design discipline and two didactic modules that complete the thematic framework. Activities of each LSF are coordinated by the teacher of the characteristic design discipline. The LSF concludes with a pass exam by the committee composed of the LSF teachers;
- The second, following the pass exam, is carried out by the student under the guidance of one of the teachers responsible for the LSFs, who assumes the role of supervisor, and consists of a critical reflection and in-depth study of the project developed in one of the three LSFs. Correlators can also be external personalities.

Committee structure The graduation session is organized with a committee composed of a minimum of 5 to a maximum of 7 teachers of the study course, including teachers who assume the roles of President and Secretary. Normally, all thesis supervisors are present in each committee.

Final exam grade attribution modalities The grades are expressed in 110s. The graduation grade is composed of the weighted average of the exam grades reported by the student in their study path, to which is added the score attributed by the graduation committee for the final thesis according to the following criteria:
- max 6 points, by majority of the committee
- max additional 2 points by unanimous committee, for theses considered of exceptional merit.
By unanimity, the committee can award the grade of 110/110 with Lode only if the weighted average of exam grades is equal to or greater than 102/110. The committee, at the public proclamation of each graduation session, confers the title of Doctor/Doctora in Design.

Summary of the technical report of the evaluation nucleus Summary of the Evaluation Nucleus Technical Report The training objectives of the proposed study course are clearly and effectively outlined and aim to capture a training demand certainly present in the reference territory, confirmed by consultations with social parties and the student population, ensuring a correct prognostic evaluation of possible employment opportunities. The range of consulted organizations appears sufficiently representative at the regional level (and, although to a lesser extent, also at the national level). The expected learning outcomes are adequately delineated, the modalities for verifying entry knowledge, the modalities for organizing teaching and courses of the study course are clearly defined. The commitment of the teaching body to align the study course teaching activities exclusively to the specific training objectives of the course and to carry out constant coordination and interdisciplinary cooperation activities is appreciated.

The available infrastructure for the study course activities appears adequate, and the accreditation requirements requested by the current discipline for the activation of new study courses are also satisfied.

The proposed study course appears consistent with the University's three-year programming plan, positioning itself in a segment of the training offer currently not present in the regional territory.

Admission Procedures Eligible to enroll are graduates of Italian and foreign secondary schools (subject to verification of equivalence of the academic qualification), with knowledge of at least one European Union language in addition to Italian.
Regarding the assessment of adequate personal preparation, the Course Council appoints a Committee that verifies through a test the possession of the required knowledge.
Exempt from the test are graduates who have achieved a final high school grade of at least a minimum threshold to ensure the possession of the required qualifications and preparation. This minimum threshold is set at 80/100.
The test consists of questions on basic knowledge in the field of cultural heritage with multiple-choice answers, only one of which is correct. To pass the test, at least 60% of the questions must be answered correctly. The test is conducted in the first semester and may be repeated in the second semester if necessary.
Students who have not passed or have not taken the test in either of the two opportunities may be assigned Additional Educational Obligations (OFA) within the framework of basic and characteristic courses. For this purpose, individual recovery paths will be defined with the instructors of the disciplinary areas where insufficient preparation was identified, or specific credit 0 learning activities organized within the Department. OFA are considered fulfilled if students have earned a minimum of 18 CFU related to basic and characteristic courses prescribed in the first year of the study plan (or in the first and second year for part-time students).
In case of failure to fulfill OFA by the specified deadline, students remain obligated to meet this requirement and cannot take second-year exams until they have done so (Article 28, paragraph 5 of the University Academic Regulations).
For all matters not covered by this article, refer to current regulations and the University Academic Regulations.

The project targets students of Bachelor's, Master's, and PhD programs in Letters, Cultural Heritage, and Archaeological and Art History Heritage, as well as professionals in public sectors (museums, superintendencies, archaeological parks) and private sectors.
The formation of a consortium involving academic and private partners enables the provision of a continuous training path aimed at developing an academic curriculum for a professional course. Specifically, a new competitive professional figure for the current job market is being defined, thanks to the application of ICT, to allow professional growth through training modules that integrate practical training with theoretical paths, laboratory activities, applied technology, and advanced diagnostic protocols. In addition to ECTS credit recognition, the training path will acquire EQF characteristics, respecting transparency and quality criteria to facilitate access to the European job market.
The teaching modules, also translated into English, will be made available as open course OER on an e-learning platform, enabling professionals to continuously update on specific techniques and application systems. The integration of teaching modules with innovative applications, such as GIS systems, augmented reality, virtual reality, and video lessons, goes beyond traditional learning methodologies, promoting the inclusion of ICT in academic training.

URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/63

Student Opinions: From the survey of student opinions as of July 31, 2023, provided by the new dynamic portal prepared by the university (see link and attached PDF), a fully positive evaluation of the Course of Study emerges (see the specific PQA page for the survey methodology: https://pqa.unich.it/rilevazione-opinioni/rilevazione-opinioni-studenti-e-docenti-2023).
The evaluation indeed records an average score of 3.53, in line with the previous year (3.55%) and 2021 (3.50).
Specifically, 67.44% of teaching activities fall under Level A; 30.23% of teaching activities fall under Level B, and only one teaching activity (2.33%) falls under Level C, with a score of 2.98, thus very close to the threshold of Level B. No teaching activity falls under Level D.
All indicators also record a high degree of satisfaction, confirming and in some cases exceeding the already positive data from previous years.
In all responses to the questionnaire provided by students, the average score of the Course of Study is higher than or equal to the area and university averages, with only a slight decline (Course 3.27; area 3.33; university 3.31) regarding question D1: "Were the preliminary knowledge possessed sufficient for understanding the topics covered in the exam program?". This data is likely due to the presence of many technical courses addressing disciplines absent from standard school curricula.
Generally, student suggestions indicate that they consider the basic knowledge and teaching load adequate.
The request for intermediate exams is numerically very limited and restricted to teaching activities with a high number of CFU.
These data suggest that some critical issues previously reported on these points have been resolved through corrective measures applied to the study path and the delivery methods of basic courses, particularly in the first year.
The Course of Study continues to monitor student opinions closely, which were discussed in a GAQ meeting on July 5, 2023, and will be further debated in the Course Council meeting scheduled for September 21, 2023.

UNIVERSITY: UNIVERSITY OF STUDIES GABRIELE D'ANNUNZIO – CHIETI/PESCARA
COURSE: [OBC7] CULTURAL HERITAGE
SECTION: GRADUATE OPINIONS
URL: https://unich.coursecatalogue.cineca.it/corsi/2024/63

GRADUATE OPINIONS The information presented in this section has been extracted from the AlmaLaurea data updated as of April 2023 (see link and attached PDF).
Graduate evaluations are favorable and exceed the university's average, particularly the positive responses (definitely yes / more yes than no) to the question of whether they are overall satisfied with the degree course and to the question about their relationship with professors reach 100% of respondents, and to the question of whether they considered the study load of the courses appropriate for the duration of the degree program, exceeding 93% compared to 90% from last year.
Also the attendance rate, in my opinion extremely indicative after the pandemic, records positive responses from over 96%, exceeding the university's average.
All these satisfaction indicators are also higher than the average of the degree class across other universities (https://pqa.unich.it/sites/st16/files/allegatiparagrafo/09-05-2023/l-1_beni_culturali.pdf).
Other indicators on the organization of teaching and the use of classrooms, libraries, and laboratories also show a generally higher level of satisfaction than the university's and national averages, while strong dissatisfaction is reported among users of computer workstations. This issue is shared by professors and has been reported multiple times. However, some restructuring and modernization interventions have been carried out on the facilities and their equipment, which should improve this aspect of the student experience.
Regarding the organization of exams, schedules, and reservations, 86.7% of students are satisfied, a figure in line with 2022 and significantly higher than previous years, exceeding both the university's and national averages.
81.8% of graduates are currently enrolled in a second-level degree course. This is an increase compared to 2022 (80%) and higher than the university's average (68.6%) and the class average across all universities (74.7%).
79.3% would enroll again in the same course at the same university, an increase from 2022 (73.3%) and higher than the university's (67.3%) and class average (71.3%).
Graduates are 69.7% women and 30.3% men, thus confirming a certain balance in this historical imbalance that characterizes this study direction.
The average age of graduates is 26.2 years, decreasing from 2022 (27.4), thanks to ongoing efforts to improve study paths and regularize student careers; the overall figure, in my opinion, is also affected by the presence of some 'senior' students, i.e., students who enroll at an advanced age, even after retirement, in this study program to pursue an interest they could not follow in their youth.
Compared to the previous year, there is an improvement in the regularity of the study path, likely due to overcoming the pandemic, which hindered access to archives and libraries necessary for completing a thesis in these disciplines.
The origin of new students remains highly diversified, practically from all high school tracks, with a predominance of Artistic High School (30.3%).
The social origin of graduates is also highly diversified, with 75.9% having no parent with a degree, while 48% come from the middle class, 31% from the executive labor class, and the remainder from the upper class (see attached PDF).
The insights from the surveys of students, graduates, and alumni were discussed in the meeting of the GAQ Review Group of the Course of Study on May 5-7, 2023, and will be thoroughly examined in the Course of Study Council meeting scheduled for September.
Learning Skills
Graduates will have developed a solid foundational education in the field of Cultural Heritage, covering both archaeological and historical-artistic areas, enabling them to subsequently choose a deeper focus in either methodological or chronological aspects.
This diversified training will allow graduates in the three pathways to acquire specific skills applicable in various occupational sectors related to the management, historical interpretation, and conservation of Cultural Heritage.
